artigo.texto: ROTTERDAM, Netherlands, Nov. 19, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- The Netherlands is approaching a major change in its residential energy landscape. From 1 January 2027, the country's net metering scheme (salderingsregeling) will officially end, changing how households with solar panels manage the electricity they generate and consume. According to market data, approximately 36% of residential addresses in the Netherlands had registered solar PV systems in 2024, up from 33% in 2023. Residential solar installations reached a combined capacity of 11,672 MWp, representing approximately 40% of the country's total installed solar capacity. Once net metering ends, households will no longer be able to offset electricity fed into the grid against electricity purchased from it. Instead, surplus electricity will receive separate compensation from energy suppliers. Meanwhile, feed-in charges (terugleverkosten) have already become an additional cost for many solar households. This shift makes maximising solar self-consumption increasingly important. SAMDUO highlights the role of accessible home energy storage and intelligent energy management in helping households make better use of their existing solar installations. SAMDUO's Nex E6000 and Nex E6000H home energy storage systems are designed to store surplus solar electricity for later use. Their plug-in design offers an accessible option for households looking to add storage to existing solar setups without necessarily undertaking a complete system overhaul. Compatibility and installation requirements depend on the existing configuration. The SAMDUO P1 Meter helps households monitor electricity consumption and energy flows. Combined with AI Mode, the system considers solar generation forecasts, household consumption, battery state of charge and dynamic electricity prices to optimise energy scheduling. The end of net metering marks a new phase in household energy management. SAMDUO aims to advance home energy solutions beyond standalone storage towards a smarter, more connected and data-driven energy ecosystem, empowering households to manage their energy and make greater use of the solar electricity they generate. About SAMDUO SAMDUO is a home energy brand developing intelligent energy solutions for European households. Built on an industrial foundation with more than two decades of experience in precision manufacturing, power and energy storage, SAMDUO combines engineering, product design and intelligent energy management to help households store, manage and use energy more proactively. Home Energy Intelligence for every home. Own Your Power.

artigo.texto: (Ohio Capital Journal) – One of the many questions looming over lame duck is if Ohio lawmakers will pass any data center regulations. Ohio legislative leaders recently commented on that possibility, and didn’t rule it out. Lawmakers went home in June without passing Ohio House Bill 646, which would, among other things, limit the size of new sales tax breaks from 100% down to 50%. But this would not apply to any of the companies with existing contracts, like Meta, Google and Amazon. “I think everything we’ve discussed before is up for discussion now. So generally speaking, it’s across the board,” Ohio Senate President Rob McColley, R-Napoleon, said when asked about data centers. Ohio House Speaker Matt Huffman, R-Lima, said he thinks H.B. 646 “was a good bill.” “There might be some other fine tuning, and I think that gives the protection to the local groups,” he said. “It incentivizes brownfields. It makes sure the water part and the electrical use, the tariffs are paid. … I think we need to work on (H.B. 646).” Ohio voters sharply rejected data centers in this year’s election. 18 Ohio communities voted on whether to curb or ban data center development in this month’s election and all 18 communities voted yes. In some communities, 70 to 80% of voters voted against measures related to data center development. “People in their local communities are really pushing back and really saying either we don’t want them or we want all these guardrails around them,” said Ohio Senate Minority Leader Nickie Antonio, D-Lakewood. “I think all of us legislators need to take a look at what they say in those local communities.” While campaigning, Gov.-elect Amy Acton said she supports a conditional moratorium on data centers “if requirements on costs, union labor, transparency, environmental standards, community benefit agreements, and development are not met.” In a quote on Acton’s campaign website, she specifies that data center developers should cover 100% of utility costs, along with “exclusively” building with union labor, and adhering to Ohio’s environmental standards. “I do think, as governor-elect, Dr. Acton should certainly be setting the vision for what happens next in Ohio,” said Ohio House Minority Leader Dani Isaacsohn, D-Cincinnati. “But data centers are among the issues that we can and should have responsible government doing something about.” Ohio has more than 200 data centers, the sixth-highest state in the country, according to Pew Research Center. Most of the data centers are in central Ohio. Cincinnati has 27 and Cleveland has 24, according to the Data Center Map. Ohio had more than 100 active moratoriums on data centers as of September. The state provided almost $1.57 billion in sales-tax exemptions on purchases of data center equipment and construction materials last year, according to the Ohio Department of Taxation. That’s nearly 12 times what state officials initially expected, according to estimates produced by the tax department in late 2024 as part of Ohio’s budgeting process. Conserve Ohio, the grassroots organization behind a proposed constitutional amendment to ban new, large scale data centers, is collecting signatures to make the 2027 ballot. Lawmakers are considering banning data center development in 16 states as of September, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures.

artigo.texto: Cumberland County data center project will not proceed after sales agreement expires CUMBERLAND COUNTY, Pa. (WHP) — A data center proposal that faced a lot of opposition from neighbors has been pulled after its sales agreement expired, officials confirmed on Monday. Pennsylvania Data Centers will not seek a renewal of its sales agreement of the proposed data center in Monroe Township. In the past, the project faced pushback from neighbors and surrounding small businesses, such as Ashcombe Farms and Greenhouse. Residents and people from surrounding areas have mixed reactions to the renewal not moving forward. Brant Gift, a retired teacher from Franklin County, said: “A lot of people will, you know, be disappointed in that, that they, came to fruition.” Warren Hardman, who lives in Monroe Township, said: “I’m a little on the relief side. You know, slightly disappointed.” Martha Nagel, from Cumberland County, said: “I’m not sure they’re we’re ready for them here in Pennsylvania. Taking up our rural. That’s what we know, what we’re known for, our rural countryside and our farms and the beauty and everything of it,” Nagel said. Nagel said she is concerned about the impact data centers could have on the rural areas. PREVIOUS | 'We are not in support:' Monroe Township farm opposes proposed data center project Monroe Township Supervisor Tim Thompson said a representative from Meadows of Ashcombe Limited Partnership confirmed the sales agreement between the two parties expired, and Pennsylvania Data Centers will not seek a renewal. It was originally proposed to be developed on the 800 block of West Granthan Road and the 1400 block of Williams Grove Road. Hardman, who has lived in Monroe Township his whole life, said the area holds a lot of memories for him. “I’m glad you know. Yeah. So, let’s keep the farmland the way it is,” Hardman said. However, Hardman said he also understands the need for more jobs and economic growth. “If we do 17 jobs for a massive data center, that’s not a that’s not a good return on investment in terms of the land use. But, yeah, I mean, right there again. We need to increase the economy and create jobs. And that’s a, you know, which seem to be the way the economy’s going,” Hardman said. The “No Data Center” signs could be seen throughout the area near Ashcombe Farms and Greenhouse, which borders the proposed site. “They’re vehemently protesting against the data centers. I think that it’s a good thing and we need to find alternative energy sources to support the data centers,” Gift said. Pennsylvania Data Centers also invested in the PAX-1 project in Middlesex Township. A legal battle is currently unfolding over that proposal to fight its development. READ MORE | Judge hears arguments over controversial PAX-1 data center: 'This is like algebra' CBS 21 reached out to the developer for a statement on the expiration of the sales agreement, but they refrained from commenting. The owner of the land says there are no current plans for future use.

artigo.texto: Proposed Wade Hampton Boulevard data center would use 5 megawatts, far less than Spartanburg County projects Councilman Frank Farmer says the Prime Storage site is not one of the large-scale data centers making national headlines GREENVILLE COUNTY, S.C. (FOX Carolina) - A proposed data center on Wade Hampton Boulevard in Greenville County would require about 5 megawatts of power, which Councilman Frank Farmer said is comparable to the electricity demand of a Walmart. The owner of the Prime Storage facility wants to rezone the property to build the data center. The site is next to Texas Roadhouse and near several homes. Recent coverage of large data centers across the country, including projects in Spartanburg County, has raised concerns about bringing similar developments into local communities. Farmer said data centers vary in size and function. “No data center is the same. They’re like fingerprints. Every single one’s different,” Farmer said. How the power use compares Farmer said the data centers receiving national attention are large artificial intelligence facilities, and the proposed project is not necessarily one of them. Here is how the proposed power requirements compare with other data center projects in the region: - Prime Storage, Wade Hampton Boulevard: About 5 megawatts - Valara, South Pine Street: At least 475 megawatts - Tyger River Industrial Park: Four proposed data centers, each projected to require about 50 to 65 megawatts Farmer said the Prime Storage project would use about as much power as a Walmart or a typical manufacturing facility. “I know five megawatts sounds big,” Farmer said. “Spartanburg, they’re dealing with 65 megawatts.” Farmer said the proposed facility would also use a closed-loop cooling system that would need to be filled about once a year with water from a facility outside Greenville County. “This is a super small scale data center. This isn’t one that uses gobs of electricity or water,” Farmer said. Farmer described the project as a low-latency data center. That means information would not have to travel as far, helping speed up data processing. What rules apply now? Farmer said the property’s proposed S-1 zoning includes protections against noxious fumes from diesel generators and requires noise to remain within the property line. Those protections are part of the zoning requirements, he said, but the county does not have an ordinance that applies specifically to all data centers. Farmer said he has been working on a countywide data center ordinance for about six months. It would be the county’s first ordinance specifically addressing data centers. He said he is gathering input from Georgia Tech representatives, industry leaders, policy experts and environmentalists. The proposed ordinance could address water use, noise, power consumption and limits on expansion, Farmer said. Residents’ concerns Residents who spoke during Tuesday’s Greenville County Council meeting raised concerns about the project, including the potential for expansion. “There’s nothing to stop them from moving outside of that building, clearing off all of those trailers and boats, and going into those storage containers as well,” one resident said. “We will have no ability to hold this company ... from building a much larger data center,” another resident said. Farmer said he understands the concerns of residents who live behind the proposed site. “There is a neighborhood behind it, and I totally understand why they would be worried,” Farmer said. “They don’t want their quality of life being impacted. I don’t want their quality of life being impacted.” What happens next Greenville County Council unanimously sent the rezoning proposal back to the Planning and Development Committee to consider additional safeguards for nearby residents. The proposal will undergo further review and require additional votes before moving forward. Farmer said that once a draft of the county’s proposed data center ordinance is ready, officials plan to hold public workshops to gather input from residents, industry representatives and other stakeholders. No timeline has been announced. RELATED COVERAGE: Feel more informed, prepared, and connected with FOX Carolina. For more free content like this, download our apps. Copyright 2026 WHNS. artigo.texto: Xcel Energy Advances 135.5-MW Battery Storage Project in Minnesota Xcel Energy has received battery units at its Blue Lake site in Minnesota, marking a construction milestone for a battery energy storage project that is part of the company's broader plan to expand energy storage capacity across the state. The Blue Lake project is part of Xcel Energy's strategy to diversify its electricity generation resources while maintaining service reliability and managing customer costs. Along with two planned projects in Becker, Minnesota, the company expects to have more than 735 megawatts (MW) of battery energy storage capacity operating in Minnesota by the end of 2027. The portfolio would be the largest in the Upper Midwest. "For more than a century, energy companies have generated electricity when customers need it and delivered it almost immediately. Battery storage changes what's possible. It allows us to store energy and dispatch it when it's needed most, giving us a powerful new tool to maintain reliability, support growing energy needs and make the most of the diverse resources that power our system," said Bria Shea, president of Xcel Energy–Minnesota, North Dakota and South Dakota. Battery energy storage systems store electricity when it is available and return it to the grid when demand increases. Advances in storage technology have also made it possible to install systems at existing energy facilities, such as Blue Lake, allowing utilities to use existing infrastructure while incorporating new technologies. The Blue Lake facility will store energy generated across Xcel Energy's Upper Midwest system, including electricity from wind, solar, nuclear and natural gas resources. The 135.5-MW facility will include 132 battery units capable of storing and delivering electricity for up to four hours. At full output, the system is expected to provide enough electricity to power approximately 125,000 homes during periods of peak demand. "The Blue Lake project demonstrates how battery storage is becoming an increasingly important part of grid operations," said Justin Meagher, Xcel Energy battery storage project manager. "These systems can respond quickly to changing conditions, store energy when it's available and provide electricity when customer demand is high. That flexibility helps us operate the electric system more efficiently while continuing to deliver reliable service to customers." The Blue Lake Battery Energy Storage System is expected to begin serving customers in 2027.

artigo.texto: AUBURNDALE, Fla. — Auburndale is drafting a moratorium on future data center projects, but the potential pause would not apply to the controversial development planned for two warehouses along Pace Road. Watch report from Chad Mills: City Manager Jeffrey Brown said city staff is working on the proposal to give Auburndale time to establish “better standards” for future data center developments. The moratorium would likely last one year. The Hillwood Development Company project would be exempt because the property is already zoned to allow a data center. The city expects the proposal to come before commissioners for a first reading at the second meeting in December, followed by a possible final vote at the first meeting in January. The public will have an opportunity to comment during both occasions. Meanwhile, the city is continuing its permitting process with Hillwood and negotiating a separate development agreement that would establish guardrails for the project. Brown said that agreement will likely require a commission vote sometime in the first quarter of 2027. A packed City Hall and calls for a moratorium The announcement comes as opposition to the proposed data center continues to draw large crowds in Auburndale. Monday evening, at the first City Commission meeting since the public learned of the project, both the commission chamber and the waiting area outside reached capacity about 30 minutes before the meeting began. Dozens of people were left outside, some waiting in the rain, for a chance to speak. The proposed project would convert two existing warehouse buildings along Pace Road into a data center near Florida Polytechnic University. Speakers raised concerns about electricity demand, water use, noise, and the project's potential impact on nearby homes and schools. A recurring demand was for the city to enact a moratorium on data center development. David Madison stood outside City Hall holding a sign opposing the project. He said he believes the development could disrupt the surrounding neighborhood and lower property values. Inside the meeting, Laura Van Amburgh challenged commissioners to protect the community. "You were all voted here to be the watchers and to safeguard our communities from things like this," she told the commission. Van Amburgh and others said a moratorium would be a good place to start. Fishback brings survey results to commissioners Former Republican gubernatorial candidate James Fishback also addressed the commission and urged city leaders to listen to the opposition and reconsider allowing the project to proceed. Fishback presented results from a text-message survey his staff conducted among registered Auburndale voters. The survey was sent to 13,057 unique cell phone numbers associated with registered voters and received 1,445 valid responses. Of those responses, 86.7% opposed the proposed data center. The survey was conducted by text message, and the results reflect people who chose to respond. During his comments to the commission, Fishback argued that the city was relying on zoning approved three years ago for a different development plan, even though the current proposal is for a data center. He compared the change to someone asking the city’s permission to install a small poolside water slide and building a full-fledged water park instead. “If I said I wanted to build a small generator and built a nuclear power plant, you would say, ‘Hell no.’ If I said I wanted to have two chickens, and I raised a poultry facility, you would say, ‘Hell no,’” Fishback said. “The people of Auburndale are saying ‘hell no’ to this data center.” He also pointed to the project's potential electricity demand and said the full buildout could require 700 megawatts of power. Fishback questioned what that demand could mean for the electric grid and the people who live in a city of roughly 22,000. "This is not about Republican or Democrat. This is not about left versus right," Fishback said. "This here tonight is about right versus wrong." Fishback also cited a statement from Governor-elect Byron Donalds, who wrote last week that communities should not be forced to accept data centers they oppose. Why the Hillwood project can move forward The debate over the project has centered in part on a decision made before Hillwood proposed building a data center at the site. The property was annexed into Auburndale in December 2022. A year later, commissioners approved a change to its future land-use designation and rezoned it as an Industrial Planned Unit Development. The original development plan included research and development buildings, an e-commerce and logistics building, and other commercial uses. After revisions, the approved zoning allowed uses including research and development, light manufacturing, health technology, and information sciences. The city says that zoning allows the property to be used as a data center. That does not mean the project has cleared every hurdle. City staff received an application Nov. 4 for the interior retrofit of the two buildings. Permitting and reviews by outside agencies are still underway. Hillwood says the project will limit water use and pay for its power Hillwood has defended the proposal, saying it was designed to address concerns about the environmental impact of data centers. The company estimates the facility will use approximately 4,665 gallons of water per day for both buildings. It plans to use a closed-loop cooling system that recirculates water rather than continuously drawing in new water to cool the computer systems. The developer says that amount is lower than the water use anticipated for the site's previous warehouse development. The Southwest Florida Water Management District has said an Environmental Resource Permit would not be required if the project uses the existing buildings and no other site changes are made. Amanda Cristina de Souza Publicado em 16 de novembro de 2026 às 20:52 A aprovação de isenções fiscais para equipamentos de tecnologia abre caminho para mais de R$ 560 bilhões em investimentos privados na construção de data centers no Brasil. Apoiada na oferta de energia renovável para consolidar o país como polo de Inteligência Artificial na América Latina, dois megaprojetos puxam essa fila: o Rio AI City, orçado em R$ 360 bilhões para a capital fluminense ao longo de dez anos, e a aposta de R$ 200 bilhões da ByteDance, gigante chinesa dona do TikTok, no Porto de Pecém, no Ceará. Breve cronologia dos data centers As gigantes globais de computação em nuvem dos Estados Unidos e da China, conhecidas como hyperscalers ou provedores de hiperescala, veem no território brasileiro espaço para expandir suas operações. A vantagem por aqui parece óbvia à primeira vista, pois enquanto o Brasil desperdiça eletricidade limpa por falta de linhas de transmissão, os servidores de Inteligência Artificial precisam de parques computacionais com alta densidade de carga para funcionar sem parar. Brasília enxerga essas empresas como clientes ideais para comprar a sobra de energia eólica e solar gerada principalmente no Nordeste. A sobrecarga da rede elétrica e tarifas mais caras nos Estados Unidos funcionam hoje como o maior aviso de perigo para o planejamento brasileiro. Lá fora, o apetite energético de um único centro de dados já equivale ao consumo de uma cidade inteira, forçando as concessionárias a religarem termelétricas a gás natural e a repassarem os custos de expansão da rede para as famílias. O presidente Donald Trump e seus aliados sentiram o peso desse problema diretamente nas urnas. Derrotas recentes em eleições estaduais e parlamentares em redutos estratégicos, como Texas e Virgínia, sinalizam o desgaste político provocado pelo aumento dos custos de energia doméstica. Uma pesquisa do instituto Gallup confirma o desgaste: 70% dos entrevistados nos EUA se opõem à construção de novos centros de dados nas proximidades de suas residências. Por que o Brasil virou um dos países mais importantes para o ChatGPT Já o presidente Lula e a equipe econômica tentam fazer o caminho inverso ao liderar uma ofensiva pró-investimento para fechar contratos antes da concorrência. O desafio real, no entanto, será blindar o bolso do brasileiro comum. Se as regras de conexão elétrica não obrigarem as big techs a bancarem sozinhas a ampliação da infraestrutura, o avanço da Inteligência Artificial pode acabar cobrando a fatura na conta de luz residencial. O consumo de água para a refrigeração de máquinas abre uma segunda frente de tensão que ameaça travar as obras no Nordeste. Servidores de alta performance esquentam rápido e exigem sistemas contínuos de resfriamento, o que pressiona mananciais em regiões já castigadas pela seca. Os grupos indígenas, como o povo Anacé no Ceará, já lideraram protestos contra o avanço dessas estruturas próximas a seus territórios no entorno do Porto de Pecém. As comunidades temem o esgotamento das reservas hídricas locais para manter computadores rodando 24 horas por dia. Essa demanda por água doce representa um dos principais desafios para a instalação de data centers de Inteligência Artificial no Nordeste. Mesmo com a oferta de energia eólica e solar, os hyperscalers, empresas que operam grandes estruturas de computação em nuvem, precisam manter os servidores refrigerados 24 horas por dia. A depender da tecnologia utilizada, esse processo pode consumir grandes volumes de água. Lixeira invisível da IA No complexo do Pecém, no Ceará, a proximidade de áreas sujeitas à escassez hídrica e de territórios tradicionais aumenta a preocupação com a expansão desses empreendimentos. O desafio está em receber investimentos bilionários em tecnologia sem pressionar o abastecimento de água nem colocar em risco a segurança hídrica das comunidades da região. Para sair do papel sem bloqueios judiciais ou desgaste socioambiental, os investidores terão de comprovar o uso de circuitos fechados de água e passar por licenciamentos. A América Latina virou o novo tabuleiro geopolítico da computação em nuvem, colocando o Brasil em rota de colisão direta com Chile e Argentina. Embora a isenção fiscal brasileira garanta uma vantagem tributária imediata na largada, o país esbarra em um gargalo físico importante diante dos vizinhos sul-americanos: o armazenamento de energia. A energia eólica e solar dependem do clima, mas a Inteligência Artificial não desliga quando o sol se põe ou o vento para. Nesse quesito, o Chile já saiu na frente do Brasil ao instalar megabaterias industriais em larga escala para garantir fornecimento contínuo aos seus centros de dados. Transformar o meio trilhão de reais prometidos em processamento ativo exigirá que Brasília e a iniciativa privada acelerem agora os investimentos em baterias e redes de transmissão. https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBM.resumo: A nova regulamentação dos Estados Unidos para exportação de semicondutores avançados pode elevar os custos de infraestrutura tecnológica no Brasil, dificultar projetos de inteligência artificial (IA) e data centers e criar diferenças competitivas entre empresas que operam no país. O alerta é da Associação Brasileira das Empresas de Software (ABES), que acompanha a regra final provisória (Interim Final Rule) publicada pelo Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), órgão do Departamento de Comércio norte-americano. A norma estabelece a exigência de licenças para exportação, reexportação e transferência de semicondutores avançados destinados ao Brasil e a outros quatro países: Indonésia, Malásia, Singapura e Tailândia. Também prevê controles sobre data centers que disponibilizem grande capacidade computacional a empresas sediadas em países sujeitos a restrições. Na avaliação da ABES, os efeitos podem atingir diretamente a cadeia de infraestrutura digital brasileira. Isso porque as exigências não se limitam a chips fabricados nos Estados Unidos: também alcançam componentes e servidores produzidos em terceiros países que utilizam tecnologia norte-americana. O alcance da regulamentação pode afetar, portanto, decisões de compra de equipamentos, cronogramas de implantação de infraestrutura e planejamento de investimentos em capacidade computacional, especialmente em projetos que dependem de processadores avançados para treinamento e operação de modelos de IA. Regras podem criar desigualdade entre provedores de infraestrutura Um dos principais pontos de preocupação é a diferença de tratamento entre empresas que operam no mercado brasileiro. Subsidiárias de companhias sediadas nos Estados Unidos ficam dispensadas da licença prévia, desde que os exportadores reportem mensalmente as operações ao BIS. Para provedores de nuvem e data centers de capital nacional ou de outras origens, universidades e centros de pesquisa brasileiros, a aquisição de infraestrutura computacional avançada passa a depender de autorizações analisadas individualmente. Segundo a ABES, essa distinção pode gerar assimetria competitiva no mercado brasileiro, com efeitos sobre custos operacionais, previsibilidade de fornecimento e capacidade de planejamento das empresas. Na prática, a necessidade de aprovação prévia pode acrescentar etapas aos processos de aquisição de equipamentos e dificultar a expansão da capacidade computacional necessária ao desenvolvimento de aplicações de inteligência artificial. Brasil pode perder atratividade para investimentos em data centers A entidade também alerta para os possíveis reflexos sobre a atração de investimentos internacionais. O Brasil reúne condições favoráveis à instalação de grandes estruturas de processamento de dados, entre elas matriz elétrica limpa e abundante, conectividade e políticas de estímulo à infraestrutura digital. Esses fatores sustentam a possibilidade de o país se consolidar não apenas como um polo regional de data centers, mas também como exportador global de serviços de processamento e armazenamento de dados. A inclusão do Brasil na lista de países sujeitos às novas restrições, entretanto, pode acrescentar incertezas regulatórias e operacionais aos projetos. Para investidores, a necessidade de obter licenças para acessar componentes de alta tecnologia representa uma variável adicional na avaliação de custos, prazos e viabilidade de novos empreendimentos. O impacto potencial alcança também o ecossistema de inteligência artificial, que depende do acesso a aceleradores e semicondutores de alto desempenho para desenvolver e executar modelos em larga escala. ABES defende negociação entre governos A regulamentação entra em vigor na data de sua publicação no Federal Register e estabelece prazo de 60 dias para o envio de comentários públicos. Entre os critérios considerados pelo BIS na análise das licenças estão o regime de controle de exportações do país de destino e o nível de cooperação com as autoridades norte-americanas. Diante desse cenário, a ABES defende uma atuação coordenada entre o governo brasileiro e o setor produtivo nas discussões com os Estados Unidos. A proposta é estabelecer uma agenda de cooperação em controle de exportações que demonstre a capacidade institucional do Brasil e preserve o fluxo das cadeias globais de suprimentos tecnológicos. A associação informou que continuará avaliando os aspectos técnicos da regulamentação com suas empresas associadas e manterá interlocução com as autoridades brasileiras. O objetivo é contribuir para a segurança jurídica, a inovação e a competitividade do setor de tecnologia nacional.

artigo.texto: The University of Michigan’s Board of Regents will vote on proceeding with the development of the planned Ypsilanti Township data center during Thursday’s monthly meeting. Ahead of the Board convening, project officials hosted a press conference to discuss recent developments, such as the project’s updated timeline and financing. The discussion was moderated by Paul Corliss, assistant vice president for public affairs and communications, and featured project lead Steve Ceccio; Robert Green, project director in the office of the executive vice president; Patricia Hurn, interim vice president for research and innovation; and engineering professor Karthik Duraisamy. If the resolution is approved during the Nov. 19 Board meeting above-ground construction is expected to begin in late 2027. The first phase of construction will cover an approximately 150,000 square-foot facility. Renderings of the potential facade of the data center were presented during Tuesday’s press conference. Ceccio said the goal of the facility’s exterior is to blend into the natural landscape. “If you look at the facade we’ve tried to make, it’s an industrial motif, but we try to have it blend into the environment,” Ceccio said. “We have a natural landscaping to harmonize with the land that’ll be abutting the river.” Construction will occur in two phases, and the total size of the development will be approximately 290,000 square feet. Approximately 50,000 square feet will be dedicated to University research, with the remaining 240,000 square feet to be utilized by research tenants, such as Los Alamos National Laboratory. Ypsilanti Township residents have vocalized a number of concerns in recent community forums regarding the data center’s impacts on their quality of life. A common concern among many has been the facility’s noise output. According to Green, the development would have the same sound output restrictions as any other campus facility, which is 61 decibels during the day and 55 at night. A normal conversation averages about 60 decibels, whereas the typical data center averages an output between 45 to 55 decibels at the property line. “We expect to test noise levels during commissioning and to continue monitoring after the facility opens to ensure noise levels are within the acceptable standards,” Green said. “The final model and design will determine the full spectrum of mitigation measures that we’ll install.”’ In an interview with The Michigan Daily, Green said noise mitigation efforts have been increased due to resident feedback. “We’re taking standards that are above and beyond what you would see with a typical facility of this nature to make sure that we are distancing those noise-producing elements of the facility away from the public access areas or away from the roadways or property lines,” Green said. “We’re taking additional measures to screen those with berms, trees, and then following up on that, we’ll be using our monitoring and modeling to see if that isn’t sufficient, then we’ll look at engineered sound barriers to, again, mitigate that noise emission.” Residents have expressed concerns during community feedback sessions about the data center’s potential to draw water from or discharge water into the Huron River. According to Green, the facility does not plan to draw or discharge water from the river. He also said they are looking to reduce potable water use. “Our model estimates that the peak water demand would be up to 650,000 gallons per day under the most demanding weather conditions and with roughly one-third of that water-drawn amount discharged back into the sanitary sewer system after its uses in the cooling process,” Green said. “We are also evaluating options to reduce the potable water use.” The University will continue to conduct environmental impact and acoustic studies during the next phase of project development. Additionally, the next phase will include the completion of design developments and construction documents, as well as refining utility plans. The first phase of construction is estimated to cost approximately $450 million. According to documentation submitted to the Board, the project will be supported by a grant provided by the state of Michigan, which totals up to $100 million and is contingent upon the development being built in Ypsilanti Township. Supplemental funding will come from “university bond proceeds with debt service paid from a combination of rental payments and general fund resources.” The first phase of construction is estimated to be completed in fall 2031. Hurn said she believes this development is necessary to keep the University competitive with research advancements. “We want to be able to meet our mission, which is to serve the public,” Hurn said. “There is no way that our research will be able to do that if we don’t move to be able to accelerate our capacities for research computing.” Hurn added that these data center developments have the opportunity to impact a variety of fields across the University. “One of the things that’s so important about this expanded capacity is, first of all, that it’s going to cut across all fields — medicine, engineering, climate science, some aspects of social and behavioral science — but all of these things are going to be taking on bigger and more complex problems than we’ve ever been able to work on before,” Hurn said. Daily News Editor Alexa Cheaney can be reached at acheaney@umich.edu.

artigo.texto: DCF Video: CoolIT's 3 MW CDU Brings Smart Monitoring and Fanless Cooling to AI Infrastructure As AI infrastructure moves toward higher rack densities and increasingly liquid-cooled architectures, the next challenge is not simply removing more heat. It's ensuring that the cooling systems themselves remain reliable, efficient, and capable of protecting increasingly valuable computing hardware. At the 2026 OCP Global Summit in San Jose, CoolIT Systems Director of Marketing Charles Robison gave Data Center Frontier a close-up look at several technologies addressing that challenge, including the company's new 3-megawatt CHx 3000 coolant distribution unit (CDU), integrated coolant health monitoring, and a fifth-generation cold plate loop designed for fanless servers. The demonstration comes at a significant moment for CoolIT, which was acquired by Ecolab for approximately $4.75 billion in July 2026. On November 16, Ecolab formally introduced its new integrated AI cooling platform at SC26 in Chicago, placing the CHx 3000 and its embedded 3D TRASAR technology at the center of a broader strategy combining liquid cooling hardware, fluid management, and digital monitoring. Looking Inside the CHx 3000 The CoolIT CHx 3000 is a liquid-to-liquid CDU rated for 3 MW of cooling capacity at a 3°C approach temperature difference, with a specified flow rate of 4,500 liters per minute. Designed for high-density AI deployments, the unit incorporates Ecolab's 3D TRASAR technology to continuously monitor the condition of the circulating coolant. In the video, Robison points directly to the sensor array that makes the integration possible. "3D TRASAR, and you can see the array of sensors here, allows coolant health monitoring," Robison explains. "It allows people to see real-time what's going on with the coolant. So before it goes out of spec, they know what's happening and they can address it." The distinction is important. Traditional cooling monitoring typically emphasizes temperature, pressure, and flow. Ecolab's technology adds visibility into fluid chemistry and contamination, allowing operators to identify deteriorating conditions before they compromise the system. According to a November 10 technical report from CoolIT, the integrated monitoring system tracks parameters including glycol concentration, pH, turbidity, conductivity, and differential pressure. These measurements can help identify conditions that contribute to corrosion, biological growth, and restricted flow through cold plate microchannels. Robison describes the monitoring capability as another layer of reliability for high-density liquid cooling infrastructure. Opening the CHx 3000 enclosure, he also walks through the unit's mechanical architecture, identifying its pumps, large 25-micron filters, heat exchanger, and control system, all accessible from the front of the CDU. Cold Plates Push Toward Fanless Servers The second part of the demonstration moves from the CDU to the server itself. Robison highlights a fifth-generation cold plate loop developed for a server OEM, describing it as a high-performance design intended to remove the need for conventional server fans. "What's unique about this cold plate design is there's—it's a fanless design," he says. "So we're doing 100% heat capture through this cold plate loop." That claim reflects a larger transition underway in AI server thermal design. As processor power demands climb, liquid cooling must increasingly address not only CPUs and GPUs but also memory, networking, storage, and power components that traditionally relied on airflow. In a September 2026 technical discussion of fanless AI servers, CoolIT described near-total liquid heat capture as an increasingly practical requirement for very high-density systems. The company identifies less than 1% of server heat remaining for air cooling as an achievable engineering target, while acknowledging that literal 100% capture is difficult to establish. The underlying direction is clear: as liquid cooling takes on virtually the entire server heat load, eliminating server fans becomes increasingly feasible. Robison concludes the walkthrough with CoolIT's range of cooling fluids, spanning pure water and multiple propylene glycol-based formulations. The display underscores another aspect of the company's expanding portfolio: matching coolant selection and fluid management to the requirements of increasingly sophisticated direct liquid cooling systems. From Cooling Capacity to Cooling Intelligence For DCF, the OCP demonstration also provides a useful continuation of our recent tour of CoolIT's manufacturing and R&D operations in Calgary, where Robison showed how the company is scaling production and testing for megawatt-class cooling infrastructure. The latest demonstration moves that story forward, illustrating how greater cooling capacity, continuous fluid monitoring, and increasingly comprehensive server-level heat capture are beginning to converge. With Ecolab's newly announced platform bringing these technologies together, the industry is moving toward an approach in which coolant quality, thermal performance, and operational reliability are managed as parts of the same system. For AI data centers increasingly defined by the density and value of the compute they house, that integration may prove as consequential as the next increase in CDU capacity. artigo.texto: Today’s advanced AI data center can be viewed as a vast, complex and interdependent digital organism in which a virtually infinite number of components must be tracked all the time, in real time. It’s a monitoring job of staggering proportions. At stake is the operation of highly critical workloads and the maintenance of return on investment for high-cost compute equipment. At risk is sub-optimal performance or, in worst-case scenarios, the nightmare of data center downtime. Sponsored Resources: Why traditional telemetry misses nanosecond power-rail events Telemetry has long been relied upon to monitor data center servers, test and measurement equipment, wireless infrastructure and other systems for real-time information about voltage, current, power, temperature and overall system health. But most systems operate at millisecond-level intervals or slower, which is six orders of magnitude longer than the transient events that now occur at the processor power rails and the tools meant to observe them. The requirements and high stakes of today’s AI data centers and workloads have called for a new generation of advanced, nanosecond-level telemetry gear. Texas Instruments has established a leadership position in this sector. The company has developed the first analog-to-digital converter (ADC) to enable 24/7, low-power, event-based remote monitoring at nanosecond resolution. Let’s unpack this statement and examine why TI’s new monitoring technology is so important for the data center industry. What is the TI ADC34DSO75? We’re talking specifically about TI's ADC34DSO75, the industry's highest-performance, 3 gigasamples per second (GSPS) ADC, delivering thousands of times faster performance than current offerings. Launched at the Open Compute Project Global Summit conference in October, the ADC34DSO75 addresses the shortcomings of existing monitoring solutions that can’t detect the nanosecond-level power-rail glitches that cause costly data center downtime. The ADC34DSO75 combines ultra-high-speed sampling with advanced on-chip digital signal processing in a small form factor, detecting and capturing transient fault events in real time. “AI deployments span tens of thousands of GPUs producing enormous compute power combined with operating conditions that change by the second,” said Shannon Lippincott, TI product marketing manager, high-speed data convertors in a technical article for TI. “Workloads continually ramp up and down, requiring server power systems to respond to dynamic demands. The result is voltage droops, overshoots and other transient events at the processor power rail, many of which can occur in nanoseconds.” Lippincott explained that although nanosecond-level telemetry exists today, many events can occur during complex workflows and result in brownouts or downtime without showing up on existing telemetry systems. Within 100 ms, a server can experience several nanosecond-scale electrical events that, left undetected, can trigger resets, retests, triage, throttling and interrupted workloads. The result: reduced AI compute performance and underutilization of processors and other components at major cost. What do undetected power glitches cost data centers? Without effective detection capabilities, technicians are forced to manually debug the situation, spending hours or days combing through hardware, firmware and system logs to isolate nanosecond-scale transients that have caused problems. The Uptime Institute reported that 57 percent of major outages cost more than $100,000, with one in five outages surpassing $1 million. Another shortfall of traditional high-speed detection technology, including those with nanosecond telemetry, is that they tend to be too large, too power-hungry and too costly for at-scale deployment across thousands of AI data center server racks. Critical advantages of TI’s ADC34DSO75 are its small size and low power consumption. It leverages advanced analog design and an integrated digital signal processor, processing and refining signals in real time while simplifying the overall architecture and reducing the need for field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs) and their complexity and high cost. It combines a signal-to-noise (SNR) ratio of 68 dBFS with low phase and amplitude noise and has half the power consumption of competing solutions within a one-inch-by-two-inch form factor. "The glitches technicians look for are like a needle in a haystack,” said Karthik Vasanth, vice president of TI’s Data Converters and Clocks business unit. “Engineers program the parameters of the needle, and the chip searches the haystack. The ADC34DSO75 detects the glitches data centers can’t see." Inside the eight-channel system-on-module board TI also built around the ADC34DSO75 an eight-channel system-on-module (SOM) board. The board measures eight voltages inside a processor with nanosecond resolution using two of the data converters, each handling four channels. The board includes a microcontroller unit (MCU) and flash memory for storing event data, so if power goes out, the information stays on the card for retrieval later. Designers can offload the full onboard memory in about 10 ms at 200 Mbps. In all, the ADC34DSO75's configurable, integrated event detection and capture enable engineers to tailor monitoring to their specific needs. And its remote event reporting capability eliminates the need to send a technician on-site or connect an oscilloscope to troubleshoot an event, minimizing downtime and reducing the security risk of physical hardware access. From nanosecond visibility to predictive fault detection The bar for data center reliability is always rising even as reliability grows in complexity. Moving forward, TI plans to combine nanosecond-level monitoring with system intelligence to support predictive fault detection and autonomous system management with the goal of anticipating and fixing problems before they occur. artigo.texto: JA lança ecossistema de energia solar e armazenamento de mesma origem em Chengdu AGÊNCIA DE COMUNICAÇÃO Conteúdo de responsabilidade da empresa 17 de novembro de 2026 CHENGDU, China, 17 de novembro de 2026 /PRNewswire/ — A JA apresentou seu ecossistema de energia solar e armazenamento de mesma origem no evento “ORIGIN — Lançamento do ecossistema de energia solar e armazenamento da JA” em Chengdu, reunindo representantes de associações do setor, instituições de pesquisa, clientes e órgãos de certificação. Guiado pela abordagem de integração de sistemas fotovoltaicos e de armazenamento de mesma origem da JA, o ecossistema alinha energia solar, armazenamento de energia, gestão inteligente de energia e atendimento ao cliente desde o início, em vez de reunir, posteriormente, produtos desenvolvidos separadamente. Em seu discurso de abertura, o presidente da JA, Yang Aiqing, afirmou que uma integração mais estreita entre energia solar e armazenamento de energia é um próximo passo natural à medida que ambos os setores amadurecem. Os clientes precisam de mais do que equipamentos de alto desempenho: precisam de sistemas de energia confiáveis e fáceis de gerenciar, projetados de acordo com suas necessidades. Começar pelo valor para o cliente pode reduzir os custos de coordenação e melhorar os resultados gerais. Liu Shuo, presidente do centro de marca e marketing da JA, observou que excelentes módulos solares e equipamentos de armazenamento não garantem automaticamente um sistema excelente. Compatibilidade, despacho e responsabilidade devem ser considerados na fase de design. Com base em 21 anos de experiência na fabricação de painéis fotovoltaicos, a JA estruturou sua abordagem em torno de origem, sinergia e convergência, conectando P&D conjunto, operações coordenadas, pré-comissionamento conjunto antes do envio e serviço unificado. Guo Yafei, copresidente do centro de operações regionais da JA, descreveu três capacidades essenciais: controle e despacho unificados, gestão coordenada de energia verde e serviço unificado. Fundamentadas em um modelo de P&D de três gerações, essas capacidades reúnem uma arquitetura de hardware unificada, uma plataforma de software e um processo de comissionamento. A JA estima que, em comparação com sistemas montados separadamente, sua abordagem pode melhorar a eficiência do sistema em 2% a 3%, reduzir o tempo de implantação e comissionamento em 20% a 30%, diminuir os custos de gerenciamento do ciclo de vida do projeto em 30% e reduzir os custos de operação e manutenção em 10% a 20%. A JA ESS também apresentou soluções baseadas na integração de sistemas fotovoltaicos e de armazenamento de mesma origem, combinando os produtos desenvolvidos pela JA com a inteligência em nível de nuvem, borda e dispositivo. Elas abordam oito áreas de aplicação: centros de dados com IA, projetos de grande escala para serviços públicos, instalações comerciais e industriais, agricultura, sistemas integrados de energia solar, armazenamento e carregamento, microrredes conectadas e desconectadas da rede, mineração e energia residencial. A JA destacou as implementações na Itália, no noroeste da China, na República Democrática do Congo e na Mongólia Interior. Para um projeto comercial e industrial típico, a modelagem da JA indica um período de retorno do investimento 28,3% menor e um aumento de 36,5% na taxa interna de retorno (TIR). Bai Yiqi, da TÜV Rheinland Greater China, apresentou planos para desenvolver padrões para verificar o valor de sistemas integrados de energia solar e armazenamento, abrangendo desempenho em nível de usina, coordenação do sistema, confiabilidade do ciclo de vida e valor do ativo, bem como um relatório técnico conjunto com a JA. Na mesa-redonda do setor, os participantes defenderam uma mudança de paradigma, passando da conexão de dispositivos individuais para o projeto e gerenciamento de sistemas integrados, apoiados por objetivos compartilhados, responsabilidades claras e padrões de avaliação consistentes. Olhando para o futuro, a JA planeja levar seu ecossistema de energia solar e armazenamento de mesma origem para mais de 180 países e regiões por meio de uma rede de mais de 5.000 parceiros, ajudando os clientes a obter benefícios de energia limpa mais eficientes, confiáveis e mensuráveis. img alt=”” src=”https://rt.prnewswire.com/rt.gif?NewsItemId=PT98450&Transmission_Id=202611171144PR_NEWS_LATAM____PT98450&DateId=20261117″ style=”border:0px; width:1px; height:1px;” /> Tópicos Relacionados: Novos Produtos/Serviços, Serviços Públicos, Concessionárias de Energia Elétrica, Produtos e Serviços Ambientais, Energias Alternativas, Ambiental, Social e Governança, Tecnologia Verde A OESP não é(são) responsável(is) por erros, incorreções, atrasos ou quaisquer decisões tomadas por seus clientes com base nos Conteúdos ora disponibilizados, bem como tais Conteúdos não representam a opinião da OESP e são de inteira responsabilidade da PR Newswire Ltda

artigo.texto: - Power - 2 min read Energy storage firms raise $16.7 billion in corporate funding in Jan-Sept 2026: Report VC funding rises 93 per cent year-on-year to $5.4 billion across 79 deals, energy storage project acquisitions more than double to 21.6 GW Corporate funding for global energy storage companies rose 49 per cent year-on-year (YoY) to $16.7 billion across 120 deals in the first nine months of 2026, compared with $11.2 billion across 85 deals in the corresponding period last year, according to a report by Mercom Capital Group. The funding, which includes venture capital (VC), debt and public market financing, was raised across 120 deals, up 41 per cent from 85 deals in January-September 2025. This was the highest number of transactions recorded in a nine-month period in the past five years, the report said. VC funding for energy storage companies increased 93 per cent to $5.4 billion across 79 deals during the period, compared with $2.8 billion across 56 deals in the year-ago period. “Energy storage corporate funding increased sharply in the first nine months of 2026, supported by growing electricity demand, the need for greater grid reliability, and expanding applications for battery storage,” said Raj Prabhu, CEO of Mercom Capital Group. Energy storage downstream companies attracted the largest share of VC funding at approximately $1.8 billion. Other major funding recipients included iron-air battery, thermal energy storage, lithium-based battery, metal-hydrogen battery, and materials and components companies. The five largest VC funding deals included Base Power's $1 billion fundraise, Form Energy's $750 million, Antora Energy's $550 million, and $300 million each raised by EnerVenue Holdings and Sila Nanotechnologies. Debt and public market financing for the sector rose 36 per cent year-on-year to $11.4 billion across 41 deals in 9M 2026, compared with $8.4 billion across 29 deals in the corresponding period last year. Public market financing accounted for $6.7 billion across 20 deals, while debt financing contributed $4.7 billion across 21 deals. Corporate mergers and acquisitions (M&A) activity also increased, with 27 transactions announced during the nine-month period, up 35 per cent from 20 transactions a year earlier. Energy storage downstream companies accounted for the largest share of M&A activity, with 14 transactions, followed by energy storage systems and materials and components companies, with four transactions each. Energy storage project acquisitions increased significantly, with approximately 21.6 GW of projects acquired across 108 transactions in 9M 2026, compared with 10.1 GW across 46 transactions in the year-ago period. Acquired capacity rose 114 per cent year-on-year, while transaction activity increased 135 per cent. Standalone energy storage projects accounted for approximately 16.5 GW of the acquired capacity, while renewable energy projects paired with storage accounted for 5.2 GW.

artigo.texto: Despite the hot topic of data centers in Virginia and nationwide, so far companies have yet to eye Halifax County as a destination. Halifax County Planning and Zoning Administrator Detrick Easley said in a recent interview that he has not received any requests to move a data center into the county. “I know a big topic in the county has been data centers,” Easley said. “I’ve seen a couple of posts. But I currently have not had anyone reach out to me about data centers.” Though there are no data center requests yet, the county is still working on a new ordinance, starting with a work order with the Berkeley Group. “We have a work order with the Berkeley Group because we don’t know about data centers,” he explained. “All we know is what we hear about the water and the noise,” he continued. “So, we felt like we weren’t educated enough, so we hired the Berkeley Group to go out and research, go to all locales and research the pros and the cons.” After that research has been done, the county may ask the Berkeley group to help create a new ordinance. “But the rumors that we have data centers coming here, they found that’s not factual,” he said. “That is not true.” Along with working on the data center ordinance, the county is also working on an ordinance for small modular reactors and battery storage. “It’s a new wave of energy,” Easily explained. “So we also have a working group working on the ordinance for SMRs.” He said there has been some interest in bringing small modular reactors to Halifax County, but they take up less land than data centers. “You wouldn’t know they were there, and that’s the way we want it,” Easley said. Easley explained that battery storage is a new wave right now to help store energy made by solar farms. “Once you get solar and solar starts making all this energy, if you don’t have the grid mass to put this solar in power, you’re losing it,” he said. “So we have a couple of developers looking now to site battery storage facilities in the county,” he explained. “They’re better because they are more compact and take less land. So, solar might take 1,000 acres, battery might only need 50 acres.” Emily Barber is a staff writer for The Gazette-Virginian. Contact her at ebarber@yourgv.com.

artigo.texto: State environmental regulators have resumed reviewing data center permits, bringing an end to an earlier directive from Gov. Greg Abbott ordering a pause on permit approvals related to data center projects. The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality received notice on Friday from Abbott’s office that officials at the state’s electric grid had completed gathering information on potential community impacts from data centers — one of multiple issues Abbott asked grid officials and electricity regulators to evaluate. “The agency has resumed its normal permit review process and will evaluate applications under all applicable state and federal laws and regulations,” TCEQ spokesperson Laura Lopez said in a written statement. In August, Abbott had called on the Electric Reliability Council of Texas and electricity regulators to audit all data centers trying to connect to the grid, as well as gather information about tax incentives, power use, water use and potential neighborhood impacts. Abbott at that time paused approval of any grid interconnections for data centers while the audit was completed. In his Sept. 21 letter to TCEQ calling for the environmental permitting pause, Abbott said the agency needed to wait until ERCOT “completes its review.” Environmental advocates at Public Citizen, responding to the news of the resumed permits, called on TCEQ commissioners to resign. “The TCEQ is asserting that ERCOT has concluded its assessment of the community impacts of data centers, and without sharing those results with communities or detailing how the TCEQ will incorporate the findings into permitting decisions, agency leadership has begun unilaterally issuing data center permits,” said Kathryn Guerra, the TCEQ watchdog campaign director for Public Citizen, in a statement. Intense opposition to data centers had been growing all year in communities across the state, where Democrats and Republicans alike fought projects they worried would destabilize the electric grid, lead to more pollution from new gas-fueled power generators and guzzle up water in a state with serious drought concerns. TCEQ handles permits related to air pollution at facilities and stormwater runoff on construction sites. The agency faced criticism in October from Public Citizen and FracTracker Alliance. The groups noticed that some data center-related construction permits were being cleared anyway — counter to Abbott’s order. TCEQ said it suspended the permits and then it shut down its entire automated electronic filing system and required physical applications be submitted for staff to review. Then in a staggering upset on Nov. 3, Abbott lost his reelection to Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who on the campaign trail vowed to keep data center approvals paused until legislators pass new state laws. Neither Abbott’s office nor Hinojosa’s media team on Tuesday immediately responded to a request for comment. “Texans are tired of this political theatre,” said Sam Law, researcher at FracTracker Alliance, in a written statement shared by Public Citizen. “We need real leadership, transparency, and a true moratorium on data center development.” ERCOT provided an update on its review of community impacts to electric regulators at the Public Utility Commission of Texas on Nov. 5. ERCOT reported receiving responses from 93% of 465 projects, which provided enough information for “a statistically meaningful analysis for the final report.” ERCOT officials plan to report their full findings to the PUC on Dec. 10 and discuss them at the next PUC open meeting Dec. 17. artigo.texto: The Hood County Commissioners Court voted 5-0 to find a third party expert to address safety concerns regarding the Apache Hill battery energy storage system (BESS) in response to a risk analysis of the facility. The analysis was conducted by Dr. Andy Wolford, who founded Risknology, a safety consulting and risk assessment firm, in Houston in 1994. Wolford and other community members have previously voiced concerns about the BESS’s location adjacent to the Rainbow’s Promise daycare off Mambrino Highway. The Apache Hill BESS project by Vitis Energy features 96 Sungrow Power Titan 2.0 battery energy storage system containers and is expandable to 120 containers. Wolford said the site density is comparable to 1,000 Tesla car batteries. The BESS is located 200 feet from the daycare. The site is intended to provide 200 megawatts of power and 400 megawatt hours of energy. “That’s about a fifth of one of the Comanche Peak nuclear reactors,” Wolford said. Wolford filed a peer review of the facility with the developer of Apache Hill BESS in June 2026, and this was forwarded through the Hood County fire marshal to the company’s fire protection and engineering contractor. In September, the contractor responded to Wolford’s critique. “I had 16 key issues for them to address,” Wolford said. “They addressed one and stated that the other 15 were invalid and they weren’t going to do anything about it.” Wolford issued a rejoinder challenging the consulting firm’s response. Because the industry and fire codes governing it are new, “it’s not backed up by operational experience and accident history,” Wolford said. Summit Fire Consulting, which performed safety studies for Apache Hill, and Risknology disagree on the safety concerns, Wolford said. “I boiled this down to three primary reasons,” Wolford said. “Number one, the lab testing was done incorrectly.” He noted that the testing was done in China and was “performed incorrectly with propagating errors.” The testing results also influenced the design of the equipment, he said, adding, “they’re wrong, and they need to be redone.” Second, “the most significant hazards that the fire company was supposed to identify, they did not,” Wolford said. He identified these as container-to-container fire propagation risk and toxic vapor cloud dispersion. A third concern, Wolford said, is that the consulting company ranked the risks “unreasonably low,” adding that “the rankings are very biased and extremely low risk, which achieves no further engineering work if you meet a risk tolerance.” Wolford’s recommendations to the commissioners court were “first and foremost” for Hood County to not issue a certificate of occupancy “until all deficiencies are resolved,” to have the county fire marshal’s office seek a response from Summit regarding Risknology’s findings, to define resource needs for county fire departments to respond to BESS facilities and to contract with a third party expert to arbitrate between Summit and Wolford’s findings. That report would empower the fire marshal to act according to third party findings. He added that the cost of resources needed to respond to BESS incidents should be paid for by those operating BESS facilities and not by the taxpayers. Wolford said the risk to children should be considered. “Do we really want a crisis involving a large number of children who are a disadvantaged evacuation population — they’re vulnerable?” he said. Wolford said that Hood County is worth requiring responsible risk management over minimum compliance, adding, “Are we wise enough to recognize that something brand new, unproven and hazardous needs extra scrutiny?” Precinct 2 Commissioner Nannette Samuelson asked County Attorney Matt Mills if the county had received a response from communication sent to the Public Utility Commission, the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality or the Attorney General “regarding risks at Apache Hill.” Mills said he was not aware of any response. Samuelson said the West fertilizer plant explosion (in 2013) was an example of “a lot of safety standards being bypassed” before a tragedy occurred. Precinct 1 Commissioner Kevin Andrews asked how higher standards can be required. “What can we do just in our world?” Wolford asked. “I think the first thing that we need to do is give (County Fire Marshal) Jeff (Young) the ability to respond however he needs to whatever pressure that the developer puts on him. It’s clear to me it’s their expectation that they’re going operational next month. … So we have to give our fire marshal the ability to either let that happen or not.” Andrews said he did receive a response from the Electric Reliability Council of Texas saying ERCOT was monitoring and following developments with the BESS. “What I don’t want to happen is for the standards to get revised due to an accident at Apache Hill,” Samuelson said. Messages left with Vitis Energy and Summit Fire Consulting seeking comment were not returned by press time.

artigo.texto: Gasgoo Munich – Shenzhen Capchem Technology Co., Ltd. (Capchem) and EVE Energy Co., Ltd. (EVE Energy) have signed a long-term supply agreement for battery electrolytes, according to Capchem. Image Source: Capchem A Five-Year Supply Agreement for 600,000 Tonnes of Electrolyte Under the agreement, Capchem expects to supply EVE Energy with a total of 600,000 tonnes of electrolyte products between 2026 and 2030. The long-term agreement is expected to have a positive impact on Capchem's operating performance over the next five years. Both companies aim to achieve mutual benefits through greater supply chain stability. Deepening Strategic Cooperation and Supply Chain Integration In recent years, Capchem has continued to deepen strategic cooperation with leading battery manufacturers, establishing long-term partnerships with multiple customers. The latest agreement marks a further step in its cooperation with EVE Energy, building on their existing relationship and extending collaboration in capacity planning and technology development. Capchem plans to leverage its technological capabilities in electrolytes, vertically integrated supply chain and global network of intelligent manufacturing facilities to coordinate production capacity and support customers' long-term material requirements. A Shift Toward Integrated Industry Competitiveness Competition in the electrolyte industry is increasingly shifting beyond pricing to encompass broader capabilities, including reliable delivery, integrated supply chain support and long-term joint technology development. Capchem said it will continue to follow its business philosophy of specialization, precision, depth and thoroughness, focusing on high-quality products and reliable delivery to create value for customers as the industry faces new opportunities and challenges.

artigo.texto: Electricity prices and reliability are on the minds of all Pennsylvanians. A recent study found that the region’s electricity grid is getting stretched to its limits, and as a result, prices have been on the rise. Pennsylvania could also start experiencing more than a dozen electricity shortfalls — and potential blackouts — annually by 2030 because of this stress on the grid. Unfortunately, with new data centers and more extreme temperatures on the horizon, energy use will continue to rise, making the strain on our grid even greater. In response to this energy demand spike, dozens of new fossil fuel projects are being proposed that would bring more air and climate pollution to our state. This includes a gas plant near Pittsburgh that would become the largest power plant of its kind in the nation — and could, by some estimates, emit 17 million tons of air and climate pollution annually. Instead of finding cheap and clean alternatives to tackle the challenge, the U.S. Department of Energy is keeping old fossil fuel power plants open that should have been retired. Here in Pennsylvania, two aging power plants that produce considerable climate emissions were kept open past their retirement date to help meet energy demand. Pennsylvania doesn’t need to keep open dirty power plants to meet the region’s energy demands. Instead, we can pair clean, renewable energy such as wind and solar with battery storage systems. This allows us to power the state and the nation with pollution-free electricity and avoid massive price hikes that some energy companies foist on consumers when electricity demand is highest and most urgent. Much like we use batteries in our everyday lives to power our TV remote or our kids’ newest toy, utility-scale batteries can also store and then supply the extra electricity needed to meet our energy demand. One of the great things about battery storage is that it allows us to capture and store extra electricity being produced from solar energy on the sunniest days. Then, in moments when the grid is strained and energy demand is high, that extra energy can be sent to the grid, providing consistent renewable power throughout the day. Red and blue states alike are taking full advantage of these benefits: Texas currently has approximately hundreds of times the battery capacity as Pennsylvania, much of which is paired with new solar developments. This buildout is in response to the 2021 winter storm Uri, which forced dayslong blackouts and resulted in hundreds of deaths across the state. Since that extreme cold, the huge investment in battery storage has helped to keep the grid up and running in subsequent winter storms and intense heat waves. In California, battery systems paired with solar arrays have been so efficient at saving and delivering energy to the grid that natural gas generation in the state has decreased, helping to reduce pollution while still meeting energy demand. With 21,000 megawatts of battery storage capacity, California has been able to use its wind and solar energy — even when the wind isn’t blowing and the sun isn’t shining — to power the state. Sadly, Pennsylvania currently isn’t taking advantage of this technology. A recent study by the PennEnvironment Research & Policy Center showed that Pennsylvania has seen little measurable growth in battery storage over the past decade. This is despite the fact that the cost of battery storage has been rapidly and substantially declining, like many other clean energy technologies. When we combine this with maximizing clean renewable energy, it can deliver real results for Pennsylvania. With batteries already being paired with renewables across the country, promoting storage here in Pennsylvania will help us take the next major step in renewable electricity production. The good news is that a proposal that would require utility companies to utilize more battery storage passed the Pennsylvania State House earlier this fall with bipartisan support. This legislation, state House Bill 2380, would allow utilities to capture excess energy produced and deploy it to our electricity grid when it’s stretched thin. If these batteries are paired with sources such as wind and solar, we can also power Pennsylvania with more clean, renewable energy. The Pennsylvania Legislature should pass this commonsense and bipartisan proposal as quickly as possible next session. Getting this bill to the governor’s desk is one of the best ways that Pennsylvania can protect our health and our climate — and keep the lights on. State Rep. Nikki Rivera, a Democrat, represents the 96th House District. Belle Sherwood is a climate and clean energy advocate for PennEnvironment.

artigo.texto: Terça-feira, 17 de novembro de 2026 Por Redação O Sul | 16 de novembro de 2026 Os Estados Unidos passaram a exigir autorização prévia para a exportação de determinados chips avançados de inteligência artificial (IA) destinados ao Brasil. A medida, anunciada nessa segunda-feira (16) pelo governo de Donald Trump, também abrange Singapura, Tailândia, Malásia e Indonésia e busca impedir que empresas chinesas utilizem estruturas de processamento de dados instaladas em outros países para acessar tecnologias americanas submetidas a restrições. A nova regulamentação do Departamento de Comércio dos EUA estabelece que os fornecedores precisarão obter licenças para enviar os semicondutores aos países incluídos na lista. Os pedidos serão analisados individualmente pelo governo americano. A exigência envolve processadores avançados da Nvidia e de outros fabricantes dos Estados Unidos. Segundo o Departamento de Comércio, a preocupação é evitar que empresas chinesas contornem as restrições impostas por Washington por meio de contratos de computação em nuvem. Nesse modelo, companhias podem utilizar remotamente a capacidade de processamento de chips instalados em data centers de outros países, sem precisar importar diretamente os equipamentos. A avaliação americana é de que os cinco países apresentam risco acima do habitual de desvio de tecnologias consideradas sensíveis. Com a nova regra, o controle não ficará restrito ao destino físico dos processadores, mas também envolverá a identificação de quem utiliza a capacidade computacional disponibilizada pelas empresas. Impacto A regulamentação também estabelece exigências para operadores de data centers que fornecem capacidade computacional significativa a empresas sediadas na China e em outros territórios submetidos a embargos americanos. Essas companhias terão prazo de até 90 dias, após a entrada em vigor da norma, para solicitar autorização e continuar prestando os serviços. As remessas de equipamentos que já estiverem a caminho terão uma isenção de 30 dias. A regulamentação prevê ainda exceções para determinadas operações, incluindo estruturas ligadas a empresas americanas e sistemas utilizados por redes sociais e varejistas. A medida não representa uma proibição geral da compra de semicondutores pelo Brasil. Entretanto, as exportações abrangidas passarão a depender de autorização do governo dos Estados Unidos, que poderá avaliar a capacidade brasileira de fiscalizar o destino dos equipamentos e impedir eventuais desvios. Disputa tecnológica A decisão ocorre em meio ao aumento das tensões entre Washington e Pequim pelo controle das tecnologias de inteligência artificial. Os Estados Unidos procuram impedir que empresas chinesas tenham acesso aos processadores mais avançados, considerados estratégicos para o desenvolvimento de modelos de IA e aplicações militares. O endurecimento das regras também acontece após suspeitas de que empresas de Singapura tenham adquirido grandes quantidades de chips americanos e disponibilizado sua capacidade de processamento a companhias chinesas. O anúncio foi feito às vésperas de uma viagem de Trump à Ásia, que inclui um encontro com o presidente chinês, Xi Jinping. As restrições ao acesso a semicondutores avançados devem integrar as discussões entre os dois governos. A inclusão do Brasil ocorre em um momento em que o país busca atrair investimentos internacionais em infraestrutura de inteligência artificial e centros de processamento de dados. A nova exigência poderá acrescentar uma etapa de autorização americana para projetos que dependam de determinados equipamentos fabricados nos Estados Unidos.
