artigo.texto: UK battery company AceOn has launched a range of 12 V sodium-ion battery packs for applications including solar street lighting, roadside equipment, medical devices and remote telemetry, which is UN38.3-certified . The StamiNa+ Core range comprises four packs from 10 Ah to 30 Ah, equivalent to 120 Wh to 360 Wh, and is now available to order following completion of UN38.3 transport testing. UN38.3 is the section of the UN Manual of Tests and Criteria covering the transport safety testing required before rechargeable lithium and sodium batteries can be shipped. Tests include altitude simulation, thermal cycling, vibration, shock, external short circuit, impact or crush, overcharge and forced discharge. AceOn said certification allows it to ship the StamiNa+ Core packs to OEMs and system integrators in the UK, Europe, Africa and other markets. The packs are rated to discharge between –40°C and +70°C and charge between –20°C and +60°C, with a claimed cycle life of 5,000 cycles to 70% remaining capacity. That low-temperature performance is one of the areas where sodium-ion developers are increasingly targeting applications traditionally served by lead-acid batteries. BESTmag reported in September that Aeson was promoting sodium-ion as an alternative to lead-acid for automotive starter and auxiliary batteries, while Clarios, Altris and InoBat have validated sodium-ion cold-cranking performance down to –40°C. AceOn said the new range is aimed at applications where conventional lead-acid batteries can struggle in extreme cold and where lithium-ion chemistry may create safety or supply-chain concerns. The company said it is also seeing interest from the defence sector. All four packs use 32140-format cylindrical sodium-ion cells in a 4S configuration and incorporate an AceOn-designed battery management system providing overcharge, over-discharge, over-current and short-circuit protection, as well as cell balancing. The range comprises two 10 Ah/120 Wh packs, a 20 Ah/240 Wh pack and a 30 Ah/360 Wh model. Maximum current is 5 A for the 10 Ah packs and 10 A for the larger variants. AceOn has also developed a dedicated 15.6 V, 5 A charger for the range. The charger and integrated BMS were designed in-house. The company’s work with sodium-ion dates back to 2017, when it integrated Faradion pouch cells into a modified SolarSDS off-grid solar system. AceOn said that early project provided field experience with the chemistry and led to subsequent development of its own sodium-ion battery management technology, including work on a zero-volt BMS. Sodium-ion cells can tolerate deeper discharge than many lithium-ion chemistries and can use aluminium current collectors on both electrodes rather than requiring copper on the anode side. AceOn said its cells contain no lithium or cobalt and use sodium compounds derived from abundant materials including salt and soda ash. The launch follows growing commercial activity in the 12 V sodium-ion market. BESTmag reported last year that Unigrid had launched a sodium-ion platform as a drop-in replacement for conventional 12 V starter batteries. AceOn is also expanding sodium-ion assembly in Africa. Its new facility near Kampala, Uganda, includes a 3,000 sq ft battery assembly and training centre as well as BMS research and development. The site is intended to supply locally assembled StamiNa+ packs to East African markets. AceOn co-founder and CEO Mark Thompson said: “We first put sodium-ion cells into one of our solar systems back in 2017, when most people had never heard of the chemistry. It proved to us that sodium-ion could do a real job in the field. Nine years on, StamiNa+ Core is a certified range we can ship anywhere in the world. “Solar street lights, roadside signs, medical devices and remote telemetry all need batteries that work in the cold, last for years and don’t depend on cobalt or lithium. That is exactly what these packs are built for, and we’re ready to talk to OEMs and integrators now. “We want to be a leader in sodium-ion pack technology. Our team designs the BMS and charger in-house, we’re now assembling packs in Uganda, and we want to work with cell manufacturers around the world to take this chemistry into every market that needs it.” Photo: AceOn’s StamiNa+ Core range comprises four UN38.3-certified 12 V sodium-ion battery packs from 10 Ah to 30 Ah, alongside a dedicated charger. The packs are rated to discharge at temperatures as low as –40°C. Credit: AceOn.

artigo.texto: Today, a team led by Harvard researchers published a highly anticipated study in Nature Sustainability. For the first time since generative AI took off, we have a peer-reviewed estimate of how much climate pollution comes from keeping America’s biggest data centers running. Headlines about it are already popping up all over. The study estimates that hyperscale data centers across America are emitting up to 31 million metric tons of carbon dioxide per year, roughly as much CO₂ as Denmark emitted in 2024. It also estimates the facilities are taking up roughly 2 percent of U.S. electricity consumption. These are big, important numbers! And yet, they’re also massive underestimations. There are a few reasons why today’s study gets nowhere near the actual amount of climate pollution coming from these ever-buzzing internet slop factories. One is the way the researchers counted the facilities’ emissions. To do this, they estimated how much electricity each data center used, then looked at how the grid in that part of the country makes its electricity—how much comes from gas, coal, renewables, and so on—to estimate how much CO₂ would be released to generate that much power. But not all data center electricity comes from the grid. Indeed, an ever-increasing number of these massive data centers are also building their own, on-site fossil fuel plants. For example, during the study period (May 2024 through April 2025), Elon Musk’s xAI got some of the electricity for its Colossus data center in Memphis from the grid—but it also got some of it by burning gas in turbines right outside the building. Lead author Gianluca Guidi confirmed that Colossus wasn’t among the 403 facilities studied. For the facilities they did study, the researchers couldn’t tell how much power came from the grid and how much was generated on-site. So they applied the regional grid mix to all estimated electricity use, which can undercount emissions at facilities that burn their own gas. Another reason the climate impact of hyperscale data centers is likely understated is that electricity consumption is not the only way these facilities heat the planet. For example, the equipment that keeps the servers from overheating is leaking heat-trapping refrigerants into the atmosphere. And when a data center runs on gas—as so many of them do—methane can escape from wells and pipelines before the gas even reaches the power plant. In addition, there are potentially hundreds of hyperscale data centers that were left out of today’s study on the climate impacts of these facilities. Yes—hundreds. That’s because we don’t actually know how many hyperscale data centers are currently up and running in the United States. (Hyperscale means “the largest and most powerful class of data centers,” according to the study. These are the kinds of facilities that can train and run large language models. See footnote to see how the study defines them).1 The researchers only landed on their number—403—after painstakingly going through a list of 675 possible hyperscale data center locations given to them by a company called Baxtel, which tracks data centers. And by that I mean they had to pull up satellite images for every single facility to answer questions like Is this the data center, or just another building on the same campus? Has it even been built yet, or is this satellite photo just old? And even after they found the right building, they still had to figure out whether it was running before they could figure out how much electricity it might be using. All told, the researchers had to leave 272 possible hyperscale data centers out of the study because they couldn’t find out enough about them. Finally, the study period ends in April 2025—meaning the climate impact of data centers has likely grown substantially. Gianluca Guidi, the study’s lead author, acknowledged this in Monday’s release. “The data center boom hasn’t slowed down since our study period ended in April 2025,” he said. “New facilities have been built, existing campuses have expanded, and demand for AI computing continues to grow. That means the electricity use and carbon footprint we’re reporting could already be substantially larger now in 2026.” And yet, even with all of these limitations (most acknowledged by the study itself, which is how I know about them), the researchers were able to pull out some important findings. They include: - The generative AI boom is mostly powered by fossil fuels. 53.9 percent of the electricity consumption of hyperscale data centers is fossil-fuel generated, with 38.2 percent coming from methane gas and 15.2 percent coming from coal. - Hyperscale data centers use as much electricity as some U.S. states. They used 82 terawatt-hours of electricity in a year (68–99 terawatt-hours of electricity across scenarios). That’s as much electricity as some individual U.S. states over the course of a year, with the upper estimate approaching the annual electricity consumption of Indiana, Michigan, and Tennessee. It represents about 1.8% of all U.S. electricity consumption. - Hyperscale data centers are consuming more than 3 times as much electricity as they were in 2018. An earlier study done before the generative AI boom put U.S. data centers’ electricity use at about 23 terawatt-hours in 2018. The new study’s central estimate is about 3.6 times as high. - Virginia alone accounted for about a quarter of the electricity use. The researchers counted 142 facilities in Virginia, more than twice as many as in any other state. Powering those facilities was associated with about 7 million metric tons of CO₂. Together, Virginia, Oregon, Ohio, and Iowa accounted for more than half the electricity used by the data centers in the study. Now, to be totally clear, I’m not saying any of this to bash the study! Quite the contrary: I think it represents an important, Herculean effort, especially given how little information Congress and state governments require tech companies to give u

artigo.texto: LEGO Manufacturing Vietnam powers on battery energy storage system - Official operation of battery marks a key milestone towards operating the factory on 100% renewable energy. - The system is the first of its scale in Vietnam. - The renewable energy solution supported by battery storage and LEGO Manufacturing Vietnams 12,400 rooftop solar panels are expected to avoid the equivalent of 20,000 tonnes of CO2e annually in the first five years of operation¹. LEGO Manufacturing Vietnam has powered on its battery energy storage system, developed in partnership with VietnamSingapore Industrial Park (VSIP), marking a key milestone in the companys ambition to operate its Vietnam factory using renewable energy. Jesper Hassellund Mikkelsen, Senior Vice President of Asia Operations and General Manager of LEGO Manufacturing Vietnam, said: This is an exciting step for the LEGO Groups sustainability ambitions in Vietnam and around the world. By bringing together innovative technology and strong collaboration with our partners, we are turning our renewable energy ambitions into reality and demonstrating what is possible when industry works together. Nguyen Phu Thinh, General Director of VSIP, said: We congratulate LEGO Manufacturing Vietnam for taking a pioneering step in adopting large-scale renewable energy solutions and demonstrating that ambitious sustainability goals can be translated into tangible action. The DPPA between the LEGO Group and VSIP is not only a significant milestone for both organizations, but also a powerful testament to how industrial developers and manufacturers can jointly create a new paradigm for sustainable manufacturing. As part of Vietnams first large-scale renewable energy solution for industrial use, LEGO Manufacturing Vietnam operates its own on-site rooftop solar panels alongside a direct Power Purchase Agreement (DPPA) with VSIP. Under this framework, electricity generated from VSIPs rooftop solar and integrated Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) is delivered directly to the factory via a dedicated transmission line. When generation exceeds demand, VSIPs battery stores the excess power and releases it as needed, ensuring a continuous and highly reliable renewable energy supply. Combined with the existing 12,400 rooftop solar panels on the factorys rooftops, the battery energy storage system is expected to cover approximately 75% of the factorys total electricity demand during the first five years of operation and help avoid approximately 20,000 tonnes of CO₂e emissions each year². LMV is exploring additional power purchase agreements to address the remaining 25% electricity demand and support its continued transition towards renewable energy. Opened in April 2025, the LEGO Groups Vietnam factory has been designed to support the companys long-term growth in the region, while advancing the companys sustainability ambitions. Facts about the battery energy storage system - Agreement type: Direct Power Purchase Agreement (DPPA) with VSIP, signed September 2025 - System: Integrated rooftop solar and battery energy storage solution operated by VSIP, supplying renewable electricity directly to LEGO Manufacturing Vietnam - Forecast renewable coverage: Combined, solar generation and battery storage are expected to support 75% of the factorys electricity demand with renewable energy. - CO2e reduction: Approximately 20,000 tonnes of CO2e per year (based on Vietnam grid emission factor of 0.561 tCO2e/MWh), including the contribution from LEGO Manufacturing Vietnams existing rooftop solar system. Facts about LEGO Manufacturing Vietnam - Jobs: For a full list of job openings, visit our career page or follow LEGO Careers and see how you can build your career. - Employees: 1,350 - Land: 44-hectares, size of 62 soccer pitches - Buildings: Five buildings that cover approximately 150,000 m2 and include office spaces, energy centre, moulding, packing buildings, a high bay warehouse and other buildings critical to factory operations. - Precision manufacturing: All LEGO factories follow the same blueprint, using high-tech equipment to produce bricks with 1/10th of a hairs width precision. - Location: Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam Environmental Sustainability Initiatives - Renewable energy: LEGO Manufacturing Vietnam is supported by Vietnams first large-scale renewable energy solution specifically designed for industrial use. The factorys renewable electricity supply is delivered through on-site rooftop solar panels and an adjacent energy centre combining large-scale solar generation with battery energy storage. Until all remaining energy needs can be accounted for through power purchase agreements, renewable energy certificates will be used. - Paper-based bags: The packaging line at LEGO Manufacturing Vietnam packages LEGO bricks in new paper-based bags, which replace single-use plastic bags. - Zero waste to landfill: The factory shares the same ambition as all LEGO operations to generate zero waste from factories which is sent to landfill. - Certification: LEED (Leadership in Energy & Environmental Design) Platinum and Gold certifications have been issued for the factorys main buildings, covering energy, water and waste. - Materials: In 2025, renewable and recycled sources accounted for 52% of the materials purchased to make LEGO® bricks, up from 33% in 2024, primarily through the use of the mass balance approach. - Investment: Sustainability investments increased by 20% in 2025 compared with 2024, and by more than three times compared with 2022. ¹ Avoided emissions are estimated using Vietnams 2026 electricity emission factor. Actual avoided emissions may vary as the emission factor changes over time. ² Based on Vietnams current grid emission factor. artigo.texto: The Minneapolis City Council passed an ordinance Thursday in a 7-6 vote to strengthen regulations on data centers ahead of the expiration of a six-month suspension on new development passed in June. If approved by Minneapolis Mayor Jacob Frey, the law will institute overlay zoning, which gives the City Council and City Planning Commission the ability to evaluate new data center proposals on a case-by-case basis. The ordinance also limits the size and geographic location of data centers, which provide storage and transmission of data for internet services. The development of new data centers is limited to two downtown districts that primarily consist of office buildings in an effort to avoid densely populated residential areas. Under the ordinance, data centers using only nonrenewable energy are capped at 50,000 square feet, while those that purchase local green energy can use up to 150,000 square feet. There are eight existing data centers in Minneapolis, with Cologix Data Center being the largest at 45,000 square feet. In an effort to limit noise pollution, servers must be located 20 feet inside a building and at least 100 feet from residential properties. The ordinance also requires potential developers to share expected water and energy use, and how they plan to manage noise. Supporters say case-by-case evaluations by elected officials will strengthen the democratic process. “This amendment is fundamentally about whether we believe residents deserve a meaningful voice in decisions that will shape the future of their neighborhoods,” Ward 2 Council Member Robin Wonsley, who represents parts of southeast Minneapolis and the University of Minnesota area, said. The ordinance follows a failed attempt Monday by progressive council members to pass a full ban, intended to reflect the wishes of the majority of the 1,600 Minneapolis residents who submitted comments to the City Council, Wonsley said. “It doesn’t bring a people-centered downtown, it’s not gonna be our ticket out of our financial woes, and our neighbors don’t want it,” Council Member Soren Stevenson, who represents parts of south central Minneapolis, said. “We should ban it.” The ban did not receive enough support from council members or Mayor Frey to pass. Data centers have been at the center of political deliberations in communities across the country, as the quickly developing Artificial Intelligence industry has increased demand for computational power. Residents in communities with large-scale data centers have faced air, noise and water pollution, as well as lower property values and strain on local energy resources, resulting in frequent power outages and higher utility costs. Council members who oppose stricter regulations say Minneapolis should prioritize the economic investment brought by data center developers. “We need a plan for economic growth, for a thriving downtown core. Being anti-jobs, anti-labor, anti-investment is not a strategy,” Council Member Elizabeth Shaffer, who represents parts of downtown and southwest Minneapolis, said. Council members supporting overlay zoning hope that evaluating individual applications could effectively respond to the rapidly changing conditions of the AI and data center industries. “The industry is rapidly evolving. It changes week by week, both in its financial conditions, in the way that the tech is evolving and also the way that the industry is finding gaps in local policies,” Council Member Aurin Chowdhury, who represents parts of southeast Minneapolis, said. Other council members preferred the existing primary zoning laws, which would establish standardized rules for all data center applications, in order to avoid tedious deliberation. “It’s better for us to have rules, apply them evenly, and not make every data center application a political fight,” Shaffer said. At a rally outside Minneapolis City Hall on Tuesday evening, residents protested in favor of a total ban and, in its absence, the adoption of overlay zoning over primary zoning. Many expressed worry about the pollution and quality-of-life risks from living near large data centers. Kalani Matus of the Climate Justice Committee spoke at the rally opposing any data center development, citing inflated demand driven by intense industry competition and speculation. City Council President Elliott Payne echoed these sentiments in support of overlay zoning at Thursday’s meeting. “The large frontier models are taking on significant debt to build these out under the speculation of future demand that might not actually ever show up,” Payne said. “It’s all speculation. It is a gold rush right now.” J.P. Morgan estimated that the industry’s five largest development companies will spend $697 billion on data center investments by the end of 2026, while major AI companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic are not expected to make a profit for several years. The City Council’s ordinance will now go to the desk of Frey, who will either approve or veto it. Frey has spoken in support of overlay zoning before, though he has also supported allowing data center development in a larger range of Minneapolis neighborhoods than the ordinance proposes.

artigo.texto: According to SNS Insider, the global Activated Carbon Market is entering a period of accelerated expansion as governments strengthen drinking water standards, industrial operators improve pollution control and manufacturers adopt advanced adsorption technologies. The global activated carbon market was valued at USD 5.31 billion in 2025, is estimated to reach USD 5.77 billion in 2026 and is projected to expand to USD 12.15 billion by 2035, registering a CAGR of 8.63% during 2026–2035. Demand is increasingly influenced by regulatory measures addressing per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), volatile organic compounds and industrial contaminants. Activated carbon remains an important filtration material because its porous structure enables adsorption of impurities from liquids and gases. Market development is also shifting toward reusable filtration media, carbon reactivation services and specialized grades for pharmaceutical manufacturing, chemical processing, energy storage and environmental remediation. Asia Pacific dominates global consumption and production, while North America and Europe are strengthening investment in advanced treatment infrastructure. Through 2035, suppliers offering certified filtration materials, reliable feedstock sourcing and reactivation capabilities are positioned to benefit from recurring industrial and municipal demand. Market Size and Forecast Demand Drivers and Constraints Primary Demand Drivers - Stricter drinking water standards: PFAS monitoring and treatment requirements are increasing demand for granular activated carbon across municipal water systems. - Industrial pollution control: Chemical plants, power facilities and manufacturing operations use carbon filtration to manage emissions, solvents and wastewater contaminants. - Expansion of water infrastructure: Urbanization and industrial development are encouraging investment in municipal and industrial purification systems. - Growing reactivation demand: Regeneration of spent carbon offers opportunities to reduce material consumption and establish recurring service contracts. - Specialty industrial applications: Pharmaceuticals, food processing, mining and energy storage are expanding the range of activated carbon applications. Potential Growth Constraints - Volatility in coal, wood and coconut shell raw material prices. - High energy consumption during carbon activation and reactivation. - Competition from membrane filtration and ion exchange technologies. - Trade barriers affecting international material sourcing. - Certification requirements and lengthy procurement cycles for drinking water applications. Demand Structure by Type Powdered Activated Carbon (2025 Market Share: 47.36%) Powdered activated carbon dominated the market with a 47.36% revenue share in 2025, supported by its rapid adsorption performance and widespread application in municipal water treatment, pharmaceutical purification, food processing and industrial emissions control. Its fine particle structure enables effective removal of dissolved organic compounds, taste-related impurities and selected contaminants. Municipal utilities frequently use powdered grades for seasonal treatment requirements, while industrial operators employ them in chemical purification and mercury capture. Through 2035, established processing infrastructure and recurring consumption are expected to sustain demand. Current trend: Continued demand from municipal water treatment and industrial purification. Major trends: Seasonal contaminant treatment, powdered carbon injection, pharmaceutical purification and optimized adsorption efficiency. Granular Activated Carbon (Forecast CAGR: 9.62%) Granular activated carbon is estimated to see the highest compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 9.62%, over 2026-2035. It is capable of being used in fixed-bed filtration systems and therefore is ideal for drinking water purification, PFAS elimination, groundwater cleanup and industrial gas purification. In contrast to powder activated carbon, granular activated carbon has the capacity to be thermally reactivated, which improves economics through the lifecycle. Current trend: Accelerating installation of granular filtration systems for contaminant removal. Major trends: PFAS treatment, carbon reactivation, fixed-bed filtration and reusable adsorption media. Demand Structure by Raw Material Coal-Based Activated Carbon (2025 Market Share: 43.84%) Coal Activated Carbon generated 43.84% of total revenue in the market in 2025, retaining its leadership due to the presence of production capacity and suitability for commercial use. Coal activated carbon is used in municipal water treatment, industrial gas purification, wastewater treatment, and emissions management. Production capacities are present in China, the USA, and Europe. Future demand from 2026 until 2035 will be determined by investments in filtration and raw material costs. Current trend: Stable industrial consumption supported by large-scale manufacturing capacity. Major trends: Water purification, industrial emissions treatment, raw material optimization and production efficiency. Coconut Shell Activated Carbon (Forecast CAGR: 9.84%) Coconut shell-based activated carbon is expected to grow at a CAGR of 9.84% through 2035, supported by demand for hard, microporous, low-ash filtration materials. These characteristics make it suitable for drinking water purification, gold recovery, food processing and selected pharmaceutical applications. Indonesia, the Philippines, India and Sri Lanka represent important supply markets. Growing interest in agricultural by-product utilization creates opportunities for producers, although seasonal shell availability and processing costs remain important commercial considerations. Current trend: Increasing preference for coconut shell-derived filtration materials. Major trends: Biomass utilization, specialty adsorption grades, gold recovery and sustainable feedstock sourcing. artigo.texto: "Expands When Charged, Contracts When Discharged"... A Clue to Solving the All-Solid-State Battery Lifespan Challenge [Reading Science] Hanyang University, Korea Electrotechnology Research Institute, and KIST Develop Bilayer Combining Silver-Carbon and Carbon Nanofiber Layers Capacity Retained at 92% After 250 Charge-Discharge Cycles...11.2 Percentage Points Higher Than Existing Structure Expansion during charging and contraction during discharging are among the main causes of shortened service life in all-solid-state batteries, a next-generation battery technology. Korean researchers have developed a bilayer structure that evenly distributes lithium inside the battery and absorbs volume changes, helping to mitigate the problem of capacity degradation. The National Research Foundation of Korea announced on November 17 that a joint research team led by Professor Lee Jongwon of Hanyang University, Principal Researcher Choi Jeonghee of the Korea Electrotechnology Research Institute, and Principal Researcher Jung Hoonki of the Korea Institute of Science and Technology (KIST) had developed a new bilayer structure that mitigates volume changes during the charging and discharging of anode-free all-solid-state batteries. Fabrication process of a double-layer all-solid-state battery and its lithium storage mechanism. (a) Fabrication of the double-layer structure combining a silver-carbon layer and a carbon nanofiber layer. (b) Lithium stored inside the carbon nanofiber layer and between the two layers after charging. (c) Reduction in internal pressure fluctuations achieved by applying the double-layer structure. (d) How sequential lithium storage mitigates volume expansion and mechanical stress. Provided by the research team led by Professor Lee Jongwon of Hanyang University. View original image All-solid-state batteries are a next-generation battery technology that can reduce fire risks by replacing the liquid electrolyte in conventional lithium-ion batteries with a solid electrolyte. Anode-free all-solid-state batteries, in particular, can reduce weight and volume and increase energy density because they do not use a separate anode active material, such as graphite, during manufacturing. The technology has attracted attention for its potential to extend the driving range of electric vehicles, but volume changes during charging and discharging have been considered a barrier to commercialization. During charging, lithium ions that have moved from the cathode gain electrons and accumulate as metallic lithium, increasing the battery's internal volume. During discharging, the accumulated lithium turns back into ions and moves, reducing the volume. Repetition of this process can destabilize contact between the electrode and solid electrolyte and cause mechanical damage inside the battery, potentially shortening its service life. To address this issue, the team designed a bilayer structure combining a thin silver-carbon layer with a carbon nanofiber layer containing abundant internal voids. The silver-carbon layer guides lithium to accumulate evenly rather than concentrating in specific areas during the initial stage of charging. As more lithium flows in, the carbon nanofiber layer stores it in its internal voids, mitigating volume expansion. By tracking lithium migration and accumulation through structural analysis and computer simulations, the team found that lithium first accumulates in the silver-carbon layer during the initial stage of charging, then fills the voids in the carbon nanofiber layer, and subsequently accumulates between the two layers. Capacity Maintained at 92% After 250 Charge-Discharge Cycles When the bilayer structure was applied to an actual pouch cell, the cell retained 92.0% of its initial capacity after 250 charge-discharge cycles, even at the relatively low pressure of 2 megapascals (MPa). This was 11.2 percentage points higher than the capacity retention rate of a cell using only the existing silver-carbon layer (80.8%). The results demonstrated the potential to improve battery service life by mitigating mechanical damage caused by charging and discharging. The joint research team that developed a bilayer structure for all-solid-state batteries. From left: Professor Lee Jongwon of Hanyang University; Principal Researcher Choi Jeonghee of the Korea Electrotechnology Research Institute; Principal Researcher Jung Hoonki of the Korea Institute of Science and Technology; and co-first authors Kang Junhee and Lee Taeyoung. Photo courtesy of the National Research Foundation of Korea. View original image However, these results were verified under experimental conditions. Before the technology can be applied to actual electric vehicle batteries, stable performance must be achieved in large-area, stacked cells, and long-term charge-discharge durability must be further validated. “This study is significant because it presents a new approach that goes beyond existing technologies for promoting uniform lithium deposition and can also mitigate mechanical damage during charging and discharging,” Professor Lee said. “We plan to develop the technology to deliver stable performance in large-area, stacked all-solid-state batteries and enable long-term operation at room temperature and under low-pressure conditions.” Hot Picks Today "Two Spend 500,000 Won in a Flash, Yet Wait Two Hours?" ... artigo.texto: A Cirion Technologies anunciou nesta quarta-feira, 18, a Datrix, nova marca da empresa para atuar no setor de data centers. A operação assume a gestão dos 12 complexos da Cirion na América do Sul, incluindo as unidades em São Paulo, Curitiba e Rio de Janeiro. Em comunicado, a Cirion destacou que a Datrix representa um novo passo na estratégia de crescimento no segmento de infraestrutura digital na América Latina. A marca busca fortalecer a presença regional da companhia e ampliar as capacidades de infraestrutura nos países em que mantém operações. Na relação com o mercado, a subsidiária deve atuar para atender hyperscalers, provedores de nuvem, empresas regionais e globais, plataformas de conteúdo e novas demandas de infraestrutura de inteligência artificial (IA). Além do Brasil, a Datrix conta com data centers na Argentina, no Chile, no Peru, na Colômbia e no Equador. A operação ocorrerá no modelo neutro (carrier-neutral), possibilitando que o cliente se conecte a diversos provedores de rede e tecnologia, com liberdade de escolha, informou a Cirion. "O papel da América Latina na economia digital das próximas décadas será definido pela infraestrutura que construímos hoje. A Datrix foi criada não apenas para sustentar esse futuro, mas para ajudar a moldá-lo", afirma Santiago Londoño, CEO da Cirion Technologies, em nota. "Nossa nova marca reflete tanto a força do nosso legado quanto a nossa ambição para o futuro", afirma o CEO da Datrix, Nelson Fonseca. "A Datrix dá a essa experiência um foco claro no que vem pela frente: o rápido crescimento da nuvem e da inteligência artificial na América Latina", complementa.

artigo.texto: Charge Power has been appointed to manage two Texas battery energy storage projects totalling 290MW/580MWh through commissioning and into commercial operation in 2027. The two projects comprise a 150MW/300MWh BESS and a 140MW/280MWh system, both connecting to the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) grid. Charge Power will act as an owner’s-side project partner rather than as battery supplier or EPC contractor. Its role will be to coordinate the engineering, procurement and construction contractors, project engineers, equipment suppliers, documentation and grid-connection requirements needed to take both projects from late-stage construction through commissioning to commercial operation date, or COD. COD is the point at which a project has completed the required testing and contractual milestones and can begin normal commercial operation and earn revenue. For projects in ERCOT, the process also involves completing the grid operator’s interconnection and commissioning requirements before the asset can participate fully in the Texas electricity market. Both projects will also use the WARAM platform for project governance, due diligence and compliance. Charge Power said the software is intended to link physical asset requirements with the documentation and evidence needed to demonstrate that those requirements have been met throughout ownership, certification and eventual asset transfer. Founder and president Ravi Pinnelli said: “Texas is one of the most demanding storage markets in the country, and the stretch between construction and commercial operation is where a project either protects its returns or loses them. “We approach every project with an owner-operator mindset, so on these projects our decisions prioritize schedule, revenue, and long-term performance the way the owner would. “Through shifting markets and an evolving energy landscape, our goal is to deliver execution certainty from day one to COD and beyond.” Charge Power said it has commissioned 3GW/7GWh of energy storage since the company was founded in 2022. The company works across US electricity markets including ERCOT, CAISO, MISO and PJM, as well as projects in Canada, India, Japan and the UK. Battery storage deployment has grown rapidly in Texas as developers seek to capture low-cost electricity during periods of abundant generation and discharge it during higher-priced periods of demand. Charge Power cited Modo Energy figures showing ERCOT battery capacity reached 16.5GW/28.8GWh by the end of June 2026, following rapid annual growth since 2020. BESTmag has previously reported on a number of large Texas projects, including Eolian’s 400MW/1.8GWh Padua BESS complex and Energy Vault’s 57MW/114MWh Cross Trails system. The chemistry and equipment suppliers for Charge Power’s two newly awarded projects were not disclosed. Photo: Charge Power’s 240MW/480MWh Anole BESS in Texas. The image illustrates the company’s growing ERCOT project portfolio but is not one of the two newly announced 290MW/580MWh projects. Credit: Charge Power.

artigo.texto: Ford Motor (NYSE:F) has commenced production of low-cost battery cells at a new plant in Michigan, US, using technology licensed from Contemporary Amperex Technology (CATL) (HKG:3750). The cells are made with a lithium-iron-phosphate (LFP) chemistry and are being shipped to a plant in Louisville, Kentucky, to be used for the company’s forthcoming Fathom midsize electric truck. Ford’s Vice President of advanced development projects Alan Clarke has spoken to the media about the use of CATL battery technology, noting that it is the fastest way for the company to build affordable electric vehicles (EVs) in the US. “CATL being the biggest in the world, it means that they’re the best supplier to get us that technology and help us learn how to produce LFP cells,” Clarke says. The move has drawn criticism from the US Government, with Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy saying in September that the agency was “deeply alarmed” by the company’s use of licensed technology from CATL. As previously reported, LFP batteries are gaining global momentum due to their long-life attributes, low cost, and high-safety characteristics. In 2025, LFP batteries accounted for over 55% of all EV batteries globally, up from nearly 50% in 2024. Unlike nickel-manganese-cobalt chemistries, LFP batteries rely on lithium carbonate rather than hydroxide. The chemistry has traditionally been concentrated in China and is popular in more urban markets rather than for longer-range vehicles. While LFP usage is not as widespread in the US, more than 50 gigawatt-hours of battery manufacturing capacity was redirected towards LFP production in 2025, across several companies including Ford and LG Energy Solution. Ford Motor’s Fathom is expected to launch in early 2027, joining the Mustang Mach-E in the company’s line of consumer EVs. As recently reported at Benchmark Week 2026 in Shanghai, CATL is focused on industry collaboration and sharing its expertise through global partnerships. As US automakers balance geopolitical pushback against the need for affordable EVs, licensing established LFP technology highlights how global partnerships remain central to scaling North America’s battery manufacturing and EV industry. Write to Amy Rotman at Mining.com.au Main image: Ford Motor

artigo.texto: In the electric vehicle (EV) battery market, where Korean batteries are under pressure, they have yet to find a breakthrough for a turnaround. As the rise of "Made in China" batteries continues, voices are growing that a counteroffensive must be launched centered on new product lineups such as mid-nickel, lithium manganese-rich (LMR), and all-solid-state batteries. According to battery industry sources and Samsung Securities on Tuesday, CATL's share of Hyundai Motor Group's EV sales was 29% as of September last year. This figure represents a 16 percentage point (p) increase compared to the same period last year. In contrast, during the same period, SK On's share decreased from 52% to 38%, and LG Energy Solution's share fell from 32% to 30%. A similar trend is observed among other automakers. Currently, within the Volkswagen Group, Korean battery makers hold a 53% market share, while Chinese firms account for approximately 45%, according to analysis. The Volkswagen Group, which had used almost 100% Korean batteries, newly adopted CATL batteries in the first half of 2024. In less than three years since then, the market share of Chinese batteries has closed in on that of K-batteries. Jo Hyeon-ryeol, a researcher at Samsung Securities, explained, "With China's Gotion also entering the Volkswagen Group's supply chain this year, it is expected that K-batteries will cede the lead to Chinese firms by 2027." He added, "Similarly, as Hyundai Motor Group has fully launched new vehicles equipped with lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries—an area where China holds an advantage—the market share of Chinese companies is likely to expand further." K-batteries are aiming to increase sales of EV batteries in the United States, where a "No China Zone" has been established, but this too is proving difficult. This is due to the shrinking front-end market resulting from the second Trump administration's abolition of EV purchase subsidies. Through the third quarter last year, GM's EV sales were approximately 214,000 units, and Ford's were about 221,000 units, representing year-on-year declines of 15.6% and 4.4%, respectively. Both companies are experiencing their first negative growth trend since 2020. Domestic battery majors such as LG Energy Solution, Samsung SDI, and SK On have adopted a strategy of weathering the EV market downturn by expanding sales of batteries for energy storage systems (ESS). However, as the strength of Chinese firms led by LFP becomes more pronounced year by year, there are concerns that K-batteries may lose their lead in the EV battery market, which is considered the industry's "main battlefield." CATL and others are leveraging cost competitiveness to target not only the LFP segment, where they have shown superiority, but also the ternary cathode market, which has been a stronghold for K-batteries. For K-batteries, it is urgent to regroup and secure market share in the EV battery sector. LG Energy Solution is increasing sales of high-voltage mid-nickel batteries, a mid-to-low-priced product that can serve as a check against Chinese-made LFP, centered on its Poland plant. LMR, which offers higher energy density at a price similar to LFP, is also considered a promising candidate. LG Energy Solution is pushing for the production of next-generation LMR prismatic batteries through Ultium Cells, its joint venture with GM. Whether all-solid-state batteries can emerge as a "game changer" is also a key issue. In the development of all-solid-state batteries, known as the "dream battery" for maximizing performance and safety through solid electrolytes, Samsung SDI is assessed to be in the lead. The company's goal is to mass-produce all-solid-state batteries within next year and apply them to EVs following their use in humanoid robots. A battery industry official said, "Even if we perform well in the ESS market, ceding the EV market to China would inevitably result in a significant blow." He added, "We must be able to create a turning point in the EV battery market next year."

artigo.texto: Essa informação foi compartilhada pelo Sr. Bui Duc Hieu, Diretor Adjunto do Departamento de Mudanças Climáticas, com a imprensa em um evento de lançamento online realizado à margem da 31ª Conferência das Partes da Convenção-Quadro das Nações Unidas sobre Mudança do Clima (COP31), em Antalya, Turquia, no dia 13 de novembro. Segundo ele, o desenvolvimento de um mercado de carbono é uma das soluções para apoiar a implementação dos compromissos nacionais de resposta às mudanças climáticas, especialmente a meta de alcançar emissões líquidas zero até 2050. “Constatamos que um mercado de carbono não é apenas uma ferramenta para gerenciar emissões, mas também precisa criar incentivos para que as empresas inovem em tecnologia, melhorem a eficiência energética e invistam em soluções de redução de emissões”, afirmou o Sr. Hieu. No contexto da implementação acelerada do Acordo de Paris sobre mudanças climáticas em todo o mundo , os mercados de carbono estão se tornando uma ferramenta política crucial para promover a redução das emissões de gases de efeito estufa, mobilizar recursos para transições verdes e apoiar o cumprimento dos compromissos internacionais. De acordo com representantes do Departamento de Mudanças Climáticas, o Vietnã encontra-se atualmente nos estágios iniciais de implementação de um sistema de comércio de emissões de gases de efeito estufa. Portanto, é necessário buscar recomendações e experiências de outros países e parceiros internacionais em relação à gestão, monitoramento e operação dos mercados de carbono para atingir a meta de operação oficial do mercado até 2029. O Vietnã fez progressos significativos no aperfeiçoamento de sua estrutura institucional e na construção da infraestrutura para seu mercado de carbono. 2026 também marca uma transição crucial do desenvolvimento de políticas para a implementação prática. Até o momento, o Vietnã alocou cotas de emissão de gases de efeito estufa para 110 instalações nos setores de energia térmica, siderurgia e cimento para o período de 2025-2026 e colocou em operação o Sistema Nacional de Registro de Cotas de Emissão de Gases de Efeito Estufa e Créditos de Carbono. Notavelmente, a bolsa de carbono doméstica foi oficialmente lançada em 29 de junho na Bolsa de Valores de Hanói . No entanto, estabelecer um novo quadro legal e infraestrutura técnica é apenas o começo. De acordo com o vice-diretor Bui Duc Hieu, durante a fase piloto, o Vietnã precisa continuar aprimorando o sistema de medição, reporte e avaliação das emissões de gases de efeito estufa, além de garantir a coordenação sincronizada entre os órgãos de gestão e os operadores de mercado, e fortalecer a capacidade e a prontidão das empresas para participar. Esses são os requisitos que precisam ser atendidos para que o mercado de carbono se torne, de fato, uma ferramenta eficaz para promover a redução das emissões de gases de efeito estufa. Ao elogiar o progresso do Vietnã na tradução do compromisso em ação, John Robert Cotton, Diretor da Parceria para a Transição Energética do Sudeste Asiático (ETP), afirmou que poucos países conseguem fazer a transição de um arcabouço legal para a operação de um mercado de carbono obrigatório em tão pouco tempo quanto o Vietnã. Enfatizando a importância da precificação do carbono para incorporar os custos de emissão aos balanços patrimoniais das empresas, Cotton disse que, a partir de 2029, quando o mecanismo de leilão de cotas começar a ser implementado, o mercado gerará receita para o orçamento do Estado, que poderá então ser reinvestida em atividades de redução de emissões na indústria. Segundo ele, "gargalos" semelhantes que dificultam o funcionamento do mercado também estão sendo encontrados em muitos outros países da região. "Nas Filipinas , a ETP está auxiliando o Ministério das Finanças na realização de uma revisão jurídica dos instrumentos de precificação de carbono. Na Indonésia, estamos trabalhando com o Ministério do Comércio e o Ministério da Indústria para avaliar o impacto das exportações de ferro e aço, cimento, alumínio e fertilizantes nos mecanismos tributários internacionais", afirmou. Reconhecendo o progresso significativo do Vietnã no desenvolvimento de seu mercado de carbono, a Sra. Leticia Guimarães, Chefe da Unidade de Mercado Global de Carbono do PNUD Vietnã, enfatizou: “O Vietnã estabeleceu uma estrutura legal clara e robusta para seu mercado de carbono. O lançamento da Bolsa em junho reafirmou sua posição como um dos países pioneiros na região da ASEAN. Também estamos muito satisfeitos com o lançamento do Portal de Informações de Mercado, que ajuda a divulgar informações importantes, lançando as bases para que as partes interessadas e os investidores tenham confiança nas próximas etapas.”

artigo.texto: Com atuação da alta à baixa tensão, passando pelas disciplinas de hidráulica e combate a incêndio, o Grupo Planem oferece soluções de engenharia de ponta a ponta para um dos maiores hyperscalers (empresas que oferecem serviços em grande escala) do mundo. O projeto, ainda em sigilo, será o primeiro campus de data centers da empresa no Brasil. O escopo cobre todo o ciclo de energia a partir do ponto de entrega da concessionária, incluindo a subestação turn-key de 138 kV/34,5 kV, a distribuição em média e baixa tensão, além das subestações abaixadoras. A atuação também contempla os sistemas hidráulicos e de combate a incêndio, além da interface técnica com a concessionária. Ao concentrar disciplinas sensíveis sob responsabilidade única, o Grupo Planem minimiza riscos de integração e fortalece a confiabilidade do conjunto. A complexidade da obra exige coordenação precisa. Além disso, os prazos impõem um desafio adicional, pois demandam frentes de trabalho simultâneas e lideranças dedicadas ao planejamento e à logística — itens fundamentais para esse desafio. Outro ponto, não menos importante, é o apagão de mão de obra que o país vem enfrentando. O Grupo Planem já atua há algum tempo com estratégias para reter e qualificar suas equipes, com remuneração acima do mercado, o que tem a ajudado a vencer desafios com prazos curtos. BIM, Primavera P6, scanner 3D, registros georreferenciados, checklists eletrônicos e inspeções técnicas de processos apoiam a precisão, a produtividade e a rastreabilidade dos serviços. O comissionamento, com testes FAT, SAT e IST, validam o desempenho conjunto dos sistemas em condições reais e cenários de falha. Com essa combinação de integração técnica, planejamento, tecnologia e controle, o projeto evidencia o know-how do Grupo Planem para atuar em data centers e outros empreendimentos de infraestrutura crítica, nos quais confiabilidade e execução disciplinada são requisitos essenciais.

artigo.texto: Two days of training end with a diploma reception. Companies eager to hire the new graduates have come ready to hand out jobs that can pay more than $100,000 a year. Welcome to the data center economy. In the race to build out America’s AI infrastructure, tech companies are struggling to find technicians with sufficient skills to install the cooling, server racks, electrical equipment and fiberoptic cables necessary to meet the off-the-charts demand for the revolutionary technology. Even as AI politics have shifted – particularly after recent midterm election – the lack of available labor to build continuing data center projects would almost certainly trump any potential construction slowdown. So the industry is going to extraordinary lengths to teach and hire people to fill those crucial jobs. Several nonprofits, online learning companies and all four of the big AI hyperscalers — Amazon, Google, Meta and Microsoft — offer various forms of free, accelerated training courses for the technical skills needed to build out data centers. Some of those positions can pay six-figure salaries. And many Americans don’t even know these jobs exist. Graduation on Friday. Orientation on Monday Javonntae Hill studied video game design. He’s in his early 30s and he was looking for a career — but didn’t quite know where to start. His girlfriend saw an advertisement for America’s Workforce Academy, a new training program Meta kicked off in August to help fill the labor skills gap. The company was willing to pay him during his four-week training and guaranteed him placement in a data center job after he received his diploma. Hill figured he’d give it a shot. Over the course of a month, in a classroom of 30 people, he got thrown into a mix of lectures and hands-on training, learning about how to place and run fiberoptic and copper cables and what each cable insulator color specifies. He was nervous: He hoped he could retain all that information for his new job. “Graduation was on Friday,” Hill said. “I started orientation on Monday.” Meta partnered with Associated Builders and Contractors, a construction industry trade group that has been training workers for decades. Unlike traditional training methods, including trade school or an apprenticeship, ABC’s accelerated courses aren’t designed to be comprehensive; they’re designed to get as many people working in data centers as possible. “It’s like the military,” said Joel Thames, head of ABC’s safety and workforce group. “Does boot camp get them trained for any scenario? No. But it gives them a foundational education before they spend time on the job site.” Hill said his nerves were unfounded: He showed up to the Ohio job site overprepared. And grateful. “I could do this for the rest of my life,” Hill said. “I’ve seen postings of jobs available, but I have a lot of loyalty toward Meta.” The problem Despite growing public opposition and a wave of new lawmakers pledging to regulate their expansion, data center construction is virtually unstoppable. AI infrastructure spending is expected to approach $1 trillion a year, annually for the foreseeable future, according to Columbia Business School economist Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh. But construction faces many logistical hurdles, including building permits, power guarantees, materials and financing. Even the deepest-pocketed AI companies that can overcome those obstacles are encountering a consistent roadblock: America has far too few qualified people to build data centers — particularly in some of the remote or rural locations where they’re being built. The United States has a shortage of 1 million engineers needed to meet data center construction estimates, PwC estimates. Many otherwise ready-to-go sites have been delayed for months while they assemble a qualified crew to build them. Only about half of the AI computing capacity scheduled to come online between now and 2028 is actually expected to meet its target date, according to Goldman Sachs. That’s a costly wait: For large AI data centers, a month of delay can cost anywhere from the low tens of millions to well over $100 million, depending on location, scale and contract terms, said Mona Dajani, co-chair of Cooley’s infrastructure, energy and real estate practice. So AI companies are addressing the challenge by ditching requirements for multi-year trade school courses or apprenticeships in favor of accelerated, high-intensity courses designed specifically for data center construction jobs. Many are offering the courses for free. A growing number will even pay learners to take the courses. Classes can run from 15 weeks to just two days, depending on the job. Desperation for labor is so high that AI companies are placing some top graduates on the job the day after they gain their certifications. ‘I had nothing to lose’ Robert Burgess had been bouncing around construction jobs in and around Canton, Mississippi. He knew how to do some low-voltage electrical work and had heard that he could make a lot more money cutting fiber for a telecom or a data center site. Burgess Googled “internet fiber training Mississippi” and a four-week Amazon training program called I2PA (Information Infrastructure Pre-Apprenticeship) surfaced at a local community college. “I had nothing to lose,” Burgess said. “I put in my email, and I got accepted.” Over the course of the training, Burgess learned how electricity is generated and delivered, how servers are installed and how they fit into a data center. Amazon trainers set up a mock data center so that Burgess and his classmates could get hands-on training. At the end: a job fair. Burgess got a job from Yates Construction and Turner Construction, which were partnering on the tail end of a data center construction site in the area. That was in 2024. artigo.texto: MARSHALL, Mich. — Ford Motor has started producing battery cells in the U.S. for its next generation of electric vehicles using technologies licensed by Chinese battery giant CATL. The automaker said Wednesday that cell production at a $3 billion plant in Marshall, Michigan — roughly 100 miles west of Detroit — started last month and the cells are now shipping out. They'll be used in prototypes for its Fathom small electric pickup truck, which CEO Jim Farley has touted as rivaling Tesla and Chinese competitors. The production marks a milestone for the Detroit automaker and is the next step toward using lower-cost lithium iron phosphate, or LFP, battery cells in U.S. vehicles. The technology was created in the U.S. but commercialized largely in China. The automaker's decision to make the batteries at the roughly 2 million-square-foot facility has been criticized by some lawmakers and U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy over Ford's ties to CATL. Alan Clarke, Ford's vice president of advanced development projects, said licensing the technology from CATL helped the automaker bring the low-cost battery chemistry to the U.S. as quickly as possible. "If we want to get to being able to produce affordable EVs in the United States, we need to also do it the fastest way possible," Clarke said Tuesday during a tour of the facility. "CATL being the biggest in the world means that they're the best supplier to get us that technology and help us learn ourselves how to produce LFP cells." The U.S. government has increased scrutiny of Chinese ties with U.S. companies even as President Donald Trump is meeting this week with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. In September, Duffy sent a letter to Farley expressing "profound concern" about Ford's ties to Chinese companies that it believes could be detrimental to the Detroit carmaker and the U.S. automotive industry. The White House a day later followed up by commending the automaker for its domestic jobs and manufacturing. Ford — the largest producer of U.S. vehicles — has routinely touted its American roots, jobs and manufacturing, especially as the Biden and Trump administrations have pushed to onshore and grow U.S. production. Ford's battery plant in Marshall is expected to be capable of producing 40 battery cells a minute, equating to 20 gigawatt-hours annually for EVs and the company's energy storage business. That's down from initial plans of up to 40 gigawatt-hours annually amid an EV pullback by the automaker and broader industry. Ford has said the production pace will help reduce battery costs and that the facility has room for additional capacity if needed. The facility is highly automated, but Ford said it's still in the early stages of certifying its processes, as it plans to ramp up cell production next year before the expected launch of the Fathom pickup during the fourth quarter of 2027.

artigo.texto: O governo dos Estados Unidos emitiu uma norma nesta segunda-feira, 16, que deve dificultar a aquisição de chips de Inteligência Artificial (IA) por empresas de data centers sediadas em cinco países, entre eles o Brasil. A norma publicada pelo Departamento de Comércio não proíbe a compra de chips. Contudo, estabelece que Brasil, Indonésia, Malásia, Singapura e Tailândia deverão obter, além das exigências de licenciamento atualmente em vigor para semicondutores avançados, uma licença adicional para exportação, reexportação ou transferência de chips de alta capacidade. Embora tenha listado cinco países, o governo de Donald Trump busca, na prática, atingir a China com a medida. A ideia é dificultar que empresas chinesas utilizem data centers em outros países para processar demandas de alta capacidade computacional usando tecnologia norte-americana. Conforme a norma, o Brasil e as demais nações são classificados pelo governo dos Estados Unidos como "países que apresentam um risco de desvio superior ao normal". Nesse sentido, a medida afirma que data centers que forneçam um volume significativo de poder computacional a empresas sediadas na China ou em países do chamado grupo D:5 (mercados sujeitos a embargos de armas dos Estados Unidos) deverão obter uma licença no prazo de 90 dias, sob pena de enfrentar futuras restrições à exportação. De acordo com a medida, a exigência de licença não alcança semicondutores destinados a empresas sediadas nos Estados Unidos ou cuja controladora final esteja sediada no território norte-americano. "A norma visa a garantir que as restrições já existentes ao acesso a tecnologias norte-americanas sensíveis não possam ser contornadas por meio de arranjos de computação remota que envolvam data centers em países terceiros", afirma o Departamento de Comércio, em comunicado. A nota oficial ainda afirma que os Estados Unidos "estão empenhados em promover a adoção global de tecnologia norte-americana para fins comerciais legítimos". Sendo assim, o governo busca atuar para que "tecnologias sensíveis não sejam exploradas por meios que ameacem a segurança nacional dos Estados Unidos". Pontos de atenção Em comunicado, a Associação Brasileira das Empresas de Software (Abes) afirma que "acompanha com atenção" a medida anunciada pelo governo norte-americano. A entidade destacou que a norma, enquanto representa uma nova camada de compliance para subsidiárias de empresas sediadas nos Estados Unidos, gera uma "assimetria competitiva" para provedores de nuvem e data centers de capital nacional, por exigir autorizações analisadas caso a caso. Além disso, para a Abes, a inclusão do Brasil em uma lista restritiva pode dificultar a atração de novos investimentos internacionais ao setor de infraestrutura digital brasileiro. Desse modo, a associação defende uma atuação coordenada entre o governo brasileiro e o setor produtivo junto aos Estados Unidos. "Essa atuação deve ter uma agenda objetiva de cooperação em controle de exportações, que demonstre a solidez institucional do Brasil e preserve a fluidez das cadeias globais de suprimentos tecnológicos", ressalta a entidade.

artigo.texto: 17/11/2026 - 13:00 As restrições dos Estados Unidos à exportação de chips de inteligência artificial podem atrasar projetos de data centers no Brasil e adiar parte da demanda por equipamentos da WEG (WEGE3), avalia o Bradesco BBI. O banco considera a notícia negativa para a fabricante de motores e equipamentos, mas mantém suas projeções, a recomendação equivalente à compra e o preço-alvo de R$ 62 por ação. A dimensão do impacto ainda é incerta e dependerá das características de cada projeto. Restrições a chips podem adiar investimentos em data centers Desde 16 de novembro, fornecedores precisam de autorização do governo americano para exportar ao Brasil determinados processadores utilizados em data centers. As exigências alcançam componentes fabricados fora dos Estados Unidos quando desenvolvidos com tecnologia americana. O objetivo de Washington é impedir que empresas chinesas utilizem operações em outros países para contornar as restrições tecnológicas impostas à China. A regulamentação do Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) citada na análise classifica Brasil, Singapura, Tailândia, Malásia e Indonésia como países com risco acima do normal de desvio ilegal desses componentes para China e Macau. Para o BBI, as exigências podem desacelerar a implantação de projetos no momento em que o governo brasileiro tenta atrair investimentos por meio do programa ReData. Como a WEG fornece equipamentos para esse mercado, eventuais adiamentos poderiam postergar encomendas. O banco ressalta que as regras não representam uma proibição total das exportações para o Brasil. Há exceções para operações ligadas a empresas americanas. O efeito dependerá da estrutura societária dos projetos, dos usuários finais dos chips e das aplicações pretendidas. Dados da Abinee, citados pelo BBI, mostram que as importações brasileiras de semicondutores atingiram US$ 6,8 bilhões entre janeiro e setembro, avanço de 51% na comparação anual. JPMorgan eleva preço-alvo da WEG para R$ 66 Em sua análise sobre a companhia, o JPMorgan reiterou a recomendação overweight, equivalente à compra, e elevou o preço-alvo da WEG de R$ 56 para R$ 66 ao fim de 2027. O novo valor representa um potencial de valorização de aproximadamente 30% em relação aos níveis considerados no relatório. A expectativa do banco é de aceleração do crescimento, sustentada principalmente pelos negócios de transformadores, sistemas de armazenamento de energia por baterias (BESS) e motores elétricos. Exposição internacional favorece a WEG com real mais fraco O JPMorgan destaca a proteção natural da companhia diante da desvalorização do real. Mais de 60% das receitas da WEG são geradas fora do Brasil, com cerca de 30% provenientes da América do Norte. Pelos cálculos do banco, cada depreciação de 5% do real acrescenta aproximadamente 4% ao EBITDA projetado da empresa. Após incorporar um cenário de câmbio mais depreciado, o JPMorgan elevou em 6% sua estimativa de EBITDA para 2027. A projeção passou a considerar crescimento de 27% nessa linha. O banco prevê receitas e lucro líquido acima do consenso de mercado em 2027 e 2028. Banco vê desconto nos múltiplos de WEGE3 Na avaliação do JPMorgan, a ação da WEG negocia a múltiplos atrativos, com desconto de aproximadamente 15% em relação à média histórica do período pós-pandemia. Os analistas argumentam que a companhia tende a se beneficiar da exposição ao dólar e da menor dependência do ciclo econômico brasileiro. Esses atributos, associados à percepção de qualidade da empresa, sustentam a visão favorável do banco para WEGE3. artigo.texto: The Commerce Department on Monday moved to close a loophole that has let Chinese companies lease Nvidia's advanced computing power from data centers in third countries, effectively circumventing controls on sensitive chip technology being exported to China. The interim final rule from Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security is the first U.S. policy response to the scandal that led Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to resign last week after reports that he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy who worked for Megaspeed, one of Nvidia's biggest Asian customers. The rule was "written by and at the direction of" the Treasury Department and the White House National Security Council, BIS said in a press release. The rule came after growing criticism of Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick for not doing enough to prevent possible diversion of Nvidia's most advanced chips to China in violation of American export controls. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, in an interview on Friday with CNBC's "Squawk Box," blamed the Commerce Department for not putting Singapore-based Megaspeed on its "entity list," which would restrict certain exports to it. Share prices of Nvidia and other companies linked to the artificial intelligence trade fell Monday morning after the interim rule was announced, among them chipmakers Micron Technology, Intel and Advanced Micro Devices. The rule is designed "to prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on U.S. technology to threaten U.S. national security and foreign policy interests," according to the text of the rule. The new restrictions "will undermine the ability of companies headquartered in countries of concern from using" advanced artificial intelligence semiconductors produced by U.S. companies to train advanced AI models, the rule says. The rule also says that a license will now "be required to export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil (and any additional country designated by the Secretary of Commerce, in consultation with the Secretary of State or the Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs) – countries which present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion." The New York Times reported on Nov. 9 that American authorities began investigating Singapore-based Megaspeed and one of its executives, Alice Huang, in 2024, "after the company started importing billions of dollars' worth of advanced Nvidia A.I. equipment into Malaysia." "Megaspeed had been planning and constructing data centers around Southeast Asia to serve Chinese clients, including Alibaba, the Chinese tech giant," The Times reported that day. "While that behavior is legal, U.S. officials were concerned that some of the Nvidia chips the company had bought were illegally routed into China." Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO last week after reports that he had an affair with Alice Huang, and that she was a spy working for China. The two are not related. China's government has denied the claim that Alice Huang was a spy. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who, as national security advisor, leads the National Security Council, warned President Donald Trump last spring that Jensen Huang was in a close relationship with Alice Huang, The Times has reported. Rep. John Mooelnaar, the Michigan Republican who is chairman of the House Select Committee on China, in a statement on the new rule that it "sends a message to the Chinese Communist Party that America is serious about closing dangerous export control loopholes China has been exploiting for years." "Our most advanced AI chips are simply not for sale to our foremost enemy," Moolenaar said. "This new rule is an important step in keeping chips out of ill-intentioned hands, strengthens our national security laws, and will help protect America's lead in the AI race." Chris McGuire, a former deputy senior director for technology and national security at the National Security Council, in a post on X called the new rule "a major step forward to countering Chinese smuggling of and access to advanced AI chips." "The work here is not done, as there are some critical loopholes that remain open and need to be closed in a follow-up rule (namely those related to activities inside the United States)," wrote McGuire, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations. "Commerce should move extremely quickly to close these. But this is the first time in over 18 months that the administration is starting to take export controls seriously, and does represent a meaningful step forward." McGuire said that the fact that the new rule was written by and at the direction of the Treasury Department and the NSC "is remarkable and unprecedented." "I have never seen a BIS rule that was not written by BIS," he wrote. "That implies that Commerce was dragged kicking and screaming over the finish line by the White House and Treasury, and instructed to publish this rule rather than the rumored weaker one that it preferred. Remarkable." Commerce's new rule was published a day after Sen. Maria Cantwell of Washington state, the ranking Democrat on the Committee on Commerce, Science and Transportation, in a letter to Lutnick said that Chinese companies such as Alibaba and ByteDance have "used overseas data centers equipped with advanced Nvidia chips to train advanced AI models." "These companies are exploiting a loophole in U.S. export controls by using advanced American chips in foreign data centers even when those chips are restricted from the [People's Republic of China]," Cantwell wrote. "Despite warnings from the Bureau of Industry and Security that certain arrangements may violate existing restrictions, the Department of Commerce failed to close this loophole, allowing PRC companies to advance their AI capabilities using sensitive American technology," she wrote.

artigo.texto: From emission pricing to green investment incentives Within the framework of the 31st Conference of Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (COP31), Vietnam launched its Carbon Market Information Portal, marking another step forward in perfecting the infrastructure and operational mechanisms of the market. The public disclosure of information on policies, regulations, and trading activities is expected to facilitate access to the market for businesses and investors, while also promoting the mobilization of resources for emission reduction activities. Previously, on June 29, 2026, the Vietnam Carbon Exchange officially launched at the Hanoi Stock Exchange, along with the commissioning of the National Registration System for Greenhouse Gas Emission Quotas and Carbon Credits. The gradual completion of the market's components lays the foundation for transparent trading, establishes a carbon pricing mechanism, and encourages businesses to invest in emission reduction solutions. According to the plan, approximately 511 million tons of CO₂, equivalent to the approved emission quota, will be allocated on a pilot basis during the 2025-2026 period to 110 facilities in three sectors: thermal power, iron and steel production, and cement. These are all energy-intensive industries with a high demand for production line modernization and the adoption of emission reduction technologies. Including these facilities in the quota allocation mechanism not only increases their responsibility for emission control but also forces businesses to reassess the long-term effectiveness of their investments. According to Mr. Bui Duc Hieu, Deputy Director of the Climate Change Department, carbon credits are not only a tool for managing emissions but also an incentive for businesses to innovate technology, use energy efficiently, and invest in emission reduction solutions. However, for the market to play this role, perfecting the legal framework and technical infrastructure needs to go hand in hand with improving the quality of emission measurement, reporting, and assessment, as well as the capacity of businesses to participate. When emission costs are factored into production calculations, businesses have more incentive to innovate technologically, save energy, and improve investment efficiency. Units maintaining energy-intensive production lines may face increased compliance costs; while businesses that proactively improve processes and reduce emissions will have an advantage in cost control and production organization. This also encourages capital flows towards clean technology projects, efficient energy use, and sustainable production development. Furthermore, the carbon quota and credit trading mechanism opens up the possibility of generating additional revenue from emission reduction results that meet the conditions for recognition and transfer . Although this revenue depends on regulations, trading capacity, and market price fluctuations, the prospect of commercializing emission reduction results can become a factor for businesses to consider when developing investment plans. Through this, the carbon market gradually links environmental goals with economic benefits, creating further incentives for businesses to transform their production models towards low emissions. Market transparency to unlock capital flows. Along with the establishment of carbon pricing mechanisms, the ability to mobilize resources for emission reduction projects is becoming a matter of concern. The demand for investment in technological innovation, improved energy efficiency, and the use of clean fuels is growing, while many businesses still face difficulties in balancing capital, especially for projects with high initial costs and long payback periods. The development of the carbon market is therefore expected to create additional financial incentives, supporting businesses in implementing the green transition process. According to John Robert Cotton, Director of the Energy Transition Partnership (ETP) for Southeast Asia at UNOPS, very few countries have been able to transition from establishing a legal framework to operating a mandatory carbon market in such a short time as Vietnam. He believes that carbon pricing is crucial in incorporating emission costs into businesses' financial calculations, thereby creating incentives for investment in emission reduction. Notably, from 2029, when the quota auction mechanism is expected to be implemented, the market could generate additional budget revenue for reinvestment in emission reduction activities in industry. Besides domestic resources, international cooperation also opens opportunities to mobilize financing for green transition. Through cooperation mechanisms under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, projects that meet emission reduction requirements can access financing from the international carbon market. However, the ability to attract capital depends on the quality of the project, the transparency of emission reduction results, and compliance with transaction standards. While the carbon market opens up opportunities to mobilize resources, the ability to convert these opportunities into actual investment capital still depends on the financial efficiency of each project. From a credit perspective, Mr. Bui Minh Giap, Chief Economist of the Asian Development Bank (ADB) in Vietnam, said that Vietnam needs approximately US$368 billion in additional investment capital by 2040 to adapt to climate change, enhance resilience, and reduce emissions, equivalent to 6.8% of GDP per year. Specifically in the electricity sector, the investment needs for developing power sources and grids in the 2026-2030 period, according to the revised Power Development Plan VIII, are estimated at around US$136 billion. The large scale of capital indicates the need to mobilize diverse resources, with bank credit continuing to play a crucial role for green transformation projects. Mr. Bui Minh
