artigo.texto: Data centers: acordo entre Amazon e Blackstone abrange 13 prédios em Indiana e no Mississippi (Adobe Stock/Divulgação) Repórter de Inteligência Artificial e Tecnologia Publicado em 16 de novembro de 2026 às 10h10. Última atualização em 16 de novembro de 2026 às 10h11. A Amazon anunciou em 16 de novembro de 2026 a venda do controle de 13 prédios de data centers nos Estados Unidos, avaliados em US$ 5 bilhões, para a Blackstone Digital Infrastructure Trust (BXDC), veículo imobiliário administrado por uma afiliada da Blackstone. A Amazon Web Services (AWS) continuará ocupando todos os imóveis como inquilina, com contratos de prazo médio inicial de 12 anos, que podem chegar a 32 anos com as renovações, e reajuste de 2,75% ao ano. A Amazon receberá dinheiro e ficará com 24,9% das duas sociedades conjuntas que serão donas dos complexos, localizados em Indiana e no Mississippi, que somam 647 megawatts de capacidade. É o primeiro investimento da BXDC desde o IPO, em maio, e a conclusão está prevista para até o fim de 2026. O modelo lembra a sociedade fechada pela Meta com fundos da Blue Owl, em 2025, para o complexo Hyperion, na Louisiana. A Amazon vai passar de proprietária a sócia minoritária e inquilina de 13 prédios de data centers recém-construídos nos Estados Unidos. Em acordo anunciado nesta segunda-feira, 16, um veículo imobiliário administrado por uma afiliada da Blackstone comprará o controle das sociedades que ficarão com os imóveis, avaliados em US$ 5 bilhões. A Amazon Web Services (AWS), braço de computação em nuvem do grupo, vai alugar todos os prédios e continuar usando a infraestrutura. A operação dá à Amazon uma forma de levantar dinheiro com instalações que já construiu e manter a capacidade disponível para seus clientes. Em troca, a companhia assume aluguéis com prazo inicial médio de 12 anos. Se todas as opções de renovação forem exercidas, a média sobe para 32 anos. O reajuste previsto é de 2,75% ao ano, e a própria Amazon garante os pagamentos da subsidiária. Os US$ 5 bilhões correspondem à avaliação bruta dos dois complexos. Na conclusão da operação, a Amazon vai transferir os imóveis para duas sociedades conjuntas, uma para cada complexo, e receber dinheiro e uma fatia de 24,9% em cada uma. A Blackstone Digital Infrastructure Trust, negociada na Bolsa de Nova York sob o código BXDC, ficará com os outros 75,1%. O pagamento em dinheiro será financiado por duas fontes. A BXDC espera aportar US$ 1,9 bilhão em recursos levantados no IPO. Subsidiárias das sociedades conjuntas devem contratar cerca de US$ 2,5 bilhões em empréstimos hipotecários, garantidos pelos próprios imóveis. Como parte do financiamento também cobrirá custos da transação, a soma dessas duas fontes indica o volume de recursos mobilizados, e o valor líquido a ser recebido pela Amazon ainda depende dos termos do fechamento. É o primeiro investimento da BXDC desde a abertura de capital, em maio. A oferta inicial foi de US$ 1,75 bilhão e, depois que os bancos exerceram integralmente a opção de vender ações adicionais, a captação líquida chegou a cerca de US$ 1,9 bilhão. A conclusão da compra está prevista para até o fim de 2026, sujeita às condições do acordo. O acordo reúne nove prédios no norte de Indiana, no mercado de data centers da região de Chicago, e quatro no Mississippi. Juntos, eles somam 647 megawatts de capacidade elétrica para equipamentos de TI. O número indica a potência que a infraestrutura pode disponibilizar a equipamentos como servidores e sistemas de rede. Para a BXDC, a compra dá acesso a prédios novos com um contrato para ocupar 100% do portfólio. Para a AWS, a locação mantém disponíveis os imóveis de que a operação depende. O contrato segue o modelo conhecido como triple net, em que o inquilino arca, além do aluguel, com despesas como impostos imobiliários, seguro e manutenção. A aquisição foi precificada a uma taxa inicial de capitalização de 7%. O indicador relaciona a renda operacional anual dos imóveis ao valor atribuído a eles. Ele serve para avaliar o preço pago pelo portfólio. O retorno para o acionista da BXDC também depende do custo da dívida e das demais despesas da operação. A parceria permite à Amazon recuperar parte do capital investido nas instalações e continuar usando os prédios. O dinheiro entra no fechamento. Os aluguéis serão pagos ao longo dos anos, com reajuste anual. Para o investidor imobiliário, o atrativo é justamente o fluxo de pagamentos de uma única locatária, respaldado pela garantia da Amazon. Prasad Kalyanaraman, vice-presidente de infraestrutura da AWS, afirmou no comunicado que a parceria permite à empresa continuar ampliando sua operação à medida que cresce a demanda dos clientes. No terceiro trimestre, a receita da AWS cresceu 39%, para US$ 46 bilhões. A expansão exige investimentos em terrenos, energia e prédios, além dos chips e servidores instalados neles. O acordo com a Blackstone traz um investidor para a parte imobiliária dessa conta. A Meta recorreu a uma sociedade com fundos da Blue Owl em outubro de 2025 para desenvolver o complexo Hyperion, na Louisiana. Os fundos ficaram com 80%, e a Meta, com 20%. Os US$ 27 bilhões divulgados naquele acordo correspondem ao custo estimado de desenvolvimento, incluindo construção e infraestrutura de energia, refrigeração e conectividade. No caso da Amazon, os US$ 5 bilhões são a avaliação de imóveis já construídos, que a AWS continuará usando como inquilina. A AWS vai alugar todos os 13 prédios. A Amazon também manterá 24,9% das sociedades que serão donas dos imóveis. Os US$ 5 bilhões são o valor bruto atribuído aos dois complexos. Na conclusão do negócio, a Amazon receberá uma parcela em dinheiro e manterá uma participação minoritária nas sociedades. A BXDC espera concluir a transação até o fim de 2026. O fechamento depende das condições do acordo e do financiamento previsto. artigo.texto: Ascenty constrói data center de IA em Sumaré Projeto tem cliente âncora contratado; companhia mantém três unidades em construção e quatro em expansão no Brasil. A Ascenty está construindo em Sumaré, no interior de São Paulo, um data center dedicado à inteligência artificial, com capacidade inicial de 60 megawatts (MW) para equipamentos de TI e 90 MW de potência total. O empreendimento, chamado Sumaré 3, já tem um cliente âncora contratado, segundo Rodrigo Radaieski, CTO da companhia, em entrevista ao TV.Síntese. O vídeo vai ao ar hoje, às 19h. “É um hyperscale”, afirmou. Segundo o executivo, as bases e os pilares da construção já foram executados. A previsão é disponibilizar a primeira fase em setembro de 2027. O projeto faz parte da expansão da empresa no Brasil, dona de 21 data centers em operação, três em construção e quatro em expansão. Na América Latina, a companhia contabiliza 26 unidades operacionais e um total de 40 ao incluir os empreendimentos em construção e desenvolvimento. Expansão concentrada em São Paulo As obras de expansão no Brasil estão concentradas em São Paulo. Segundo o CTO, a localização atende à demanda dos clientes e à necessidade de reduzir a latência, ou seja, o tempo de comunicação entre os dispositivos dos usuários e os data centers. O executivo afirma que essa proximidade também importa para aplicações de inteligência artificial. A empresa mantém unidades no Rio de Janeiro e em Fortaleza. Radaieski também conta das negociações para novos projetos, que atribuiu ao avanço do Redata, regime de incentivos ao setor. “O Redata acelerou bastante o mercado, então tem muitas discussões, a gente deve fazer anúncios em breve”, disse. No caso de Sumaré 3, a intenção é solicitar o enquadramento no regime após a regulamentação. Além daquela projeto, a Ascenty está adaptando instalações existentes para receber cargas de maior densidade. “Só no ano de 2025 nós fizemos 400 ações dentro dos data centers para buscar essa eficiência energética”, afirmou. Entre os exemplos citados estão ajustes de temperatura, posicionamento de grelhas e circulação do ar. Rede de fibra integra a estratégia A expansão dos data centers é acompanhada pela infraestrutura própria de conectividade. Segundo o CTO, a Ascenty possui 4 mil quilômetros de fibra óptica, somando as redes no Brasil e no México. Essa infraestrutura conecta unidades da empresa, data centers de outros operadores e estações de chegada de cabos submarinos. No Brasil, a rede própria tem conexões em São Paulo, incluindo Praia Grande, no Rio de Janeiro e em Fortaleza. A rede atende tanto clientes corporativos que contratam links quanto empresas que demandam fibras apagadas, dedicadas à conexão entre instalações. Segundo o executivo, os hyperscalers contratam grandes quantidades dessas fibras para interligar data centers, replicar dados e manter redundância. Ele diz que o ativo é estratégico e não há nenhum plano de spin off dele.

artigo.texto: HADLEY — Lightning Hill is the name generations of Hadley residents have given to the peak of Breckenridge Road, where a gravel pit could soon become the location of a stand-alone battery energy storage system. “It is incredibly prone to lightning strikes,” said Linda Hannum, of Sylvia Heights. For residents who have organized to halt the placement of a 5-megawatt facility in the 5-acre site above Zatyrka Park, where there is a playground, gazebo and walking trails, the fact that lightning regularly splits trees and tears off bark makes the location above the town’s aquifer unsuitable for this project. On Thursday, nearly 30 people went to the Hadley Senior Center dining room, joined by another dozen or more attending virtually, to appeal to the Board of Health to take a stand against the development. They contend that the Board of Health could intervene after the Planning Board last month approved site plans, a solar project special permit and a business use in aquifer special permit for ZP Battery Devco’s 5-megawatt system. The meeting came two nights after the Conservation Commission voted 3-0 against the project. Commission members cautioned that they typically only weigh in on matters when wetlands are involved but still determined the project likely wasn’t appropriate for the neighborhood. “We are asking for you to join the Conservation Commission in opposing this project outright,” Hannum said. Planners had initially rejected the development in January 2025, concerned with potential impacts on the aquifer and public safety should there be a fire or leaks, before facing a lawsuit in Hampshire Superior Court in which the company argued the board’s decision was legally untenable and “unreasonable, arbitrary and capricious.” The Lightning Hill nickname for the top of Breckenridge Road, along with the gravel pit remaining an active site with unstable material at its base, are among neighbors’ many objections to the development. Since the agenda only called for public comment on the project, the Board of Health made no decision and took no action on the request. Neither the developer nor the landowner, Karl’s Excavating, was present to rebut any of the information presented. Hannum said she understands that the health board will likely have to prove there is a risk to the aquifer. Her hope is that the information residents provided, supplemented with photographic evidence from the site and pictures of a similar development that caught on fire and burned in Warwick, New York, will be sufficient. Members of the group organizing opposition, though, said they understand this is only a starting point. The aquifer is the big concern for Carol Soules of Sylvia Heights. Soules said the porous soil and fragile and unstable embankments should have necessitated a hydrogeologic study, which was not required for the proposal to proceed. “I feel like there are risks to [the] health and safety of residents,” Soules said. “The developer should find a safer place.” There are potential noise concerns, too. Donna Kurkul of Frallo Drive said residents below the gravel pit can already hear everything that happens there, and the battery noise will be excessive. Gail Mengel of Sylvia Heights said that a catastrophe could happen, and it’s unclear if the town has the resources to handle an emergency, whether a fire or a leak. Greg Owen of Breckenridge Road said the town should mitigate the threat and plan for the worst-case scenarios, adding that the best hazard prevention would be to prohibit such a development altogether. Others suggested that the project would be more appropriate along Route 9, where there are already areas paved over and fewer residential homes. Kristi Nelson of Sylvia Heights said that those concerned with the development are green energy advocates who understand the need to support solar and battery energy storage, but harming drinking water is not a good trade-off. “We feel very strongly it should not be in this location,” Nelson said.

artigo.texto: Pela regra, os operadores de data centers nos cinco países vão precisar de autorização do governo americano para comprar chips de IA avançados da Nvidia e de outros fabricantes americanos. O objetivo é impedir que a China e outros adversários dos EUA usem capacidade computacional instalada fora do país e baseada em processadores projetados nos Estados Unidos. “A regra foi elaborada para garantir que as restrições existentes ao acesso à tecnologia americana sensível não possam ser contornadas por meio de acordos de computação remota que envolvam data centers em terceiros países”, afirmou o departamento em comunicado. Segundo o órgão, os avanços na computação em nuvem tornaram cada vez mais viável acessar remotamente os sistemas americanos de IA. A nova regra busca alinhar esse tipo de acesso às normas que já valem para o acesso físico à tecnologia. As ações da Nvidia chegaram a cair 2,9% nesta segunda-feira, e o índice de semicondutores da Filadélfia recuou até 5,5% Como a regra afeta o Brasil e os outros países da lista Os pedidos de licença serão analisados caso a caso. Empresas com sede nos EUA que operam nos cinco países ficam de fora da exigência e podem continuar enviando chips de IA para lá sem licença. A isenção também vale para data centers usados em sistemas de recomendação de varejistas online e redes sociais. O texto divulgado na segunda-feira prevê que as novas exigências entram em vigor quando a regra for publicada no Federal Register, o diário oficial do governo americano. Escândalo na Nvidia pressiona o Departamento de Comércio A regra saiu dias depois de Jensen Huang deixar o cargo de CEO da Nvidia. Ele admitiu ter tido um caso com Alice Huang, ex-executiva da Megaspeed International, empresa com sede em Singapura. Os EUA suspeitam que Alice seja espiã chinesa, e hoje ela está na China. A Megaspeed é investigada nos EUA por possíveis violações dos controles de exportação e nega irregularidades. Depois da saída repentina de Huang, o Departamento de Comércio e autoridades como o secretário Howard Lutnick passaram a ser mais cobrados pela forma como conduzem os programas de controle de exportação. Nos últimos dias, o secretário do Tesouro, Scott Bessent, culpou Lutnick por não fazer o suficiente para aplicar as restrições que já existem. “Como eu disse, muitos outros departamentos estavam pressionando por isso, e quem redigia era o Comércio”, afirmou Bessent no programa Sunday Morning Futures, da Fox News. O comunicado do Departamento de Comércio diz que a regra foi escrita pelo Departamento do Tesouro e pelo Conselho de Segurança Nacional, e por orientação deles. Isso sugere que a pressão de autoridades de fora do Comércio pesou na publicação. Na semana passada, o site Axios informou que Trump havia autorizado uma nova ofensiva contra empresas suspeitas de desviar chips avançados de IA para a China, mas que Lutnick atrasou a execução da ordem. Nesta segunda-feira, Trump disse que Jensen Huang não colocou a segurança nacional em risco.

artigo.texto: O Conselho Municipal de Meio Ambiente de Campinas (Comdema) convidou três instituições de ensino e pesquisa para avaliar os possíveis impactos da construção de um mega data center na Fazenda Pau d'Alho, em Barão Geraldo. Os ofícios foram publicados no Diário Oficial desta quarta-feira (18) e buscam ampliar a análise dos efeitos do empreendimento sobre o meio ambiente e as atividades científicas na região. Os convites foram enviados à PUC-Campinas, ao Centro de Pesquisa e Desenvolvimento em Telecomunicações (CPQD) e ao Centro Nacional de Pesquisa em Energia e Materiais (CNPEM). A Unicamp já participa das discussões, por meio de professores de diferentes áreas. O complexo é um projeto da Terranova, ligada à gestora de investimentos Actis, e poderá alcançar 400 megawatts (MW) de capacidade até 2029. Quando foi anunciado, em agosto, esse valor correspondia a 40% da capacidade de processamento de dados em operação no Brasil. O Comdema afirmou que também está organizando um grupo de trabalho (GT) com especialistas em tecnologia, energia, recursos hídricos, legislação e saúde. A expectativa é apresentar um primeiro relatório técnico em até 90 dias, para ajudar o conselho a avaliar o empreendimento. Em nota, a Terra Nova negou que o projeto vá consumir 3,24 milhões de litros de água por dia e afirmou que seguirá as normas ambientais. Segundo a empresa, as obras ainda não começaram e o primeiro prédio deve entrar em operação em 2028. Leia o posicionamento completo abaixo. 🔎 Quais são as preocupações? Projeto do data center em Campinas (SP) — Foto: Terranova Os data centers são grandes instalações que abrigam servidores responsáveis por armazenar e processar informações, inclusive para sistemas de inteligência artificial. Como funcionam continuamente, esses equipamentos precisam de muita energia e de refrigeração para evitar o superaquecimento. No caso de Campinas, o Comdema quer esclarecer principalmente: - Água: o conselho apontou uma estimativa de consumo de até 3,24 milhões de litros por dia em determinadas condições de refrigeração. - Energia: a alta demanda de eletricidade e os possíveis efeitos sobre a infraestrutura regional. - Calor: a possibilidade de aumento da temperatura no entorno do empreendimento. - Ruídos e vibrações: possíveis interferências em equipamentos científicos sensíveis. - Resíduos eletrônicos: o descarte de baterias, processadores e outros componentes. - Impactos urbanísticos: a compatibilidade do complexo com o planejamento ambiental da região. Em agosto, a Terranova afirmou que utilizará um sistema de refrigeração com água circulando por pequenos tubos próximos aos servidores. Segundo a empresa, a tecnologia funciona em circuito fechado, sem evaporação da água utilizada no processo, o que reduziria o consumo hídrico. 🔬 Por que as instituições foram convidadas? Vista aérea do laboratório Sirius, em Campinas — Foto: Reprodução/EPTV Uma das principais preocupações é a proximidade do empreendimento com o CNPEM, onde funciona o Sirius, um acelerador de partículas utilizado em pesquisas científicas. Segundo o conselho, os equipamentos exigem condições rigorosas de estabilidade, e vibrações provocadas pelas obras ou pelo funcionamento do complexo poderiam interferir nas atividades. Por isso, o CNPEM foi convidado a contribuir com estudos sobre esses possíveis efeitos. O CPQD poderá ajudar na avaliação da eficiência energética, dos sistemas de refrigeração e do descarte de resíduos eletrônicos. Já a PUC-Campinas foi chamada para colaborar com análises sobre os impactos ambientais e urbanísticos. A Unicamp participa do grupo por meio de pesquisadores de diferentes áreas, e a Reitoria também demonstrou interesse em acompanhar os trabalhos, segundo os ofícios. Questionamentos sobre o projeto A instalação do complexo já havia sido questionada pelo Comdema em agosto, quando o conselho pediu a suspensão dos licenciamentos da subestação de energia. Entre as preocupações estavam o consumo de água e energia, os possíveis impactos ambientais e a concessão de autorizações separadas para a subestação e o data center. Em setembro, o Ministério Público de São Paulo (MP-SP) instaurou um inquérito civil para apurar os impactos e a regularidade do projeto, após receber três denúncias, incluindo uma do próprio conselho. Na época, a Prefeitura de Campinas informou que apenas a subestação havia recebido autorizações e que as demais etapas do empreendimento continuavam em análise. A administração afirmou que os procedimentos adotados seguiram a legislação municipal. A Terranova também declarou, em setembro, que cumpria as exigências legais para avançar no licenciamento. A empresa destacou as contrapartidas previstas, como a preservação de áreas verdes, a construção de vias públicas e a implantação de estações de tratamento de água e esgoto. O projeto prevê investimento inicial de US$ 500 milhões e geração de aproximadamente 3 mil empregos, diretos e indiretos. A primeira fase está prevista para 2027. O que diz a empresa? "A TERRANOVA acompanha com respeito o trabalho do Comdema e das instituições de pesquisa de Campinas, e está à disposição para o diálogo técnico ao longo do desenvolvimento do projeto. O projeto do campus tem como compromisso atender à legislação e às normas aplicáveis para ruído, vibração, calor e resíduos. O objetivo é que a energia venha 100% de fontes renováveis ou de baixa emissão, como prevê a lei federal dos data centers (REDATA, Lei nº 15.504/2026). O volume de 3,24 milhões de litros de água por dia indicado não corresponde ao projeto do Campus Campinas. O resfriamento funciona em circuito fechado, sem captação de rios ou poços e sem resfriamento evaporativo, que é o tipo de sistema que demanda grandes volumes diários de água. No primeiro prédio, o circuito é abastecido uma única vez, com cerca de 1.040 m³ de água de reuso transportada por caminhão-pipa, sem uso da rede pública, e na operação só repõe pequenas perdas. artigo.texto: Smartphone batteries have become an important part of the buying decision, especially for people who spend hours gaming, watching videos or scrolling through social media. With the iQOO 15, the company is focusing on battery life through its fourth-generation silicon anode technology. The smartphone comes with a 7,000mAh battery, and iQOO claims that it can deliver up to 10.5 hours of continuous gaming, 32.6 hours of video streaming and 22.6 hours of social media usage on a single charge. But what exactly is silicon anode technology, and how does it help a smartphone battery last longer? To understand this, it is important to know how a smartphone battery works. A battery has two main parts called the anode and cathode. During charging and discharging, lithium ions move between these two parts to store and release energy. Most traditional smartphone batteries use graphite in the anode. Silicon, however, can store more lithium ions than graphite. This means it has the potential to hold more energy in the same amount of space. This is where silicon anode technology comes in. By using silicon-based materials in the battery's anode, manufacturers can increase energy density. In simple terms, a battery can store more power without necessarily becoming much bigger. However, silicon also has a limitation. It expands and contracts during charging and discharging, which can affect battery life and stability over time. Battery makers therefore have to work on ways to manage this expansion. The fourth-generation technology used in the iQOO 15 is designed to improve energy density and battery performance. However, iQOO has not publicly explained every material change that separates this generation from earlier versions. The phone also uses second-generation semi-solid battery technology, which the company says helps maintain stable performance across temperatures ranging from -20°C to 40°C. According to iQOO's laboratory figures, the 7,000mAh battery can offer up to 10.5 hours of continuous gaming. For people who mainly use their phones to watch videos, the company claims up to 32.6 hours of continuous video streaming. Social media users can also get up to 22.6 hours of usage, according to the company's figures. These numbers are based on iQOO's internal testing and should not be treated as guaranteed everyday battery life. Actual results will depend on factors such as screen brightness, network strength, gaming settings, background applications and the type of content being played. The phone also supports 100W wired FlashCharge and 40W wireless charging. It includes bypass charging, which allows power to go directly to the phone's system instead of charging the battery while gaming. This is d esigned to reduce battery heat during long gaming sessions. Another feature is Battery Life Extender mode. The company says this helps users return to their previous activity when the phone is connected to a charger after its battery runs critically low. The iQOO 15 also features Qualcomm's Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 processor and an 8K vapour chamber cooling system. These features are meant to support demanding tasks such as gaming while helping manage heat. artigo.texto: Much attention has been given to artificial intelligence, cloud computing and the technology driving the modern economy. Those topics certainly deserve discussion. Yet for local residents, the more important question is far simpler: What do these projects mean for our communities? The answer begins with jobs and investment, but it does not end there. The arrival of large-scale data centers represents one of the most significant private investments ever contemplated in this region. Drawn by reliable electric power, strategic location, available land and access to major markets, technology companies are increasingly viewing West Virginia as an attractive destination for future development. The benefits begin long before a facility becomes operational. During construction, hundreds and potentially thousands of local and regional workers may be employed in site preparation, building construction, utility installation, electrical work and equipment deployment. These projects create opportunities for heavy equipment operators, electricians, steel workers, concrete specialists, truck drivers, engineers, surveyors and countless others. Once operational, the facilities create a new layer of highly skilled employment opportunities, including data center technicians, network engineers, facility operators, security professionals, maintenance personnel and management staff. These positions typically provide competitive wages, specialized training and long-term career opportunities. Data centers represent extraordinary concentrations of private investment. The land, buildings, electrical infrastructure and equipment associated with these facilities collectively create a property tax base unlike anything most communities have previously experienced. Once placed on the tax rolls, those assets generate recurring revenue year after year. Where does the data center revenue go? Economic development projects are often measured by the number of jobs created. While employment matters, residents should also ask another important question: Where does the revenue go? The answer is straightforward. Tax revenues generated by these facilities are distributed through existing state and local systems and ultimately support essential public services. Those revenues benefit public schools, county government, emergency services, public safety operations, infrastructure improvements, and important statewide initiatives. The combined Monarch and Tamarack developments in Mason County are expected to generate approximately $231.2 million annually in property tax revenue. Of that amount, more than $90 million would support county schools, nearly $47.5 million would flow to county government and more than $7 million would support Fire and EMS services. Additional funding would support statewide initiatives, including the Personal Income Tax Reduction Fund, the Economic Enhancement Grant Fund and improvements to West Virginia's electric grid. Putnam County's proposed Google development, while smaller in scale, would still generate approximately $40.9 million annually in property tax revenue. Local schools would receive approximately $17.4 million each year, the County Commission more than $8.2 million, and Fire and EMS services approximately $1.6 million, with additional revenues supporting statewide priorities. Combined, these projects are projected to generate more than $272 million in annual property tax revenues. For Mason County schools alone, the projected annual distribution exceeds $90 million. Putnam County schools stand to receive more than $17 million annually. These are investments in classrooms, teachers, educational technology, facilities, and opportunities for future generations. County governments would gain resources that could strengthen emergency services, improve infrastructure, address deferred maintenance, expand recreational opportunities and better prepare for future growth. Perhaps most importantly, this revenue stream is not a one-time payment or a temporary grant. It is generated year after year for as long as the facilities remain in operation. This is no longer simply a discussion about technology projects or industrial development. It is a discussion about whether West Virginia can position itself to capture the benefits of one of the fastest-growing sectors of the modern economy. Reasonable questions should be asked. Citizens deserve transparency. Public officials should be held accountable for the decisions they make. Those principles are fundamental to good government and responsible economic development. At the same time, it is important to recognize opportunity when it appears. Years from now, the success of these projects will not be judged by the size of the facilities or the sophistication of the technology they contain. They will be judged by whether they helped build stronger schools, safer communities, better public services, greater economic opportunity, and a higher quality of life for the people who call Mason and Putnam Counties home. That is the true promise of this moment. It is a once-in-a-generation opportunity, and one worthy of thoughtful consideration. Clark S. Barnes, of Scott Depot, is a former state senator and president of the Heritage Hills Development Corporation.

artigo.texto: Data center estaria em trâmite na ONS Mapa traz data center anunciado há quase 2 anos para Maringá, mas ministério não registra criação de ZPE Embora não seja apareça publicamente com o pedido de criação de uma Zona de Processamento de Exportação, no Ministério do Desenvolvimento, Indústria, Comércio e Serviços, Maringá consta do Mapa da ONS – Mapa de Datacenters do Brasil do Maravalley, comunidade que mostra a distribuição dos datacenters em operação, construção e planejamento no país. Para se implantar um datacenter é necessário ter uma ZPE, criada mediante edição de decreto presidencial após terem tido seus projetos aprovados pelo Conselho Nacional das Zonas de Processamento de Exportação (CZPE). Até julho não havia nenhum pedido protocolizado no MDIC. A informação no mapa é que, ao lado de outros 17 projetos, foi encaminhado ao Pnast (Política Nacional de Acesso ao Sistema de Transmissão) e está sob análise do ONS – Operacionador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico. No site não possível constatar a existência do protocolo. Hoje no país são quatro ZPEs ativas: Pecém (PE), Paranaíba (PI), Cáceres (MT) e Uberaba (MG), e outras em instalação: Açu (RJ), Aracruz (ES), Araguaína (TO), Bacabeira (MA), Barcarena (PA), Bataguassu (MS), Imbituba (SC), Senador Guiomard (AC) e Suape (PE). Em 23 de janeiro do ano passado o prefeito Silvio Barros (PP) anunciou que Maringá tinha iniciado à tramitação junto ao governo federal para a criação de uma ZPE, que abrigaria o maior data center de inteligência artificial da América Latina, em parceria com a RT-One, que anunciou recentemente a implantação modular e poderá alcançar capacidade de até 400 megawatts (MW) para equipamentos de tecnologia. A empresa informou que o investimento será de R$ 6 bilhões e que adotará sistema direct-to-chip em circuito fechado (resfriamento líquido). A expansão acelerada dos grandes data centers (especialmente voltados para IA) gerou uma forte polêmica em torno do consumo de energia e recursos naturais. Os servidores funcionam 24 horas por dia e exigem uma quantidade colossal de eletricidade, comparável ao consumo de grandes cidades ou a centenas de milhares de residências por unidade. Além disso, pode impactar na conta de luz, dada a expectativa de que o consumo gere escassez. Além da eletricidade, os sistemas de resfriamento consomem grandes volumes de água e geram ilhas de calor e poluição sonora nas comunidades vizinhas. Oficiamente, o governo federal presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva defendeu que a energia “do povo” não deve subsidiar ou ser consumida por essas grandes infraestruturas estrangeiras, sugerindo condicionar a instalação de data centers à autoprodução de energia (como geração própria ou contratos específicos). A recente vitória dos democratas nos Esta Unidos fez investidores das bolsas da Europa ponderarem sobre as incertezas relacionadas ao futuro da inteligência artificial e dos data centers. artigo.texto: Just 400 hyperscale data centers connected in the US used as much electricity as the state of Michigan in a single year, new Harvard research has found. The study, published Monday in Nature Sustainability, also finds that the majority of that electricity was generated using fossil fuels, and data center emissions are three times higher than they were before the AI boom. Federal and state governments do not track data center use separate from the rest of the power sector, despite mounting projections that data centers are putting serious strain on the American power grid. Individual data centers’ power use is often considered proprietary business information, and data center operators and utilities do not have to disclose specific numbers to the public. The Harvard study specifically focuses on hyperscale data centers—the largest types of facilities, which have become flashpoints in community opposition across the country. While often used for AI inference or training, not all of the hyperscalers surveyed in this study are being used for AI. “Hyperscalers have been growing fast, even before the AI boom,” says Jon Koomey, an energy researcher who was not a part of the study. To assemble their dataset, the Harvard researchers put together a list of 403 hyperscale data centers around the country that were operational between May 2024 and April 2025 using a mix of industry research and satellite data. The team then modeled these facilities’ energy use in a variety of scenarios and calculated the energy mix of the regional grids to estimate individual facilities’ carbon emissions. Not all regions were created equal: Data centers in Virginia, Oregon, Ohio, and Iowa—the first of which is home to Data Center Alley—were responsible for more than 50 percent of the energy use in the study. “Knowing for certain data centers how much they use over a year is a really useful thing,” says Koomey, who notes that a peer-reviewed study is more rigorous than some back-of-the envelope calculations. Koomey has been involved in a regular report from Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory since 2007 that approximates the energy and water use of the industry. “Sometimes we know it, but sometimes it’s behind an NDA, and no one ever sees it.” While based on recent data, the study may already be outdated—a reflection of how fast the data center industry is moving. The average size of a facility in the new study is 40 megawatts, which is relatively small compared to some of the data centers under development today. Developers are building campuses that are hundreds or even thousands of megawatts, and there are proposals for still larger data centers. “Some of the massive campuses being proposed today are substantially larger than the typical facility in our dataset,” says Gianluca Guidi, a postdoctoral research fellow at Harvard’s T. H. Chan School of Public Health and the lead author of the study. The study also does not look at developers who choose to build power plants onsite, known as behind-the-meter power—a factor Koomey calls a “wild card” in accurately assessing total data center power use. Plans for behind-the-meter power generation have skyrocketed at proposed data center sites across the US over the past year, with as many as 189 gigawatts in the pipeline earmarked for data centers alone. Many of these plants rely increasingly on inefficient natural gas turbines. BloombergNEF estimated last week that if all of the behind-the-meter power plants in the development queue in the US get built, it could increase overall US emissions by 10 percent. While the federal government hasn’t tracked data center energy use to date, that could change soon, and it could be a boon to researchers and the public. The Energy Information Agency, the arm of the federal government that tracks energy use across various sectors, conducted three pilot surveys of data center power use across 10 states this year. Those pilot surveys are now complete, EIA spokesperson Lee Tucker tells WIRED, and the agency is currently using them to design a potential voluntary survey for the sector.

artigo.texto: By Hervé Jeannin, co-rapporteur for the EESC opinion on the potential of the sodium battery manufacturing sector Europe’s energy transition requires an industrial base capable of delivering it. Batteries power electric mobility, facilitate the integration of renewable electricity and help households and businesses manage their energy consumption. Our ability to manufacture them will shape Europe’s competitiveness and energy security. Yet intense international competition and dependencies on materials, components and equipment are weakening this essential industry. As co-rapporteur for the European Economic and Social Committee’s opinion on sodium battery manufacturing, I am convinced that sodium technologies offer a tangible opportunity to strengthen Europe’s capabilities while making better use of its own resources. Beyond lithium: what makes sodium batteries different? Today, lithium-ion batteries dominate the global market, powering everything from smartphones to electric vehicles and energy storage systems. Their production is heavily concentrated in Asia, particularly China, which leads in battery manufacturing and the processing of key materials. Sodium-ion batteries offer an emerging alternative: they use sodium instead of lithium, reducing reliance on certain critical raw materials. Although they generally store less energy for the same weight, they could be cheaper to produce and are particularly promising for stationary energy storage and more affordable electric vehicles. China is already investing heavily in this technology, making it essential for Europe to develop its own manufacturing capacity before another strategic dependency takes hold. Sodium batteries: an opportunity for Europe Sodium is abundant in Europe. Suitable battery chemistries can reduce dependence on lithium, cobalt and nickel, while the hard carbon used for anodes can be derived from wood or agricultural waste. The EESC highlights the possibility of producing sodium batteries entirely from European raw materials. Turning this potential into strategic autonomy requires European capabilities across the entire value chain, from processing to recycling, and, above all, strong political commitment to driving the development of European solutions encompassing both raw materials and manufacturers. Sodium should complement lithium-ion technologies. Each application calls for a different balance between energy density, cost, safety and durability. Sodium-ion batteries generally have slightly lower energy density, but weight and size matter less for stationary storage than for electric vehicles. Storing renewable electricity for households, businesses and grids therefore represents a particularly relevant market opportunity. Public support must reflect technological maturity. Sodium-ion batteries offer prospects for deployment in the nearer term; sodium–saltwater systems require further research, particularly into solid electrolytes, to explore their potential for marine applications and longer-term storage. Our opinion also identifies the possibility of using sodium recovered from desalination by-products, linking water resilience to energy storage, subject to technical and environmental assessment. From innovation to industrial production The immediate challenge is industrial scale-up. A laboratory breakthrough alone does not create a competitive factory. Companies must demonstrate the reliability of their solutions, secure customers and finance production equipment. Small businesses often struggle to shoulder these risks. The EESC therefore calls for an updated industrial roadmap for lithium and sodium batteries, coordinated by the European Battery Alliance, with targeted investment support and cooperation with research and technology organisations. Investing in Europe’s battery industry The EESC’s opinion on the Battery Booster strategy makes a specific request: broaden funding to cover chemistries beyond lithium and explicitly include sodium. Support should reach SMEs, suppliers and recyclers alongside cell manufacturers, and should not be limited to electric vehicles. Critical chemicals, electrolytes and European-made machinery also deserve investment. Dependence on imported inputs and equipment leaves vulnerabilities that building more cell factories alone cannot resolve. Affordable energy, predictable permitting procedures and timely funding are essential. The EESC calls for stronger and better-targeted funding for the Battery Booster strategy in the next EU Budget. Our opinion on sodium advocates an overall budget of at least EUR 220 billion for FP10. International cooperation must help build lasting European expertise. Both opinions call for technology transfer; the Battery Booster opinion recommends making state aid, public procurement and subsidies conditional on technology transfer and local content. Investment must strengthen European research (80% of current projects are not launched for lack of funding in Europe), skills and suppliers, while ensuring that requirements for products entering the EU market are applied fairly. Sustainability, jobs and regional development Circularity must be built in from the outset. Ecodesign should facilitate disassembly and materials recovery, while production should minimise energy consumption and the use of hazardous substances. Recycling requires economically viable facilities, harmonised collection and the efficient transport of used batteries to authorised facilities within the single market. Materials recovery capacity must grow in step with production. Industrial ambition must also benefit workers and regions. The Battery Booster opinion makes job quality and compliance with EU standards conditions for public support. Adequate staffing, training, investment in prevention and effective inspections are essential. Workers must be involved in identifying risks arising from new processes. artigo.texto: Data centers precisam se conectar às comunidades Sustentabilidade significa ir além da eficiência energética, passando pela otimização de múltiplos recursos e pela criação de impacto positivo para as comunidades que abrigam esses edifícios, avalia Ana Cunha, da Deerns Por Ana Cunha* – A expansão da IA mudou a forma como projetamos e operamos data centers. Com o aumento da densidade e potência dos racks e da demanda por capacidade computacional, questões como energia, água, resfriamento, disponibilidade de rede, emissões e adaptação tecnológica deixam de ser questões isoladas e passam a fazer parte de uma mesma equação que define estrategicamente o valor do ativo “data center” e até a viabilidade do seu licenciamento (permiting) técnico e social. Nesse cenário, falar em sustentabilidade significa ir além da eficiência energética, passando pela otimização de múltiplos recursos e pela criação de impacto positivo, especialmente para as comunidades que abrigam esses edifícios. Torna-se prioritário compreender como diferentes dimensões ambientais, técnicas, regulatórias e sociais se relacionam e como afetam a resiliência e o valor do ativo no longo prazo. Uma mudança que já é perceptível na Europa. Obrigações de reporte e instrumentos como a Taxonomia Europeia, a EED (Diretiva da Eficiência Energética) e a CSRD (Diretiva europeia sobre Relatórios de Sustentabilidade Corporativa) aproximam cada vez mais o desempenho de sustentabilidade das decisões de financiamento, investimento e de relacionamento ou captação de clientes. Sustentabilidade deixa, assim, de ser apenas uma agenda de conformidade e passa a integrar a equação econômica do empreendimento e de aceitação social na fase de licenciamento. Indicadores de desempenho sustentável e operacional também podem influenciar a avaliação de risco econômico e reputacional, a atratividade do ativo e o acesso a instrumentos de financiamento, tão importantes na fase atual de capital “caro”. Isso não significa que o Brasil deva reproduzir o modelo europeu. Os mercados partem de condições diferentes, mas os clientes de data centers de grande escala são cada vez mais internacionais e buscam otimizar práticas, indicadores e valor. A Europa possui um ambiente regulatório mais maduro e enfrenta restrições importantes relacionadas à água, à energia renovável e à capacidade (ou saturação) da rede. O Brasil, por sua vez, conta com uma matriz elétrica predominantemente renovável e vive uma fase de expansão da infraestrutura digital. O ponto de convergência entre eles está na relação entre sustentabilidade e capital. Enquanto o mercado europeu utiliza critérios de desempenho e mecanismos financeiros cada vez mais associados à sustentabilidade, o Brasil pode combinar suas características energéticas com mecanismos fiscais para estimular novos investimentos. O Redata se insere nesse contexto como parte de uma nova equação para a expansão da infraestrutura digital brasileira, embora seus efeitos concretos devam ser avaliados à medida que o mecanismo avance. Mas existe um risco em transformar essa discussão em uma competição por indicadores. O PUE (Eficácia no Uso de Energia) continua sendo uma métrica fundamental para avaliar a eficiência energética de um data center, mas nenhum indicador isolado conta toda a história. Muitas vezes uma solução pode melhorar o PUE e piorar o WUE (Eficácia no Uso de Água); outra pode otimizar o consumo energético e, ao mesmo tempo, dificultar o reaproveitamento do calor residual. Além de que um local energeticamente eficiente ainda pode operar com energia não renovável tendo assim um fraco REF (Fator de Energia Renovável). É por isso que precisamos de uma abordagem sistêmica e multicritérios refletida desde as fases preliminares. Uma decisão de engenharia e de consultoria estratégica de sustentabilidade produz efeitos em diferentes dimensões do projeto, que precisam ser consideradas não só desde a concepção do ativo, mas até mesmo desde a seleção do terreno. Essa visão ganha ainda mais importância diante da inteligência artificial. Um data center preparado para cargas convencionais de cloud não necessariamente terá as mesmas características de uma instalação voltada para cargas de IA. A maior densidade de potência exige novas estratégias e tecnologias de resfriamento e modifica requisitos de infraestrutura. Por isso, a sustentabilidade começa antes do primeiro megawatt. A escolha do terreno, a disponibilidade de energia e água, os riscos climáticos, a arquitetura, o sistema de resfriamento, a possibilidade de reutilização de calor e a capacidade de adaptação futura precisam fazer parte das primeiras decisões. Inovação, porém, não significa simplesmente adotar a tecnologia mais nova. Em infraestrutura crítica, novas soluções precisam ser acompanhadas de segurança operacional e gestão de riscos. A experiência técnica é fundamental para avaliar sua aplicabilidade e integrá-las ao projeto sem dissociar sustentabilidade de funcionalidade, resiliência e custo total de propriedade (“Total Cost of Ownership”). Há ainda uma dimensão que muitas vezes fica fora das discussões predominantemente técnicas que é o território. Um data center não existe isoladamente, pois depende de energia, conectividade, fornecedores, trabalhadores e serviços. Sua implantação também pode gerar impactos sobre a região, e questões como ruído, impacto visual, demanda por água e energia ou ausência de benefícios locais podem comprometer a aceitação do projeto. Por outro lado, a infraestrutura digital também pode contribuir para o desenvolvimento desse local. Reaproveitamento de calor, capacitação profissional, contratação local, conectividade e integração com outros edifícios e sistemas urbanos podem criar benefícios que ultrapassam os limites físicos do data center. É na fase inicial, desde a seleção do terreno, que podem ser identificar as oportunidades de sinergias entre o data center e o território onde será instalado. artigo.texto: Key Takeaways - The plant's assembly lines can produce 40 cells per minute, making them among the fastest prismatic LFP battery lines outside China. - The project, which uses CATL-licensed technology, achieved commercial mass production after navigating setbacks including US political scrutiny and a downsizing. Ford Motor's (NYSE: F) plant in Michigan has rolled out its first lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery cells using technology licensed from CATL (HKEX: 3750), marking the US auto giant's official entry into battery manufacturing. The prismatic LFP cells, produced at BlueOval Battery Park Michigan in Marshall, Michigan, are headed to the Louisville Assembly Plant to power prototypes of the Fathom electric pickup truck, Charles Poon, vice president of hardware engineering at Ford, said in a statement on Wednesday. With commercial-scale deliveries from the wholly owned and operated plant, Ford will become the first automaker to introduce LFP batteries for the mainstream US consumer automotive market, helping push pure electric vehicle (EV) prices lower. To significantly reduce vehicle cost and weight, Ford chose proven technology from CATL, the world's largest battery maker, and integrated the prismatic LFP battery pack directly into the vehicle design as a structural chassis component. The plant's assembly lines can produce 40 cells per minute, making them among the fastest prismatic LFP battery lines outside China, and use AI image recognition technology to pursue a low defect rate at the parts-per-billion level. Following the shipment of the first cells, Ford plans to bring a supporting battery pack plant into operation in Marshall in 2027 to prepare for the official launch of the Fathom electric pickup. Manufacturing experience gained from the on-schedule launch of the Michigan plant is helping a battery energy storage system plant in Glendale, Kentucky, prepare for its start of production in 2027, Ford Energy president David Carroll said on Thursday. The bumpy partnership began in February 2023, when Ford initially announced a $3.5 billion investment to build a plant with an annual capacity of 35 gigawatt-hours (GWh), with CATL providing technology licensing and operational support. After US Republican lawmakers questioned whether federal subsidies could indirectly flow to CATL, the project was temporarily halted in 2023 before restarting in November of the same year with investment and annual capacity cut to $2 billion and 20 GWh, respectively. Facing policy headwinds such as the early termination of US federal EV tax credits in September 2025, Ford recorded $19.5 billion in related asset impairment charges in December 2025, but kept the LFP project and decided to expand into the energy storage business. Ford announced in June this year that the plant had completed full-process trial production of its first cells and was conducting tests under CATL standards, and has now achieved the official roll-out and shipment of automotive power cells within the year as planned.

artigo.texto: A new international platform, named the Global Energy Storage Alliance (GESA), aimed at enhancing cooperation on energy storage was launched at the China Pavilion during COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye. The GESA initiative was established through the joint efforts of the China Energy Storage Alliance (CNESA), China Southern Power Grid Energy Storage Co. and the China Renewable Energy Engineering Institute (CREEI), together with additional industry stakeholders. Discover B2B Marketing That Performs Combine business intelligence and editorial excellence to reach engaged professionals across 36 leading media platforms. The alliance seeks to address the role of energy storage in power-system flexibility and renewable energy integration as countries accelerate their adoption of clean energy sources. Senior officials attending the launch included Li Gao, China’s Vice Minister of the Ministry of Ecology and Environment, and Xiong Minfeng, Deputy Director-General of the Department of International Cooperation of the National Energy Administration of China. Also present were Francesco La Camera, Director-General of the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA), and Selwin Hart, Special Adviser to the UN Secretary-General on Climate Action and Just Transition. The event took place during a side meeting focused on digital-intelligent innovation and green electricity. GESA was introduced amid mounting challenges faced by the sector, such as energy security concerns, varying technical standards across countries, and gaps in financing and business models, particularly in emerging markets. CREEI International Cooperation Department director, lead scientist and director-general assistant Dr Jiang Hao, stated that the initiative aims to promote large-scale, diversified, and innovation-driven energy storage around the world. The goal is to position storage as a central part of new power systems through international collaboration and support the global energy transition and climate efforts. CNESA secretary-general Liu Wei outlined six priority areas for GESA: facilitating global dialogue, developing databases and standards, advancing technology deployment, fostering business model innovation, enhancing supply-chain coordination, and supporting investment and project cooperation. According to Liu, GESA is intended to serve as an open and inclusive platform for cooperation. China Southern Power Grid Energy Storage Co. deputy general manager Sun Liqun highlighted the evolution of energy storage, identifying challenges such as fragmented standards and difficulties in project development and remuneration. He pointed to gaps in short- and long-duration remuneration, as well as obstacles in financing and business models. Representatives from organisations including Acwa, EVE Energy, the International Hydropower Association, Trina Solar, the Long Duration Energy Storage Council, and the World Resources Institute also attended the launch. The alliance is inviting further participation from industry associations, research institutions, companies, and international bodies worldwide. Recently, at COP31, leaders from Africa and Europe called for greater investment in clean energy and manufacturing to help turn Africa’s renewable resources and critical minerals into jobs and industrial development.

artigo.texto: Support WBUR Kraft-backed data center proposal met with opposition from Sutton residents Residents in Sutton, Massachusetts expressed outrage at a planning board meeting Monday over a proposal to build $16 billion data center campus in their town. The proposed project is backed by The Kraft Group, which owns the New England Patriots. The data center campus would span 10 buildings and draw 900 megawatts of electricity, according to a town memorandum on the project. If built, it would be the among largest data centers in the country. Because the town currently has no zoning laws related to data centers, Sutton’s planning board is exploring options to add a bylaw for data centers to be built in the town. Town officials said at the meeting that the campus would bring in nearly $28 million in tax revenue each year, which could lower the tax bill of an average single-family home and help close the town’s growing budget deficit. But residents in attendance said they are worried about the data center’s impact on the environment, public health and home values. Shawn Buzzell, who has lived in Sutton for three years, stood outside the town hall collecting signatures on a petition before the meeting. He said the petition, which had more than 300 signatures as of Monday night, calls for a special town meeting for residents to vote on the petition’s definition of data centers and prohibit their construction in Sutton. He said he’s against the proposed data center because he’s concerned that it will put residents at risk of higher electricity costs and noise pollution. “They’re sticking them in the middle of people’s neighborhoods,” Buzzell said. “They wedge these in there and it’s not because it’s the right place to put it, it’s because it’s the cheapest place to put it. They end up ruining a lot of people’s lives, destroying quality of life, destroying household resale value, just so they can make themselves a little bit more extra money, and that’s not fair.” Crystal Smith, a Sutton resident for 15 years, said she has been following the news about data centers, but never expected one to be built in the “tiny town” of Sutton. “We don’t have the space for that, we don’t have the resources for that and it would impact way too many things here,” Smith said. About 75 residents attended Monday night’s planning board meeting. Some held signs that read, “NO DATA CENTERS” and “NO DATA CENTERS IN SUTTON.” Others chimed in during the meeting, voicing their disapproval of the project. WBUR reached out to The Kraft Group for comment, but did not receive a response in time for publication. In a memorandum outlining the project, the town said the proposal is tentative. Applications with the town have yet to be filed and "important details on power, water, equipment and site impacts are still to come," the memo reads. Gov. Maura Healey signed an executive order in September requiring data center projects to get local approval before they can obtain state permits. Under the order, data center projects are also required develop energy resources to support their operation or to create a "Ratepayer Protection Fund" if they can't supply their own power infrastructure. The proposed data center would draw 900 megawatts of power, roughly the amount of electricity required to power 450,000 homes.

artigo.texto: Blenden Township unable to reach decision on controversial battery energy storage system BLENDON TOWNSHIP, Mich. (WOOD) — The Planning Commission of Blendon Township met Wednesday night to decide on a controversial battery energy storage system, known as a BESS. Neighbors worry about proposed battery energy storage system in Blendon Township The Wednesday meeting regarding the facility developments lasted nearly three hours, with outraged residents and town commissioners ultimately unable to reach an agreement. The project was initially proposed by Key Capture Energy, which has been trying to develop a 100-Megawatt BESS for the past 15 months. Commissioners ended up splitting their votes three to three on the decision for approval, which has left the project in limbo. Throughout the entire process, residents have been concerned about the environmental impact of a BESS. They called attention to the risks of a fire at the BESS and how the facility could have long term impacts on the area and its farms. Key Capture Energy says that the BESS would be safe and highly regulated, but commissioners expressed reservations over what a potential fire could mean for nearby property values, pointing to fires that have broken out at other BESS facilities. Advertisement "Any type of development has a risk of fire loss of a larger than typical compared to a home, or as our counterparts experienced the common amount of hazardous chemicals that could contaminate the environment during and after a failure," Planning Commissioner Ben Van Zweden said at the Wednesday meeting. "I consider their submission being conclusive that they did not address failure with this is a possibility. There have been fires at BESS facilities, so there should be data on that." Key Capture Energy says that a nearby Van Buren substation makes Blendon Township an ideal location for the project. "The biggest benefit is a stable and reliable electric grid," said Chris Linsmayer, director of public affairs and community relations at Key Capture Energy. "So the way that these work is they store energy at periods of low demand, typically when prices are low and then that energy is available to dispatch back onto the grid." The commissioners are now working on revisions to the BESS application and are planning to bring those to the next board meeting. One option Key Capture Energy says they would consider is going to the state to seek approval through Public Act 233, which reduces local control over land-use decisions and would potentially giveo the Michigan Public Service Commission the authority to approve the project. Residents of Blenden Township as well as commissioners shared their unease about what that path would mean for the town and if it would be benefitted at all based on agreements made with Key Capture Energy.o Copyright 2026 Nexstar Media, Inc. artigo.texto: - Solar installations keep growing, and the market enters a new stage India has steadily accelerated solar project construction, and solar has become a major part of its renewable energy development. According to data published by the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE), cumulative installed solar capacity reached 174.55 GW as of October 31, 2026, of which ground-mounted utility-scale capacity was about 127.33 GW. From April to October 2026, India added about 24.29 GW of solar capacity, including about 3.50 GW in October alone. Annual additions also show the pace of development. In FY2025–26, India added 44.61 GW of solar capacity, up roughly 87.2% from 23.83 GW in FY2024–25, which indicates a clear acceleration in project development and construction. As electricity demand grows and the energy mix continues to transition, solar demand keeps expanding. Beyond large ground-mounted plants, rooftop solar, commercial and industrial distributed generation, and hybrid energy projects are becoming additional sources of new demand. Under the PM-Surya Ghar rooftop scheme, about 6.526 million households had benefited as of early November 2026, and cumulative rooftop installations reached about 19.1 GW, further boosting the distributed solar market. Still, rapid capacity growth places greater demands on grid infrastructure and power absorption. As solar accounts for a larger share of the power mix, how well generation growth matches transmission capacity will directly affect whether new projects can connect to the grid and perform as expected. - Growing capacity and grid absorption constraints highlight the need for energy storage As solar capacity expands, some regions of India have begun to face a mismatch between renewable output and grid acceptance capacity, and solar curtailment is drawing growing attention. Solar curtailment refers to situations where a solar plant can generate electricity but part of that output cannot be delivered to the grid because of insufficient transmission capacity, supply-demand mismatches, or dispatch restrictions. For solar projects, curtailment reduces actual electricity sales, affects returns on investment, and may weaken the incentive to develop future projects. According to Grid Controller of India data submitted to Parliament by the MNRE, solar curtailment reached 8,133 GWh from April to June 2026, with 2,417 GWh in April, 3,235 GWh in May, and 2,481 GWh in June. This shows that while solar capacity has grown rapidly, grid transmission and absorption capacity has not fully kept pace with generation, and the power supply-demand mismatch is becoming more visible. As more solar projects come online, expanding transmission capacity and building supporting energy storage will become key directions for reducing curtailment and improving solar utilization. Transmission delays are also affecting renewable grid connections. In the first quarter of 2026, India lost about 300 GWh of renewable generation due to transmission constraints, roughly two-thirds of the renewable curtailment in interstate grid projects over the same period. In addition, some transmission projects are behind schedule, and about 20 GW of renewable projects face grid connection delays of more than four months. This points to a continuing gap between renewable project development and grid construction. Against this backdrop, energy storage has become an important complement for improving solar absorption. Battery energy storage systems (BESS) can store electricity during solar peak output and release it at night or during demand peaks, shifting power across time periods to ease the timing mismatch between generation and consumption. According to the Central Electricity Authority (CEA) statistics on energy storage projects as of August 31, 2026, about 3.03 GW / 9.08 GWh of BESS projects are in operation, about 28.21 GW / 79.92 GWh are under construction, about 7.32 GW / 24.13 GWh have been awarded, and about 18.31 GW / 63.53 GWh are at the tendering stage. These figures show that India has a large pipeline of storage projects, but projects under construction, awarded, or in tendering are not the same as storage capacity already in operation. Looking at project progress, India’s BESS pipeline has grown substantially, but operating capacity remains limited, with projects under construction and at the tendering stage making up the bulk of the pipeline. The focus of the storage market is gradually shifting from project planning and tendering toward construction, grid connection, and actual operation. As storage projects come online, their role in easing peak-period supply-demand imbalances, improving solar utilization, and strengthening grid regulation will become more apparent. In addition, on July 31, 2026, the Indian government approved the Pradhan Mantri Surya Sarovar Yojana, which plans to develop 5,000 MW of floating solar paired with at least two hours of storage, corresponding to about 10,000 MWh. The project will be implemented over FY2026–27 to FY2030–31, further reflecting India’s direction of combining solar generation with storage. Overall, the growth focus of India’s solar market is extending from new capacity additions to grid transmission, absorption, and storage support. Transmission construction progress and the commissioning of storage projects will be important factors affecting the actual generation performance of solar projects and future market demand. - Localization policies continue to advance, and DCR and ALMM are reshaping module procurement While expanding solar capacity, the Indian government has also continued to promote domestic solar manufacturing, aiming to reduce reliance on imports and build a domestic supply system covering more segments of the industrial chain. India currently drives industrial localization mainly through the Domestic Content Requirement (DCR), the Approved List of Models and Manufacturers (ALMM), and the Production Linked Incentive (PLI) schem

artigo.texto: Rare look inside Port Washington's $15M AI data center project drawing mixed reactions A $15 million AI data center project in Port Washington, developed by Vantage in partnership with Oracle and OpenAI, is under construction and drawing both community curiosity and criticism. 12 News got a rare look inside one of the largest AI data centers in the country. Get an exclusive look behind-the-scenes in the video player above. The 672-acre site, with an additional 1,000 acres reserved for expansion, is larger than the entire Village of Whitefish Bay. The construction site sees 3,500 workers daily, and Port Washington Mayor Ted Neitzke has been leading van tours of the site to engage locals and address concerns. “Our restaurants are thriving, and our bars are thriving, and our hotels are thriving, and our downtown businesses are thriving,” Neitzke said during one of the tours. The project The first phase of the project includes four data center buildings, each with a footprint large enough to hold two Lambeau Fields. “This is one of the four data center buildings being built here. 800 thousand square feet each,” Neitzke said. “It’s comparable to other data centers that are being built across the country. But definitely as someone who has been in construction for a large part of my life, this is definitely fantastic to watch and build,” he added. Vantage says the center will be operational by early 2028, providing internet and cloud services while storing, processing, and distributing data. “Almost everything you’re seeing here is manufactured, made, or fabricated here in Wisconsin. So it’s not just a Port Washington thing. It’s statewide,” Neitzke said. The project is expected to bring significant tax benefits to the community, transforming agriculturally zoned land assessed at a few million dollars into a site valued at $120 million. This increase is anticipated to support the majority of city services for Port Washington. Responses after tour Tour participants shared their impressions of the project. “It’s really something else,” one attendee said. “I didn’t know what the Vantage Center was really for. And now I know a lot more, so that’s good,” another participant said. When asked if they thought the project was positive for the area, they replied, “Sure. Sure.” Al Poull, whose family has lived on a nearby farm for 126 years, acknowledged the changes brought by the project. “Things change, you know? It’s just the way it is,” Poull said. Criticism Despite the enthusiasm from some locals, the project has faced criticism and opposition. One contentious meeting resulted in the arrest of three women. Clean Wisconsin and other groups have raised concerns about the environmental impact of AI data centers and the power plants required to support them. Video below: Data center dust and noise fight continues near Port Washington “Wisconsin is incredibly vulnerable right now to AI data centers,” a Clean Wisconsin representative said. “When you have something as large as what’s going on in Port Washington, that will be vastly bigger in terms of energy needs than anything Wisconsin has ever seen before, where so much has to be given to that, these are resources we all rely on. That needs to be a conversation that needs to happen well before right now when the construction is going on and it’s almost done,” the representative added. Neitzke acknowledged the unexpected backlash. “Surprised? Yes. Caught off guard is probably the better way to describe it. Did not see that coming,” he said. Transparency The mayor has emphasized transparency during the tours, addressing concerns about water usage, power supply, and electricity rates. “It does not use a lot of water. Power is protected, your electricity rates do not go up,” Neitzke said. He believes the data center is a transformative project for the community. “I really believe that data centers are the newest of all the utilities. And a utility is something everyone needs, right? Clean water, clean sidewalks, electricity, and now information,” Neitzke said. Neitzke has also been advising elected officials across the country on how to navigate similar projects. “Right now, local communities are in an amazing position to negotiate. And I don’t know why anyone wouldn’t. As you saw out there, I mean, it’s an amazing project,” he said. Construction on the data center began in December 2022 and is scheduled to be completed by 2028.

artigo.texto: Brian Fellon is senior vice president at Xpansiv, a market platform for energy and environmental commodities. Winter Storm Fern hit Texas in January 2026 with extreme cold and hazardous precipitation. But unlike Winter Storm Uri in 2021, the lights stayed on. The Electric Reliability Council of Texas’ post-event report captured how the grid remained intact without Energy Emergency Alerts, public conservation calls or systemwide outages. During Fern, ERCOT’s battery energy storage resources were indispensable for covering peak-demand reserves, while all resource types contributed to meeting broader system demand. The critical lesson is that grid performance is highly dependent on coordinating nascent technologies and real-time operations with legacy generation assets. That lesson is now being tested at scale across the country. The U.S. electricity sector is undergoing its most abrupt transformation since deregulation. After nearly two decades of flat demand, load growth is accelerating from data centers, transportation and industrial electrification. The forward demand curve has never been this steep, and ERCOT's long-range planning assumptions contemplate peak load reaching more than four times today’s record levels. Across the PJM Interconnection footprint, forecasted load growth is raising expectations that tens of gigawatts of new supply may be needed over the coming decade to maintain system reliability. This demand jump is colliding with aging grid infrastructure, constrained transmission, record-long interconnection queues and a shifting policy landscape. These factors are reconfiguring wholesale power markets and revaluing baseload and dispatchable generation, while establishing battery storage as essential grid infrastructure. Batteries are often described as a foundational solution because they respond instantly, start and stop without thermal plants’ mechanical constraints, and uniquely shift energy from off-peak to on-peak periods. In practice, the grid does not simply benefit from batteries as fixed capacity in the conventional sense. It benefits from dynamic, flexible battery storage systems that are specifically configured to accelerate responsiveness, along with the telemetry, data feeds, market interfaces and 24/7 readiness required to perform under normal and stressed conditions alike. That distinction matters as storage scales, owners compete for arbitrage opportunities and electricity markets evolve. In organized wholesale markets, dispatch is not a single daily event. It’s a sequence of day-ahead scheduling, intraday adjustments and real-time dispatch, translated into 5-minute price intervals. For chemically-constrained assets like batteries, timelines are crucial because spot market decisions are inseparable from current and future state-of-charge, known as SoC. Every megawatt discharged at a given time affects what can be delivered later. Fortunately, policy and market design are adapting to support this reality. FERC’s Order No. 841 requires ISOs/RTOs to remove barriers to storage participation and adopt participation models that recognize storage’s physical and operational characteristics. That mandate expanded the range of products storage can provide, with more options for revenue production. Although not governed by FERC, ERCOT went even further than Order 841. In December 2025, ERCOT implemented Real-Time Co-optimization Plus Batteries (RTC+B), which co-optimizes energy and reserves in real time while accounting for what battery resources can actually deliver. One month later, during Winter Storm Fern, ERCOT credited RTC+B with helping redistribute ancillary services across the system during a localized transmission emergency. The same change that helped ERCOT lean on batteries during Fern also changed how those batteries earn revenue. As these rules open new ways for storage to participate, the mix of market products that pay off keeps shifting. The new paradigm, and what’s needed Market participants and grid operators need timely, accurate information about what a battery can deliver under variable constraints. Unreliable data or inconsistent operations aren’t theoretical problems, because they show up directly in project economics after commercial operations begin. Similarly, optimization only creates value if it’s converted into timely, accurate and compliant market submissions. There has never been a greater need for validated bid and offer workflows, automated checks against asset constraints and market rules, reliable ISO/RTO connectivity, clear audit trails, and the ability to rapidly adjust trades as forecasts, prices, outages and SoC conditions change. The same need for accuracy and coordination extends into real-time operations. Wholesale markets and grid conditions don’t simply pause at 5 p.m. when the workday ends for most electricity consumers. Scarcity pricing, forced outages and weather disruptions often happen during off-hours. Sophisticated storage operators utilize defined escalation pathways, telemetry monitoring and situational awareness tools to coordinate instantly when grid conditions require immediate support. A practical checklist for battery owners and operators includes: - Treat data and telemetry as mission-critical infrastructure. Validate data quality and latency end-to-end, not just at the device level. - Run multi-market playbooks, not single-product strategies. Markets change; build the adaptive capability to shift with them. - Treat market submission as a core operating capability. Whether built in-house or outsourced, deploy resilient controls, versioned workflows and exception handling. - Operationalize SoC discipline. Establish SoC guardrails tied to existing obligations, revenue targets and forecast uncertainty. Review after-action performance during unforeseen events. ERCOT has shown what adaptive market design can deliver. Other markets should follow. Operators can only do so much on their own. Market rules decide how
