artigo.texto: Singapore is expanding its international carbon market network after authorizing its first carbon credit project in Rwanda and signing a new carbon trading agreement with Bangladesh. Both developments, announced at COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, show how Singapore is turning its Article 6 partnerships into practical projects and new sources of climate finance. The Rwanda project is expected to reduce about 780,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (CO₂e) between 2026 and 2030. It will distribute 300,000 ceramic water filters to households and early childhood centres, giving more people access to safe drinking water. Singapore also signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with Bangladesh to explore future carbon trading. The two countries will work toward a formal agreement that could allow Bangladesh to transfer eligible carbon credits to Singapore. These steps form part of a wider plan to build a regional carbon market hub. Singapore is also working with the World Bank and private groups to improve project funding, carbon registries, and access to buyers. Singapore Approves First Rwanda Carbon Project Under Article 6 On November 14, Singapore’s National Environment Agency (NEA) announced its first project authorization under its carbon market agreement with Rwanda. Singapore-based Climate Bridge International developed the Safe Water Supply Project. It will distribute 300,000 ceramic water filters across Rwanda, focusing on the Western Province. The filters will provide clean drinking water without the need to boil it using firewood or charcoal. This can lower fuel use, reduce emissions, and improve indoor air quality. - The project is expected to benefit around 1.8 million people and reduce about 780,000 tonnes of CO₂e from 2026 to 2030. The first 10,000 filters began distribution in June 2026, with the rest planned for 2027. This is the first project authorized under Singapore’s six operationalised Article 6 agreements. More than 20 other projects are also being assessed under its agreement with Rwanda. However, authorization does not mean that all 780,000 credits have already been issued or transferred. The project must still undergo independent checks and credit issuance. The two countries must also approve the transfer of eligible credits. Under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, countries must make a corresponding adjustment when they transfer credits internationally. This prevents both countries from counting the same emissions reduction toward their climate targets. The Singaporean official document reads: “The Singapore-Rwanda IA comprises three stages, corresponding to different stages of a carbon credit project’s development and implementation. At each stage, Singapore and Rwanda assess applications against their respective requirements. For Singapore, projects must meet Singapore’s eligibility criteria for International Carbon Credits (ICCs).” Singapore and Bangladesh Explore Carbon Trading Singapore and Bangladesh also signed an MoU on November 14 to develop carbon market cooperation under Article 6. The agreement sets the stage for talks on a legally binding implementation agreement. This would establish how both countries approve projects and transfer eligible carbon credits from Bangladesh to Singapore. The two governments also plan to share knowledge and support the growth of high-quality carbon markets. Bangladesh could gain new funding for projects that cut emissions and support sustainable development. Singapore could gain another source of international credits for companies covered by its carbon tax. Permanent Secretary Melvyn Ong remarked: “Carbon markets are a new area of partnership for Singapore and Bangladesh, and this MOU is an exciting next step in our relationship. Together, we will work towards an Implementation Agreement and enable the development of high-integrity carbon credit projects that support both countries’ climate goals.” The MoU is an early step, however. It does not yet allow Bangladesh to transfer credits for use under Singapore’s carbon tax system. That will require a formal agreement and approved projects. The deal adds to Singapore’s growing network of carbon market partners across Asia, Africa, and South America. Singapore Expands Its Article 6 Network Singapore has signed carbon market agreements with 12 countries: Papua New Guinea, Ghana, Bhutan, Peru, Chile, Rwanda, Paraguay, Thailand, Mongolia, Vietnam, the Philippines, and Laos. Six agreements have been operationalized, with project application processes open for Ghana, Bhutan, Peru, Rwanda, Thailand, and Mongolia. These partnerships follow Article 6.2 of the Paris Agreement, which allows countries to trade emissions reductions toward their climate goals. Singapore’s rules also include safeguards. Five percent of proceeds from authorised credits must support climate adaptation in host countries or the UN Adaptation Fund. In addition, 2% of authorised credits must be cancelled at issuance to help reduce global emissions. These rules aim to ensure that carbon trading supports wider climate action, rather than simply moving credits between countries. The two partners signed a 2027–2029 activity plan under the Singapore Carbon Markets for Development Programme at COP31. - The plan will focus on three areas: carbon market systems, project funding, and technical support. It will help countries develop carbon registries and digital systems to track and verify emissions reductions. artigo.texto: Global energy storage cell shipments increased by 82.28% YoY between January and September 2026, according to InfoLink CATL retained its leading position, while CORNEX entered the global top 5 for the first time InfoLink has raised its global energy storage cell shipment forecast for 2026 to 1,043.5 GWh InfoLink Consulting reports that global energy storage cell shipments grew by 82.28% year-on-year (YoY) to 747.63 GWh in the first nine months (9M) of 2026. Shipments in the first half of 2026 totaled 467.84 GWh, up 94.76% YoY. Shipments grew by 8.59% quarter-on-quarter (QoQ) in Q3 2026. Manufacturers increased shipments in August to avoid the 2% consumption tax on lithium-ion batteries that came into effect in China on September 1, InfoLink adds. The tax, announced in July 2026, will increase to 4% from September 1, 2027 (see China to Introduce Phased Solar Cell and Battery Consumption Tax). August 2026 recorded the year’s highest monthly shipments, followed by a more than 5% month-on-month (MoM) decline in September. However, InfoLink expects shipments to resume growth in Q4 2026. The market is becoming less concentrated as mid-sized manufacturers expand their shipments. The combined market share of the top 10 manufacturers fell to a record low of 81.9%. CATL continued to lead the global rankings, followed by HiTHIUM, EVE Energy, CORNEX, and CALB. Together, these five manufacturers accounted for nearly 56.5% of global shipments. Among the notable changes in the rankings was CORNEX's rise to 4th position, a year after entering InfoLink’s global top 10. The company has also expanded its product portfolio with a battery energy storage system (BESS) featuring 588 Ah cells. Meanwhile, Sunwoda secured a place among the global top 10 suppliers, supported by its partnerships with major customers such as Sungrow and Huawei. Utility-Scale Energy Storage Utility-scale energy storage cell shipments, including commercial and industrial (C&I) applications, reached 650.30 GWh in the first three quarters of 2026, up 74.79% YoY. CATL, HiTHIUM, and EVE Energy occupied the top 3 positions in this segment, followed by CALB and BYD. Shipments in Q3 alone grew by more than 10% QoQ. The transition towards higher-capacity battery cells is progressing at different speeds among manufacturers. Leading manufacturers have started supplying 500+ Ah cells in large volumes. For some mid-sized manufacturers, however, production is still at the pilot stage. InfoLink expects shipments of these cells from mid-sized suppliers to pick up around Q2 2027. Several manufacturers have already introduced products based on higher-capacity cells. For instance, Pylontech began mass production of its 588 Ah and 601 Ah cells in September 2026, while HiTHIUM has introduced a utility-scale storage system based on 1,175 Ah cells (see HiTHIUM’s Prismatic LFP Cells, C&I ESS & Utility BESS At REI). Competition in this segment is also extending beyond China. LG Energy Solution, which rose to 9th position in utility-scale cell shipments in Q3 2026, has introduced a cell with dimensions similar to those of the 648 Ah cells already being mass-produced by leading Chinese manufacturers. Residential Energy Storage Residential energy storage cell shipments grew by 189.62% YoY to 91.22 GWh during 9M 2026. However, shipments declined by more than 15% QoQ in Q3. Great Power led residential storage cell shipment rankings for the first time, followed by REPT BATTERO and EVE Energy. Together, the three manufacturers accounted for more than 60% of all shipments in this segment. Residential storage is also seeing a shift toward higher-capacity cells. Alongside existing 100 Ah and 122 Ah cell formats, manufacturers are increasingly adopting 314 Ah and 392 Ah cells. InfoLink has raised its global energy storage cell shipment forecast for 2026 from 1,026 GWh to 1,043.5 GWh. The consultancy now expects shipments to reach 1,343.7 GWh in 2027, representing nearly 30% YoY growth.

The company develops a water-based zinc battery using polymer technology designed to absorb and deliver power quickly. HoriZn lists artificial intelligence data centers and commercial and industrial properties among the applications for its technology. New investors contributed 60% of the capital raised. The financing also included continued backing from investor directors Lord Michael Spencer and Michael Alen Buckley. The financing will support its next phase of growth and plans for battery manufacturing. HoriZn also received its first grant through Innovate UK’s Battery Innovation Program. The £300,000 (~$400,000) funding will support deploying the company’s battery technology at a U.K. data center in early 2027. Jane Hunter, CEO of HoriZn, said, “I am delighted with the support the business received from investors in this successful bridge round. The company has an exciting year ahead as we run the battery through its paces in a working data center and scale for future manufacture. We recently moved to an innovation campus in Cambridge, which will enable us to build our groundbreaking technology to address customer problems that are not solved by lithium-ion. This additional investment will support us on the path to battery manufacture, while the grant from InnovateUK directly supports our first commercial deployment.” HoriZn recently moved its office and laboratory operations to The Press, a science and innovation campus in Foxton, Cambridge. According to the company, the site can support a pilot production facility that could be developed as early as 2027. According to Mercom’s recently released 9M 2026 Funding and M&A for Energy Storage report, VC funding for energy storage companies in 9M 2026 totaled $5.4 billion across 79 deals, a 93% YoY increase compared to $2.8 billion across 56 deals in 9M 2025. artigo.texto: St. Cloud moves closer to data center moratorium Following a lengthy and, at times, heated debate, city leaders in St. Cloud failed to pass the data center policy and ordinance changes they had in front of them. It did approve moving forward more discussion, including setting a public hearing for Dec 21, surrounding placing a one-year moratorium on data centers. Still, some council members expressed concerns with the negative impact a moratorium would have on the city’s economic growth. The changes would have created a policy statement about data centers — which would have included how data centers would benefit the city and the importance of carefully considering projects to address community concerns — and ordinances to address several factors of any future projects. City staff said there are no proposed data centers in the city; this was just an effort to be prepared for future proposals, pointing to the city’s infrastructure, resources and desire to grow the city’s tax base as reasons data centers could be an important aspect of the city’s future. The policy statement would have also stressed the need to carefully consider all projects to “avoid projects with an unreasonable detrimental effect on surrounding properties and the environment.” The ordinance changes would have required developers to share how much energy and water they expect to use, where data centers can operate — including larger hyper-scale data centers being at least a quarter mile from homes — and the need for projects to have council support. In what was at times a convoluted meeting with council members trying to navigate proposed amendments and changes to the items in front of them, the council did not move forward with both the policy statement and ordinance changes. Many community members pushed back during the public hearing — most stressing the potential harmful impacts to the environment. Ahead of the meeting, some protested with signs outside city hall, including Sue Hanley, who’s called St. Cloud home for a year and a half with no plans to move. “What do they bring to the table? We know the resources they need, absolutely: energy, water, all kinds of things that are going to be taken from our community. What do we get in return for that sacrifice?” Hanley told 5 EYEWITNESS NEWS. Another big issue people have is with the tax breaks and subsidies that have been offered to data center projects across the state. We pressed the city, mayor and all city council members on whether the city has offered tax breaks and subsidies to data center developers or if it plans to do so in the future. Only the city administrator wrote back to us, sharing, “No, the City has not given any tax breaks or subsidies to any data centers.”

artigo.texto: Salt Lake adopts 180-day pause on data center development SALT LAKE CITY (KUTV) — The Salt Lake City Council adopted a temporary ordinance pausing data center development in the city for up to 180 days, giving officials time to study regulations for the industry. The council plans to use the pause to consult with residents, industry representatives, experts and other levels of government. From there, the council "intends to initiate formal petitions to amend the Salt Lake City Code to adopt zoning regulations pertaining to data centers." The 180-day period is the maximum allowed under state law, Councilwoman Victoria Petro said. The vote comes after permit applications for a proposed data center in Salt Lake City’s Northpoint area drew opposition from nearby residents. The ordinance will temporarily pause any progress on that and any other data center projects on Salt Lake City land. Dennis Bangerter, who lives across the street from the proposed site, said he believes development approvals are moving too quickly. “We’re just kind of caught in the middle of a puzzle that they’re trying to do too many things,” he said. Chris Souther, who lives nearby, said he has noticed more noise and air pollution as the neighborhood has changed. He says that has impacted more than just the quality of life, but also property value. "My life savings is gone because the city decided to commercialize to make a bigger tax base for themselves," Souther said. Petro said residents have not had enough input into the development of the data center industry. “You can’t leave our neighbors out of it,” she said. “You have to engage them.” Petro represents the area and said residents’ concerns about noise, light, energy use and water use will be part of the council’s review. “I am constantly working against clocks trying to preserve the sanity for my neighbors who want to stay," Petro said. Petro said the council will seek input from residents, experts and other stakeholders during the pause. She hopes the city will develop “an evidence-based, truth-based way to regulate an industry that could either be beneficial or harmful.” But Petro cautioned that the city may have limited ability to stop the Northpoint project. She said it is already vested and the landowners have the zoning they need. “We will struggle to even play defense,” Petro said. “The only way we can be sure things will be different is if our constituents and every other stakeholder comes to the table and finds a path forward.” Petro said the council is not inherently opposed to data centers, but is concerned about the speed of development, lack of information, and potential harm to residents, the environment and wildlife. “We are hostile to abuses of our environment and our neighbors that could make a project like this detrimental for time to come,” she said. _____

artigo.texto: Filiais da Blackstone Digital Infrastructure Trust Inc. (BXDC) assinaram em 11 de novembro de 2026 um acordo com entidades ligadas à Amazon para adquirir 75,1% de cada uma de duas joint ventures imobiliárias. As empresas conjuntas deteriam 13 data centers com capacidade total de 647 MW de potência de TI. A Blackstone anunciou o acordo em 16 de novembro: o valor bruto agregado informado para o portfólio é de US$ 5 bilhões, e o fechamento era esperado para o quarto trimestre de 2026, sujeito a condições. O documento protocolado na SEC detalha os termos da operação. Para entender o negócio, separe três papéis: participação nos imóveis, gestão das joint ventures e locação dos data centers. O que a BXDC pretende adquirir O acordo prevê que a BXDC fique com 75,1% de cada joint venture; as partes ligadas à Amazon manteriam os 24,9% restantes. No conjunto, as empresas deteriam nove edifícios no norte de Indiana e quatro no Mississippi. A taxa de capitalização inicial informada para a operação é de 7,0%. A compra envolve participações em empresas que deteriam os imóveis, não a transferência da operação de serviços de nuvem da AWS. O arranjo prevê que a Amazon continue como locatária do portfólio. Como seriam o financiamento e a locação A BXDC esperava aportar US$ 1,9 bilhão em recursos de seu IPO e levantar cerca de US$ 2,5 bilhões em novos empréstimos hipotecários non-recourse para cobrir as necessidades restantes da transação, inclusive custos. Esses valores descrevem o financiamento previsto no acordo. Os imóveis seriam alugados integralmente à Amazon Data Services, Inc. por contratos triple-net. O prazo inicial médio ponderado seria de 12 anos; com todas as extensões, o prazo médio ponderado chegaria a 32 anos. As extensões são opções, não uma garantia de que serão exercidas. O contrato prevê reajuste anual de 2,75%, e Amazon.com, Inc. garantiria as obrigações de pagamento do aluguel. Quem ocuparia os data centers e quem administraria as joint ventures A Amazon seria a locatária, enquanto o membro da empresa conjunta ligado à BXDC administraria os negócios e assuntos de cada joint venture. As partes locatárias ligadas à Amazon teriam direitos de aprovação sobre determinadas decisões importantes e fundamentais, conforme os termos do acordo protocolado na SEC. O contrato, portanto, trata separadamente da ocupação dos imóveis e da gestão das empresas conjuntas. Prazo e condições de fechamento Ao anunciar o acordo em 16 de novembro, a Blackstone informou que esperava concluí-lo no quarto trimestre de 2026, condicionado ao cumprimento das condições de fechamento. O contrato estabelece 31 de dezembro de 2026 como prazo-limite, sujeito a prorrogações. Se uma das partes deixar de concluir a operação quando estiver obrigada a fazê-lo, poderá haver uma taxa de rescisão de US$ 150 milhões, conforme as condições do contrato. A Blackstone apresentou a expectativa de fechamento junto com o anúncio da operação.

artigo.texto: The rapid expansion of data centers is adding pressure to the U.S. power grid heading into winter, as electricity demand climbs and extreme weather threatens to strain supplies. The North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC) warned in its new winter reliability assessment released on Wednesday that electricity demand continues to rise rapidly, driven in part by the growth of data centers and other large industrial loads. The increase comes as a strengthening El Niño climate pattern raises the prospect of extreme winter weather that could push some regions' power systems closer to their limits. “While the resource outlook has improved, the unpredictable weather of El Niño and rapid load growth present unique challenges this winter,” NERC President and CEO Jim Robb said in a press release announcing the assessment. “We anticipate operators will need everything in their tool kit—including requests for emergency support—to maintain reliable operations.” Read More on U.S. Newsweek reached out to NERC by email for comment on Wednesday. How Is Data Center Growth Affecting the U.S. Power Grid? Electricity demand is expected to increase in 21 of the 23 regions assessed by NERC this winter, reflecting widespread growth in power needs across much of North America. While data centers are not responsible for all the growth, NERC identifies their expansion alongside large industrial loads and broader electrification as factors driving demand higher. The challenge is that the grid must be able to meet that additional demand even during periods of extreme weather, when households and businesses may also be using considerably more electricity. However, data centers could also play a role during a grid emergency. If electricity supplies fall short, or are expected to, grid operators in areas with large loads can seek emergency authority from the Department of Energy to direct those customers to switch to backup generators as a last resort, reducing demand and helping avoid an energy shortfall. U.S. Power Grid Regions With ‘Elevated’ Risk This Winter The report found that several parts of North America could face reliability challenges under stressed conditions this winter. Quebec, the Canadian Maritimes and parts of the U.S. Southeast are classified as at elevated risk, while New England faces concerns tied to limited natural gas supplies and parts of the central U.S. face localized transmission constraints. No region was classified as high risk. The picture has shifted since last winter, when the Pacific Northwest and several other regions were among those facing elevated concerns. NERC’s assessment can change from year to year as electricity demand, available generation, imports and transmission conditions evolve. Where Is Data Center Growth Occurring Fastest in the U.S.? Despite growing pushback from some state leaders, including Texas Governor Greg Abbott and New York Governor Kathy Hochul, data center development continues to expand rapidly across the U.S. Major projects are underway in states, including Texas, Virginia, Utah, Ohio and Louisiana, as companies race to build the infrastructure needed to meet rapidly growing demand for artificial intelligence and cloud computing. Atlanta has overtaken Northern Virginia as the country's biggest market for data centers under construction, while Texas has emerged as a major center of the broader boom. El Niño Could Threaten U.S. Power Grid This Winter Despite growing demand from data centers, the greater uncertainty this winter comes from extreme weather, as El Niño increases the potential for disruptive cold, ice and storms in parts of the country, including southern areas less accustomed to severe winter conditions. Extreme cold can put power grids under pressure in several ways. Electricity demand rises as homes and businesses use more energy for heating, while freezing temperatures and ice can disrupt power plants, fuel supplies and other grid infrastructure. The risk can be especially pronounced in southern regions that historically have not had to design or prepare equipment for prolonged extreme cold. What Happens Next Grid operators have been urged to take the coming winter season seriously. “I am asking everyone in the power and natural gas sectors to ensure your operations are prepared for extreme cold and ice,” Robb said this week ahead of the assessment’s release. “Please be sure that you’re prepared, properly winterized and are actively monitoring conditions.” Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Anna Skinner and Dave Siminoff.

artigo.texto: Here’s How Much Electricity Powerful Data Centers Use A new study reveals the environmental costs of hyperscale data centers—most of which are powered by fossil fuels such as coal and natural gas. Across the country, large data centers have become a charged political issue. But basic information, including how much energy they use and how much pollution they emit, has been largely lacking. A paper recently published in the journal Nature Sustainability documents the consumption and output of the largest and most powerful data centers across the United States. Those roughly 400 hyperscale centers use almost as much electricity in a year as massive, mature industries like steel and aluminum and even as much as all the collective homes, businesses, and facilities in some individual states. “It's pretty extraordinary—a few hundred buildings are consuming as much as an entire state,” says Gianluca Guidi, a data scientist at Harvard’s T.H. Chan School of Public Health and the study’s lead author. Most of the electricity comes from burning fossil fuels, causing the combined centers to emit more than 25 million metric tons of carbon dioxide (CO2) a year, the study found. Carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas largely responsible for climate change. (Solar panels that plug into your wall are about to be everywhere.) Hundreds more hyperscale data centers, each of which contain tens of thousands of computer servers that power the artificial intelligence industry and cloud computing, are planned or under construction, so their electricity demands are poised to grow significantly, Guidi says. “Communities and policymakers need reliable, independent data on what these facilities mean for our air, health, and the climate. This study is an important step,” Gina McCarthy, the former administrator of the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, said in a statement. The researchers calculated the number of hyperscale centers using a database from a commercial research company along with satellite imagery documenting their size. Then, using the research company’s information along with their own calculations of size and operating hours, they estimated annual electricity consumption for each facility. Finally, data from the Environmental Protection Agency revealed the mix of electricity sources used by utilities serving each center. The study covers the year between May of 2024 and April 2025. Collectively, the centers required between 68 and 99 terawatt-hours of electricity (a terawatt is a trillion watts) during the study year. Roughly half, 54 percent, came from fossil fuels, including natural gas (38 percent) and coal (15 percent). Another 21 percent used nuclear energy, and a quarter employed hydropower, solar, wind, and other renewables. Prior to this calculation, the last estimate quantifying hyperscale centers’ energy consumption published in a scientific journal appeared five years ago, using data from 2018. It calculated cumulative energy use then at 23 terawatt hours. “This was before the AI boom rapidly expanded the number of these centers. Our data shows it’s now at least three time higher,” says Francesca Dominici, a Harvard data scientist and coauthor of the paper. The earlier research also found carbon emissions were roughly three times lower than they are now. The implications of this much electricity consumption go beyond the strain many electric grids are currently experiencing. The study authors say their future research will study how much these data centers take a toll on human health. Research clearly links emissions from fossil-fuel-based energy generation with changes to the climate, as well as health harms like lung and heart disease. Even low levels of chronic exposure to pollution, including from fossil-fuel power plants, damages the heart, according to a study published in July in the journal Radiology. Cardiac computed tomography (CT) scans that had been performed in more than 11,000 Canadians concluded those living in areas with higher fine particulate pollution have more calcium plaque and artery obstruction. This occurred even in places where the particulate matter fell below allowable government standards. “There was no lower level at which we didn't see an association, which indicates there may be really no safe level of air pollution exposure,” says Kate Hanneman, a cardiac radiologist at the University of Toronto, who conducted the research. (Debunking three myths about air pollution.) Exposure to emissions from coal-powered plants—some 15 percent of the hyperscale centers’ energy consumption—may be particularly harmful, says Corwin Zigler, an environmental scientist at Brown University. Older people exposed to its sulfur-dioxide-laden pollutants have especially high death rates, Zigler reported in Science in 2023. In recent years, coal plants have installed technologies reducing their emissions, but “still, the burden is not zero,” Zigler says. The Nature Sustainability study found very large data centers are concentrated in specific parts of the country, with four states—Virginia, Oregon, Ohio, and Iowa—consuming more than half of the electricity use reported. This concentration means some locations bear more burden than others. Research published last year by the same authors, examining computer centers mining for bitcoins, found higher concentrations of particulate pollution in some regions of the country. Some of that pollution remained close to the data centers, but other particulates appeared hundreds of miles away, thanks to wind and atmospheric patterns that disperse them. Similarly, coal power pollution impacts health far from the plant locations. “If you live in Boston, some of that pollution you're breathing came from Ohio or Kentucky or Missouri or Indiana,” Zigler says of his research. artigo.texto: 13/11/2026 A Abeeólica (Associação Brasileira de Energia Eólica) pretende apresentar uma ADI (Ação Direta de Inconstitucionalidade) no STF (Supremo Tribunal Federal) para questionar o custeio do leilão de baterias, disseram fontes à Agência iNFRA. Pelas regras atuais, os encargos da contratação dos sistemas de armazenamento serão pagos apenas pelos geradores. Mesmo com o risco de um “desgaste político”, os agentes temem que o leilão marcado para dezembro ocorra com “fragilidades regulatórias”, de acordo com interlocutores. Também está previsto que empresas associadas entrem com uma ACP (Ação Civil Pública) na Justiça pedindo a suspensão do certame até a aprovação do PL (Projeto de Lei) 3.716/2026, que compartilha os encargos com os consumidores. O objetivo, de acordo com fontes, é pressionar pela rápida tramitação do projeto no Congresso. A estratégia foi aprovada no conselho da Abeeólica há cerca de três semanas, mas foi decidido que só dariam andamento a ela após se certificarem de que o PL não seria aprovado a tempo do certame. Segundo fontes, a expectativa era que o projeto fosse debatido na reunião de líderes partidários da Câmara dos Deputados na última terça-feira (10) e votado no plenário nesta quinta-feira (12). Isso viabilizaria a apreciação no Senado na próxima semana. A matéria, no entanto, não entrou na pauta da Câmara. O leilão está previsto para 2 e 4 de dezembro. Relatório Contribui para a percepção de risco do setor a probabilidade de que outros temas do setor sejam incluídos na matéria. Isso poderia atrasar ainda mais a aprovação do texto. A avaliação de fontes é que há margem para uma tentativa de rever pontos debatidos na MP (Medida Provisória) 1.304, transformada na Lei da Reforma do Setor Elétrico (Lei 15.269/2025). O PL está sob relatoria do deputado Danilo Forte (PP-CE), próximo a pautas de agentes renováveis, mas que não são consensuais no setor e entre os parlamentares. Um dos principais temas já defendidos pelo deputado é a ampliação do ressarcimento financeiro aos geradores pelo curtailment (cortes de geração obrigatórios). Ele conseguiu aprovar uma emenda na Câmara durante a tramitação da MP 1.304, mas que foi vetada pelo presidente Lula. Outros temas que podem estar no relatório, como circula nos bastidores, são a obrigatoriedade de que projetos de hidrogênio verde contratem energia de usinas novas ou recém-construídas, além do retorno dos incentivos nos custos dos fios de transmissão para fontes renováveis. Apesar de serem pautas benéficas às eólicas, segundo fontes, a Abeeólica defende que o relatório do PL 3.716 fique livre de temas polêmicos. Isso facilitaria a aprovação de forma célere, sem colocar em risco a realização do certame na data prevista. Mudanças no edital O diretor-geral da ANEEL (Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica), Sandoval Feitosa, disse à imprensa que qualquer modificação legal sobre o leilão iria requerer o adiamento do certame. Segundo ele, a reguladora precisaria de prazo para ajustes no edital. No MME (Ministério de Minas e Energia), no entanto, a percepção é que o edital aprovado não exige alterações caso o custeio seja estendido aos consumidores, disseram fontes. Existe ainda a possibilidade de incluir no projeto que tramita no Congresso emenda para dispensar a ANEEL do prazo necessário para modificações no edital. Contudo, há relatos de resistências a isso. Posição do governo O governo federal evitou apoio ao PL antes das eleições, pelo risco de ter atrelado a si o discurso de aumento de custos aos consumidores de energia elétrica. No entanto, técnicos do MME estariam alinhados à proposta, de acordo com fontes. O tema também foi levado à Casa Civil, que teria solicitado aos geradores um estudo comprovando que a medida não seria prejudicial aos consumidores e de que forma contribuiria para o sistema elétrico. Segundo relatos, a avaliação é que o órgão da Presidência da República estaria mais sensibilizado à pauta. Fonte: Agência Infra

artigo.texto: Flow battery manufacturers are expanding grid-scale energy storage capacity as utilities seek alternatives to lithium-ion batteries for six- to twelve-hour electricity storage. Dalian Rongke Power, Sumitomo Electric, Invinity Energy Systems, CellCube, VRB Energy, ESS Tech, VFlowTech, H2 Inc., Delectrik Systems, CMBlu Energy, Jena Flow Batteries and Elestor are competing through vanadium, iron, organic and hydrogen-based technologies. Flow batteries store energy in electrolytes and use electrochemical stacks to convert it into electricity. Unlike conventional lithium-ion batteries, their power capacity and energy capacity can be expanded relatively independently. This architecture is attractive for renewable energy integration, grid balancing and long-duration storage. However, manufacturing costs, round-trip efficiency, pumping losses, project financing and maintenance determine commercial competitiveness. 1. Dalian Rongke Power: 1 GWh Vanadium Battery Operating in China Dalian Rongke Power has one of the largest disclosed vanadium redox flow battery portfolios. Its 200 MW / 1,000 MWh CTG Jimusaer project in Xinjiang reached full-capacity operation at the end of 2025. Other references include Xinhua Wushi at 175 MW / 700 MWh and the first 100 MW / 400 MWh phase of Dalian ConCurrent, commissioned in 2022. Rongke also delivered a 12 MW / 60 MWh Panzhihua installation using leased vanadium electrolyte. These four references total 475 MW / 2,160 MWh, although they have different commissioning histories. Electrolyte leasing may reduce initial capital requirements, but customers must evaluate recurring payments and residual-value provisions. 2. Sumitomo Electric: Operating VRFB Projects and 20-Year Service Contract Japan’s Sumitomo Electric has extensive experience in vanadium flow batteries. Its Minami-Hayakita references include a 17 MW / 51 MWh system operating since April 2022 and a separate 15 MW / 60 MWh demonstration system continuing commercial operation. At Kashiwazaki, completed phases total 24 MWh, with another 1 MW / 8 MWh installation scheduled for spring 2027. Sumitomo also secured an 11 MW / 33 MWh Minami-Hayakita project for completion by May 2029, including a 20-year service agreement. The Sumitomo Electric project announcement details its latest contract and operating references. Long-term maintenance commitments are important because flow batteries require pumps, membranes, sensors and stack servicing. 3. Invinity Energy Systems: 77.2 MWh Orders and 12.5 GWh Pipeline UK-based Invinity Energy Systems supplies VS3 and Endurium vanadium flow battery platforms. The company reported 34.2 MWh of customer orders in the first half of 2026. A subsequent 43 MWh Dairyland Power contract increased secured 2026 orders to 77.2 MWh. Its prospective project pipeline exceeded 12.5 GWh, while the global installed fleet had cumulatively dispatched 11 GWh of electricity. The 20.7 MWh Copwood system had been delivered, although grid connection and full commissioning remained pending at the interim reporting date. Invinity targets a 66 percent product-cost reduction for Endurium deliveries in 2027. Its 2026 interim financial results distinguish confirmed orders from prospective opportunities. The main investment considerations are manufacturing costs, gross margins, cash requirements and delivery performance. 4. CellCube: Modular Vanadium Storage and Electrolyte Recovery CellCube, associated with Austrian developer Enerox, provides modular vanadium flow battery technology. Its systems separate electrolyte storage from electrochemical stacks, allowing developers to configure discharge duration. Vanadium electrolyte can retain recoverable material value, potentially supporting end-of-life economics. However, electrolyte tanks, pumps, civil construction and electrical infrastructure increase upfront costs. Customers should verify current manufacturing arrangements, completed installations, stack replacement costs and warranty responsibility. 5. VRB Energy: Vanadium Batteries for Renewable Integration VRB Energy develops vanadium flow battery systems for stationary storage and renewable electricity integration. The company has been associated with projects in China and international markets. Its commercial assessment requires distinguishing technology ownership, manufacturing responsibilities and project warranties. Relevant indicators include commissioned capacity, actual production, customer references, electrolyte supply and technical service coverage. Prospective projects should not be treated as operating installations or secured revenue. 6. ESS Tech: Iron Flow Batteries Target Lower Material Costs US-based ESS Tech develops aqueous iron flow batteries using relatively abundant materials. Its technology targets long-duration electricity storage without relying on vanadium or lithium-ion cell chemistry. Iron-based systems may reduce exposure to certain critical mineral prices. However, lower raw-material costs do not automatically translate into cheaper delivered electricity. Manufacturing yields, energy efficiency, operating availability, maintenance and stack durability remain important. Buyers should request independently verified operating hours, delivered energy, degradation and warranty information. 7. VFlowTech: Singapore-Based Modular Vanadium Batteries VFlowTech develops vanadium redox flow battery systems for commercial, industrial and grid applications. Its modular approach targets renewable energy integration and longer-duration electricity storage. Potential revenue streams include battery equipment, energy management software, installation and maintenance. For tropical markets such as India and Southeast Asia, customers should examine cooling requirements, auxiliary consumption and performance at high ambient temperatures. Commercial expansion will depend on repeat orders, local service partners, manufacturing scale and financing. 8. H2 Inc.: South Korean Vanadium Flow Battery Techn

artigo.texto: Portugal has opened two tenders offering a combined 1,050 MVA of grid capacity for energy storage Of the total, standalone batteries account for 750 MVA, while renewable projects with co-located storage receive 300 MVA Applications will be accepted till December 22, 2026, according to DGEG Portugal has opened two competitive tenders offering a combined 1,050 MVA of grid connection capacity for energy storage projects as the country expands battery storage deployment. The tenders, launched by Portugal’s Directorate-General for Energy and Geology (DGEG), allocate 750 MVA for standalone battery energy storage systems (BESS) and 300 MVA for renewable power generation projects with co-located storage. Developers can apply for a minimum capacity of 50 MVA per application. There is no maximum capacity limit per applicant. Applications for both tenders must be submitted by December 22, 2026. The 750 MVA tender is designed exclusively for standalone battery storage installations across different grid connection points. Developers will bid for capacity and indicate their preferred grid connection locations. Projects must have installed storage power equivalent to at least 100% of their awarded grid injection capacity. They must also provide a minimum of four hours of storage at maximum injection power. The second 300 MVA tender is for renewable energy generation projects paired with battery storage. The storage component must have a minimum power rating equivalent to 20% of the awarded grid injection capacity. It must also provide at least four hours of storage at maximum injection power. The tender includes additional consideration for agrivoltaic projects that combine solar power generation with agricultural activities on the same land. The framework also provides financial benefits to municipalities hosting the projects. Local authorities will receive a share of auction revenues and annual compensation from project developers. The two tenders are part of Portugal’s broader efforts to strengthen electricity storage, improve grid flexibility and support renewable energy integration. Portugal’s National Energy Storage Strategy sets a target of 6.9 GW of installed storage capacity by 2030.

artigo.texto: Duke Energy plans to invest up to $756 million in two massive battery storage facilities in eastern North Carolina, a move the utility says could help keep electricity reliable and reduce costs for customers as demand for power continues to grow. The projects, announced Tuesday, Nov. 17, will be built next to Duke's existing H.F. Lee natural gas plant in Goldsboro. Together, they will provide 410 megawatts of battery storage capacity, more than doubling the amount Duke currently operates across North Carolina. Other WRAL Top Stories The announcement comes one day after the North Carolina Utilities Commission approved Duke Energy's updated long-term energy plan, which calls for major investments in natural gas, solar power, battery storage, and potential new nuclear generation. How could batteries save customers money? Unlike traditional power plants, batteries don't generate electricity. Instead, they store energy when it's available and release it when demand rises. That flexibility could help Duke manage growing electricity needs without relying as heavily on more expensive sources of power during peak periods. In an email to WRAL, Duke Energy spokesperson Bill Norton explained that batteries can store surplus solar energy generated on sunny afternoons and release it during periods of high demand, including cold winter mornings before the sun rises. Norton said that reduces the need to purchase electricity from neighboring utilities or operate less efficient power plants, ultimately lowering fuel costs. Battery storage can also make renewable energy more useful by allowing solar power generated during the day to be used after sunset. The Wayne County facilities will use four-hour lithium-ion batteries, meaning they can deliver their full rated output for up to four hours before needing to recharge. Duke has not provided a specific estimate of how much the Wayne County projects could save customers on their electricity bills. Federal tax credits help offset costs Duke says the Wayne County investment qualifies for a 50% federal tax credit because of its location in an energy community and its use of domestically manufactured components. The company is also prioritizing former coal plant sites for battery storage projects because they already have land and transmission infrastructure, reducing the need for additional construction. "To lower costs for our customers, we're prioritizing former coal plant sites like this, which have available land and transmission infrastructure," Norton told WRAL. The new facilities will be located near the H.F. Lee natural gas plant, on a site with a history of coal-fired electricity generation. While the federal incentives will reduce eligible project costs, the company has not detailed how much of the remaining investment customers will ultimately pay through electricity rates. Part of Duke Energy's larger energy strategy Duke currently operates 308 megawatts of battery storage across 14 facilities in North Carolina. Its largest existing facility is a 100-megawatt installation in Knightdale, which WRAL toured in March. Duke confirmed the Wayne County projects will use the same type of battery containers and technology as the Knightdale facility. "We want more renewables on the grid. We want all of that diverse mix that we have," Duke Energy spokesperson Jeff Brooks said. "It will take all of that, from carbon-free nuclear to natural gas to hydro renewables to battery storage." The newly approved Carbon Plan and Integrated Resource Plan calls for up to 5,400 megawatts of battery storage across Duke's Carolinas system by 2034, including 2,700 megawatts of additional storage beyond previously approved plans. The plan also includes new solar generation, additional natural gas plants, and continued development work on potential nuclear facilities. Environmental advocates have questioned the plan's continued reliance on natural gas, arguing that greater investments in renewable energy and energy efficiency could help reduce costs. Battery storage offers one way to make solar power more flexible, although batteries must be charged using electricity generated elsewhere and cannot replace all the functions of conventional power plants. What's next for the Wayne County project? Construction is expected to begin in early 2027. The first facility will have 260 megawatts of capacity and is scheduled to begin operating in fall 2028. A second, 150-megawatt facility is expected to be completed by the end of that year. The investment could generate up to $2 million in additional annual property tax revenue for Wayne County, according to Duke Energy. The company already pays approximately $5.8 million annually in local taxes for its existing energy infrastructure. Nine permanent jobs are expected to support the new batteries and other regional solar and storage facilities. Duke is also expanding battery storage at the former Allen coal plant near Charlotte, where approximately 400 megawatts of storage is planned by late 2028. The first 50-megawatt installation began serving customers last year. As electricity demand grows across North Carolina, these investments could help utilities make better use of existing power supplies while larger generation projects are developed. For customers already facing rising electricity bills, the question is whether those improvements will translate into measurable savings.

artigo.texto: Elon Musk Tesla’s Powercore could change how data centers get power Tesla unveiled Powercore, a solid-state transformer that could ease one of the grid’s worst bottlenecks. Tesla has unveiled Powercore, a solid-state medium voltage transformer that also handles the jobs of an inverter and a circuit breaker in a single unit. “Solid state medium voltage transformer, inverter and breaker – reliable, safe and secure,” the company’s Tesla Megapack account posted on X Tuesday, adding that the product is “Made in America” and will be “Operating 2027.” Elon Musk followed with his own post: “Advanced solid state transformers at scale from Tesla.” Tesla rates Powercore at 7.4 MW, or 9 MVA, of continuous output at 34.5 kV AC, with grid-forming support for 10 MVA of peak power. Specs shared by Sawyer Merritt list a peak efficiency of 98.86 percent, a DC range of 800 to 2,000 volts and a built-in solid-state breaker that clears faults in about 100 microseconds. Tesla has not announced pricing, a factory location or a first customer. The product fills a gap Tesla left open last year. When it introduced Megapack 3 and Megablock in September 2025, Tesla said it would build its own transformers, but shared almost nothing about them. Megablock groups four Megapack 3 units with a transformer and switchgear into a single medium voltage block, as Teslarati reported. Powercore appears to be that missing piece. A typical battery or solar project today uses low voltage inverters to turn DC into AC, then a large oil-filled transformer to step that power up to grid voltage. A solid-state unit handles both steps with power electronics, which means less equipment, a smaller footprint and no flammable oil. Grid-forming capability lets it actively help hold voltage and frequency steady rather than simply following the grid. Introducing Powercore Solid state medium voltage transformer, inverter and breaker – reliable, safe and secure 7.4 MW/9 MVA continuously at 34.5 kVac w/ grid-forming support for 10MVA of peak power Made in America. Operating 2027 https://t.co/sHxqnpWJrf — Tesla Megapack (@Tesla_Megapack) November 17, 2026 Timing is a big part of the pitch. Lead times for conventional transformers have stretched into years as AI data centers and renewable projects crowd utility interconnection queues. Tesla energy executive Max de Zegher pointed to the problem in a post Musk shared, noting that “transformers have barely changed since the 1890s: copper coils in a tank of oil,” while batteries, solar and compute all run on DC. Powercore, he wrote, delivers “one conversion and about half the losses.” Tesla has also said its Megapack supply for 2027 is nearly sold out. Tesla deployed 13.7 GWh of energy storage in the third quarter, its second best quarter on record. On Tuesday, the company also said customer solar systems deployed by Tesla Energy now generate more than twice the electricity its global operations consume each year.

artigo.texto: Superando desafios e abraçando o superciclo de investimentos em data centers. Segundo Do Thanh Thang, Diretor de Otimização de Operações para o Leste Asiático da Schneider Electric, os data centers em todo o mundo estão apresentando um forte crescimento. Este também é o momento em que o mercado está entrando em um super ciclo de investimentos. O rápido desenvolvimento da inteligência artificial ( IA ), da computação em nuvem e da economia digital está transformando os centros de dados, de meras infraestruturas de armazenamento em plataformas essenciais para a economia digital. À medida que a IA se desenvolve, a demanda por poder computacional, armazenamento, conectividade e processamento de dados aumenta, exigindo que a infraestrutura dos centros de dados seja moderna, flexível e escalável. Em seu discurso no recente seminário "Data Centers no Vietnã: Infraestrutura Estratégica para a Era da IA", organizado pelo jornal Industry and Trade Newspaper, o Sr. Ha Dang Son, Presidente do Centro de Pesquisa em Energia e Crescimento Verde, afirmou que a tendência de transformação digital e a revolução digital são necessidades urgentes para o Vietnã e a região no período vindouro. Segundo pesquisadores do mundo todo, o mercado de data centers e serviços relacionados à digitalização e inteligência artificial na região Ásia-Pacífico representa atualmente cerca de 34% da demanda global, sendo que a ASEAN sozinha responde por aproximadamente metade desse valor. A tendência de digitalização e desenvolvimento de data centers já está presente em países vizinhos como Singapura , Tailândia e Malásia. No entanto, o Vietnã é considerado um dos países de crescimento mais rápido da região. “Isso também representa um desafio significativo para o investimento em infraestrutura e a preparação de serviços relacionados para garantir o desenvolvimento. Os investimentos em data centers devem assegurar sustentabilidade e competitividade com outros países da região”, afirmou Ha Dang Son. O Sr. Ha Dang Son analisou que, com o aumento da densidade e da eficiência dos centros de dados, a densidade energética por rack disparou em comparação com o passado, chegando a ser de 3 a 4 vezes maior. Para modelos específicos, o nível é ainda mais alto (podendo atingir 1 MW para uma única unidade de gerenciamento de dados). "Isso levanta a questão de como ainda podemos criar centros de dados altamente eficientes, garantindo simultaneamente um fornecimento de energia sustentável que esteja alinhado com a tendência verde emergente", afirmou o Sr. Son. Além disso, o sistema de refrigeração (que representa aproximadamente 20-30% do consumo de energia) também precisa ser otimizado. Este é um problema relacionado ao planejamento e à seleção dos padrões mais adequados às características específicas do Vietnã, visto que cada país terá características diferentes dependendo da localização do data center. Do ponto de vista de uma unidade de investimento e operação de data centers, o Sr. Nguyen Tien Long, Diretor Adjunto de Negócios da FPT International Telecommunications Co., Ltd. (FTI), uma subsidiária da FPT Telecom, identificou três tendências em mudança nos sistemas de data center que atendem à IA. Você também pode gostar Em primeiro lugar, a eficiência energética por unidade de área, bem como por utilização de racks, aumentou significativamente nos últimos tempos. Em segundo lugar, o investimento em sistemas de refrigeração é necessário para atender às demandas de sistemas de computação de alto desempenho. O Sr. Long explicou que estávamos acostumados com data centers tradicionais que utilizavam sistemas de refrigeração a ar. No entanto, para data centers de alta densidade, precisamos migrar para um novo sistema chamado Refrigeração Líquida. Em terceiro lugar, esses sistemas exigem velocidades de conexão muito altas. Antes, nos conectávamos a 1G, 10G ou até mesmo 100G, mas agora precisamos de conexões de 800G ou 1 Terabit. Segundo o Sr. Long, os atuais centros de dados do Vietnã utilizam principalmente refrigeração a ar. Portanto, o desafio é a modernização para um novo sistema de refrigeração líquida, bem como a atualização de outros componentes dentro do centro de dados. Isso apresenta desafios técnicos significativos e exige um cronograma de implementação rigoroso para atender às demandas dos clientes e do mercado. 60% dos novos centros de dados serão destinados a aplicações de IA. A respeito desse assunto, o Sr. Do Thanh Thang, Diretor de Otimização de Operações para o Leste Asiático da Schneider Electric, afirmou o forte desenvolvimento de data centers em todo o mundo. Segundo o Sr. Thang, estamos em um superciclo de investimentos em data centers. O relatório mais recente da JLL, do início de 2026, indica que o mundo deverá adicionar aproximadamente 100 GW de data centers globalmente entre agora e 2030, o que representa uma duplicação da capacidade. Desse total, 60% dos novos data centers atenderão aplicações de IA. “Em países vizinhos, já surgiram grandes data centers (também conhecidos como fábricas de IA). Essas fábricas de IA são projetadas especificamente para atender a todas as necessidades ao longo do ciclo de vida da aplicação de IA, desde o treinamento e o refinamento até a consulta e a inferência”, explicou o Sr. Thang. Como parceira global em tecnologia de energia, a Schneider Electric observa um forte impacto dessa onda de investimentos nas necessidades de fornecimento de energia, sistemas de refrigeração e gerenciamento de energia para data centers. Você também pode gostar O Sr. Do Thanh Thang salientou que a densidade de potência normal atual ronda os 5 a 10 kW por rack, mas que será muito superior no futuro. Os fabricantes já estão mesmo a considerar um cenário de 1 MW por rack. Além disso, os centros de dados de IA operam de maneira muito diferente dos centros de dados convencionais. Por exemplo, o treinamento de IA exige a mobilização de um número muito grande de chips de GPU, às vezes milhares funcionando simultanea

artigo.texto: State environmental regulators have resumed reviewing data center permits, bringing an end to an earlier directive from Gov. Greg Abbott ordering a pause on permit approvals related to data center projects. The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality received notice on Friday from Abbott’s office that officials at the state’s electric grid had completed gathering information on potential community impacts from data centers — one of multiple issues Abbott asked grid officials and electricity regulators to evaluate. “The agency has resumed its normal permit review process and will evaluate applications under all applicable state and federal laws and regulations,” TCEQ spokesperson Laura Lopez said in a written statement. In August, Abbott had called on the Electric Reliability Council of Texas and electricity regulators to audit all data centers trying to connect to the grid, as well as gather information about tax incentives, power use, water use and potential neighborhood impacts. Abbott at that time paused approval of any grid interconnections for data centers while the audit was completed. In his Sept. 21 letter to TCEQ calling for the environmental permitting pause, Abbott said the agency needed to wait until ERCOT “completes its review.” Environmental advocates at Public Citizen, responding to the news of the resumed permits, called on TCEQ commissioners to resign. “The TCEQ is asserting that ERCOT has concluded its assessment of the community impacts of data centers, and without sharing those results with communities or detailing how the TCEQ will incorporate the findings into permitting decisions, agency leadership has begun unilaterally issuing data center permits,” said Kathryn Guerra, the TCEQ watchdog campaign director for Public Citizen, in a statement. Intense opposition to data centers had been growing all year in communities across the state, where Democrats and Republicans alike fought projects they worried would destabilize the electric grid, lead to more pollution from new gas-fueled power generators and guzzle up water in a state with serious drought concerns. TCEQ handles permits related to air pollution at facilities and stormwater runoff on construction sites. The agency faced criticism in October from Public Citizen and FracTracker Alliance. The groups noticed that some data center-related construction permits were being cleared anyway — counter to Abbott’s order. TCEQ said it suspended the permits and then it shut down its entire automated electronic filing system and required physical applications be submitted for staff to review. Then in a staggering upset on Nov. 3, Abbott lost his reelection to Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who on the campaign trail vowed to keep data center approvals paused until legislators pass new state laws. Neither Abbott’s office nor Hinojosa’s media team on Tuesday immediately responded to a request for comment. “Texans are tired of this political theatre,” said Sam Law, researcher at FracTracker Alliance, in a written statement shared by Public Citizen. “We need real leadership, transparency, and a true moratorium on data center development.” ERCOT provided an update on its review of community impacts to electric regulators at the Public Utility Commission of Texas on Nov. 5. ERCOT reported receiving responses from 93% of 465 projects, which provided enough information for “a statistically meaningful analysis for the final report.” ERCOT officials plan to report their full findings to the PUC on Dec. 10 and discuss them at the next PUC open meeting Dec. 17.

artigo.texto: Maharashtra’s emissions trading scheme is being presented as a way to make industrial pollution control financially meaningful rather than relying only on penalties and restrictions. Announced at an Impact Assembly in Mumbai organised by The Earthshot Prize, the proposed expansion will initially cover Maharashtra before being extended to Rajasthan, according to a report by Loksatta – Mumbai. The initiative is expected by its proponents to help improve air quality for about 21 crore people across the two states. The central idea is to place an overall limit on the pollution that participating factories can emit and allow permits linked to unused pollution capacity to be traded. A factory that emits less than its permitted level could sell its surplus allowance to another industrial unit. In theory, this creates two simultaneous pressures: cleaner factories can gain financially, while factories that continue to emit more face a higher economic cost. That design changes the logic of industrial regulation. Conventional enforcement generally focuses on setting standards, inspecting facilities and penalising violations. An emissions market adds a price signal to those requirements. The purpose is not to make pollution acceptable, but to make pollution reduction financially valuable and continued high emissions financially burdensome. Whether that shift produces cleaner air will depend on how the cap is set, how emissions are measured and how consistently the system is enforced. The supplied announcement does not provide those operational details. The model is based on Gujarat’s experience, which the report describes as a successful experiment and as the world’s first system to establish an economic trading mechanism around industrial pollution. Under the model, factories receive an overall pollution limit. Units that remain below their limits can trade their unused permissions, while units that exceed their own reduction capacity can bear the cost of acquiring additional permissions. The arrangement is intended to reward investment in pollution-control equipment and production systems. A factory that reduces particulate emissions could potentially create a tradable surplus, giving it a financial return in addition to the environmental benefit. The incentive is therefore different from a rule that simply requires every unit to install the same equipment or meet the same reduction pathway. It attempts to direct reductions towards facilities that can achieve them more efficiently, although the source material does not specify how the Maharashtra programme will identify those facilities. Particulate matter is the immediate pollution concern identified in the announcement. Fine particles released by industrial activity contribute to deteriorating air quality, and industrial development can intensify that problem when emissions controls do not keep pace with production. The Maharashtra proposal thus links industrial policy with urban and regional public health. The impact will not be confined to factory premises: emissions move through the air sheds in which workers, nearby communities and urban residents live. This is particularly important for a state with large industrial and urban regions, but the announcement does not identify the districts, industrial clusters or categories of factories that will enter the first phase. It also does not state the number of facilities to be covered, the initial emissions cap, the particulate pollutants to be traded or the date on which trading will begin. Those details are not peripheral. They will determine whether the scheme operates as a meaningful reduction programme or merely as a compliance mechanism with limited effect on actual air quality. The institutional arrangement announced so far places the Emissions Market Accelerator in a supporting role. The organisation will assist with expanding the Gujarat model to Maharashtra and later Rajasthan. The report does not identify the precise responsibilities of the Maharashtra government, the Maharashtra Pollution Control Board or other regulatory bodies in administering the market. It also does not specify who will issue allowances, verify factory emissions, maintain the trading platform or impose consequences for inaccurate reporting. Those administrative functions are central to the credibility of any pollution market. A tradable allowance has value only when the underlying emissions data are reliable and when the total quantity of allowances is controlled. If a factory’s emissions are under-measured, its apparent compliance may not reflect its actual pollution. If the overall cap is too generous, trading can continue without delivering a significant reduction. If enforcement is inconsistent, firms that invest in cleaner technology may not receive the expected economic advantage. The announcement’s reference to approximately 21 crore people is a measure of the proposed geographic reach rather than evidence of an achieved health outcome. That figure combines the populations of Maharashtra and Rajasthan as the scheme is expanded. The supplied material does not include baseline air-quality data, projected particulate reductions, health indicators or an implementation timetable. It therefore establishes the scale of the policy ambition, but not yet its measurable environmental performance. The sequencing is also significant. Maharashtra is to receive the first phase of the expansion, followed by Rajasthan. This suggests that the programme will be adapted across states rather than introduced simultaneously. However, the report does not explain whether both states will use the same emissions limits, monitoring standards or trading rules. Differences in industrial composition, regulatory capacity and pollution sources could affect how the model works in each jurisdiction. artigo.texto: Canadian Solar’s energy storage subsidiary, e-STORAGE, has partnered with renewable energy developer X-ELIO to deploy 590 MW/1.43 GWh DC of battery energy storage capacity. This will be spread across five projects in the US and Australia. The projects include four installations in Texas and one in New South Wales. The largest project in the list is a 200 MW/482 MWh project in Texas. For all these projects, e-STORAGE will supply its SolBank 3.0 battery systems built using battery cells manufactured at Canadian Solar’s facilities, along with power conversion systems and plant controls. The projects include 22-year long-term service agreements (LTSA). Shipments are already underway, with commercial operations expected in 2027 and 2028. The duo announced the agreement at RE+ 2026. EDF power solutions Australia, the Australian arm of French energy company EDF, has acquired the Holloway BESS project from SynCo Global. The proposed 250 MW / 1,000 MWh facility will be located near Armidale in New South Wales, within the New England Renewable Energy Zone (REZ). The four-hour battery system will store excess renewable electricity and supply power during periods of peak demand. EDF targets a final investment decision for late 2027 and to commence operations in 2029. Coreshell Technologies has raised $30 million in a Series B funding round. The round was co-led by silicon and specialty alloys producer Ferroglobe and investment firm Access Industries, with participation from ADS, Helios Ventures, Pegasus Tech Ventures, Mana Ventures, and Entrada Ventures. Coreshell said the funding will support technology commercialization, manufacturing expansion, and customer programs as it seeks to scale ‘China-free’ batteries for US industries. A lithium-ion battery producer, Coreshell replaces conventional graphite anodes with US-produced metallurgical silicon (MGS). The company has also secured a $50 million grant from the US Department of Energy to support domestic battery manufacturing. In October 2026, Coreshell announced an eight-year agreement with South Korean cathode materials producer L&F to secure access to lithium for its cathode supply chain. Ferroglobe also supplies its anode materials. US-based NeoVolta has signed a $116 million master purchase agreement with an unnamed energy solutions provider to supply battery energy storage systems (BESS) in 2027. Its majority-owned subsidiary, NeoVolta Power will supply its systems that comply with Foreign Entity of Concern (FEOC) requirements. The agreement will support the company's manufacturing expansion at its facility in Pendergrass, Georgia, as it scales up domestic battery production. Japanese utility company Kansai Electric Power has agreed to acquire a minority stake in Prospect Power Storage, a 150 MW / 600 MWh battery energy storage project in Rockingham County, Virginia, US. It is making the investment through its US subsidiary, KPIC USA, from infrastructure developer Elevate Infrastructure and investment firm ArcLight Capital Partners. The project is the largest standalone battery storage facility currently operating in the PJM Interconnection region. The project has been operational since May 2026 and is backed by a 15-year power purchase agreement (PPA) with Dominion Energy Virginia. The investment marks Kansai’s first battery storage project outside Japan. China’s Envision Energy is partnering with German battery storage developer and operator ju:niz Energy for a 442 MWh battery energy storage system (BESS) in Bavaria, Germany. Named Smareg 13 (Vöhringen II), the project will be the companies’ third collaboration, bringing their combined project capacity to nearly 600 MWh. ju:niz Energy will handle the project’s development, financing, construction and long-term operation, while Envision will supply its Gen 8 BESS platform. The system will offer four-hour storage duration and grid-forming capabilities. It will be located next to ju:niz Energy’s operational Smareg 12 facility. UK-based clean energy developer Pathfinder Clean Energy (PACE) has secured a £68 million portfolio financing facility from Novuna Business Finance. artigo.texto: According to a new SEIA & Benchmark Mineral Intelligence report US energy storage installations have exceeded 200 GWh Utility-scale projects accounted for 12.2 GWh of Q3 additions, led by Texas, Arizona, and California Analysts forecast cumulative installations to reach 708 GWh by 2030 The US energy storage market has crossed 200 GWh of cumulative installed capacity, as battery deployments continue to expand across all segments, as per a new report. The total 215.9 GWh includes 14.3 GWh of new capacity in Q3 2026, taking installations during the first nine months of the year to 48.3 GWh. The figures are from the U.S. Energy Storage Market Outlook Q4 2026 (ESMO), released by the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA) and Benchmark Mineral Intelligence. According to the report, utility-scale projects accounted for the bulk of Q3 installations, adding 12.2 GWh. Three GW-scale projects came online during the quarter, supporting growth in the utility-scale segment. Commercial and industrial (C&I) storage contributed 1.3 GWh, while residential systems added 746 MWh. The report said battery energy storage system (BESS) installations in Q3 at 14.3 GWh remained flat quarter-on-quarter (QoQ), but increased 23% year-on-year (YoY) for the first three quarters of 2026. Overall US installations were up 20% YoY during the January-September period. Texas led utility-scale storage deployment through Q3, adding 12.3 GWh. Arizona followed with 7.7 GWh, while California recorded 6.8 GWh. The report also highlighted the impact of solar and energy storage deployment on electricity prices. According to SEIA analysis, the growth of these technologies helped reduce average wholesale electricity prices by 42% in Texas and 51% in California between summer 2021 and summer 2026 (see Solar & Storage Cut Wholesale Electricity Prices In CAISO & ERCOT). Eleven states had already exceeded their previous annual energy storage installation records by the end of Q3, despite three months remaining in 2026. These included Colorado, Massachusetts, Utah, Michigan, Georgia, Mississippi, Virginia, Iowa, Montana, Alabama, and Illinois. As states move from targets to centralized procurements, Benchmark Minerals Senior Analyst Pete Tillotson says energy storage pipelines are growing across utility mandates and bulk capacity contracts, thanks to “investment appetite and flexibility requirements”. In 2026, analysts project the annual installed BESS capacity of the US to reach 73.8 GWh, up 26% from 59 GWh installed in 2025 which was an increase of 30% over the previous year, comprising both utility and behind-the-meter (BTM) installations. This implies around 26 GWh of new additions in Q4 2026. SEIA and Benchmark Mineral Intelligence have raised their forecast for cumulative installations by 2030 by 3.7% to 708 GWh across grid-connected and behind-the-meter (BTM) applications. Annual installations are projected to exceed 129 GWh by 2030. Along with installations, domestic manufacturing is also seeing an uptick as per the report. Ultim Cells of LGES and General Motors began Lithium-ion Phosphate (LFP) commenced cell production for stationary storage in Tennessee in July 2026, while Samsung SDI opened LFP production at its StarPlus Energy facility in Indiana in October. This brought the total US battery cell manufacturing capacity to 92.4 GWh, a 50% increase, according to the report. Battery module manufacturing capacity exceeded 109 GWh following the opening of an additional facility in Q3. Analysts forecast that LFP will account for 92% of lithium-ion BESS deployments in 2026, up from 77% in 2023. Lithium-ion batteries are expected to account for over 97% of all BESS installations in 2026. Other technologies, including flow batteries, sodium-ion and lead acid batteries, continue to lag behind lithium-ion. Recently US flow battery and sodium-ion cell manufacturer ESS Tech filed for relief under Chapter 7 (see US Battery Maker ESS Tech Files For Chapter 7 Bankruptcy). The complete report is available for purchase on Benchmark Mineral Intelligence website. Meanwhile on the policy front, following the results of the mid-term elections in the US, SEIA said more than 300 solar and storage companies recently urged Congressional leaders to pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA). The industry says the legislation could accelerate storage deployment, reduce project costs, lower prices, and improve access to affordable electricity.
