artigo.texto: Empresa suíça apresentou em Londres a estratégia para que a computação de IA deixe de pressionar a rede elétrica e passe a ajudar a sustentá-la. E se o prédio que mais consome energia de uma cidade pudesse, em certos momentos, devolver eletricidade para a rede? É essa a aposta que a Hitachi Energy, empresa suíça de tecnologia para redes elétricas, levou ao seu Investor Day, evento para investidores realizado em Londres em novembro de 2026. A ideia é transformar os data centers de inteligência artificial, hoje vistos como grandes consumidores, em contribuidores do sistema elétrico. O pano de fundo é uma corrida. A computação de IA pode ser instalada em pouco tempo, mas as usinas, linhas e subestações que a alimentam levam muito mais para ficar prontas. Esse descompasso é o problema que a empresa quer atacar. Um consumo que não para de crescer Segundo a Hitachi Energy, a demanda global por eletricidade deve quase dobrar até 2050, empurrada pela eletrificação de transportes, edifícios e indústrias. Os data centers entram como um acelerador extra: a estimativa é que consumam cerca de 950 terawatt-hora por ano até 2030, quase o dobro do nível atual e mais do que o consumo anual de eletricidade do Japão. Para dar conta disso, a Agência Internacional de Energia calcula que o mundo precisará construir ou modernizar aproximadamente 80 milhões de quilômetros de linhas de energia nos próximos 25 anos. É o equivalente a toda a rede global em operação hoje. Como um data center vira fornecedor de energia No modelo defendido pela empresa, o data center não depende só de uma grande conexão com a rede. Ele combina geração no próprio local, armazenamento de energia, eletrônica de potência (equipamentos que controlam e convertem a corrente elétrica) e gestão inteligente de consumo. Quando a geração local supera a demanda dos computadores, o excedente pode ser exportado. Esses sistemas também podem prestar serviços técnicos à rede, como resposta de frequência, regulação de tensão e suporte de potência reativa, o que ajuda a integrar mais energia renovável, que oscila conforme sol e vento. Para quem opera data centers, a empresa vê acesso mais rápido à energia, uso mais enxuto de capital, maior resiliência e novas receitas com venda de eletricidade e serviços de rede, sujeitas às condições de mercado de cada local. A parceria com a Ansaldo e o truque das frequências A solução nasce de uma parceria estratégica recém-anunciada com a Ansaldo Energia. A Ansaldo entra com turbinas a gás e geração; a Hitachi Energy, com transformadores, equipamentos de alta tensão, eletrônica de potência, armazenamento e automação de rede. Uma peça central é o conversor estático de frequência. Ele permite que quem gera e quem recebe a eletricidade operem em frequências diferentes. Na prática, turbogeradores de 50 Hz da Ansaldo poderiam atender mercados de 60 Hz, como os Estados Unidos, sem redesenhar a turbina. Segundo a Hitachi Energy, o princípio já foi testado em larga escala: desde 2014, uma instalação de 413 MW na Alemanha converte energia de 50 Hz em 16 2/3 Hz para a rede ferroviária da Deutsche Bahn. Combinada a armazenamento e controles avançados, a eletrônica de potência também ajuda a lidar com as variações bruscas de carga típicas da computação de IA. As metas financeiras para 2030 Segundo a Hitachi Energy, a empresa busca crescimento anual composto de receita na casa dos 15% entre os anos fiscais de 2024 e 2030, com margem EBITA ajustada de 19% a 21%. A carteira de pedidos deve se aproximar de US$ 100 bilhões, sustentando receitas anuais de cerca de US$ 38 bilhões. Para o ano fiscal de 2026, a projeção é de receita de US$ 23,6 bilhões e margem EBITA ajustada de 15,7%. A companhia estima que clientes industriais e data centers representem uma oportunidade de mercado anual de US$ 130 bilhões até 2030. Para sustentar o crescimento, executa um programa global de investimentos de US$ 9 bilhões em fábricas, engenharia e tecnologia, e persegue retorno sobre o capital investido de 30% a 40%. Elevou ainda a meta de contribuição da IA em suas próprias operações para mais de US$ 350 milhões anuais no EBITA ajustado até 2030, e quer ampliar serviços digitais, como manutenção preditiva, com a plataforma HMAX. O que isso pode significar para a Amazônia A pauta é global, mas o debate chega à região. Data centers exigem energia firme e abundante, e a Amazônia tem rede em que muitas comunidades ainda dependem de geração isolada. A discussão de como integrar geração local, armazenamento e serviços de estabilidade à rede é a mesma que atravessa os sistemas da região, onde fontes renováveis precisam conviver com a necessidade de estabilidade. O material da empresa não cita projetos na Amazônia, mas o modelo mostra uma tendência: quem planeja infraestrutura digital precisará planejar junto a energia que a sustenta, e a forma como isso for feito definirá quem se beneficia, as comunidades do entorno ou apenas o próprio data center. Os próximos passos serão acompanhados nos resultados trimestrais da companhia e na implantação das primeiras soluções integradas com a Ansaldo Energia, que dirão se a promessa de data centers como ativos da rede sai do papel até 2030. artigo.texto: O que são mega data centers, onde estão os projetos no Brasil e por que precisamos de leis rigorosas para proteger o povo e a natureza das Big Techs. A era da Inteligência Artificial (IA) virou uma corrida tecnológica que exige cada vez mais territórios, recursos e dados. Mas dá tempo de agir antes que os danos se tornem irreversíveis. No Brasil, mega projetos das gigantes da tecnologia avançam em meio a isenção de impostos, enquanto comunidades e consumidores enfrentam os prejuízos. “Antes de seguir expandindo os data centers que só aumentam os lucros bilionários das Big Techs, o Brasil deve saber o custo e definir as regras para que o povo brasileiro não pague a conta dos impactos” explica Julia Catão, especialista em Tecnologia do Greenpeace Brasil. O que são Mega Data Centers? São centros de dados de hiperescala que concentram milhões de servidores para processar, armazenar e transmitir enormes volumes de dados, podendo consumir energia equivalente a países inteiros, sobrecarregando as redes elétricas locais e milhões de litros de água potável. A principal diferença está no tamanho e na capacidade: os data centers operam os serviços digitais que usamos no dia a dia (enviar mensagens, assistir a vídeos e acessar plataformas); já os mega data centers são instalações computacionais de escala industrial e atendem sobretudo às Big Techs para desenvolvimento de IA. Quais os impactos dos Mega Data Centers? Diferente de estruturas menores, os mega data centers causam danos de proporção industrial e prejudicam principalmente a população local: - Aumento na conta de luz: usam a rede local e elevam os custos da energia nas residências – nos EUA, as tarifas chegaram a triplicar para mercados, custo que é repassado aos consumidores. - Consumo de água: apesar de existir “circuito fechado”, há perdas e reposição; nos EUA, o consumo anual chegou a 1 trilhão de litros d’água. - Poluição sonora: geradores fazem ruído insuportável, alto e constante, afetando a qualidade de vida das famílias vizinhas. - Emissões de gases de efeito estufa: a possibilidade de usar fontes fósseis, ampliando as emissões que agravam a crise climática. - Pressão sobre os territórios: ocupam áreas enormes que podem chegar a mais de 100 campos de futebol, disputando terras, água e energia com comunidades locais. - Concentração de poder: domínio de empresas estrangeiras sobre o mercado e as infraestruturas impede o avanço tecnológico no país. Nos EUA, onde mais tem data centers no mundo, a população fez vários protestos contra e o tema foi decisivo nas eleições. Nova York suspendeu novas instalações de hiperescala até ter leis mais rígidas e países europeus também pausaram projetos como Irlanda, Holanda e Dinamarca. Quais são os projetos de Mega Data Center no Brasil? O Brasil já possui data centers (cerca de 225 e quase metade fica no estado de São Paulo), mas projetos de hiperescala estão chegando em todo país: instalações maiores e com muito mais impactos. O mais avançado está em construção no território indígena do povo Anacé, em Caucaia (CE), região metropolitana de Fortaleza. Segundo o Governo do Ceará, abrigará as tecnologias de IA do TikTok e a previsão é começar a operar no segundo semestre de 2027. Confira abaixo projetos de mega data centers em andamento no Brasil. Lei Redata e a importância de regular data centers no Brasil No Brasil, o Redata (Lei 15.504/2026), sancionada em setembro, criou o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter. Na prática, concede isenções de impostos para atrair centros de dados ao país — uma renúncia fiscal estimada em R$ 7 bilhões, segundo Secretaria Especial da Receita Federal, ou seja, recursos públicos que deixam de ser arrecadados. Aprovado sem participação social ou diálogo com as comunidades atingidas, o Redata abre brechas preocupantes, como o incentivo à combustível fóssil. O desenho da lei favorece as Big Techs em detrimento do povo brasileiro e do clima global. Enquanto estados norte-americanos e países europeus discutem limites rígidos, o Brasil se torna alvo da expansão acelerada. O que são Big Techs e quem controla a corrida da Inteligência Artificial? As Big Techs são gigantes da tecnologia que estão entre as empresas mais ricas e influentes do mundo, como Google, Amazon, Meta, Nvdia, Microsoft e TikTok – seus fundadores e administradores ocupam o topo da lista de bilionários da Forbes. São exemplos de como a “inovação” acontece quando é controlada por poucos: lucros recordes, cortes de empregos e a falsa promessa de que automação trará benefícios, porém na prática acumulam violações trabalhistas, sociais e ambientais. Por que regular Big Techs e Data Centers? Regular não é censurar ou frear o desenvolvimento tecnológico, é assegurar que a população faça parte com salvaguardas que respeitem os ciclos da natureza, o bem-comum e que tragam retorno para a sociedade. Para isso, precisamos de criar regras: - Regulação das Big Techs (ambiente digital e democracia): estabelece limites e responsabilidades para as grandes empresas de tecnologia, incluindo transparência sobre algoritmos, proteção de dados e direitos digitais. - Regulação de data centers (infraestrutura física e recursos naturais): impõe análise de riscos e leis firmes para a construção e operação desses empreendimentos, considerando os impactos socioambientais. Parem os mega data centers! Nove organizações — Instituto Terramar, Amazônia Sem Data Center, CTRL+Z, Data_Labe, Instituto Decodifica, Mulheres pelo Clima do Vale do Paraíba, Coding Rights, Filha do Sol e Greenpeace Brasil – se uniram para frear o avanço de data centers de IAs no Brasil até que sejam assegurados: - Consentimento e Transparência: Participação social ativa e consulta livre, prévia e informada para as comunidades tradicionais. - Licenciamento Ambiental completo: Estudo e relatório de impacto assegurando transição energética justa e proibindo instalação em áreas de importância ecológica. - Fim da isenção de impostos: Quem lucra com i

artigo.texto: Lawmakers call for national data center construction pause Lawmakers say pause would give Congress time to pass artificial intelligence regulations WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Members of Congress are calling for a national moratorium on data center construction until the artificial intelligence field can be regulated. They said data centers are not helping local communities and, in many cases, are actively harming them. Rep. Jim McGovern (D-Mass.) said the White House is not doing enough on artificial intelligence. “The alarm bells are flashing. And the president and the White House are asleep at the switch when it comes to AI,” he said. McGovern said big tech leaders are becoming oligarchs and are enriching themselves at the expense of local communities with data centers. “These billionaires want to come into our communities, tell us what to do, and make a profit by driving up our utility prices, and wrecking our environment,” he said. Rep.-elect William Lawrence (D-Mich.) said data centers do not provide the same community value as an automotive plant. “The value, the billions of dollars that is being raised to build these data centers, is built on the promise that it’s going to put people out of work,” he said. Lawmakers said pausing new construction would give Congress time to pass regulations and protect communities from future construction. Rep. Chellie Pingree (D-Maine) said she wants transparency in dealings between big tech and the government. “We don’t want back door deals and secret handshakes between big tech and the government. We want transparency, community engagement, and strong regulations that protect our air, water, climate and communities,” she said. It is not yet clear whether the plan has enough support to pass in the next Congress. The Trump administration has attempted to rename AI - artificial intelligence - as SI - super intelligence. artigo.texto: SpaceX plans $50B data center campus in Cochise County COCHISE COUNTY, AZ (AZFamily) — SpaceX has announced plans to build a $50 billion data center campus in Cochise County, and several community groups are organizing to stop it. SpaceX, Elon Musk’s rocket and AI company, has created an online link for the facility that includes a rendering of the proposed campus. The data center would sit on nearly 750 acres near Willcox Playa and would be the largest in the state. Developers have changed their tactics amid opposition to data center facilities. Many now are trying to work with communities to get projects approved. SpaceX is highlighting the economic impact of the project. Residents raise concerns Tara Clayton lives in Cochise County and is the organizing director for Rural Arizona Engagement. The group fought and killed a large data center project in Pinal County over the summer. “I’ve been hearing from the community that they’re extremely concerned about the integrity of this SpaceX data center,” Clayton said. “Whether they’re telling us the absolute truth about some of these benefits that we might be receiving or the chemicals that might be involved in this facility, how it could potentially impact our water supply here locally or local wildlife, quality of life,” Clayton said. Clayton said it’s important that the county leaders listen to the community and take their opinions into account. Environmental questions Ken Gillingham, a professor of environmental and energy economics at Yale University, has been researching data centers. He said SpaceX has used diesel generators to power some of its facilities. “SpaceX has acquired a reputation for not being the most environmentally oriented of the large hyperscalers,” Gillingham said. “There are other claims that they have not been following environmental protections in a very, very serious way.” Jobs, grid upgrades and state review SpaceX said the project would create more than 5,000 construction jobs and 1,000 permanent jobs. According to the company’s application, SpaceX would invest more than $3 billion in power grid upgrades. Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes said in an interview with On Your Side’s Christine Stanwood that she has concerns and that her office is taking a closer look. Mayes raised the question of “whether that would destabilize our grid in the southwest and maybe even potentially in the West.” SpaceX claims the project would reduce neighbors’ electricity bills and lower property taxes. What’s next The project still must go before the county’s Planning and Zoning Board, which will hold a hearing Dec. 9. Arizona’s Family Investigates called and emailed the Planning and Zoning department and all three members of the Board of Supervisors but has not heard back. artigo.texto: America’s hyperscale data centers together use as much electricity as some entire U.S. states and produce millions of metric tons of carbon dioxide over the course of a year, according to a new study published Monday in Nature Sustainability. The number of hyperscale data centers, which are larger and more powerful than traditional data centers, and are often used to train and run large-scale AI models, has exploded in recent years. Between 2019 and 2024, the number of data centers around the world doubled from a little over 500 to over 1,100, with more than half located in the United States. That number is only expected to grow: the research firm Synergy estimates that the total capacity of U.S. data centers will double in the next three years, largely driven by the growth of hyperscale data centers. American voters rallied against data center development in the midterm elections this November, with many citing economic and environmental concerns. In 40 out of 41 local ballot initiatives across the country, citizens voted to limit or prevent data center development. Yet few studies have quantified just how much electricity each hyperscale data center uses, and what fuels generate the electricity, the researchers say. “Even though there were a lot of [public and scientific] statements about the environmental impact of data centers, when we started this research, we realized that there was basically very little, if none, peer-reviewed data,” says Francesca Dominici, director of the Harvard Data Science Initiative and senior author of the paper. The study provides one of the first facility-level estimates of the electricity use and carbon dioxide emissions of hyperscale data centers since the rise of AI. The researchers used satellite imagery to build a list of 403 hyperscale data centers across the U.S., and then estimated the annual electricity consumption for each facility between May 2024 and April 2025 under a range of operating scenarios. They then used data from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency to calculate their emissions. They found that, together, the data centers used between 68 and 99 terawatt-hours (TWh) of electricity—with the upper estimate equivalent to what some states, like Indiana, Michigan, and Tennessee, use in a year. In the lower scenario, the facilities still consumed approximately the annual electricity sold to customers in Wisconsin, roughly 70 TWh, or Minnesota, around 65 TWh. More than half of the electricity powering the data centers comes from fossil fuels, primarily natural gas and coal. The facilities studied produced a combined estimated 25.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide—roughly the annual emissions of Denmark. Half of the electricity use of all the data centers studied was concentrated in just four states: Virginia, Oregon, Ohio, and Iowa, the report found. Virginia has long been known as “data center alley” due to its high number of data centers, but size and power capacity can also impact electricity consumption. The researchers identified 26 hyperscale facilities in Iowa, combined electricity consumption for which was approximately 7.2 TWh, with the average facility having substantially higher estimated electricity demand than the average facility in Virginia, where 142 hyperscale facilities account for approximately 21.4 TWh of annual electricity consumption. However, the emissions impacts were not always the same. Virginia, Iowa, and Ohio have the most emissions attributable to hyperscale data centers, while Oregon, which is home to more hyperscale data centers than Iowa and Ohio, has significantly fewer emissions due to a cleaner energy grid. “For the same amount of electricity consumed, the regional electricity mix associated with data centers in Wyoming produces approximately seven times more carbon dioxide than in Oregon,” says Gianluca Guidi, Harvard data scientist and the study’s lead author. “So these environmental impacts are not necessarily inevitable. Geography matters.” Without clean energy alternatives, U.S. data centers are projected to consume more natural gas than most countries by 2035, according to a report from BloombergNEF. The electricity demand and carbon emissions are likely even higher than the research shows. The team did not have enough data to assess every single hyperscale data center in the U.S. at the time, and more data centers have emerged since their study concluded in April 2025. The researchers hope to continue to quantify the environmental impacts of hyperscale data centers to better understand their impact on air pollution, water, and health, adding that, as AI continues to scale, its infrastructure growth must be done sustainably. “We tend to imagine AI as something that is almost immaterial, but in the end, the infrastructure power is profoundly physical,” says Guidi. “Behind every algorithm, there are enormous buildings, power plants, water resources, and ultimately also communities that live with the consequences.”

artigo.texto: One flashpoint for the tech industry’s all-in push on large language models has been the sudden rush to turn investment money into hyperscale data centers. The rush hasn’t allowed anyone to plan how to supply the required electricity cleanly or with minimal impact on ratepayers. Instead, it has been difficult to even collect information on what’s being built. A new study has tallied energy use and estimated emissions for hyperscalers operating in the United States between May 2024 and April 2025. They weren’t able to differentiate between AI compute and more traditional data services, but it provides a clear point of reference to track moving forward. Finding the centers The team started with a list of 675 facilities from a commercial database based on news reports, company statements, and satellite imagery. They dropped any that didn’t have a reported electrical capacity or that they couldn’t verify was a suitably large building with the expected cooling and electrical connection equipment. That reduced the list to 403 data centers with an average electrical capacity of about 40 megawatts. In a way, that makes this a very conservative estimate, since 272 facilities believed to be large data centers were left out. But if you’re interested in AI data centers, specifically, it’s also true that some of the facilities included may not fall in that category. That fact also introduces some uncertainty in the actual power usage of these data centers. Relying on other research, they use a range—some conventional data centers run at an average of about 48 percent of capacity, while AI training loads have been running higher, at around 70 percent. Putting that together, the total power usage for the year by these 403 data centers was estimated at 68 to 99 terawatt-hours. That amounts to 1.5 to 2.2 percent of total US electricity use, on par with the total used by Wisconsin or Indiana.

artigo.texto: When the dust was still settling after November’s election, Elon Musk posted on X that “data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.” This might sound like a crazy idea. But is it? Musk’s post was a reaction to the electorate’s overwhelming rejection of data centers. Voters backed regulations and politicians vowing to halt new construction, concerned about the tremendous energy and water resources needed to power data centers, along with the noise pollution. While it may be technically feasible to someday launch data centers into low orbit to run off of solar electricity — and companies like Google and SpaceX are exploring the idea — for now, this remains science fiction beset by massive technical and financial hurdles. But Musk’s post brings up an interesting discussion: Why not build in the equivalent of the cosmos, meaning in a place with lots of, well, space? The two main components a data center needs are land and energy — the more abundant and cheaper, the better. The other necessity is a welcoming regulatory environment. A small town in North Dakota is the only place where voters supported data centers. The state has plentiful and cheap land and is a major producer of natural gas and wind energy. So why not construct miles and miles of data centers there or in a similar place that’s actually welcoming them? Or what about Canada? Prime Minister Mark Carney is trying to lure technology companies to build there, touting the cooler climate, open spaces, and abundant renewable energy, largely supplied by hydroelectric power. The energy-rich province of Alberta is offering a “concierge service” to ease the approvals process. Meta took the plunge this summer, breaking ground on a $13 billion complex. Even if most Americans don’t want data centers in their backyards, the fact remains that these buildings are the backbone of our modern economy, providing computational power far beyond the needs of artificial intelligence. Data centers enable cloud computing and allow modern financial services, health care, and entertainment streaming to function. To be clear, the editorial board isn’t suggesting thrusting all of our worries onto North Dakota or Canada. Communities there deserve the same protections as any place — developers should pay for their own energy and grid upgrades, and ideally power their centers using renewable energy. Tax incentives should be tied into local economic benefits. Even if a rural place could extract these arrangements, a big if, concentrating large data centers across a place such as the Northern Great Plains would still be a heavy lift. “The difficulty is one of scale and of timelines,” Mohammad Hajiesmaili, who researches carbon-intelligent computing at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, told the editorial board. “Some proposed campuses would draw more than a gigawatt each, and one gigawatt running around the clock is more electricity than the entire city of Boston uses in a year.” That would require new power generation and transmission lines, which could take years to plan, permit, and build, with no guarantees what demand could look like in a few years. Clustering data centers also adds risk — a power outage, severe weather, or a cyber or physical attack could bring a concentrated system to its knees. Just like with an investment portfolio, diversification is key to minimizing the possibility of a catastrophe. Building large data centers in remote areas in conjunction with smaller projects near populated areas, including in Massachusetts, might be the best path forward. From a computing standpoint, there are clear advantages to locating some data centers closer to where computing power is needed, namely better speed and reliability. Transmitting data across vast distances also adds cost. Data travels through fiber-optic cables incredibly fast, about two-thirds the speed of light, but distance can still matter. Autonomous vehicles rely on real-time data. Doctors performing robotic surgery need lightning quick computing. Military operations cannot afford a lag. But for the overwhelming majority of us using a chatbot, or even scientists or businesses doing research, we can afford to wait a few extra milliseconds for our answers. The results of the midterm election present an opportunity to slow down and think through an optimal national strategy. Data centers are also only going to get more energy efficient, so pumping the brakes could be a good thing to control costs, conserve energy, and protect the environment, a win-win-win. Economists have compared the buildout of data centers today to the railroad boom of the late 19th century, when financial speculation and intense competition led to laying far more rails than needed. To be clear, railroads presented a leap forward just as data centers do today. But in 1873, the checks came due, the economy collapsed, and the United States and Europe entered a six-year depression. Let’s hope it doesn’t come to that and we can learn from history’s mistakes. Editorials represent the views of the Boston Globe Editorial Board. Follow us @GlobeOpinion.

artigo.texto: Whitley County residents weigh in on data center rules FORT WAYNE, Ind. (WPTA) - The Whitley County Plan Commission just heard from the public Wednesday night on proposed rules for data centers. The debate, which took place at Columbia High School, was over a drafted proposal that addresses where data centers could be built, how far they’d have to be from homes, and requirements for noise and water use. I’m asking everybody to keep an open mind, demand responsible development, look at the actual numbers, and consider the long-term opportunities,” another speaker added. artigo.texto: Alberta put its data center rules and its oil sands emissions policy into one bill on November 18, 2026. Mining Weekly reported that the province unveiled limits on large data centers and dropped the oil sands emissions cap, and Reuters and other outlets ran the same story. The legislation behind both moves is Bill 42, the Energy, Environment and Utilities Statutes Amendment Act, 2026. It is proposed law, not enacted law. The data center half is the part developers will study first. Facilities of 10 megawatts or larger would sit at least 600 metres from the nearest home, stay off the province’s best farmland and its irrigated land, and answer to the Alberta Utilities Commission. The rules arrive as Canadian operators race to add AI capacity, including the Toronto platform we covered in Vertical Data’s 150 MW pipeline. The oil sands half is quieter. Bill 42 would repeal the Oil Sands Emissions Limit Act, a 2016 law that set a 100 million tonne annual ceiling and never took effect through regulation. This analysis walks through what the bill says, what Alberta has left unconfirmed, how the rules stack up against other jurisdictions, and what to watch as the legislature takes it up. Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. What Alberta Bill 42 Changes at a Glance Alberta introduced Bill 42 on November 18, 2026. The title signals a broad housekeeping bill covering energy, environment and utilities statutes, and the contents bear that out. Two items drive the headlines, and a third gets less attention. The province would set new siting and regulatory rules for large data centers, repeal the Oil Sands Emissions Limit Act, and require financial security for closing and reclaiming new oil and gas wells. The province laid out the data center package in its own announcement on new restrictions for data centres. The table below condenses the confirmed provisions and flags what the province has not yet pinned down. Two cautions apply before anyone reads this as settled policy. First, a bill introduced on November 18 still has to move through the legislature, and the sources we reviewed give no passage date or in-force date. Second, several details that matter to builders, such as the water number, are missing from the public material. We flag each gap as we go. The 10 MW Threshold: Which Data Centers Get Caught The line sits at 10 megawatts. Anything at that scale or above faces the new siting rules, and the Alberta Utilities Commission becomes its regulator. Smaller facilities fall outside the package as described. How big is 10 MW? It is large for an enterprise server room and small for a modern AI campus. A single AI-focused project can run far beyond it. Giga Energy’s $1 billion lease for a 60 MW Texas AI site, which we covered on this site, would clear the Alberta threshold six times over. A midsize colocation hall or an edge facility serving a city could land near the line, which is where the drafting will matter most. There is also a wording wrinkle. The province describes the covered facilities as 10 megawatts or larger in the setback and land provisions, while the regulator provision speaks of data centers larger than 10 megawatts. The gap looks like loose phrasing rather than a policy split. Still, a developer sizing a project at exactly 10 MW should read the bill text rather than rely on press summaries, since one word decides whether the project needs commission review. The threshold also shapes behavior. Rules that bite at a fixed capacity invite projects sized just under the line, or phased builds that start small and expand. Large-load rules in other markets face the same design problem, and Alberta has not said how it would treat staged expansions. That silence is worth watching when the committee stage opens. The 600-Metre Setback: 1,970 Feet From Your Front Door The setback rule is the easiest to picture. A covered data center would need a minimum of 600 metres between its site and the nearest home or residential dwelling. For US readers, that is about 1,970 feet, or 0.37 miles. The distance is measured to the nearest dwelling, so a single farmhouse near the edge of a parcel counts. Reports describe the buffer as a response to community effects such as noise and lighting. Large facilities run cooling fans and backup generators around the clock, and lit perimeters add glare at night. A 600 metre gap does not erase those effects, but it moves most of them beyond the property line of a typical residence. Municipal Add-Ons and Reduced Setbacks Reporting on the bill says municipalities could set stricter setbacks than the provincial minimum, and that some projects could win a reduced setback if the affected landowners and the Alberta Utilities Commission agree. We treat both as reported rather than confirmed, because the official release does not carry them. If they hold, they create a floor with local ratchets and a negotiated exit, which is a common pattern in setback law. The landowner-consent route would matter most in rural areas where a single neighbor controls the land around a proposed site. A developer could buy or lease the adjoining parcels, secure agreement, and ask the commission to shrink the buffer. Whether that route stays open in the final bill is one of the first things industry lawyers will test. Here is a simplified screen a developer might run before spending money on a site. artigo.texto: A Assembleia Legislativa do Paraná (Alep) aprovou na terça-feira (17) o Programa Paranaense de Incentivo a Centros de Dados (Prodatapr), que autoriza o Governo do Estado a conceder benefícios fiscais para atrair data centers. O projeto é dos deputados Luiz Fernando Guerra (Novo), Maria Victoria (PP) e Pedro Paulo Bazana (PSD). O Projeto de Lei 55/2026 estabelece diretrizes para a instalação e a expansão dessas estruturas, com foco na economia digital, na atração de investimentos privados e na geração de empregos especializados. A proposta também busca aproveitar a produção de energia renovável e a conectividade do Paraná. Segundo a justificativa, o objetivo é tornar o Estado um polo de data centers na América Latina e fortalecer a cadeia produtiva de tecnologia. Energia renovável e uso racional da água O programa incentiva novos empreendimentos, a ampliação da infraestrutura de telecomunicações e parcerias entre empresas, universidades e centros de pesquisa. Na área ambiental, estimula o uso de fontes renováveis de energia, o aproveitamento do biometano, o uso racional da água e tecnologias sustentáveis de resfriamento dos equipamentos. Os data centers armazenam e processam grandes volumes de informações usadas por empresas, governos, bancos, hospitais, universidades e plataformas digitais. Com o avanço da inteligência artificial, essas instalações ganharam importância na disputa mundial por investimentos em tecnologia. “A inteligência artificial, a computação em nuvem e os serviços digitais dependem de uma infraestrutura robusta de processamento de dados. Temos energia, universidades, profissionais qualificados e um ambiente favorável à inovação. Queremos transformar essas vantagens em investimentos, empregos e oportunidades para os paranaenses”, afirmou Maria Victoria. Formação de profissionais Luiz Fernando Guerra destacou a necessidade de preparar mão de obra para o setor. “Com esse projeto, o Paraná terá diretrizes para planejar a expansão dos data centers, dar mais previsibilidade a quem pretende investir e identificar os empreendimentos estratégicos para o Estado. Para operar e manter essas estruturas, as empresas vão precisar de profissionais preparados”, disse. Para Bazana, a expansão deve beneficiar também o interior. “Defendo que a expansão dos centros de dados fortaleça também as empresas locais, estimule a formação profissional e leve empregos qualificados ao interior”, declarou. artigo.texto: The US has installed more than 200 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of battery storage, with nearly 50 GWh coming online in the first nine months of 2026 alone. The US added 48.3 GWh of battery storage through September, up 20% from the same stretch last year, according to the latest report from the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA) and Benchmark Mineral Intelligence. Q3 was a little slower: The US installed 14.3 GWh in those three months, down 1% year over year. Texas is in the lead Texas added 12.3 GWh of grid-scale batteries through September, more than any other state. Arizona came in second at 7.7 GWh, followed by California at 6.8 GWh. And 11 states had already broken their annual storage installation records with three months to go – Colorado, Massachusetts, Utah, Michigan, Georgia, Mississippi, Virginia, Iowa, Montana, Alabama, and Illinois. Utility-scale batteries did most of the work in Q3, accounting for 12.2 GWh of new capacity. Businesses and industrial sites added another 1.3 GWh, and residential added 746 megawatt-hours (MWh). That was the best Q3 yet for home batteries, though installs through September were still down 12% year over year. Some homeowners moved up their installations last year before the federal residential clean energy tax credit ended. “States are moving from targets to centralized procurements,” said Pete Tillotson, a senior analyst at Benchmark. In September, New York awarded contracts for eight battery projects that can deliver about 950 megawatts (MW) combined. SEIA and Benchmark now expect 708 GWh of storage across the grid, homes, and businesses by 2030, up 3.7% from their previous forecast. The US can also make more battery cells here. A Tennessee factory opened in July and an Indiana factory opened in October, bringing US cell manufacturing capacity to 92.4 GWh, up 50%. What about people’s electric bills? Solar and batteries helped bring down average summer wholesale power prices by 42% in Texas’s ERCOT market and 51% in California’s CAISO market between 2021 and 2026, according to SEIA’s inflation-adjusted analysis. When batteries had power to spare during peak hours, grid operators could call on expensive power plants less often. You wouldn’t know it from looking at the total on residential electric bills. The cost of generating power for households fell in both markets, but the cost of delivering it to homes rose. Overall, residential bills rose 22% at the two California utilities SEIA examined and 3% across its Texas utility sample, driven by higher transmission and distribution costs. California is upgrading its grid to reduce the risk of wildfires. Texas is expanding its grid for rising demand and make it more resilient to storms. artigo.texto: Ohio Becomes the Epicenter of Data Center Backlash After Tax Credits Cost State’s Schools $374 Million Angela Huffman, a sixth-generation farmer, spent 15 years in agriculture policy in Columbus, OH, and Washington, DC. But her focus lately has been 10 miles from her Wharton, OH, sheep farm. On June 4, Huffman picked up her local newspaper, the Daily Chief-Union. The above-the-fold headline revealed a developer was eyeing a $900 million data center in nearby Upper Sandusky. The headline "stopped me cold," Huffman says. The proposal would have planted a 146-acre Smartland Energy data center campus, with a natural gas power plant, on the north edge of town. "We were already worried about a big development coming in and extracting the town's resources," Huffman tells Realtor.com®. Townsfolk were already concerned after another recent proposal for a soybean processing plant. "What does that do to the community?" she says. Huffman, CEO of Farm Action, says her family has owned its nearby farm for six generations. Organizing concerned neighbors, they began filling planning commission meetings and peppering officials with questions about the impact of the development. They also questioned if it should be approved on industrial zoning, as neighbors had hoped. A petition opposing the project drew 1,100 signatures. Many residents worried about how such a major project could change their rural way of life. And Upper Sandusky wasn't alone. Ohio was the heart of data center resistance in the midterms. Voters in 18 of its 88 counties backed 21 bans or restrictions on development of those projects. One of those was in Upper Sandusky, where voters approved a charter amendment blocking large data centers within the limits of the 6,600-person town. "They wanted to use about a third of the water the whole town uses today," Huffman says. "I'm not against AI or development, but can a town of this size absorb a development like that?" Data center tax breaks come into view But the state already hosts dozens of large centers. And they already exact a cost. A new study shows that the state's data center tax break derived its schools of almost $374 million in revenue in 2025 alone. Republican Gov. Mike DeWine paused the tax breaks in May after the state realized developers were exempted from $2.1 billion in taxes in 2024 and 2025, far more than initally projected. Gov.-elect Amy Acton has promised further scrutiny. Good Jobs First and Policy Matters Ohio studied where those missing tax dollars would have gone. The state's Fair School Funding Plan allocates some sales tax to schools. So by exempting data center developers from the 5.75% sales tax, those schools missed out on revenue. "Ohio lawmakers made a choice to give data center companies a blank check, and now Ohio's schools are paying the price," said Hannah Halbert, Policy Matters Ohio's executive director. "In 2025 alone, the state gave up enough revenue from this single tax break to fully update the Fair School Funding plan and close the gap." This comes at a time when homeowners were being asked to make up the difference. Many Ohio schools aimed to raise money through levies this year, but many were unsuccessful. The Ohio Policy Education Institute found just 24 of 66 levies on the May 2026 ballot had passed. Upper Sandusky's school district was one of the losers—missing out on $383,000 in revenue, according to the report. While voters have approved levies for its schools in 2015, 2018, and 2023, it's still been forced to cancel classes this year because it can't install air conditioning in century-old buildings that are too expensive to rebuild. "Our schools were struggling," Huffman says. "It tells you a lot about when these big tech companies come along, and if they are paying their fair share." Wider backlash Voter anger has put data center incentives in the spotlight. NBC exit polls show 76% of voters opposed data center building in their communities, and a majority considered them "crucial" to their votes. Polls show broad concerns that the pace of data center construction could drive up power costs, raise land prices, and create environmental problems. Recent Realtor.com research on data centers found they're increasingly moving into rural areas. That's despite a major spending spree by the industry. Ohio was barraged with $1.8 million in data center ads in the fall, Pew Research Center found—more than Texas, Wisconsin, and other large states. AI and crypto political action committees spent an estimated $65 million backing Republican Sen. John Husted, who lost reelection to Democrat Sherrod Brown on Nov. 3. Developers, after all, have big plans in the state, having pitched $168.7 billion in new projects. Regulation of data center developments and AI could be a major factor for new Democratic leaders in Columbus and Washington, DC. Sober to that reality, tech stocks tanked after the election. Acton says she supports a conditional moratorium on data centers. She wants to see them cover their utility costs, build with union labor, and abide by environmental standards. She also says she wants to see incentives "reined in" for the large developments. AI companies address future scrutiny Artificial intelligence companies have spent the days since the election promising they'll work with cities and residents on data centers. OpenAI published a "blueprint for responsible development" promising to slow the technology. Meta spokesperson Andy Stone cited a commitment "to pay our own energy and water costs so they're not passed onto consumers, fund new and upgraded grid infrastructure, and support local communities." Ohio isn't alone, either. Virginia, another data center hot spot, spent over $4 billion in data center incentives over 10 years, according to a state report. artigo.texto: What happened in Marshall, Michigan Ford said Wednesday it has started U.S. battery cell output for its next wave of electric vehicles using technology licensed from China's CATL. The first cells rolled out last month at the Marshall complex, and they are already shipping for prototype builds of the Fathom small electric pickup that CEO Jim Farley has positioned against Tesla and Chinese competitors. Ford framed this as a step toward wider use of lithium iron phosphate cells - the lower cost LFP chemistry - in U.S. vehicles. The chemistry was developed in the U.S. but reached commercial scale largely in China. Alan Clarke, who oversees advanced development projects as a vice president at Ford, said the CATL license enables Ford to introduce the low-cost chemistry in the United States as rapidly as possible. While guiding visitors through the plant on Tuesday, Clarke said, "If we want to get to being able to produce affordable EVs in the United States, we need to also do it the fastest way possible." "CATL being the biggest in the world means that they're the best supplier to get us that technology and help us learn ourselves how to produce LFP cells." Capacity, pace, and the ramp Ford says the highly automated Marshall operation should be able to turn out 40 battery cells per minute, equating to roughly 20 gigawatt-hours a year for its EV lineup and energy storage business. That goal is below the company's earlier plan that called for up to 40 gigawatt-hours annually, reflecting an EV slowdown at Ford and across the sector. The company also said the site has room to add capacity if needed. Ford remains at an early phase of certifying its processes and plans to ramp cell production next year ahead of the Fathom's expected launch in the fourth quarter of 2027. The automaker said moving faster on throughput will help lower battery costs. In September, Duffy sent CEO Jim Farley a letter expressing "profound concern" about Ford's relationships with Chinese companies that he said could harm the automaker and the U.S. auto sector. The White House a day later commended the company for its domestic jobs and manufacturing. As the largest producer of U.S. vehicles, Ford has consistently highlighted its American heritage, employment, and factories while both the Biden and Trump administrations press for more domestic production. The bottom line: Ford is anchoring its next EV wave to lower cost LFP cells and a licensed design from the world's biggest cell maker. artigo.texto: This article is part of the thematic channel The Carbon Observer: subscribe to the newsletter Kigali - I wrote this op-ed from the Carbon Markets Africa Summit in Kigali, a great event that brought together investors, project developers and governments committed to making Africa a major hub for Article 6 carbon markets. One message particularly resonated with me. In her keynote speech, Rwanda's Minister of Environment emphasised that Africa needs bankable projects capable of attracting investment and supporting economic development. And that is exactly the point. Carbon finance could play a central role in mobilising capital, creating jobs and supporting a more sustainable development pathway. But something caught my attention: across discussions, meetings and keynote speeches, plenty about carbon finance and investment opportunities was discussed. Yet, Article 6.4 and its Paris Agreement Crediting Mechanism (PACM) were almost absent from the conversation. For many of the people actually developing and financing projects, Article 6.4 remains more of a theoretical framework than a practical opportunity. Developers do not really oppose the mechanism, they simply do not see a compelling reason to adopt another complex system in a market that is already extremely difficult to navigate. Developers are already dealing with changing methodologies, host-country authorisations, corresponding adjustments and increasingly demanding buyer requirements. Article 6.4 introduces yet another set of rules and approval processes without demonstrating a clear commercial advantage. After years of negotiations, the mechanism is finally becoming operational. As of October 2026, five methodologies have been approved, including two new clean-cooking methodologies. Meanwhile, 1,512 projects and programmes have requested transition from the old Clean Development Mechanism (CDM), with 418 having received host-country approval by June. Transitioning existing projects, however, is not the same as attracting new investment under the new methodologies. In conversations with experts and developers, one concern kept emerging: methodological conservatism increasingly seems to be treated as synonymous with environmental integrity. Stricter baselines and more demanding monitoring requirements could significantly reduce credit issuance. Developers must also account for mandatory deductions of 5% for the Adaptation Fund and at least 2% for overall mitigation, alongside administrative fees, host-country levies and, where applicable, reversal-risk buffer contributions. To understand the potential economic impact, I ran a quick-and-dirty simulation. This is not a financial model or an Article 6.4 price forecast, just a simple exercise to illustrate how project economics could change. Let's assume a project originally generates 100,000 credits annually, sold at $10 each, generating $1 million in carbon revenue. If more conservative accounting reduces issuance by 40%, and we apply the mandatory 7% UNFCCC deductions, only 55,800 credits remain available for sale. What price would the developer need to charge to maintain the same carbon revenue? In the most demanding scenario, a credit previously sold at $10 would need to sell for almost $30 just to preserve the same carbon revenue. Is the market prepared to pay that difference? The concern is not conservatism itself, but the accumulation of conservative assumptions without sufficiently recognising improvements already made to address historical over-crediting. Conservatism should ensure accurate crediting, not become an objective in itself. Meanwhile, international carbon markets are progressing. According to Sylvera, projected demand for internationally adjusted credits under CORSIA and government purchasing programmes could approach one billion tonnes through 2030. Unlike Article 6.4, these pathways can leverage established standards, methodologies and registries that developers already know, and which are beginning to support deliveries to governments and airlines. Why move to an entirely new mechanism when existing systems are already opening access to compliance markets? The answer may come from future demand. The European Commission has proposed auctioning up to 260 million EU ETS allowances to finance the purchase of international credits between 2036 and 2040. At an illustrative EUA price of €120 in the late 2030s, this could generate approximately €31 billion in purchasing resources. This is not a guaranteed budget or credit price, but it illustrates the scale of the potential opportunity. Such purchasing power could make Article 6.4 more attractive, establish a new market benchmark and potentially encourage other countries to follow a similar approach. But this raises two fundamental questions. Will buyers pay the higher prices needed to make these projects viable, while keeping international credits cost-effective? And perhaps more importantly, will enough eligible and authorised credits be available? Lower issuance per project means more investment is needed to generate the same volume. Host-country authorisation remains a sovereign decision, while credit-vintage eligibility and restrictions across NDC periods create additional uncertainty. For Europe, securing up to 260 million credits between 2036 and 2040 would require a substantial project pipeline developed and financed years in advance. The market cannot wait until 2036 to start developing the projects Europe may need in 2036. This brings me back to the message from Rwanda's Minister of Environment: “Africa needs bankable projects.” Article 6.4's success will ultimately depend on strong demand signals and its ability to reduce risks for project developers and investors. This means simplifying procedures, providing greater regulatory certainty, establishing a clear and transparent pathway for host-country authorisation, and turning regulatory ambition into bankable projects that attract capital and deliver measurab

artigo.texto: A Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) informou seus clientes que pretende interromper o fornecimento de chips para operadores de data centers que alugam mais de 50% de suas unidades de processamento gráfico (GPUs) para empresas chinesas, de acordo com uma reportagem da CNBC publicada na terça-feira, 17 de novembro de 2026. A política anunciada surge num momento em que as autoridades americanas introduzem medidas adicionais destinadas a limitar o acesso das empresas chinesas à tecnologia avançada de inteligência artificial americana, incluindo recursos computacionais fornecidos por meio de serviços de nuvem no exterior. A CNBC, citando duas pessoas familiarizadas com o assunto, informou que a Nvidia havia alertado seus clientes nos últimos meses sobre as possíveis implicações da proposta da Lei de Segurança de Acesso Remoto (RASA). A legislação ampliaria a autoridade do governo dos EUA para regulamentar o acesso a serviços de computação em nuvem, aproximando as restrições de acesso remoto dos controles já existentes sobre as exportações físicas de semicondutores. Segundo o relatório, a Nvidia também alertou que as regras propostas poderiam gerar riscos legais tanto para os fabricantes de semicondutores quanto para seus clientes. A Nvidia teria definido uma meta de 51% de clientes fora da China O Financial Times noticiou no início de novembro que a Nvidia havia instruído verbalmente seus clientes de data centers a alocar pelo menos 51% de seus serviços a clientes não chineses em contratos futuros. A exigência relatada afetaria operadoras cujos modelos de negócios dependem fortemente do fornecimento de capacidade computacional para empresas chinesas. De acordo com os atuais controles de exportação dos EUA, a Nvidia está impedida de vender certos processadores de IA avançados diretamente para a China. No entanto, os órgãos reguladores têm tido autoridade mais limitada sobre o acesso à mesma tecnologia por meio de infraestrutura em nuvem localizada fora do país. A legislação RASA proposta visa abordar essa distinção, estendendo a supervisão regulatória aos serviços de computação remota. Segundo a CNBC, o projeto de lei foi aprovado pela Câmara dos Representantes dos EUA em janeiro, mas ainda não havia recebido a aprovação do Senado. O Departamento de Comércio dos EUA introduz restrições adicionais ao acesso remoto O Departamento de Comércio dos EUA, por meio do Bureau de Indústria e Segurança (BIS), anunciou na segunda-feira uma regra final provisória destinada a impedir que empresas chinesas acessem remotamente processadores de IA restritos, informou a CNBC. A medida faz parte dos esforços de Washington para fortalecer a aplicação dos controles de exportação de semicondutores e abordar o uso de centros de dados em terceiros países para obter capacidade computacional. A questão atraiu atenção após relatos de que empresas chinesas de inteligência artificial buscavam acesso a hardware da Nvidia por meio de instalações no exterior. Em 5 de novembro, a CNBC noticiou que a desenvolvedora chinesa de IA Moonshot AI havia tentado acessar processadores da Nvidia por meio de data centers na Europa. Anteriormente, em julho, o governo Trump havia acusado a Moonshot de obter acesso aos chips por meio de centros de dados no Leste Asiático. Essas alegações dizem respeito a possíveis métodos de acesso a recursos computacionais restritos e não comprovam, por si só, que ocorreram violações dos controles de exportação. O secretário do Tesouro pede maior fiscalização da Nvidia Os acontecimentos seguem a saída do CEO da Nvidia, Jensen Huang, o que gerou maior atenção às práticas de gestão e controle de exportação da empresa. O secretário do Tesouro dos EUA, Scott Bessent, pediu no domingo uma “reestruturação drástica” na Nvidia, de acordo com a CNBC. Suas declarações vieram na sequência de relatos que alegavam que Huang havia se envolvido em um relacionamento extraconjugal com uma mulher que, segundo as autoridades americanas, era suspeita de realizar atividades de espionagem em nome da China. As alegações relatadas não foram comprovadas como evidências de irregularidades. Bessent também sugeriu que outros executivos da Nvidia deveriam ser investigados quanto ao cumprimento das restrições de exportação dos EUA. Em entrevista à Fox News, ele questionou se a Nvidia teria incentivado vendas que ele classificou como potencialmente ilegais, numa tentativa de aumentar a receita e os lucros. Os comentários representam preocupações levantadas pelo Secretário do Tesouro, e não conclusões definitivas sobre a conduta da Nvidia. Nvidia destaca as limitações da supervisão de produtos pós-venda A Nvidia já abordou anteriormente os desafios associados ao monitoramento de como seus processadores são usados após a venda. Em um documento enviado à Comissão de Valores Mobiliários (SEC) em agosto, a empresa afirmou que buscava cumprir os requisitos de controle de exportação aplicáveis, mas reconheceu as limitações em sua capacidade de supervisionar os produtos depois que eles saem de sua posse. A Nvidia afirmou não ter “controle físico de seus produtos após a venda”, explicando que depende de programas de conformidade operados por clientes e parceiros comerciais. A divulgação ilustra as dificuldades que os fornecedores de semicondutores enfrentam no monitoramento do uso final de processadores avançados, principalmente quando o hardware é implantado em infraestrutura de nuvem que atende clientes em várias jurisdições. As alterações relatadas nas políticas de vendas da Nvidia, juntamente com a legislação proposta e as novas medidas do Departamento de Comércio, podem afetar os operadores de centros de dados que fornecem serviços de computação de IA para empresas chinesas. A Nvidia também é negociada na B3 por meio da BDR (BOV:NVDC34). Este conteúdo é apenas para fins informativos e não constitui aconselhamento financeiro, de investimento ou de qualquer outra natureza profissional. artigo.texto: Massachusetts pilot program offers free batteries and extra cash A Massachusetts utility has announced plans to use home batteries to help 125 low-income families save money and keep the lights on during power outages — all at no cost to them. If successful, the pilot program could serve as a model for similar initiatives throughout the state, as utilities pursue a mandate to create a more affordable, robust, and equitable electric system. National Grid this month launched BatteryBackup+, a partnership with residential power-storage company Haven Energy that will bring the no-cost batteries to homes in Fall River, a working-class former mill city where the median household income hovers just above half the statewide average. Participants will receive a battery capable of providing at least four hours of backup power, as well as $150 annually for five years. To qualify, residents must already be signed up for National Grid’s low-income discount rate, or meet the equivalent income limits — about $103,000 per year for a four-person household, for example. Haven will handle installation and maintenance of the systems, and manage the batteries’ enrollment and deployment in programs that share their power with the grid to alleviate strain at times of high demand. After 10 years, participants will be able to work with Haven to take over ownership and management of the batteries or remove them. The utility’s overall goal is to develop and refine a strategy for making the grid more efficient and resilient while giving a financial boost to families who are the most vulnerable to soaring energy prices. “We’re really excited about what we get to learn from this,” said Joshua Tom, National Grid’s director of energy transition solutions. The idea of aggregating residential batteries to create benefits for the grid is not new. When batteries work in concert to send power into the system, it can reduce the need for energy from pricier, dirtier plants. In the long term, such arrangements can also help avoid expensive grid upgrades that would be paid for by customers. States are increasingly leaning into the concept. Vermont’s Green Mount Power harnesses this potential with a network of 10,000 residential batteries. Massachusetts’ ConnectedSolutions model, launched as a pilot in 2016, has been adopted or adapted by nearby states including Connecticut and Rhode Island. New Jersey just launched its own program paying residents to share their battery capacity with the grid. Haven’s business model takes advantage of this trend. As in the Fall River pilot, the company handles the installation and management of residential batteries. Haven then earns money from enrolling the equipment in state programs, using some of the revenue to make the investment more affordable for customers. Haven currently operates in seven states — including elsewhere in Massachusetts — with eight more coming soon. In most places, customers pay a monthly fee for their batteries and the company’s services, starting at $29. Fall River is not Haven’s first foray into a no-cost model. Last year, the company launched a program in California providing free batteries to low-income households. So far, the program has contracted with about 2,500 homes and completed installations in about 60% of them. The National Grid pilot is different from the California offering in a few ways. The initiative is an element of National Grid’s Electric Sector Modernization Plan, a strategic document required by Massachusetts in which electric utilities lay out their road maps for modernizing the grid to meet growing demand in an affordable and environmentally responsible way. The utility hopes its experience in Fall River will help it learn more about how to recruit low-income customers and convince them to participate in such programs. “One of the things we’re testing out is how do you get scalable, cost-effective, grassroots customer engagement,” said Steven Caldwell, National Grid’s vice president of energy efficiency and clean transportation. The pilot is also investigating a new question: Can aggregated batteries alleviate strain on a specific portion of the grid, rather than providing only broader system benefits? The utility aims to install 1.2 megawatts of capacity in homes along three grid feeders that National Grid identifies as having reliability and capacity challenges. “They’re targeting areas that maybe haven’t had the infrastructure updates that needed to happen,” said Sherri Bence, Fall River’s municipal energy manager. “We are at this crossroads where we need to start being a little more innovative.” Sarah Shemkus is a reporter at Canary Media who is based in Gloucester, Massachusetts, and covers New England. read next - Virtual power plants New net-zero community will become Michigan’s first virtual power plant

artigo.texto: The largest data centers in the US collectively emit an estimated 25.7 million metric tons of carbon emissions annually â almost as much as Denmark, according to a study published in the journal Nature Sustainability. Harvard researchers found 403 data centers used almost 2% of US electricity, with most of the power being generated from fossil fuels. Sites in Iowa, Ohio, and Virginia accounted for about half the estimated emissions. The study provides the first peer-reviewed estimates of emissions generated by US data centers since the start of the AI boom, although it is not a comprehensive inventory. Without a publicly available list of facilities, researchers pieced together information using a commercial dataset, satellite imagery, and data on the power mix supplying each regional electricity grid. The findings are likely an underestimate as they exclude data centers that researchers could not sufficiently verify, as well as facilities that rely on on-site power generation.

artigo.texto: Pakistan is seeking investment and technological partnerships with Finland in electric vehicles (EVs), battery energy storage and advanced industrial technologies as the country works to expand its electric mobility sector. The opportunities were discussed during a meeting between Prime Minister’s Adviser on Industries and Production Haroon Akhtar Khan and a Finnish delegation led by Jarno Syrjälä, Finland’s Under-Secretary of State for International Trade. During the meeting, both sides explored potential cooperation in electric vehicles, battery storage solutions, mineral processing and advanced industrial technologies. Haroon Akhtar Khan highlighted Pakistan’s recent policy initiatives, including the National Industrial Policy, National Tariff Policy and New Energy Vehicle Policy. He said electric vehicles had become an important part of modern transportation and encouraged Finnish companies to explore investment opportunities in Pakistan’s EV and industrial sectors. The adviser also invited Finnish businesses to consider investment in Pakistan’s mineral processing industry. Finnish companies, including Metso and Wärtsilä, are already involved in projects such as Reko Diq. Other Finnish firms, including Nokia and Vaisala, also have an established presence in the country. He added that the government was working to simplify regulatory procedures and remove obstacles to facilitate foreign investment. The discussions also focused on the 14th Finland-Pakistan Business Summit, scheduled to take place in Islamabad on November 16 and Karachi on November 17. The event aims to strengthen business-to-business ties and create new opportunities for companies from both countries. Although no specific Finnish investment, EV manufacturing plant or battery production project was announced, the discussions signal Pakistan’s efforts to attract foreign expertise and technology to support its electric mobility ambitions. Greater cooperation with Finnish companies could help Pakistan develop its EV ecosystem, strengthen battery storage capabilities and expand its industrial technology base.

artigo.texto: Desejando direcionar até 10% do consumo de energia para data centers projetados, Brasil teme restrições de vendas de processadores ONS já recebeu pedido de 159 empreendimentos para acesso aos sistemas de transmissão de 20,7 GW que podem ser afetados pelas restrições dos EUA. Clique aqui e escute a matéria A decisão do governo Donald Trump de incluir o Brasil entre os países que terão restrições para importar chips desenvolvidos nos Estados Unidos para uso em data centers, mesmo que os semicondutores sejam fabricados fora da jurisdição da Casa Branca, pode ter um forte impacto no desejo do Brasil de ser um grande destino desse investimento. Se forem ampliadas as restrições, especialmente para os Data Centers de aprendizado de agentes de Inteligência Artificial, dezenas de projetos que já estão sendo comunicados ao Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS) podem ser prejudicados e revistos, embora tecnicamente a exigência apenas acrescente um componente a mais do que eles já precisam para se habilitar no Brasil. O setor de Data Center e Inteligência Artificial foi tema de um dos painéis da Conferência Ibero Brasileira de Energia em Lisboa Portugal (Coniben) horas antes do anúncio americano com executivos do ONS, Sumara Ticom, da Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE) Thiago Prado, o diretor da Amptank Tiago Barreto de Chaves e o Diretor de Inovação e Novos Negócios da CCEE, trataram do tema a partir das necessidades de energia para fazer funcionar os Data Center. O desafio no Brasil é que o setor pediu ao ONS, entre janeiro de 2025 e outubro de 2026, acesso à transmissão e demais instalações de transmissão, nada menos que 20,7 GW, dos quais 159 empreendimentos com pareceres favoráveis. Parecer de acesso é a autorização para um data center receber a energia que precisa para funcionar. Instalados, eles vão usar quase 20% da demanda máxima de energia entregue pelo Sistema Interligado Nacional. Até agora, o ONS já concedeu 123 pareceres para projetos com viabilidade confirmada que vão exigir 14,2 GW. Desse, 7,9 GW já têm contrato assinado (que vão consumir 3,8 GW) e outros em andamento que vão precisar de mais 4,1 GW. O interesse é tão forte que, dos 159 pedidos, apenas 36 foram negados e 77% (123) aprovados. Prevendo essa demanda, o governo se antecipou e, em 2025, criou o que chamou de Política Nacional de Acesso ao Sistema de Transmissão (PNAST). Com ela veio um pacote de aprimoramentos regulatórios, criou-se uma fila única de pedidos a sistemas de transmissão de toda essa energia e criou um janela, avaliação conjunta e regras comuns para alocar a margem disponível. Funcionou. Já este ano, quando abriu a primeira temporada de acessos, viu o interesse dos investidores. Ao menos 71 projetos se cadastraram pedindo 2,8 GW. Do total de 65 ( necessitando de 2,6 GW), foram admitidos outros 7, seguiram após verem a margem disponível e 58 desistiram. A informação mostra ao investidor onde a rede pode recebê-lo hoje e ao planejamento onde expandir. O problema é que esses projetos exigem muita energia. O que torna o desafio do governo em fazer com que a chegada dos data centers seja eficiente para o sistema e para todos os consumidores. O que obriga a EPE a trabalhar para fazer os estudos nas regiões com mais pedidos e antever onde a rede já pode recebê-los, tratar dos insumos para que eles entrem sem transferir os riscos. Porém, o fato de, a partir desta segunda-feira (16), fornecedores precisarem de autorização do governo americano para enviar os processadores avançados a empresas brasileiras, com pedidos analisados caso a caso, não deve fazer com que o interesse pelas compras de chips diminua. Mas ninguém gostou de que o Brasil está numa lista que inclui Singapura, Tailândia, Malásia e Indonésia, que, segundo a norma, apresentam risco acima do normal de desvio ilegal desses chips para a China ou Macau —alvos de embargos junto com Rússia, Irã, Coreia do Norte, Síria e Cuba. Com base no que já está cadastrado, o que a EPE trabalha e que o Brasil vai multiplicar o uso de energia apenas para Data Center por 10. Sair de um consumo de 3 TW/hora em 2026 para 30 TW/hora em 2036. Muito maior que a própria taxa de crescimento do consumo de energia elétrica no Brasil, estimada em 3,4% ao ano. Isso quer dizer que o Brasil pode ter um consumo muito próximo de 10% de toda a carga do país no horizonte de 10 anos. Essa demanda levou a EPE a criar uma área no site da empresa de planejamento energético do Brasil que tem até acordo de confidencialidade com as empresas interessadas apenas para começar a entender o projeto Data Center. O objetivo é que essas informações possam ajudar a pensar em eficiência energética e no comportamento da carga por sistema mais recentemente. Em outra frente a cooperação a própria Nvidia que passou a além de vender os seus processadores, passou a ajudar a desenhar os parques usando recursos de Inteligência Artificial para fazer o projeto e o desenho e extrair o melhor desses processadores. E como tudo o que está complexo pode ficar mais complicado, a EPE avalia que futuramente, aumentando a densidade de potência dos Data Centers, haverá uma evolução tecnológica com um uso mais intensivo da tecnologia de corrente contínua, o que trará mais complexidade ao planejamento e à operação do Sistema Interligado Nacional. Os Data Centers recebem a energia em corrente contínua e no parque de máquinas, os processadores seriam alimentados em corrente contínua, de modo a dar mais segurança ao sistema. Para a EPE e o ONS, isso representa um novo desafio para o gerenciamento de toda essa energia, o que vai exigir ações para habilitar os sistemas de transmissão.

artigo.texto: This week: Two high-stakes data center public hearings in Spotsylvania and Stafford SPOTSYLVANIA, Va. (7News) — Two important hearings will take place this week in Spotsylvania and Stafford counties on proposed massive data center projects. On Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026, the Stafford County Planning Commission will hold a public hearing on the massive Kings Corridor data center complex on and near the Rappahannock River. On Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026, the Spotsylvania County Board of Supervisors will hold a public hearing on the Crossroad Technology Campus in the Lee Hill area. The data center applicant is requesting a special use permit in Spotsylvania County to develop a 555-acre data center campus. One property is at 3215 Eagle Drive. The other two properties have not been assigned addresses. According to the county, the properties are located on the north side of Eagle Drive (Route 736), Lee Hill School Drive (Route 635), and Mills Drive (Route 17) and lie adjacent to the CSX Railroad corridor on the west side. RELATED | Spotsylvania Planners recommend approval for 555-acre Amazon data center In September, 7News reported that the Spotsylvania County Planning Commission recommended approving a new data center campus in the Lee Hill area. The planning commission voted 4-2 to approve the Crossroads Technology Campus. The data center mega-site would sit across the street from a park, and homeowners have told 7News they’re concerned about how close it will be to their homes. Right now, the 550-acre site is filled with trees and wildlife. Much of it would be leveled for a data center campus with multiple buildings, including three substations to power the data center complex. RELATED | Spotsylvania residents push back on data centers and the county’s low data center tax Over the summer, 7News reporter Nick Minock spoke with homeowners living next to the proposed data center development. “We are worried about all sorts of things. Will it affect our home prices?” asked Trillane Burlar. “Will we be able to sleep at night with the noise? Will our children get asthma from the additional particulates in the air from the generators?” “I would really like to see a limit on how many data centers we bring here,” said Cynthia Staats. “At the bare minimum, we need to slow it down. We need to understand what the long-term impacts are to our neighborhoods, communities, water, [and] utilities.” “Not only do we love our home because it's our sanctuary and it's our place where we come to restore and revive, but we also have invested a lot of money in our home, and we would like to know that it continues to appraise,” said Sarah Burlar. “I've been looking much more into the environmental impacts, the noise problem that's going to be affecting everyone, because constant hum and noise is actually bad for our health,” said Kevin Johnson. “We wouldn't be able to sit on our decks and enjoy the peacefulness of our neighborhood with having the 24/7 light and noise pollution; that is a big, big concern of ours,” said Catherine Williams. “3,100 feet is too close.” RELATED | Stafford residents oppose massive data centers proposed near Rappahannock River Meanwhile, several Stafford County residents who live in a neighborhood on the Rappahannock River are concerned about a proposal that would place data centers and a substation near – and in some cases right next to – their homes. “I hate it,” said Arlene, who would live directly next to the data centers. “It makes me want to cry.” The data center complex, known as Kings Corridor, would cast a shadow over Arlene’s house during the day, and bright lights from the data centers would shine through her windows at night. “It makes me very sad, and I'm praying that it doesn't come about,” said Arlene. “And we should keep it farm.” The location the data center developer is eyeing is currently farmland and an agricultural area with homes and subdivisions next door. The developer is proposing four sites along Route 3, also known as Kings Highway, for massive data center complexes. Homes are right next to all four locations. The newly proposed data center alley is a short drive from Fredericksburg, King George County, and George Washington’s boyhood home in Stafford County. One of the data center locations is right across the river in Spotsylvania County. The homeowners there would have a view of an industrial site instead of a serene river with trees at Bald Eagle's nest. RELATED | Stafford County postpones data center project hearing after county staff urged denial “They need to know that there is one very large data center being put literally right across a river from a very large subdivision, and they're very likely going to see the light effect of that at night,” said Stafford County resident Kevin French. David lives in the house right next to Arlene’s home, and he’s concerned about data center noise. “I've had a choice [to live anywhere in] the entire country,” said David, who is a veteran and physician. “I chose here, and this is an idyllic area with a lot of nature. We've got a river here. We've got eagles. We've got wildlife. That'll all disappear.” The Parsons are concerned about their property value and the data centers impacting the water next to their homes, which run on well water, but that’s not all. “I'm just worried about the Rappahannock because it is an endangered river,” said Sharon Parsons.
