artigo.texto: RS offers ebm-papst solutions for rack-level thermal challenges in high-density data centers ebm-papst DiaForce, AxiForce, and RadiCal series fans help mitigate rack-level hot spots, minimize harmonic vibration, reduce parasitic power draw, and improve energy efficiency in critical data center infrastructure. FORT WORTH, Texas , Nov. 17, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- RS, a high-service global product and service solutions provider for industrial customers, offers high-performance ebm-papst air-moving products engineered to solve rack-level thermal management challenges in high-density data centers, including several series of robust, compact, and versatile fans. As processing demands soar, these proven fan technologies allow data center operators, system builders, and thermal engineers to optimize airflow, overcome high static pressure resistance, minimize harmonic vibration, reduce parasitic power draw, and reliably protect critical assets from thermal damage and mechanical stress. Rapid growth in artificial intelligence, machine learning, and high-performance computing has pushed server rack power densities from 3–5kW a decade ago to 40–100kW or more per rack today. Because server chips convert nearly all electrical energy into heat, unmitigated thermal energy creates localized hot spots that facility-level air conditioning cannot effectively dissipate, risking component degradation, silicon melting, and unplanned downtime that averages around $9,000 per minute. While liquid cooling adoption is growing, fan-based forced-air cooling remains the global standard for roughly 90% of data centers due to lower capital costs, easier maintenance, legacy facility compatibility, and zero risk of fluid leaks near high-voltage electronics. Effectively cooling these densely populated server chassis requires specialized fans engineered to overcome extreme aerodynamic resistance from PCBs, power supplies, and cabling without introducing excessive noise, harmonic vibration, or energy penalties. ebm-papst offers a variety of precision engineered fans through RS that directly resolve these common rack-level thermal and mechanical constraints. Key product lines include: - DiaForce series diagonal compact fans: Designed to combine the high volumetric airflow of axial fans with the high static pressure capabilities of centrifugal blowers, these single-stage units deliver up to 50% higher air performance than single-stage axial fans with static pressure matching traditional counter-rotating units. Their unique single-motor diagonal design cuts motor count in half compared to dual-motor counter-rotating setups, significantly reducing the harmonic vibration energy that causes hard drive read/write errors while lowering acoustic noise by 6–12 dB(A) with superior tonality. Available in standard 40mm, 80mm, and 120mm footprints, DiaForce fans provide high-efficiency cooling for high-density server chassis and uninterruptible power supply systems. - AxiForce series compact axial fans: Engineered specifically for high-static-pressure server rack environments, these compact axial fans feature optimized blade aerodynamics, lower noise profiles, reduced electrical power draw, and robust environmental construction compared to legacy axial designs. They are available in compact frame sizes ranging from 40mm to 200mm, directly corresponding to vertical rack unit (U) heights from 1U chassis (40mm) up to 4U and larger enclosures (120mm and 172mm). This structural alignment enables reliable, space-efficient thermal protection across server chassis, power supplies, and rack enclosures. - RadiCal series AC and EC centrifugal fans: Featuring backward-curved impellers from 190mm to 250mm with aerodynamically shaped blades, these centrifugal fans minimize energy losses, flow separation, and turbulence to achieve maximum aerodynamic efficiency. Available with GreenTech EC motor technology and variable speed controls, they reduce energy consumption by up to 50% compared to traditional AC alternatives to curb facility-wide parasitic power draw. Their high-volume airflow capabilities make them ideal for computer room air conditioners, air handling units, supply fan grids, rear-door heat exchangers, and in-row cooling architectures. "As data centers scale to handle generative AI and high-performance computing, thermal management has shifted from a facility-wide consideration to a precise, component-level engineering discipline," said Steve Berestecky, Director of Information Technology & Clean Room Air Technologies at ebm-papst. "Evaluating fans strictly on total volumetric airflow is no longer sufficient when dense internal components create intense aerodynamic impedance. By matching static pressure requirements, optimizing air velocity at critical component sites, and utilizing intelligent PWM control loops, ebm-papst solutions like our DiaForce, AxiForce, and RadiCal series fans allow engineers to master thermal density, curb parasitic power consumption, and protect operational uptime." To learn more about high-performance ebm-papst air-moving products available through RS, visit the links embedded here and check out the new RS Expert Advice article, "High-density rack-level data center cooling," featuring Steve Berestecky. For assistance identifying, procuring, deploying, and maintaining ebm-papst products engineered to optimize data center server rack cooling and maximize uptime, please contact your local RS representative at 1.866.433.5722 or reach out to the RS technical solutions team. artigo.texto: Rwanda carbon market goes to Antalya with 29 projects on its register Rwanda has registered 29 carbon market projects and opened its Article 6 agreement with Singapore to renewable energy and clean cooking proposals, and at COP31 in Antalya, where Prime Minister Justin Nsengiyumva leads the delegation, its pavilion programme includes the launch of a carbon registry and a distributed renewable energy fund. Credits from Rwandan carbon projects have sold at between $14 and $45 a tonne and brought in about $1.5 million, the Rwanda Environment Management Authority (REMA) said in September, from a register of 29 projects running across renewable energy, electric mobility, forestry, waste management, agriculture and land conservation. Some of those projects are already selling credits and others are with external auditors for verification, according to REMA, whose Deputy Director General, Faustin Munyazikwiye, said the projects “are at different stages of development”. Rwanda became Singapore’s first East African partner under Article 6 when the two governments signed an implementation agreement on 6 May 2025, Singapore’s sixth such agreement overall, under which Singapore-based companies can use eligible Rwandan credits to offset up to 5% of their taxable emissions. Singapore will put the value of 5% of the authorised credits towards adaptation in Rwanda and cancel 2% at first issuance, and the call for proposals that opened on 30 January covers renewable energy and efficiency alongside clean cooking, electric mobility, waste management and improved forest management. The joint committee overseeing the agreement, which Munyazikwiye co-chairs, met in Kigali on 16 October to speed up approvals, and the lessons from it are the subject of a session at Rwanda’s COP31 pavilion that will also launch the country’s carbon registry. At the same pavilion the Rwanda Green Fund is launching its Distributed Renewable Energy Fund, the first fund of its investment arm, the Ministry of Environment said on 10 November, alongside a biodiversity window and the Cabinet-endorsed Country Platform for Climate and Development, which coordinates national climate priorities with the investment raised for them. Household electricity access reached 85.4% by the end of 2025, with 60.1% of households on the national grid and 25.3% relying on solar, according to Rwanda Energy Group, and the government’s target is universal access by 2029. The World Bank’s Renewable Energy Fund project, which runs subsidies and loans for solar home systems through local savings and credit cooperatives, aims to connect at least 445,000 households from a $15 million subsidy window, and Franz Drees-Gross, the World Bank Group’s Regional Director for Infrastructure in Western and Central Africa, called Rwanda “a shining example for Africa of what it takes to electrify a country”, The New Times reported in October. Under its third nationally determined contribution, submitted last year, Rwanda commits to a 53% cut in greenhouse gas emissions by 2035, about 14.86 million tonnes, with 7% of the reduction to come from its own resources and 46% depending on external finance or technical support, against a total finance need of $12 billion to 2035. Its delegation is asking COP31 for a clear roadmap to the $300 billion a year climate finance goal agreed at COP29, and for high-integrity carbon markets under Article 6. Rwanda will also use COP31 to call for universal ratification of the Kigali Amendment, which commits countries to cut their use of climate-warming hydrofluorocarbons by 80% by 2047, after Kigali hosted the 38th Meeting of the Parties to the Montreal Protocol from 2 November on the amendment’s tenth anniversary. Full implementation could avoid up to 0.5°C of warming by 2100, and close to 1°C with more efficient cooling, and the Minister of Environment, Dr Bernadette Arakwiye, told the Kigali meeting that “signals only matter when they are backed by clear rules”. Speaking in Kigali in October, Arakwiye said the government is studying whether “a share of the proceeds from carbon transactions can be recycled through the Rwanda Green Fund”, so that the credits Rwanda sells now pay for the feasibility studies and baseline data its next projects need before investors will look at them. artigo.texto: St Bess collects $413m in property taxes up to October Loading article... WESTERN BUREAU: Despite the widespread devastation caused by Hurricane Melissa, St Elizabeth is reporting a steady collection in property tax payments, netting $413.6 million in the first seven months of the 2026-2027 financial year. The improved revenue performance has triggered calls from councillors for a greater portion of the revenue to be channelled into community development projects, particularly in areas still recovering from the hurricane. Black River Mayor Richard Solomon, who is also the chairman of the St Elizabeth Municipal Corporation, said the $413,626,794 collected up to October 31 represents 64.2 per cent of its $644.26-million annual target. The sum collected is approximately $144.14 million short of matching the $557.76 million collected for the entire 2025-2026 financial year, with five months remaining. Deputy Mayor Donald Simpson, councillor for the Malvern Division, commended the residents for honouring their tax obligations despite the financial challenges. “I think it’s a great achievement. We really have to congratulate the citizens of the parish because, you know, people in general don’t like to be taxed,” he said. “But when you go through these sorts of circumstances and you still remember that you have to pay your property tax and you make it your duty to pay property tax, I think we really have to congratulate the citizens of St Elizabeth.” Solomon endorsed the sentiments, noting that property tax revenue is important for the efficient operation of municipal corporations and funding for local government services. He hailed the collection team for its outreach efforts, particularly the mobile collection unit, which has been visiting communities to facilitate payments. According to the corporation’s report, property tax collections for October 2026 exceeded those collected in the corresponding month last year by approximately $10.27 million. The parish’s annual property tax target was reduced by approximately $11.85 million, from $656.12 million in 2025-2026 to $644.26 million for the current financial year. Audie Myers, councillor for the Siloah Division, stressed that residents should reap tangible benefits from the funds collected. “We want to see it reflected now in the parish. It’s time for us to get something now within the parish to do something on the roads,” said Myers, declaring that residents were making sacrifices to meet their tax obligations. Everton Fisher, councillor for the Balaclava Division, suggested that the funds could be used to assist communities still struggling with the hurricane’s impact. Solomon also acknowledged the need for taxpayers to see direct benefits from improved collections. “We have to revisit the timetable and see how best we can connect this programme, so that people can realise the benefits that can be derived from the improved collection,” he said. albert.ferguson@gleanerjm.com

The record date for both dividends is November 30, 2026, and the payment date is Thursday, December 10, 2026. For more information on Hyperscale Data and its subsidiaries, Hyperscale Data recommends that stockholders, investors, and any other interested parties read Hyperscale Data's public filings and press releases available under the Investor Relations section at hyperscaledata.com or available at www.sec.gov. About Hyperscale Data, Inc. Through its wholly owned subsidiary Sentinum, Inc., Hyperscale Data owns and operates a data center at which it offers colocation and hosting services for the emerging AI ecosystems and other industries. Another of Hyperscale Data's wholly owned subsidiaries, Ault Capital Group, Inc. ("ACG"), is a hybrid private equity firm and operating company that acquires, finances, builds and actively manages businesses across financial services, digital assets, industrial services, hospitality, defense technologies and other sectors. Hyperscale Data currently expects the divestiture of ACG (the "Divestiture") to occur in 2027. Upon the occurrence of the Divestiture, the Company would be an owner and operator of data centers to support high-performance computing services, as well as a holder of the digital assets and the third wholly owned subsidiary of the Company, Omnipresent Robotics, LLC. Until the Divestiture occurs, the Company will continue to provide, through ACG and its wholly and majority-owned subsidiaries and strategic investments, mission-critical products that support a diverse range of industries, including an AI software platform, equipment rental services, defense/aerospace, industrial, automotive and hotel operations. In addition, ACG is actively engaged in private credit and structured finance through Ault Lending, LLC, a licensed lending subsidiary. Hyperscale Data's headquarters are located at 11411 Southern Highlands Parkway, Suite 190, Las Vegas, NV 89141. On December 23, 2024, the Company issued one million (1,000,000) shares of a newly designated Series F Exchangeable Preferred Stock (the "Series F Preferred Stock") to all common stockholders and holders of the Series C Preferred Stock on an as-converted basis. The Divestiture will occur through the voluntary exchange of the Series F Preferred Stock for shares of Class A Common Stock and Class B Common Stock of ACG (collectively, the "ACG Shares"). The Company reminds its stockholders that only those holders of the Series F Preferred Stock who agree to surrender such shares, and do not properly withdraw such surrender, in the exchange offer through which the Divestiture will occur, will be entitled to receive the ACG Shares and consequently be shareholders of ACG upon the occurrence of the Divestiture. artigo.texto: Long-duration energy storage (LDES) companies are attracting investment as utilities, renewable energy developers and data-centre operators seek electricity storage lasting eight to 100 hours. Form Energy, ESS Tech, Energy Dome, Highview Power, Hydrostor, Eos Energy, Invinity Energy Systems, Sumitomo Electric, Sage Geosystems and Malta are competing with iron-air, flow batteries, zinc batteries, compressed air, liquid air, geothermal and thermal storage technologies. The long-duration energy storage industry is expanding beyond conventional lithium-ion batteries as electricity grids require additional flexibility to accommodate solar and wind generation. Unlike shorter-duration batteries, LDES technologies target extended discharge periods, potentially reducing dependence on fossil-fuel generation during prolonged renewable energy shortfalls. However, the market faces major commercial challenges, including high capital expenditure, limited operating references, project financing, efficiency losses and uncertain customer demand. According to Sightline Climate’s H1 2026 energy storage leaderboard, 23 vendors were assessed on technology, financing, deployment progress and capital economics. Tesla and Chint Power led the overall assessment. Among non-lithium providers, Energy Dome ranked third with 78 points, followed by Highview Power with 65, Hydrostor with 63, ESS Tech with 58 and Sage Geosystems with 57. The leaderboard uses an eight-hour threshold for LDES. Its scores are screening indicators, not independent guarantees of profitability or operational performance. 1. Form Energy: 100-Hour Iron-Air Batteries and $750 Million Funding Form Energy develops iron-air batteries designed to discharge electricity for approximately 100 hours. The company reports testing more than 34,700 sub-scale cells, 6,200 full-scale cells and 170 modules. Its approximately 800 MW / 80 GWh agreement pipeline includes a proposed 300 MW / 30 GWh Xcel Energy–Google project and a 10 MW / 1,000 MWh FuturEnergy Ireland project. Form Energy raised $750 million through Series G financing and secured a $270 million credit facility. The combined $1.02 billion financing commitments demonstrate access to capital but do not represent project revenue or commissioned capacity. Manufacturing scale, project delivery and independently verified efficiency remain critical investment tests. 2. ESS Tech: Iron Flow Batteries and 500 MWh Framework ESS Tech develops aqueous iron-flow batteries through its Energy Base platform and is also developing sodium-ion technology under Bridge. A non-binding Juniper framework covers at least 500 MWh, including a proposed 10 MW / 80 MWh project in California. An 8.5 GWh letter of intent involving Alsym represents a potential opportunity, not confirmed equipment sales. Iron-flow batteries offer an alternative to lithium-based systems, but commercial performance depends on manufacturing costs, operating efficiency, equipment reliability and customer orders. Investors should distinguish signed purchase contracts from non-binding agreements and assess liquidity, warranty liabilities and operating cash flow. 3. Energy Dome: 200 MWh Operating CO₂ Battery and Ireland Expansion Energy Dome stores electricity through a carbon dioxide compression and expansion process. Its 20 MW / 200 MWh Sardinia installation provides ten hours of rated storage duration and an operating commercial reference. The company is also developing a 23 MW / 200 MWh project in Ireland, supported by a ten-year capacity contract, with operation targeted for 2028. In India, NTPC has identified an 18 MW / 144 MWh CO₂ battery project at Kudgi. The Indian project represents eight hours of storage duration. Energy Dome’s operating reference strengthens its commercial position, but future growth depends on construction costs, project financing, repeat orders and actual operating efficiency. 4. Highview Power: Liquid-Air Storage and 3.2 GWh Project Opportunity Highview Power develops liquid-air energy storage systems that liquefy air during charging and expand it through turbines to generate electricity. Its Carrington project is rated at 50 MW / 300 MWh, equivalent to six hours. Consequently, Carrington falls below Sightline Climate’s eight-hour LDES threshold, despite being relevant to longer-duration storage. Highview’s proposed 3.2 GWh Hunterston development represents a larger opportunity. However, proposed capacity is not equivalent to an operational installation. Investors should examine financing, construction schedules, equipment efficiency, turbine maintenance and the cost of replicating projects at additional locations. 5. Hydrostor: 5.6 GWh Compressed-Air Storage Pipeline Hydrostor develops advanced compressed-air energy storage using underground storage formations and captured thermal energy. Its planned Silver City project in Australia is rated at 200 MW / 1,600 MWh. The Willow Rock project in California is designed for 500 MW / 4,000 MWh. Together, the two projects represent 700 MW / 5,600 MWh of proposed capacity. Both have eight-hour rated duration, but neither should be classified as an operating project. Hydrostor’s commercial risks include geological suitability, underground engineering, permitting, financing and construction execution. 6. Eos reported a $765 million backlog representing approximately 3.2 GWh and $344.1 million in cash, including restricted cash. artigo.texto: Google bets on superhot geothermal to power Oregon data centers The geothermal startup Quaise Energy has landed a major first customer for its novel, superhot project in central Oregon. On Tuesday, the Houston-based firm announced that Google has agreed to buy 50 megawatts of carbon-free power from Quaise’s first commercial project, called Project Obsidian, near the Newberry Volcano. Quaise will deploy advanced drilling techniques and unique rock-melting technology to access significantly hotter geothermal resources than traditional plants can. Google said it plans to use the energy to help run its existing data center operations in northwest Oregon as early as 2030. The deal is valued at more than $500 million, Quaise confirmed. The startup is working to find offtakers for an additional 200 MW in future capacity at the Oregon site. “We started Quaise to make the Earth’s most abundant energy source universally accessible — and this agreement marks a critical next step, not just for Quaise but for the entire clean energy sector,” Carlos Araque, Quaise’s CEO and president, said in a Tuesday statement. Quaise is one of at least four U.S. geothermal companies to land agreements with tech giants to pursue next-generation plants. Fervo Energy, the startup that’s furthest along in project development, recently inked a landmark deal to supply Google with nearly 400 MW of clean electricity from the Cape Station facility in southwest Utah. Sage Geosystems and XGS Energy are both partnering with Meta to develop facilities in Nevada and New Mexico, respectively. Tech firms are seeking to secure sources of clean, around-the-clock power for their vast buildout of data centers. For geothermal startups, winning customer contracts like these is an essential step toward raising the financing they need to build first-of-a-kind facilities. Their technologies, while promising, have yet to be deployed widely at commercial scales — and questions remain about how effectively they’ll be able to operate over long periods of time. Google is investing in other nascent technologies, too, including long-duration energy storage and advanced nuclear power. “The scale of power that we’re looking for and also the scale of impact we’re trying to have on the grid requires us to foster that ecosystem,” Lucia Tian, who leads Google’s advanced energy technologies team, told the Wall Street Journal. Quaise said its Oregon project will cost about $350 million to build. The company raised $180 million in equity financing in August, which included investment from the oil-and-gas drilling firm Nabors Industries. (Another startup, Mazama Energy, recently nabbed $135 million to accelerate its own superhot geothermal project near the Newberry Volcano.) At the Project Obsidian site, Quaise will initially use oil-and-gas drilling technologies to develop an enhanced geothermal system. The emerging approach involves fracturing rocks and pumping them full of water to create artificial reservoirs. Surrounding rocks heat the water, which is used to drive turbines on the surface to produce power. Fervo is deploying this method at Cape Station, which began selling power from an initial 33-MW unit in September — becoming the first utility-scale, next-gen geothermal facility to hit such a milestone worldwide. Quaise’s goal is to go deeper and hotter. After using conventional tools to drill down some 2.5 miles, the company plans to switch to its millimeter-wave drilling techniques, which involve deploying high-frequency beams that melt and vaporize rocks. Quaise aims to tap into superhot rock, with temperatures above 572 degrees Fahrenheit, to derive more energy from a relatively smaller number of wells. The startup is still testing the unique technology it plans to deploy for the Google-backed power plant. Quaise said it drilled through more than 330 feet of granite at its field site in central Texas last year, and is now working to reach down over 3,200 feet, or about 0.6 mile, at the same site. Maria Gallucci is a senior reporter at Canary Media. She covers emerging clean energy technologies and efforts to electrify transportation and decarbonize heavy industry.

artigo.texto: A Smiths Group plc (LSE:SMIN) reportou um aumento de 6,1% na receita para o trimestre encerrado em 31 de outubro de 2026, impulsionado pela aquisição da DRC, embora a receita orgânica tenha permanecido inalterada devido à crise no Oriente Médio que afetou sua divisão John Crane. O grupo de engenharia britânico afirmou que a DRC contribuiu com 5,6 pontos percentuais para o crescimento da receita reportada durante o trimestre, beneficiando-se da demanda associada à expansão de data centers. O desempenho variou entre as operações do grupo, com o crescimento nas atividades de construção e aeroespaciais da Flex-Tek sendo compensado pela queda na receita da John Crane e da Thermal Solutions. A receita da John Crane cai 3% em meio à crise no Oriente Médio A John Crane reportou uma queda de 3% na receita orgânica durante o primeiro trimestre, refletindo a contínua interrupção das atividades comerciais e da entrada de pedidos no Oriente Médio. O crescimento nas Américas compensou parcialmente a fraqueza regional, enquanto a entrada de pedidos permaneceu forte em todos os mercados fora do Oriente Médio e da África. A divisão manteve um forte índice de pedidos em relação ao faturamento, indicando que os pedidos recebidos excederam a receita reconhecida durante o período. A Smiths afirmou que a carteira de encomendas continuava a proporcionar visibilidade sobre a atividade futura, embora as condições comerciais no Oriente Médio permanecessem uma restrição ao desempenho a curto prazo. A receita orgânica da Flex-Tek aumenta 3,9% A Flex-Tek apresentou um crescimento orgânico de receita de 3,9%, impulsionado pelos seus negócios de construção e aeroespacial. A operação de construção registrou um crescimento de receita de um dígito alto, beneficiando-se de novos contratos com clientes e iniciativas de preços, apesar das condições ainda desfavoráveis no mercado imobiliário residencial dos EUA. O setor aeroespacial também registrou crescimento, impulsionado pela execução de pedidos existentes e pelas contribuições das renovações de contratos de longo prazo garantidas durante o exercício financeiro anterior. Na divisão de Soluções Térmicas, a receita diminuiu após a conclusão de um grande projeto de aquecimento de altíssima temperatura que havia contribuído para o resultado do período comparativo do ano anterior. Entretanto, a DRC continuou a beneficiar-se do investimento em infraestrutura de centros de dados, contribuindo para o aumento da receita reportada pelo grupo. A meta de margem operacional foi mantida em aproximadamente 21% O Grupo Smiths reiterou sua meta de alcançar uma margem de lucro operacional de aproximadamente 21%. A empresa espera que a rentabilidade se beneficie da alavancagem operacional, do seu Plano de Aceleração e das reduções de custos proporcionadas pelo programa Smiths Excellence. O investimento em iniciativas de crescimento estratégico continua em conjunto com medidas destinadas a melhorar a eficiência operacional. O diretor executivo, Roland Carter, afirmou que a empresa espera que o crescimento orgânico da receita acelere durante o restante do ano fiscal, impulsionado pela carteira de pedidos existente e pelas iniciativas comerciais em andamento. Ele também destacou o crescimento dos negócios de construção e aeroespacial da Flex-Tek, bem como a demanda pelos produtos da DRC por parte de clientes de data centers. Progresso nos planos de descarte de amianto e pagamento de dívidas de empresas A Smiths confirmou que seu plano de desinvestimento da divisão de amianto da John Crane, nos EUA, está progredindo. O grupo também está se preparando para quitar um título de € 650 milhões com vencimento previsto para fevereiro de 2027. A administração manteve suas expectativas de melhoria no crescimento orgânico da receita ao longo do ano fiscal, com o desempenho dependendo da execução contínua de sua carteira de pedidos, das iniciativas de crescimento e das condições comerciais em seus mercados de atuação. artigo.texto: O governo dos Estados Unidos incluiu o Brasil na lista de países sujeitos a restrições para a compra de chips avançados destinados a data centers. A medida também atinge Singapura, Tailândia, Malásia e Indonésia. Com a decisão, a exportação desses processadores para empresas brasileiras dependerá de autorização do Departamento de Comércio dos EUA, com análise individual de cada pedido. Segundo o Escritório de Indústria e Segurança (BIS), o objetivo é impedir que tecnologias americanas consideradas sensíveis sejam acessadas indiretamente por meio de centros de processamento de dados instalados em outros países. A restrição pode dificultar a expansão de data centers e projetos de inteligência artificial no Brasil, setores que dependem de processadores de alto desempenho. A medida não representa uma proibição total das vendas, mas estabelece novas exigências para sua autorização.

artigo.texto: A SOLV Energy (NASDAQ:MWH) anunciou uma carteira de projetos de US$ 9,2 bilhões em 30 de setembro de 2026, ao apresentar suas atividades comerciais e planos de desenvolvimento de infraestrutura durante a conferência de energia limpa RE+ 2026 em Las Vegas. A empresa afirmou que o tamanho médio de seus projetos agora ultrapassa 400 megawatts de capacidade de corrente contínua (MWdc), com o crescimento dos negócios concentrado nas regiões Sudoeste, Centro-Sul e Centro-Oeste dos Estados Unidos. A conferência marca a primeira participação da SOLV Energy na RE+ desde que se tornou uma empresa de capital aberto no início de 2026. A empresa fornece serviços de engenharia, aquisição e construção, além de operações e manutenção, suporte técnico e soluções de infraestrutura de alta tensão para projetos de energia. A aquisição amplia os serviços de transmissão e alta tensão A SOLV Energy destacou sua recente aquisição da ASB Energy Services, que amplia suas capacidades em transmissão, distribuição, infraestrutura de alta tensão e serviços de campo. A aquisição amplia a gama de serviços que a empresa pode fornecer nas fases de desenvolvimento, construção e operação de projetos de infraestrutura energética. A SOLV Energy afirmou que a maioria de seus clientes atualmente utiliza mais de um de seus serviços, incluindo engenharia, aquisição e construção, operação e manutenção, serviços técnicos e soluções de alta tensão. A empresa indicou que esse modelo de serviço permite dar suporte aos clientes em diferentes estágios da vida útil de um ativo energético. George Hershman, CEO da SOLV Energy, comentou sobre a demanda por infraestrutura energética. “A necessidade de energia confiável e escalável continua a crescer, criando oportunidades em todas as etapas do ciclo de vida dos ativos de energia”, disse Hershman. “Os clientes procuram parceiros que possam entregar projetos com sucesso e dar suporte ao desempenho dos ativos a longo prazo.” Os clientes estão cada vez mais focados em requisitos de infraestrutura de longo prazo A SOLV Energy afirmou que seus clientes estão cada vez mais considerando suas necessidades de infraestrutura em períodos mais longos, em vez de abordar projetos individuais de forma independente. A empresa atribuiu essa tendência à mudança na demanda por eletricidade e à necessidade de desenvolvimento e gestão coordenados dos ativos energéticos. Helena Kimball, Diretora de Receitas da SOLV Energy, afirmou que os clientes estão buscando parcerias com fornecedores de serviços capazes de dar suporte a múltiplos projetos à medida que suas necessidades aumentam. “Em vez de avaliar projetos individualmente, muitos estão buscando estabelecer relacionamentos com parceiros em quem confiam e com quem podem crescer ao longo do tempo”, disse Kimball. A empresa afirmou que sua combinação de serviços de construção, manutenção, técnicos e de alta tensão visa atender a essas necessidades de longo prazo. O crescimento do armazenamento de energia e dos centros de dados está entre as prioridades do setor A SOLV Energy também confirmou que Hershman tem participação agendada em um debate informal organizado pela Associação das Indústrias de Energia Solar (SEIA) no dia 17 de novembro. A discussão abordará os desenvolvimentos na infraestrutura de energia, incluindo o papel do armazenamento de energia e a expansão dos centros de dados. Essas áreas estão se tornando parte de discussões mais amplas do setor sobre demanda de eletricidade, capacidade de infraestrutura e integração de recursos adicionais de geração de energia. A participação da SOLV Energy no evento ocorre após a divulgação de sua carteira de pedidos de US$ 9,2 bilhões e do aumento no tamanho médio dos projetos para mais de 400 MWdc. A empresa não forneceu projeções financeiras adicionais nem um cronograma revisado para converter sua carteira de pedidos em receita nas informações apresentadas. artigo.texto: The U.S. Commerce Department on November 16 issued an interim rule that restricts indirect access to advanced American AI chips through overseas data centers, Bloomberg reported, as President Donald Trump prepared to travel to the Philippines and China. The rule adds export-license requirements for covered chips shipped to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil. It also gives overseas data centers that serve certain foreign customers 90 days to obtain licenses. We already walked through the mechanics in our earlier report on the five-country license requirement and 90-day deadline. This piece takes a different angle. It asks what these AI chip curbs mean for the people who rent GPU time, train models and serve inference from Southeast Asia and Brazil, and for the AI model market that leans on that compute. Trump was scheduled to meet Xi Jinping in China, and the timing colors how Washington, Beijing and regional capitals read the move. Reporting so far leaves several details open, including chip model numbers, performance thresholds and the names of affected data centers. We mark those gaps as we go, and we keep every figure tied to what outlets have actually confirmed. Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. The AI Chip Curbs at a Glance Start with what is on the record. The measure is an interim rule from the Commerce Department, and it works through export licensing rather than a ban on any single product. It covers advanced chips from NVIDIA Corporation and other U.S. manufacturers. It also reaches the data centers that sell access to that hardware, which is the part that makes it different from a classic shipment rule. One caution on framing. Some headlines say the curbs hit Asian data centers. That wording summarizes the story, but the confirmed measure is a licensing and remote-compute restriction that applies to specified countries and uses. Brazil sits on the list too, so the geography is wider than Asia alone. Why Remote Access to AI Chips Became the Target Traditional export controls govern boxes crossing borders. A buyer who cannot import accelerators directly can still rent time on servers somewhere else, send training jobs over the internet and collect the results. That path never touches a customs desk. The new rule goes after it by putting obligations on the data centers that provide the computing power, not only on the sellers of the silicon. The Associated Press framed the action as an effort to restrict China from indirect access to AI technology. That matches the language in the rule as reported, which targets overseas data centers providing “significant volumes of computing power” to companies headquartered in countries including China, Russia and Iran. Those data centers must obtain U.S. licenses and conduct end-user checks. This shift matters because earlier limits focused almost entirely on hardware. Our analysis of why US chip export controls fell short showed how much room remained once a buyer found a third-country intermediary. Washington now treats rented compute as the same kind of exposure as purchased compute. Whether that works in practice depends on enforcement, and the reporting does not describe any company-specific enforcement action yet. The Five Countries and the Higher-Than-Normal Risk Label Reuters reported that the rule names Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil as places where advanced chips face a “higher-than-normal risk” of diversion or rerouting to unauthorized buyers. Shipments of covered chips to those countries now need a U.S. export license. The label describes risk, not a finding of wrongdoing, and the reporting we reviewed does not accuse any of the five governments of facilitating diversion. The list reads like a map of where data center capital has been landing. Singapore and Malaysia have drawn heavy investment in server capacity, and Bloomberg’s headline called the region an Asian data center hotbed. Indonesia and Thailand are building out as well. Brazil is the odd one out geographically, which tells you the logic here is about transshipment risk and compute hosting, not a regional campaign against Asia. For operators in those countries, a license requirement changes timelines more than it changes demand. A shipment that used to clear in routine fashion now waits on a federal decision. Procurement teams will need to model that delay into capacity plans. How long licenses take is not stated in the reporting, so any estimate today is a guess. The 90-Day Clock for Overseas Data Centers Covered overseas data centers have 90 days to obtain licenses if they want to keep providing the specified services. If the clock runs from the November 16 announcement, that window closes around mid-February 2027. Reports do not say when the 90 days formally begin, so treat that date as arithmetic and not as a published deadline. What happens at the end of the window is also unclear. The practical reading is that a site without a license must stop providing the covered service to the restricted customers, or lose access to further covered chips. The reporting available does not spell out penalties, and we will not guess at them here. Compare that with the usual rhythm of export policy. Rules often land with immediate effect and leave industry scrambling. A 90-day runway gives operators time to audit customer lists, find out who sits behind each account and file paperwork. It also gives Washington leverage, because a data center that wants a license has a reason to cooperate on end-user checks. Who Is Exempt: U.S.-Headquartered Operators The new country-specific licensing requirements do not apply to U.S.-headquartered companies operating data centers in the five countries. That carve-out favors American cloud and colocation firms with footprints in Southeast Asia and Brazil, since they can keep building without the new license step on those

artigo.texto: A Abeeólica (Associação Brasileira de Energia Eólica e Novas Tecnologias) pediu à Justiça Federal uma liminar para suspender os primeiros leilões de armazenamento de energia em baterias do país, previstos para 2 e 4 de dezembro. A entidade, que representa a indústria nacional de geração eólica, protocolou na 2ª feira (16.nov.2026) uma Ação Civil Pública para impedir a realização do certame até que sejam definidas as regras sobre quem pagará pela contratação dos sistemas e como as despesas serão divididas. A duas semanas da disputa, a associação argumenta que é inconstitucional o trecho da lei que determina que somente os geradores arquem com os custos das baterias. Também contesta a proposta da Aneel (Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica) para distribuir as despesas entre as diferentes fontes de geração. O processo questiona os critérios de rateio sugeridos pela agência, com participação entre 25% e 100%, conforme a flexibilidade de cada fonte. Pelo modelo, geradores eólicos, solares e nucleares pagariam mais; as usinas térmicas teriam custos intermediários, e as hidrelétricas arcariam com as menores parcelas. Para a Abeeólica, algumas empresas poderiam pagar até 4 vezes mais que outras, sem critérios jurídicos claros. As regras de divisão das despesas foram submetidas pela Aneel a consulta pública, mas ainda não receberam aprovação definitiva. A entidade afirma que, sem regulamentação concluída, os agentes de geração não conseguem calcular os riscos e os impactos econômicos antes de apresentar ofertas. A ação, protocolada na 17ª Vara Federal Cível do Distrito Federal, pede a interrupção de todas as fases do certame, da disputa à adjudicação, homologação e assinatura dos contratos. A associação sustenta que as baterias devem reforçar a segurança e a estabilidade de todo o sistema elétrico nacional, beneficiando diretamente os consumidores conectados à rede. Por isso, argumenta que deixar a conta exclusivamente com os geradores viola princípios de isonomia, livre concorrência e segurança jurídica. A controvérsia envolve a Lei 15.269 de 2025, que atribuiu aos geradores os custos da contratação. Nos leilões tradicionais de reserva de capacidade, a cobrança é feita de todos os consumidores finais. Para a Abeeólica, as baterias deveriam seguir essa regra, pois também se destinam a garantir potência ao sistema. A ação cita estimativas do TCU (Tribunal de Contas da União) de que os contratos do leilão podem totalizar de R$ 108 a R$ 153 bilhões. No Congresso, há discussões para mudar a lei e retirar dos geradores a obrigação exclusiva de custear os sistemas. Em 13 de outubro, a Câmara aprovou urgência para o PL (Projeto de Lei) 3.716 de 2026, apresentado pelo deputado Arnaldo Jardim (Cidadania-SP) e relatado pelo deputado Danilo Forte (PP-CE). A proposta revoga o trecho da lei de 2025 e prevê a aplicação da regra geral de divisão dos custos. Segundo a Aneel, se o texto for aprovado antes do leilão, será necessário alterar o edital: as despesas passariam a ser compartilhadas pelos usuários finais do SIN (Sistema Interligado Nacional), incluindo os consumidores. As baterias armazenam energia produzida quando há maior oferta e a devolvem à rede nos períodos de aumento do consumo. Na geração solar, podem ser carregadas durante o dia e acionadas no início da noite, quando a produção solar diminui e a demanda é maior. O armazenamento ajuda a reduzir o desperdício e dá flexibilidade ao sistema, permitindo equilibrar rapidamente geração e consumo. Ainda assim, não substitui os investimentos necessários para ampliar as redes de transmissão e distribuição.

artigo.texto: Ford starts shipping CATL battery cells from Michigan plant Ford has shipped its first CATL battery cells from Michigan, a milestone dogged by political scrutiny of the Chinese tie-up and shaky quarterly profits. In this article 3 sections Ford Motor Co (NYSE: F) has shipped its first CATL battery cells from a Michigan factory, a concrete step in a strategy the carmaker has pursued since 2023 but one that remains politically fraught in Washington. The cells, manufactured using technology licensed from China’s CATL, left the BlueOval Battery Park in Marshall, Michigan, on Wednesday 18 November 2026, bound for the Louisville Assembly Plant in Kentucky, where they will power pre-production units of Ford’s new Fathom electric pickup, as UPI reported. The cells are lithium iron phosphate, or LFP – a battery chemistry that trades some energy density for lower cost and longer cycle life, and one that Chinese manufacturers have dominated for years. Ford’s VP of advanced development, Alan Clarke, said CATL’s scale made it “the best supplier” to help the company learn the chemistry quickly, framing the licensing arrangement as a fast-track rather than a dependency, according to UPI. A licence, not a joint venture – Ford insists The structural distinction matters because it has become the crux of a running argument in Washington. Ford has been explicit that the Marshall plant is wholly owned and operated by the carmaker, which employs the workforce and runs the supply chain, with CATL providing technology and services under contract rather than equity, according to reporting from CarPro. That framing has not satisfied every critic in the current administration. US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the department “remains deeply alarmed by Ford’s continued reliance on licensed technology from Chinese battery manufacturer CATL” at the Marshall facility, according to InsideEVs. Ford’s response, as relayed by the same outlet, was that the arrangement is “a limited technology-licensing and services agreement, not a joint venture or foreign-owned manufacturing operation” – a rebuttal that effectively concedes the political sensitivity even as it rejects the characterisation. CATL’s presence on a Pentagon list of companies alleged to have military ties has kept that scrutiny alive since the deal was first struck, per CarPro. For Ford, Marshall is as much a test of whether a US-owned plant running licensed Chinese chemistry can pass political muster as it is a manufacturing milestone. The scale Ford is chasing Ford says the Michigan lines can run at 40 cells a minute, which the company describes as among the fastest LFP prismatic production rates outside China, according to Yahoo Finance. The Detroit News reported the plant is designed to eventually run two such lines at full ramp-up. The facility itself represents a $3 billion investment, according to the International Business Times, with production having quietly begun in October before Wednesday’s shipment made the milestone public. Ford’s own target is to begin assembling cells into finished battery packs at a neighbouring facility in 2027, with the first production Fathom pickups reaching buyers by the end of that year, according to Fox17/WOOD-TV, which also reported that Michigan governor Gretchen Whitmer attended the launch and credited state support for landing the project. Ford’s long-term goal for the site is roughly 1,700 jobs, more than 70% of them drawn from the Marshall, Albion and Battle Creek area, the same report said. A milestone against an uneven balance sheet The announcement lands at an awkward moment for Ford’s core profitability. The carmaker’s quarterly net income has swung sharply over the past two years – from a $1.92 billion profit in the second quarter of 2023 to a $36 million net loss in the second quarter of 2025, before returning to diluted earnings per share of $0.50 in the third quarter of 2026, according to Ford’s own filings with the SEC. Quarterly revenue has moved in a similarly uneven band, from $40.7 billion in the first quarter of 2025 to $50.5 billion a couple of quarters later, per the same disclosures. Battery self-sufficiency is, in that context, as much a cost-control bet as a technology one: LFP chemistry is cheaper than the nickel-based cells Ford has relied on, and bringing production onshore is meant to insulate the company from both tariff exposure and supply shocks further down the line. Markets, for their part, treated the news as background noise rather than a catalyst. Ford shares closed at $11.31, down 0.57% on the day and down 5.31% over the preceding 20 trading sessions, with volume running at 1.12 times the 20-day average – a pattern consistent with the stock’s existing short-term drift rather than a reaction unique to the battery news. What happens next is less about the shipment itself than about what comes after it. Ford has pointed to 2027 as the year it expects to move from shipping test cells to assembling full packs at Marshall, and ultimately to putting Fathom pickups built on this chemistry into customers’ hands. Whether the licensing structure it has built around CATL can survive sustained political pressure in Washington may end up mattering as much to that timeline as the engineering does. artigo.texto: Relatórios Estudo de Harvard conclui que os combustíveis fósseis fornecem energia à maioria dos data centers hiperescaláveis dos EUA Adicione Unite.AI às suas fontes preferidas no Google Pontos-chaveOs combustíveis fósseis forneceram aproximadamente 54% da eletricidade atribuída aos… Ver mais - Os combustíveis fósseis forneceram aproximadamente 54% da eletricidade atribuída aos data centers de hiperescala dos EUA. - As emissões atribuídas a um data center dependem da matriz de geração da sua rede regional. - O estudo não conseguiu separar o uso de eletricidade específico da IA da computação de uso geral em instalações individuais. Um estudo liderado por Harvard, publicado em 16 de novembro de 2026 na Nature Sustainability, estima que 403 data centers hiperescaláveis dos EUA consumiram aproximadamente 82 terawatts-hora (TWh) de eletricidade no cenário central, o equivalente a cerca de 1,8% do consumo total de eletricidade dos EUA. Os combustíveis fósseis forneceram cerca de 54% da geração atribuída, principalmente gás natural, com 38%, e carvão, com 15%. A estimativa central das emissões atribuíveis de dióxido de carbono (CO2) foi de aproximadamente 25,7 milhões de toneladas métricas, dentro de uma faixa de 21 a 31 milhões de toneladas métricas entre os cenários. Nos diferentes cenários de carga das instalações, o consumo estimado de eletricidade variou de aproximadamente 68 a 99 TWh. Harvard afirmou que a estimativa mais alta se aproxima do consumo anual de eletricidade de estados como Indiana, Michigan e Tennessee. Como foram elaboradas as estimativas das instalações As estimativas abrangem o período de maio de 2024 a abril de 2025. Os pesquisadores usaram imagens de satélite para compilar a lista de instalações e modelaram o consumo anual de eletricidade de cada local em diferentes cenários operacionais. Em seguida, usaram dados da Agência de Proteção Ambiental para atribuir as emissões de acordo com a combinação de usinas de energia na rede regional de cada instalação. O artigo descreve seu método central de contabilização como um método de atribuição baseado na localização e na produção total da autoridade de balanceamento. Na prática, a abordagem distribui entre as instalações a geração e as emissões das usinas da rede regional pertinente. O resultado é uma estimativa das fontes de eletricidade e das emissões discriminada por instalação, em vez de leituras diretas dos medidores de cada local. As redes regionais moldam a pegada Segundo a medida de produção total ponderada pelo consumo de eletricidade usada no artigo, a intensidade de carbono foi de aproximadamente 314 gramas de CO2 por quilowatt-hora, em comparação com a média de produção total dos EUA, de aproximadamente 348 gramas. Essa média agregada mais baixa coexiste com grandes variações regionais: cerca de um quarto da eletricidade foi consumida em regiões da rede com intensidade de carbono acima da média nacional, e muitas instalações estavam concentradas em áreas onde a geração a carvão contribui significativamente para o abastecimento. Virginia, Oregon, Ohio e Iowa responderam, em conjunto, por mais da metade do consumo de eletricidade analisado. Portanto, uma média nacional não representa todos os complexos de data centers; as emissões atribuídas a uma instalação dependem da combinação de fontes de geração de sua rede regional. O que as estimativas não esclarecem Os dados disponíveis não abrangiam todos os data centers hiperescaláveis dos EUA, e os pesquisadores não conseguiram separar, em cada instalação, a eletricidade usada em operações especializadas em IA daquela destinada à computação de uso geral. As instalações dão suporte a serviços como computação em nuvem, treinamento de grandes modelos de linguagem e implantação global de ferramentas de IA; por isso, os totais não podem ser interpretados como consumo exclusivo de IA. O autor principal, Gianluca Guidi, afirmou no anúncio de Harvard que o consumo de eletricidade e a pegada de carbono relatados “já podem ser substancialmente maiores agora, em 2026”. Trata-se de uma projeção baseada nas instalações construídas e nos complexos ampliados após o período do estudo, além do crescimento contínuo da demanda por computação de IA, e não de uma nova medição. O estudo não mediu diretamente os efeitos sobre a saúde, que os pesquisadores planejam investigar em trabalhos futuros. A autora correspondente, Francesca Dominici, descreveu duas vias: o dióxido de carbono impulsiona as mudanças climáticas, que afetam a saúde por meio de ondas de calor, fumaça de incêndios florestais, inundações e outras vias; além disso, as usinas de combustíveis fósseis liberam material particulado fino, óxidos de nitrogênio e dióxido de enxofre, associados a doenças cardíacas e pulmonares e à morte prematura. As pessoas que vivem perto dessas usinas e a favor do vento em relação a elas podem arcar com custos para a saúde mesmo estando longe do próprio data center. Dominici afirmou que o objetivo é oferecer ao público, aos formuladores de políticas, aos investidores e aos incorporadores uma base mais concreta para decidir onde instalar data centers e como abastecê-los de energia. Essa estrutura amplia a contabilização, que deixa de se limitar a um único total nacional e passa a abranger as redes regionais e suas usinas — o nível em que se encontram a escolha de locais para data centers hiperescaláveis, o fornecimento de eletricidade e as emissões atribuíveis.

artigo.texto: EU 2040 Climate Goal Faces Pressure From Carbon Market Compromise A leaked document reviewed by Euronews indicates that reforms to the European Union's Emissions Trading System could weaken the bloc's 2040 climate target. The Irish Presidency of the EU Council has softened a proposal set for discussion by EU ambassadors on Wednesday, as political pressure mounts over reconciling emissions goals with industrial competitiveness and high energy costs. The compromise text aims to secure political backing for the carbon market beyond 2030, but climate advocates caution that concessions meant to protect European industry may reduce the system's contribution to the 2040 target, leaving other economic sectors to cover the gap. Free Allowances and Investment Plans The Council text keeps the European Commission's July proposal to slow the decline in carbon allowances, extend free permits for industry and bring international carbon credits into the EU market so that domestic emissions can be offset through projects abroad. Under the Irish Presidency's proposal, industrial companies would retain 80 percent of their free allowances if they submit an investment plan, even if they later fail to carry out the proposed decarbonisation investments. The remaining 20 percent would depend on starting construction of eligible projects. Free allowances are permits companies receive without buying them at auction, designed to shield EU producers from competition in countries with less stringent climate rules, such as China and the United States. The proposal represents a significant political concession to industries worried about losing those allowances and raises questions about whether the ETS will provide enough incentive to cut emissions. International Credits and the 2040 Target On international carbon credits, the Council has retained the Commission's proposal to set aside allowances equivalent to 260 million tonnes of CO2 to finance their purchase. It also leaves open a possible pilot phase between 2031 and 2035 to test the system before full implementation. The Council has maintained stringent quality and integrity requirements for international credits, making the ETS reduction trajectory increasingly dependent on their availability. If industries cannot buy them, the 2040 climate target could be jeopardised, since it requires at least an 85 percent domestic net emissions reduction, with international credits accounting for the remaining 5 percent. Negotiation Timeline and Member State Divisions The Irish Presidency is seeking consensus among the 27 EU countries before talks move to more politically sensitive questions of climate ambition and burden-sharing. It hopes to secure an agreement at the Environment Council on December 11, while the European Parliament is expected to vote during its December 14-17 plenary session in Strasbourg. The presidency faces an uphill battle given deep divisions among member states and the complexity of the negotiations. According to a second document reviewed by Euronews, EU countries are already divided over how quickly carbon permit supply should shrink, whether companies should use international credits to meet obligations and how far industrial sectors should be shielded from rising carbon costs. Taken together, these demands risk diluting the ETS when it is expected to drive a large share of the bloc's next phase of emissions cuts. Governments generally want to preserve the ETS as a source of revenue for decarbonisation, but concerns are growing about costs imposed on energy-intensive industries competing with manufacturers in China or the United States. Some capitals argue permit numbers should decline to raise carbon pricing and encourage divestment from fossil fuels, while others fear the impact of withdrawing free allowances on struggling industries. A slower reduction would ease pressure on power plants and factories, potentially tempering carbon prices and giving companies more time to adapt, but it would also mean fewer emissions cuts in ETS-covered sectors, making the 2040 target harder to reach. Analysis Questions Reform Compatibility A recent analysis by the Oko-Institut, commissioned by the environmental campaign group WWF Germany, warned that the Commission's proposed ETS reform is incompatible with the EU target of cutting net emissions by 90 percent by 2040. Lisa Okken, an industrial policy expert at WWF Germany, said the Commission was choosing to take risks on climate protection rather than safeguard the future of European industry, and argued that the proposed reform lacks the carbon price signal needed to drive urgent modernisation. She said the gap was being filled with complicated accounting measures and excessive flexibility. Environmentalists also cited concern over a proposal to allow additional emissions beyond the existing cap in exchange for future permanent carbon removals through expensive technologies designed to capture CO2 from the air. The study noted that it remains unclear whether such removals can be delivered at the required scale, since the necessary capacity does not exist today. - 1. artigo.texto: SNOQUALMIE, Wash. — In the race to meet the nation’s growing power demands, states and utilities are rapidly building new “battery farms” that can store energy for when customers need it most. But as the facilities grow, so too does community opposition. The systems store banks of batteries in buildings or shipping containers. While they can take many forms, developers are increasingly building large, multi-acre projects designed to meet the needs of local utilities. The electricity stored by such systems nationwide has grown tenfold since 2022, and it’s projected to double again by the end of 2028. State lawmakers and renewable energy advocates say battery storage is urgently needed to stabilize the grid and support the transition to clean power. But in some communities, residents are wary of proposals to build industrial battery systems in their neighborhoods, noting that battery fires can produce toxic smoke and are difficult to extinguish. As the backlash has grown, nearly 200 communities have passed or proposed moratoriums to block battery farms from being built near them. Backers say modern systems are designed to be much safer than previous versions, with data showing that fire risk has dropped significantly. But some industry leaders fear the perception of danger — along with a rising tide of community activism stirred by the buildout of data centers — could threaten an industry that’s becoming integral to the nation’s energy future. ‘Meteoric growth’ Most energy storage on the U.S. grid takes the form of battery energy storage systems, commonly known as BESS. Such facilities host banks of batteries, typically lithium-ion — a technology that has become more capable and cost-effective with the development of electric vehicles. At present, battery storage capacity nationwide exceeds 50 gigawatts, up from just 5 gigawatts at the beginning of 2022. Another 54 gigawatts is slated to come online in the next two and a half years. That projected total of more than 100 gigawatts would be enough to power roughly 75 million homes, although battery farms are designed to provide electricity for one to four hours, as opposed to the more continuous supply of conventional power plants. “The meteoric growth is continuing,” said Noah Roberts, executive director of the U.S. Energy Storage Coalition, an industry group. “For state policymakers who are focused on the energy transition and decarbonizing the grid, (battery) storage is essential.” Policymakers and energy planners have increasingly pushed for battery farms as more renewable energy sources have come online. Solar farms, for instance, can produce massive amounts of cheap electricity during the afternoon hours — but peak demand is in the evening, when people get home from work and turn on household appliances. With batteries on the grid, that surplus solar energy can be stored and saved for when it’s needed, instead of firing up more costly “peaker” gas plants to meet evening demand. Industry leaders say battery systems can also improve reliability and affordability, even in states without clean energy goals. They note that Texas and California are home to a majority of the battery projects on the grid so far. While typically on opposite ends of the political spectrum, both states produce large amounts of wind and solar energy, while facing heavy power demands that have at times required energy conservation measures and put the grid at risk of blackouts. Battery systems, backers say, have already stabilized their grids considerably. Adding to the appeal of battery farms is the fact that they can be put in place quickly, in a matter of months, compared with much longer timelines for other energy projects. “As we’re dealing with a power supply crisis, energy storage is the obvious solution for adding capacity and getting more out of the grid that we’ve already paid for,” Roberts said. State policies have been a driver of the industry’s growth. Thirteen states have enacted targets requiring their utilities to deploy certain amounts of energy storage by specific dates. In Maryland, Democratic Del. Lorig Charkoudian authored a law in 2025 directing state regulators to issue bids for projects totaling 1,600 megawatts of energy storage. “It’s basically a no-regret path,” Charkoudian said in an interview earlier this year. “Over time once we bring more renewables on, they will be that much more valuable because there’s battery storage.” Charkoudian noted that the Trump administration has stalled permitting for offshore wind and other renewable projects, while phasing out clean energy tax credits. The federal push against those forms of energy has made battery farms a more attractive option, as they’ve met with less resistance and still qualify for a 30% tax credit. Community concerns For all of the potential that battery farms offer the grid, some communities are not eager to host them. Much of the opposition centers around the risk for out-of-control fires and toxic smoke. Most prominently, the Moss Landing Power Plant in Monterey County, California, caught fire in early 2025, burned for several days and released 55,000 pounds of toxic metals into nearby wetlands. Lithium-ion batteries, when ignited, can trigger a reaction known as thermal runaway that is nearly impossible to extinguish. Across the country, community activists have been alarmed to see battery farms proposed near schools, playgrounds and senior care facilities. “They’re making us collateral damage,” said Phoenix Artemisia, an activist in Watsonville, California, who has helped lead efforts to oppose a proposed battery storage facility there. “We have 12 schools within two miles of us here, but these out-of-state developers are telling us what we’re going to do in our backyard.” The Watsonville project has stirred up significant community opposition, Artemisia said, prompting the developer to seek approval from state regulators in order to bypass local officials. artigo.texto: Oklahoma currently has 64 data centers operating or in progress. Editor’s note: This story was updated on 11/16/2026 with new information from the U.S. Data Center map, and updates to local project. Our Data Center Info Hub features an interactive map, data center profiles, frequently asked questions, and a form to ask us your questions about data centers in your area. Driven by affordable land, access to power, and growing demand for cloud and AI services, companies ranging from global tech giants to regional providers are expanding their presence in Oklahoma. According to the US Data Center Map, data as of Oct 2026. https://dcmap.us, Oklahoma has: - 64 data center projects overall - 34 operational data centers - 6 data centers under construction - 20 data centers planned - 2 paused data center projects - 2 inactive data centers Below is a running list of data center projects across the state. This article will be updated as new facilities are announced, approved, or completed. Claremore Project Mustang (Approved) Project Mustang is an approved data center development at the Claremore Industrial Park by Beale Infrastructure. Plans call for multiple data center buildings and office space, with power supplied by Grand River Dam Authority and water and wastewater services provided by the City of Claremore. City leaders say the property is already zoned for industrial use and that the developer would pay for required infrastructure upgrades. The Claremore City Council approved plans Monday, May 18, for “Project Mustang.” Claremore City Hall reached standing-room capacity during the meeting, with dozens of people waiting outside and rotating in to comply with fire code limits. Public comment lasted nearly two hours before the council voted on the proposal. Related Story: Claremore approves Project Mustang data center plan The agreement allows Beale Infrastructure to seek a 25-year ad valorem tax exemption for each phase of the project. Company representatives said the development would still contribute more than $250 million toward Rogers County schools, municipal services and community programs over time. Some residents have raised concerns about water usage, environmental impacts and transparency. City officials and the developer say the project would not raise taxes or utility rates and could bring long-term investment and jobs. Muskogee County Google Data Centers (Summit and Council Hill) (Early Development) Google plans to build two new data center campuses near Summit and Council Hill as part of a $9 billion investment in Oklahoma. The facilities are expected to support Google’s cloud and AI services, including Search, Maps and Google Cloud. The company says the projects will be paired with clean energy agreements expected to add hundreds of megawatts of renewable power to Oklahoma’s grid. Construction timelines have not been released. Related Story: Google to build two data centers in Muskogee County as part of $9B Oklahoma investment In April, OG&E announced that it will power the Muskogee data centers as well as a data center coming to Stillwater (see below) “OG&E is pleased to support Google and together advance growth in our home state, ensuring our current customers benefit from data center expansion that meets the technology needs of the 21st century economy at some of the lowest rates in the country,” said Sean Trauschke, Chairman, President and CEO of OGE Energy Corp. “This unique agreement is a model for future data center partnerships and forms the basis for a new large-load tariff that OG&E will submit in the coming weeks that protects our current customers from bearing the costs of this growing demand and Oklahoma’s goals for economic growth.” Core Scientific (Under Construction) A Core Scientific data center in Muskogee at 4800 S 24th St W. is operational, as of Aug. 14, 2026, according to the U.S. Data Center map. Two more Core Scientific high-performance computing (HPC) data centers in Muskogee are under construction. Oklahoma City American Tower EDC Oklahoma (Planned) American Tower EDC Oklahoma is a construction-ready edge data center* development located at 1309 Northeast 122nd Street in Oklahoma City, Oklahoma. According to American Tower, the facility would be on 83.5 acres and provide 4MW of capacity. The American Tower EDC Oklahoma company says that zoning has been approved and that the facility can be ready in 18 months once a customer signs an anchor lease. *An edge data center is a smaller, decentralized facility positioned near the source of data generation. Cerebras Systems operates a 10-megawatt data center in Oklahoma City in partnership with Scale Datacenters. The facility supports large-scale AI computing and uses a closed-loop, direct-to-chip liquid cooling system. CloudBurst Oklahoma City Campus - 3 Data Centers (Under Construction) The CloudBurst Oklahoma City Campus is planned to be an expansive location with a total capacity of 200MW covering at least three data centers. It is planned for the area near 2000 S Council Rd. Cogent Data Center (Operational) The Cogent Data Center in Oklahoma City is 5,294 square feet of colocation space designed for 42U cabinets. The Cogent data center is what’s known as a “carrier hotel,” meaning that it has equipment, space, and/or bandwidth available for rental to retail customers. Lumen Technologies operates the Oklahoma City 1 data center, supporting enterprise, government and network infrastructure. MIDCON Recovery Solutions operates a 60,000-square-foot data center in northwest Oklahoma City’s Quail Springs Business Park, designed to meet Tier IV standards. RACK59 operates a 30,000-square-foot colocation data center at 7725 West Reno Avenue, offering redundant power and on-site substation access. TierPoint operates multiple Oklahoma City facilities providing colocation and enterprise services ValorC3 operates a 65,000-square-foot Tier III+ data center designed to withstand severe weather, including EF5 tornadoes.

artigo.texto: BOTETOURT COUNTY, Va. – A Botetourt County judge is taking more time to decide whether construction on a controversial 300-acre Google data center campus should be halted. Following a hearing Monday, the judge gave attorneys for the three parties involved, Botetourt County, Google shell company Helio, and Botetourt County resident Robert Dallas, until Friday to submit additional briefs explaining their arguments. The judge said he wants more time to review the evidence and relevant case law before deciding whether the county violated Virginia’s Freedom of Information Act. John Fishwick, who represents Dallas, argued the county failed to adequately disclose that supervisors would be voting on the project’s performance agreement during a June 2025 meeting. Fishwick said the county did not provide the public with enough information about the agreement before the vote, arguing that the lack of disclosure violated state law. “We think we have a strong case. We think we’ve made it,” Fishwick said. “We’re pleased with how the evidence came in today. We put a lot of evidence in front of the judge. Ultimately, that’ll be his call.” The county maintains it made information about the project available to the public, including posting the performance agreement online after the deal was finalized. “Once the deal was consummated, it was all out in the open. Anyone could issue a FOIA request for the deal. The deal was placed on the website,” said Julian Harf, an attorney representing Botetourt County. However, the judge questioned the timing of that disclosure, pointing out that the details of the agreement were not made public until several hours after supervisors voted on it. “I have a fundamental disagreement as far as the temporal issue and whether you can disclose three and a half hours after the vote, and that somehow satisfies the statutes,” the judge said. The judge also acknowledged a fundamental disagreement between the parties over what qualifies as disclosure under the state’s open meeting requirements. A ruling could come as early as Monday, after the judge has had additional time to review the arguments and determine whether the remedies Dallas is seeking are permitted under the Freedom of Information Act.

artigo.texto: Lawmakers call for national data center construction pause WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Members of Congress are calling for a national moratorium on data center construction until the artificial intelligence field can be regulated. They said data centers are not helping local communities and, in many cases, are actively harming them. Rep. Jim McGovern (D-Mass.) said the White House is not doing enough on artificial intelligence. “The alarm bells are flashing. And the president and the White House are asleep at the switch when it comes to AI,” he said. McGovern said big tech leaders are becoming oligarchs and are enriching themselves at the expense of local communities with data centers. “These billionaires want to come into our communities, tell us what to do, and make a profit by driving up our utility prices, and wrecking our environment,” he said. Rep.-elect William Lawrence (D-Mich.) said data centers do not provide the same community value as an automotive plant. “The value, the billions of dollars that is being raised to build these data centers, is built on the promise that it’s going to put people out of work,” he said. Lawmakers said pausing new construction would give Congress time to pass regulations and protect communities from future construction. Rep. Chellie Pingree (D-Maine) said she wants transparency in dealings between big tech and the government. “We don’t want back door deals and secret handshakes between big tech and the government. We want transparency, community engagement, and strong regulations that protect our air, water, climate and communities,” she said. It is not yet clear whether the plan has enough support to pass in the next Congress. The Trump administration has attempted to rename AI - artificial intelligence - as SI - super intelligence. artigo.texto: Texas data center permits moving forward again following Abbott pause AUSTIN, Texas - Texas environmental regulators have begun reviewing permits for data centers again just months after outgoing Gov. Greg Abbott issued an order halting the controversial projects. What we know: The Texas Commission of Environmental Quality (TCEQ) said it was notified that the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) completed its audit looking at whether these data centers could have an impact on the state’s power grid and natural resources. "The agency has resumed its normal permit review process and will evaluate applications under all applicable state and federal laws and regulations," Ryan Vise, director of external relations for TCEQ, said in a statement emailed Tuesday night. A pause on data center permits The backstory: Abbott directed ERCOT to audit all data center projects in August, effectively putting a pause on any pending projects until regulators had gathered the information requested. A letter the governor sent to the TCEQ in September specifically requested that no projects be approved by the agency until the audit was completed. The governor said that, after the review, the TCEQ must only approve audited data centers that follow his directives. SpaceX gets permit What's next: It appears that at least one permit has already been approved since the pause was lifted. Politico reported earlier this week that the TCEQ had issued an air pollution permit to SpaceX for a $24 billion data center project being planned in Starbase, where the company is based. Projects draw controversy Local perspective: These data center projects have drawn concerns from residents across the state who worry about the potential impact on their communities. Some cite worries over noise, light and water pollution, and the closeness of the facilities to their neighborhoods. Activists in Cameron County have previously organized protests against the proposed SpaceX data center, claiming that it and others in the Rio Grande Valley will "use up water" and increase energy bills. Hundreds have popped up in recent years, with Abbott previously welcoming the artificial intelligence agency. Gina Hinojosa, his Democratic opponent in the midterm elections, often criticized him over his attitude toward data center development in the state. Incoming governor promises moratorium Dig deeper: Hinojosa will officially be sworn into the governor’s office in January after defeating Abbott in a stunning upset. Among her campaign promises was an immediate moratorium on data centers. She said she would keep the projects paused until lawmakers could develop stricter regulations. Some state lawmakers have already proposed removing tax breaks and requiring all agreements between data centers and municipalities to be made publicly available. Findings of audit not yet released The findings from ERCOT’s review have not yet been publicly released. The agency last provided an update on Nov. 5 to the Public Utility Commission of Texas, in which it said 93% of companies had responded to its request for information. The Source: The information in this article comes from an emailed statement from the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality, reports by Politico and previous Fox Local reporting.
