artigo.texto: In March, Super Micro faced a crisis. Two employees at the U.S. server giant, including one of its co-founders, had just been charged in federal court with attempting to transfer Nvidia AI chips to China, in violation of U.S. export laws. Weeks later, Super Micro retained the services of Ballard Partners, a lobbying firm known for its close ties to the Trump administration. Ballard would help the company with “advocacy regarding AI data center infrastructure policy” and “export control regulations affecting advanced computing hardware,” according to records maintained under the Lobbying Disclosure Act. Super Micro is one of three firms involved in Southeast Asia’s data center boom that have called on Ballard since the beginning of Trump’s second term. The region has emerged as a hotbed for server companies providing remote access to Nvidia chips for Chinese AI companies. Ballard’s other clients include EdgeConneX, a U.S. firm that operates data centers in Kuala Lumpur and Jakarta, with three more under construction elsewhere in Malaysia and the Philippines, and Equinix, another data center operator for which Ballard has been “tracking executive orders and action regarding power, energy, and data center development.” Equinix, too, has expanded operations in Southeast Asia since Trump retook office. Ballard’s work on behalf of data center operators raises questions about vectors of influence in the Trump administration, whose approach to chip export policy has come under fresh scrutiny following revelations about Jensen Huang’s affair with former Megaspeed executive and alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang (黃樂). Super Micro has also returned to the spotlight this week, following a statement from Singapore’s government saying that the company had provided “limited cooperation” with its investigation into Alice Huang last year. Since the second quarter of this year, Super Micro has paid Ballard $100,000 each month as the company has come under increasing scrutiny for its role in a network of AI infrastructure providers that Nvidia assembled in East Asia to get around U.S. export controls. The lobbyists on the Super Micro account include two former high-level officials with recent experience in the Trump White House. Thomas Boodry, a former aide to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, served as special assistant to President Trump and senior director for legislative affairs at the National Security Council. Micah Ketchel served as a Trump special assistant, too, and a senior advisor to the former national security advisor, Michael Waltz. Domino Theory has reached out to Boodry for comment. Ketchel could not immediately be contacted. Both men left the administration around the time that Waltz — who accidentally added a journalist to a group chat containing classified battle plans for Yemen — transitioned out of his role as national security advisor. Founded in Tallahassee, Florida, in 1998, Ballard Partners did not expand outside of Florida until 2017, establishing an office in Washington when Trump became president. Brian Ballard, the firm’s founder, has had close ties to the president for more than a decade. When Trump first ran for president in 2016, Ballard chaired the campaign’s finance committee in Florida. Ballard Partners has also acted as a talent pipeline for Trump. The firm’s alumni include his former Chief of Staff Susie Wiles and former Attorney General Pam Bondi. In a recent interview, Calley Means, a former top aide to Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., told CBS News that Ballard “controlled” White House policy. Ballard’s more than $88 million in lobbying revenue in 2025 was the highest of any firm since the Lobbying Disclosure Act went into effect in 1996, even after adjusting for inflation, according to CBS News. In the first three quarters of this year, it has already earned $98 million. The firm’s clients have included Lenovo, a Chinese computer maker that a House committee accused of building a back door for the Chinese government to spy on users in late 2023. Lenovo denied these allegations. Ballard has also worked for ByteDance, the Chinese tech giant that struck a joint venture deal to keep operating its social media platform TikTok in the U.S. earlier this year. More than $1 million of Ballard’s recent revenue has come from EdgeConneX, which first hired them in late 2024 for lobbying related to “International Data Center development opportunities,” according to disclosure records. Ballard’s most recent lobbying disclosure on behalf of EdgeConneX came in the third quarter of 2025, when it contacted an office at the White House. Since then, it has continued to receive $50,000 each month for its services, despite reporting no further lobbying activity. EdgeConneX has been rapidly expanding its AI data center capacity in Malaysia, where Chinese AI firms have increasingly turned for remote access to Nvidia-powered servers. It is currently building two data center campuses, in Cyberjaya and Johor, designed specifically to handle AI workloads. “These facilities also serve as gateways for global cloud and cloud-based services expanding throughout Southeast Asia and beyond,” reads a description of the project on the company’s website. A 2020 press release described EdgeConneX as a “long-term member of the Nvidia DGX-Ready Data Center program.” Providing cloud services remotely to Chinese AI firms from Southeast Asia has been legal since January 2025, when the U.S. Commerce Department revoked a Biden-era rule restricting the practice. artigo.texto: The Churchill County Planning Commission has recommended new rules for data centers and other industrial development, including a requirement that the largest data centers come before the commission for a special use permit. Commissioners voted 5–1 on Nov. 12 to forward the proposed ordinance, with revisions made during the meeting, to the Churchill County Commission, with Commissioner Mark Hyde dissenting. The county commission will make the final decision. The recommendation followed a lengthy discussion about water use, backup generators, industrial chemicals and the amount of public review that should be required as interest in data centers grows. Under the recommendation summarized by county staff before the vote, data centers with a capacity of 100 megawatts or more would require a special use permit in all three industrial zoning districts. Those permits come before the Planning Commission for a public hearing. Facilities under 10 megawatts would require a conditional zoning permit in each of the three districts. For facilities from 10 to 100 megawatts, a special use permit would be required in the I-1 district, while a conditional zoning permit would apply in the I-2 and I-3 districts. Commissioners also agreed to recommend adding battery energy storage systems to the county’s use table, with a special use permit required in the three industrial districts. The permit categories became a central point of debate. Commissioner Dennis Mills argued that the largest data centers should come before the board and receive public attention. Other commissioners said they wanted standards that would give potential investors certainty while preserving the possibility of industrial development. Commissioner Joe Frey questioned whether some of the proposed requirements would duplicate state or federal regulations and whether the county had enough capacity to enforce additional rules. He said the county should remain cautious without allowing fear to drive its approach. The proposed ordinance extends beyond data centers. The draft in the meeting packet would establish standards for new industrial uses and substantial expansions, addressing water, power, chemicals, traffic, noise, building appearance and sanitation. The draft calls for water-efficient cooling methods and annual reporting of operational water use. Depending on the project, applicants could also be asked for information such as estimated power consumption, a power provision plan, traffic studies and emergency planning documents. Commissioners discussed reporting requirements for industrial spills and other incidents. In staff’s summary of the revisions, a state-reportable spill, an explosion or a fire requiring a fire department response would be reported to Churchill County within 10 days. Staff said copies of state reporting forms would be acceptable, and annual reporting would remain part of the recommendation. Commissioners also agreed to remove a proposed requirement that backup generators meet an EPA Tier 4 standard. Staff said that language was specific to diesel generators and could unintentionally limit the types of backup power used. The revisions summarized at the meeting would apply the backup-generator provisions to facilities with more than two megawatts of combined backup-generator capacity. Resident Michelle Anderson raised concerns about public access and the commission’s oversight during opening public comment. She questioned whether replacing some special use permit hearings with administrative approvals would reduce opportunities for public review.

artigo.texto: Patrocinado por: Data centers: empresas brasileiras passam a precisar de licença dos EUA para receber chips avançados de IA (Envato) (Costfoto/NurPhoto/Getty Images) Repórter de Inteligência Artificial e Tecnologia Publicado em 19 de novembro de 2026 às 06h01. Regra do Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), do Departamento de Comércio dos Estados Unidos, publicada no Federal Register em 19 de novembro de 2026, passa a exigir licença para exportar, reexportar ou transferir chips avançados de IA ao Brasil, à Indonésia, à Malásia, a Singapura e à Tailândia. Vendas a destinatários com sede nos EUA ou controlados de lá, como as donas da AWS, do Azure e do Google Cloud, ficam isentas de licença, desde que o exportador, reexportador ou transferidor envie relatórios mensais ao BIS. Empresas brasileiras precisam de autorização caso a caso. A ABES diz que a regra cria condições desiguais de competição, e o governo brasileiro montou uma força-tarefa para medir o impacto. Os Estados Unidos devem publicar nesta quinta-feira, 19, a regra que passa a exigir licença para exportar chips avançados de inteligência artificial (IA) ao Brasil. A exigência não vale para todos. Se o destinatário for subsidiária de uma empresa americana, como as donas da AWS, do Azure e do Google Cloud, basta que o fornecedor dos chips envie relatórios mensais a Washington. Se for uma empresa brasileira, é preciso pedir autorização ao governo americano e esperar a resposta, caso a caso. A regra foi anunciada na segunda-feira, 16, pelo Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), órgão do Departamento de Comércio dos Estados Unidos que controla exportações de tecnologia. A norma entra em vigor na data de publicação no Federal Register, o diário oficial americano, e vale também para Indonésia, Malásia, Singapura e Tailândia. Para a Associação Brasileira das Empresas de Software (ABES), que representa cerca de 2.000 empresas de software e tecnologia no país, a regra pode "criar condições desiguais de competição entre empresas brasileiras e subsidiárias de companhias norte-americanas". Em Brasília, o governo montou uma força-tarefa para medir o impacto da medida. A regra é uma norma provisória com efeito imediato, o que os americanos chamam de interim final rule. O texto foi disponibilizado para consulta pública prévia no Federal Register na segunda-feira e tem duas partes. A primeira exige licença para exportar, reexportar ou transferir chips avançados de IA aos cinco países da lista. O controle vale também para componentes e servidores fabricados em outros países que usem tecnologia americana. Não se trata de uma proibição de venda ao Brasil: cada pedido será avaliado caso a caso. A segunda parte vale para data centers em qualquer lugar do mundo. Quem oferecer grande capacidade de computação a empresas sediadas na China, ou controladas a partir de lá, precisa de autorização. O objetivo é fechar a brecha que permitia a empresas chinesas usar chips americanos pela nuvem, alugando capacidade em outros países. Data centers que já prestam esse tipo de serviço a clientes abrangidos pela regra e querem continuar têm 90 dias, a partir da entrada em vigor, para obter a licença. A regra também abriu um período de 60 dias para comentários públicos, até 19 de janeiro de 2027, em que empresas e governos podem pedir mudanças. O ponto mais sensível para o mercado brasileiro é a diferença de tratamento entre empresas. A exigência de licença não vale quando o destinatário final tem sede nos Estados Unidos ou pertence a um grupo controlado de lá, como as donas da AWS, do Azure e do Google Cloud. Nesses casos, basta que o exportador, reexportador ou transferidor dos chips envie relatórios mensais ao BIS com informações como as partes envolvidas, os produtos e as datas de embarque. A obrigação é de quem vende ou transfere os equipamentos, não do comprador. Provedores de nuvem e operadoras de data center de capital brasileiro, ou de outros países, não têm essa saída. Para cada operação coberta pela regra, precisam pedir autorização individual, analisada pelas autoridades americanas. Segundo a ABES, empresas que disputam os mesmos clientes passam a enfrentar procedimentos diferentes para comprar equipamentos de IA. Na avaliação da entidade, a exigência de licença "pode elevar custos, dificultar investimentos em data centers" e afetar a atratividade do país para projetos de infraestrutura de IA e nuvem. A associação também chama a atenção para quem fica fora do debate comercial. Universidades e centros de pesquisa que precisam de computação avançada podem ser afetados. E mesmo nas vendas isentas de licença haverá um custo extra de conformidade, com os relatórios mensais que os fornecedores passam a enviar ao governo americano. Segundo o governo americano, o Brasil foi incluído pela expansão acelerada do setor de data centers e pela presença de operações de nuvem da Huawei no país. Washington não acusa o Brasil de desviar chips deliberadamente para a China. Na análise dos pedidos de licença, o BIS considera o regime de controle de exportações do país de destino e o grau de cooperação com os Estados Unidos. Em nota, o governo brasileiro afirmou que "não se trata de proibição, mas de necessidade de autorização" e disse ainda não ser possível avaliar o efeito concreto sobre as importações. A força-tarefa é liderada pelo ministro do Desenvolvimento, Indústria, Comércio e Serviços, Márcio Elias Rosa, e pela ministra da Gestão e da Inovação em Serviços Públicos, Esther Dweck. A ABES defende que o governo e o setor privado negociem com as autoridades americanas, com foco na cooperação em controle de exportações e na manutenção das cadeias de fornecimento de tecnologia. Para a entidade, "o Brasil reúne condições para ampliar sua participação no mercado internacional de serviços de data centers", com sua matriz elétrica, disponibilidade de energia, conectividade e políticas de incentivo. artigo.texto: Lansing residents push town board to ban data centers, crypto mining LANSING, N.Y. (WBNG) --More than 20,000 people have signed a petition opposing a proposed AI data center in Lansing. Residents are now taking that opposition to the Town Board and pushing for a ban on data centers and cryptocurrency mining facilities. The company TeraWulf has proposed a 300-megawatt facility along the shores of Cayuga Lake. Residents say the potential costs to their community are too high. Resident Renee Vogelsang said, “AI data centers suck up all of our energy, raise our electricity bills, waste our water, and harm our climate and environment.” What the proposal includes The proposed project would include three buildings to house computing equipment. Plans also call for clearing more than 40 acres of forested land and constructing new power infrastructure. Residents worry about the impact on the lake, local wildlife and the region’s tourism industry. Resident John Dennis said, “And in terms of jobs, the Finger Lakes ecotourism and wineries produce 4.6 billion in annual visiting spending a year, and it’s time for the 10 miles of the town of Lansing’s border on the lake to become integrated back into that economy.” Dennis said he believes the region should be focused on protecting the natural resources that already support its economy. Assemblymember raises cost concerns State Assemblymember Anna Kellis, who represents the 125th District, said the concerns go beyond the immediate impact of construction. She said taxpayers could be left paying for the infrastructure needed to power the facility. “But what will still be here is the debt that is then passed on to all taxpayers for paying for the capital infrastructure for the grid, the energy grid that was built up in order to provide those electrons and that energy to those data centers,” Kellis said. “We are the ones who would be stuck with that cost.” Kellis also pointed to potential increases in electricity costs, greenhouse gas emissions and water usage. She said the economic promises made by data center developers do not necessarily guarantee long-term benefits for the communities hosting them. Resident Ken Wolkin, who lives near Cayuga Lake, also shared concerns. “They are bullies who encroach and impinge upon our legislative and democratic processes and they continue to push their development plans even despite our sustained and ongoing refusal to consent to a data center in Lansing,” Wolkin said. Town Board considers zoning change The Town Board is considering a zoning change that would make data centers and cryptocurrency mining facilities disallowed uses in Lansing. A vote on the proposal is currently scheduled for Wednesday. The date could change. Residents who have spent months organizing against the project said the decision could help determine the future of their community. Copyright 2026 WBNG. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: UK-EU carbon market plan sparks clash over British energy bills Ahead of Friday's UK-EU summit in Brussels, ministers say linking carbon markets shields £6.5 billion in exports, while critics warn it raises energy bills. Chief editor: Ken Kariuki 0701401086 Britain and the European Union are preparing to link their carbon markets at a Brussels summit on Friday, Nov. 20, 2026, prompting a sharp dispute between Downing Street and free-market critics over whether the deal will protect exporters or raise domestic energy bills. In an official factsheet published Tuesday, Nov. 17, the UK Cabinet Office said linking the UK Emissions Trading Scheme (UK ETS) with the EU ETS could add up to £3.8 billion a year to the British economy and shield about £6.5 billion in steel and aluminium exports from the EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM). Critics at the Prosperity Institute, writing in City AM on Wednesday, Nov. 18, countered that aligning with higher European carbon prices would raise British carbon prices by around 32% and leave the wider economy worse off. The clash highlights a central policy trade-off behind Prime Minister Andy Burnham's European reset: shielding export-heavy manufacturers from EU border tariffs requires accepting higher domestic carbon-price floors across power generation and industry. How Carbon Market Linkage Works Both the UK ETS and EU ETS operate as cap-and-trade systems that require power plants, heavy factories, and airlines to buy permits for their greenhouse gas emissions. Because the UK system has traded at lower carbon prices than the EU's scheme, British exports entering the bloc face CBAM charges designed to equalize carbon costs at the EU border. Linking the two trading schemes would create a shared permit price and secure mutual exemptions from border carbon levies. Beyond emissions trading, the Cabinet Office factsheet outlines a food and drink trade deal projected to add up to £5.1 billion annually by cutting border paperwork, alongside a Youth Experience Scheme for study, work, and travel. Downing Street's economic case rests on protecting export competitiveness. By avoiding CBAM charges on approximately £6.5 billion of steel, aluminium, and related industrial exports, ministers argue the linkage prevents new trade friction while keeping Britain inside its manifesto red lines against rejoining the EU single market, customs union, or freedom of movement. Competing Cost Estimates and Evidence Limits Critics argue the government's calculation omits the domestic cost of converging toward EU permit prices. Writing in City AM, Prosperity Institute researcher Joseph Dinnage pointed to a 2024 Frontier Economics report cited by ministers, noting that while separate markets could cost British exporters £0.2 billion to £0.8 billion in EU CBAM payments between 2026 and 2030, keeping UK carbon prices lower would simultaneously save the domestic economy £3.5 billion to £8 billion in carbon taxes. Neither side's headline number tells the full story on its own. The Cabinet Office's £3.8 billion figure represents an upper-bound economy-wide projection ("up to") rather than a guaranteed windfall, while the Prosperity Institute's recommendation to abolish the Climate Change Levy, Carbon Price Support, the UK ETS, and the proposed UK CBAM would eliminate domestic carbon pricing altogether, leaving British steelmakers exposed to EU border tariffs and raising Exchequer revenue questions. Brexit Politics and Delayed Long-Term Options The carbon dispute unfolds alongside broader political caution inside Labour ahead of Friday's summit with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and EU leaders. Speaking at the Lord Mayor's Banquet in London on Monday evening, Nov. 16, Burnham declared that "the Brexit we were given has not worked" and said Britain had "lost more than we gained" over the past decade. Yet by Tuesday, Burnham indicated there was "no rush" to set out broader options for Britain's long-term EU relationship, postponing a planned options framework until December amid cabinet unease over reopening Brexit divisions. Meanwhile, former prime ministers Boris Johnson and David Cameron cautioned against moving toward rejoining the bloc, and the Cabinet Office's factsheet stressed that Friday's agreements require no payments into the EU budget beyond proportionate administrative costs for shared databases and IT systems. artigo.texto: Os créditos de carbono negociados entre países ganharam um livro-caixa global. A ONU Mudança do Clima lançou na COP31, em Antália, na Turquia, a primeira versão do registro internacional previsto no artigo 6.2 do Acordo de Paris, segundo o secretariado da convenção do clima. O registro vai servir aos países que não têm, ou não conseguem acessar, um registro próprio. Com ele, poderão anotar e acompanhar os chamados ITMOs, sigla em inglês para resultados de mitigação transferidos internacionalmente. O que é o artigo 6.2 O artigo 6.2 do Acordo de Paris permite que um país compre de outro uma redução de emissões e a conte na própria meta climática. Para que a mesma tonelada de carbono não seja contada duas vezes, cada transferência precisa ser registrada e rastreada. É esse o papel do novo sistema. O que já funciona Na primeira versão, os países participantes podem: - abrir seções e contas próprias; - registrar atividades de redução de emissões; - emitir resultados de mitigação e ligá-los às autorizações; - registrar transferência, compra, uso e cancelamento de ITMOs. As funções foram demonstradas num evento na COP31 na segunda-feira (16). Entrada em etapas Os países que pedirem uma seção no registro vão entrar aos poucos. O processo deve incluir uma oficina no início de 2027, seguida de treinamento e testes antes do acesso ao sistema real. Versões futuras vão trazer relatórios e integração com registros nacionais e com o mecanismo de créditos do Acordo de Paris. O desenvolvimento do software começou em janeiro de 2026, e uma versão mínima foi apresentada aos países em maio. Por que isso importa para a Amazônia O mercado de carbono entre países é uma das apostas para levar dinheiro à conservação de florestas. O Peru, vizinho amazônico, já fez a primeira transferência de resultados de redução de emissões da América Latina, para a Suíça, como a Revista Amazônia mostrou. E estados amazônicos brasileiros, como o Pará, pedem que seus programas de REDD+ jurisdicional possam participar desse mercado. Um registro confiável é condição para que esse dinheiro chegue sem fraude e sem dupla contagem. Acompanhe a cobertura diária na página especial da COP 31. Perguntas frequentes O que é um ITMO? Oklahoma leaders discuss nuclear power, data centers during State of Business Forum At a State of Business Forum, leaders said Oklahoma is in position to attract new nuclear development and AI data centers. Oklahoma is exploring nuclear power and data centers as key industries to drive its economic future, with leaders discussing the state’s potential at the State of Business Forum Tuesday. But to attract the next wave of jobs and investment, Oklahoma will have to compete. The conversations were part of the forum hosted by the State Chamber of Oklahoma, where industry leaders explained why Oklahoma is catching their attention. "Having a state that’s willing to hold its hand up and say, ‘Hey we want to host this stuff here. We have the right infrastructure. We’re an energy state, and we’re hungry for opportunities,’ Oklahoma fits all those in a unique way," Jacob DeWitte, co-founder of the nuclear power company Oklo, said. DeWitte moved to Tulsa last year as Oklahoma submitted its bid for a federal nuclear lifecycle innovation campus. He said the state’s oil and gas history could position it as a leader in nuclear energy. "I think, ultimately, Oklahoma has the potential and positioning to be really the hub for new nuclear development," DeWitte said. >> Video Below: Oklahoma reveals new details of nuclear facility bid, but many questions remain The demand for artificial intelligence is also driving interest in data centers, and Amazon’s Brian Huseman stressed the importance of Oklahoma seizing this opportunity. "Although I work for Amazon, I am definitely on team Oklahoma. I do not want to see our state like in 10 years regret that we were not able to take part in the building of this new kind of interstate highway system," Huseman said. Chad Warmington, president and CEO of the Oklahoma State Chamber, said the state needs to act quickly to attract companies. "The companies that are going to come here are going to come here because we move quickly, and I think we have the regulatory framework in place to do that," Warmington said.

artigo.texto: Data centers – O Departamento de Comércio dos Estados Unidos prepara uma regulamentação que exigirá autorização do governo americano para a compra de chips avançados de inteligência artificial por operadoras de data centers de cinco países, incluindo o Brasil. A medida também abrange Indonésia, Malásia, Cingapura e Tailândia. A iniciativa pretende impedir que a China e outros países considerados adversários tenham acesso indireto à tecnologia americana por meio do aluguel de capacidade computacional em estruturas instaladas no exterior. LEIA: Novo curso do Sindplay ensina a transformar ideias em soluções inovadoras Segundo o Departamento de Comércio, a norma busca evitar que as restrições existentes sejam contornadas por acordos de computação remota. As empresas afetadas também terão de realizar verificações mais rigorosas sobre seus clientes. A expectativa é que as novas exigências dificultem o uso de chips americanos no treinamento de modelos avançados de IA por organizações de países considerados de alto risco, como China, Rússia e Irã. A regulamentação surge após o escândalo envolvendo a Nvidia e seu ex-CEO, Jensen Huang, que renunciou ao cargo depois de vir à tona seu relacionamento com Alice Huang, ex-executiva de uma companhia de Cingapura investigada por suspeita de envolvimento em espionagem para a China. A empresa nega irregularidades. O episódio aumentou a pressão sobre autoridades americanas responsáveis pela fiscalização das exportações de tecnologia. O secretário do Tesouro, Scott Bessent, criticou a atuação do Departamento de Comércio, comandado por Howard Lutnick, por considerar insuficientes os mecanismos de controle existentes. A discussão também expôs divergências dentro do governo Trump. Enquanto o Departamento de Comércio supervisiona as regras, o Tesouro e o Conselho de Segurança Nacional defendem medidas mais rigorosas para impedir que empresas chinesas obtenham acesso indireto aos processadores. A nova norma, que prevê análise individual dos pedidos de licença, deverá entrar em vigor em até 90 dias. Empresas americanas que operam nos países afetados terão exceções, assim como data centers utilizados em sistemas comerciais de recomendação de varejistas on-line e redes sociais. O anúncio ocorre poucos dias antes da viagem de Donald Trump à China, onde o presidente americano deverá se reunir com Xi Jinping para uma cúpula econômica. As restrições também provocaram reação no mercado financeiro. Na manhã do anúncio, ações da Nvidia recuaram mais de 2%, enquanto Intel e Micron registraram perdas superiores a 6% e 7%, respectivamente. O índice Philadelphia Semiconductor, que reúne empresas do setor, caiu mais de 5%. Fonte de divergências dentro do governo dos EUA A possibilidade de empresas chinesas utilizarem data centers estrangeiros para acessar chips americanos tem provocado disputas internas na administração Trump. Nos últimos meses, Scott Bessent, Marco Rubio e Jamieson Greer defenderam controles mais abrangentes sobre essas estruturas, diante do risco de transferência indireta de tecnologia para a China. O comunicado oficial informou que a regulamentação foi elaborada pelo Departamento do Tesouro, por determinação da própria pasta e do Conselho de Segurança Nacional. A participação dessas instituições reforça a pressão de setores do governo por regras mais rígidas para o acesso internacional à capacidade computacional americana. artigo.texto: As LIPA eyes more battery storage, LI developer envisions alternative method As New York State doubles down on large energy-storage plants which could lead to a second wave of lithium-ion based projects and alternative battery technologies before the end of the decade, a Long Island entrepreneur is proposing one of the first plants using an alternative called flow-batteries. Last week, the state announced a second bulk-energy storage solicitation, seeking projects that could add 1,000 megawatts of battery storage plants across the state by 2030. It expands on awards from the first round announced this summer that saw two of eight new projects awarded for Long Island -- in Holtsville and Manorville. All are part of Gov. Kathy Hochul’s plan for 6,000 megawatts of battery storage by 2030, and come as Long Island continues to collectively resist the strategy with moratoriums in nearly all towns. Concerns here are based largely on reports of thermal runaway events at four New York plants in 2023, including one in East Hampton, where high levels of forever chemicals were reported earlier this month at a site dealing with a spreading toxic plume following fire suppression efforts. The New York State Energy Research and Development Authority’s competitive solicitation announced on Nov. 12 is “open to a range of eligible storage technologies,” the agency said. Non-lithium batteries are eligible for 25-year contracts in the new solicitation, versus 15-year contracts for lithium-ion battery proposals, NYSERDA said in responses to Newsday. - As New York State doubles down on soliciting for large energy-storage plants proposals, a Long Island entrepreneur is proposing one of the first plants using an alternative called flow-batteries. - Last week, the state announced seeking projects that could add 1,000 megawatts of battery storage plants across the state by 2030. - Meanwhile, Larry Siegel, a businessman from Wantagh with a background in energy finance, said he is in the early stages of developing a non-lithium ion battery storage project for eastern Long Island which would use flow-battery technology to provide 5 megawatts of storage for the grid. NYSERDA’s NY Green Bank will help fund the new battery projects with a “range of financing options” to advance energy storage, the agency said, and its siting team will work “closely with local governments to provide tailored education, technical assistance and model local laws.” LIPA expressed support for the state’s latest battery solicitation, saying in a statement that it “welcomes NYSERDA’s efforts to advance innovation in energy storage and help promising technologies become commercially viable options for meeting New York’s energy needs.” Meanwhile, Larry Siegel, a businessman from Wantagh with a background in energy finance, said he is in the early stages of developing a non-lithium ion battery storage project for eastern Long Island which would use flow-battery technology to provide 5 megawatts of storage for the grid. Siegel, in an interview, said his newly formed Tobay Energy has identified a location for the plant on a site less than an acre. He said he recently met with PSEG Long Island, which runs the grid under contract to LIPA, about connecting his project to the electric grid. It could be ready by 2028, he said. Flow batteries use liquid electrolytes rather than solid lithium-ion cells to store energy, using zinc bromine or vanadium to the store power for up to four hours of discharge onto the grid. Batteries can help stabilize the grid in the face of intermittent energy from solar and wind arrays, one of the reasons they are crucial as LIPA prepares to make way for up to 924-megawatts of wind energy early next year. Siegel said he’s still finalizing a design and specific manufacturer for the project, and that much will depend on the cost of connecting to local power lines. “All over Long Island, there’s a demand for a large number of these batteries, but it’s just very hard to build them because of the moratoriums,” Siegel said, noting that Islip Town recently approved a ban on batteries over a certain size that could nix a LIPA contract for a 79-megawatt battery. “Even Brookhaven is not in a rush to approve them,” Siegel said of the town where multiple projects have been proposed because it has a special zone for batteries and no moratorium. More recently, town supervisor Dan Panico has assured concerned residents nothing will be approved until the town is sure they are safe. Siegel said flow batteries are not subject to thermal runaway fires that lithium batteries are, and said they are already in use in the state and across the country. He pointed to a July contract awarded to manufacturer Eos Energy to build zinc-based battery storage systems for a “Golden Dome for America” defense system for the U.S. Department of War. “It’s going to cost me more” to work with flow-energy batteries, Siegel said. “There’s less profit in it because the costs are higher, but I think it’s the way to go.” The Wantagh resident, who said he previously worked for the U.S. Department of Energy, grew up in Patchogue. “I know the market, I see other site locations that will never get built,” said Siegel, who has attended community meetings where residents have objected to lithium-ion batteries. “I know what’s going on out here. There are a lot of projects that have been abandoned on Long Island.” His proposed flow battery of 5 megawatts has challenges, he acknowledged. “I do have a hurdle to convince investors about these flow batteries,” he said. “They have questions. artigo.texto: Loudoun County leaders approve 10-month pause on data center applications LOUDOUN COUNTY, Va. - Loudoun County's Board of Supervisors voted Tuesday night to put the breaks on future data center development with a 10-month pause on data center applications. What we know: The vote comes after an hours-long meeting where supervisors heard from frustrated residents and industry leaders. Before the decision, some residents were losing hope. The pause is intended to give supervisors time to take a closer look at how much more growth the area can actually handle, including the impact on electricity, infrastructure and neighborhoods. During Tuesday's meeting, supervisors raised concerns about the backlog that could result from putting a halt to all new digital infrastructure projects. The Data Center Coalition argued that these facilities should drive Loudoun County's economy, and generated about $1.3 billion in tax revenue in 2026. They also argued that the county should not abruptly change course in a way that creates uncertainty, invites legal challenges and disrupts investments. On Tuesday night, the coalition warned that developers could take legal action. Certain developers with existing zoning applications, like ZRTD applications, may still move forward, depending on the status of their projects and a case-by-case review. The Source: Information in this article is from a Loudoun County Board of Supervisors hearing and original FOX 5 DC reporting.

artigo.texto: Durham has just 75 days of easily accessible water remaining if no rain falls, and Falls Lake has dropped to its lowest level since the drought crisis of 2007. As water supplies dwindle across the Triangle, some residents are pointing the finger at a rapidly growing industry: data centers. Other WRAL Top Stories Comments on recent WRAL social media posts about the drought have raised concerns about the facilities consuming large amounts of drinking water. But water consumption figures provided by Raleigh and Durham show that other customers account for much more of the cities' water demand. Drought is caused by a lack of precipitation, but water consumption can determine how long communities' supplies last. How much water do Durham's data centers use? Durham officials have identified six customers with facilities that could be classified as data centers. Four of those facilities collectively consume approximately 1.88 million gallons of water per month, accounting for just 0.2% of the city's overall water use. At the other two facilities, officials cannot distinguish water used to cool data centers from water used for other purposes. Data center water consumption also tends to increase during the hotter summer months, according to the city. Residential customers account for the largest share of Durham's water demand: - Residential: 52% - Commercial and industrial: 36.6% - Institutional, including schools and places of worship: 11.4% Durham estimates it has 145 days of total water supply remaining, including 75 days of easily accessible water. Those projections are based on a 30-day running average of demand on the city's reservoirs and assume no rainfall. Who uses the most water in Raleigh? In Raleigh, nearly two-thirds of water demand comes from residential customers. Just 4% goes to the entire industrial category. Raleigh Water official Ed Buchan said the utility serves a handful of traditional data centers, including facilities that handle banking information, but no large-scale generative AI data centers. “But we don't really have any significant demand from industrial customers, and certainly none from generative AI,” Buchan said. “So that is not an issue in our service area.” Despite the Triangle's rapid population growth, Raleigh's water demand has increased relatively modestly over the past two decades. In 2007, Raleigh Water's average demand was 52 million gallons per day. Today, it's about 60 million gallons per day, including water supplied to additional wholesale customers. Buchan attributes that trend in part to more efficient household appliances and conservation habits that developed during the previous drought crisis. One of the biggest drivers of additional water demand during the summer is lawn irrigation, which can account for 17 million to 18 million gallons of water per day. Not all data centers use the same amount of water Water consumption can vary significantly depending on how a data center is designed and cooled. Cooling towers and evaporative cooling systems can consume large amounts of water, while closed-loop systems and air cooling can substantially reduce water consumption. Durham officials said a proposed data center in Research Triangle Park would use city water for standard office needs but not for cooling. Instead, the facility has proposed using reclaimed water from Durham County. Officials also said data centers would be subject to the same drought-related water restrictions as other customers. Can North Carolina handle future data center demand? In Richmond County, where Amazon Web Services is developing a massive data center campus, economic development officials say they evaluated the project's water needs alongside engineers and public works staff. “We're not having to expand our water treatment plant,” a Richmond County economic development official told WRAL earlier this year. “We have plenty of capacity to supply AWS at peak buildout in the hottest days of the summer.” Amazon is also funding water distribution infrastructure upgrades needed to serve the campus, according to county officials. Those assessments are based on projected demand, rather than actual water consumption from a fully operational campus. In the Triangle, both Raleigh and Durham have temporarily paused approvals for certain new data center developments as they consider regulations for future projects. Raleigh's moratorium lasts six months, while Durham's lasts nine months. Buchan said Raleigh Water has contacted utilities across the country that already serve large data centers to learn how they manage the industry's water demand. While the available figures do not indicate that data centers are a major driver of current water demand in Raleigh or Durham, the industry's rapid expansion raises a longer-term question: how much additional demand can North Carolina's water systems handle, particularly during prolonged drought? Water officials urge conservation Raleigh Water is encouraging customers to conserve water even though mandatory restrictions have not been implemented. Buchan recommends reducing lawn irrigation, taking shorter showers and checking homes for leaks. “That said, the whole region is clearly in a very serious drought situation,” Buchan said. “So we would ask our customers and anybody listening to this to try to conserve water, no matter where you're at.”

artigo.texto: Sungrow has unveiled a new generation of commercial and industrial energy storage solutions at its Global Energy Pioneer Summit (GEPS) 2026 in Hefei, China, introducing the PowerStack 3.0 alongside an expanded PowerKeeper battery storage family. Held from 10 to 13 November 2026, the summit brought together more than 1,200 attendees from over 80 countries, including installers, distributors and engineering partners. The announcements reflect a growing focus on making energy storage easier to deploy, manage and scale, particularly for businesses looking to improve their use of solar generation, manage electricity costs and maintain operations during grid interruptions. While much of the discussion around battery storage in Australia centres on households, the commercial and industrial sector faces a different set of challenges. Businesses must consider available installation space, peak electricity demand, operational continuity and the financial returns of larger battery systems. Sungrow’s latest developments aim to address these requirements through modular hardware, smarter energy management and greater integration between solar, storage and charging infrastructure. PowerStack 3.0 Brings Modular Energy Storage to Different Business Needs The headline announcement was the global launch of Sungrow PowerStack 3.0, a commercial and industrial energy storage system built around what the company describes as a Scene-in-One architecture. Rather than deploying separate equipment for each application, PowerStack 3.0 uses a Multi-Scenario Dock with four dedicated modules: - PCS Module: Power conversion and standalone battery storage applications. - Solar Module: Integration of photovoltaic generation and battery storage. - Charging Module: DC-coupled integration of solar, batteries and electric vehicle charging. - Microgrid Module: Support for independent power systems and operation during grid outages. This approach allows installers and system designers to configure solutions around the requirements of a particular site without necessarily introducing additional standalone equipment. For example, a commercial facility might begin with battery storage to manage electricity costs, while another installation could require integrated solar generation and EV charging. The standalone storage configuration also supports two-hour and four-hour discharge durations through different power module arrangements. For businesses operating in areas with unreliable electricity supplies, the microgrid configuration supports switching between grid-connected and off-grid operation. Sungrow claims the system can achieve a 0 ms transition without a separate static transfer switch cabinet, potentially helping critical equipment remain operational during outages. Improved Efficiency and a Smaller Installation Footprint Beyond its modular architecture, PowerStack 3.0 introduces several hardware improvements. Manufacturer-stated specifications and comparisons against the previous generation. Figures have not been independently verified by DRN. The system uses a silicon carbide (SiC) power conversion system alongside 684 Ah stacked battery cells. Sungrow also claims an energy density of up to 256 kWh per square metre, with support for side-by-side, back-to-back and face-to-face installation configurations. Environmental protection includes an IP55 rating and C5-level corrosion protection, with a specified operating temperature range of -30°C to 50°C. Safety provisions include three-level fuse protection and a four-layer fire safety design. These specifications are particularly relevant for industrial locations where space, environmental exposure and system reliability can significantly influence installation decisions. Bubbly AI Takes on Battery Design, Commissioning and Management Artificial intelligence also features prominently in Sungrow’s latest energy storage strategy. PowerStack 3.0 incorporates Bubbly, the company’s proprietary AI assistant, designed to support projects throughout their operational lifecycle. Its capabilities extend beyond monitoring electricity consumption. During planning, Bubbly combines satellite imagery and 3D modelling to produce proposed system designs, including installation layouts and financial calculations. According to Sungrow, this approach can deliver more than 12% higher returns compared with a conventional self-consumption operating mode. The AI platform also monitors operating conditions continuously, identifying more than 30 potential risks and providing diagnostic recommendations. For a 10 MWh installation, Sungrow claims Bubbly can produce a fault diagnosis report with maintenance recommendations in approximately one minute. These performance and financial claims remain manufacturer estimates, and actual outcomes will depend on site conditions, electricity tariffs and system configuration. The existing PowerKeeper system, paired with Sungrow’s SH50/80/125CX hybrid inverter range, supports installations from 50 to 125 kW, with battery capacity ranging from 50 to 1,000 kWh. artigo.texto: O mercado de carbono do Acordo de Paris irá gerar créditos de carbono de alta qualidade? (Jornal Dan Tri) - O novo mecanismo previsto no Artigo 6.4 do Acordo de Paris começou a operar com padrões rigorosos, causando uma redução de até 40% no número de créditos concedidos a projetos e instaurando um processo de triagem mais rigoroso para as empresas vietnamitas. Considerado outrora como uma "tábua de salvação" financeira para ajudar as empresas a adotarem práticas sustentáveis, o mercado de créditos de carbono tem enfrentado recentemente uma onda de ceticismo quanto à sua qualidade real. A tendência de projetos exagerarem os números de redução de emissões e apresentarem falta de sustentabilidade tem dissuadido até mesmo gigantes globais da tecnologia. Por exemplo, em abril, a Microsoft suspendeu temporariamente suas compras de novos créditos de carbono, refletindo a maior cautela dos compradores internacionais. Sob essa pressão, o Artigo 6.4 do Acordo de Paris – o mecanismo centralizado de concessão de créditos supervisionado diretamente pelas Nações Unidas – entrou oficialmente na fase de implementação com o objetivo de restabelecer a ordem no cenário das emissões de carbono. Aperto excessivo na liberação de crédito: queda de 40% na produção. Um ponto de virada importante ocorreu em fevereiro, quando o Órgão de Monitoramento da Convenção-Quadro das Nações Unidas sobre Mudança do Clima (UNFCCC) aprovou os primeiros créditos, nos termos do Artigo 6.4, para um projeto de fogão a lenha limpo em Mianmar. Notavelmente, esse projeto havia sido originalmente registrado no âmbito do Mecanismo de Desenvolvimento Limpo (MDL) durante a era do Protocolo de Quioto. De acordo com uma análise da Clean Air Task Force (CATF) – uma organização não governamental internacional especializada em pesquisa climática independente – quando comparado usando a nova metodologia e fatores de cálculo mais cautelosos para biomassa não renovável, o projeto recebeu aproximadamente 40% menos créditos em comparação com o sistema MDL anterior. Você também pode gostar A "evaporação" de quase metade dos créditos de carbono é uma clara evidência de que as Nações Unidas estão a tornar a sua fórmula de cálculo mais rigorosa. O novo mecanismo obriga as partes a comprovarem que as reduções de emissões são reais, em vez de se basearem em cenários exagerados. Até à data, o organismo regulador aprovou apenas cinco metodologias, incluindo a captura de gás de aterro, o tratamento industrial de N₂O, as energias renováveis e a cozinha limpa. A transição dos projetos MDL legados para o Artigo 6.4 também está progredindo bastante lentamente. Embora o prazo para os países anfitriões aprovarem as transferências seja 30 de junho, os dados do início de 2026 mostram que apenas cerca de 13% dos créditos MDL submetidos foram aprovados. Isso indica que muitos governos estão considerando reter os créditos para fins de redução de emissões domésticas, em vez de vendê-los internacionalmente em larga escala. O "padrão ouro" em termos de qualidade e o desafio complexo das florestas. Em princípio, um crédito de carbono representa uma tonelada de CO2 equivalente que é reduzida ou removida da atmosfera. No entanto, para que um crédito tenha valor comercial sustentável, o Artigo 6.4 estabelece cinco condições rigorosas: complementaridade (o projeto só sobrevive graças ao financiamento de carbono), longevidade (por quanto tempo o carbono é armazenado), linha de base de emissões precisa, risco de fuga de emissões (não transferir a poluição para outro lugar) e um sistema independente de medição, relato e verificação (MRV). Embora os projetos de engenharia industrial possuam processos de medição relativamente claros, os aspectos de crédito de carbono na silvicultura e no uso da terra representam o maior desafio. As plantações podem ser destruídas por desastres naturais, pragas e doenças, ou o carbono acumulado no solo pode ser liberado quando a propriedade muda de mãos. Uma avaliação realizada pela organização sem fins lucrativos CATF, que analisou 20 regras de créditos florestais na América do Norte, revelou diversas lacunas na determinação da linha de base e na mitigação do risco de retorno de carbono. Embora os créditos florestais já tenham representado quase 40% do mercado voluntário, a metodologia para reflorestamento e recuperação de florestas só foi introduzida no processo de revisão da UNFCCC em outubro, e não há data definida para a aprovação final da estrutura. O dilema entre manter os padrões ambientais e facilitar o fluxo de capital privado é um grande problema. Se as regulamentações forem muito brandas, os créditos de acreditação se tornarão inúteis. Por outro lado, se os procedimentos forem muito complicados e os custos de acreditação muito altos, os países em desenvolvimento terão dificuldades para acessar o mercado. Isso impacta diretamente o roteiro do Vietnã. Você também pode gostar A onda de padronização internacional está impactando diretamente o progresso do Vietnã. Em 1º de abril, o Governo emitiu o Decreto 112/2026/ND-CP (em vigor desde 19 de maio). Este é um importante documento legal que estipula claramente o mecanismo para a troca de resultados de redução de emissões, tanto no âmbito do Artigo 6.2 (acordos bilaterais entre governos), quanto do Artigo 6.4, além de outras formas voluntárias. Anteriormente, em 14 de agosto, o Governo também aprovou a Resolução 235/NQ-CP, formalizando oficialmente o acordo de cooperação do Artigo 6 assinado com Singapura , com vigência a partir de setembro de 2025. Este acordo abre caminho para que empresas vietnamitas vendam créditos internacionalmente reconhecidos para a ilha. De acordo com dados do UNEP-CCC de 5 de novembro, o Vietnã possui 3 acordos bilaterais e 20 atividades registradas no âmbito do Artigo 6.2, embora nenhum crédito tenha sido oficialmente emitido ainda pelo canal do Artigo 6.4. No âmbito nacional, a bolsa de carbono também está operacional desde 29 de junho. De acordo com dados do PNU

artigo.texto: POWER Act: Clean energy advocates demand data center regulations Lawmakers, advocates hope to pass massive plan before veto session ends SPRINGFIELD, Ill. (WAND) – Clean energy advocates from across the state are pushing lawmakers to pass data center regulations during the second week of veto session. Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle agree that Big Tech companies need to bring their own energy sources, pay their fair share for power, and use closed-loop water systems. Advocates say the POWER Act could also establish consumer protection and pollution control policies. “People are tired of waiting for the state to protect our local water supplies and from the dirty fossil fuel plants powering them,” said Springfield environmental activist Lori McKiernan. “People are tired of fighting against backroom deals without a real seat at the table.” The Illinois Environmental Council said the POWER Act would ban NDAs and require full access to any agreements signed. Some argue local governments should decide where data centers can be located and prevent the facilities from being approved within three miles of residential communities. The POWER Act could require data centers to develop energy supply and capacity need plans with renewable and battery storage protections that add new capacity to the power grid. “The protections in the POWER Act are the guardrails we need to protect ratepayers, communities, and our natural resources,” said Sen. Ram Villivalam (D-Chicago). “The impacts of data centers are too large to ignore.” Lawmakers could finalize data center regulations during lameduck session in early January if they fail to pass a bill Dec. 1 to 3. “I think that this has more political power and urgency behind it in getting things done than anything that I’ve ever seen in Springfield,” Illinois Environmental Council CEO Jen Walling said. “I think that people all over the state, bipartisan basis, are pushing legislators to act.” The renewed push comes after the Illinois Environmental Protection Agency and Illinois Power Agency released the 2026 reliability mitigation plan Monday. The joint report proposed extending the 2030 emission limits for gas- and oil-fired power plants under the Climate and Equitable Jobs Act to 2033. Advocates argue data centers haven’t been held accountable for their impact on grid reliability and energy costs. “Data centers claim to be the technology of the future, and yet they’re proposing extending the life of gas and coal plants to operate their facilities,” said IEC’s Cate Caldwell. “They’re operating behind closed doors, ignoring the concerns of local communities. And they’re sucking up our resources to line their shareholders’ pockets. That’s the past. That’s regression, and those days are over here in Illinois.” Copyright 2026 WAND. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: 247 – A COP31 apresentou nesta terça-feira (17) um acordo internacional para diminuir o impacto ambiental dos data centers, estruturas responsáveis pelo processamento de dados e pelo funcionamento de tecnologias digitais. De acordo com a Sputnik, o Brasil e outros oito países aderiram ao Compromisso de Antália sobre Inteligência Artificial nos eventos que ocorrem na Turquia. A iniciativa estimula a redução das emissões, o uso eficiente de água e energia e a adoção de práticas sustentáveis. O pacto não estabelece metas obrigatórias, mas prevê avaliações anuais durante as conferências climáticas até 2030. A presidência turca da COP31 desenvolveu a iniciativa em parceria com a União Internacional de Telecomunicações (UIT) e a Organização das Nações Unidas para a Educação, a Ciência e a Cultura (Unesco). A proposta busca enfrentar os efeitos ambientais associados à expansão da infraestrutura digital, especialmente diante do crescimento das atividades que dependem de centros de processamento de dados. Acordo busca reduzir consumo de energia e água O Compromisso de Antália estabelece diretrizes para incentivar práticas ambientais nos data centers. Entre as prioridades estão a ampliação da eficiência energética, a redução do consumo de água e o aumento da participação de fontes limpas no abastecimento dessas instalações. A iniciativa também contempla a economia circular, modelo que incentiva o reaproveitamento de materiais e a redução do desperdício ao longo dos processos produtivos. Outro ponto envolve o gerenciamento de equipamentos eletrônicos que chegam ao fim de sua vida útil. O documento defende procedimentos adequados para o descarte desses resíduos, buscando diminuir os impactos ambientais associados à infraestrutura tecnológica. O conjunto de orientações procura estimular mudanças na operação dos centros de processamento de dados, considerando tanto as necessidades energéticas quanto a utilização de recursos hídricos. Brasil participa de compromisso internacional A adesão brasileira coloca o país entre os participantes do entendimento anunciado durante a conferência climática na Turquia. Além do Brasil, outras oito nações assumiram o compromisso de incentivar medidas voltadas à sustentabilidade da infraestrutura digital. O caráter voluntário da iniciativa permite que os governos participantes desenvolvam ações sem a imposição de metas vinculantes de redução de emissões. O acordo estabelece, ainda assim, um mecanismo de acompanhamento anual nas conferências do clima, com avaliações previstas até 2030. A proposta busca manter a discussão sobre os impactos ambientais dos data centers na agenda internacional, permitindo que os países acompanhem as iniciativas implementadas ao longo desse período. Ausência de big techs dos Estados Unidos gera dúvidas Embora o entendimento tenha recebido o apoio de nove países, a iniciativa ainda enfrenta questionamentos sobre sua capacidade de produzir resultados concretos. O principal ponto de incerteza envolve a ausência das maiores empresas de tecnologia dos Estados Unidos, que figuram entre as principais operadoras mundiais da infraestrutura de processamento de dados. Sem a participação dessas companhias, o alcance das medidas dependerá da adesão voluntária dos governos e dos operadores interessados em incorporar as recomendações. O documento também não determina percentuais obrigatórios de redução das emissões, fator que limita sua capacidade de impor mudanças diretamente às empresas do setor. Mesmo com essas restrições, os participantes pretendem acompanhar anualmente o desenvolvimento das ações, mantendo o tema nas próximas conferências internacionais sobre o clima. Inteligência artificial poderá contribuir para soluções climáticas O compromisso não aborda apenas os impactos ambientais associados à operação dos sistemas digitais. A iniciativa também incentiva o desenvolvimento de aplicações de inteligência artificial voltadas ao enfrentamento das mudanças climáticas. Entre os exemplos apresentados está a utilização da tecnologia para melhorar a previsão de eventos climáticos extremos. O acordo também contempla mecanismos de cooperação tecnológica com países em desenvolvimento, buscando ampliar o acesso a instrumentos digitais que possam contribuir para a agenda ambiental. Essa orientação relaciona o desenvolvimento de sistemas de inteligência artificial à necessidade de reduzir seus efeitos ambientais e, simultaneamente, aproveitar suas aplicações no monitoramento e na resposta aos desafios climáticos. Pacto inclui proteção aos trabalhadores diante da automação Outra dimensão do Compromisso de Antália envolve as consequências da automação sobre o trabalho. O documento contempla medidas destinadas à proteção dos trabalhadores diante das transformações associadas à utilização crescente de inteligência artificial. A proposta integra essas preocupações sociais às diretrizes ambientais e tecnológicas, ampliando o alcance das discussões sobre a infraestrutura digital. No Brasil, o conteúdo do acordo apresenta pontos de convergência com iniciativas como o programa Computadores para Inclusão, mencionado entre as ações relacionadas à agenda tecnológica nacional. A proposta brasileira de sediar o Instituto de Inteligência Artificial para Mudanças Climáticas (AICI) também se relaciona aos objetivos do compromisso, especialmente no desenvolvimento de aplicações tecnológicas voltadas à questão ambiental. Com a adesão de nove países, o Compromisso de Antália estabelece uma agenda de cooperação sobre emissões, consumo de energia, utilização de água, resíduos eletrônicos e aplicações climáticas da inteligência artificial. O acompanhamento anual até 2030 permitirá observar os avanços das iniciativas voluntárias, em um cenário no qual as maiores empresas norte-americanas de tecnologia ainda não participam do pacto. artigo.texto: Utilities could be left holding the bill for billions in infrastructure spending committed in anticipation of artificial intelligence data centers that are delayed, downsized or canceled, industry observers and experts told Utility Dive. Opposition to data center construction has crossed traditional party lines, while Democratic gains in the midterms are adding pressure on earlier-stage investments across key markets. Together, these dynamics raise the stakes for project approvals and utility cost recovery, they say. “From a financing perspective, prolonged uncertainty will increase the cost of capital, reduce available leverage and make investors more hesitant to commit significant development dollars before power is secured,” said Andrejka Bernatova, managing partner of investment firm Dynamix Capital Partners, which invests in energy infrastructure. Even in regions that theoretically have enough capacity to accommodate new large loads, projects may struggle to secure a credible path to power on the timelines they need. “Interconnection, permitting, and financing all matter, but they are part of the same execution question of whether the team can get reliable power to the site and actually deliver,” Bernatova said. “A customer commitment or a large announced capacity number does not answer that by itself.” Ultimately, Bernatova expects investors to favor markets that offer certainty around power availability and timelines, potentially eroding the competitive advantage of markets like Texas, which until recently attracted substantial data center investment. Over the summer, Gov. Greg Abbott, R, announced a pause on new data center interconnections pending an audit of the queue. In the midterms, he lost his bid for reelection to Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who has pledged to maintain pressure on the industry after taking office next year. Ballot-box rebuke puts utility investment safeguards in focus Nearly all of the 46 municipal ballot measures tracked by Bloomberg that addressed data center development resulted in restrictions, moratoriums or bans. That unfavorability extends to a substantial share of the development pipeline. An estimated 191 GW of planned data center capacity faces new risk, with exposure concentrated in Texas, Ohio and Georgia, where incoming Democratic governors campaigned on pausing or restricting construction, according to a report from energy analytics firm Orennia that was shared with Utility Dive. Texas accounts for nearly half of the pre-construction in development in the U.S., so a statewide approval freeze would have an outsized impact on the national buildout, but the “impact of delayed or unrealized data center build-out on power prices varies widely across technologies and markets,” Orennia said. If 20% of projected data center demand in the Electric Reliability Council of Texas region fails to materialize, solar and wind generators could see their average wholesale revenue fall 38% and 37%, respectively, according to the report. Implied heat rates, a measure of the economics of gas-fired generation relative to fuel costs, could decline 39%. In the same scenario, two-hour battery storage arbitrage spreads could fall below new-build break-even requirements. In PJM, delaying half of the planned data center buildout by two years could reduce four-hour battery storage arbitrage spreads by 16% and lower solar and wind capture prices and implied heat rates by about 12% through 2030, the modeling suggests. The election results are unlikely to produce sweeping federal AI legislation but could lead to congressional hearings and greater transparency requirements, according to D.C.-based research and advisory firm Capstone. Its analysts expect much of the policy debate to take place at state utility commissions and local siting boards. Despite a proliferation of large-load tariffs over the past year, safeguards may still leave customers exposed in the event of a slowdown, some say. “Existing tariffs and regulatory frameworks likely won’t fully protect customers because they were designed for a different century,” Louisa Eberle, principal at the Regulatory Assistance Project, warned in a written statement. Eberle also called for reforms to utility business practices “to turn this data center surge into updated infrastructure, cleaner energy and a better deal for average customers.” The push for lower electricity bills is prompting policymakers to look more closely at how utilities use existing grid infrastructure. Richard Caperton, vice president of policy at SPAN, a maker of smart electrical panels, anticipates greater emphasis on data center projects that can be served without major new grid investments. “I’m really thrilled to see governors like Abigail Spanberger [in Virginia] campaign on affordability and then embrace utilization as the solution,” he said. In April, Gov. Spanberger signed legislation requiring Dominion Energy and Appalachian Power to report how effectively they use existing grid infrastructure. The State Corporation Commission can use those metrics to establish improvement targets and evaluate utility spending. “Winning candidates who emphasized lowering electricity prices are already looking for ways to deliver on their promises quickly,” Caperton said. “I expect that will lead to more policies and programs that boost grid utilization being ratified and implemented in early 2027. How those policies affect data center development and utility investments will vary by state.” A ‘necessary’ shakeout puts project commitments to the test Stephen Rose, CEO of infrastructure software provider Render Networks, said he expects to see a “pause and necessary shakeout” in data center development. “Fully permitted projects with real capital will keep moving,” Rose said. “The speculative end takes the hit: developers land-banking without firm power, and the contractors who staffed up for projects that won't break ground.” Rose cited AEP Ohio's large-load tariff,

A avaliação predominante, compartilhada pelo autor, deputado Arnaldo Jardim (Cidadania/SP), é que incluir outros temas no parecer pode atrasar ou inviabilizar a votação antes dos leilões de baterias de 2 e 4 de dezembro. A manifestação ocorre em meio à expectiava de que o parecer de Danilo Forte (PP/CE), relator do projeto, incorpore outros temas como mudanças na autoprodução e no ressarcimento dos cortes de geração. Participaram do almoço os deputados Joaquim Passarinho (PL/PA), presidente da Comissão de Minas e Energia da Câmara, Evair de Melo (Republicanos/ES) e Heitor Schuch (PSD/RS). A presidente da Associação Brasileira das Empresas Geradoras de Energia Elétrica (Abrage), Marisete Pereira, defendeu a aprovação do texto original, posição também sustentada por Rui Altirei, presidente da Associação Brasileira dos Produtores Independentes de Energia Elétrica (Apine). Já o presidente da Associação Brasileira de Soluções de Armazenamento de Energia (Absae), Fábio Lima, reforçou apenas que a contratação das baterias precisa ocorrer. Bárbara Rubim, da Associação Brasileira de Energia Solar Fotovoltaica (Absolar), também defendeu a aprovação “da maneira como proposto pelo deputado Arnaldo Jardim”. Assim como a Associação Brasileira da Indústria de Hidrogênio Verde (Abihv). O presidente do conselho da entidade, Luis Viga, apontou a necssidade de preservar a segurança jurídica do setor elétrico e evitar o encarecimento da energia renovável, com impacto direto sobre os projetos de hidrogênio verde. Para a entidade, a imposição de adicionalidade na autoprodução, ao restringir o uso de usinas existentes e exigir nova geração, compromete a competitividade desses empreendimentos. As manifestações reforçaram a pressão para concentrar o projeto na mudança do rateio, sem reabrir outras disputas da reforma do setor elétrico. Em carta divulgada no evento Abeeólica, Abihv, Abrage, Abragel, Absae, Absolar e Apine não citam a aprovação do texto original, mas pedem ao Congresso a ‘priorização da tramitação e à aprovação da matéria” para garantir a segurança jurídica do leilão. A Abeeólica, entretanto, já entrou com uma ação civil pública para suspender os leilões de baterias, questionando a cobrança dos custos exclusivamente dos geradores. Também estava na mesa da entidade a possibilidade de uma Ação Direta de Inconstitucionalidade (ADI) no STF. Jardim articula apoio com governo e MME Jardim afirmou perceber uma posição favorável do Ministério de Minas e Energia (MME) ao texto, mas indicou que a articulação dentro do governo ainda busca uma posição conjunta sobre a proposta. Segundo ele, há um diálogo interno no governo para alinhar uma posição conjunta. Com o debate no Congresso concentrado na agenda fiscal, as associações devem se mobilizar para abrir espaço à votação do PL das baterias. O desafio é transformar o apoio à mudança no rateio em um acordo para aprovar a proposta na Câmara e no Senado nas duas semanas que restam até os leilões. A reforma da reforma O relator, Danilo Forte, não participou do almoço, assim como a Associação Brasileira de Energia Eólica e Novas Tecnologias (Abeeólica) e Associação Brasileira de Geração de Energia Limpa (Abragel). A eixos apurou que o parecer de Danilo Forte deve incorporar mudanças na autoprodução e no ressarcimento dos cortes de geração, o curtailment. O desconto nas tarifas de uso da rede deve ficar fora. O projeto pode se transformar, assim, em uma reforma da reforma do setor elétrico, cerca de um ano depois da aprovação da legislação relatada no Senado por Eduardo Braga (MDB/AM). Foi essa reforma, sancionada em novembro de 2025, que estabeleceu o custeio da contratação de baterias exclusivamente pelos geradores. Agora, o projeto de Jardim busca rever essa escolha, enquanto o parecer de Forte pode reabrir outras disputas enfrentadas na negociação do marco. Forte havia prometido apresentar o parecer na terça-feira passada (10), o que não aconteceu. O projeto tramita em regime de urgência desde 13 de outubro. O próprio autor tenta conter a ampliação do texto. Segundo a MegaWhat, Jardim trabalha para convencer o relator a concentrar o parecer na mudança do rateio, por avaliar que a inclusão de outras pautas pode dificultar a aprovação. “Em vez de você agregar apoio, você torna mais complexa a decisão”, afirmou Jardim na sexta-feira (13), durante evento de setor de energia em Portugal. Adicionalidade e curtailment ampliam a disputa Um dos pontos que deve estar no parecer vincula a autoprodução à adicionalidade — a exigência de nova capacidade de geração para o enquadramento no regime. A adicionalidade é uma disputa recorrente no Congresso. Rejeitada nas discussões do marco do hidrogênio, voltou na MP 1.307/2025, editada pelo governo para as ZPEs e que caducou, e reapareceu na reforma do setor elétrico. Agora, a exigência de nova geração para a autoprodução pode retornar no parecer das baterias, reabrindo o conflito sobre o aproveitamento das usinas existentes, em meio a uma crise de curtailment. O outro ponto trata exatamente do ressarcimento dos cortes de geração, uma das principais pressões sobre o caixa das geradoras renováveis. O governo já abriu um caminho para compensar parte das perdas passadas. A regulamentação publicada em julho alcança cortes por indisponibilidade externa e confiabilidade elétrica entre setembro de 2023 e novembro de 2025. Ficaram de fora os cortes por sobreoferta de energia. Permaneceu também a discussão sobre as perdas acumuladas depois daquele período e sobre o tratamento dos eventos futuros. artigo.texto: Will the Paris Agreement's carbon market generate high-quality carbon credits? (Dan Tri Newspaper) - The new mechanism under Article 6.4 of the Paris Agreement has begun operating with stringent standards, causing the number of project credits granted to decrease by up to 40%, opening up a rigorous screening process for Vietnamese businesses. Once seen as a financial "lifeline" to help businesses go green, the carbon credit market has recently faced a wave of skepticism regarding its actual quality. The tendency for projects to exaggerate emission reduction figures and lack sustainability has deterred even global tech giants. For example, in April, Microsoft temporarily suspended its purchases of new carbon elimination credits, reflecting the heightened caution of international buyers. Under that pressure, Article 6.4 of the Paris Agreement – the centralized credit granting mechanism directly overseen by the United Nations – officially entered the implementation phase with the goal of restoring order to the carbon game. Tightening the credit disbursement valve: A 40% drop in output. A major turning point occurred in February, when the Monitoring Body of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) approved the first credits under Article 6.4 for a clean cooking stove project in Myanmar. Notably, this project had originally been registered under the Clean Development Mechanism (CDM) during the Kyoto Protocol era. According to an analysis by the Clean Air Task Force (CATF) – an international non- governmental organization specializing in independent climate research – when compared using the new methodology and more cautious calculation factors for non-renewable biomass, the project received approximately 40% fewer credits compared to the previous CDM system. You may also like The "evaporation" of nearly half of the credit output is clear evidence that the United Nations is tightening its calculation formula. The new mechanism forces parties to prove that emissions reductions are real, rather than relying on exaggerated scenarios. To date, the regulatory body has only approved five methodologies, including landfill gas capture, industrial N2O treatment, renewable energy, and clean cooking. The transition from legacy CDM projects to Article 6.4 is also progressing quite slowly. Although the deadline for host countries to approve transfers is June 30th, early 2026 figures show that only about 13% of submitted CDM credits have been approved. This indicates that many governments are considering retaining credits for domestic emission reduction purposes, rather than selling them off internationally on a massive scale. The "gold standard" for quality and the challenging problem of forests. In principle, one carbon credit represents one ton of CO2 equivalent that is reduced or removed from the atmosphere. However, for a credit to have sustainable commercial value, Article 6.4 sets out five stringent conditions: complementarity (the project only survives thanks to the carbon funding), longevity (how long the carbon is stored), accurate emission baseline, emission leakage risk (not shifting pollution elsewhere), and an independent measurement, reporting, and verification (MRV) system. While industrial engineering projects have relatively clear measurement processes, the credit-based aspects of forestry and land use present the greatest challenge. Crops can be destroyed by natural disasters, pests and diseases, or accumulated carbon in the soil can be released when ownership changes. An assessment by the non-profit organization CATF, reviewing 20 forest credit rules in North America, has revealed a number of gaps in baseline determination and carbon return risk mitigation. Although forest credits once accounted for nearly 40% of the voluntary market, the methodology for reforestation and reforestation was only introduced into the UNFCCC review process in October, and there is no date set for final approval of the framework. The dilemma between upholding environmental standards and facilitating the flow of private capital is a major headache. If regulations are too lenient, accreditation credits will become useless. Conversely, if procedures are too complicated and accreditation costs too high, developing countries will struggle to access the market. This directly impacts Vietnam's roadmap. You may also like The wave of international standardization is directly impacting Vietnam's progress. On April 1st, the Government issued Decree 112/2026/ND-CP (effective from May 19th). This is an important legal document that clearly stipulates the mechanism for exchanging emission reduction results under both Article 6.2 (bilateral agreements between governments), Article 6.4, and other voluntary forms. Previously, on August 14th, the Government also approved Resolution 235/NQ-CP, officially formalizing the Article 6 cooperation agreement signed with Singapore , effective from September 2025. This handshake paves the way for Vietnamese businesses to sell internationally accredited credits to the island nation. According to UNEP-CCC data as of November 5th, Vietnam has 3 bilateral agreements and 20 registered activities under Article 6.2, although no credits have yet been officially issued through the Article 6.4 channel. On the domestic stage, the carbon exchange has also been operational since June 29th. According to data from the UNDP, the total pilot quota for the 2025-2026 period is approximately 511 million tons of CO2 equivalent, directly allocated to 110 large facilities in three heavy-emission sectors: thermal power, iron and steel, and cement. On November 13th, Vietnam further announced the launch of the Carbon Market Information Portal at COP31 to ensure transparency of all project data for investors.
