artigo.texto: EUA impõem restrição ao Brasil em compras de chips para data centers O governo dos Estado Unidos incluiu o Brasil na lista dos países que enfrentarão restrições para importar chips fabricados no país norte-americano para data centers. Com a decisãodo Escritório de Indústria e Segurança do Departamento de Comércio dos Estados Unidos (BIS, na sigla em Inglês), fornecedores brasileiros precisarão de autorização do governo de Donald Trump para enviar os processadores avançados a empresas brasileiras, com pedidos analisados caso a caso. Segundo o Departamento de Comércio, a norma visa garantir que as restrições existentes ao acesso a tecnologias americanas sensíveis não possam ser contornadas por meio de acordos de computação remota que envolvam centros de dados em países terceiros. Além do Brasil, a restrição inclui Singapura, Tailândia, Malásia e Indonésia, que, segundo a norma, apresentam risco acima do normal de desvio ilegal desses chips para China ou Macau —alvos de embargos junto com Rússia, Irã, Coreia do Norte, Síria e Cuba. Norma norte-americana exige que empresas dos países restringidos solicitem licenças de exportação dos EUA para os chips mais avançados, em um esforço para reduzir o contrabando desses produtos. A proposta dos EUA aborda o cenário tecnológico em evolução. “Alinhando ainda mais as proteções que regem o acesso remoto a recursos computacionais avançados com os controles existentes sobre o transporte físico de tecnologia americana sensível”, disse o Departamento de Comércio. continue lendo - O que se sabe sobre a reunião para a 'paz mundial' que reunirá Trump, Xi e Putin AFP · há 1 hora - Justiça ordena transferência de Peña a prisão militar após denúncias de privilégios Estadão Conteúdo · há 2 horas - Alliana diz que pagamento a aposentados do Ueno Bank acontecerá nesta semana AFP · há 3 horas - Rascunho da COP31 defende acelerar o fim do uso dos combustíveis fósseis AFP · há 6 horas

artigo.texto: Consumo de eletricidade – A expansão da inteligência artificial (IA) exige uma infraestrutura física cada vez maior, que depende de grandes quantidades de eletricidade para processar dados e manter servidores em funcionamento. O impacto ambiental dessa estrutura, porém, pode ser maior do que se imaginava. Uma pesquisa da Universidade Harvard, nos Estados Unidos, identificou o consumo energético e as emissões de centenas de centros de dados, revelando a dimensão da demanda elétrica provocada por essas instalações. Publicado em 16 de novembro de 2026 na revista científica Nature Sustainability, o estudo analisou 403 instalações classificadas como hyperscale data centers, centros de dados de grande porte utilizados para computação em nuvem, armazenamento digital e inteligência artificial. LEIA: Diferença salarial entre brancos e negros chega a 71% no Brasil Os pesquisadores estimaram que essas estruturas consumiram aproximadamente 82 terawatts-hora (TWh) de eletricidade entre maio de 2024 e abril de 2025, considerando o cenário central de funcionamento. O volume representa cerca de 1,8% de toda a eletricidade consumida nos Estados Unidos no período. Além da demanda energética, o funcionamento dos centros de dados foi associado à emissão de aproximadamente 25,7 milhões de toneladas de dióxido de carbono (CO₂). O resultado é entre duas e três vezes superior às estimativas anteriores referentes a 2018, embora os períodos e as metodologias utilizadas não sejam diretamente comparáveis. A pesquisa também apontou que aproximadamente 54% da eletricidade atribuída às instalações analisadas foi gerada a partir de combustíveis fósseis. Os dados estão disponíveis no estudo publicado na Nature Sustainability, que apresenta uma avaliação detalhada da relação entre centros de dados, consumo energético e emissões de carbono. Satélites ajudaram a identificar o consumo dos centros de dados A falta de informações detalhadas sobre o funcionamento dessas instalações é um dos obstáculos para avaliar seus impactos ambientais. Empresas de tecnologia divulgam relatórios de sustentabilidade, mas nem sempre disponibilizam dados específicos sobre o consumo de eletricidade de cada centro de dados. Para contornar essa limitação, os pesquisadores utilizaram imagens de satélite para identificar as instalações e estimar sua demanda energética. As informações foram cruzadas com dados da Agência de Proteção Ambiental dos Estados Unidos (EPA), permitindo identificar as fontes de energia utilizadas pelas redes elétricas regionais. A combinação dos dados possibilitou relacionar o funcionamento dos centros de dados às emissões das usinas responsáveis pelo fornecimento de eletricidade. Virgínia, Oregon, Ohio e Iowa concentraram mais da metade do consumo energético analisado. Apesar dos resultados, os cientistas ressaltam que as instalações estudadas atendem a diferentes serviços digitais, e não exclusivamente à inteligência artificial. Por isso, não é possível atribuir todas as emissões identificadas apenas aos sistemas de IA generativa. Emissões também podem afetar a saúde da população Os impactos ambientais dos centros de dados não se limitam ao aquecimento global. Quando a eletricidade utilizada pelas instalações é produzida por usinas a carvão ou gás natural, a geração de energia também pode liberar poluentes como material particulado fino, óxidos de nitrogênio e dióxido de enxofre. Essas substâncias estão associadas a problemas respiratórios e cardiovasculares, o que pode afetar comunidades próximas às usinas, mesmo que os centros de dados estejam localizados a centenas de quilômetros de distância. Francesca Dominici, professora de Harvard e uma das responsáveis pelo estudo, destaca que investigar os efeitos dessas emissões sobre a saúde humana será uma das próximas etapas da pesquisa. O levantamento, entretanto, estimou as emissões de carbono e não mediu diretamente a ocorrência de doenças ou mortes relacionadas às instalações analisadas. Consumo de energia pode aumentar até 2030 O avanço da inteligência artificial deve ampliar ainda mais a demanda por eletricidade. Segundo a Agência Internacional de Energia (IEA), o consumo global de energia dos centros de dados poderá dobrar até 2030, enquanto a demanda das instalações especializadas em IA poderá triplicar. Em 2025, os centros de dados foram responsáveis por aproximadamente 1,5% do consumo mundial de eletricidade. A agência também estima que as emissões globais relacionadas à energia utilizada por essas instalações estejam próximas de 150 milhões de toneladas de CO₂ por ano, podendo chegar a 350 milhões de toneladas em 2035, considerando o cenário central. O crescimento da infraestrutura também pode sobrecarregar redes elétricas locais, exigindo investimentos em novas usinas, linhas de transmissão e sistemas de refrigeração. O consumo de água representa outro desafio, especialmente em regiões que já enfrentam escassez hídrica. Energia limpa pode reduzir o impacto ambiental da IA A redução dos impactos ambientais da inteligência artificial não depende exclusivamente do desenvolvimento de computadores mais eficientes. A localização dos centros de dados e as fontes de eletricidade utilizadas também são determinantes. Instalações abastecidas por fontes de baixa emissão, como energia solar, eólica e nuclear, podem apresentar uma pegada de carbono operacional significativamente menor. Alternativas incluem o reaproveitamento do calor produzido pelos servidores, melhorias nos sistemas de refrigeração e o desenvolvimento de modelos de IA que demandem menos energia. Durante a COP31, realizada na Turquia, governos e organizações internacionais apresentaram uma iniciativa voluntária voltada ao incentivo de energia limpa, eficiência energética e maior transparência ambiental no setor tecnológico. artigo.texto: Malta Maritime Forum calls for a fairer emissions trading system Prime minister's arguments at EU summit lauded Malta Maritime Forum calls for a fairer system and backs the Prime Minister’s stand in the national interest. The Malta Maritime Forum (MMF) has welcomed the 'firm position' taken by the prime minister at the recent European Political Community meeting in Ireland, where, it said, he echoed the MMF’s criticism of the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS). The MMF views the ETS as harming Europe and Malta, and must be changed. "The ETS was poorly designed. It was passed in record time, without a proper, broad consultation process with the maritime industry. The result is an impractical system that created unfair competition for European ports," it said. "The ETS is not delivering the climate results it promised. The EU cannot apply its laws outside its own territory. As a result, Europe is losing business, investment and maritime connectivity to North Africa, where the ETS applies differently or may not apply at all," it explained. " Whilst shipping routes are increasingly diverting southwards, emissions are not falling; they are simply moving elsewhere, together with the jobs and investment that go with them." Robert Abela made the same point at the summit meeting, saying the EU is shooting itself in the foot with ETS. The impact of ETS is disproportionate on Malta relative to other Member States because it has no alternatives such as rail or inland waterways to keep goods moving, and it is the most open economy in the EU27. The MMF said it is ready to continue working with the government on fair and practical solutions and to present them to the EU with a unified national voice. One key proposal is to apply the ETS to the cargo, whether containerised or not, rather than to the vessel carrying it. " Any solution must ensure a level playing field and avoid putting EU ports and shipping services at an unfair disadvantage," it stressed. artigo.texto: Um projeto aprovado pela Assembleia Legislativa do Estado do Paraná (Alep) estabelece diretrizes para incentivar a instalação e a expansão de data centers no estado. O Projeto de Lei 55/2026 cria o Programa Paranaense de Incentivo a Centros de Dados (ProdataPR). Aprovada na terça-feira, 17, a proposta é uma iniciativa dos deputados Luiz Fernando Guerra (Novo), Maria Victoria (PP) e Bazana (PSD). O projeto visa ao desenvolvimento da economia digital, à atração de investimentos privados, à geração de empregos especializados e ao aproveitamento das vantagens competitivas do Paraná, especialmente na produção de energia renovável e na conectividade. De acordo com a deputada Maria Victoria, o texto tem o objetivo de criar condições para posicionar o Paraná como um dos principais destinos de investimentos em infraestrutura digital, inteligência artificial e novas tecnologias no Brasil. O deputado Luiz Fernando Guerra destaca a importância do planejamento para que a expansão dos data centers no Paraná seja acompanhada pela formação de profissionais para o setor. Já o deputado Pedro Paulo Bazana (PSD) diz que a proposta busca transformar o potencial tecnológico do Paraná em oportunidades de desenvolvimento para os municípios. Data centers Os data centers são estruturas essenciais para o funcionamento da economia digital. Neles são armazenadas e processadas grandes quantidades de informações utilizadas por empresas, governos, instituições financeiras, hospitais, universidades e plataformas. Com o avanço da inteligência artificial, essas instalações ganharam importância estratégica na disputa mundial por investimentos tecnológicos. Conforme a justificativa do projeto, o ProdataPR tem a finalidade de consolidar o Paraná como polo estratégico de data centers na América Latina, gerando empregos qualificados e fomentando a cadeia produtiva de tecnologia. O texto ainda autoriza o Governo do Estado a conceder benefícios fiscais às empresas beneficiárias do programa. A proposta estabelece diretrizes para estimular novos empreendimentos, aumentar a infraestrutura de telecomunicações e incentivar parcerias entre empresas, universidades e centros de pesquisa. Outro diferencial é a preocupação com a sustentabilidade. O projeto incentiva a utilização de fontes renováveis de energia, o aproveitamento do biometano, o uso racional da água e a adoção de tecnologias sustentáveis de resfriamento dos equipamentos. A aprovação da proposta ocorre em um momento de expansão do setor no Brasil. Em setembro de 2026, foi sancionada a Lei Federal n.º 15.504, que instituiu o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Data Center (Redata). A legislação federal prevê incentivos tributários condicionados a compromissos de sustentabilidade, investimentos em pesquisa e desenvolvimento e utilização de energia renovável ou de baixa emissão. artigo.texto: O Departamento de Comércio dos Estados Unidos publicará norma que obriga operadoras de data centers no Brasil, Indonésia, Malásia, Cingapura e Tailândia a obterem licença prévia para comprar chips avançados de inteligência artificial destinados a esses centros de dados, produzidos pela Nvidia e por outros fabricantes americanos. A medida visa impedir que a China e outros adversários dos EUA acessem capacidade computacional localizada no exterior que utiliza processadores projetados nos Estados Unidos. A decisão ocorre na esteira do escândalo que levou à renúncia do ex-CEO da Nvidia, Jensen Huang, na semana passada, após revelação de relacionamento com uma executiva chinesa suspeita de espionagem. Os países listados apresentam risco de contrabando acima do normal, segundo o governo americano. A norma foi elaborada para garantir que restrições existentes a tecnologias americanas sensíveis não sejam contornadas por acordos de computação remota envolvendo data centers em terceiros países. A regulamentação fecha brecha que, na visão de muitos em Washington, permitia à China contornar a proibição de compra dos chips de IA mais avançados. Ela estabelece restrições para data centers no exterior que forneçam volumes significativos de capacidade computacional a empresas sediadas em países de alto risco, lista que inclui China, Rússia e Irã. Os centros também deverão realizar verificações rigorosas sobre clientes. A regra, que entra em vigor em 90 dias, deve prejudicar a capacidade dessas empresas de usar chips americanos para treinar modelos avançados de IA. Ações de fabricantes de chips caíram na manhã desta segunda-feira. Papéis da Nvidia recuaram mais de 2%, da Intel mais de 6% e da Micron mais de 7%. O Philadelphia Semiconductor Index caiu mais de 5%, e o Nasdaq também abriu em baixa. O plano surge dias antes da viagem do presidente Donald Trump à China para cúpula econômica, na qual se reunirá com Xi Jinping. A proposta foi divulgada dias após Huang renunciar, após admitir relacionamento extraconjugal com Alice Huang, ex-executiva da Megaspeed International, empresa de Cingapura investigada por possíveis violações de controles de exportação e suspeita de envolvimento em espionagem para a China. A empresa nega irregularidades, e Alice Huang está atualmente na China. Após a queda de Huang, o Departamento de Comércio e autoridades de alto escalão, incluindo o secretário Howard Lutnick, enfrentaram maior escrutínio. O secretário do Tesouro Scott Bessent responsabilizou Lutnick por não ter feito o suficiente para garantir cumprimento das restrições. A norma alinha regras de acesso remoto às restrições já existentes para acesso físico. Há exceção para empresas com sede nos EUA que operam nos países listados, que podem continuar enviando chips sem licença, e para envios a data centers usados como sistemas comerciais de recomendação por varejistas online ou redes sociais. Analistas afirmam que a aplicação ficará a cargo do Departamento de Comércio, e ainda não está claro como será implementada. A minuta estabelece que as exigências entram em vigor com a publicação no Federal Register, que ainda não havia ocorrido até as 9h desta segunda. A possibilidade de a China acessar chips via aluguel de capacidade em data centers do Sudeste Asiático e outras regiões tem sido fonte de divergências no governo Trump. O escândalo da Nvidia elevou o tema aos mais altos escalões, gerando atritos entre o Departamento de Comércio e outros setores. O anúncio afirmou que a norma foi redigida pelo Departamento do Tesouro e por determinação deste e do Conselho de Segurança Nacional, instituições que defendiam regras mais rigorosas. Licenças serão analisadas caso a caso. Nos últimos meses, Scott Bessent, Marco Rubio e Jamieson Greer defenderam restrições abrangentes, enquanto Lutnick resistia a uma versão mais enxuta.

artigo.texto: The voluntary carbon market debate we’re having is wrong For several years now, one question has dominated the technical debate over voluntary carbon markets: should host countries be required to apply “corresponding adjustments” — accounting entries that prevent the same emission reduction from being counted twice — when their carbon credits are purchased by foreign companies? The question sounds like a dry accounting matter. It is not. Depending on how it is answered, the result could be either a more credible voluntary carbon market or a smaller and less effective one — with the costs falling disproportionately on the countries and projects that need climate finance most. A new EDF paper, Corresponding Adjustments and the Voluntary Carbon Market makes the case that the debate, as currently framed, is asking the wrong question. What corresponding adjustments are — and where they apply A corresponding adjustment is an accounting entry applied to a host country’s national emission balance when it transfers a mitigation outcome internationally. The logic is simple: If a country sells reductions to a foreign buyer, it should not also count those reductions toward its own Paris Agreement commitment. The same tonne of CO₂ cannot discharge two obligations simultaneously. This accounting obligation is legally clear in two contexts. Under Article 6.2 of the Paris Agreement, CAs are required for government-to-government transfers of mitigation outcomes. Under CORSIA, the international aviation offsetting scheme, CAs are required when airlines use credits to discharge their compliance obligations. Both cases involve legal obligations being discharged through the same transaction — which is precisely why double-counting matters. The contested question is different: Should CAs also be required for purely voluntary transactions, where a company purchases credits to support its own net zero commitment, not to satisfy any legal obligation? Two questions that keep getting conflated The CA debate suffers from a persistent failure to distinguish between two fundamentally different questions. - The accounting question: Are CAs legally required for voluntary corporate transactions under the Paris Agreement? The answer is no. The Paris Agreement and its implementing decisions are entirely silent on what corporate climate claims may or may not be made on the basis of carbon credits. The leap from “sovereign accounting requires CAs for government-to-government transfers” to “corporate offsetting claims require CA-backed credits” is a normative position, not a treaty requirement. - The policy effectiveness question: Would mandating CAs for voluntary transactions, in practice, produce better climate outcomes? This is an empirical question — and the honest answer is that we do not yet have the evidence to resolve it. Conflating these two questions has consequences. When CAs are treated as a matter of accounting integrity, those who oppose them are forced to defend double-counting. When they are treated as a policy instrument with costs and benefits, the burden shifts to proponents to demonstrate that the benefits outweigh the costs. The second framing is the correct one. Do CAs improve climate outcomes? Whether mandating CAs would strengthen or weaken global climate outcomes depends on three empirical parameters that remain poorly understood. - Host country responsiveness: If countries systematically reduce their own domestic climate ambition when private carbon finance flows in — substituting international private money for domestic public commitment — then even additional project-level credits generate no net global benefit. This is the displacement concern at the heart of the pro-CA argument. It is a legitimate concern. But the evidence for it, across the heterogeneous landscape of VCM host countries, does not yet exist at the scale needed to justify a blanket policy response. - Supply sensitivity: World Bank modelling suggests that CA-related fees could exceed $25 per tonne of CO₂ in many host countries — enough to render the most finance-dependent, highest-additionality projects unviable. For projects where carbon revenues are the margin between proceeding and not, this is not a marginal cost. The authorization infrastructure needed to implement CAs efficiently is also, as of today, absent in most potential host countries. Mandating CAs before that infrastructure exists would not reform the market — it would freeze it. - Buyer differentiation: The pro-CA position assumes that CA backing is what makes corporate claims credible. But neither the ICVCM’s Core Carbon Principles, the VCMI’s Claims Code of Practice, nor the SBTi’s framework for beyond-value-chain mitigation currently requires CA backing for valid corporate claims. If buyers and the public do not, in practice, distinguish meaningfully between CA-backed and non-CA credits when the underlying quality is high, the market case for mandating CAs weakens considerably. Who pays when we get CA requirements wrong? The cost structure of CA requirements is not neutral. The most additional projects — those entirely dependent on carbon revenue to proceed — face the steepest barriers from authorization fees. Low-additionality projects, which would happen regardless of carbon finance, are comparatively unaffected. A policy designed to protect environmental integrity should not systematically penalize the most genuinely additional activities. The geographic pattern is similarly concerning. The countries with the greatest mitigation potential and the greatest need for climate finance are typically those with the least authorization infrastructure. The CDM precedent is instructive: Administrative requirements contributed to a heavy concentration of activity in a small number of large, institutionally sophisticated economies, with relatively little reaching least-developed countries. There is no reason to assume CA requirements would produce a different distribution.

artigo.texto: A Assembleia Legislativa do Paraná (Alep) aprovou, nesta terça-feira (17), o Projeto de Lei 55/2026, que cria o Programa Paranaense de Incentivo a Centros de Dados (PRODATAPR). A proposta estabelece diretrizes para estimular a instalação e a expansão de data centers no Estado. O projeto é de autoria dos deputados Luiz Fernando Guerra (Novo), Maria Victoria (PP) e Pedro Paulo Bazana (PSD). Entre os objetivos estão atrair investimentos privados, ampliar a infraestrutura tecnológica e incentivar a formação de profissionais para trabalhar no setor. Os data centers são estruturas utilizadas para armazenar, processar e distribuir grandes volumes de informações. Eles atendem empresas, instituições financeiras, hospitais, universidades, órgãos públicos e plataformas digitais. Com o crescimento de serviços de computação em nuvem e inteligência artificial, esse tipo de infraestrutura passou a ter maior importância para o setor de tecnologia. Projeto prevê incentivos fiscais O texto autoriza o Governo do Paraná a conceder benefícios fiscais às empresas que participarem do programa. A proposta também prevê medidas para ampliar a infraestrutura de telecomunicações e estimular parcerias entre empresas, universidades e centros de pesquisa. Outro ponto é a formação de mão de obra especializada. O projeto estabelece diretrizes para incentivar cursos e parcerias voltados à qualificação de profissionais que poderão atuar na construção, operação e manutenção dos centros de dados. Na justificativa, os autores apontam a produção de energia renovável e a estrutura de conectividade do Paraná como fatores que podem favorecer a instalação desses empreendimentos. Proposta inclui medidas ambientais O programa também prevê diretrizes relacionadas à sustentabilidade. Entre elas estão o incentivo ao uso de fontes renováveis de energia, o aproveitamento do biometano, o uso racional da água e a adoção de tecnologias de resfriamento que reduzam os impactos ambientais. A proposta busca ampliar a participação do Paraná no setor de infraestrutura digital e estimular a instalação de empreendimentos em diferentes regiões do Estado. Setor também recebe incentivo federal A aprovação do projeto estadual ocorre após a sanção da Lei Federal 15.504, em setembro de 2026, que instituiu o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Data Center (Redata). A legislação federal prevê incentivos tributários para empresas do setor, condicionados ao cumprimento de compromissos relacionados à sustentabilidade, aos investimentos em pesquisa e desenvolvimento e ao uso de energia renovável ou de baixa emissão.

artigo.texto: Solar and battery storage can do a lot of the heavy lifting in a renewable electricity system. Add wind, and supplying reliable power gets nearly 20% cheaper, according to new analysis from energy think tank Ember. Wind fills gaps when solar output drops, so the system needs fewer batteries to keep electricity flowing. Ember’s analysis, produced with the Global Wind Energy Council (GWEC), found that adding wind to solar and battery storage cuts the median cost of meeting 90% of electricity demand from $105 to $86 per megawatt-hour. The median cost of solar and wind power covering all demand is $89/MWh, with batteries and a little backup. More wind means fewer batteries Solar and wind don’t follow the same schedule. Their output varies by time of day and across seasons, allowing one to offset the other’s shortfalls. That matters because storing enough electricity to get through a long stretch of weak solar output gets expensive. Wind reduces the amount of energy the batteries need to store in the first place. In the US, adding wind reduces the modeled battery requirement to meet 90% of demand from 20 hours of electricity use to 12 hours. Europe sees the same reduction, while China’s requirement falls from 18 hours to 12. The savings also put cheaper renewable power within reach of more regions. With wind included, regions that account for 75% of global electricity demand can meet 90% of their electricity demand at less than $100/MWh. With solar and batteries alone, that share is only 50%. “We already know that solar and wind are cheap,” said Daan Walter, principal at Ember. By combining solar, wind, and batteries, we can deliver reliable power at remarkably low costs almost everywhere in the world. That’s a pretty fundamental shift in the economics of energy. What happens when it’s cloudy and still? The researchers also looked at prolonged periods of low output. Globally, weighted by electricity demand, a week of low solar output occurs roughly four times a year. A week in which both solar and wind output are low occurs only about once every four years. That’s a global average, so individual locations will have different experiences. Ember defines a lull as seven consecutive days of output below half the source’s average. Combining wind and solar reduces the gaps in low output. New coal and gas doesn’t make financial sense The findings also raise questions for developers planning new fossil fuel plants. Ember identifies 845 GW of coal and gas capacity in planning worldwide. Adding wind raises the share located in regions where solar, wind, and battery storage can meet 90% of demand for under $100/MWh from 71% to 90%. In China alone, wind brings another 91 GW of planned coal and gas capacity into the range where renewables are cheaper. Include backup to cover all demand, and 706 GW of the planned fossil fuel capacity sits in regions where the renewable-based alternative costs less than $100/MWh. Without wind, that figure falls to 520 GW. For investors financing fossil fuel plants in the pipeline that are expected to run for decades, there is likely already a cheaper renewable alternative available to meet the same electricity demand, so it’s worth scrutinizing the project’s economics. Ember’s interactive Wind + Solar + Battery Atlas lets users explore reliable electricity costs in their own region. artigo.texto: Montrose County drafting data center regulations during moratorium MONTROSE, Colo. (KJCT) - Montrose County is drafting regulations for data centers while a moratorium on data center applications is in place. The Planning Commission will hold a public hearing on the regulations Thursday at 6 p.m. Discussion of data centers has grown over the last couple of years. Moratorium in place Montrose County approved a six-month moratorium on data center applications in July. Tallmadge Richmond, Montrose County planning and development director, said the county does not accept applications while a moratorium is in place. “That gives us time to basically research and analyze what these facilities are, what kind of impacts they have,” Richmond said. Draft regulations The county is in the process of drafting data center regulations. Meetings are being held to adjust potential amendments to zoning regulations and to hear from the public. Richmond said the Planning Commission heard public comment the last time the item was heard and then they adjusted the draft based on that. “So it is to continue hearing public comment, but also see if the draft now captures what the Planning Commission was looking for,” Richmond said. The current draft would allow data centers in the general agricultural district and the general industrial district. Both would be allowed by special use. Richmond said that designation means any future data center proposed in Montrose County would have public hearings related to that specific facility and location. Minimum standards Under the draft, all facilities would need to meet minimum standards in several categories. They include energy and water usage, thermal and noise impacts, and others. Richmond said the standards acknowledge potential negative impacts to surrounding properties and identify minimum standards to mitigate them. Next steps The regulations must be finalized by the Planning Commission and approved by the county commissioners before they are adopted. The county is also considering an extension of the moratorium while the regulations are finalized. The moratorium will end when the regulations are finalized. Public hearing details The Planning Commission will hold a public hearing to discuss the regulations Thursday at 6 p.m. The hearing will be held in the Montrose County Public Works Board Room.

artigo.texto: The UL-certified, ITC-eligible system is built at the company’s award-winning Megafactory 1, with deployments planned at commercial sites across North America AUSTIN, Texas and VANCOUVER, British Columbia, Nov. 17, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Moment Energy today unveiled Nova, its next-generation battery energy storage system (BESS). Nova is the world's first BESS made with repurposed electric vehicle batteries to achieve both UL 1973 and UL 9540 certification. The certifications help support its use in commercial, industrial and large-scale energy storage applications. Nova is now in production at the company’s award-winning Megafactory 1 for deployment across North America. The BESS enables commercial customers to reduce energy costs, improve site reliability and uptime, and integrate clean energy into their operations. Moment Energy has already deployed systems powering critical infrastructure including airports, hospitals, agricultural and manufacturing sites. Nova is made in North America and independently verified as fully compliant with Foreign Entity of Concern (FEOC) requirements. Moment Energy has also been independently verified as a non-Prohibited Foreign Entity. Together, this makes Nova the only third-party verified BESS eligible for the U.S. federal Investment Tax Credit (ITC) in 2027 and beyond. "Access to affordable power is a defining factor determining where businesses can grow and what they can build. Today, businesses across North America are being throttled by power capacity constraints,” said Edward Chiang, Co-Founder and CEO of Moment Energy. “We see a future where reengineered EV batteries become essential infrastructure for powering businesses and onshoring manufacturing and supply chain. Nova brings that vision to life, combining safety, engineering and North American manufacturing to deploy the safest and highest-performance batteries ever made: EV batteries to supercharge our aging grid.” Designed for Performance, Flexibility and Long-Term Value The Nova platform is designed to integrate batteries from multiple types of EVs into its flexible stationary storage platform. Moment Energy’s proprietary AI-powered battery management system (BMS) continuously evaluates and optimizes batteries across different states of health to maximize performance, efficiency and reliability throughout the system's life. Each Nova block delivers 200 kW of power / 500 kWh of energy within a 2.94 m by 1.80 m (9.65 ft x 5.9 ft) footprint. This compact, scalable design brings substantial energy storage capacity to commercial sites where space is an important consideration, while also enabling Nova to deploy in large-scale installations in the tens of MWhs. Nova helps commercial energy users save by supporting grid services and utility bill savings, as well as providing resilient backup power during grid outages. Nova’s swappable architecture allows individual battery packs to be replaced as they age over time, instead of replacing the entire system. Durable infrastructure such as the enclosure and concrete pad can remain undisturbed, while the battery packs are serviced and replaced. This design extends the system's lifespan to more than 20 years with Moment Energy’s capacity augmentation service. "With Nova, we’ve solved the engineering challenges that have prevented BESS made with EV batteries from scaling commercially,” said Gurmesh Sidhu, Co-Founder and Chief Product Officer of Moment Energy. “Every element of the platform has been engineered to maximize flexibility, simplify servicing and give customers confidence that the system will reliably power their critical infrastructure for decades." Batteries Made in North America As battery storage becomes increasingly critical for commercial energy users, battery supply has become a global issue of international trade and national security, with the large majority of batteries currently imported from China. By establishing a new domestic supply chain from the abundant supply of retiring EV batteries, Moment Energy's Nova allows the U.S. and Canada to keep critical minerals and battery software in North America. Repurposing is an important step in the circular economy, unlocking years or even decades of residual value in a battery after its useful life for electric vehicle applications is over, preventing batteries from entering landfills. Nova brings that value into commercial energy infrastructure through a platform engineered, manufactured and supported in North America. Engineered and Certified for Safety Nova is the first BESS built from EV batteries that is certified to UL 9540 by UL Solutions. Nova has achieved UL 1973 and UL 9540 certifications, key safety certifications also commonly held by first-life battery systems, and has been tested to UL 9540A for evaluating thermal runaway fire propagation in BESS. With these certifications, Nova meets the listing requirements of electrical codes of the United States and Canada for stationary storage. Additionally, Megafactory 1 is certified to UL 1974, the standard for sorting, grading and repurposing electric vehicle batteries. “Repurposing electric vehicle batteries for stationary energy storage creates new technical considerations that must be carefully evaluated,” said Jeff Smidt, senior vice president of Testing, Inspection and Certification, Industrial, at UL Solutions. “UL Certification demonstrates that the evaluated battery and energy storage system met applicable safety requirements. This achievement provides important third-party evidence supporting the responsible use of repurposed batteries in commercial and industrial energy storage applications.” Nova combines these UL certifications with integrated safety features and engineering for demanding commercial environments: Nova’s rigorous safety engineering allows the system to be installed in the outdoor built environment, alongside the buildings and facilities it serves. artigo.texto: Duke Energy has unveiled plans to invest up to $756 million in its largest battery storage complex yet, adding 410 megawatts (MW) of grid capacity in Wayne County, North Carolina. Announced on November 17, 2026, the two-phase H.F. Lee Battery Storage project is scheduled to begin construction in early 2027 and enter service by late 2028. Situated adjacent to Duke Energy‘s existing H.F. Lee natural gas power plant in Goldsboro, the complex will more than double the 308 MW of battery storage the utility currently operates across 14 North Carolina sites. By building on a former coal plant property using North American-manufactured batteries, the development qualifies for a 50% federal tax credit designed to reduce costs for ratepayers. Two-Phase Buildout Doubles North Carolina Storage Fleet The installation is divided into two four-hour lithium-ion battery systems. H.F. Lee Battery Storage 1 will deliver 260 MW when it comes online in fall 2028, followed by the 150 MW H.F. Lee Battery Storage 2 facility by the end of 2028. At full output, the combined 410 MW complex will supply enough instantaneous electricity to power roughly 300,000 homes during peak demand periods. That capacity is more than four times the size of Duke Energy’s current largest operational battery facility in North Carolina, a 100 MW site in Knightdale. Work on the Goldsboro site will reuse grid interconnections at the H.F. Lee Energy Complex, where a 920 MW combined-cycle natural gas plant replaced a retired 1951 coal-fired station in 2012. How Do Federal Tax Credits and Grid Rules Shape the Deal? Federal clean-energy tax incentives form a central pillar of the project’s economics. Locating the batteries inside a designated energy community alongside domestic content requirements for North American battery manufacturing unlocks a 50% federal tax credit, lowering the net capital cost passed on to utility customers. The announcement arrived one day after the North Carolina Utilities Commission issued a November 16, 2026 order advancing 2,700 MW of new battery storage toward a 5,400 MW fleet target by 2034. Within its broader 2025 Carolinas Resource Plan, the utility has outlined plans for 6,540 MW of battery storage by 2035 as it shifts capital toward dispatchable capacity following Duke Energy’s decision to halt offshore wind plans off North Carolina and advances four planned solar projects in Florida. Local Tax Base and Workforce Impact in Wayne County County officials estimate the two battery facilities could generate up to $2 million in additional annual property tax revenue once operational. Duke Energy is already Wayne County’s largest taxpayer, contributing $5.8 million each year for its existing H.F. Lee generating complex and related local power infrastructure. Nine permanent full-time positions will support operations at the Goldsboro battery complex alongside regional solar and storage assets. Kendal Bowman, Duke Energy’s North Carolina President, said the utility is “reinvesting in our existing power plant communities that have powered North Carolina and South Carolina for decades,” while Wayne County Board of Commissioners Chairman Joe Daugherty noted that the tax revenue and grid reliability will support long-term industrial recruitment across Eastern North Carolina. Across the broader U.S. grid-storage pipeline targeting 2028 delivery, construction is also underway on the 553 MWdc Cold Creek Solar and Storage Project in Texas after developer Doral Renewables closed nearly $900 million in project financing earlier in 2026. artigo.texto: Luiz Araújo, da Agência iNFRA O governo federal formalizou nesta semana as regras do ProBioQAV (Programa Nacional de Combustível Sustentável de Aviação), que estabelece metas de redução das emissões de carbono para as companhias aéreas. A regulamentação da ANAC (Agência Nacional de Aviação Civil), publicada na terça-feira (17), prevê um período de transição, com redução ou dispensa das metas caso as empresas comprovem a indisponibilidade de SAF (Combustível Sustentável de Aviação). Criado pela Lei do Combustível do Futuro, o programa prevê metas anuais de redução das emissões em voos domésticos, começando em 1% em 2027 e chegando a 10% a partir de 2037. A obrigação alcançará companhias que emitirem mais de dez mil toneladas de carbono por ano em operações de passageiros ou cargas. O cálculo considerará o consumo de combustível de cada empresa e o percentual de redução previsto para o período. O principal instrumento para o alcance das metas é o uso do SAF. Contudo, as regras permitem o cumprimento das obrigações sem abastecimento físico, já que os créditos serão contabilizados a partir dos CS-SAF (Certificados de Sustentabilidade do SAF), documentos que comprovam a redução de emissões e podem ser comercializados. Também admitem o uso parcial de combustíveis de menor emissão, certificados estrangeiros e créditos do SBCE (Sistema Brasileiro de Comércio de Emissões), limitados a 15% da meta em 2027 e 2028, 10% em 2029 e 5% a partir de 2030. A possibilidade de redução ou dispensa das metas por falta de SAF valerá enquanto não estiver em funcionamento a plataforma de emissão e registro dos CS-SAF. Para obter a flexibilização, as companhias deverão comprovar tentativas de aquisição do combustível, apresentando informações sobre a disponibilidade do produto, respostas dos fornecedores e motivos que impediram o abastecimento. Até a entrada em operação do sistema, o uso de SAF poderá ser comprovado por documentos equivalentes aos exigidos para a emissão dos certificados. A regulamentação também permite que as companhias aproveitem, no ano seguinte, reduções de emissões superiores às metas exigidas. O mecanismo deverá observar as condições estabelecidas pela ANAC e poderá ser utilizado para compensar parte das obrigações futuras. A medida se soma aos instrumentos alternativos previstos para o cumprimento das metas anuais. Fiscalização e penalidades O acompanhamento será feito por três instrumentos, cujos procedimentos foram detalhados em portaria complementar: o PME (Plano de Monitoramento de Emissões), o RE (Relatório de Emissões) e o RC (Relatório de Cumprimento). O primeiro detalhará os métodos de medição do consumo de combustível e das emissões, enquanto os demais apresentarão os dados anuais e a comprovação do cumprimento das metas. O prazo excepcional para entrega do PME será 15 de dezembro deste ano. O RE deverá ser apresentado até 31 de março do ano seguinte ao período de referência, e o RC, até 31 de maio. A ANAC será responsável pela verificação das informações, sem exigir, como regra geral, auditorias independentes. O descumprimento das obrigações poderá resultar em multas de R$ 84 mil pela ausência do PME ou do RE e de R$ 750 por tonelada de carbono que deixou de ser reduzida. O pagamento da penalidade não eliminará a obrigação, e o saldo pendente deverá ser incorporado à meta do ano seguinte. A regulamentação também prevê sanções por inconsistências nos relatórios, ausência de documentos e irregularidades na utilização de certificados ambientais. Embora as regras da ANAC já estejam formalizadas, a implementação integral do ProBioQAV ainda depende da regulamentação e da entrada em operação do sistema de certificados sob responsabilidade da ANP (Agência Nacional do Petróleo, Gás Natural e Biocombustíveis).

artigo.texto: Bloomberg reported on Nov. 16, 2026, that CATL is considering a China-wide battery-swapping network, citing people familiar with the company’s plans. The proposed system could involve partnerships with automakers, work on vehicle design from the development stage and battery leasing. In battery swapping, a driver exchanges a depleted battery for a charged one instead of waiting for it to recharge. Bloomberg placed the strategy against pressure on CATL’s margins and automakers’ interest in diversifying their battery suppliers. Starting collaboration at the vehicle-design stage would bring automakers into planning for the proposed system, while leasing could make battery ownership part of the model. The reported strategy links CATL’s station network with automaker partnerships and vehicle design. CATL’s reported network in China A Jan. 8, 2026 report by Movilidad Eléctrica put CATL’s Chinese network at 1,325 stations at the end of 2025: 1,020 for passenger cars and 305 truck stations managed by Qiji Energy. The outlet also described a construction plan in which CATL subsidiary Contemporary Amperex Energy Service Technology (CAES) would build the first 1,000 stations, with outside organizations involved in stations 1,001 through 10,000. It reported a separate target of more than 2,500 passenger-car stations in over 120 Chinese cities by the end of 2026.

artigo.texto: The 400 largest data centers in the United States emit more greenhouse gas emissions in one year than the entire nation of Denmark, according to a new report from Harvard University. From May 2024 to April 2025, data centers accounted for nearly 2% of total U.S. energy consumption and produced more than 25 million metric tons of CO2. Amna Nawaz spoke with the study's lead author, Gianluca Guidi. Amna Nawaz: The 400 largest data centers in the United States emit more greenhouse gas emissions into the air in one year than the entire nation of Denmark. That's according to a new report from Harvard University. The study found that, from May 2024 to April 2025, data centers accounted for nearly 2 percent of total U.S. energy consumption and produced more than 25 million metric tons of carbon dioxide, a level two or three times higher than an earlier estimate in 2018. I'm joined now by the lead author of that study, Gianluca Guidi, a postdoctoral research fellow at Harvard focusing on AI and public health. Gianluca, welcome to the "News Hour." Thanks for joining us. Gianluca Guidi: Yes, thank you for having me. Hello, everyone. Amna Nawaz: So, what was most surprising to you from this report? What really stood out to you in the way of the findings? Gianluca Guidi: Yes. So think about it, right? So Denmark is an entire country, and with millions of people, homes, hospitals, and industries. And we're talking about, like, comparable annual carbon emissions from just 403 data centers. So those are just like 400 buildings. And that's an extraordinary scale. And those facilities are just only a fraction of the industry and how the industry looks like right now. Amna Nawaz: You point out in the report too you weren't even able to capture all of the information from many data centers. So what do we not yet know about the impact that they could be having? Gianluca Guidi: Yes, that's a great question. The study dates back like -- it's almost a year-old by now. And since then, there's been, like, an incredible build-out. We have preliminary results of newer studies that tells us there are around 1,000 hyperscale data centers. So that's just more than the double of what we reported in our study. Amna Nawaz: So many more data centers, meaning the numbers in here, in actuality, now the scope of emissions could be much higher than your report suggests. Is that correct? Gianluca Guidi: That is correct. Yes, that is correct. And together with the emissions, you have the water consumption and potentially also public health consequences. So, in a way, we have that a technology that is actually moving faster than our ability to understand its consequences. Amna Nawaz: Tell us more about that, the intersection of the build-out of these data centers and the impact on public health. What are you finding there? Gianluca Guidi: Yes. In this specific study, we haven't addressed yet the public health, but what's happening basically is that, once you have a powered demand and a power that is produced at the power plant level, not only you're producing, we're producing carbon emissions, but we're also producing hazardous pollutants that travel and eventually somebody breathes them, and the effects for the health are pretty dangerous. And there's plenty and ton of scientific research about this. Amna Nawaz: The power pull as well when we talk about the power use in -- of these data centers, there are states you point out, like Virginia, Iowa, Oregon, and Ohio that account for half of the electricity use. Why is that and what kind of downstream impacts does that have for residents in the area? Gianluca Guidi: Yes, that's correct. So, basically, the states offer the infrastructure, the land and the electricity that large data centers need. But there's a catch. So the benefits of these expansion aren't necessarily felt by the same communities that bear its environmental costs. So, more electricity demands can mean more power plans and, therefore, as we're saying, more pollution and more pressure on local infrastructure. So those consequences don't stop at the data center's fence. Amna Nawaz: There are those who will argue, Gianluca, I'm sure you have heard, that we need to build out these AI data centers, that the country has to do it to remain competitive, that it's necessary for our economy, for national security, and that the impact of that on the environment or for residents in the area is a necessary evil, in other words. Would you agree with that? Is that -- can that argument be made? Gianluca Guidi: Yes, I see that, and there's a big backlash happening right now. I wouldn't call them like a necessary evil. I mean, I am an AI researcher myself, and I have to say I'm really excited about this technology and what it can do. but there are better ways to build it, so -- that might cost more, they might take longer. The question is whether we're willing to prioritize doing it right over doing it first. Amna Nawaz: The report, as you mentioned, is now several months old, almost a year-old. There are a lot of things you don't address in it. For the average citizen to understand how this might impact their lives, what are the questions you think need to be answered next? Gianluca Guidi: Yes, here's what concerns me the most. We're building this AI infrastructure faster than we can independently understand its consequences. So, our study, as you were saying, was just published, like -- but the data are already over a-year-old. So scientific evidence shouldn't arrive after the infrastructure, and neither should, I believe, the public participation. And the main concerns would be the water consumption, the electricity, so such that putting the power grid into like -- in strain and potentially therefore, as I was saying before, the public health consequences. Amna Nawaz: That is Gianluca Guidi of Harvard. He's a postdoctoral research fellow there focusing on AI and public health. Gianluca, thank you so much for your time. It's good

artigo.texto: As the world looks for ways to restore degraded land and remove carbon dioxide (CO2) from the atmosphere, oasification offers another approach to nature-based restoration. It focuses on improving how drylands capture and retain water, allowing vegetation to recover and ecosystems to become healthier. Beyond its environmental benefits, oasification could also create opportunities for carbon removal projects and nature-based finance. But how does it work, and can it become part of the growing carbon market? What Is Oasification? Understanding the Concept Oasification is a land-restoration approach that aims to reverse desertification by improving how degraded land captures and retains water. It focuses on restoring the natural conditions needed for vegetation to grow, particularly in arid and semi-arid regions where water is limited. The concept was developed by Spanish researchers Andrés Martínez de Azagra, Jorge Mongil, and J. Rojo. Their 2004 paper, Oasification: A Forest Solution to Many Problems of Desertification, describes how small earth structures can collect and infiltrate rainwater and surface runoff, improving soil moisture and supporting vegetation growth. Oasification is closely linked to the fight against desertification, which occurs when land in dry regions loses its productivity due to climate conditions and human activities such as deforestation, overgrazing, and unsustainable farming. The scale of this challenge is significant. According to the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD), drylands cover approximately 40.6% of Earth’s land area, excluding Antarctica. The UN also reported that 77.6% of the world’s land experienced drier conditions between 1990 and 2020 than during the previous 30 years. Unlike approaches that focus mainly on planting trees, oasification first addresses the land’s ability to capture and retain available water. It can complement reforestation by creating better conditions for vegetation to establish and survive. How Does Oasification Work? Restoring Land by Making Better Use of Water Oasification works by improving how degraded land collects, absorbs, and retains rainwater. Rather than relying on large irrigation systems, it uses relatively small structures and land-management techniques to direct available water toward areas where vegetation can grow. One common technique is rainwater harvesting. Small basins, trenches, terraces, and contour barriers are built along slopes to slow down surface runoff. These structures collect rainwater that would otherwise flow downhill and carry away valuable topsoil. The captured water can then seep into the ground, increasing soil moisture and supporting plant growth. Another important part is soil restoration. By slowing water runoff, oasification helps reduce erosion and allows soil particles and nutrients to settle. This can improve soil conditions and create a better environment for seeds, roots, and microorganisms. Vegetation is then introduced or allowed to recover naturally. Native trees, shrubs, grasses, and other suitable plants help stabilize the soil, provide ground cover, and support local biodiversity. Their roots also help improve soil structure and water infiltration. The process works as a cycle. Better water retention supports plant growth, while growing vegetation protects the soil and adds organic matter. Over time, these improvements can help degraded land recover its productive capacity. However, oasification must be adapted to local conditions. Rainfall, soil type, slope, and available water all influence which techniques will work. It is not a one-size-fits-all solution, but an approach that combines water management, soil protection, and vegetation recovery. Not all carbon added to the soil remains stored permanently. Some organic matter decomposes and releases CO2 back into the atmosphere. Projects must, therefore, measure net changes in carbon stocks over time. Oasification and Carbon Sequestration: How Restored Land Can Capture CO2 Beyond restoring degraded land, oasification could also contribute to climate change mitigation by increasing the amount of carbon stored in vegetation and soil. This is where the approach becomes particularly relevant to nature-based carbon removal and carbon markets. Plants absorb carbon dioxide (CO2) from the atmosphere through photosynthesis and store carbon in their trunks, branches, leaves, and roots. When oasification improves soil moisture and supports vegetation growth, it can create better conditions for increasing this natural carbon storage. As trees and other plants grow, they can accumulate more carbon in their biomass. Soil also plays an important role. Fallen leaves, dead roots, and other organic materials break down and add carbon to the soil. Greater vegetation cover can help protect this organic matter from erosion and support the long-term buildup of soil organic carbon. The scale of the opportunity is significant. The IPCC estimates that approximately 20–30 billion tonnes of carbon have been released into the atmosphere through desertification-related processes, including deforestation, overgrazing, and conventional tillage. This highlights the climate value of protecting and restoring degraded land. However, carbon storage does not happen immediately. Vegetation needs time to establish, while soil carbon gains can take years or even decades to become measurable. Results also depend on rainfall, soil conditions, plant species, and long-term land management. The IPCC identifies natural vegetation restoration and tree planting on degraded land as activities that can enrich carbon in topsoil and subsoil over time. It also recognizes that measures to combat desertification can support soil carbon sequestration. For oasification projects, this means carbon benefits could come from two main sources: - increased carbon in growing vegetation, and - additional organic carbon stored in the soil. artigo.texto: Setting ground rules: City of Irondale votes on data center regulations Irondale, Ala (WBMA) - Irondale City Council says it is setting the ground rules for possible future data center developments. Tuesday night, the City voted to adopt regulations for future data center project proposals. City Councilman Aaron Sims says he had been researching data centers for months, and used that information to draft the new ordinance. Under Irondale's new code, if a future data center required upgrades to the power grid, the developer would be fully responsible for funding the upgrades. The code also requires any future data center to use a 'closed loop' water system, that is designed to cut down on excessive water use. Irondale Mayor James D. Stewart, Jr., says as of now, there are no data center projects on the table for the city.

artigo.texto: Meta climática de 2040 da UE sob pressão por acordo no mercado de carbono Um documento vazado analisado pela Euronews indica que as reformas do Sistema de Comércio de Emissões da União Europeia, o EU ETS, poderiam enfraquecer a meta climática de 2040 do bloco. A Presidência irlandesa do Conselho da UE suavizou uma proposta que será discutida por embaixadores da UE na quarta-feira, em meio ao aumento da pressão política para conciliar as metas de emissões com a competitividade industrial e os altos custos de energia. O texto de compromisso busca garantir apoio político para o mercado de carbono após 2030, mas defensores do clima alertam que as concessões destinadas a proteger a indústria europeia podem reduzir a contribuição do sistema para a meta de 2040, deixando outros setores econômicos para cobrir a lacuna. Licenças gratuitas e planos de investimento O texto do Conselho mantém a proposta de julho da Comissão Europeia de desacelerar a redução das licenças de carbono, estender as permissões gratuitas para a indústria e trazer créditos de carbono internacionais para o mercado da UE, de modo que as emissões domésticas possam ser compensadas por meio de projetos no exterior. Segundo a proposta da Presidência irlandesa, as empresas industriais manteriam 80 por cento de suas licenças gratuitas se apresentarem um plano de investimento, mesmo que depois não realizem os investimentos de descarbonização propostos. Os 20 por cento restantes dependeriam do início da construção de projetos elegíveis. As licenças gratuitas são permissões que as empresas recebem sem comprá-las em leilão, concebidas para proteger os produtores da UE da concorrência em países com regras climáticas menos rigorosas, como a China e os Estados Unidos. A proposta representa uma concessão política significativa às indústrias preocupadas em perder essas licenças e levanta questões sobre se o ETS oferecerá incentivo suficiente para cortar emissões. Créditos internacionais e a meta de 2040 Sobre os créditos de carbono internacionais, o Conselho manteve a proposta da Comissão de reservar licenças equivalentes a 260 milhões de toneladas de CO2 para financiar sua compra. Também deixa em aberto uma possível fase-piloto entre 2031 e 2035 para testar o sistema antes da implementação plena. O Conselho manteve requisitos rigorosos de qualidade e integridade para os créditos internacionais, tornando a trajetória de redução do ETS cada vez mais dependente de sua disponibilidade. Se as indústrias não puderem comprá-los, a meta climática de 2040 poderá ser comprometida, já que ela exige pelo menos 85 por cento de redução líquida doméstica das emissões, com os créditos internacionais respondendo pelos 5 por cento restantes. Cronograma das negociações e divisões entre os Estados-membros A Presidência irlandesa busca consenso entre os 27 países da UE antes que as negociações avancem para questões politicamente mais sensíveis, como ambição climática e repartição de encargos. Ela espera fechar um acordo no Conselho de Meio Ambiente em 11 de dezembro, enquanto o Parlamento Europeu deve votar durante sua sessão plenária de 14 a 17 de dezembro em Estrasburgo. A presidência enfrenta uma batalha difícil diante das profundas divisões entre os Estados-membros e da complexidade das negociações. Segundo um segundo documento analisado pela Euronews, os países da UE já estão divididos sobre a velocidade com que a oferta de licenças de carbono deve encolher, se as empresas devem usar créditos internacionais para cumprir obrigações e até que ponto os setores industriais devem ser protegidos do aumento dos custos de carbono. Em conjunto, essas demandas correm o risco de diluir o ETS justamente quando se espera que ele impulse grande parte da próxima fase de cortes de emissões do bloco. Os governos em geral querem preservar o ETS como fonte de receita para a descarbonização, mas crescem as preocupações com os custos impostos a indústrias de uso intensivo de energia que competem com fabricantes na China ou nos Estados Unidos. Algumas capitais argumentam que o número de licenças deve cair para elevar o preço do carbono e incentivar o desinvestimento em combustíveis fósseis, enquanto outras temem o impacto da retirada das licenças gratuitas sobre indústrias em dificuldade. Uma redução mais lenta aliviaria a pressão sobre usinas e fábricas, potencialmente moderando os preços do carbono e dando às empresas mais tempo para se adaptar, mas também significaria menos cortes de emissões nos setores cobertos pelo ETS, tornando a meta de 2040 mais difícil de alcançar. Análise questiona compatibilidade da reforma Uma análise recente do Oko-Institut, encomendada pelo grupo ambientalista WWF Alemanha, alertou que a reforma do ETS proposta pela Comissão é incompatível com a meta da UE de cortar as emissões líquidas em 90 por cento até 2040. Lisa Okken, especialista em política industrial do WWF Alemanha, disse que a Comissão está optando por correr riscos na proteção climática em vez de resguardar o futuro da indústria europeia, e argumentou que a reforma proposta carece do sinal de preço do carbono necessário para impulsionar uma modernização urgente. Segundo ela, a lacuna está sendo preenchida com medidas contábeis complicadas e flexibilidade excessiva. Ambientalistas também manifestaram preocupação com uma proposta que permitiria emissões adicionais além do teto existente em troca de futuras remoções permanentes de carbono por meio de tecnologias caras destinadas a capturar CO2 do ar. O estudo observou que ainda não está claro se tais remoções podem ser entregues na escala necessária, já que a capacidade necessária não existe hoje.

artigo.texto: Moratorium? Tax break? Colorado cities face data center policy choices As data centers continue to pop up across Colorado, municipalities are facing a difficult choice: weighing the economic benefits against growing concerns from the communities they serve. While some municipalities are passing moratoriums on data centers, Douglas County leaders recently granted a $19 million tax break in business personal property taxes to a new Flexential data center that's under construction in Parker. That data center is set to open next year. Across Colorado, community members have been saying no to data centers. "A lot of people feel very blindsided about the data centers popping up, and so they don't feel heard, which I understand, and I understand their disappointment," one Douglas County resident said in a recent meeting. "We needed this moratorium, and you all failed us, and you failed yourselves," an Aurora resident said in another meeting. Residents have shared worries about water, electricity, noise and pollution. "I'm scared for the water, scared for the pollution, scared for my air, my quality of life. The noise that this data center might create- that's why I'm so disappointed in this," one Colorado resident recently said. But one CEO in the rapidly growing industry says data centers are a necessity in modern life. Flexential's CEO and a public policy expert weighed in on the heated debate surrounding them. "Your connected life can't happen without a data center," said Ryan Mallory, CEO of Flexential. "All of the social media apps that you're using run through our sites, as well as a lot of the streaming services that everybody's using at home." Headquartered in Denver, Flexential has data centers across the country. Its fifth Colorado center is in development in Parker. "This is an industrial shell that has power and cooling that customers can then put their own IT infrastructure into," Mallory said. While Mallory says AI-focused customers only make up 11% of Flexential's centers, he says AI data centers are fueling the U.S.'s economic growth right now. "The GDP in the United States is growing about 3%, 3.5%. That's fueled primarily by AI infrastructure data centers," Mallory said. But with communities mobilizing against them, how should local leaders respond? "It's a lot of hard and fast feelings," said Billy Wynn, the lead author of a recent report on data centers, prepared by the Romer Institute of Evidence-Based Policy for the city of Colorado Springs. "It's a very nascent and kind of burgeoning issue," Wynne said. The report recommends municipalities handle data center applications with transparency, invite the public to participate and develop standard rules and processes. "Do it in a transparent way, develop policies that are broadly applicable, not case by case, ad hoc negotiations. Give the public a bona fide opportunity to express their interests, concerns, questions," Wynne said. "[We] really want to be treating different facilities as similarly as much as possible." It also recommends clarifying evidence-based standards around water and energy use. Mallory says Flexential uses an efficient closed-loop system rather than evaporative cooling. "Our site in Parker will use the same amount of water as about six homes," Mallory said. He says data centers bring tax revenue that can be beneficial for communities. Wynne says there are a lot of unknowns in the rapidly changing space, and evidence should guide communities weighing data centers. "Let's do our best to look at the facts, and then have a more informed debate about it," Wynne said. Flexential's CEO also spoke on the impact of the recent election on data center buildout after the stock market plummeted following the midterms. While Mallory attributes that to standard volatility, he does think that Democratic lawmakers could slow data center permitting and buildout. "At the end of the day, the people that lose out isn't going to be Flexential. It's going to be the communities that we serve," Mallory said.

artigo.texto: BYD’s next-generation Han will offer up to 875 km of CLTC range (approximately 718 km WLTP estimated), while its most powerful electric version delivers 520 kW (697 hp). The new sedan is expected to debut at the Guangzhou Auto Show on November 27. It arrives as October domestic deliveries of the outgoing Han fell 68.9% year-on-year to 2,236 units. Three electric versions and a 400 km PHEV The new Han EV comes in three versions, with outputs ranging from 245 kW (329 hp) to 520 kW (697 hp). All three EV versions use LFP Blade batteries supplied by BYD’s FinDreams subsidiary. The entry-level rear-wheel-drive version has a 76.744 kWh battery and a 245 kW (329 hp) rear motor. It delivers 775 km of CLTC range (approximately 635 km WLTP estimated). The Long-Range RWD increases battery capacity to 88.682 kWh and motor output to 300 kW (402 hp), taking the claimed range to 875 km CLTC (approximately 718 km WLTP estimated), according to iFeng. At the top of the range, the Performance AWD uses the same 88.682 kWh battery but adds a 200 kW (268 hp) front motor to the 320 kW (429 hp) rear unit. Combined output reaches 520 kW (697 hp), with a CLTC range of 730 km (approximately 599 km WLTP estimated). It weighs 2,351 kg and has a listed top speed of 270 km/h, compared with 240 km/h for both RWD versions. The Han DM-i plug-in hybrid pairs a 1.5-litre turbocharged engine with a 200 kW (268 hp) electric motor. The engine produces 115 kW (154 hp) maximum power, or 110 kW (148 hp) maximum net power. A 45.36 kWh LFP battery provides 300 km of WLTC or 400 km of CLTC electric range (approximately 328 km WLTP estimated). Listed fuel consumption with the battery depleted is 4.6 L/100 km. The DM-i weighs 2,115 kg and has a top speed of 200 km/h. Chinese media also report that the new Han supports BYD Flash Charging. Compatible vehicles are claimed to charge from 10% to 97% in nine minutes. Larger body and redesigned exterior The new Han is 5,156 mm long and 1,969 mm wide, with a 3,030 mm wheelbase. That makes it 161 mm longer and 59 mm wider than the outgoing car, with 110 mm more between the axles. Depending on the version, height is either 1,507 mm or 1,492 mm. It is also longer than the 5,050 mm Han L, although the 5,256 mm BYD Da Han remains larger. Uncamouflaged photographs show a revised front end, led by a horizontal light bar, illuminated star-diamond elements and a Han emblem on the hood. Recessed door handles and multi-spoke wheels measuring 18, 19 or 20 inches feature along the sides, while the rear retains its full-width Chinese knot-style light bar. Roof-mounted LiDAR is standard on the 300 kW and 520 kW versions and optional on the entry-level EV and DM-i. It supports BYD’s God’s Eye B (DiPilot) driver-assistance system. Inside, photos show a floating central touchscreen, a digital instrument display, a column-mounted gear selector and two 50W wireless charging pads. Sales decline puts pressure on the replacement The Han’s domestic deliveries fell 47.6% year-on-year to 119,821 units in 2025, down from a peak of 274,016 in 2022, according to China EV DataTracker. In October, its 2,236 deliveries represented 1.1% of BYD’s domestic volume. The Xiaomi SU7 sold 12,954 units that month, while the Xpeng P7+ managed 2,247, just 11 more than the Han. BYD has not announced pricing for the new model. The outgoing Han starts at 168,800 yuan (23,700 USD).

artigo.texto: Beril Canakci 19 November 2026•Update: 19 November 2026 Carbon emissions linked to the world’s data centers are projected to rise 70% by 2030 as growing demand for artificial intelligence (AI) drives electricity consumption higher, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said Thursday. In its annual World Energy Outlook 2026 report, the Paris-based agency projected that global electricity consumption by data centers would double to about 1,000 terawatt-hours by 2030, with AI accounting for much of the increase. Data centers, which house the computer servers used to run AI systems and other digital services, require large amounts of electricity to operate and keep equipment cool. The expansion is expected to increase demand for electricity generated from fossil fuels, particularly in the United States and China, contributing to higher carbon emissions. The IEA projected that natural gas would supply about 60% of electricity used by US data centers by 2030, while coal would account for roughly half of the power consumed by China’s AI data centers. In the European Union, renewable energy is expected to provide about 70% of data center electricity needs by the end of the decade. The agency also warned that rapid growth in electricity demand from AI infrastructure was putting additional pressure on power grids and equipment supply chains, highlighting the need for investment in electricity networks.

artigo.texto: Massive data center proposal faces pushback from Stafford County residents STAFFORD COUNTY, Va. - A massive data center development is putting Stafford County in the spotlight as the proposal goes before the Planning Commission for a vote. What we know: The proposed development, which spans four projects along the Kings Highway corridor near the Rappahannock River, consists of 37 facilities and 14 electrical substations. The scale of the project is larger than 1,000 football fields placed side by side. Stafford County Data Center Proposal More than 100 people signed up to speak when the proposal was introduced to the Planning Commission. While some attendees expressed support for the development, the proposal is already facing significant pushback from residents, with opponents calling it an absolute outrage. Critics argue the development could significantly alter the area and negatively impact local farmland, the Rappahannock River and the historic surroundings near Ferry Farm, George Washington's childhood home. Residents have also raised concerns about construction and its potential impact on the region's water supply. In response, developers told the Planning Commission they are committed to working with the community. They say that if all four projects are approved, the development could generate more than $268 million in revenue by 2036 and create nearly 1,200 jobs. Developers also said habitat rehabilitation along the Oak Creek shoreline and wetland restoration along the Rappahannock River would be prioritized. What's next: If the Planning Commission ultimately recommends approval of the projects, the proposal will still require final approval from Stafford County's Board of Supervisors. The Source: Information in this article is from a Stafford County Planning Meeting and original FOX 5 DC reporting.

artigo.texto: Our Next Energy Inc. (ONE), a Novi-based U.S. energy storage technology company and battery manufacturer, has signed an agreement with New York’s Wen Acquisition Corp. to take ONE public and trade on the Nasdaq Stock Market under the ticker symbol ONEE. “Over the last five years, LFP (lithium iron phosphate) has grown from roughly 20 percent to 60 percent of the global battery market, yet China produces approximately 99 percent of the world’s LFP cells,” says Mujeeb Ijaz, founder and CEO of ONE. “We built ONE to close that gap with a secure American and allied supply chain. “We believe our combination with Wen will give us a public platform to scale ONE into this $40 billion addressable market with access to growth capital as we scale our operations to meet rising demand.” Most LFP cells made in America today come from foreign-owned factories or rely on licensed Chinese technology. ONE uses its own domestic technology, from electrode active materials through fully integrated energy storage systems. Two recent federal actions make that distinction matter, according to ONE. The FY2026 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) extends battery restrictions to cells and components produced by a foreign entity of concern (FEOC) or under FEOC technology licenses. Executive Order 14421, signed in August 2026, restricts battery energy storage systems and other grid equipment tied to covered foreign entities from the U.S. bulk-power system. ONE says it’s well positioned to meet this moment. It makes its cells in Van Buren Township and integrates them in Novi with its own battery management systems (BMS) into packs and containerized energy storage systems for defense, rail, and grid customers that require safety, durability, and a secure domestic supply chain. “ONE has done the hard part of building an American LFP cell and pack business, with factories operating and customers in markets that increasingly require domestic supply,” says Julian Sevillano, CEO of Wen. “With two operating factories, binding customer contracts, and federal policy appearing to move its way, ONE is positioned to lead the reshoring of critical battery manufacturing in the United States.” The boards of directors of both Wen and ONE have approved the proposed transaction, which is expected to close in the first half of 2027, subject to approval by Wen’s shareholders and ONE’s stockholders and the satisfaction of other customary closing conditions, including Wen’s registration statement on Form S-4 being declared effective by the Securities and Exchange Commission, the expiration or termination of the waiting period under the Hart-Scott-Rodino Antitrust Improvements Act of 1976, as amended (HSR Act) and the satisfaction or waiver of a minimum cash condition. Additional information about the proposed transaction, including a copy of the business combination agreement, will be provided in a Current Report on Form 8-K to be filed by Wen with the SEC and available at sec.gov. For more information about ONE, visit one.ai.
