artigo.texto: Low Carbon says new UK BESS projects 'demonstrate clear benefits' of co-location with solar PV The 30MW Birch BESS and 35MW Sandon Brook BESS represent the first battery storage projects the company has brought into commercial operation in the UK. UK renewables investment and asset management company Low Carbon has energised two battery energy storage systems (BESS) in Essex with a combined 65MW capacity. The 30MW Birch BESS and 35MW Sandon Brook BESS represent the first battery storage projects the company has brought into commercial operation in the UK. The projects are both co-located with operational solar PV plants owned by Low Carbon. The Birch project shares a 132kV grid connection with the 39MW Birch Solar Farm and 49.9MW Layer Solar Farm, while Sandon Brook has its own connection but is located alongside the 49.9MW solar plant of the same name. Both solar plants secured Contracts for Difference (CfDs) in allocation round 5 (AR5) and are covered by long-term route-to-market (RTM) power purchase agreements (PPAs). Low Carbon said that there is “increasing emphasis” on making smarter use of existing grid capacity and that battery storage is “playing a crucial role supporting market dynamics and enabling more renewable generation to come online”. The company’s managing director of portfolio management, Steven Hughes, said: “Birch and Sandon Brook demonstrate the clear benefits of battery co-location, which is a key part of our business model as we continue to grow our portfolio of operational battery assets across the UK and Europe.” While the two projects are Low Carbon’s first to enter commercial operations, co-located BESS assets feature in many of its plans. That includes its Beacon Fen Energy Park, which was consented by the government in August, which will pair 400MW of solar PV with up to 600MW of batteries.

artigo.texto: Tuesday, November 17th 2026 U.S. Cracks Down on China Renting AI GPUs Through Overseas Data Centers Yesterday, the U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) released an interim final rule to address remote access to advanced AI chips and servers. This rule significantly addresses a long-standing gap in U.S. export controls, where Chinese companies that are barred from accessing NVIDIA's latest GPUs have been renting overseas computing power instead of purchasing the chips outright. Notably, BIS states that the rule was written by and at the direction of the Department of the Treasury and the National Security Council. Under the new rule, a license is required to ship any advanced accelerators to any data center worldwide that provides more than 12 million "aggregate TPP" of computing power to companies headquartered in Macau or Country Group D:5, which includes China. TPP, or Total Processing Performance, is BIS's metric for chip computing power, calculated as a chip's peak dense throughput multiplied by the bit length of the operation. For example, an H100 rates about 15,800 TPP. "Aggregate TPP" sums up every accelerator in the facility, so the cap equates to roughly 750 H100s or around 330 B200s. The limit also applies to "linked data centers" and indirect access, such as a cloud reseller training models for a Chinese firm. Data centers already serving such customers have 90 days to obtain a license. Only "commercial recommender systems" are exempt, and anything that generates text, images, video, or code does not qualify.The rule also requires a license for advanced AI chips shipped to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil, which the Commerce Department says carry a higher-than-normal risk of diversion. Shipments to U.S.-headquartered companies are exempt if they meet new reporting requirements. Foundries and packaging houses also lose some of the methods to clear advanced-node chips for designers in restricted countries. Finally, the rule formally rescinds the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule, eliminating its country tiers, the Data Center VEU program, and model-weight controls. Reflecting the current trends and the times under the U.S. administration led by Donald Trump, the document uses "Super Intelligence" instead of "AI," citing Executive Order 14434. Source: BIS

artigo.texto: Abeeólica vai à justiça para suspender leilão de sistemas de baterias Associação argumenta que os certames não deveriam ocorrer antes da definição das regras de cobrança e questiona a legalidade da proposta da Aneel de estabelecer pesos diferentes para cada tipo de fonte A Abeeólica (Associação Brasileira de Energia Eólica e Novas Tecnologias) entrou na Justiça Federal contra as regras propostas pela Aneel (Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica) para dividir entre os geradores os custos da contratação dos sistemas de baterias. A entidade pede a suspensão dos dois leilões de reserva de capacidade previstos para dezembro e contesta tanto a atribuição dos encargos aos geradores quanto a metodologia de rateio em discussão na agência reguladora. A ação civil pública foi protocolada nesta segunda-feira (16) na 17ª Vara Federal Cível do Distrito Federal. A associação argumenta que os certames não deveriam ocorrer antes da definição das regras de cobrança e questiona a legalidade da proposta da Aneel de estabelecer pesos diferentes para cada tipo de fonte de geração. Os leilões estão marcados para os dias 2 e 4 de dezembro. A Abeeólica pede uma decisão liminar para suspender os procedimentos, incluindo as etapas de adjudicação, homologação e assinatura dos contratos. Até o momento do ajuizamento, a metodologia de rateio ainda não havia sido regulamentada. A entidade sustenta que a contratação de baterias atende à segurança e à confiabilidade do sistema elétrico, benefícios que alcançam os consumidores finais. Por isso, considera inadequado transferir exclusivamente aos geradores a conta de um serviço destinado a garantir o fornecimento de energia em momentos de maior demanda. A contestação tem duas frentes. A principal questiona a própria regra legal que atribuiu aos geradores o pagamento dos custos das baterias. Subsidiariamente, a associação pede que os leilões não sejam realizados com o modelo de rateio diferenciado por flexibilidade das fontes proposto pela Aneel. O primeiro leilão de baterias Os dois certames de dezembro serão os primeiros leilões de reserva de capacidade do país voltados especificamente à contratação de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias. A iniciativa busca ampliar a capacidade do sistema elétrico de responder a momentos de maior demanda e oferecer maior flexibilidade à operação. Os contratos terão duração de 15 anos, com início previsto para agosto de 2028. Os empreendimentos deverão disponibilizar potência por pelo menos quatro horas consecutivas, com possibilidade de até dois ciclos diários de operação. A remuneração será baseada na disponibilidade dos sistemas. A realização dos leilões ocorre em meio à expansão das fontes renováveis na matriz elétrica brasileira. A geração eólica e solar, por depender das condições climáticas, pode variar ao longo do dia. As baterias permitem armazenar energia em períodos de maior oferta e devolvê-la ao sistema quando necessário, contribuindo para reduzir a necessidade de cortes na geração renovável e reforçar a segurança do abastecimento. A estrutura dos certames foi dividida em duas etapas. O leilão de 2 de dezembro será destinado a projetos que atendam aos requisitos mínimos de conteúdo nacional estabelecidos pelo BNDES (Banco Nacional de Desenvolvimento Econômico e Social). O segundo, marcado para 4 de dezembro, contemplará os demais sistemas de armazenamento. A disputa sobre quem paga a conta O ponto central da controvérsia está na mudança promovida pela Lei 15.269, de 2025. A legislação alterou a Lei 10.848, de 2004, e estabeleceu que, no caso de sistemas de armazenamento por baterias, os custos da contratação de reserva de capacidade serão rateados exclusivamente entre os geradores de energia, conforme regulamentação da Aneel. A regra criou uma exceção ao modelo geral de custeio da reserva de capacidade. Nas demais modalidades, os encargos são distribuídos entre os usuários finais de energia elétrica. A Abeeólica argumenta que as baterias têm a mesma finalidade sistêmica de outras formas de contratação de potência e que, portanto, seus custos deveriam seguir a lógica geral. Na avaliação da associação, a mudança transfere aos geradores a despesa de um serviço cuja principal finalidade é beneficiar consumidores residenciais, comerciais e industriais. A entidade também sustenta que a regra pode afetar a competitividade das empresas e criar distorções entre diferentes tecnologias de geração. A ação cita estimativas do TCU (Tribunal de Contas da União) segundo as quais os contratos dos leilões podem movimentar entre R$ 108 bilhões e R$ 153 bilhões ao longo de sua duração. A petição também calcula que, considerando a contratação de 5 gigawatts e o preço-teto de R$ 1,76 milhão por megawatt ao ano, o encargo poderia alcançar R$ 17 por megawatt-hora. O rateio por flexibilidade Além de questionar a atribuição dos custos aos geradores, a Abeeólica contesta a metodologia apresentada pela Aneel na Consulta Pública 37/2026. A proposta estabelece pesos diferentes para a participação de cada fonte no pagamento do encargo, de acordo com critérios de flexibilidade operacional. Os percentuais em discussão variam de 25% a 100%. Na prática, fontes consideradas menos flexíveis teriam participação maior no rateio, enquanto aquelas com maior capacidade de ajustar a geração ao longo do tempo arcariam com uma parcela menor.

artigo.texto: Havells India lança sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias na REI Expo 2026 A Havells India apresentou seus sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias na REI Expo 2026, segundo a pv magazine, posicionando o armazenamento dentro de um portfólio mais amplo de energias renováveis que também abrange inversores híbridos, carregadores de veículos elétricos, inversores solares e módulos. A empresa criou uma unidade de negócios dedicada a renováveis em abril para ampliar sua presença no setor. Reshu Madan, presidente e chefe de unidade de negócios da Havells, indicou que a primeira prioridade da empresa são os segmentos residencial e comercial e industrial, com expansão posterior planejada para aplicações em escala de utilidade e agrícolas. A Havells firmou parceria com a norueguesa Pixii para levar à Índia soluções modulares de armazenamento em baterias com controles definidos por software. A linha inicial atenderá aplicações de 3 kW a 125 kW, com sistemas maiores na sequência. A empresa também pretende oferecer pacotes integrados de solar com armazenamento para clientes residenciais, comerciais e institucionais. O portfólio modular incluirá a família PowerShaper, com o PowerShaper XLP nas capacidades de 112 kW e 225 kW, e a família PowerNode, a partir de 125 kW para uso comercial e industrial de maior porte. Aseem Goyal, chefe de unidade de negócios de Renováveis da Havells India Ltd, explicou que o design modular permite adicionar ou substituir unidades individuais com o sistema em operação, de modo que os clientes dimensionem a capacidade de armazenamento conforme suas necessidades, sem subdimensionar nem superdimensionar. A parceria com a Pixii tem o objetivo de levar a tecnologia aos clientes indianos a custos competitivos, aproveitando a rede de distribuição e a base de instaladores da Havells. A Havells também planeja uma futura família de produtos, a MegaNode, voltada ao armazenamento em escala de utilidade. A empresa continua vendo espaço para armazenamento off-grid e em microrredes em áreas remotas, mesmo com a expansão da conectividade à rede. Goyal observou que os mercados off-grid estão encolhendo gradualmente após os esforços do governo para levar eletricidade a todo o país, mas bolsões em estados como Uttar Pradesh e Bihar, além de localidades remotas, ainda apresentam oportunidades. As operações de mineração são outro mercado potencial. No segmento solar, a Havells oferece módulos monocristalinos PERC bifaciais e TOPCon, com produtos TOPCon classificados em até 620 Wp. A empresa fabrica alguns modelos de inversores conectados à rede na Índia e importa unidades de maior capacidade. A Havells também é investidora estratégica da Goldi Solar, que tem 16 GW de capacidade de fabricação de módulos e está entrando na produção de células solares. Goyal descreveu o arranjo como a combinação da força de fabricação da Goldi no mercado de IPP com o alcance de distribuição da Havells. A Havells fabrica e vende módulos não DCR com sua própria marca e espera obter em breve a aprovação na ALMM List-II para seus módulos DCR. A empresa está localizando sua cadeia de suprimentos de armazenamento em baterias em torno de eletrônica de potência, baterias, software e sistemas de rack. Ela começou a localizar o software de gestão de energia e trabalha na localização de racks, com a fabricação local de baterias prevista para começar em breve. A Havells pretende ir além de produtos individuais e avançar para soluções integradas. Madan disse que o objetivo é conquistar a confiança do cliente e melhorar a experiência do consumidor por meio de uma solução completa, e não apenas do produto. A empresa espera se tornar um player relevante em energias renováveis nos próximos três a quatro anos. A confiabilidade dos produtos, as garantias e o suporte pós-venda continuam centrais, com garantia de 10 anos nos inversores, ante as ofertas típicas do setor de seis a oito anos, e garantia mínima de 10 anos nos produtos de armazenamento em baterias, que pode ser estendida por cinco anos. Este relatório fornece uma análise aprofundada do mercado de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias em escala de rede na Índia, cobrindo tamanho de mercado, crescimento, demanda, oferta, fluxos comerciais, preços, cenário competitivo e previsões até 2035. O estudo é projetado para fabricantes, distribuidores, importadores, exportadores, investidores, equipes de compras, consultores e equipes de estratégia que precisam de uma visão consistente e orientada por dados da dinâmica do mercado e de uma definição analítica transparente do escopo do produto. Cobertura do Produto Os Sistemas de Armazenamento de Energia em Baterias em Escala de Rede são grandes instalações estacionárias de armazenamento eletroquímico de energia projetadas para armazenar e descarregar eletricidade no nível de utilidade, transmissão ou distribuição. O escopo abrange sistemas completos turnkey que compreendem racks de baterias, sistemas de conversão de potência, gerenciamento térmico, controles e balance of plant, bem como invólucros containerizados ou construídos para esse fim, classificados tipicamente de vários megawatts a centenas de megawatts e capazes de fornecer serviços de rede, como regulação de frequência, firmeza de capacidade, integração de renováveis e corte de picos. Incluídos - Sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias de íons de lítio em escala de rede - Sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias containerizados - Sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias em edifícios construídos para esse fim - Projetos turnkey de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias - Sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias com conversão de potência integrada - Sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias de propriedade de concessionárias - Sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias conectados à rede para serviços auxiliares Excluídos - Armazenamento de baterias comerciais e industriais atrás do medidor - S

artigo.texto: Two City Council members want to place a one-year moratorium on development of data centers in Jacksonville, according to legislation set to appear before Council. The ordinance, which is scheduled for formal introduction on Nov. 22, would create a task force to analyze regulation of data center development. Introduced by Council members Jimmy Peluso and Moné Holder, the legislation states that allowing development of data centers “to proceed without appropriate regulatory standards could create risks to the City’s water resources, electrical infrastructure capacity, land use planning objectives, and long-term community development strategy.” The legislation would also create a task force to study the effects of data centers in Jacksonville. That group would be composed of, at a minimum, the city’s Office of Economic Development, Department of Public Works, Environmental Quality Division and Planning Department. Those effects would include water supply and wastewater treatment capacity, electrical grid capacity and infrastructure requirements, land use compatibility, community impacts, other environmental considerations and best practices adopted by other Florida municipalities. The legislation allows for data centers already operating in Duval County to continue to do so. There are currently six operating in Jacksonville, according to a JEA spokesperson. “JEA does not currently have the electric and water capacity to serve a hyper-scale data center. Hyper-scale data centers run 24/7 with 80 percent or higher load factor and demand 100-500 megawatt (MW) of power. There are not any hyperscale facilities in Jacksonville,” JEA spokesperson Karen McAllister wrote in an email. “We do have six small-scale data centers in Jacksonville. They require less than 5 megawatts of power and do not necessitate major upgrades. Hyper-scale is about 100-500 MW of demand. For perspective, 500 MW equates to energy usage by 280,000 homes. In comparison, a small-scale data center (assuming 5 megawatts) uses as much energy as 2,800 homes.” Phil Perry, chief communications officer for the city of Jacksonville, said the city administration had “concerns about energy and water resources, and our citizens are concerned about their costs. Additionally, JEA has been clear that currently their electric grid cannot support a hyper-scale data center.” Perry said the administration was preparing to review the legislation. In October, Daily Record news partner News4Jax found that several companies had contacted JEA with inquiries about data center build-out. Those requests ranged in demand for power from 10 MW to 1,248 MW. According to News4Jax, a steel company places the largest demand on JEA, drawing a peak of nearly 64 megawatts for its plant’s furnace, plus an additional 18 megawatts for other portions of the facility. JEA also cannot service many of the largest data center requests, News4Jax reported. “Each of these sites would need their own dedicated substation or potentially multiple substations in order for JEA to serve them,” JEA’s interim Chief Administrative Officer Jordan Pope told News4Jax. “With supply chain constraints being a concern, especially because of the growth of data centers, long lead items such as substation transformers can take years to acquire and then install.” The proposal from Peluso and Holder comes as news analysts attributed much of the results of the November U.S. midterms to a “data center revolt.” A Nov. 6 story by the BBC said polling “found 56% of surveyed voters said data centres were a ‘crucial or major’ factor in their vote, while 76% said they would oppose the construction of a new data centre in their community.” “Americans in a variety of demographic and partisan subgroups have become more negative in their views of data centers,” the Pew Research Center wrote in a story about its own data center polling. “Men and women alike, as well as adults across age groups and education levels, have become more likely since January to say data centers have a mostly bad impact on the things we asked about.” Proponents of data centers say development of the projects can benefit communities by expanding their tax base, creating jobs and providing infrastructure investment. In a July story, Forbes pointed to Virginia’s Loudoun County as an example of the beneficial impact of data centers to communities. According to Forbes, the county hosts more than 230 data centers, representing approximately 56.5 million square feet that were fully built or under construction at the time of the story. Forbes reported that than 17,000 direct and indirect jobs related to the projects had been created within the county, including in specialized trades, technology, professional services and security. Kerri Stewart, chief administration officer for Miller Electric Co. and a member of the Florida Digital Infrastructure and Security Alliance, said she had no concerns about the moratorium as of its introduction. “This legislation contemplates a task force that allows for thoughtful consideration about community concerns,” she said in a text message. Speaking as a FDISA board member, she said she hoped the city “truly intends to become educated on the impacts — good and bad — that could arise with/without clear regulations that address the public’s hopes for positive economic impact and concerns about strains on the grid and watershed.” "As an executive at Miller Electric, we hope that we will be able to share our experiences building data centers of all sizes around the Southeastern US. artigo.texto: Chesterfield supervisors approve battery energy storage facility CHESTERFIELD, Va. (WWBT) - The Chesterfield County Board of Supervisors on Wednesday approved a proposal to build a 100-megawatt battery energy storage facility off Watkins Centre Parkway. “I think this is going to add to the capacities that we are going to need,” Supervisor Kevin Carroll said. The Munster Battery Energy Storage Facility will store electricity to be used later when demand is high. “It helps keep the lines at more of a constant line, voltage, instead of real highs and lows and that helps in a lot of ways for a lot of reasons,” Supervisor Jim Ingle said. The newly approved facility will be next to another battery energy storage facility. The two facilities will share an electrical substation. Renewable energy sources, such as solar and wind, fluctuate. Battery storage helps make sure none of the energy produced goes to waste. A handful of people spoke during public comment. Multiple speakers pointed to the benefits of the project. “It will actually reduce our electric bills over time and also clean our air,” one man said. Concern was also raised that the extra energy will go to the growing number of data centers being built in the county instead of the people who live there. “Our water, our air, our electricity is meant to be for people, and it’s important that we are prioritizing that,” Billy Davies of the Sierra Club said. Chesterfield currently has nine data center projects. All but two have been approved. Project Loch, one of Google’s sites, is planned to go right by the newly-approved battery energy storage facility. In response to the data center comments, Board of Supervisors Chair Mark Miller pointed to the energy expected to come from the fusion power plant, which should be running by the early 2030s. “I know that I would’ve never approved data center unless we knew that we were having another form of energy coming here. And I believe in fusion,” Miller said. Copyright 2026 WWBT. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: (KNSI) – Residents filled St. Cloud City Hall Monday night to oppose data centers. By the end of the night, the city council had turned down rules meant to control where data centers could go and how they’d operate, and started work on a one-year moratorium instead. Over a meeting that ran about five hours, 23 people spoke against allowing data centers in the city. No one spoke in favor. Pipefitters Local 539 sent letters supporting responsible data center development. Council member Mark Johnson voted against the city’s proposed policy and in favor of the moratorium. He told KNSI News what he heard from people that made him want to slow down. “I think there’s a lot of things we don’t know. How much water is it going to use? How much electricity? Is our electric bill going to go up? Is it going to be too noisy?” Right now, the city has no rules written specifically for data centers. Staff drafted two changes to fix that before any developer came forward, and the council voted on both. Community Development Director Matt Glaesman said no data center company has brought a serious proposal to the city. He added that the city has not signed any nondisclosure agreements with data center developers and won’t sign any, in the name of transparency. The first vote was on a policy statement for the city’s comprehensive plan, the long-range guide for how St. Cloud grows. It would have set limits on where data centers could locate, keeping them away from neighborhoods and requiring the city to address noise, strain on public resources and the environment. It also recognized data centers as part of the local economy and tax base. The vote was 4-3 in favor, but changing the comprehensive plan takes a two-thirds vote, so it failed. Scott Brodeen, Dave Masters, Council President Mike Conway and Tami Calhoun voted yes. Hudda Ibrahim, Karen Larson and Johnson voted no. Before that vote, Larson tried to replace the policy with a public hearing on a one-year moratorium. That failed 3-4 with herself, Ibrahim and Johnson in favor. The second vote was on the zoning rules themselves. Small data centers would have been allowed in downtown, highway commercial and industrial areas. Large hyperscale facilities would have needed a special permit, could only go in one industrial district and would have had to stay at least a quarter mile from homes. Every project would have had to turn in studies on noise, environmental impact and community impact, along with a plan for shutting the site down. Larson moved to swap those rules out for a one-year moratorium on data centers and communication facilities. Calhoun joined Larson, Johnson and Ibrahim, and that motion passed 4-3. Brodeen, Masters and Conway voted no. Conway said people focus too much on the biggest hyperscale data centers without realizing there are several sizes, and the city would handle each one differently. He wanted the council to act Monday night. “So I’m a little disappointed with that we’re gonna kick the can down the road a little bit farther. I’d like to have seen us put some guardrails in with this meeting.” Johnson said the moratorium isn’t necessarily a permanent no. “It buys us time to be able to do more research, be better prepared, if we do come to a place where we decide that we do want data centers, I just want us to be as well-prepared as we can.” St. Cloud resident Mike Sjogren spoke several times during the meeting in favor of a moratorium. He said no data center would ever be built near his home because there isn’t enough land there, even for a small one. His worry is for other parts of the city. “I am concerned how it’s going to affect the people of St. Cloud, either in commercial zones, you know, next to schools or close to schools, or commercial zones that are close to neighborhoods.” Sjogren said he hopes a pause will give Minnesota lawmakers time to set statewide guidelines. He isn’t sure the moratorium will survive the final vote. “Seeing the different sides that the city council people took, I just don’t know what’s going to happen with the same city council come December.” The moratorium ordinance will be introduced on December 7th. A public hearing and a possible final vote are set for December 21st. ___ Copyright © 2026 Leighton Media. All rights reserved. artigo.texto: University of Dubuque forum explores benefits, risks of AI and data centers DUBUQUE, Iowa — The University of Dubuque hosted a public forum Tuesday night to explore the potential benefits and drawbacks of artificial intelligence and data centers, giving community members an opportunity to learn about the technology and ask questions. Students spent the semester researching data centers from several perspectives, including their potential impact on water use, energy demand, land use and the environment, as well as ethical and public policy concerns. Donovan Tann, an English professor at the University of Dubuque, said the forum was designed to challenge the idea that technological changes are inevitable and demonstrate that communities have choices about how those changes affect them. In a statement to Iowa's News Now following the event, Tann emphasized that he does not believe technological change is inevitable. “I said that the event is designed to respond to people who say ‘this is inevitable’ and that instead, we show the options available to communities,” Tann said. Tate Glaspie, who examined the potential environmental impacts of data centers, said communities must weigh the benefits of the technology against its potential consequences. “It could be a huge beneficial thing to overall improve the quality of life. But the main concern that I know for people is, are we sacrificing a huge aspect of our quality of life in order to basically make our life simpler and, you know, more convenient,” Glaspie said. Several academic divisions across the university collaborated on the event, including aviation and flight, computing and applied technology, humanities, natural sciences and theology. In addition to student research presentations, the forum featured a 90-minute panel discussion and question-and-answer session with three journalists from across the region. The panelists included Dubuque-based freelance journalist Benjamin Fisher, Wisconsin Watch reporter Tom Kertscher and The Gazette's Linn County local government reporter Grace Nieland. The forum aimed to help community members better understand the technology and make informed decisions about data center development. “It is more of a moral obligation that we take into account all factors that could potentially harm our quality of life in order to make sophisticated and educated decisions,” Glaspie said.

artigo.texto: Appear Inc Begins Pre Production of Solid-State Battery, Targets Mid-2027 Launch Field trials complete across motorcycles, e-bikes and scooters. Pre-production underway. Limited production on track for mid-2027, with full-scale production in 2028. SAN FRANCISCO, Nov. 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — Appear Inc., a San Francisco-based developer of next-generation solid-state battery technology, today announced that it has moved from proving its technology to producing it. The company has completed field trials on three types of electric vehicle: motorcycles, e-bikes and scooters. It has also completed advanced manufacturing trials and started pre-production manufacturing with a manufacturing partner. Alongside this technical progress, Appear has added new distributors and strategic partners in selective established and emerging markets. The company remains on track to begin limited commercial production in mid-2027, followed by full-scale production in 2028. The technology Most electric vehicles today run on lithium-ion batteries, which use a liquid electrolyte to move charge between the electrodes. Solid-state batteries replace that liquid with a solid material. This is widely seen as a path to safer batteries, with no flammable liquid to leak or ignite, and to more energy in a smaller, lighter cell. Appear’s solid-state technology is built around three priorities: safety, performance and manufacturability. For motorcycles, e-bikes and scooters, where weight, range and safety matter on every ride, that combination is especially valuable. From the lab to the production line Following its advanced manufacturing trials, Appear has moved into pre-production with its manufacturing partner and is refining its processes for volume manufacturing. Building a route to market New distributors and strategic partners in selective established and emerging markets are expected to give Appear regional market access and distribution channels at launch. Partner details remain confidential. Prashant Rurs, Founder & CEO of Appear Inc, said: We are moving beyond development and validation and into commercialization, “We remain on track to begin limited production in mid-2027 and to scale up to full production in 2028.” READ the latest Batteries News shaping the battery market Appear Inc Begins Pre Production of Solid-State Battery, Targets Mid-2027 Launch, source

artigo.texto: Canadian EV battery re-engineering company Moment Energy has launched a new battery energy storage system (BESS) called Nova. Nova is the first BESS made from repurposed electric vehicle batteries that achieves UL 1973 and UL 9540 safety certifications from US testing and certification company UL Solutions. Nova has also been tested to the UL 9540A standards for the evaluation of thermal runaway, Moment Energy says. Jeff Smidt, senior vice president of testing, inspection and certification, industrial, at UL Solutions said, "UL Certification demonstrates that the evaluated battery and energy storage system met applicable safety requirements." Nova is now in production at Megafactory 1 in British Columbia, the company's facility that's certified to UL 1974, a standard determining the sorting, grading and repurposing of EV batteries. Moment Energy has been verified as a non-Prohibited Foreign Entity by the US government, so investments in Moment Energy battery systems are eligible, therefore, for the federal Investment Tax Credit from 2027. Related:Veolia to recycle EV batteries in the EU, calls for regulation of domestic strategic metals Moment Energy takes end-of-life EV battery packs from vehicles at around 70% state-of-health (SoH), then removes underperforming cells and reconfigures them to form units specifically designed for utility-grade battery storage systems. Each Nova 2.94m x 1.80m (9.65 ft x 5.9 ft) block provides around 200kW/500kWh, and individual battery packs can be replaced as they reach end-of-life without altering the overall BESS enclosure, producing a projected lifespan of the Nova of around 20 years. The Nova BESS comes in a Type 3R enclosure with an ISO 12944-complaint C4 coating, operates in temperatures from -25°C to 50°C (-13°F to 122°F), functions at altitudes up to 2,000 metres (6,500 ft) and has an IEEE 693 high seismic rating. Edward Chiang, co-founder and CEO of Moment Energy, said: "We see a future where re-engineered EV batteries become essential infrastructure for powering businesses and onshoring manufacturing and supply chain. Nova brings that vision to life, combining safety, engineering and North American manufacturing to deploy the safest and highest-performance batteries ever made: EV batteries to supercharge our aging grid." Moment Energy's battery storage systems are used in data centres, airports, hospitals, factories and micro-grids, the company says. First deliveries of Nova are planned for Q1 2027. In January 2024 Moment Energy received US$15 million in Series A funding from the Amazon Climate Pledge Fund and Voyager Ventures. Series B funding of US$40 million for the company came in May this year from Evok Innovations, Liberty Mutual Investments, the W23 Global Fund and Acario, the latter the wholly-owned subsidiary of natural gas supply company, Tokyo Gas. artigo.texto: Ecobiz.asia – The ASEAN Common Carbon Framework (ACCF) is seeking a more formal role within ASEAN and closer alignment with global carbon market standards as it moves into a new two-year phase focused on turning regional cooperation into practical outcomes. The framework’s 2026–2028 strategy includes expanding its membership, strengthening coordination with international carbon market initiatives and establishing an ASEAN Community of Practice to facilitate knowledge-sharing and consultations on longer-term projects. The priorities follow the renewal of the ACCF’s Memorandum of Collaboration at the 31st UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye, on Nov. 12, 2026. The five founding signatories extended their cooperation for another two years, while the Philippines-based Aboitiz Foundation Inc. joined as an observer. The ACCF was established at COP29 in November 2024 to support the development of high-integrity and interoperable carbon markets across Southeast Asia. Its founding members are the Malaysia Carbon Market Association (MCMA), ASEAN Alliance on Carbon Markets (AACM), Singapore Sustainable Finance Association (SSFA), Indonesia Carbon Trade Association (IDCTA) and Thailand Carbon Markets Club (TCMC). Under the chairmanship of SSFA, which began in the second half of 2026, the ACCF will focus on three areas: strengthening carbon credit supply and demand, improving market infrastructure and building regional capacity. On the demand side, it plans to develop an interim pathway for corporate use of high-integrity carbon credits and a due diligence framework to help financiers assess carbon project investments. On market infrastructure, it will seek greater clarity on the legal status of verified carbon credits and explore ways to reduce cross-border barriers to harmonisation and the fungibility of credits across ASEAN markets. The framework will also work with international partners to provide technical and advisory support for carbon finance and bring its work to ASEAN forums. Oi-Yee Choo, ACCF co-chair, co-lead of SSFA’s Carbon Markets Workstream and chief executive of Climate Impact X, said the organisation would work closely with Singapore as it assumes the ASEAN chairmanship in 2027, complementing regional market-building efforts from the private sector. The framework also aims to broaden its regional representation through new members, including Aboitiz Foundation, which joined as an observer. “By plugging in to initiatives such as the Coalition to Grow Carbon Markets, we will also bring ASEAN’s perspective to the global agenda and help ensure carbon markets develop more equitably,” Choo said. The renewal also marks a step towards aligning ASEAN’s carbon market development with global efforts to promote credible corporate use of carbon credits. All five founding signatories now support the Shared Principles developed by the Coalition to Grow Carbon Markets, a government-led initiative co-chaired by Kenya, Singapore and the United Kingdom. Launched at the COP30 Business and Finance Forum in November 2025, the principles set out six pillars for companies to use carbon credits credibly alongside deep emissions reductions within their own operations. Renard Siew, president of MCMA, said the ACCF had originated as a priority deliverable under Malaysia’s ASEAN chairmanship, championed through the ASEAN Business Advisory Council Malaysia to advance regional carbon market cooperation. He said the next phase should move beyond dialogue towards tangible outcomes that build market confidence, strengthen institutional capacity and unlock cross-border opportunities. “The ambition should not simply be to grow carbon markets, but to ensure they deliver meaningful climate impact, mobilise investment and create lasting value for the region,” Siew said. Dharsono Hartono, permanent chair of AACM, said closer coordination, knowledge-sharing and joint efforts to address common challenges would help strengthen confidence in carbon credits originating from ASEAN and create more opportunities for cross-border cooperation. Riza Suarga, president of IDCTA, said the framework should now translate its commitments into concrete action, particularly by supporting the development and implementation of carbon projects that meet high standards of quality, transparency, credibility and environmental integrity. Gloyta Nathalang, chair of TCMC, said cooperation between governments and businesses could strengthen credit quality and market interoperability while respecting the different priorities of ASEAN member states. She said TCMC would contribute by sharing knowledge and bringing the practical experience of project developers and buyers into the framework’s work. Aboitiz Foundation President Ana Margarita Hontiveros said the foundation’s participation as an observer would allow it to share experience and learn from regional partners, representing the Philippines’ nature-based solutions industry and carbon coalition groups. She said regional carbon market cooperation should deliver benefits beyond the generation of credits, including opportunities for communities and the protection of natural resources. Since its establishment, the ACCF has gained recognition in several regional policy platforms, including the joint media statement of the 57th ASEAN Economic Ministers’ Meeting and the ASEAN Joint Statement on Climate Change to COP30. Its work has also been cited in the ASEAN Capital Markets Forum’s guidance for an ASEAN voluntary carbon market. Over the past year, the framework has supported national and independent carbon standards aligned with benchmarks set by the Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market (ICVCM) and the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA), according to the initiative. artigo.texto: Empresas ligadas a data centers perdem US$ 4,2 tri As perdas eliminaram quase metade dos US$ 9,4 trilhões em valor de mercado que essas mesmas empresas haviam acumulado nos 12 meses anteriores Atualizado Empresas globais dos setores de manufatura, serviços públicos e mineração perderam US$ 4,2 trilhões em valor de mercado desde junho, depois que a aposta nos fornecedores de equipamentos e infraestrutura para a inteligência artificial começaram a se reverter. Empresas frequentemente associadas à construção de centros de dados foram as mais atingidas pela onda de vendas, segundo uma análise do “Financial Times”, em meio à oscilação da confiança dos investidores no boom da IA. As perdas eliminaram quase metade dos US$ 9,4 trilhões em valor de mercado que essas mesmas empresas haviam acumulado nos 12 meses anteriores, quando os investidores direcionaram recursos para fabricantes de tudo, desde motores a jato adaptados para fornecer energia a centros de dados de grande escala até os avançados sistemas de fibra ótica necessários para conectar os racks de servidores de IA. A Caterpillar, uma das principais fornecedoras de geradores a gás para centros de dados, viu seu valor de mercado encolher US$ 214 bilhões, ou 44%, desde que suas ações atingiram um recorde histórico em 30 de junho, segundo dados da FactSet. A Oklo, uma empresa de energia nuclear, sofreu uma queda de 49%, apesar de ter assinado um contrato com a Meta em janeiro. A Comfort Systems, fabricante de sistemas de aquecimento, ventilação e ar-condicionado, e a Corning, fabricante de equipamentos de fibra ótica, também perderam cerca de metade de seus valores no mesmo período. Paul Kedrosky, investidor de capital de risco e pesquisador do Instituto de Tecnologia de Massachusetts (MIT), diz que os investidores erraram ao começar a tratar empresas industriais tradicionais como se fossem fabricantes de semicondutores. A queda ocorre em meio à turbulência mais ampla das ações ligadas à IA, com investidores questionando se o aumento dos investimentos de capital financiados por dívida pelas grandes empresas de computação em nuvem, somado à crescente oposição política à construção de centros de dados nos Estados Unidos, poderá provocar um colapso do setor. O movimento atingiu grupos industriais cujos resultados estão cada vez mais atrelados à expansão dessa infraestrutura. O setor foi o segundo de pior desempenho entre as ações que fazem parte do índice Standard & Poor’s (S&P 500) desde o começo do terceiro trimestre, atrás apenas do de tecnologia. Há quem diga que as empresas fornecedoras do setor estão assentadas em bases sólidas e que a demanda continua muito superior à oferta. Os gastos com a construção de centros de dados - excluindo-se os equipamentos de Tecnologia da Informação e chips - chegaram a US$ 96 bilhões nos EUA nos 12 meses encerrados em setembro, segundo dados governamentais. Tendências mais amplas, como a eletrificação e a reestruturação das cadeias de suprimentos, continuam a sustentar as atividades principais de muitas empresas industriais. Richard S. Warzala, executivo-chefe da Allient, fabricante de sistemas de controles industriais, diz que a demanda por IA não vai diminuir. "Eles [alguns Estados] podem impor uma moratória à instalação de novos centros de dados, mas aqueles cujas obras já começaram precisam ser concluídos", disse ele em teleconferência sobre os resultados da empresa em 5 de novembro. Os resultados do terceiro trimestre mostraram uma demanda vigorosa. Diversos fabricantes de turbinas a gás afirmaram ter recebido encomendas de bilhões de dólares nos primeiros nove meses de 2026. A Caterpillar informou que sua carteira de pedidos atingiu o recorde de US$ 78 bilhões e que as vendas de equipamentos para geração de energia cresceram 75% em relação ao mesmo período do ano passado, graças à demanda dos centros de dados. A carteira de pedidos da Siemens de equipamentos elétricos destinados a centros de dados cresceu 60% em 2026, alcançando € 7 bilhões. Já a Eaton, que também fornece equipamentos elétricos, informou que suas encomendas dobraram em relação ao ano passado. Ainda não está claro qual será o impacto das moratórias e restrições à construção de centros de dados, amplamente apoiadas pelos eleitores americanos nas eleições legislativas de meio de mandato realizadas este mês. Pesquisadores do Citigroup afirmaram, em relatório divulgado após as eleições, que, embora esperem que regras mais rigorosas provoquem maior volatilidade no setor de centros de dados, restrições generalizadas à construção continuam sendo improváveis. Joseph Dominguez, da Constellation Energy, disse a investidores que a reação do mercado após as eleições foi um “exagero” e que os democratas “se preocupam muito” com a proteção de empregos operacionais em centros de dados. Outros afirmam que eventuais proibições apenas deslocariam os projetos de construção para regiões com ambientes regulatórios mais favoráveis. “No fim das contas, se houver demanda por essas instalações, elas serão construídas em algum lugar”, afirma Ryan, do Deutsche Bank. (Tradução de Mario Zamarian)

artigo.texto: Empresas interessadas em instalar ou ampliar data centers no Brasil ainda aguardam a regulamentação do Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter (Redata) para acessar os benefícios fiscais previstos na Lei 15.504/2026. Embora a legislação tenha sido sancionada em setembro, a utilização dos incentivos depende de um decreto do governo federal, que deverá estabelecer os critérios de habilitação, as condições técnicas e os procedimentos para adesão ao programa. Segundo informações divulgadas pelo UOL nesta segunda-feira (16), a expectativa é que o decreto seja assinado após o retorno do governo da Conferência das Nações Unidas sobre Mudanças Climáticas (COP31), possivelmente por volta de 27 de novembro. Até a publicação das regras, as empresas não conseguem utilizar os benefícios do regime. O Redata foi criado para estimular investimentos em infraestrutura digital, computação em nuvem e inteligência artificial no país. O programa prevê a suspensão de tributos na aquisição de equipamentos de tecnologia da informação e comunicação utilizados na implantação, modernização e ampliação de centros de processamento de dados. Quais benefícios estão previstos no Redata A Lei 15.504/2026 prevê a suspensão de PIS/Pasep, Cofins, Imposto sobre Produtos Industrializados (IPI) e Imposto de Importação, observadas as condições estabelecidas para cada tributo. No caso do Imposto de Importação, o benefício alcança equipamentos e componentes sem produção nacional equivalente. A suspensão dos tributos poderá ser convertida em isenção definitiva após o cumprimento das contrapartidas e a entrega dos produtos aos empreendimentos habilitados. O atraso na regulamentação, porém, reduz o período disponível para aproveitar parte dos incentivos. Segundo o UOL, a suspensão de PIS/Pasep, Cofins e IPI tem efeitos até 31 de dezembro de 2026, em razão da transição da Reforma Tributária sobre o consumo. Já o benefício relativo ao Imposto de Importação permanece previsto por cinco anos. Regulamentação deve definir critérios técnicos Um dos pontos que ainda precisam ser esclarecidos é o enquadramento das fontes de energia consideradas de baixa emissão de carbono. A legislação exige que os data centers atendam à demanda de energia elétrica com fontes renováveis ou de baixa emissão, mas não detalha quais alternativas serão aceitas nessa segunda categoria. A possibilidade de inclusão do gás natural está entre os temas em discussão no governo. Segundo o portal Eixos, há divergência entre os ministérios da Fazenda e de Minas e Energia sobre o enquadramento do combustível. A definição deverá constar das regras complementares. Outro ponto envolve a definição de quais equipamentos importados poderão receber o benefício. A lei restringe a suspensão do Imposto de Importação aos produtos sem produção nacional equivalente, mas a regulamentação deverá esclarecer os procedimentos para essa avaliação. A discussão envolve interesses de fabricantes instalados no Brasil e empresas de tecnologia que dependem da importação de equipamentos específicos para seus projetos. Empresas terão contrapartidas para acessar o regime A adesão ao Redata não será automática. As empresas precisarão obter habilitação junto ao Ministério da Fazenda e cumprir compromissos relacionados a investimentos, fornecimento de serviços ao mercado interno e sustentabilidade. Entre as principais exigências previstas na lei estão: - Destinar pelo menos 10% da capacidade efetiva de processamento, armazenamento e tratamento de dados ao mercado brasileiro; - Investir o equivalente a 2% do valor dos produtos adquiridos com os benefícios fiscais em projetos de pesquisa, desenvolvimento e inovação no país; - Utilizar fontes de energia renováveis ou de baixa emissão para atender à demanda contratual de eletricidade; - Apresentar índice de eficiência hídrica para resfriamento dos equipamentos igual ou inferior a 0,05 litro de água por quilowatt-hora. Para empreendimentos instalados nas regiões Norte, Nordeste e Centro-Oeste, a legislação prevê redução de 20% em duas das contrapartidas: o percentual destinado ao mercado interno e o investimento em pesquisa e desenvolvimento. Com a regulamentação ainda pendente, empresas do setor continuam sem acesso efetivo ao regime. A publicação do decreto será necessária para esclarecer as condições de habilitação e permitir que os investimentos planejados considerem os benefícios fiscais e as exigências definitivas do programa.

Nov 17, 2026 Soneil Spark Unveils Towable Mobile Battery Energy Storage System at RE+ 2026 Soneil Spark this week introduced its Mobile Battery Energy Storage System, a portable modular battery unit built into a towable trailer, according to Solar Power World. The company, which offers bespoke modular energy solutions, is presenting the product at RE+ 2026. The Mobile BESS is designed to supply temporary backup and off-grid power by drawing electricity from the grid, a generator, or solar sources. Sonya Jain, the company's chief executive, said in a statement that the power follows the business wherever it goes and that the unit can be towed to locations where energy demand grows; customers can begin with a single unit and add more as requirements change, she added. Soneil Spark described the setup as straightforward, requiring no crane, trenching, or utility interconnection wait. The company positions the system for job sites that may be months from permanent service, film sets and events where generator noise and fumes are problematic, utility crews restoring power after storms, and remote mines or farms beyond the grid's reach. At sites already using generators, the Mobile BESS synchronizes with them to cover peaks and start-up gaps, allowing the generators to run fewer hours. In locations where diesel use is restricted, the company said the unit offers a quiet alternative. Unlike containerized storage intended to be placed once, the Mobile BESS is built to be towed and to operate in any weather, according to the company. Target applications include generator and equipment rental, construction, emergency and backup power, utilities, electrical contractors, events, film and entertainment, and off-grid sites such as mining and agriculture. artigo.texto: It’s never been easy to run a battery startup in the U.S. There have been more failures than successes over the last 20 years, and whipsawing federal policy has caused more than a few battery companies to shut shop. Not all of them die, though. Our Next Energy (ONE) had some close calls, but soon it will go public via SPAC, the company exclusively told TechCrunch. ONE says it is valued at $600 million pre-money, and it expects the merger with Wen Acquisition Corp. will bring $400 million in gross proceeds assuming no redemptions. The combined company will trade on the Nasdaq under the ticker “ONEE,” and the pro forma implied equity value is $1 billion. Over the years, ONE has raised $483 million, according to PitchBook, and at one point was valued at $1.3 billion. It has also received tens of millions of dollars in incentives tied to investments and job creation in Michigan. ONE is the brainchild of former Ford and Apple engineer Mujeeb Ijaz, who designed a way for electric vehicles to draw power from two batteries of different chemistries. In ONE’s first setup, it paired lithium-iron-phosphate (LFP) and with a manganese-rich chemistry, which would let each chemistry play to its strengths: LFP could be used day in, day out, while the more fragile but energy-dense, manganese-rich one would work for long, infrequent road trips. An initial prototype traveled over 600 miles on a single charge. But the EV market didn’t take off as quickly as anticipated, and automakers wanted to buy at lower prices (usually from China). Both of those reasons helped sink ONE’s first attempt at a Series C in late 2023. The startup had to lay off a chunk of its staff, and eventually vacated its lease for a planned $1.6 billion factory in Michigan. The rough patch led to Ijaz’s ouster as CEO in December 2023, only to have him return to the position in March 2025 after a new round of funding closed. (His brother’s investment firm co-led the round.) Part of the critique aimed at ONE during Ijaz’s first tenure as CEO was that the company spent too much time developing new products instead of focusing on one or two, as most startups tend to do. When Ijaz came back to the helm last year, he said that ONE would leave the automotive market and focus on grid-scale batteries. ONE isn’t alone in pivoting away from vehicle batteries. American automakers, which had similarly rosy views of EV adoption, also bet big on battery factories and supply chains. When sales didn’t pop in the U.S. like they have in China or Europe, they had to find an outlet for that capacity, and the grid started looking like the obvious target once it started groaning under the weight of AI data centers. Both Ford and GM have announced their own energy storage products. Many new grid-scale batteries use LFP, which is safer and cheaper than those used in most EVs in the U.S., and Ijaz saw an opportunity for ONE there as well. “We go back to the origins of LFP in this country and even to some of the factories that are in China,” he said. Indeed, just over a decade ago Ijaz led the automotive division at A123 Systems, the company that first commercialized the chemistry. Soon, Ijaz saw other opportunities for ONE’s batteries, including defense and locomotives. The defense play isn’t surprising. Nearly every battery company I talk with these days mentions defense, in part because it’s a market that Chinese companies can’t play in. Building an American supply chain means that a company can sell batteries at a premium, shielded as they are from Chinese competition. It’s a higher-margin market, though much smaller than EVs. My recent conversation with Ijaz last week was the first time I’d heard a company pitch rail companies as potential customers, though. Ijaz said ONE is “finding a lot of traction in” that market. The company has built a hybrid locomotive that uses a 2.8 megawatt-hour battery, and another he calls a micro-hybrid, which uses a smaller battery to start the diesel engine faster, similar to a stop-start system on a fossil fuel car or truck. “Our customers are seeing a 50% improvement in diesel fuel consumption, which is a big deal,” Ijaz said. Currently, ONE has three business lines, which could be a sign of its old culture creeping back into the picture. But Ijaz said the addition of defense and rail were driven by the bottom line: Grid-scale battery customers are also “very much like automotive customers, where they were willing to buy from China as long as the price was low enough,” he said. “Believe me, I would have loved to have made that grid business into the single business of the company. But the customers would look and then be taken away to a Chinese option because of the pricing, and the tariffs also leading them to that conclusion,” Ijaz said. “And so we decided that we needed a more durable market, and we looked for who in the customer base valued an American battery company.” Today, ONE operates a pack assembly plant in Novi, Michigan, which can put together packs from cells at a rate of 3 gigawatt-hours per year. The plant uses cells from China-based and non-China-based suppliers, as well as ONE’s own cells from a smaller factory nearby, which is currently being upgraded to make 50 megawatt-hours of batteries per year. In its investor pitch, which TechCrunch has reviewed, ONE distills its business lines into defense and rail. Drones and submarines make up the majority of what ONE sees as a $16.2 billion market. Defense-focused data centers get lumped in there, too, contributing $4.1 billion to the defense business. (That appears to be the main outlet for grid-scale batteries.) The other line, which serves the rail industry, is expected to be worth $28.2 billion. Both markets are sizable, but they pale in comparison to the EV sector, which is worth about $73 billion today, and could grow to $200 billion by the end of the decade, according to Grand View Research. artigo.texto: Resumo - Fundo BXDC, da Blackstone, assume maioria de duas joint ventures com a AWS - Transação é avaliada em cerca de US$ 5 bilhões e deve fechar ainda em 2026 - BXDC fica com 75% dos ativos; AWS mantém 25% e arrenda o portfólio inteiro - São 13 estruturas recém-construídas em campi no norte de Indiana e no Mississippi - Blackstone mira mercado potencial de US$ 1 trilhão em data centers nos próximos 5 anos - Ações do BXDC subiam quase 7% em Nova York na manhã do anúncio A Blackstone anunciou nesta segunda-feira (16) a compra de uma participação majoritária em duas joint ventures com a Amazon Web Services (AWS). O negócio, estimado em US$ 5 bilhões, marca a primeira aquisição do Blackstone Digital Infrastructure Trust (BXDC), fundo voltado para data centers. Com a operação, o fundo assumirá o controle de 13 instalações em dois complexos de data centers da AWS. As estruturas ficam no norte de Indiana e no Mississippi, nos Estados Unidos. Segundo Nick Pell, diretor-presidente do BXDC, o fundo terá 75% de participação nos ativos. Enquanto isso, a AWS permanecerá com os 25% restantes. Além disso, a divisão de computação em nuvem da Amazon arrendará todo o portfólio por um período inicial de 12 anos. O contrato também prevê a possibilidade de prorrogação por até 32 anos. A expectativa é que as empresas concluam a transação ainda em 2026. Após a conclusão, a joint venture assumirá uma dívida equivalente à metade do valor da aquisição. Por volta das 9h30, em Nova York, as ações do BXDC avançavam cerca de 7%, após o anúncio do acordo. “Este acordo direto com a Amazon cria um roteiro para realizarmos mais operações desse tipo com hyperscalers ou desenvolvedores”, afirmou Pell. Aposta da Blackstone em infraestrutura para IA Com a aquisição, a Blackstone busca ampliar sua presença no financiamento de infraestrutura para inteligência artificial (IA). Além disso, a gestora pretende atrair mais investidores individuais para seus fundos. Atualmente, a companhia administra cerca de US$ 1,4 trilhão em ativos alternativos. Desse total, aproximadamente US$ 200 bilhões estão ligados a data centers. O portfólio inclui a QTS Realty Trust, empresa especializada na construção e operação dessas instalações. Criado em maio, o BXDC concentra seus investimentos em data centers que já estão em operação. O fundo busca ativos avaliados entre US$ 250 milhões e US$ 1,5 bilhão. Além disso, a estratégia prioriza instalações que possuem contratos de locação de longo prazo com grandes empresas de tecnologia, conhecidas como hyperscalers. Segundo as projeções do BXDC, esse mercado poderá movimentar US$ 1 trilhão nos próximos cinco anos. Durante uma teleconferência com analistas, Pell também destacou o volume de novos projetos nos Estados Unidos. “Somente em 2027, estamos acompanhando mais de US$ 300 bilhões em novos data centers pertencentes a desenvolvedores e hyperscalers cuja entrega é esperada nos Estados Unidos”, afirmou. O executivo acrescentou que a companhia identifica oportunidades para 2028 e os anos seguintes. Além disso, mais da metade dos projetos acompanha o crescimento de novos polos tecnológicos. Entre eles estão Richmond, na Virgínia, e San Antonio, no Texas. Oferta limitada aumenta valor dos data centers A demanda por infraestrutura de inteligência artificial continua em expansão. No entanto, a construção de novos data centers enfrenta limitações que podem aumentar o valor das instalações existentes. Segundo Mike Forman, diretor de investimentos do BXDC, a combinação de demanda elevada e oferta restrita favorece os ativos que já operam. “À medida que as restrições de oferta aumentam diante de uma demanda que continua muito forte, ativos já estabilizados, que já existem, já possuem energia disponível e já contam com um inquilino, tornam-se mais valiosos”, afirmou. Nesse cenário, a Blackstone pretende comprar instalações de desenvolvedores e fundos que precisam recuperar parte do capital investido. Para Pell, o BXDC também poderá funcionar como uma alternativa de liquidez para esses investidores. “Há muitos desenvolvedores e fundos fechados buscando vender ativos e reciclar capital. Estamos oferecendo uma alternativa para eles por meio do capital dos investidores públicos do BXDC”, explicou. Dessa forma, a gestora busca aproveitar a necessidade de financiamento do setor para ampliar seu portfólio.

artigo.texto: UK hotel operators face growing pressure from electricity network charges that can remain high even when energy consumption falls. For multi-site hotel groups, these fixed costs are becoming an important factor in energy procurement, property investment and long-term financial planning. One charge attracting attention is the Transmission Network Use of System (TNUoS) charge. It helps fund the high-voltage electricity network that moves power across Great Britain. Although it is less visible than wholesale electricity prices, it can have a significant effect on the total cost of supplying large commercial properties. The challenge for hotel businesses is that lower electricity consumption does not always lead to a proportionate reduction in bills. Some network costs are based on a property’s connection and charging category rather than the amount of electricity it uses. This is prompting a closer look at commercial battery energy storage systems, on-site generation and smarter electricity management. Yet the financial case for these investments depends on how each hotel is charged. Battery storage can reduce some electricity costs, but it cannot automatically remove fixed TNUoS charges. Why electricity network charges matter for hotels Electricity bills contain more than the cost of generating or purchasing power. They also include charges for transporting electricity through transmission and local distribution networks, alongside other regulated costs and supplier charges. For hotels, this distinction matters because electricity demand is difficult to eliminate. Guest rooms, kitchens, lifts, ventilation, lighting, refrigeration and digital systems all require reliable power. Many properties operate around the clock, while demand can change considerably with occupancy, weather and the use of conference or leisure facilities. The UK’s electricity network charging arrangements create different cost pressures depending on a property’s location, voltage connection and supply agreement. TNUoS charges recover the costs of the national transmission network. Distribution Use of System (DUoS) charges fund the local networks that deliver electricity to individual premises. These charges can be passed through to commercial customers by electricity suppliers, although the way they appear on bills varies between contracts. For international hotel groups, understanding these distinctions is essential. Two properties with similar electricity consumption may face different network costs because of their connection arrangements, location or charging classification. How TNUoS residual charges affect hotel operating costs TNUoS charges have two broad elements: a locational component and a residual component. The locational element reflects differences in the costs associated with using the transmission network in different areas. The residual element recovers transmission costs that are not collected through locational charges. Under reforms introduced by the UK energy regulator Ofgem, residual transmission charges for final electricity demand are recovered through fixed charges rather than being linked directly to electricity consumed during particular periods. For non-domestic customers, the charging framework uses bands determined by relevant site characteristics, including historical consumption or capacity measures, depending on the connection category. This creates an important distinction for hotel energy managers. Reducing electricity use during a winter evening can help control certain consumption-related charges. However, it does not directly eliminate the fixed TNUoS residual charge. The distinction is particularly relevant when assessing investment proposals for batteries or other technologies intended to reduce exposure to network costs. A hotel may reduce the amount of electricity purchased during expensive periods without achieving an equivalent reduction in its fixed transmission charges. For multi-site operators, the financial exposure can be substantial in aggregate. It also creates a need for property-level analysis rather than assuming that every hotel will benefit equally from the same energy-saving measures. Why winter evening electricity demand remains important Winter evenings are a challenging period for electricity management in Great Britain. Demand across the electricity system can be high as homes and businesses use more lighting, heating and other electrical equipment. Hotels may also experience overlapping demand from guest services, restaurants, kitchens, leisure facilities and building systems. Although fixed TNUoS residual charges are not avoided by reducing consumption during these hours, other elements of electricity pricing can still make peak demand expensive. Some commercial electricity contracts expose customers to time-varying wholesale prices, network charges or peak-demand costs. Local distribution network tariffs may also vary by time of day and connection type. For hotels with suitable contracts, reducing electricity imports during costly periods can therefore deliver savings. The financial opportunity depends on the structure of the electricity agreement, the relevant network tariff and the hotel’s actual demand profile. This makes it important to distinguish between avoiding expensive electricity imports and avoiding fixed network charges. The two objectives require different calculations and may justify different investments. artigo.texto: Solar energy has emerged as one of the fastest-growing sources of renewable energy globally. How do you see its role evolving in the coming decade as countries work towards their clean energy and net-zero targets? The amount of electricity generated worldwide from solar photovoltaics surpassed that from nuclear and wind in 2025 and is destined to surpass that from coal in the early 2030s. Past then it will be our largest source of electricity generation, with electricity supplying an increasing portion of our total energy needs. How significant is the contribution of solar power in reducing global carbon emissions, and what more needs to be done to accelerate the shift from conventional energy sources? There are now over 3 terawatts of solar photovoltaics installed worldwide that will generate 3.5 petawatt-hours of electricity in 2026. If displacing coal from electricity generation or oil from transport, this will have reduced global CO2 emissions by over 3 gigatons. Solar is being installed at over 0.5 terawatts per year, but this needs to be increased to at least twice this. The more that is installed now, the lower will be global temperature rise Solar technology has advanced considerably over the years. What have been the most significant breakthroughs in solar cell efficiency, and what innovations can we expect to see in the coming years? Over the last decade, solar panel efficiency has increased from about 16% to values as high as 25%. We have made a solar system in our lab that converts sunlight with over 40% efficiency. This is by using a stack of four cells, each specialised for a different colour range in sunlight. If this approach can be commercialised at low cost, we would expect commercial panels to operate at such efficiencies at some time in the future. Despite the rapid growth of solar energy, what are the key challenges that continue to limit its wider adoption, particularly around energy storage, grid integration, efficiency and reliability? The availability of low-cost Li-ion storage batteries has overcome earlier barriers to large-scale integration. Solar plus batteries are now providing a more reliable electricity supply than traditional coal generators, not only in Australia but in countries like Pakistan and many African countries with notoriously unreliable electricity supply. How can next-generation solar technologies, including advancements in PERC and TOPCon cells, help improve the performance, affordability and scalability of solar power? Improving solar cell performance not only lowers the costs of solar panels not only by lowering the amount of glass, cover sheets, frames and terminals required but also costs of transport, support structures and wiring required when being installed. As solar energy becomes more cost-competitive, what steps are needed to make it a reliable and accessible energy source for both developed and emerging economies? The International Energy Agency announced in 2020 that solar was now providing “some of the cheapest electricity in history,” but because it used to be expensive, this has taken time to become more widely known. Private citizens in emerging economies have only recently realised this and are now taking the initiative in procuring solar to provide a reliable electricity supply. Looking ahead, which countries or regions do you believe have the greatest potential to drive the next phase of solar innovation, and how important will international research collaborations be in achieving this? Australia pioneered both the PERC and TOPCon cell technologies that have dominated recent solar production, so it is likely to play a major role in leading progress here. China and India are the two countries likely to dominate solar production, helped by the strong demand in their local markets. artigo.texto: A proposta da Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) de ampliar a aplicação de tarifas horárias para consumidores de baixa tensão recebeu manifestações favoráveis de Luiz Barroso, CEO da consultoria PSR, e de diversas entidades do setor elétrico. As avaliações destacam o potencial da mudança para melhorar a sinalização dos custos da energia, incentivar o deslocamento do consumo para horários mais baratos e estimular investimentos em tecnologias como baterias e sistemas de gestão energética. A antiga tarifa branca, que passará a se chamar Tarifa Hora Certa, pode passar a ser obrigatória aos consumidores de baixa tensão com consumo médio mensal igual ou superior a 500 kWh. Essa foi a conclusão das áreas técnicas da agência após a consulta pública 46/2025. O objetivo da medida é sinalizar os custos de atendimento do sistema ao longo do dia e incentivar o deslocamento do consumo para períodos de menor custo. A implantação será dividida em três etapas, sendo que a primeira, prevista para abril de 2028, vai abranger unidades com consumo mensal superior a 1.800 kWh. Em abril de 2029, será a vez daqueles com demanda superior a 1.000 kWh por mês. A última etapa, em abril de 2031, vai incluir quem consome mais de 500 kWh mensais. Consumidores com MMGD terão o mesmo tratamento que aqueles que não geram a própria energia. O desenho apresentado pela área técnica incorporou contribuições da consulta pública, incluindo mecanismos de proteção aos consumidores durante a transição. Apesar disso, a proposta recebeu críticas de associações ligadas à geração distribuída, que apontam a necessidade de aperfeiçoamentos antes da implementação. Entre as preocupações estão a criação de condições econômicas mais favoráveis à instalação de baterias e a preservação da segurança jurídica dos sistemas de geração distribuída já existentes. Na avaliação de Barroso, a cobrança do consumo e dos excedentes de geração por posto tarifário poderá criar incentivos econômicos para que consumidores com MMGD invistam em sistemas de armazenamento de energia. O executivo também considera acertada a ampliação do universo de consumidores expostos à sinalização horária, uma vez que os custos de atendimento à demanda variam ao longo do dia e devem ser refletidos nos preços da energia. Outro segmento que poderá ser beneficiado pela mudança é o da mobilidade elétrica. Com a diferenciação das tarifas por horário, os proprietários de veículos elétricos terão incentivos para realizar as recargas nos períodos de menor custo, contribuindo para distribuir melhor a demanda e otimizar o uso da infraestrutura elétrica. “A proposta da Aneel de uma tarifa horária para consumidores a partir de determinado nível de consumo é extremamente bem-vinda. O custo de atender a demanda varia por hora e ampliar o universo de consumidores que percebem este sinal econômico é uma decisão acertada”, afirmou Barroso. O executivo também considera positiva a criação da chamada tarifa plana, alternativa destinada aos consumidores que não desejarem ficar imediatamente expostos à variação dos preços ao longo do dia. Para ele, essa modalidade apresenta uma definição mais adequada do que a estrutura da tarifa convencional atualmente existente. Barroso ainda elogiou o processo de elaboração da proposta pela área técnica da Aneel, ressaltando a maturidade conceitual dos estudos, a análise das contribuições recebidas e a estruturação do modelo regulatório. “A construção de toda a proposta da área técnica possui muita maturidade conceitual no entendimento do problema, na escuta e processamento das contribuições e na construção da proposta apresentada. A leitura da nota técnica fornece a certeza que foi um processo estruturado e muito pensado em termos técnicos por parte da agência. Espero que a diretoria acate”, afirmou. Entidades defendem modernização da estrutura tarifária Além da manifestação de Barroso, entidades representativas do setor elétrico encaminharam à diretoria colegiada da Aneel, em 13 de novembro, uma carta conjunta nº 001/2026, na qual manifestam apoio à iniciativa de modernização das tarifas de distribuição de energia elétrica. Na avaliação das entidades, a modernização da estrutura tarifária é uma agenda necessária diante das transformações da matriz elétrica brasileira, da expansão das fontes renováveis variáveis, da abertura do mercado de energia e das mudanças nos padrões de consumo e nas tecnologias disponíveis. A carta sustenta que a estrutura tarifária é um dos principais instrumentos para promover eficiência econômica, orientar decisões de consumo e investimento e assegurar uma distribuição adequada dos custos entre os usuários do sistema elétrico. As entidades defendem que os preços reflitam de maneira mais precisa os custos associados à utilização da infraestrutura de geração, transmissão e distribuição. A sinalização econômica por horário também poderia reduzir distorções e subsídios cruzados implícitos, além de incentivar o uso mais eficiente dos recursos disponíveis. Outro ponto destacado é o papel mais ativo que os consumidores poderão assumir na operação do sistema. Com tarifas que reconheçam a variação temporal dos custos, será possível estimular o deslocamento de cargas, a incorporação de soluções de armazenamento de energia e a adoção de tecnologias de gestão do consumo. Para as signatárias, esses mecanismos podem melhorar a coordenação entre oferta e demanda, reduzir pressões sobre a infraestrutura elétrica e contribuir para a modicidade tarifária no longo prazo. A carta também ressalta que a modernização deve observar princípios como causalidade de custos, eficiência alocativa, isonomia e sustentabilidade econômico-financeira do setor. Na avaliação das entidades, a mudança não deve representar privilégio ou restrição a uma tecnologia específica, mas promover uma alocação mais eficiente dos custos e benefícios associados ao uso da rede elétrica.
