artigo.texto: A leaked compromise proposal seeks to shield European industry from rising carbon costs, but environmental groups warn that concessions on free emissions allowances and international carbon credits could undermine the bloc's 2040 climate ambitions. The European Union's 2040 climate target risks being undermined by reforms to the bloc's carbon market, the Emissions Trading System (ETS), according to a leaked document seen by Euronews. The Irish Presidency of the EU Council has softened a proposal, to be discussed by EU ambassadors on Wednesday, amid growing political pressure on the ETS as national governments struggle to reconcile emissions targets with industrial competitiveness and high energy costs. The compromise text seeks to secure political support for the bloc's carbon market beyond 2030. However, climate advocates warn that concessions to protect European industry could weaken the system's contribution to the 2040 target, leaving other sectors of the economy to make up the shortfall. The Council text retains the European Commission's July proposal to slow the decline in carbon allowances, extend free permits for industry and introduce international carbon credits into the EU carbon market, allowing emissions at home to be offset through projects abroad. But negotiations are further reshaping the plan, especially around how much flexibility governments and industry will have to avoid domestic emissions cuts. Free allowances and international credits Under the Irish Presidency's proposal, industrial companies would retain 80% of their free allowances if they submit an investment plan, even if they subsequently fail to carry out the proposed decarbonisation investments. The remaining 20% would be conditional on starting construction of eligible projects. Free allowances are permits that companies receive without having to buy them at auction. They are designed to protect EU producers against competition from countries with less stringent climate rules, such as China and the US. The proposal marks a significant political concession to industries concerned about losing free allowances, raising questions about whether the ETS will provide sufficient incentives to cut emissions. The compromise would shield industry from carbon costs for longer, while leaving governments to ensure that this protection translates into investment in European production and clean technologies. On international carbon credits, the Council has retained the Commission's proposal to set aside allowances equivalent to 260 million tonnes of CO2 to finance their purchase. It also leaves open the possibility of a pilot phase between 2031 and 2035, allowing the EU to test the system before implementing it in full. The Council has also maintained stringent quality and integrity requirements for international credits, making the ETS emissions reduction trajectory increasingly dependent on their availability. However, if industries can't buy them, it could jeopardise the 2040 climate target, since it requires at least an 85% domestic net emissions reduction, with international credits accounting for the remaining 5%. The Irish Presidency is seeking to build consensus among the 27 EU countries before negotiations turn to more politically sensitive questions of climate ambition and burden-sharing between member states. It hopes to secure an agreement at the Environment Council on December 11. The European Parliament is expected to vote during its December 14-17 plenary session in Strasbourg. Fragmentation at national level The Irish Presidency faces an uphill battle given the depth of divisions among member states and the complexity of the negotiations. EU countries are already divided over how quickly the supply of carbon permits should shrink, whether companies should be allowed to use international carbon credits to meet their obligations and how far industrial sectors should be shielded from rising carbon costs, according to a second document seen by Euronews. Taken together, the demands risk diluting the ETS when it is expected to drive a large share of the bloc’s next phase of emissions cuts. In general, governments want to preserve the ETS as a source of revenue for decarbonisation, but concerns are mounting about the costs it imposes on energy-intensive industries competing with manufacturers from China or the United States. EU capitals are split over the total number of emissions permits available to companies — some argue they should decline to increase carbon pricing and encourage divestments in fossil fuels. Others fear the impact of withdrawing free allowances on their struggling industries. A slower reduction would ease the pressure on power plants and factories to cut emissions, potentially tempering carbon prices and giving companies more time to adapt. But it would also mean fewer emissions cuts in the sectors covered by the ETS, making the 2040 target harder to reach. Environmental groups sound the alarm A recent analysis by the Öko-Institut, commissioned by environmental campaign group WWF Germany, warned that the Commission's proposed ETS reform was "incompatible" with the EU's target of cutting net emissions by 90% by 2040. “The Commission would rather gamble on climate protection than safeguard the future of European industry," said Lisa Okken, industrial policy expert at WWF Germany. "Its proposed reform lacks the carbon price signal needed to incentivise the urgent modernisation of European industry. This gap is being filled with complicated accounting tricks and excessive flexibility.” Another key concern cited by the environmentalists is the proposal to allow additional emissions beyond the existing emissions cap in exchange for future permanent carbon removals through expensive technologies designed to capture CO2 from the air. "It remains unclear whether these removals can be delivered at the scale required, as the necessary capacity simply does not exist today," reads the study.

artigo.texto: As data centre construction starts to gather pace in Africa, supporters say investment in AI infrastructure could help expand electricity access for the roughly 600 million Africans who lack it. But critics fear growing energy demand from the sector could strain already weak power systems and divert resources from communities and industries struggling to secure reliable electricity supplies. On Monday at the UN climate summit in Antalya, three African countries - Somalia, Uganda and Sierra Leone - endorsed a new voluntary pledge proposed by the Turkish presidency which aims "to make AI part of the climate solution - sustainably powered, efficiently designed, transparently measured and available to all". The pledge's signatories - so far just nine countries as well as over 40 companies and some civil society groups - commit to power and build AI infrastructure and hardware sustainably, for example by running data centres with zero- or low-emission energy, supporting their integration into electricity grids, and designing efficient cooling, energy and water systems. The pledge also calls for stronger financial and technical support - including access to computing capacity - to help developing countries use AI to address climate challenges, such as improving energy efficiency, optimising electricity systems and meeting renewable energy needs. It does not, however, explicitly propose that they should be helped to build data centres for that purpose. Bashir Jama, Somalia's minister of environment and climate change, said his country supports the pledge's call to reduce AI's environmental footprint "through cleaner energy, efficient use of electricity and water, transparent measurement and responsible management of electronic waste". In September, the Rockefeller Foundation launched an "Emergent Grid" initiative that will set up small-scale AI data centres running on solar mini-grids in African villages. Funded through the Mission300 Accelerator, a World Bank-led programme to bring electricity to 300 million Africans by 2030, pilot projects are planned for Kenya, Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), Sierra Leone and Djibouti. artigo.texto: Following the signing of the connection construction agreement earlier this year, the grid connection agreement marks a further significant step towards delivering the project. Together, the two agreements establish the key contractual framework for construction and subsequent operation of the grid connection. The BESS will have a storage duration of four hours and will be connected directly to the extra-high-voltage grid. It will be able to store electricity during periods of high generation or low demand and release it back to the grid when needed. Stadorf will make an important contribution to integrating renewable energy, increasing the flexibility of the power system and making efficient use of existing energy infrastructure. Michael Zimmermann, Managing Director of Elements Green Deutschland, said: “Signing the grid connection agreement marks another milestone for Stadorf. Together with the connection construction agreement, we now have the key contractual foundations in place for connecting this 400 MW project to the grid. This is significant progress for Elements Green and underlines our ability to successfully advance complex energy infrastructure projects of this scale.” Stadorf is part of Elements Green’s extensive German battery storage pipeline. The company is developing several large-scale battery storage projects for connection to the extra-high-voltage grid and is pursuing a long-term strategy as an integrated developer, investor and operator of energy infrastructure. “Germany needs not only additional renewable generation capacity but, above all, the high-performance and flexible infrastructure to make the energy transition a technical and economic success. Large-scale battery storage systems such as Stadorf will play a central role in this,” Zimmermann added. With the key grid connection agreements now in place, Elements Green is focusing on the next stages of technical and commercial implementation. This includes detailed planning of the grid connection infrastructure, preparations for construction and continued coordination with the project and technology partners involved.

artigo.texto: Deputados do Paraná aprovam projeto de lei que incentiva instalação e expansão de data centers no estado — Foto: Divulgação/Gov.br Deputados estaduais da Assembleia Legislativa do Paraná (Alep) aprovaram, nesta quarta-feira (18), em segunda discussão, uma política estadual para incentivar a instalação e a expansão de data centers no estado. O projeto autoriza o Poder Executivo a classificar datas centers como empreendimentos de interesse estratégico estadual, dar prioridade administrativa a estes projetos, firmar parcerias com universidades e centros de pesquisa e regulamentar benefícios fiscais. Os autores da proposta, os deputados Luiz Fernando Guerra (Novo), Maria Victoria (PP) e Bazana (PSD), apontam que o Paraná reúne condições favoráveis para atrair grandes centros de processamento de dados, como matriz energética predominantemente renovável, disponibilidade de energia, redes de fibra óptica de alta capacidade, ecossistema de inovação consolidado e capital humano qualificado. Segundo a justificativa, a proposta pode estimular a economia digital, a pesquisa tecnológica, a inteligência artificial e a geração de empregos especializados. Conforme o texto da proposta, o objetivo é atrair investimentos de infraestrutura digital para o estado, consolidar o Paraná como polo estratégico de data centers na América Latina, entre outros. Na versão original, o projeto criava o Programa Paranaense de Incentivo a Centros de Dados (PRODATA-PR) e autorizava benefícios fiscais de ICMS (Imposto sobre Circulação de Mercadorias e Serviços) para empresas do setor. Entre eles estavam suspensão, isenção ou redução do imposto. Porém, no substitutivo aprovado pela Comissão de Constituição e Justiça, o texto passou a ser mais genérico. Com a mudança, ele apenas autoriza o Poder Executivo a regulamentar eventuais benefícios fiscais, respeitando a legislação federal e a disponibilidade orçamentária, sem conceder incentivos específicos diretamente na lei. LEIA TAMBÉM: - Política: Sergio Moro anuncia ex-procurador da Lava Jato como secretário Anticorrupção do Paraná - Final feliz: Bilhete com telefone de contato ajuda idoso com amnésia a voltar para casa após se perder - Vídeo: Motorista joga caixas de cigarros contrabandeados pela janela enquanto foge da PRF com carro sem um dos pneus Data centers são alvos de discussões Os data centers são grandes instalações que abrigam servidores responsáveis por armazenar e processar informações, inclusive para sistemas de inteligência artificial. Como funcionam continuamente, esses equipamentos precisam de muita energia e de refrigeração para evitar o superaquecimento. Em setembro de 2026, foi sancionada uma lei federal que instituiu o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Data Center (Redata). Na prática, o programa reduz a cobrança de impostos sobre equipamentos usados na instalação e na expansão de data centers, desde que as empresas cumpram uma série de requisitos. No entanto, a instalação desses empreendimentos também tem gerado controvérsias. Nos Estados Unidos, por exemplo, moradores de regiões que concentram grandes centros de processamento de dados relatam impactos como ruído permanente gerado pelos sistemas de refrigeração e pelos geradores de energia de emergência, além de preocupações com o aumento do consumo de água e energia elétrica. Em algumas regiões do país norte-americano, comunidades afirmam que a chegada dos data centers altera a dinâmica urbana sem necessariamente trazer benefícios proporcionais em empregos. O debate também envolve questões ambientais e de planejamento urbano. No Brasil, os problemas são semelhantes. Em São Paulo, o Conselho Municipal de Meio Ambiente de Campinas (Comdema) convidou três instituições de ensino e pesquisa para avaliar os possíveis impactos da construção de um mega data center na Fazenda Pau d'Alho, em Barão Geraldo. Também naquele estado, o Ministério Público abriu um procedimento para apurar a instalação de dois data centers na cidade de Salto. A representação menciona o receio do potencial aumento no consumo de água na cidade, que tem problemas constantes no abastecimento. No Pará, o primeiro data center de IA na Amazônia gera debate por risco de formação de "ilhas de calor" em uma região já castigada por temperaturas extremas. artigo.texto: Duke Energy customers across North Carolina are facing higher electricity bills starting in January, but new rules will require large data centers to shoulder more of the financial risks associated with their growing energy demand. After opening in downtown Raleigh one year ago, Alejandro Leon Jr., owner of Olé Sports Bar and Lounge, said a new challenge is on the horizon for his establishment: Higher electricity bills. Other WRAL Top Stories “We’ve been eating that up and now unfortunately with that spike its obvious that the consumers are going to have to pay all that up front. Very unfortunate," Leon said. Leon says the rate hike would put business owners like himself in a crunch. “I was pretty disappointed that North Carolina approved the spike," Leon said. For Durham resident Midori Brooks, who recently received a $900 electricity bill, the prospect of another rate increase means she may need to take on a second job. Brooks has lived in the same home since 1995 and has watched her electricity bills climb. She recalls paying about $225 to $250 a month in previous years. Now, even with her husband working full time and Brooks working part time, the family is struggling to keep up. “I have to figure out whether I'm gonna pay at least a portion of the light bill and still be able to feed my three grandkids,” Brooks said. About $200 of her recent $900 bill was a past-due balance, she said, reflecting how difficult it has already become for her family to keep up with electricity costs even before the new rate increases take effect. The North Carolina Utilities Commission on Monday approved two-year rate plans for Duke Energy Carolinas and Duke Energy Progress, largely accepting negotiated settlements that reduced the utility's original requests. Residential electricity rates are projected to rise about 9.5% over the next two years for Duke Energy Carolinas customers and 9.3% for Duke Energy Progress customers. Duke released new figures Tuesday detailing how those increases will translate into monthly electricity bills. The increases will begin Jan. 1, 2027, in the middle of the winter heating season. How much more will customers pay? According to projections released Tuesday by Duke Energy, a typical residential customer using 1,000 kilowatt-hours of electricity per month would see the following increases: Duke Energy Carolinas (Charlotte, Durham, the Triad and much of western North Carolina): - January 2027: $6.53 more per month - January 2028: An additional $4.66 per month - Total monthly increase by 2028: $11.19 Duke Energy Progress (Raleigh, much of eastern North Carolina and the Asheville region): - January 2027: $9.62 more per month - January 2028: An additional $5.89 per month - Total monthly increase by 2028: $15.51 That amounts to approximately $134 to $186 in additional annual electricity costs by 2028 for a typical household, based on Duke's projections. Actual bill impacts will vary depending on electricity usage and other charges. Under the settlements, Duke would collect approximately $834 million in additional annual revenue across all customer classes by the second year of the rate plans. Regulators authorized a 9.8% return on equity for both utilities, down from Duke's initial request of 10.95%. That figure represents the authorized return on shareholder equity invested in the utility, not the percentage increase in customers' electricity bills. The rate plans include approximately $7.2 billion in capital investments over two years, along with a mechanism to refund customers for certain infrastructure projects that are delayed or canceled. Duke also agreed to contribute a combined $20 million in shareholder funds to support electricity bill assistance and home repairs that help low-income households access weatherization programs. Duke said it worked with customers and other stakeholders to reduce its initial rate increase requests while maintaining investments needed to strengthen the power grid and accommodate North Carolina's growth. “We listened to our customers and worked closely with stakeholders to find a more cost-effective way forward,” said Kendal Bowman, Duke Energy's North Carolina president, in a statement Tuesday. “This outcome keeps affordability at the forefront while allowing us to make the investments needed to strengthen reliability and support North Carolina's continued growth.” For some low-income customers, however, the financial impact could be significantly greater. A $42 monthly credit available to qualifying customers through Duke's Customer Assistance Program is scheduled to expire at the end of December, just as the new rates take effect. Brooks said some of the programs that Durham families have relied on for help with utility bills have lost funding. “I know I'm struggling, so I can imagine how the seniors are going to be struggling with a fixed income,” Brooks said. The commission directed Duke to submit revised revenue calculations within 10 days of its orders and updated rate schedules for approval within 30 days. New rules for data centers For the first time, regulators established a separate electricity rate schedule for large data centers with power demands of at least 50 megawatts. The decision comes as artificial intelligence and cloud computing drive unprecedented growth in electricity demand across the Carolinas. Between March 2024 and April 2026, Duke signed contracts to provide 6.7 gigawatts of electricity capacity to new large customers in North Carolina and South Carolina. Data centers account for 92% of that contracted demand, according to the commission. Meeting that demand will require billions of dollars in new power plants, transmission lines and other infrastructure. Regulators found that Duke's existing and proposed billing structures did not adequately address the financial risks associated with that expansion. artigo.texto: Geral COP31 propõe controle de emissões de data centers O crescente impacto ambiental dos data centers entrou na mira de um novo pacto global lançado durante a COP31, em Antália, na Turquia. Batizado de Compromisso de Antália sobre Inteligência Artificial e articulado pela presidência turca junto à União Internacional de Telecomunicações (UIT) e à Unesco, o acordo, anunciado nesta terça-feira (17), busca frear a pegada ecológica da infraestrutura digital, exigindo maior eficiência energética e hídrica dos centros de processamento de dados. Articulado pela presidência turca em parceria com a União Internacional de Telecomunicações (UIT) e a Unesco, o acordo conta com a adesão do Brasil e incentiva o uso de energias limpas, a eficiência no consumo de água e energia, a economia circular e o descarte adequado de lixo eletrônico nos centros de processamento de dados. Embora tenha caráter voluntário e não estabeleça metas obrigatórias de corte de emissões, o pacto prevê acompanhamento anual nas conferências do clima até 2030. Além do Brasil, oito países aderiram ao pacto, incluindo Coreia do Sul e a gigante chinesa Alibaba. Entretanto, o acordo enfrenta dúvidas sobre seu alcance prático por não ter atraído as principais big techs dos Estados Unidos, maiores operadoras globais dessa infraestrutura. A iniciativa incentiva ainda o uso da própria IA para soluções climáticas, como previsão de eventos extremos, prevê apoio tecnológico a países em desenvolvimento e inclui medidas de proteção aos trabalhadores diante da automação — ponto alinhado a ações brasileiras como o programa Computadores para Inclusão e a proposta de sediar o Instituto de Inteligência Artificial para Mudanças Climáticas (AICI). Brasil é o 4º país a apresentar novo relatório de transparência do Acordo de Paris Também nesta terça-feira (17), o Brasil tornou-se a quarta nação do mundo a cumprir a etapa das regras de prestação de contas do Acordo de Paris. O principal destaque do levantamento é a queda de 27% nas emissões nacionais de gases de efeito estufa entre 2022 e 2024, resultado extraído da série histórica analisada desde 1990. Coordenado pelo Ministério da Ciência, Tecnologia e Inovação (MCTI) e aprovado pelo Comitê Interministerial sobre Mudança do Clima, o material integra dados científicos e resultados de políticas públicas em uma única publicação para dar mais agilidade aos processos. Além de detalhar o cumprimento das metas climáticas brasileiras, o relatório traz um diagnóstico sobre os riscos do aquecimento global e as estratégias de adaptação do país, reunindo também informações sobre educação ambiental, pesquisas científicas e as necessidades de financiamento e transferência de tecnologia. De acordo com a pasta, o documento, que foi submetido em inglês — idioma oficial da ONU —, terá em breve versão em português no portal do ministério e o conteúdo enviado passará pelo crivo de especialistas internacionais e por um fórum multilateral da convenção para revisão técnica. artigo.texto: Sutton residents continue ardent opposition to Kraft-backed data center At a packed planning board meeting in Sutton, Massachusetts, Monday night, residents were adamant in trying to convince the planning commission to shut down a Robert Kraft-backed data center proposal before it goes any further. The proposal from the Kraft Group and its Unified Global Packaging Group business involves building a massive data center on a former sand lot on the north side of Sutton. It would include 10 buildings and draw roughly 900 megawatts of power, which is enough to power a city. Residents said they are worried about that kind of drain on the power grid and on local water resources. They are also dreading the noise. "I'm frustrated that it's even being thought of as a possibility here," said Crystal Smith. Some residents are trying to fast-track an effort to shut the project down. Shawn Buzzell has launched a petition against the project. He already has signatures in the town of less than 10,000 residents. "I think that a development of a smaller scale might be something that the town would entertain," Buzzell said. "Just not in this fashion and not on this scale." The planning board meeting comes on the heels of a Select Board meeting that generated staunch opposition and public outcry over the project. "We are governing backwards. Right now as a town— we are taking steps out of order; we haven't done the proper action in the past to address this issue before a proposal like this arrived on our doorstep with a big red bow," said Sarah Osterman Stone. The planning board said Monday night that it's in no hurry and said they would not rule out a 1-year moratorium on data centers while they explore adding a bylaw. Like many towns, Sutton is facing a budget deficit, and the town select board says it's their responsibility to at least consider investments that would cover the gap and lower property taxes, posting a statement on the town website that reads in part: "Considering an opportunity is not the same as supporting it," the town said. "Our obligation is to understand it fully: its potential benefits, its potential costs, and its potential impacts. Only with that understanding can the Town, and ultimately Town Meeting, make an informed decision." The Kraft Group also released a statement, saying that it's always looking for meaningful, long-term economic investments: "We are committed to working collaboratively with local officials, residents and other stakeholders as the planning process moves forward to pursue a responsible development that delivers lasting benefits to the community. Most importantly, this project will only move forward if the community and the town of Sutton want it."

artigo.texto: Technology First Read An Electrician's Tale: Working on Data Center Projects Before Drawings Exist Mission critical schedules bring electrical contractors on before the design is close to construction ready, the first thing you contribute isn’t labor, but information. We get onboarded to data center projects that barely have drawings. Not bad drawings; no drawings at all. What exists may be early concepts or an intent somebody wrote down: we want a 300-MW facility, we think this area is going to be where the data halls are, these are the systems we’re thinking we’re going to leverage. No equipment spec. Architectural design isn’t figured out, either, so you can’t even start coordinating where things are going to go. And we’re on the project anyway. So, what are you contributing at that point? Not installation. Capacity, and people in the room. Where the Decisions Ultimately Get Made I think about in relation to the software development life cycle. A solution architect sits down with the customer and comes up with a grand idea. If all you do is hand that off to a developer, it’s really challenging for the developer to build it unless the documentation is phenomenal. A lot of these projects are at exactly that stage. You have an owner with high demands and a budget. You can’t just hand everything off to an engineer, and the engineer can’t just hand everything off to a contractor. There isn’t time for that. So, you bring everybody into the discussion upfront. That’s awareness of capacity. Awareness of lead times on material. Logistics. All the expertise a contractor can bring to steer a decision the right way — before the drawings get created, so those things don’t hit later. Because that’s what goes wrong on these jobs. Too many decisions get made without all the proper data or information that would have been valuable at the time, and they end up biting the project later. Get the stakeholders into the big-room discussions early and they can make what would have become an issue down the road nonexistent. Coordination Isn't a Project Phase Anymore Think about building a house. You don’t want the plumber and the tile guy scheduled in the bathroom at the same time. It’s sequenced. Put people on top of each other and you end up with more issues. Coordination used to run the same way: this group does their stuff in an area, then the next group gets that area, then the group after that. Installation still works that way. Coordination doesn’t. It’s moved to everybody getting all of their stuff in, coordinated together, in live models, and it all happens at the same time. You’re working the drawings side by side with the other groups, sharing continuous iterations of what can, should and shouldn’t be, and the answer keeps moving because the design is still moving. So being on the same platform, on the same file, is critical. You need the history tracked and the metadata attached, so you can see what changed and who changed it. That’s the piece a lot of tools in this space are thin on. We Moved This Off Paper 10 Years Ago About 10 years ago we recognized that field practice was printing out drawings and laying out the electrical scope with pens, paper and highlighters. That markup lived on that sheet. Drawing gets revised, you start over. So we moved that effort into the office, onto a digital platform — Bluebeam, in our case — and made it scalable. Drawing gets revised now, you slip sheet it and all your markups are retained. That became our single source of truth. The people doing it were field guys. We brought them into the office, and now they’re the pros at it. The Risk Lives in the Handoffs Follow the data through our process. It comes out of our building information modeling team. It hits the fab floor as a PDF: a sheet with the map of everything, and on the next page a 3D view they can spin without opening a model — Okay, this conduit’s on this side of the strut, it looked funny on the build sheet and here’s why. Then it goes to the crew receiving those assemblies in the field. At every one of those handoffs, somebody could be looking at the wrong version. We also just established a sister company focused on modular electrical construction. That makes all of this more critical, not less. The BIM team, the fab floor and the crew receiving the kit all have to be on the same set of files. Where it still falls short: our heavy use is on PC. When you want to hand a guy a set of drawings on a tablet and let him walk around, there isn’t a great solution yet that retains all the metadata. That’s a real gap. What the Technology is For Earlier this year I was at an AI and robotics conference, and the whole theme was the opposite of what people expect. It’s not replacing people. It’s the things humans can’t do, or shouldn’t do, for safety reasons. In our trade, think about energization: The gear is installed, commissioned, and now it’s getting turned on, and a human has to get into an insanely big suit that is hopefully going to protect their life. My safety director wouldn’t appreciate the word “hopefully,” but it’s a huge risk. Nobody wants to do that, and nobody should have to, if there are other options. Technology in construction should be the same idea. It should increase productivity or increase the availability of the right information. That second one is where this industry has had a lot of its issues — getting the right information to the point of installation when it’s needed. That’s where technology helps, if it’s done the right way. It Isn't One Thing People ask what I’d tell another electrical contractor before their first data center job, like there’s one thing. There isn’t. Is your local labor force ready for the scale of the project? Are you set up for modeling and prefab? because these jobs typically require it. Can your schedule hold? artigo.texto: Resumo - Data centers nos EUA oferecem vagas com salários acima de US$ 100 mil por ano - Faltam técnicos para refrigeração, racks, parte elétrica e fibra óptica - Treinamentos de dois dias já terminam com cerimônia de diploma - Amazon, Google, Meta e Microsoft oferecem cursos gratuitos e acelerados - Falta de mão de obra supera qualquer freio na construção civil do setor - Muitos americanos nem sabem que esses empregos existem Nos Estados Unidos, a construção da infraestrutura de inteligência artificial criou um gargalo inesperado: faltam técnicos. Na disputa por profissionais, empresas de tecnologia já oferecem vagas com remuneração acima de US$ 100 mil por ano. E parte dessas contratações recai sobre pessoas que acabaram de concluir cursos relâmpago. A trajetória pode ser rápida: bastam dois dias de formação para que os alunos recebam seus diplomas numa solenidade. Mal o certificado fica pronto e as companhias, sedentas por mão de obra, já brigam pelos novos profissionais. Por que faltam técnicos Para dar conta da demanda disparada pela tecnologia, as companhias precisam de gente capaz de montar os sistemas de refrigeração, instalar racks de servidores, lidar com equipamentos elétricos e puxar os cabos de fibra óptica que sustentam os data centers. O problema é que encontrar profissionais com essas habilidades virou um desafio. Ainda que o ambiente político em torno da IA venha se transformando, sobretudo após as últimas eleições de meio de mandato, a falta de trabalhadores pesa mais do que qualquer eventual desaceleração nas obras. Diante disso, o setor vem se organizando para formar e contratar quem possa preencher essas vagas. Cursos gratuitos e salários de seis dígitos Diferentes origens respondem pela qualificação desses trabalhadores. Para capacitar nas habilidades técnicas que a edificação de data centers requer, cursos rápidos e sem custo são oferecidos por entidades sem fins lucrativos, por plataformas de ensino digital e pelas quatro gigantes da nuvem com inteligência artificial: Amazon, Google, Meta e Microsoft. Há posições nesse setor cuja remuneração chega à casa dos seis dígitos. Mesmo assim, a maioria dos americanos nem imagina que empregos assim estejam disponíveis. Javonntae Hill é um exemplo de quem entrou nesse universo. Formado em design de videogames e na casa dos 30 anos, ele procurava uma carreira, mas não tinha clareza de por onde começar.

artigo.texto: Ford has started producing lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries for its Fathom electric pickup truck at a Michigan plant. InsideEVs reported on Nov. 18, local time, that Ford has begun manufacturing mass-production-grade LFP battery packs at BlueOval Battery Park Michigan in Marshall, Michigan, a few hours west of Detroit. The batteries produced this time will first be installed in Fathom prototypes. Full-scale mass production is expected to begin next year. For Ford, it marked a turning point in bringing the battery supply chain into the United States alongside development of a new electric pickup. The plant was presented as the first case in the United States of local production of LFP batteries used in vehicles for mass-market consumers. LG Energy Solution also produces LFP batteries in the United States, but its supply is for stationary energy storage systems for GM and Tesla. Ford’s 2 million-square-foot facility is dedicated to automotive LFP batteries. Production capacity was also spelled out. Annual capacity is 20 gigawatt-hours, and the plant can make 50 battery packs per hour. It has a vertically integrated structure in which finished battery packs come out after lithium and iron phosphate powder are fed in. Key processes, including production of anode and cathode materials, are carried out inside the plant. Ford sees the plant as a core facility directly tied to the Fathom launch schedule. Allan Clarke (앨런 클라크), vice president of Ford Advanced Development Projects, said at a media briefing, "Ford is moving quickly to launch the Fathom." He said Ford built a new universal EV platform, a new production system at the Louisville assembly plant and a U.S. LFP battery production system in a short period. He said building a battery plant, a unicastings plant and a highly automated vehicle production facility in less than five years is faster than the pace in China. A licensing deal with China’s CATL underpins the plant’s technology. Ford established the production system by adopting CATL’s battery technology. Ford owns and operates the plant, while CATL engineers supported setup of complex production equipment, worker training and establishment of a quality-control system. Ford explained that the prismatic LFP cells for the Fathom are Ford-specific specifications, not CATL’s existing global product lineup. Ford said the plant also meets requirements under the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA). It said raw materials used for battery production are not sourced from entities designated by the U.S. government as a foreign entity of concern. It said that while the technology came from CATL, the core materials are structured not to rely on sources of concern to the United States such as China, Russia and North Korea. Meng Wang (멍 왕), head of battery cell industrialisation and chief engineer at Ford, said of the background to cooperation with CATL, "To reduce time to market, we decided to learn from a top-tier partner." He added that CATL transferred key knowledge to Ford, including equipment functions, manufacturing processes and quality control. A future timeline was also laid out. Fathom preorders will begin in early 2027, and production and deliveries are expected to begin by the end of next year. Ford will therefore put to the test both commercialisation of an electric pickup backed by lower-cost batteries and localisation of battery production in the United States.

The 2026 midterms didn’t only swell the ranks of progressives and green economic populists in Congress — they also ushered in a stunning number of Native American leaders in down-ballot races across the country. Among the state legislative races involving Indigenous candidates that have been called so far, Native American candidates won 83 percent of the time, according to ICT. Montana led the way: 12 of 13 Indigenous candidates there, all Democrats, won legislative seats, including Natalie Weeks-O’Neal (Fort Peck Assiniboine and Sioux) in House District 31 and Katie Fire Thunder (Oglala Lakota) in House District 59. In Nevada, Brian Wadsworth, a former Pyramid Lake Paiute Tribal Council member, won a seat on the Washoe County Commission representing the county’s rural north, becoming the first tribal member from any of the county’s tribal nations to serve on it, Wadsworth told Truthout. Native Republicans won too, including Emily McIntire (Muscogee) in Oregon and Heather Ellison (Navajo) in New Mexico. In Alaska, Mary Peltola defeated the incumbent to became the first Native person to represent the state in the U.S. Senate. Many of these candidates spoke to voters’ concerns on the campaign trail about the affordability of groceries and health care. In Northern Nevada, voters also raised concerns about water, land, and unchecked growth. And the offices these candidates won are increasingly in locales where fights over land, water, and AI data centers get decided, as the federal government weakens its obligation to consult tribes. “We have about 120 proposed hyperscale data centers for Indian Country,” said Krystal Two Bulls, executive director of environmental advocacy group Honor the Earth. Locally, “these fights are currently being fought and won,” Two Bulls told Truthout. A U.S. Senate permitting bill, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, despite its name, focuses on narrowing environmental review processes and threatens tribal consultation on projects affecting tribal water, land, and cultural sites. “That’s pretty much going to gut any kind of protections or legs that tribes can stand on to push back against these corporations,” said Two Bulls. The bill passed a preliminary vote on November 9 but has yet to clear the next hurdle in the Senate. National wins among Native politicians could augur change at the state level, especially in states with multiple Indigenous candidate victories. Montana’s wins were historic: “It’s not lost on us that we’re making history, being the largest American Indian caucus in the United States at the state level,” said Weeks-O’Neal, adding that the state’s main media has yet to cover this fact. Two Bulls expressed hope that the Indigenous bloc will be able to exert real leverage, saying: “They can actually throw a lot of wrenches into the fast tracking that’s currently happening.” Despite Two Bulls’ forward-looking ambitions for the new class of Native politicians, especially around AI, Weeks-O’Neal faces extant costs to her district: The Zortman mines, which extracted gold from the Little Rocky Mountains in the 1980s and ’90s, contaminated Montana’s water and still cost $3 million a year to treat. “The water is devastated. It is tainted in perpetuity. That means forever,” she said. “Whatever profit was made from the mine, I mean, I can’t imagine.” The site has been re-listed for $52.5 million with geologists estimating “that only 20% of the gold and silver [was] harvested, leaving plenty of reserves for investors or operators,” the listing states. House District 31 includes much of the Fort Peck Reservation, whose median age is 30 and median household income is roughly $53,000, far below the national median of around $87,000. It’s no surprise then that voters’ primary concern is affordability, especially groceries. “They were struggling to even feed their families,” said Weeks-O’Neal. Trump’s administration has moved to slash the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, which could cut off access for 6.3 million people nationally. Meanwhile Katie Fire Thunder’s constituents in South Bozeman, which is one of the wealthiest areas in the state, are also worried about affordability: Rising property taxes, driven by soaring land values, are creating a crisis for retirees on fixed incomes who are being priced out of homes they’d expected to keep for life. “That tax burden is being shifted on to residential and property owners,” she said, joining the call alongside Weeks-O’Neal. Rep. Thedis Crowe (Blackfeet), reelected in House District 15, which borders Canada and includes part of the Blackfeet Reservation, said protecting the water compacts negotiated by the Blackfeet Nation and the Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes is a top priority, because both are “headwaters tribes.” He said data center bills expected in the coming session will force lawmakers to weigh impacts on rural and tribal communities, and on water quality. Weeks-O’Neal said too many of those decisions in Montana have been left to counties, which she said “is just way too much power given to county entities,” and that it was part of why she ran for the Montana House of Representatives. In northern Nevada, that county power is exactly what Brian Wadsworth just won. Wadsworth lives in Nixon, on the Pyramid Lake Paiute Reservation, about an hour from Reno. Rush-hour traffic along I-80 by the area’s industrial center was once quite rare, he said. Now, “it’s literally a daily occurrence,” something “that we haven’t seen in our lifetimes.” Wadsworth told Truthout that voters are fed up with unchecked growth and have been asking cities to examine the area’s economic growth and really grapple with infrastructure issues. “We definitely have a lack of adequate roads here in Washoe County,” said Wadsworth. artigo.texto: Economia Brasil pode contestar restrições dos EUA à venda de chips para data centers O governo do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva está considerando a possibilidade de questionar as novas limitações impostas pelos Estados Unidos sobre a comercialização de chips avançados de inteligência artificial destinados a data centers no Brasil. Essa medida, anunciada nesta segunda-feira, colocou o Brasil entre cinco países que precisarão de autorização do governo americano para importar esses componentes, utilizados em grandes centros de processamento de dados. Fontes próximas ao governo dizem que uma possível negociação com os EUA ou contestação das regras ainda está em aberto. Por enquanto, o tema não gerou grande preocupação dentro do Executivo, e não há uma decisão tomada sobre eventuais respostas à decisão dos americanos. Os Estados Unidos detêm um controle significativo sobre a fabricação e distribuição desses chips, que são essenciais para o funcionamento de sistemas avançados de inteligência artificial, o que lhes confere forte influência sobre o comércio internacional desse mercado. Os data centers são locais que reúnem servidores e equipamentos responsáveis por armazenar e processar grandes quantidades de informações. Com o avanço da inteligência artificial, esses centros passaram a exigir chips mais potentes, capazes de realizar os cálculos necessários para desenvolver e operar essas tecnologias. A nova regulamentação foi divulgada pelo Departamento de Comércio dos Estados Unidos e também inclui Indonésia, Malásia, Cingapura e Tailândia. O objetivo é evitar que empresas chinesas acessem tecnologia americana por meio de centros de dados instalados em outros países, burlando as restrições já impostas por Washington. Desde 2022, os EUA limitam a venda de chips avançados para a China, exigindo autorização para a exportação de certos componentes e equipamentos usados na fabricação desses chips. Em 2023, as regras foram reforçadas e agora abrangem novas exigências para países que o governo americano considera mais vulneráveis ao uso indevido dessas tecnologias. Membros do governo brasileiro apontam que anteriormente houve preocupação com a possível escassez de chips no mercado global, devido ao aumento da demanda por equipamentos para inteligência artificial, mas essa preocupação foi superada. Segundo as novas regras, as empresas afetadas terão que obter licenças do governo dos EUA para importar determinados chips avançados. A regulamentação prevê exceções para empresas baseadas nos Estados Unidos, desde que cumpram os requisitos de fornecimento de informações, e determina que os pedidos de autorização serão analisados caso a caso pelas autoridades americanas.

artigo.texto: The San Joaquin County Board of Supervisors has extended its moratorium on the development of hyperscale data centers in the unincorporated County for an additional 10 months and 15 days. The move allows time for a comprehensive review of potential environmental and economic consequences and opportunities for community input. “We owe our residents answers before allowing development that could have negative consequences for our environment and economy,” said Chair and Third District Supervisor Sonny Dhaliwal. “This extension gives us the time needed to thoroughly evaluate the potential effects of these large-scale facilities and ensure that any future decisions reflect the best interests of our communities.” Traditional data centers store, manage, and process digital information, while artificial intelligence (AI) data centers are designed to support the intensive computing demands of developing and operating AI systems. These facilities can require substantial electricity, water, and infrastructure resources, raising important questions about their long-term effects on surrounding communities. Last month, the Board adopted an interim urgency ordinance establishing a temporary moratorium and directed the Community Development Department (CDD) to conduct an initial 10-day review of AI data centers. Following that review, CDD presented its preliminary findings and recommended extending the moratorium to allow for a more comprehensive evaluation. During the extension, CDD will examine the experiences of other jurisdictions, conduct community outreach with stakeholders, assess potential demands on local resources, and explore regulatory options. The department will also work with a consultant to prepare a more detailed analysis to help guide future policy decisions. “We simply don’t have enough information to make an informed decision on something that could have lasting consequences for our community,” said CDD Director Jennifer Jolley. CDD is expected to present its comprehensive report to the Board in June 2027.

artigo.texto: Monticello data center proposal leaves homeowner, buyer facing big losses MONTICELLO, Minn. (FOX 9) - A proposed hyperscale data center in Monticello has one homeowner ready to leave and another buyer starting over. Homeowner says proposed project changed everything What we know: Kathy Cohen said she moved into her Monticello house in February, not long after her husband died, so she could be closer to her grandchildren after moving from Hopkins. She said she did not know that a proposed 3 million-square-foot hyperscale data center was planned blocks away and said her realtor never brought it up. "It never even occurred to me that they would have this in the works, or I would’ve never bought this house," she said. Cohen said possible future construction would be too disruptive, and she said she also worries about the environmental impact. She said she has been told she could lose as much as $50,000 if she sells, but she still plans to move. Cohen also said she plans to disclose the project to prospective buyers when she lists the house. Buyer says backing out could cost $30,000 What they're saying: Rebecca Webeck said she and her two sons recently signed a purchase agreement for a brand-new house in Monticello. But after they learned it was near the proposed data center site, they pulled out of the sale and now expect to lose as much as $30,000. "With me being disabled and my boys helping with my medical stuff, it took us a while to get to this point, and so it’s devastating for us to have to completely start over again and lose all that money," she said. Webeck also said her realtor never said anything about the proposed project. She said the experience will make her ask much more directly about data centers in future home searches. Attorney says disclosure rules are limited What's the law: Rob Shainess, an Edina-based real estate attorney, said there is no law that specifically requires realtors to tell buyers about proposed data center projects. But he said state law does require them to share anything they know that could adversely affect a buyer’s use and enjoyment of a home. That leaves key questions about whether either realtor knew about the proposal and whether they knew it would negatively impact the property. Shainess said buyers probably do not have any legal recourse because proposed projects are not final and "any impact on the property is amorphous and only potential." The Source: FOX 9's Mike Manzoni interviewed Kathy Cohen and Rebecca Webeck and spoke with a real estate attorney.

artigo.texto: Hitachi Energy fecha primeiro contrato de IA para energia de data center no Brasil Acordo com a BCR-i prevê manutenção preditiva em subestação de 560 MVA que atende data center no estado de São Paulo. A Hitachi Energy assinou seu primeiro contrato HMAX Energy no Brasil com a BCR-i Brasil para implementar um sistema de monitoramento e manutenção preditiva em uma subestação de 560 MVA que atende um data center no estado de São Paulo. O acordo prevê o uso de IA para analisar as condições dos equipamentos elétricos e identificar riscos de falhas operacionais. A solução combina informações coletadas dos ativos elétricos, monitoramento em tempo quase real e modelos analíticos para orientar intervenções técnicas. Segundo a Hitachi Energy, o serviço busca substituir parte das rotinas de manutenção baseadas em intervalos predeterminados por procedimentos orientados pelas condições dos equipamentos. Subestação atende infraestrutura digital A instalação é operada pela BCR-i Brasil, grupo especializado em gestão de infraestrutura e serviços técnicos, e a capacidade de 560 MVA corresponde à potência aparente da subestação. Raphael Campos, Head de Operação e Manutenção da BCR-i Brasil, afirma que o contrato permitirá integrar os serviços de operação elétrica da companhia às ferramentas de análise de dados fornecidas pela Hitachi Energy. “Garantir a máxima confiabilidade no fornecimento de energia é fundamental para atender a setores que exigem alta disponibilidade, como os data centers”, afirma o executivo. A Hitachi Energy ficará responsável pelo fornecimento do HMAX Energy, que reúne serviços de acompanhamento técnico e ferramentas de IA aplicadas à gestão dos ativos durante seu ciclo de vida. “Os data centers estão no centro da era da IA e operam com a expectativa de 100% de disponibilidade. Isso exige uma transformação na forma como a infraestrutura energética é gerenciada, incorporando mais inteligência, capacidade de antecipação e integração”, diz Fernanda Alves, gerente do Service Hub para a América Latina na Hitachi Energy. Expansão pressiona demanda por energia O acordo ocorre em meio ao crescimento da infraestrutura de processamento e armazenamento de dados no Brasil, associado à expansão da computação em nuvem e das aplicações de IA. Segundo projeções da Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE) citadas pelas empresas, o consumo de eletricidade no Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN) deverá crescer 4% ao ano até 2030, quando a carga elétrica total poderá atingir 98,8 GW. A expansão dos data centers é apontada como um dos fatores de aumento da demanda. A continuidade do fornecimento elétrico é um requisito operacional dessas instalações, que dependem de energia para servidores, sistemas de armazenamento, equipamentos de rede e refrigeração. Nesse contexto, o modelo contratado pela BCR-i busca identificar alterações no desempenho dos componentes elétricos antes que provoquem interrupções nos serviços. (Com assessoria de imprensa)

artigo.texto: Advanced graphene architectures have demonstrated an enhancement of 30 to 50 percent in energy storage performance compared to conventional electrode materials, addressing long-standing limitations in device capacity, charge kinetics, and operational longevity. In an extensive technical review published in the Journal of Materials Science: Materials in Energy, researchers Jahanvi Thakur and Shreya systematically evaluated the synthesis methodologies, intrinsic physical characteristics, and device implementations of graphene-based materials. The investigation encompasses electrochemical storage platforms including supercapacitors, lithium-ion batteries, sodium-ion batteries, and solid-state systems. Conventional energy technologies frequently encounter severe engineering trade-offs, such as limited energy densities, slow charge and discharge rates, restricted cycle lives, and material degradation caused by mechanical stress during prolonged cycling. Graphene, structured as an atomically thin two-dimensional honeycomb sheet of carbon atoms, provides a versatile physical foundation capable of mitigating these technical bottlenecks across multiple commercial and industrial sectors. The extraordinary baseline physical characteristics of graphene provide the foundational rationale for its electrochemical efficacy across diverse energy conversion and storage platforms. Monolayer graphene possesses a theoretical specific surface area of approximately 2630 square meters per gram, establishing an expansive interface for electrostatic charge accumulation and active electrochemical species interaction. In terms of electronic transport, the delocalization of pi-electrons across the hexagonal carbon lattice facilitates ballistic carrier movement, yielding electrical conductivities as high as 10 to the sixth power Siemens per meter, which exceeds that of metallic copper by more than a factor of one hundred. Graphene also displays an exceptional thermal conductivity of approximately 5000 Watts per meter-Kelvin, allowing devices to dissipate high thermal fluxes generated during intense charge and discharge cycles, alongside a thermal stability that resists degradation at temperatures exceeding 3000 degrees Celsius in inert environments. Mechanically, graphene exhibits a tensile strength reaching 130 gigapascals and an elastic strain tolerance of 20 percent, ensuring robust mechanical resilience against the destructive stresses that typically accompany repeated electrochemical cycling. Synthesis methodologies strongly dictate the structural integrity, sheet morphology, defect distribution, and final electrochemical capabilities of graphene-derived materials. Chemical vapor deposition stands as the premier fabrication route for growing continuous, large-area monolayer and bilayer graphene films characterized by high crystalline order and minimal defect concentrations. Operative at temperatures between 800 and 1000 degrees Celsius, chemical vapor deposition decomposes carbon-bearing precursors such as methane, ethylene, or acetylene over catalytic transition metal substrates, notably copper and nickel foils. The resulting films achieve sheet resistances as low as 20 ohms per square, electrical conductivities between 10 to the fifth and 10 to the sixth Siemens per meter, and Raman intensity ratios of the defect-induced D-band to the graphitic G-band below 0.1. However, the requirement for high thermal budgets, specialized catalyst substrates, and delicate post-growth metal etching processes introduces mechanical defects that complicate cost-effective, large-scale industrial device manufacturing. To overcome throughput limitations inherent to vapor deposition, wet-chemical, mechanical, and thermal exfoliation techniques provide scalable pathways for bulk graphene manufacturing. The chemical reduction of graphene oxide derived through modified Hummers oxidation of graphite remains one of the most accessible approaches, producing functionalized reduced graphene oxide flakes. This route relies on reducing agents such as hydrazine, sodium borohydride, or ascorbic acid to restore conjugated carbon networks, though incomplete reduction often leaves residual oxygen-containing functionalities that modulate electrical conductivity. Complementary hydrothermal and solvothermal approaches treat graphene oxide dispersions in sealed autoclaves at temperatures between 150 and 250 degrees Celsius, where reactive organic solvents provide elevated reduction degrees, yielding highly conductive powders suitable for ink formulation and composite manufacturing. The transition toward environmentally sustainable manufacturing has motivated the development of biomass-derived graphene and green synthesis protocols utilizing agricultural waste and organic residues. Thermal processing routes, including high-temperature pyrolysis in inert atmospheres and hydrothermal carbonization in aqueous media, successfully convert forestry and agricultural wastes into functional carbon structures. Quantitatively, biomass-derived graphene materials exhibit electrical conductivities ranging from 10 to the second to 10 to the fourth Siemens per meter, specific surface areas spanning 500 to 1800 square meters per gram, and Raman defect ratios between 0.8 and 1.3. Although these values reflect greater disorder than pristine chemical vapor deposition films, the resultant hierarchical porosity, structural vacancies, and heteroatom sites accelerate ionic diffusion pathways and generate additional electrochemically active charge storage centers. Sustainable synthesis strategies also incorporate the direct electrochemical reduction of carbon dioxide and the utilization of biodegradable solvents, establishing circular production paradigms that reduce reliance on toxic reagents. artigo.texto: New Delhi/Mumbai: The Maharashtra Government on Tuesday announced the country's first sulphur dioxide (SO2) emissions trading scheme to improve air quality. The scheme will be implemented by the Maharashtra Pollution Control Board (MPCB) in collaboration with Emissions Market Accelerator, Environment and Climate Change Minister Pankaja Munde said. Speaking at an event in Mumbai, Munde said the government wanted to develop, in collaboration with industries, solutions that balance environmental protection with economic development. Under the emissions trading scheme, participating industrial units will be given permits specifying their permissible sulphur dioxide emissions. Industries that can reduce emissions at a lower cost will be able to make additional reductions and sell their surplus permits, while those facing higher costs of emission reduction can purchase them, an official release said. Michael Greenstone, professor of economics at the University of Chicago, director of the Energy Policy Institute and co-chair of Emissions Market Accelerator, said research had shown that market-based schemes could achieve effective emission reductions while lowering the cost of pollution control for industries. The MPCB and the University of Chicago Trust also signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) to use artificial intelligence and machine learning in environmental regulation and industrial inspections. The initiative will be implemented through the Energy Policy Institute at the University of Chicago India. Under the agreement, the two institutions will jointly develop and pilot an AI-based framework for environmental inspections. The system will analyse data available with the MPCB to identify industrial units that are more likely to violate environmental regulations, the release said. Training programmes will also be organised for MPCB officials and field inspectors on AI, environmental data analysis and the use of modern technologies. A decision on expanding the system across Maharashtra will be taken based on the findings of the pilot project. artigo.texto: Demand for electricity to power data centers is hindering the state’s plans to reduce pollution and fight climate change. Under an ambitious law signed by Gov. JB Pritzker in 2021, the state set out to retire all fossil-fuel power plants between now and 2050. Stream NBC 5 for free, 24/7, wherever you are. But big new data centers are requiring so much electricity that it’s become difficult for the state to shut down all coal, gas and oil sources used to meet demand, a pair of state reports released Monday found. The reports confirmed fears that environmental and climate advocates have had for more than a year. Cleaner sources of power, including wind and solar farms, are not being built quickly enough to keep up with the new demands from the data centers being used to power artificial intelligence. That’s bad news for the planet because oil, gas and coal create carbon dioxide, the major contributor to global warming. The same pollution causing climate change is also bad for our health, causing respiratory problems and exacerbating a number of other threats. “Fossil fuel power plants emit thousands of tons of lung-damaging chemicals,” said Brian Urbaszewski, director of environmental health at Respiratory Health Association in Chicago. “These are chemicals that have an immediate and harmful effect on people.” In central and southern Illinois, seven coal plants still operate. The goal has been to shut four of them down by 2030 and that goal remains, according to one of the two reports. Three publicly owned coal-fired plants have longer timelines before they are closed. Local Eleven so-called peaker plants, which burn oil or natural gas as power backups, were expected to close in 2030 or 2031. But power demands from data centers mean those plants should continue to operate until 2033 to help prevent blackouts, the report recommends. Those peaker plants are limited-use, oil-fueled or gas-power sources shut down for most days in any given year, but are designed to guard against blackouts and can be fired up when energy use is peaking, like on the hottest day of the year, when many air conditioners are running. In Chicago, peakers are still active at the long-closed Fisk coal-fired power plant in Pilsen. There are also peakers in Waukegan, where a former coal plant that has operated for more than 90 years will keep operating until 2033 under the state recommendation. “That’s disappointing,” said Mayra Mendez, executive director of Clean Power Lake County. She said the Waukegan peakers produce strong smells that cause a burning sensation in the nose. “Our community is tired of dirty energy.” Some advocates feared the state would recommend building new natural gas plants but that is not being advised, state officials said. The state will continue to rely on nuclear power and upgrades to plants in hopes of producing more energy which is free of carbon dioxide, according to the reports. Enough power for now Illinois is not running out of power yet but the forecast for data centers is so large, and the operations potentially being built so quickly, the situation could create an emergency to provide more electricity. Each new hyperscale data center can require enough electricity to power a mid-sized city. State lawmakers in Springfield are expected to debate the impact of data centers and power demand, possibly next month. Hearings on the state findings are expected later. The reports are the Resource Adequacy Mitigation Plan released by the Illinois Power Agency and the Illinois Environmental Protection Agency and the Integrated Resource Plan, released by the Illinois Commerce Commission.

artigo.texto: Publicidade O setor de data centers no Brasil pode enfrentar um combo desafiador nos próximos meses. De um lado, os Estados Unidos aprovaram a exigência de restrições para a exportação de chips avançados de inteligência artificial com destino para diversos países, dentre eles, o Brasil. Do outro, as taxas de juros devem seguir elevadas por mais tempo que o esperado, pressionando investimentos. Para o Morgan Stanley, entretanto, o setor brasileiro de data centers seguem sustentando uma perspectiva positiva. De acordo com o banco, as tendências estruturais de adoção de IA e computação em nuvem (Cloud) devem compensar os obstáculos de natureza cíclica decorrentes desses desafios. Ainda que a nova regra dos EUA determine que o envio de chips ocorra através de uma licença governamental de exportação, o país já deixou claro que as solicitações serão avaliadas caso a caso. Além disso, poderá ser aplicada uma exceção condicional à regra para exportações destinadas a usuários finais (ou empresas controladoras) com sede nos Estados Unidos. Anthropic desafia a turbulência do mercado e se aproxima do maior IPO da história Mesmo com a queda das ações de tecnologia, dona do Claude vê demanda sete vezes superior à oferta, pode captar mais de US$ 90 bilhões e estrear avaliada em cerca de US$ 1,4 trilhão Goldman Sachs rebaixa Brasil por crescimento fraco e ‘pouco espaço’ para cortar juros Esses fatores reduzem as chances de uma recuperação rápida da Bolsa e justificam uma postura mais defensiva De acordo com os analistas do Morgan, essa exceção poderá fazer toda a diferença. Segundo estimativa do banco, mais de 60% da capacidade adicional esperada para o Brasil é controlada por entidades norte-americanas, o que poderá mitigar os impactos sobre os data centers nacionais. Desafios administráveis Com as restrições ou não, o Morgan Stanley já havia publicado uma visão positiva para o setor brasileiro de data centers, sustentada por três pilares. Continua depois da publicidade De acordo com o banco, o setor tem contado com tendências estruturais de crescimento da demanda doméstica, fatores externos favoráveis e, ainda, uma boa administração dos impactos das taxas de juros mais altas. Neste último caso, o banco destaca o posicionamento positivo do presidente Lula em relação ao arcabouço fiscal mais favorável aos data centers locais. Para o Morgan, esse posicionamento deve permanecer durante o quarto mandato. Além disso, ainda que a volatilidade do cenário macroeconômico e das taxas de juros represente um obstáculo para o setor, os analistas observam que as variáveis nas quais o Brasil apresenta vantagens competitivas são mais importantes para a expansão da capacidade instalada do que os custos mais elevados de financiamento. Continua depois da publicidade Mesmo com os desafios macroeconômicos, pesquisas realizadas pelo próprio Morgan Stanley mostram que Cloud (computação em nuvem) e IA estão entre as categorias de gastos com tecnologia que mais crescem e apresentam maior resiliência no Brasil. A estimativa do banco é de que o consumo doméstico de serviços de computação em nuvem cresce cerca de 26% ao ano, na comparação anual. Ao mesmo tempo, apenas quase 40% desse consumo é gerenciado localmente. Segundo o banco, essa baixa capacidade de processamento local, combinada ao potencial de atrair cargas de trabalho internacionais provenientes de países que não estão sujeitos às restrições, deve sustentar uma trajetória robusta de crescimento para a indústria brasileira de data centers nos próximos anos. artigo.texto: Criticism of data centers is less about the physical building infrastructure and more about the public’s broad concerns about artificial intelligence and tech companies, according to several University of Virginia studies. Maura Austin, a research scientist at the University of Virginia’s National Security Institute, said that as data center pushback has intensified over the last few months, it’s largely been bipartisan. But, Austin said, people are thinking about data centers “as combined with their thoughts on AI, and they are harboring a strong distrust for the federal government and for Big Tech as well. And those feelings of distrust translate into an uneasiness about the future and about the economic instability that they believe is being wrought by AI and the developments there, and they’re taking out that unease in their resistance to data centers.” Broadly, Austin said, many people have a negative feeling about data centers but can’t explain why. As a result, they point to the physical buildings. There are hundreds of data centers across Northern Virginia, and many are in Loudoun County. In some cases, local governments are working to change the way data center projects are approved, in an effort to slow their growth. Generally, Austin said, residents who live close to new data center projects don’t envision benefits locally. “They don’t expect data centers to bring jobs,” Austin said. “They don’t expect to experience any more benefits from AI by having a data center close by, which makes sense. I don’t think that you get faster access to AI models just because you have a data center down the street.” There are concerns about noise, water usage and data centers driving up energy bills, Austin said, which means data centers are “occupying this particularly tricky space, where they are not bringing any known benefits to the local community, and they are bringing a lot of expectations for costs and burdens.” Some tech companies, Austin said, are working to make water use more transparent or taking responsibility for energy infrastructure and announcing they’ll absorb the costs. But, based on the studies’ findings, “What people are looking for is to feel more secure in their economic futures,” she said. Spending on proenvironmental efforts, local libraries or schools, or direct payments to households would all increase support for data center projects, Austin said the research found. Direct payments to households were the best-performing initiative to increase the public’s support for data centers. “We’re relying on the acceptance of the people in these communities in order to continue this critical infrastructure build-out, and the way forward is to meet the people at the negotiations table, and that means listening to their concerns and listening to their needs,” Austin said. artigo.texto: EUA fecham a brecha do acesso remoto: data centers no exterior precisarão de licença para servir a China O Departamento de Comércio publicou nesta segunda (16) uma regra provisória que exige licença sempre que um data center, em qualquer país, fornecer mais de 12 milhões de TPP a empresas sediadas na China, Macau e outros destinos restritos. O Brasil entra numa lista separada de cinco países. O Departamento de Comércio dos Estados Unidos publicou nesta segunda-feira, 16 de novembro de 2026, uma regra provisória — uma *interim final rule* — desenhada para impedir que empresas chinesas tenham acesso a chips avançados de inteligência artificial por via remota. O alvo é uma brecha conhecida: em vez de comprar ou receber fisicamente o equipamento, a empresa aluga capacidade computacional em data centers fora dos Estados Unidos, inclusive em países que não estão sujeitos às mesmas restrições. Abaixo, o que exatamente a regra exige, os dois mecanismos que ela cria — o limite de capacidade computacional e a lista de cinco países que inclui o Brasil —, o que fica de fora, o que acontece a partir de agora e por que o anúncio cai justamente na semana em que Xi e Trump se encontram. 1 · O que foi publicado, em resumo Ponto de atenção — a regra não proíbe chips nem data centers. Ela cria uma etapa burocrática: a licença. Quem precisa dela é quem exporta, reexporta ou transfere o equipamento sabendo que ele alimentará um data center que dará volume relevante de computação a empresas de um grupo restrito. Sem licença, a operação não pode acontecer — e a análise é caso a caso, não automática. 2 · Como a brecha funcionava A lógica é simples e foi explicada por praticamente toda a cobertura. Os Estados Unidos já impediam que empresas chinesas comprassem os chips de IA mais avançados — aqueles fabricados por companhias como a Nvidia — e que os recebessem em território chinês. O que não estava igualmente controlado era o caminho indireto: uma empresa chinesa pode contratar, em Singapura ou na Malásia, o uso de um data center equipado com esses mesmos chips americanos. Nada é exportado para a China; só a capacidade de computação é acessada por rede. A formulação do próprio BIS, no comunicado que acompanha a regra, é esta: “A regra foi desenhada para garantir que as restrições existentes ao acesso à tecnologia americana sensível não possam ser contornadas por meio de arranjos de computação remota envolvendo data centers em países terceiros.” O que dá nome ao problema é o volume. Vinte mil chips em um data center estrangeiro não mudam nada; um data center configurado para servir grandes volumes de computação a um único cliente chinês, sim. É essa diferença de escala que a regra tenta capturar com um limite numérico, em vez de tentar controlar toda operação de nuvem. 3 · O primeiro mecanismo: o limite de 12 milhões de TPP O coração da regra é um número. A unidade de medida é o TPP — *total processing performance*, a métrica que o controle de exportação americano usa para medir a potência de um chip de computação avançada. A partir de agora, quando o exportador sabe que o equipamento irá para um data center que fornecerá mais de 12 milhões de TPP agregados a uma empresa restrita, a licença é obrigatória. Alguns pontos importantes sobre como esse limite funciona: · O cálculo é agregado: soma a capacidade dos chips, e não a de um chip isolado. · A soma vale para um data center ou para data centers interligados, que compartilhem recursos como um sistema único — o que impede a fragmentação artificial do volume entre instalações. · Quem é alcançado pela regra: empresas sediadas na China, em Macau ou em países do chamado Grupo D:5, e também empresas cujo controlador final tenha sede nesses lugares. · A regra alcança o acesso indireto: um cliente que esteja fora do grupo restrito entra no escopo quando treina modelos para uma empresa alcançada, participa desse treinamento ou fornece modelos a ela. A comparação que ajuda a dimensionar o limite: 12 milhões de TPP correspondem, aproximadamente, à capacidade máxima de cerca de 750 chips Nvidia H100 ou H200. Não é um limiar baixo — é um volume de cluster, e não o uso individual de nuvem. 4 · O segundo mecanismo: a lista de cinco países A regra tem uma segunda parte, independente da primeira. Ela passa a exigir licença para exportar, reexportar ou transferir semicondutores avançados cobertos pelo controle com destino a cinco países: A justificativa oficial é que esses países “apresentam risco de desvio acima do normal”. Para os três primeiros — Indonésia, Malásia e Singapura —, há um motivo específico: são os três centros da rede da Megaspeed, a empresa que estaria comprando milhares de chips da Nvidia para fornecer capacidade computacional a empresas chinesas e, com isso, contornar as restrições já existentes. Há uma exceção relevante nessa parte da regra: a exigência de licença não se aplica a chips destinados a empresas sediadas nos Estados Unidos ou cujo controlador final tenha sede americana, desde que cumpridos os requisitos de relatório periódico. É importante não confundir essa exceção com o controle de uso final da seção anterior: são dois mecanismos distintos, com escopos distintos. 5 · O que fica de fora A regra exclui explicitamente um caso, e a definição dessa exceção é reveladora. Ficam fora da proibição os usos de acesso computacional dedicados exclusivamente a **sistemas comerciais de recomendação** — aqueles que ordenam, filtram ou sugerem produtos, serviços ou conteúdo —, sujeitos a condições de relatório. A definição, porém, fecha a porta logo em seguida: a exceção não alcança sistemas projetados ou usados para **gerar** novo texto, imagens, áudio, vídeo, software ou outro conteúdo, mesmo que também tenham função de recomendação. Em outras palavras: a regra deixa de fora o motor de recomendação de uma loja ou de uma rede social e mantém dentro o treinamento e a operação de modelos generativos.
