artigo.texto: Insight and analysis on the data center space from industry thought leaders. Rethinking High-Voltage Commissioning for AI Data Centers AI data centers are driving more direct high-voltage connections, making specialist HV commissioning essential for safe, reliable, and on-schedule delivery. The rapid global buildout of digital infrastructure to support the artificial intelligence boom is reshaping the design, construction, and commissioning requirements of data center projects. As computing capacity grows and rack densities rise to unprecedented levels, facilities are increasingly demanding power supplies measured in the tens and hundreds of megawatts. For many developments, securing that capacity means moving beyond conventional distribution networks and, where possible, connecting directly to high-voltage (HV) transmission infrastructure. Those connections can provide the capacity needed to support the next generation of AI facilities. They also significantly increase the complexity of the electrical environment. That raises both the difficulty and the risk for commissioning teams. Yet not every project fully acknowledges that the demands of HV data center commissioning extend well beyond conventional low-voltage (LV) certification and verification. HV infrastructure must be treated as a specialist engineering discipline, with its own competencies, testing methodologies, safety procedures, and assurance requirements. Incorporating it into an existing data center commissioning scope without appropriate specialist oversight risks leaving critical elements of the project insufficiently verified. The Changing Electrical Landscape Traditionally, data centers have relied on utility supplies delivered through distribution networks, with transformers stepping voltage down before electricity reaches the facility’s LV infrastructure. From there, uninterruptible power supplies, switchgear, and distribution systems provide the conditioned power required by critical IT loads. Now, the scale and nature of the AI boom are changing that equation. As AI data center development trends toward gigawatt-scale demand, local distribution networks in some markets cannot support new projects without major upgrades. That has contributed to extended approval processes and multiyear delays for some projects. Direct connections to higher-voltage networks, including 66kV, 110kV, and 150kV systems, are becoming an increasingly compelling alternative. However, connecting a data center directly to transmission infrastructure introduces additional complexity and cost. Substations, power transformers, HV cables, switchgear, protection systems, and utility interfaces all become integral parts of the critical power architecture. In many cases, some or all of those elements would have sat well outside the project boundary only a few years ago. From a commissioning perspective, that increases both the volume and the importance of the work required to bring a project from design through initial handover. Every HV element requires appropriate inspection, testing, and verification before energization, and commissioning that equipment brings its own risks and inherent complexities. HV Commissioning Requires Specialist Expertise HV commissioning differs fundamentally from conventional LV commissioning in both its technical requirements and its safety implications. At higher voltage levels, electrical hazards include arc flash, flashover, and fatal electric shock, even when personnel are exposed without direct contact with live conductors. The consequences of incorrect installation, protection settings, or switching procedures can be severe. Equipment failure during energization can damage expensive infrastructure, disrupt the wider electrical network, and cause significant project delays, in addition to the personal risk to teams working on the system. HV commissioning is its own discipline, with its own standards, testing methodologies, and safety protocols. It is not simply an extension of LV commissioning. The stakes are higher, and developers need to assess a project’s HV commissioning requirements during project planning rather than treating them as an extension of the broader electrical commissioning program. HV Commissioning from Installation to Verified Performance A structured HV commissioning program should define the inspection, testing, and acceptance requirements for every major component, supported by detailed inspection and test plans. The process begins with a comprehensive review of design documentation, equipment specifications, installation records, and manufacturer requirements. Site inspections then verify that equipment has been installed correctly, that connections and terminations are satisfactory, and that the installation reflects design intent. Individual equipment testing forms a substantial part of the program: - Power transformers require electrical testing to confirm insulation integrity, winding condition, and the correct operation of associated monitoring and protection devices. - HV cables and terminations must be tested to verify insulation performance and installation integrity. - Switchgear and circuit breakers need both mechanical and electrical verification, including checks of operating mechanisms, interlocks, contact resistance, and switching functionality. Any deficiencies identified during testing must be resolved and documented before the equipment progresses toward energization. - Protection-system verification means relays must be checked against approved protection studies and settings schedules, with secondary injection testing used to verify relay operation. - Grid-interface testing is particularly important because data center supply performance often depends on interactions among multiple systems delivered by different contractors and organizations. - Power-quality assessment forms part of this broader assurance process as well. artigo.texto: Restrições a data centers nos EUA podem atrasar, mas não travar o avanço da inteligência artificial. Estimativas da XP Investimentos calculam que pausas estaduais reduzam de 1% a 5% o capex de IA das oito empresas que lideram a construção no país. Segundo os analistas, esse efeito seria causado por atrasos e custos, e não por algum movimento na demanda. Plebiscitos locais rejeitam projetos das big techs No Texas, a pausa no estado já existe e deve durar cerca de 13 meses, até uma nova lei estadual passar a vigorar, a partir de agosto de 2027. Apesar de outros estados prometerem pausas parecidas, ainda não há decretos em vigor. Impacto no capex e na capacidade até 2030 Até 2027, não há expectativas de mudanças significativas na produção, uma vez que obras e encomendas já estão sendo executadas e parte da capacidade que atrasaria pode voltar em outros estados ou com geração própria nos próprios data centers. Já de 2028 a 2030, os caminhos estaduais tiram de 1,2% a 4,9% do capex das empresas e de 4 a 15 GW de capacidade ligada em 2030. De acordo com a XP, o investimento soma US$ 5,1 trilhões neste período, com US$ 1,8 trilhão no último ano, no cenário base. Cenário de estresse e exposição por empresa Conforme os analistas, uma moratória federal, abordada pela casa como cenário de estresse/sensibilidade, mudaria drasticamente a escala, com um corte de cerca de 26% sobre o capex projetado. De acordo com a XP, cada empresa deve sentir as mudanças com base no lugar onde constrói e a perda vai depender de quantos projetos elas têm nos estados com pausa. SpaceX e CoreWeave perdem mais em proporção, por terem uma fatia maior da expansão nos estados com possibilidade de pausas. Desafios de energia e preferências da XP O grande desafio é fornecer energia suficiente para essas estruturas e integrá-las ao sistema elétrico. Segundo os analistas, gerar energia no próprio terreno seria a saída natural, mas turbinas e motores já estão vendidos por anos e não resolveriam completamente o problema. A XP reiterou a preferência por nomes com menor impacto esperado em cenário de estresse de crédito, como Alphabet, Amazon e Microsoft. Com informações do InfoMoney

artigo.texto: Regra dos EUA exige licença, analisada caso a caso, para a compra de chips avançados de IA no Brasil, incluído no mapa de risco de Washington. A exigência pode alterar cronograma, custos e o perfil de clientes de data centers como o da ByteDance, dona do TikTok, em construção em Caucaia Catharina Queiroz catharina@ootimista.com.br A nova restrição dos Estados Unidos à venda de chips de inteligência artificial, desenhada para conter o avanço da China, acende um sinal de alerta no Ceará. O Estado abriga, no Complexo do Pecém, as obras de um data center ligado à ByteDance, dona do TikTok, empreendimento estimado em R$ 200 bilhões e desenvolvido em parceria com a Omnia, plataforma de data centers do Pátria Investimentos. A medida foi apresentada pelo Bureau de Indústria e Segurança (BIS), órgão do Departamento de Comércio americano. O texto está em inspeção pública, e a publicação no Federal Register, à qual a vigência está vinculada, é prevista para quinta-feira (19). O objetivo é impedir que empresas chinesas usem data centers instalados em outros países para acessar semicondutores avançados e treinar seus próprios modelos de IA. O Brasil aparece na lista ao lado de Singapura, Tailândia, Malásia e Indonésia. O BIS classifica o país como território de risco acima do normal. Na prática, a compra de determinados processadores e servidores usados em infraestrutura de IA passa a exigir uma etapa adicional de licença, com análise caso a caso. Data centers em qualquer lugar do mundo também precisarão de autorização quando os equipamentos fornecerem alto volume de computação a empresas sediadas na China. A regra chega no momento em que o governo brasileiro se prepara para regulamentar o setor com incentivos aos data centers e em que a ByteDance quer ampliar sua operação no Brasil. Para o titular da Secretaria de Ciência, Inovação e Tecnologia de Caucaia, Machidovel Trigueiro, a decisão altera o cenário, mesmo sem impor bloqueio. “A regra americana não é sanção nem veto: é exigência de licença, analisada caso a caso. Mas muda o jogo. O chip avançado virou instrumento de política externa e o Brasil entrou no mapa de risco de Washington”, disse ao O Otimista. “Arrisco dizer que os data centers do Ceará não param, porque energia limpa, cabos submarinos e ZPE seguem sendo vantagens raras. Mudam o cronograma e o perfil dos clientes. Em Caucaia, o projeto ligado à ByteDance passa a depender de autorização americana para receber GPUs de ponta, o que traz prazo, custo e incerteza”, destaca. O secretário faz ainda uma cobrança às empresas responsáveis pelo empreendimento. “E aqui cabe um recado às gestoras do projeto: o cenário mundial é dinâmico, mas o território que vão habitar é perene, não muda. Caucaia sente falta de contrapartidas computacionais que cumpram minimamente a função social do empreendimento, e seria inteligente da parte delas ter esse olhar, tão importante quanto a geopolítica. Licença se negocia em Washington, legitimidade se constrói no território”, complementa. O CTO da Digital College, Daniel Monteiro, lembra que os chips de alto desempenho, fabricados principalmente pela americana Nvidia, são a base da economia criada pela IA. “Quando os Estados Unidos restringem o acesso a esses equipamentos, o impacto vai muito além da tecnologia. Estamos falando de competitividade, geração de empregos e desenvolvimento econômico”, afirma. Segundo ele, o Brasil não tem condições de desenvolver, no curto ou no médio prazo, um chip com desempenho equivalente, o que pode elevar custos e atrasar a implantação de soluções tecnológicas. No Ceará, avalia, o efeito tende a ser maior. “O Estado está se posicionando como um grande polo da indústria digital. Há um investimento expressivo em data centers, conectividade e energia, e esses investimentos são feitos, sobretudo, para receber esses chips”, explica. Para ele, a questão vai além da disputa comercial entre Estados Unidos e China. “Abrir mão dos chips americanos, que são os melhores e os que melhor processam a inteligência artificial, é muito arriscado e exige muito cuidado.” O Otimista entrou em contato com a Omnia, responsável pela obra do data center, mas a companhia informou que não comentará o assunto. O espaço segue aberto para pronunciamento da ByteDance. O que diz o Ministério do Desenvolvimento, Indústria, Comércio e Serviços: O governo brasileiro tomou conhecimento do comunicado do Departamento de Comércio dos EUA e acompanha com atenção eventuais desdobramentos da medida. Importante destacar que não se trata de proibição de exportações de semicondutores avançados para o Brasil nem para os demais países citados no comunicado, mas sim de necessidade de autorização para que as operações se concretizem, motivo pelo qual não é possível avaliar, no momento, o efeito concreto da medida sobre as importações brasileiras desses insumos. artigo.texto: - Salt Lake City paused new data centers for six months to review regulations. - The City Council voted unanimously, addressing concerns over a proposed Northpoint project. - Mayor Mendenhall supported the pause to reassess zoning and environmental impacts. SALT LAKE CITY — Utah's capital city quickly pushed through a new ordinance pausing all new data centers within city limits for up to six months so it can better review a proposed project on its west side. The Salt Lake City Council voted unanimously on Tuesday to approve the measure after quickly adding it to its agenda this week. It essentially creates a moratorium on new data centers, allowing the city and potentially the state to adopt new data center regulations. "While policy would be the best protection for everyone in the long term — and I will advocate for that at any level of government — I'm also going to use any amount of soft power I have to influence whoever can make a decision to back off plans that can hurt people or the land out there," Salt Lake City Councilwoman Victoria Petro told KSL before the vote. The measure popped up on the City Council this week in an apparent response to a proposed data center that recently made headlines. A San Francisco-based architect filed a commercial building permit with the city for a one-story data center in June. Little else is known about the project, which would be located at 2258 W. 2950 North in Salt Lake City's Northpoint neighborhood. Qlevr LLC, a Florida-based digital infrastructure company, then applied for an air quality permit at the same site with the Utah Division of Air Quality on Sept. 30. That, too, only provided vague details, only saying it would run on grid power with fuel storage tanks and diesel-fired emergency generators. "That particular development is a thorn in my side," said Petro, whose district covers the Northpoint area. She explained that the development flew under the city leadership's radar until recently, and the developer hasn't provided much readily available information. The location is particularly vexing for her and the city. Salt Lake City recently completed a new plan for the Northpoint area to map out developments within the city's final rural edge. That came as residents pleaded with the city to help stop massive warehouses that wreaked havoc on them. It would potentially create a new challenge with noise and environmental concerns. "This is just heaping trauma upon trauma on one community," she said, adding that many residents aren't anti-data center but against the impacts they can have without any type of regulation. What the city voted on Tuesday follows a similar moratorium that Salt Lake County leaders approved in September, but that measure only applied to unincorporated land within the county, not Northpoint. It's also similar to a six-month pause the city approved in March to cap nonresidential water to 200,000 gallons per day. What started as a temporary measure to potentially thwart an immigration detention center on the west side ended up in a permanent ordinance approved in September. The new pause would give the city time to craft a new policy to address data centers, as the concerns over them mount. It would also carry through mid-May, potentially allowing the state to craft new data center policies that could go into effect by the time Tuesday's order expires. State leaders suggested making improvements to data center policy earlier this month after it seemed to be one of the key local issues during this year's election cycle. It's a "healthy pause" for the city, Salt Lake City Mayor Erin Mendenhall said earlier on Tuesday, asserting that the city's technology plans and zoning never considered data centers at the scale that has been proposed in recent years. Many vary in how they use water, which is something the city is very interested in, so she believes it makes sense to review new centers before approving them. "I think it's appropriate for our city and any other city that does land use to reconsider and take a hard look at zoning that's out there so that we can make sure what happens here is reflective of our capacity," she said.

artigo.texto: SEATTLE, Wash. — A bill moving quickly through U.S. Congress would bring permitting reform for energy and data center projects, while also rescinding input from tribal nations and walking back environmental protections. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), sponsored by four bipartisan senators, was introduced on Sept. 30, but was never heard or read in committee hearings where stakeholders typically give feedback. Instead, it went straight to the Senate floor for a procedural vote Tuesday. Washington Senator Maria Cantwell said she didn’t get the bill until Sunday night. “This process has been one in which we didn’t have hearings, didn’t have a markup, [and] basically came to the Senate floor without much notice and debate,” Cantwell said. “Right at the aftermath of an election, and, so, I just feel like it hasn’t gotten the attention that it deserves.” The bill would reform the permitting process for projects related to the electricity grid to accommodate an increasing load of electricity. The goal is to speed up approval for energy projects to develop renewable energies like solar and wind, as well as traditional oil, gas, and coal projects. It does this by limiting the scope of several review processes designed to protect environments, endangered species, and sensitive historical sites. “While Washington Wild supports infrastructure for energy transmission and future solutions, bedrock environmental laws and tribal consultation should not be held hostage to do so.” Washington Wild executive director Tom Uniack said. BAAJA would prioritize ensuring the certainty of a project moving forward, rather than revisit legal, analytical, or clarity errors in the original permit, making them difficult for future administrations to reverse course. It would limit the Endangered Species Act (ESA) by changing the definition of “best available science” that ensured agencies and developers must prioritize protection of endangered species. It also requires states to take on the review project to ensure federal projects meet ESA standards, something the organization Earth Justice says few states, if any, have the resources to do. “This is really concerning, because it is legislation and there’s a finality to that, if they make the wrong choice,” Uniack said. BAAJA also changes the National Environmental Review Act processes by altering the best available science requirement and exempting many projects from the review completely. It changes the Clean Water Act by doubling the length of water pollution permits, limiting state and tribes’ ability to protect waters in its jurisdiction, and makes it easier for developers to fill in wetlands -- regardless of flooding or wildlife concerns. “I’m for building transmission, but last I checked, that was not the problems with transmission. It wasn’t because, oh my god, we had to run over the Clean Water Act, because we couldn’t get transmission,” Cantwell said. The bill aims to lower electricity costs by requiring data centers to pay for electricity and projects that require increasing electrical capacity, and, with shorter review periods, lowering the cost of projects. Sovereign Indigenous Tribes are speaking out, because both the National Environmental Policy Act process and the National Historic Preservation Acts have ensured a seat at the table for feedback and consultation on projects that directly or indirectly impact tribal nations. “My people have already paid far too much for this country’s energy development,” Yakama Nation tribal councilmember John Washines said. “We should not be asked to sacrifice our salmon and our treaty rights yet again.” ©2026 Cox Media Group

artigo.texto: ROCHESTER — A timeline for a temporary moratorium on data center development in Rochester remains uncertain. “I don’t expect it to take longer than a year, and our hope is to get there sooner,” Community Development Director Irene Woodward told the Rochester City Council during a roughly 90-minute review of the proposal Monday. ADVERTISEMENT The council voted 5-1 to approve the moratorium, making way for staff study of potential data center impacts, along with developing definitions and guidelines for future development. The development pause begins with official notice of approval. “It gives us the opportunity to define the application process,” Woodward said, noting the goal is to ensure the community and developers know what is possible and what the development process entails. Council member Shaun Palmer, who cast the sole vote against the moratorium, questioned whether existing model ordinances could be adopted in an effort to reduce the potential timeline to three months. Woodward said model ordinances will be reviewed, but it will take time to tweak one, if used, since staff must ensure it meets community expectations and fits within the city’s unified development code without causing new conflicts. Council member Dan Doering said time is needed, but the move doesn’t mean data centers won’t be allowed under revised ordinances. “It’s not about automatically saying no to them,” he said. “It’s about fully knowing the pros and cons before making a long-term decision that could have a profound impact on our community.” ADVERTISEMENT Woodward said the city cannot outright ban data centers, but regulations can ensure development fits community expectations. While the process for developing future regulations is expected to involve public engagement efforts, the City Council heard concerns from both sides of the issue Monday. With 11 people speaking during a public hearing, the majority encouraged the council to support the moratorium as presented by staff, voicing concerns about environmental impacts and development issues seen in other communities, including Pine Island. “I am pleased that you are looking at this proactively and not just waiting until a center is on our doorstep and a deal is already made and proposed,” Rochester resident Mary Vlazny told the council. Evan Vlaeminck, an asset manager for the Rochester Technology Campus, which sits on the former IBM campus, said he’s concerned the moratorium could harm existing businesses needing to expand their data centers during the moratorium period. “A year is a very long time, certainly with respect to business,” he said. “Many deals can come and go in that time.” Council member Andy Friederichs suggested limiting the moratorium to new development, making way for expansion, but the proposal failed to get the needed support. ADVERTISEMENT The moratorium allows existing operations to operate and adapt to changing needs, but it’s also intended to be broad enough to rule out expansions that could transform existing facilities into something beyond their existing scope. Woodward said existing Rochester data centers were developed before the city implemented its new development code in 2023, and no applications for development or expansions are under city review. Whether an expansion would be restricted by the moratorium would depend on several factors, she said, noting a building permit application would spur a review to determine if the proposed work is allowed. She said the uncertainty related to requirements in existing code is what prompted the moratorium and planned study of data center impacts. “There are different ways to define a data center, and that is what we don’t have clearly defined,” she said. The temporary pause on potential development is the latest effort throughout the state. Egan lays claim to being the first Minnesota city to enact a temporary moratorium on development of new data centers. The Feb. 17 Eagan City Council decision came as four data centers were under construction in the Twin Cities suburb with a population of nearly 69,000. ADVERTISEMENT Meanwhile, a split Minneapolis City Council took action on Nov. 12 to approve new development rules, which will require council approval for individual data centers after proposals are made. The decision follows a review that included a five-month moratorium, which was implemented in June. Woodward said Rochester’s moratorium is designed to end earlier, if the council approves updates to the city’s development code. “We are planning to keep this moving,” she said of the timeline and state statute that allows a one-year moratorium with the possibility of requesting an 18-month extension. “If we bring back an ordinance before that time, the moratorium would expire.”

artigo.texto: By Lucia Yu, Senior Manager of Development, Key Capture Energy MANORVILLE – Long Islanders opened their electric bills this year to increases of up to 20%. The state’s grid operator forecasts that Long Island’s power grid will be operating with very slim margins starting in 2027. Battery energy storage is one of the fastest ways to help address both rising costs and the risk of blackouts. Key Capture Energy is developing battery energy storage projects across Long Island, including KCE NY 37 in Manorville. The two questions our team hears the most are “why here?” and “is battery energy storage safe?” Why Long Island? Long Island’s grid connections to the rest of the state are stretched thin, and getting energy here can be a challenge, especially on summer afternoons and evenings when air conditioners and appliances are all running at once. That raises the risk of blackouts on an island that has already seen its share of outages. In February, a winter storm knocked out power for nearly 50,000 Long Island residents and just a few months later, heavy wind and rain resulted in blackouts and brownouts that impacted more than 10,000 customers. Without continued investment in the grid, even standard weather events could become increasingly difficult for Long Island’s electric grid to manage. Storage is uniquely able to address both costs and the potential of electrical shortfalls. Batteries charge when power is cheap and plentiful and store it for when it’s needed, like on hot summer afternoons that are the hours that strain the grid and drive up prices. That’s why New York set a goal of 6 gigawatts of storage by 2030, a buildout that State regulators have said could save nearly $2 billion in system costs. KCE NY 37 is a part of that buildout. In September, NYSERDA selected it as one of eight projects in the state’s first bulk energy storage solicitation. It will provide millions of dollars in local taxes, union construction wages and other community benefits. Is battery energy storage safe? Simply put, yes. There are roughly 1,000 large scale projects like KCE NY 37 operating across the country and since today’s modern safety testing codes have been in place, the occurrence of fires at BESS facilities has plummeted. Here in New York, the state updated its fire code to be one of the strictest in the country. Today, every project must undergo an independent third-party safety review during the local permitting process to ensure these updated codes are met and develop an Emergency Response Plan in coordination with the local fire department. Developers are also required to offer training for local first responders prior to a facility starting operations and annually afterwards. KCE has met with the Manorville Fire Department and Brookhaven fire officials to discuss the project. We look forward to ongoing dialogue with local emergency personnel to finalize a comprehensive emergency response plan and address any outstanding questions. These steps and the pre-operational fire department training will ensure that first responders are equipped and ready in the very unlikely event of a safety incident at the facility. New York’s fire leaders have said again and again that battery storage is safe when it is built to New York’s updated code. Residents are also right to ask what the 2023 East Hampton battery storage fire means for their community, particularly after PFAS contamination was found in nearby groundwater. The New York State Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC) is continuing to investigate that contamination, but its preliminary findings identify the facility’s fire suppression system, rather than its batteries, as the likely source of any contamination. That system used Novec 1230, a chemical fire-extinguishing agent that can break down into a PFAS compound if combined with water. KCE NY 37 and our projects across Long Island will not use Novec 1230 or a similar suppression agent. Unlike East Hampton’s indoor facility, which also utilized an older battery chemistry called nickel-manganese-cobalt (NMC), KCE’s projects will use outdoor systems with lithium-iron-phosphate (LFP) batteries built to New York’s updated fire safety codes. Everyone should be confident in the safety of today’s modern BESS systems, including KCE NY 37, because they incorporate the lessons learned from incidents like the East Hampton fire and are specifically designed to prevent and mitigate the impacts of a fire, in the rare case one were to happen. Battery energy storage built to New York’s updated safety codes is safe. It can ease Long Island’s energy challenges, help stabilize electric bills, and ensure businesses and households have the reliable grid needed to power Long Island’s economy. Lucia Yu is Senior Manager of Development at Key Capture Energy (KCE). KCE is a battery energy storage developer and operator headquartered in Albany with projects across New York.

artigo.texto: Chinese battery maker CATL opens office in Argentina — South China Morning Post Chinese battery manufacturer Contemporary Amperex Technology Co Ltd (CATL) has opened a commercial office in Argentina, South China Morning Post reports, citing Argentine media. The company plans to use it to expand supplies of energy storage systems. CATL already supplies batteries for the country’s largest electricity storage project and has presented its solutions to 35 companies interested in a government tender. Last week, CATL representatives met in Buenos Aires with generating companies and banks. The company said it intends to become the leading supplier of energy storage systems in Argentina. The office is also expected to become a base for developing storage projects for mining enterprises, data centers and wind power plants in Patagonia. Projects and tenders Argentina’s largest private electricity producer, Central Puerto, uses CATL cells in two projects with a combined capacity of 205 MW. Construction of the larger one, the 150 MW Nuevo Puerto facility, is about 80% complete. Commercial operation is planned to begin in mid-December under a 15-year contract with distribution company Edenor. Last year, Argentine authorities announced the first tender for 500 MW of energy storage systems near Buenos Aires to reduce the number of power supply disruptions. Due to high demand, contracts were concluded for 713 MW: they were signed directly with distributors, while Cammesa, which manages the wholesale electricity market, acted as guarantor. More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram. In July, Argentina’s Energy Secretariat allocated another 700.5 MW among 20 projects in other regions of the country. The auction received 235 technical applications, and the estimated investment volume amounted to $700 million. Average prices were about a quarter lower than in the first round. Renewable energy developer Genneia received 421 MW, or about 60% of the total volume. Financing in yuan Financing remains one of the main issues for market participants, as battery containers are imported from China. Christian Damonaz of the Argentine unit of Bank of China proposed lending in yuan and said that this currency offers acceptable rates and stability against the US dollar. ICBC’s Argentine unit provided Genneia with 358.8 million yuan, or $50 million, last year for renewable energy projects. CATL also reported that its revenue from energy storage systems rose 87.5% year-on-year in the first half of the year. According to Harry Lau, the company’s representative in Latin America, CATL has contracts in the region for more than 15 GWh of energy storage systems, including for the Oasis de Atacama project in Chile.

artigo.texto: COLUMBUS, Ohio — A leaked Ohio bill could allow data centers to qualify as "public utilities," giving them the ability to seize private property. Ohioans rejected data centers on every ballot measure this election, but after that massive loss, Republican lawmakers may be moving to allow tech hubs one way or another. For decades, Gretchan Francis has been fighting to keep her multigenerational family farm. "It's not the farm that it once was," Francis said in an interview. "It's only 60 acres; it's not 160 acres." Using eminent domain law, which allows the government to take property for public use, the state has seized her land numerous times for highway development. "I understand that it is necessary, but I think it has to be done in the right way," she said. While ODOT has always been able to do this, farmers like her are fearing that new legislation would take their livelihoods for a controversial cause. A draft bill leaked to us exclusively would expand the list of who qualifies to take land. The draft changes the definition of "public utility," from just an entity being owned or operated by municipal corporations, an electric cooperative and an agency holding a certificate of public convenience and necessity granted by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission. The legislation adds "and an agency holding a certificate of environmental compatibility and public need from the power siting board for constructing an electric transmission line and associated facilities or gas pipeline and its associated facilities." This could mean a transmission developer may be able to seize land to power or place a data center, according to legal experts. "That would be devastating," Francis said. "I think anybody would feel the same way if their personal land was taken for a data center. That sounds like it's a corporate, private, for-profit type of need, not for a public need." In June, we discovered that the Ohio Business Roundtable, a powerful trade group that lobbies at the Statehouse, recommended that lawmakers change eminent domain law, and “should extend possession authority to energy infrastructure projects once public use and necessity have been established.” RELATED: Ohio farmers fear new proposal would allow data centers to take property The Ohio Farm Bureau, which is adamantly against changing eminent domain, had been preparing for this fight since. "We are aware of efforts to further erode the limited protections that landowners have, allowing for quick take of property without first paying for the property and determining a landowner’s rights and compensation through a court of law," the Bureau’s Evan Callicoat said. The Farm Bureau isn't opposed to data centers, but they are opposed to a violation of property rights, Callicoat said. He feared that with this proposed idea, it's broad enough that farmers could lose their land to data centers, not getting paid for it for months or years. The Roundtable calls the program "deposit and build," and it's modeled after a system that 45 other states use. "This recommendation is about making sure that Ohio's grid is reliable and affordable for Ohioans and that economic development can continue in the state," the Roundtable's Alexandra Denney said in an interview Monday. The Ohio Power Siting Board controls the installation of utility facilities, including power lines, some gas pipelines, and wind farms. The Public Utilities Commission of Ohio can also help utility companies acquire land. A utility will approach a homeowner for land and must provide them with a "fair" market price. If the owner refuses to sell, the utility company will take them to court and will need to determine "necessity" for the land. If a court sides with the utility company, deeming it necessary to take, the appraised value of the land is given to a court account. However, the owner can appeal this decision to fight for more money. While this court battle is going on, construction is not allowed to begin. The draft bill changes the appraisal process, making it easier to seize land immediately. "Ratepayers and Ohioans are paying the price because it's driving up costs and it's also delaying the critical infrastructure that we need to have a reliable grid," Denney said about construction delays. While Denney was aware of the appraisal portion of the legislation, she categorically denied any changes to eminent domain. After I read the bill out loud, she said she would need to "look at" the changes in the definition of public utilities. She said that Ohioans choosing to restrict or ban data centers in 21 different cities has nothing to do with the timing of this proposal. "That is not the intent of the Ohio Business Roundtable to expand the ability to use eminent domain to anybody that doesn't already have that ability," Denney said. Soon-to-be Senate President Republican Bill Reineke (R-Tiffin), who is working on the bill, echoed her sentiment. “We keep talking about lowering costs, and one way we can do that is expanding infrastructure for public utilities to keep rates down. That’s what this is about," Reineke said in a statement. "It’s important to me that landowners keep their rights, and this would not extend eminent domain to anyone who doesn’t already have that privilege — rather, it is a framework to simplify our existing process that would put us in line with 45 other states." He added that one of his top focuses was to make sure there was enough energy and lower costs. But the legislation does specifically change who is considered a public utility, both for electrical transmission and for gas. Even without being a private electric transmitter who applies for a certificate, Francis believes it is feasible that a utility company can help take land in order to power a data center. artigo.texto: Data centers dos EUA emitem tanto CO₂ quanto a Dinamarca, aponta Harvard | Vero NotíciasData centers dos EUA emitem tanto CO₂ quanto a Dinamarca, aponta Harvard Os 403 maiores data centers dos Estados Unidos emitiram 25,7 milhões de toneladas de dióxido de carbono entre maio de 2024 e abril de 2025, volume equivalente às emissões anuais da Dinamarca, segundo estudo da Universidade de Harvard. Publicado nesta segunda-feira (16) na revista Nature Sustainability, o levantamento aponta que as emissões desses centros de dados triplicaram desde 2018, impulsionando preocupações sobre o impacto ambiental da infraestrutura digital. Virgínia, Oregon, Ohio e Iowa concentraram mais da metade do consumo de eletricidade analisado. Segundo os pesquisadores, a maioria dos centros utilizava energia gerada a gás, e o estudo busca ampliar a transparência sobre os impactos ambientais da inteligência artificial. Um estudo do Ministério da Fazenda estima que a aprovação do projeto de lei que regulamenta economicamente as big techs pode gerar benefícios de R$ 15,3 bilhões a R$ 50,6 bilhões anuais para consumidores e empresas brasileiras. Os valores representam entre 0,1% e 0,4% do PIB. O levantamento, elaborado pela Secretaria de Reformas Econômicas, analisou 20 segmentos do mercado digital, incluindo comércio eletrônico, publicidade, aplicativos de transporte e inteligência artificial. Os setores movimentaram cerca de R$ 410 bilhões em 2025. O Ministério da Fazenda estima que ampliar a concorrência entre plataformas digitais pode gerar benefícios de R$ 15,3 bilhões a R$ 50,6 bilhões anuais para consumidores e empresas, com menores preços e comissões. O estudo avalia um projeto que amplia os instrumentos do Cade para fiscalizar grandes plataformas e combater barreiras à concorrência. O texto tramita com urgência na Câmara e aguarda votação no plenário. O ajuste fiscal pode reduzir em R$ 280 milhões os recursos destinados a projetos esportivos, estimam as organizações Atletas pelo Brasil e Instituto Esporte e Educação. As entidades divulgaram comunicado contra a medida. O projeto amplia de 10% para 20% o corte linear de benefícios tributários. As organizações pedem que a Lei de Incentivo ao Esporte seja excluída da redução para preservar o financiamento dos projetos. O Ibovespa caiu 1,83% nesta segunda-feira (16), aos 169.295,41 pontos, em meio a preocupações com as contas públicas brasileiras e ao aumento da aversão ao risco nos mercados internacionais. Investidores avaliam se o pacote fiscal será suficiente para estabilizar as contas. O Morgan Stanley reduziu sua recomendação para o Brasil e projetou o Ibovespa em 160 mil pontos no fim de 2027. O secretário especial da Receita Federal, Robinson Barreirinhas, afirmou nesta segunda-feira (16) que o projeto de ajuste fiscal não restringe os créditos tributários da Contribuição sobre Bens e Serviços (CBS). Segundo Barreirinhas, os créditos da CBS continuarão podendo ser compensados. O texto permite restringir outras compensações tributárias caso o governo esteja distante da meta fiscal, incluindo créditos ligados a benefícios fiscais.

artigo.texto: The Hidden Efficiency Gap in Data Center Containment The Gap Nobody Budgeted For Data center operators measure nearly everything to ensure efficiency at the highest level, from inlet temperatures to rack density, airflow per kilowatt to PUE. Yet an unobtrusive gap above the hot contained aisle or missing roof above the cold contained aisle has been leaking conditioned air, forcing the cooling system to work harder than it needs to be, driving up cooling costs since the day the facility was commissioned. And no one has been measuring its detriment to performance. It’s easy to miss. The open seam sits at ceiling height for HAC or above the racks for CAC and is barely perceptible to some. However, the gap rarely appears on an efficiency dashboard, because it’s not an oversight nor a design defect. The gap is a deliberate allowance, that’s been quietly shaping the cooling bill of almost every contained facility that has relied on it. The real story is not that the gap exists. It’s why the industry has treated it as an unavoidable compromise. Why the Gap Exists The open seam above the hot aisle containment or missing roof above the cold aisle for cold aisle containment is a result of fire code, not a construction fault. In the United States, a combination of national model codes, specialized National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) regulations 13 (installation of sprinkler systems) and 75 (protection of IT equipment) standards, along with the International Fire Code plus state or local municipal amendments enforced by local Authorities Having Jurisdiction (AHJs), regulate data center fire safety. A sprinkler can only protect what its water spray can reach. Fire code mandates require the unobstructed dispersal of sprinkler heads to protect the space, and a he ad that is blocked, shadowed, or poorly positioned may fail to control the fire. The problem is that a fully sealed ceiling impedes sprinkler coverage. It can be done. The sprinkler layout could be designed at the same time as the rack, tray, and containment layout rather than afterward. But this would require renewed verification and approvals after any increase or relocation of racks and cabinets, change of cable trays or busways, additional lighting or cooling lines, or modification of containment and airflow. With the rapid evolution of AI racks, adding higher-density or higher-power equipment (such as liquid cooling or battery systems) also changes the hazard classification and can trigger additional requirements. To adhere to fire code and not impede sprinkler coverage, data center designers made the easier call and left a gap. It is a reasonable, safety-first decision that allows for adaptation and refitting as and when required. It is also one that operators have paid for ever since, in wasted cooling energy. The industry has long treated this as a fixed trade-off between containment and compliance. While that choice has protected facilities, safety and efficiency have been set against each other, and efficiency has lost by default. This trade-off has gone unchallenged for years, because no one could offer containment that fire protection engineers and code officials would accept as fully sealed. What the Gap Costs at Scale Containment has one job: to keep hot exhaust air and cold supply air from mixing. Every pathway that lets them meet forces the cooling plant to compensate. It matters more than its size suggests. The loss is not a one-off event to be fixed after an incident. It is a constant, built into the facility's operating cost from the first day of operation. Sealed When it Should Be The answer is a contained cold or hot aisle that stays fully sealed in normal operation and changes its behavior in an emergency. Two components work together to make that possible: - A melting fuse plug with airflow flaps: A sealed ceiling with airflow flaps that under normal operating conditions stay closed. If aisle temperatures rise, the melting fuse plug is activated, opening the airflow flaps releasing hot air to the sprinkler activation. - Dissolving panels: When the sprinklers activate, the EPA approved non-combustible panels dissolve on contact with water; sprinkler discharge is never blocked and panels never fall, so there is no obstruction to egress. The principle is simple: containment is in full effect when conditions are normal, but when safety requires the space, the flaps and dissolving panels combine, giving operators efficiency when they need it and safety when it counts. Reviewed and Approved Promising efficiency gains in a life-safety context can often lead to mistrust. Efficiency improvements that cannot demonstrate fire code compliance are not improvements at all. They are liabilities waiting to surface during inspection, or worse, during an incident. Most efficiency gains ask a lot: major capital, long downtime or a redesign from the ground up. The distinction here is that this is not a workaround. It is a design that has been reviewed and approved directly by fire protection engineers and AHJs. It also works for both new builds and legacy facilities. - New builds can specify either fully sealed hot or cold aisles with airflow flaps from the outset, so the gap is never created. - Legacy facilities can close a leak or add a roof system over the cold aisle that has existed since commissioning, without rethinking the architecture. In both cases the result is the same: fully sealed hot aisles with airflow flaps that meet fire code without compromising safety. Compliant Containment The hot aisle seam above hot aisle containment and missing roof system above the cold aisle for cold aisle containment has been tolerated for as long as it was thought to be the price of compliance, but that reasoning no longer holds. Each day these openings stay open is another day of avoidable cooling cost. artigo.texto: Researchers at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology have developed a structural lithium-sulfur battery cathode capable of maintaining stable electrical performance inside curved and hollow structures. Led by Professor Il-Kwon Oh from the Department of Mechanical Engineering, the research team fabricated the electrode by growing ultrafine nanowires directly onto woven carbon cloth, creating a monolithically integrated scaffold designed to serve simultaneously as a mechanical support and an energy storage medium for drones and robotic systems. In robotics and unmanned aerial vehicle engineering, maximizing energy storage capacity while minimizing device weight and occupied volume remains a primary design constraint. Conventional vehicle architectures rely on separate structural airframes and discrete, rigid battery packs, restricting the extent to which overall platform weight can be reduced. Structural energy storage addresses this challenge by converting load-bearing airframe parts, such as landing gear or robotic limbs, into functional battery components. Implementing multifunctional structural batteries in practice requires energy storage cells that conform to non-planar structural geometries. Unmanned aerial vehicle landing legs and robotic support frames frequently incorporate curved, hollow, or tubular surfaces that cannot accommodate conventional flat battery configurations. To resolve this geometric restriction, the KAIST team focused on engineering an electrode architecture capable of conforming to tightly curved, three-dimensional enclosures without sacrificing mechanical durability or electrochemical activity. The engineering team selected a lithium-sulfur electrochemical system, which utilizes sulfur as the active cathode material. Lithium-sulfur chemistries provide theoretical potential for high energy storage capacity at a relatively low material weight compared to traditional alternatives. Within this system, the cathode acts as a critical functional electrode that governs the redox reactions occurring during electrical charge and discharge cycles. Despite these theoretical storage advantages, lithium-sulfur systems encounter operational obstacles that hinder long-term performance. Elemental sulfur has poor electrical conductivity, and intermediate compounds termed lithium polysulfides dissolve into the electrolyte during operation. The migration of these dissolved polysulfides away from the cathode disrupts the reversible electrochemical reactions required for efficient energy retention, accelerating capacity loss over repeated cycling. Conventional electrode fabrication techniques introduce additional structural vulnerabilities when subjected to physical movement. Active materials are typically applied as a surface slurry coating onto a conductive substrate, making the layer susceptible to cracking or complete delamination under repeated bending or external mechanical stress. When active material detaches from the underlying current collector, the electrical pathways are severed and the electrode degrades rapidly. To overcome delamination and polysulfide migration simultaneously, the KAIST researchers grew nickel cobalt selenide nanowires directly on the surfaces of interwoven carbon fibers. Nanowires are ultrafine structures with dimensions measured on the scale of nanometers, where one nanometer represents one billionth of a meter. The nickel cobalt selenide compound, consisting of nickel, cobalt, and selenium, catalyzes sulfur-related redox reactions while chemically anchoring lithium polysulfides to limit their dissolution and migration away from the reaction zone. Because the nickel cobalt selenide nanowires are grown directly out of the woven carbon cloth substrate rather than spread as a secondary surface coating, the cathode establishes firmly anchored, continuous electrical conduction pathways. In cyclic mechanical deformation tests, the monolithic electrode underwent 1,000 bending cycles at a tight curvature radius of 2.5 millimeters. Following testing, the nanowires remained intact and securely attached to the carbon fiber surfaces, displaying no structural collapse, cracking, or material detachment. To verify the practical viability of the electrode within non-planar enclosures, the researchers assembled the material into functional lithium-sulfur pouch cells. They incorporated the resulting cells into multiple curved and angular housings, including oval, square, and drone-leg structural components. In each configuration, the integrated lithium-sulfur battery successfully powered a light-emitting diode, demonstrating reliable electrical discharge across varied structural contours. The team also subjected the integrated structural battery to external mechanical load testing to evaluate electrical stability under severe mechanical strain. When installed within a cylindrical housing, the battery retained 99.8 percent of its initial operational voltage even under external mechanical forces sufficient to fracture the surrounding structural frame. In a parallel loading evaluation, a connected light-emitting diode maintained steady illumination without flickering or interruption during structural failure. Looking toward practical deployment, the authors noted that the electrode architecture could eventually be paired with load-bearing composite materials, such as carbon fiber and resin matrices, to construct multifunctional drone legs and robotic airframes. However, the researchers emphasized that further experimental research remains necessary to quantify precisely how much structural weight can be eliminated and the degree to which operational flight times or robot mission durations can be extended in operational conditions. The study, titled “Monolithically integrated NiCo2Se4 nanowire–carbon cloth cathode scaffolds for non-planar lithium-sulfur structural-battery integration,” was published in the journal Advanced Composites and Hybrid Materials

artigo.texto: – Collaboration to assess next-generation ultralight solar cells for space-based computing infrastructure – Partnership brings together Korean space energy technology and French orbital infrastructure expertise Bremen, Germany – Flexell Space, a space energy company, announced that it has signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with ALATYR, a French company developing orbital data centers, to explore solar power solutions for space-based computing infrastructure. The collaboration will assess the potential application of Flexell Space’s next-generation solar cell technology to orbital infrastructure designed for large-scale computing and data storage. The companies intend to exchange technical requirements relating to power demand and operating conditions and explore opportunities for future joint development and validation. ALATYR develops orbital data centers designed to support artificial intelligence (AI) computing and mission-critical workloads. Its CITADEL modular infrastructure architecture and BYLD robotic system are designed to enable assembly, maintenance, and upgrades in orbit. The architecture separates the service life of the supporting infrastructure from the replacement cycle of computing hardware, enabling computing modules to be renewed in orbit while retaining the infrastructure that powers, cools, and supports them. Reliable power generation is essential to making orbital data centers viable. As these facilities grow, solar power systems must address not only electrical performance but also mass, launch and deployment efficiency, manufacturing costs, and long-term reliability. Flexell Space is developing next-generation space solar cells based on CIGS (copper indium gallium selenide) and perovskite technologies. With a focus on lightweight, flexible designs and large-area manufacturing, the company aims to provide power solutions for satellites and larger space infrastructure. Through the collaboration, Flexell Space intends to gain a clearer understanding of orbital data center requirements and assess how its technology could support this emerging application. “This MoU marks an important milestone in strengthening cooperation between Korea and Europe, particularly France, in space energy and infrastructure,” said Kyumin Lee, Business Development Manager at Flexell Space. “By combining our next-generation solar cell technology with ALATYR’s orbital infrastructure expertise, we aim to build a lasting partnership and lay the groundwork for joint development and validation of power solutions for future orbital data centers.” He added, “By bringing together our complementary capabilities, we aim to establish a practical foundation for future development and validation.” “Our orbital infrastructure is designed to serve successive generations of computing hardware,” said Emeric Lhomme, Chief Executive Officer of ALATYR. “That makes solar cell efficiency and longevity central to our approach: our power systems must continue to deliver reliable performance as computing modules are replaced and upgraded. With Flexell Space, we will explore how next-generation lightweight solar technologies could meet the demands of that extended service life.” The companies plan to begin by exchanging information on their technologies and development priorities, followed by a phased assessment of solar cell and power system compatibility. Specific development activities and validation approaches will be discussed through subsequent technical consultations. About Flexell Space Flexell Space is a space energy company that originated as an internal venture at Hanwha Systems. The company develops next-generation space solar cells and power solutions based on CIGS and perovskite technologies, with a focus on low-cost, large-area, ultralight products. Through collaboration with global partners, Flexell Space is advancing the commercialization of solar cell technologies for satellites and a broad range of space infrastructure. About ALATYR ALATYR is a French company developing a new layer of critical digital infrastructure in space. The company designs orbital data centers that evolve with computing technology, rather than being replaced with each hardware generation. Its infrastructure is designed to remain productive over the long term and expand with demand, creating a lasting extension of the cloud in orbit to increase computing capacity and strengthen the resilience of essential digital services worldwide.

artigo.texto: Spotsylvania County residents call on officials to scrap 'sweetheart deal' for data center SPOTSYLVANIA, Va. (7News) — Stafford and Spotsylvania counties are moving ahead with plans to approve more data centers, according to recent actions by their boards of supervisors. In recent years, both counties have approved data center developments. On Tuesday, the Spotsylvania County Board of Supervisors voted 4-3 to approve the Crossroads Technology Campus, a massive data center project planned for a 550-acre site near neighborhoods. SEE ALSO | Jawando’s pick for Montgomery County police chief faces scrutiny over past audit When she introduced the motion to approve the project in her district, Spotsylvania County Supervisor Lori Hayes said the developer agreed to noise mitigation, generator emissions standards and setbacks from homes. She said the developer also agreed not to use groundwater for cooling. Hayes told 7News that 66% of the site would remain forested. Supervisors Tim McLaughlin, Hayes, Drew Mullins and Deborah Frazier voted to approve the special use permit. Supervisors Chris Yakabouski, Jacob Lane and David Goosman voted against it. Despite more than 50 guarantees and the developer’s promise of $30 million in annual tax revenue for the county, dozens of homeowners told the board they don’t want to be surrounded by data centers. SEE ALSO | Fares as high as $8.25 a ride? Metro seeks to address $132M budget gap Spotsylvania County resident Kelly Shaeffer told 7News reporter Nick Minock that she doesn’t want to see data centers from her home, hear their constant hum and generator noise, or see her home’s value decrease because of the facilities’ proximity to her neighborhood. Her neighborhood is surrounded by several proposed data center sites. “Do you fear Spotsylvania County is going to become Loudoun County data center alley?” Minock asked. “Oh yeah, I absolutely do, especially with the tax rate that they're giving,” Shaeffer said. Spotsylvania County offers one of the lowest tax rates for data centers in Virginia. “Our board decided to put in place an Amazon local performance agreement [for Amazon data centers] that provides them $1.25 per $100 of computer and peripherals,” said Cindy Staats. “On top of that, they get 60% back of the generated tax revenue for ten years, and then they get 20% back for the next ten years. On top of that, they get an accelerated depreciation schedule.” “Would you call this a sweetheart deal?” Minock asked. “Oh, it is a very much a sweetheart deal,” said Staats. Both Spotsylvania County homeowners who spoke with 7News said they were disappointed that the board approved the Crossroads Technology Campus. “Disappointed because I feel like the residents have brought up some really valid concerns and unanswered questions that we still have on this project,” said Staats. “And a lot of residents just even ask them to pause or to defer the vote until we could get answers on those questions and the fact that they chose not to do that and to kind of push forward was really disappointing.” “It feels like we can't even catch up with how quickly they're [data centers] popping up,” said Shaeffer. “Like last night was the public hearing for Crossroads. And then tonight is the public hearing for the one across the river. And it's just back-to-back. And it's like we can't fully get our feet underneath us to try and fight. I know they've made the argument that they've kind of zoned all the data centers to be here. But my issue with that is why would you then spend the money to have all these residential areas pop up? Like, if I knew that this was specifically zoned [for] all these data centers my husband and I wouldn't have bought here and I think all of our neighbors wouldn't have bought here.” Stafford County also has a data center tax rate of $1.25 per $100 of assessed value, less than one-third of Loudoun County’s rate for data center computer equipment. Now, one developer is proposing four data centers near George Washington’s boyhood home. The project, off Kings Highway, spans more than 1,400 acres and would put data centers on the Rappahannock River. The proposed data center and substation would tower over Arlene’s home, as 7News previously reported. "It makes me very sad and I am praying it doesn't come about,” said Arlene. The developer’s attorney said the project, if approved, would generate $245 million in total tax revenue, about 20% of Stafford County’s total budget. The attorney said it would provide funding for schools, local roads and other public services, which he said is needed because residents’ taxes have increased 57% over the past five years. Spotsylvania and Stafford counties, King George County and the city of Fredericksburg have some of the region’s lowest tax rates on data center equipment, at $1.25 per $100 of assessed value. Fairfax, Fauquier, Prince William and Loudoun counties charge higher rates. Fairfax County charges $4.57 per $100 of assessed value for data center equipment. Prince William County’s rate is $4.50, while Fauquier and Loudoun counties charge $4.15. Loudoun County Supervisor Kristen Umstattd said the Fredericksburg-area localities should raise their tax rates so they can see the same tax revenue benefits as Loudoun County. “What we get out of a $4.15 tax rate is money for our schools, 100% of our general fund covered by data center tax revenues,” Umstattd said. “And it's 45% of our entire budget, including the schools.” While Spotsylvania and Stafford counties continue to approve data centers, Loudoun County is beginning to pump the brakes. After years of allowing dozens of data centers and substations near homes, the Loudoun County Board of Supervisors voted Tuesday night to pause new substations for data centers. Loudoun County currently has more than 230 data centers, with 100 more planned. artigo.texto: Publicidade Receba notícias do Congresso em Foco: Relações exteriores Congresso em Foco 16/11/2026 15:52 O Departamento de Comércio dos Estados Unidos passou a exigir licença do governo norte-americano para exportação, reexportação ou transferência de semicondutores avançados de inteligência artificial destinados ao Brasil. A nova regra, divulgada nesta segunda-feira (16) pelo Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), órgão responsável pelos controles de exportação, também alcança Indonésia, Malásia, Singapura e Tailândia. Segundo o governo dos Estados Unidos, os cinco países foram incluídos na nova exigência por apresentarem um risco considerado "acima do normal" de que equipamentos avançados de computação sejam desviados para empresas ou países submetidos a controles norte-americanos. A medida atinge chips de alto desempenho utilizados, entre outras aplicações, na infraestrutura necessária para desenvolver e operar sistemas avançados de inteligência artificial. Os pedidos de licença envolvendo os cinco países serão analisados individualmente pelas autoridades norte-americanas, que avaliarão se a operação pode contrariar interesses de segurança nacional ou de política externa dos Estados Unidos. Há ainda uma exceção para determinadas operações cujo usuário final seja uma empresa sediada nos EUA ou controlada por uma companhia norte-americana, desde que sejam cumpridas exigências de informação ao governo. A regra faz parte de uma ofensiva mais ampla do governo dos Estados Unidos para impedir que empresas de países sujeitos a restrições, especialmente aquelas vinculadas a destinos classificados no grupo D:5, tenham acesso indireto à capacidade computacional de chips norte-americanos. O grupo inclui países como China, Rússia, Irã e Coreia do Norte. O governo norte-americano identificou como uma das preocupações o uso de data centers instalados em terceiros países. Nesse modelo, uma empresa impedida de comprar diretamente determinados semicondutores poderia acessar remotamente a capacidade de processamento de equipamentos instalados em outro território. O Departamento de Comércio afirma que a nova norma busca fechar essa possibilidade e aproximar as regras de acesso remoto das restrições já aplicadas ao envio físico da tecnologia. Tags Temas

artigo.texto: In a recent study, researchers investigated biodegradable polymer electrolytes engineered for use in green electric double-layer capacitor devices. The research examined solid polymer blend electrolytes composed of chitosan and methylcellulose paired with potassium thiocyanate salt and modified using glycerol as a plasticizing agent. The development addresses the implementation of environmentally friendly biopolymer matrices capable of supporting functional electrochemical storage systems, with an emphasis on establishing sustainable materials for capacitor applications. Impedance spectroscopy evaluations demonstrated that the addition of glycerol plasticizer effectively enhanced the overall electrical properties of the chitosan/methylcellulose/potassium thiocyanate electrolyte system. By incorporating glycerol into the ternary biopolymer blend, the investigators identified clear modifications in electrical response compared to unmodified formulations. These impedance findings confirmed that plasticization served a critical functional role in optimizing the bulk electrical characteristics required for practical solid polymer electrolyte performance. Structural and morphological analyses confirmed that glycerol incorporation induced measurable physical alterations within the solid polymer blend. X-ray diffraction measurements showed a reduction in diffraction peak intensity alongside noticeable peak broadening, indicating structural reorganization in the polymer electrolyte network. Furthermore, scanning electron microscopy revealed a homogenous dispersion of glycerol throughout the solid polymer electrolyte matrix, demonstrating uniform integration of the plasticizer across the combined chitosan and methylcellulose structure. The dielectric behaviour of the electrolyte system provided additional insights into the internal charge transport dynamics. The loss tangent peaks exhibited a systematic shift toward higher frequencies, which the authors identified as direct evidence that the time required for ion transport decreased as plasticizer concentration increased. Complementing these observations, an electric modulus study was performed to suppress electrode polarization phenomena and enable clear observation of the relaxation peaks associated with ionic motion. Conductivity testing revealed that the plasticized polymer electrolyte reached a maximum ionic conductivity of 2.305 x 10^-4 S/cm, a performance level deemed adequate for device production. To clarify the transport mechanism, transference number measurements were performed on the electrolyte. The measurement confirmed that the dominant fraction of conducting species consisted of ions, establishing that ionic mobility governs the electrical conductivity of the plasticized polymer blend rather than electronic transport pathways. Electrochemical stability assessments using linear sweep voltammetry confirmed the capacity of the electrolyte to resist electrical breakdown under applied voltage. Furthermore, cyclic voltammetry was conducted to examine ion storage and interface reactions at the boundary between the electrodes and the electrolyte. The resulting cyclic voltammograms displayed a characteristic rectangular pattern, while galvanostatic charge-discharge testing produced an almost ideal profile, confirming that the fabricated capacitor operates through non-faradaic charge storage processes. Overall performance testing of the assembled electric double-layer capacitor demonstrated low equivalent series resistance and high specific capacitance as key experimental outcomes. The resulting energy storage device achieved energy densities ranging from 9.6 to 7.61 Wh/kg and power densities ranging from 1791 to 1475 W/kg across testing conditions. The researchers noted that these combined structural and electrochemical results substantiate the operational viability of biodegradable solid polymer electrolytes in advancing green capacitor storage technology. artigo.texto: St. Joseph County Council advances proposal to ban non-legacy hyper-scale data centers The Area Plan Commission voted unanimously against the proposal earlier on Tuesday SOUTH BEND, Ind. (WNDU) - The St. Joseph County Council took the next step Tuesday on a proposal that would ban non-legacy hyper-scale data centers, hours after the Area Plan Commission voted unanimously against it. Tuesday was the first reading of the proposal, which would prohibit future hyper-scale data centers in unincorporated parts of St. Joseph County that exceed one million square feet. County Council President Bryan Tanner sent the proposal to the Land Use Planning Committee. Tanner said the proposal also creates definitions that are not currently in the county’s development code. “It is institutionalizing a new definition that hasn’t historically existed in our development code for what a hyper-scale data center is,” Tanner said. “There will also be a new definition for what is considered a legacy data center.” Officials said a meeting focusing on public comment and discussion of the proposal will be held in December. artigo.texto: A movement opposing data center development in Rapid City appears to be gaining momentum in City Hall. Put simply, residents pressed the City Council with two options: halt data centers in the community or face potential recall petitions. As City Hall packed Monday night, citizens broke decorum standards, applauding, cheering and offering City Council an ultimatum. No one spoke in favor of data center development at the meeting. Several called back to advocate Jeff Shelton’s comments last week, pushing for a year-long moratorium on the matter, some threatening potential recall petitions, and recommending Council put the matter on the agenda at the Monday meeting. This comes as Council was considering but ultimately pushed back ordinances tied to data center development. Justin Huntley is the former flood plan and air quality manager for the city. He said it’s time to act. “Part of the programs I was involved with – we worked on the data center ordinance," Huntley said. "A lot of people put a lot of time into that. By delaying that ordinance, you’re leaving the window open for things to happen that nobody in this city wants. I would just ask that you, immediately, either approve the ordinance as written and amend it as needed, or apply the moratorium as soon as possible.” Resident Gabbi DeMarce said it simply doesn’t have to be this way. “You are looking at only a fraction of residents in Rapid City that do not support decisions made that subsidize, support, or depend on harmful, unnecessary projects like data centers, simply because it has always been that way," DeMarce said. "I urge you all to extend this moratorium. You have nothing to lose from data center companies and everything to lose in public trust and support.” A recent, Council-backed survey of residents found deep seeded opposition to data center development. Resident Taylor Gunhammer’s impassioned plea perhaps best reflects the growing tension in Council chambers. “It’s not Peter Thiel’s community, it’s not Elon Musk’s community, and we won’t stand for you selling it to them – we don’t want it," Gunhammer said. "We, the people, are not the hammer in your hand, you are the hammer in ours. If you serve the people of this community, as you claim to, there is nothing to discuss. We gave our ruling. You don’t have one. You work for us.” Rapid City Mayor Jason Salamun has called upon the Council to act quickly. Council ultimately did not motion put the matter on the Monday night agenda.

artigo.texto: Article Summary - Hundreds rallied at the state Capitol Wednesday for passage of the POWER Act, which would regulate data centers. - The bill’s Senate sponsor said the bill is a “big solution” for a “big problem.” - The legislation would, among other things, require big tech companies to pay for the energy used to power giant data centers. This summary was written by the reporters and editors who worked on this story. SPRINGFIELD — Hundreds of residents and environmental advocates rallied at the state Capitol Wednesday to urge lawmakers to regulate data centers. The residents came via bus, car and Amtrak from around the state to call for passage of the POWER Act, a bill that would require data centers to pay to create the energy they consume, mandate transparency around water use, limit noise levels and diesel generator use, ensure local community benefit agreements, and more. The bill failed to progress during the spring legislative session, but advocates hope to see it passed during the veto session. “Illinoisans are tired of fighting alone for basic protections without help from the state legislature,” said Lori McKiernan, a local Springfield community organizer and Sierra Club member. “Time is up. Our legislators must take action on data centers.” Over the summer break, lawmakers have been meeting with environmental advocates, organized labor, and representatives of the data center industry to negotiate the details. The Senate Energy and Public Utilities Committee was set to hold a hearing on the POWER Act at 4:30 p.m. Wednesday. Sen. Ram Villivalam, D-Chicago, is the lead sponsor of the Senate bill. He called the roughly 1,000-page bill a “big solution” for a “big problem,” and described the legislation as the “most comprehensive data center legislation in the nation.” “You’re here because this matters,” Villivalam told the crowd. “When something affects your families, your homes, your neighbors, and of course our bills, your voices deserve to be heard.” Battling big tech Data centers have existed for years in Illinois, housing servers and hardware that store data and power the digital world, supporting email, video streaming and other web services. But in recent years, as major technology firms race to create generative artificial intelligence, they have begun to build hyperscale data centers — massive buildings and campuses that sometimes consume the energy of a small city. Their actual and projected energy consumption have driven up energy costs for regular residents and small businesses. The rally comes shortly after the release of two reports from state agencies proposed delaying the planned closures of 11 fossil fuel plants, as required under the state’s landmark energy bill, in order to guarantee enough energy supply to meet the growing demand. But environmental advocates don’t want to see the state’s landmark climate goals delayed in order to power hyperscale data centers. “Big tech, they’re counting on us to be intimidated by their big money. They’re counting on us to be overwhelmed by the fight in front of us,” Illinois Environmental Council organizer Cate Caldwell said at the rally. “But as I look at this crowd today, I think big tech should be intimidated by us.” There won’t be a vote this week, but lawmakers could take up the issue when they return for their final days of the veto session next month. Capitol News Illinois is a nonprofit, nonpartisan news service that distributes state government coverage to hundreds of news outlets statewide. It is funded primarily by the Illinois Press Foundation and the Robert R. McCormick Foundation.
