artigo.texto: Japan said on Tuesday (November 17, 2026) that Southeast Asian nations will be able to access its crude oil storage facilities as part of efforts to prepare the region for a future energy crisis. The announcement came as leaders of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) met in Manila, where energy security has been high on the agenda. Keep track | ASEAN Summit LIVE updates: PM Modi at ASEAN-India Summit; Quad meeting likely after President Trump arrives Addressing regional leaders, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said her country's "hydro-tanks" would be available for use under the proposed initiative for cooperation on oil stockpiling. ASEAN members have been grappling with fuel shortages and price hikes after the West Asia conflict squeezed the flow of crude to the region. The regional bloc has previously called for "unimpeded" passage through the Strait of Hormuz, which was closed following U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran. Under the Japanese POWERR Asia initiative, ASEAN nations will be able to use Japan's excess storage capacity for crude oil. "We have suggested to utilise our crude oil stockpiling facilities in Japan, which is not utilised," Japan's Foreign Ministry press secretary Toshihiro Kitamura told reporters on the sidelines of the ASEAN summit. "By utilising those unused facilities in Japan, we can stockpile the other countries' crude oil and in case of crisis... it's a kind of joint stockpiling system." Japan has 254 days' worth of oil reserves, Mr. Kitamura said, while at the outbreak of the West Asia war in February some ASEAN countries had less than a month's worth. An ASEAN-backed study for joint stockpiling of oil has also recommended using facilities in Thailand and Indonesia, but Kitamura said a final decision had not been made. "It's under specific discussion," Mr. Kitamura said. "But as a government in Japan, we are ready to work with ASEAN countries to utilise our own facilities," he said. Longer term, Tokyo plans to assist ASEAN countries to build their own "stockpiling facilities". "I think this is very important in order to prepare ourselves for future possibilities, crises." Philippine Energy Secretary Sharon Garin said a memorandum of cooperation signed with Japan on Monday (November 16) included assistance to "put up many more facilities to store more oil, whether (that) is diesel, gas or crude oil", in the archipelago nation. "What this means is the Philippines will be more prepared in ensuring there is adequate oil for our homes and businesses, whatever the situation is," Ms. Garin told reporters. "With our reserves in place, we would be better positioned to support our transport, markets, and industries." Published - November 17, 2026 02:50 pm IST

artigo.texto: Empresas, profissionais e instituições ligados ao setor de data centers podem participar da Pesquisa Nacional de Data Centers, que recebe respostas até o dia 30 de novembro. A iniciativa busca reunir informações sobre o mercado brasileiro e identificar desafios e oportunidades para o desenvolvimento da infraestrutura digital no país. A pesquisa é conduzida pela Agência Brasileira de Desenvolvimento Industrial (ABDI), em parceria com o Centro de Pesquisa e Desenvolvimento em Telecomunicações (CPQD), como parte do Projeto ECOS – Data Centers Sustentáveis. O levantamento pretende reunir dados e opiniões de empresas, operadores, fornecedores, instituições públicas, universidades e outras organizações que atuam no segmento. Entre os temas abordados estão investimentos, infraestrutura, disponibilidade de energia, conectividade, formação de profissionais, sustentabilidade, regulação e inovação tecnológica. As informações coletadas serão utilizadas na elaboração de um diagnóstico sobre o setor de data centers no Brasil. O estudo deverá servir de base para identificar oportunidades de expansão, fortalecer a cadeia produtiva nacional e orientar possíveis políticas públicas relacionadas à infraestrutura digital e à soberania tecnológica. Além do questionário, o projeto realizou entrevistas técnicas, visitas presenciais e workshops em diferentes regiões do país. Os encontros foram organizados para discutir questões específicas de cada mercado regional. Em Campinas (SP), os debates abordaram infraestrutura energética e digital, inovação tecnológica, ambiente regulatório e oportunidades para ampliar a participação da indústria nacional na cadeia de data centers. Em Fortaleza (CE), o foco esteve na conectividade internacional por cabos submarinos, no potencial de geração de energia renovável, na infraestrutura de transmissão e nas condições para atrair novos investimentos. Já em Porto Alegre (RS), as discussões trataram da resistência da infraestrutura digital a eventos climáticos extremos, da segurança operacional, da conectividade regional e da continuidade de serviços essenciais. A participação na pesquisa permanece aberta até 30 de novembro e pode ser feita por organizações e profissionais ligados ao setor. Como participar: o questionário está disponível no site da ABDI, na página do Projeto ECOS – Data Centers Sustentáveis: https://www.abdi.com.br/projeto-ecos/#participe-da-pesquisa

artigo.texto: OLYPHANT — More than 200 people cheered on 27 Lackawanna County residents who urged council Tuesday not to settle a data center developer’s lawsuit and forgo the public hearing process for Project Triboro in exchange for $101 million. Council chose not to listen. Olyphant Borough Council voted 5-2 during a special meeting to approve the settlement with ERCOR Triboro LLC allowing it to move forward with plans to develop seven 420,000-square-foot data centers and a substation within the footprints of four previously approved warehouses off Marshwood Road and Route 247. Council President Jimmy Baldan and council members Beth Frushon, Eric Hartshorn, Tony Delfino and Fred Hartman voted in favor of the settlement. Council Vice President Robert Hudak and Councilman Mike Abda dissented. In an identical 5-2 vote, the council members approved a 15-year, $101 million community benefits agreement with ERCOR Triboro that was widely opposed by the community. Project Triboro will still be subject to the land development process under Olyphant’s planning commission as they modify their plans from warehouses to data centers — a detail project representatives stressed Tuesday night. But Project Triboro will not be required to navigate the conditional use hearing process, where residents would have had the opportunity to cross-examine data center representatives at public hearings and present their own evidence. Victor, New York-based ERCOR sued Olyphant in June in a bid to sidestep that process and develop its data centers as principal permitted uses. People crowded the Rescue & Restore Church sanctuary during the nearly three-hour meeting that culminated in council’s decision. As furious residents shouted at council and data center officials, half a dozen Olyphant police swarmed the front of the sanctuary after a hasty adjournment following the votes. “Give us each a million dollars for our house, then you could have our freaking town you dirtbags,” a woman yelled as the meeting adjourned. “I hate you all.” Borough police maintained a heavy presence throughout the night, including shutting down Willow Avenue and surrounding streets for the duration of the meeting. Police received credible threats of violence; officers arrested a Taylor man Tuesday, charging him with terroristic threats and harassment, Police Chief James DeVoe said. The man’s name was unavailable Tuesday night. Following a brief presentation by ERCOR Triboro and Emergent Data Centers, who partnered with ERCOR to design and develop the data centers, residents addressed council. Every speaker opposed the settlement and CBA, either asking council to table its decision or to outright deny it. Lifelong resident Nicole Pasko, 27, one of the first speakers Tuesday, stood before council and described her pride in Olyphant and its small-town charm. “By allowing this corporation to buy you and your cooperation, you are directly sewing shut the mouths of your constituents,” Pasko said. “Grow a backbone and say, ‘No.’ Listen to those that voted you into these positions. Your vote tonight shows exactly what you think about the people of our town, our opinions and our futures.” As residents discussed the night’s proceedings on the sidewalk in front of Rescue & Rescue Church after the decision, Lackawanna County Commissioner Bill Gaughan said council’s complete disdain for public comment was embarrassing. Gaughan, who also spoke during the meeting, criticized council members for failing to explain their decision. “For them again not to explain their vote is a complete dereliction of duty on their part,” Gaughan said, calling it their basic responsibility. “They didn’t even do that, and it just shows a complete lack of respect for the people.” Check back for updates.

artigo.texto: LEBANON, OH -- Warren County commissioners are preparing to take another look at regulations governing data center development when they meet Dec. 1, as the county continues evaluating how large-scale facilities could affect local communities and resources. During the commissioners' Nov. 17 meeting, county officials reported that planning and zoning staff are developing proposed regulations for discussion at an upcoming work session. The discussion follows the commissioners' Sept. 29 decision to establish a temporary moratorium on data center development in areas governed by county zoning. The moratorium provides time for officials to examine potential impacts and establish appropriate regulations before considering new development proposals. County Preparing New Regulations During Tuesday's meeting, county officials reported attending a recent Ohio-Kentucky-Indiana Regional Council of Governments (OKI) symposium focused on data centers. The gathering included representatives from government agencies and the data center industry, including Amazon. According to the discussion, an Amazon representative indicated that the company welcomes clear zoning regulations because uncertainty about local requirements can make development planning more difficult. County officials also reported that Warren County has not received a data center development application. The county's current moratorium includes a provision for periodic review every 60 days, with the next review scheduled for Dec. 1. At that meeting, planning and zoning staff expect to present draft regulations for commissioners to evaluate and discuss. Water, Power and Community Impacts Commissioners previously raised concerns about the potential demands large data centers could place on water supplies, electricity and other infrastructure. Unlike traditional commercial buildings, large data centers can require substantial electrical capacity and cooling systems to support computer equipment operating around the clock. Officials have been considering how zoning regulations could address these facilities while protecting surrounding communities. The commissioners discussed several potential regulatory approaches during their September work session, including conditional-use approvals, site plan requirements and the creation of a separate zoning classification for data centers. What Happens Next? The Dec. 1 meeting is expected to provide commissioners with an opportunity to review proposed regulations and offer additional direction to county planning staff. No final zoning regulations were adopted during the Nov. 17 discussion. For now, the temporary moratorium remains in place as Warren County continues determining how future data center proposals should be evaluated. artigo.texto: HILLSBORO, Texas (KXXV) — The proposed Provident data center has now pulled out of its agreement to come to Hillsboro. - “They’re taking a lot of the farmland, and I’m not happy about that," said Sheila Brazil. - In August 2026, the city announced that Provident no longer had the property under contract. “We’re going to have to pay their water and their electric bill, and I don’t think that’s fair," said Shelia Brazil, a Hill County resident. In this case, Sheila Brazil thinks less is best. Brazil, a Hill County resident, said that with Provident Data Centers backing out of coming to Hillsboro, she’s completely okay with it. “They’re taking a lot of the farmland, and I’m not happy about that," said Brazil. According to the City of Hillsboro, the city's economic development corporation entered into a contract with Provident in September 2024 for the potential sale of approximately 300 acres. In August 2026, the city announced that Provident no longer had the property under contract. “That contract on the land, everything before close is a matter of due diligence. So they were going through their processes to see whether the project could come to fruition. There’s a lot of uncertainty, statewide, around data centers, and at the time they were in a month-to-month contract extension period and decided to terminate," said Jessica Trew, the executive director for the Hillsboro Economic Development Corporation. Trew explained that the initial contract for Provident was for nine months to complete its due diligence. Afterwards, she said the company started asking for contract extensions. Trew said she’s unsure why Provident ended the contract. 25 News reached out to Provident Data Centers, but we have not heard back. TA Smith, the founder of the Texas Coalition Against Data Centers, said he’s not sure what to believe. "Everyone keeps saying Provident is backing out… are they? They might have backed out on paper; they may have publicly backed out, but have they actually left?" said TA Smith, founder of the Texas Coalition Against Data Centers. But Provident may not be the only data center backing out on projects. Data Center Watch reports at least 75 data center projects worth billions were blocked or delayed in the first quarter of 2026. Smith said regardless of the reason, this is good news. “At the moment it gives you a sigh of relief, but again next month it’s a different story and that same company…there’s nothing against them coming back...here’s a new proposal with a new zoning board committee," said Smith. Trew said the EDC isn’t for or against data centers, and the property once sought by Provident cannot be used for farmland. Brazil said whatever comes to Hill County can impact many people. “And we care about what comes up, what comes here, and what’s going to affect us," said Brazil.

artigo.texto: As developers pursue new data center projects in SF, the Board of Supervisors voted Tuesday to extend a moratorium on new facilities, citing unanswered questions about their environmental impacts and demands on the city's power grid. San Francisco supervisors voted unanimously Tuesday to extend the temporary ban for 10 months and 15 days, as the Chronicle reports. The extension, recommended by the Land Use and Transportation Committee on Monday, gives the Planning Department more time to examine the facilities' potential effects and develop regulations before the city considers approving additional projects. The vote follows a report released last week by the Planning Department that identified significant gaps in the city's understanding of existing data centers, including their electricity and water consumption, pollution, and effects on surrounding neighborhoods, as SFist reported previously. The department stopped short of recommending whether San Francisco should allow more facilities, but outlined several policy changes officials could consider, including restricting standalone data centers in residential and commercial areas and requiring developers to assess impacts on nearby communities. According to Mission Local, the report also recommended updating the city's definition of a data center, which currently relies on language dating back to 2001, to better align with the state's definition. The department's assessment examined the city's three standalone facilities but acknowledged that San Francisco does not maintain a complete inventory of smaller data centers operating inside other buildings. Data Center Map, meanwhile, identifies 15 potential facilities throughout the city, many of them downtown. Two of the larger standalone facilities are located along Paul Avenue in Bayview Hunters Point, a neighborhood that has experienced disproportionate air pollution for decades due to industrial operations, truck traffic, and a former PG&E power plant that closed in 2006. District 10 Supervisor Shamann Walton, who represents the neighborhood and introduced the original moratorium in October, said the city needs to understand how the facilities affect residents before allowing additional development. “We really don't know the impact of data centers to our communities,” Walton said before Tuesday's vote. The Planning Department's report also warned that larger facilities could place substantial demands on an electricity grid already approaching its transmission capacity. A 50-megawatt data center could use as much electricity as 25,000 new homes, potentially competing with housing, hospitals, and businesses for limited power resources, as previously reported. Other concerns include air pollution and noise from backup generators. Developers have explored potential data center projects at the shuttered SF Centre mall downtown and in Dogpatch. NOVVA, an existing facility at 400 Paul Ave. in Bayview, had also planned to expand from nine to 36 megawatts by 2028, but those plans are now on hold. The moratorium comes as San Francisco attempts to balance its ambitions to remain a center of the AI industry against the infrastructure demands of the facilities needed to support it. As the Chronicle notes, Mayor Daniel Lurie has made attracting tech investment part of his economic strategy, while labor groups have argued that data centers could create union construction jobs and help fund needed infrastructure improvements. In a letter Monday, Building and Construction Trades Council leader Rudy Gonzalez, who ran Supervisor Connie Chan’s campaign for US Congress, opposed a permanent ban, arguing that developers should have a path to approval if they meet enforceable environmental and labor standards and cover the costs of the infrastructure they require. He also urged the city to distinguish large commercial facilities from smaller research and development sites. Walton acknowledged the union's concerns and said he intends to involve labor and community groups in developing future restrictions. Per the Chronicle, public speakers at Monday's committee hearing, meanwhile, questioned whether data centers would deliver meaningful employment benefits, given the relatively small number of workers needed to operate them. Others raised concerns about pollution and the concentration of facilities in communities already facing environmental burdens. San Francisco now joins Oakland and Seattle in extending temporary restrictions while officials work on regulations. As SFist reported last week, Oakland supervisors also voted unanimously to extend that city's moratorium for another 10 months and 15 days, through October 5, 2027. Oakland is reviewing potential effects on its electricity grid, water supply, and air quality after receiving inquiries from developers, including Behring Companies, which proposed putting a data center inside a downtown office building. artigo.texto: ACME Solar Holdings Limited has announced the commissioning of an additional Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) component with a capacity of 52.32 MW / 209.28 MWh for its firm and dispatchable renewable energy project in Bikaner district, Rajasthan. The newly commissioned storage component is scheduled to achieve its commercial operation date (COD) on November 19, 2026. Following this latest development, the cumulative commissioned capacity of the project’s battery energy storage component has reached 247.67 MW / 990.68 MWh. The overall installed storage capacity of the project stands at 247.67 MW / 1,321 MWh, marking further progress in the company’s efforts to strengthen its renewable energy and storage portfolio. The project is being developed through a wholly owned subsidiary of ACME Solar Holdings Limited. The company has also entered into a Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) with SJVN Limited for the supply of electricity generated under the firm and dispatchable renewable energy project. The commissioning of the additional BESS capacity represents an important step towards improving the project’s energy storage capabilities and supporting the reliable supply of renewable power. Battery storage systems play a significant role in managing the intermittent nature of renewable energy generation by storing electricity and making it available when required. With the latest addition, ACME Solar continues to advance its integrated renewable energy development strategy, combining solar power generation with battery storage solutions. The project also highlights the growing importance of energy storage infrastructure in supporting India’s transition towards a more reliable and flexible renewable energy system. artigo.texto: China is targeting 300 million kilowatts (300 GW) of installed new energy storage capacity by 2030, with an average storage duration of approximately three hours, under its latest policy roadmap. The target is part of the 15th Five-Year Plan New Energy Storage Implementation Plan, released on November 13 by the National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC) and the National Energy Administration (NEA). The plan aims to move the energy storage sector from policy-driven expansion towards market-oriented development and operation. The blueprint builds on the rapid growth achieved during the 14th Five-Year Plan period. China’s installed new energy storage capacity increased from around 3 million kilowatts at the end of the 13th Five-Year Plan to 136 million kilowatts. This expansion has strengthened the country’s ability to integrate renewable energy, improve power system stability and maintain electricity supplies during periods of peak demand. Under the new framework, authorities will focus on expanding storage applications across different parts of the electricity system while improving market mechanisms, industry management, industrial development and international cooperation. The plan identifies three major application areas: power generation, electricity grids and innovative business models. On the power generation side, energy storage will support large-scale renewable energy bases and improve the ability of renewable projects to participate in electricity markets. On the grid side, storage systems will help strengthen regulation capabilities, balance electricity supply and demand, and improve overall grid stability. The plan also encourages coordination between storage projects and emerging electricity business models. Grid-side energy storage currently accounts for more than 50% of China’s total installed new energy storage capacity. It is expected to remain a major contributor to additional capacity during the 15th Five-Year Plan period. According to an NEA official, future deployment will prioritise electricity supply security, renewable energy absorption and grid stability. To support these objectives, authorities plan to improve inventory management, introduce capacity-based electricity pricing mechanisms and guide the appropriate location of storage projects. These measures are intended to ensure that storage facilities are developed according to regional electricity requirements. Improving project profitability is another major priority. China’s energy storage industry has gradually developed a three-part revenue model based on capacity payments, electricity market transactions and frequency regulation auxiliary services. However, the government plans to strengthen these mechanisms to ensure more sustainable financial returns for project developers and operators. The implementation plan proposes better recognition of energy storage capacity value, including capacity tariff mechanisms for independent grid-connected storage projects. It also calls for improved charging and discharging price signals and more flexible peak-and-valley electricity tariffs that reflect actual supply and demand conditions. Industrial and commercial consumers, along with industrial parks, will also be encouraged to invest in energy storage solutions. The government will align the pace of capacity expansion with regional grid requirements, electricity price affordability and market absorption capacity. Through these measures, China aims to establish a commercially sustainable energy storage industry by 2030, with market mechanisms playing a greater role in investment decisions, project development and operational performance. Vacco recites many of the usual reasons given for expensive housing in New York, everything from lack of supply to unionized construction labor. These are all to be considered, but like our entire political class, Vacco is silent about one obvious solution: property tax reform. A mayoral commission published findings and recommendations that were cravenly left behind by Mayor Bill de Blasio on his last day in office and ignored ever since. Equitable reform would provide thousands annually in immediate relief for the overwhelming majority of homeowners (97% of Staten Island ones). Which areas would it hurt? Park Slope, for one — a very affluent area long since paying the lowest effective rates in the city, now enjoying five-figure annual discounts paid for by unfairly taxed, striving homeowners from Bay Ridge to Whitestone. Most landlords would see their property tax burden decrease as well, easing the imposition of badly needed rent regulations. It’s about time the burden is finally borne appropriately by Brooklyn brownstone, Central Park condo and Upper West Side elites, not the other way around. artigo.texto: Loudon County Is the Data Center Capital of the World. Now It's Paused Building New Ones. Data centers have cut residents’ tax rates and funded schools. Loudoun’s board paused new approvals anyway. The nationwide data center backlash has reached the industry's home turf. On Tuesday night, the Board of Supervisors for Loudoun County, Virginia—the data center capital of the world—voted to pause approval for new data center projects for the next 10 months. The pause was passed in a 7–1 vote, with one supervisor abstaining. The measure will halt board approval for new data center and substation applications potentially until next September while the county develops new rules. Projects in the Route 28 tax district, a special commercial tax district in eastern Loudoun, are exempt. In the meantime, pre-approved projects can continue. The vote comes amid mounting concerns from residents over developments near residential areas, noise disturbances, air quality, and impacts on the electrical grid. "The fact of the matter is that this development of data centers has moved a lot faster than the board has been able to respond," said Supervisor Juli Briskman, who proposed the pause, according to reporting from Bisnow. "And we did have a lot of missed opportunities to respond and get this under control, as our constituents have been begging us to do, and this is a golden opportunity to do that tonight." Loudoun County has the highest concentration of data centers in the world, with around 233 of these facilities already up or under construction. As industry advocates pointed out during the meeting, this has brought immense economic benefits to the county. According to county data, data centers are expected to generate around $1.3 billion in tax revenue in FY 2027. Data center revenue alone is expected to make up roughly 40 percent of the county's total budget. This revenue has contributed to a steady decrease in the county's real property tax rate over the past decade. The rate has fallen to $0.805 per $100 of assessed value from $1.145 in 2016, making it the lowest rate in northern Virginia, according to the county. At the same time, the county increased funding for the school system by $105 million this year, thanks in large part to data centers. Board Chair Phyllis Randall, who voted in favor of the pause, acknowledged the economic benefits, but stressed that her duty to her constituents comes first. "I'm also an elected official, and I'm supposed to move to some degree with the constituents, so when constituents have switched, I'm not supposed to just say well three years ago you weren't saying that so I'm not going to do anything different," she said, according to reporting from local CBS affiliate WUSA9. Not everyone on the board was so convinced. Supervisor Caleb Kershner, who abstained from the vote, had some choice words for the measure. "This, ladies and gentlemen, is a pure political vote to try to win votes," he said. "This is really bad governance to do it this way. We expose ourselves to litigation." He argued that if developers successfully challenge the resolution in court, it could cost the county big time, citing a potential estimate of up to $60 million in legal costs. Even though he called the pause "legally defensible," the county attorney echoed Kershner's warnings about the potential threat of litigation. Despite their benefits, data centers have recently faced staunch opposition from local communities in the United States. On election night, localities across the country considered at least 40 ballot measures to rein in the industry, most of which passed. In the third quarter of 2026, construction of these facilities slowed down for the first time in a year, according to Cleanview, a data center research firm. Now, Loudoun County, which has felt the benefits of data centers firsthand arguably the most in the country, has voted to slow down the industry. If the data center capital of the world is having second thoughts, this could spell even more trouble for the rest of America's AI buildout.

artigo.texto: BYD supera Toyota na preferência por eletrificados, diz pesquisa Pesquisa da Webmotors mostra que metade dos donos de eletrificados tem modelos chineses; pós-venda ainda é desafio para novas fabricantes As marcas chinesas estão ganhando espaço na preferência dos consumidores brasileiros e já superam montadoras tradicionais em diferentes indicadores do mercado automotivo, segundo pesquisa da Webmotors Autoinsights. A BYD ultrapassou a Toyota na intenção de compra de veículos eletrificados, enquanto fabricantes como Omoda Jaecoo, Geely e GAC também aparecem entre as marcas emergentes mais consideradas pelos motoristas. No levantamento sobre eletrificados, realizado em junho com mais de 1.200 usuários da plataforma, a BYD lidera a intenção de compra, com 24% das menções, ante 17% em 2025. A Toyota, que ocupava a primeira posição no ano passado, caiu de 28% para 19%. A presença chinesa também aparece entre quem já possui um eletrificado. Cerca de metade dos proprietários ouvidos tem um carro de marca chinesa. A BYD concentra 25% das menções, seguida por Toyota (14,2%), GWM (9,4%) e Caoa Chery (4,7%). Omoda Jaecoo, GAC e Geely também aparecem na lista. O avanço também aparece nas buscas da plataforma. Entre junho de 2025 e junho de 2026, os contatos de compradores com vendedores de eletrificados da BYD cresceram e chegaram a 2,9 vezes o volume registrado pela Toyota. A GWM teve alta de 119% no período. Para Eduardo Jurcevic, CEO da Webmotors, a competitividade das fabricantes chinesas está relacionada à escala de produção e à oferta de tecnologia. "As marcas chinesas chegaram a esse mercado com uma vantagem de escala: a eletrificação já representa 52% das vendas de carros de passeio na China, e o país exportou 2,6 milhões de eletrificados em 2025, alta de 104% em um ano. Isso permitiu trazer um portfólio amplo de híbridos e elétricos, com preços e condições muito competitivos", afirma. Apesar do avanço, a confiança nas fabricantes ainda é um obstáculo. Em outra pesquisa da Webmotors, realizada em setembro, apenas 17,6% disseram que comprariam uma marca nova ou pouco conhecida. Outros 44,8% descartam essa possibilidade. Quando as marcas são apresentadas pelo nome, porém, a resistência diminui. Omoda Jaecoo lidera a intenção de compra entre as fabricantes emergentes, com 30,8%, seguida por Geely (27,9%) e GAC (22,5%). A principal preocupação dos consumidores é a disponibilidade de peças e serviços de manutenção, citada por 28,9% dos entrevistados. O custo-benefício aparece em seguida, com 28,2%. "O pós-venda é, sim, a principal barreira, mas não é a única, e não se vence de uma vez só", afirma Jurcevic, acrescentando que a reputação das fabricantes e o valor de revenda também pesam na decisão de compra.

artigo.texto: Client news A&O Shearman advises Macquarie Capital on strategic joint venture with Revera Energy for UK battery storage A&O Shearman has advised Macquarie Capital on the formation of a strategic joint venture with Carlyle-backed Revera Energy, a global independent energy platform backed by global investment firm Carlyle, under which Macquarie Capital will make an initial investment alongside Revera in two transmission-connected battery energy storage system (BESS) projects in Scotland. The projects, both now under construction, are Windyhill BESS (200 MW / 400 MWh), located in Bearsden, which reached financial close and notice to proceed in February 2026 and remains on track for commercial operations in Q4 2027, and Hunterston BESS (400 MW / 800 MWh), located in North Ayrshire, which reached financial close and notice to proceed in September 2026, with commercial operations expected in Q3 2028. The partnership provides scope for further investment opportunities across Revera’s UK portfolio, including the 400 MW Kincardine BESS, and supports the UK's Clean Power 2030 Action Plan. The A&O Shearman team was led by partner Dan Graham and senior associate Arabella Robinson, with support from associates Ine Deblaere and Livia Gauntlett. The team also included energy, natural resources and infrastructure partners Edward Moser and Alexander Chenery, senior associates Saskia Volhard Martin and Arvindh Rai, and associates Kamilla Marianayagam and Aidan Swietochowski; tax partner James Burton, counsel Sorsha Taylor and associate Maria Clezy; antitrust partner Thomas Masterman and associate Amol Vani; and environment and sanctions partner Matthew Townsend and senior associate Danae Wheeler. artigo.texto: Springfield City Council to consider defining data centers, extending pauses on applications Three proposals on Monday’s agenda would add a city code definition and extend pauses through Feb. 24 SPRINGFIELD, Mo. (KY3) - The Springfield City Council on Monday night will take up three proposals. One would define what a data center is under city code. The other two would extend pauses on development and utility applications while the city works on potential regulations. The current pause expires Tuesday. The proposed extensions would run through Feb. 24. What the proposals would do Council Bill 2026-235 would amend the city’s Land Development Code by adding definitions related to data centers. The bill is up for second reading tonight. Council members can amend or adopt it, and a vote is required for it to be adopted. Unless an amendment is offered, the bill would be voted on tonight. The other two proposals would extend existing pauses on development and utility-related applications through Feb. 24. The ordinance says the Land Development Code does not currently define data centers. It says the amendment establishes a common definition of “data center” and related terms only, as a first step before consideration of later text amendments and public hearings. Steve Childers, the city’s director of planning and development, said the city has not yet written a definition for data centers. He said the city needs that definition before it can establish rules for where data centers can go and how they can operate. “We’re just taking the time to get it right, taking the time to do the due diligence we need in order to be able to do the research, pull it all together and present council with a draft ordinance that they could consider,” Childers said. Any future regulations would still have to go through additional review and public hearings. How the ordinance defines data centers Under the proposed definition, a data center is a building, or a room or portion of a building, used to house information technology equipment for the storage, management, processing or transmission of digital data. The definition lists server farms, artificial intelligence training or processing, image processing, cloud computing, email services, and cryptocurrency or other digital-asset mining, among other uses. The definition also includes backup generators, energy storage systems, on-site electric generation, cooling equipment, electrical equipment, and any substations that primarily serve the data center. The ordinance would classify data centers into three types: - Accessory data center: Located within the principal building on the lot, with a data center floor area of no more than 20% of the building’s gross floor area. It serves only the owner or a tenant of the premises, does not sell, lease, or otherwise provide data storage, processing, or computing capacity to others, and has a maximum power demand of less than 1 megawatt. - Micro data center: Not an accessory data center, with a floor area of no more than 10,000 square feet and a maximum power demand of less than 5 megawatts. - Large-load data center: Not an accessory data center, with a maximum power demand of 5 megawatts or more or a floor area of more than 10,000 square feet. The ordinance says data centers other than accessory data centers that are on the same lot or premises, on adjacent lots, or under common ownership or control and share infrastructure or a point of interconnection with the electric utility would be treated as one data center. Their floor area and maximum power demand would be combined. The ordinance would take effect immediately upon passage. The Planning and Zoning Commission held a public hearing on the amendments Oct. 15 and recommended approval, with additional changes, by a vote of 7 to 0. Existing pause and public input City Council enacted Special Ordinance 28306 on June 29 to delay the acceptance and processing of applications relating to the evaluation, establishment, servicing or expansion of a data center facility until Nov. 17. The ordinance says the city held three public engagement sessions on data centers during the delay, and city staff is reviewing the feedback. The current moratorium has put at least one proposed project on hold. Trent Overhue, who was working to develop a data center at 2900 National Ave., asked a judge for permission to keep moving forward despite the moratorium. The Greene County Circuit Court denied the request for a preliminary injunction Nov. 9. When asked about a formal interview with KY3, Overhue declined. How data centers differ Matt Powell, executive director of the Missouri Cybersecurity Center of Excellence, said many people’s digital lives rely on data centers, from online banking to storing photos and shopping online. He said data centers support technology people use in everyday life, including banks giving customers access to their money, photos and family albums on phones, and GPS on phones. “You know that phrase, it’s on someone else’s computer. That’s essentially what it is,” Powell said. Powell said data centers have large amounts of storage capabilities and are used for accessing and storing people’s data. Powell said not all data centers are the same. Some primarily store information, while others use much more electricity to power the computing behind things like artificial intelligence. Powell said data centers are essentially hubs that allow data to flow throughout the world. “At one point it used to be thought of, well, the internet’s a bunch of invisible wires that connect everyone together,” Powell said. “Well, think of data centers as those hubs. You know, that data is going to ... it goes faster, it’s able to travel further and faster when we have hubs that support that data and push it along, kind of like a relay race, right? So it’s relaying information from one point to another.” The council meeting begins at 6:30 p.m. at the Regional Police-Fire Training Center on Bat

artigo.texto: Irondale sets rules for data centers before any are proposed, but resident raises loophole concerns Irondale is putting rules in place for potential data centers before any companies come knocking. The City Council voted unanimously to approve an ordinance regulating data center development after a second reading and a chance for residents to comment. Mayor James Stewart Jr. said no data centers have been proposed in the city, and no companies have expressed interest in building one. The regulations follow a six- to seven-month study led by a city councilor. Stewart said the goal is to prepare for potential development while protecting residents. Under the ordinance, data center companies must pay for any necessary power grid upgrades, keep noise within a specified limit and use a closed-loop cooling system. The ordinance also establishes a community benefit agreement intended to support schools, infrastructure and nonprofit organizations and requires the data center company to complete a certification every year to hold it responsible. Stewart said he hopes the ordinance will help residents make informed decisions about data centers while providing safeguards for the community. “A lot of this has to do with education,” Stewart said. “We’re hoping that the ordinance provides that information. It gives you the opportunity to be able to educate our citizens more, but then it also, at the end of the day, protects our community.” The mayor said three residents spoke during the meeting, and one opposed bringing data centers to Irondale. That resident didn’t want to go on camera but expressed concerns about specific language data centers can use to find loopholes around the established regulations. She also feels like the six-to seven-month study is outdated and so much has changed with data centers since it was done. She said she felt like a moratorium on data centers would’ve been better, but Stewart said that would only allow for the city to do more research, which it's already done.

artigo.texto: Georgetown panel recommends denial of rezoning for northeast data center after outcry GEORGETOWN, Texas — Georgetown's Planning and Zoning Commission unanimously recommended denying a rezoning request Tuesday night for a proposed data center in northeast Georgetown, following opposition from residents concerned about the project's proximity to neighborhoods and future development. More than 100 people signed up to speak at Tuesday's meeting as commissioners considered a request to rezone approximately 28 acres near East University Avenue and Northeast Inner Loop. Commissioners ultimately voted unanimously to recommend denying the proposal, citing concerns about how close the data center would be to nearby neighborhoods and its potential impact on future development. Residents raised concerns about potential light and noise pollution, as well as how the project could affect the surrounding area. The proposal includes a data center, on-site generators and closed-loop cooling systems. A representative of the developer, Phillip Niels, said the project would use low-level lighting and was designed to limit noise compared to larger artificial intelligence data centers. ALSO| More camp safety law changes could be on their way in Texas Niels also said the project could generate millions of dollars in property tax revenue for the city. "If this project is built as planned, it will be the largest taxpayer in Georgetown," Niels said. "Should deliver 10 to 15 million dollars a year in property taxes." The rezoning request would increase the maximum allowed data center building footprint from 5,000 to 290,000 square feet. Among those opposing the location were Judy Fabry and Kerry Brun, who said they have lived about half a mile from the proposed site for more than 30 years. "It's too close to houses. It will ruin any other development in that area. And we need a grocery store out there," Fabry said. "There's a lot of downsides, I think. I don't even know what an upside of having a data center would be," Brun said. Despite the commission's unanimous recommendation to deny the rezoning request, the proposal is not yet officially rejected. Georgetown City Council is expected to consider the rezoning request and the commission's recommendation on Dec. 8. Because the Planning and Zoning Commission recommended denial, the City Council would need a 6-1 vote to overturn that recommendation and approve the rezoning request. This is a developing story and will be updated as more information becomes available.

artigo.texto: Data centers no Brasil terão que ter licença prévia dos EUA para comprar chips de IA da Nvidia Medida dos EUA também atinge Singapura, Malásia, Tailândia e Indonésia para impedir que empresas chinesas usem chips avançados da Nvidia Resumo - Departamento de Comércio passou a exigir licença prévia para a compra de chips avançados de IA da Nvidia. - Objetivo da medida é impedir que empresas chinesas e de Macau acessem tecnologia americana por meio de servidores no exterior. - A restrição atinge data centers no Brasil, Singapura, Malásia, Tailândia e Indonésia. - Exigência vale para centros que fornecem mais de 12 milhões de unidades de processamento a empresas de Macau ou do Grupo D:5 (como a China). - Norma foi adotada logo após um escândalo de espionagem forçar a renúncia de Jensen Huang do comando da Nvidia. O governo dos Estados Unidos emitiu nesta segunda-feira, dia 16, uma norma para impedir que empresas chinesas utilizem chips avançados de inteligência artificial (IA) dos EUA em centros de dados de outros países. Dentre os países afetados estão data centers no Brasil, Singapura, Malásia, Tailândia e Indonésia. Na prática, data centers que fornecem mais de 12 milhões de unidades de desempenho de processamento a empresas de Macau ou dos países do Grupo D:5, que inclui a China, precisam obter licença prévia do governo americano para comprarem chips avançados de IA da Nvidia. Conforme o Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), a norma evita que restrições a tecnologias sensíveis dos EUA sejam contornadas por data centers de países terceiros. As empresas norte-americanas que operam nesses países, incluindo o Brasil, mas bloqueiam o acesso a países restritos ficam isentas da exigência da licença. A medida, adotada pelo Departamento de Comércio americano, é tomada logo após um escândalo de espionagem ter forçado a renúncia de Jensen Huang como diretor-executivo da Nvidia, em meio a relatos de que ele ajudou a facilitar o acesso da China à tecnologia de sua empresa, em violação às normas americanas. Proibição à China Em virtude de medidas sucessivas dos governos de Joe Biden (2021-2025) e Donald Trump, está proibida a venda dos processadores de tecnologia americana mais avançados para empresas chinesas. Washington justifica essas restrições pelo receio de que a China desenvolva uma IA de ponta para fins militares e, mais recentemente, também para conter o avanço de Pequim para a superinteligência. A superinteligência marcaria o momento em que a IA superaria as capacidades humanas de raciocínio e compreensão, e muitos consideram que quem alcançar esse estágio primeiro obterá uma vantagem decisiva nos campos tecnológico e estratégico. O secretário de Comércio dos Estados Unidos, Howard Lutnick, foi acusado por vários observadores de ter trabalhado para flexibilizar as regras de exportação de chips americanos para a China. Na sexta-feira, 13, o secretário do Tesouro, Scott Bessent, criticou publicamente seu colega de governo por essa questão. O documento que apresenta as novas regras de exportação foi publicado pelo Departamento de Comércio, mas foi "redigido pelo Departamento do Tesouro e pelo Conselho de Segurança Nacional, a pedido de ambos", segundo um comunicado do governo americano. Impactos para o Brasil De acordo com o especialista em gestão e governança de riscos digitais, cibersegurança e proteção de dados digitais, Paulo Nascimento, na prática, os data centers brasileiros de grande porte precisam adquirir esses processadores de ponta. “Só que a partir de agora eles precisam de uma autorização dos EUA e essa exigência acaba sendo ativada quando esse poder computacional vai ultrapassando determinado limite, que é de 750 chips NVidia H-100”, exemplifica Nascimento. Ele aponta os principais riscos para os data centers instalados ou em processo de instalação no Ceará. “Primeiro é o atraso e o encarecimento dos projetos porque agora vai depender dessa licença americana, que pode ou não ser concedida. Segundo, a incerteza para novos investimentos. Os investidores vão pensar duas ou três vezes antes de colocar alguns bilhões em projetos que dependem de autorização de um outro país. E o terceiro risco, seria uma vantagem competitiva para as operadoras americanas, que estão isentas dessa exigência”, elenca. De acordo com o professor do Departamento de Telemática do Instituto Federal do Ceará (IFCE), campus Fortaleza, Wendell Rodrigues, a decisão pode, sim, afetar o País. “Isso não vai impactar quem já tenha esse acesso a esses chips, mas nas novas aquisições e novos projetos. Aqui mesmo no Instituto Federal a gente deve adquirir nos próximos meses toda uma plataforma baseada em chips avançados de inteligência artificial conhecida como GPUs”, cita. Para o idealizador do projeto Iracema Digital, Mauro Oliveira, “a regra inclui o Brasil por risco presumido de desvio, sem apresentar um caso concreto envolvendo o País. Somos suspeitos do que poderíamos fazer”. Ele lembra, contudo, que empresas sediadas nos EUA, ou controladas por matrizes americanas ficam dispensadas da licença. “A big tech americana instalada em solo brasileiro segue recebendo seus chips. A empresa brasileira entra na fila”, critica. Por sua vez, o diretor do Fórum Brasileiro de Internet das Coisas, Vivaldo José Breternitz, minimiza o impacto da decisão sobre o Brasil. “É mais oba-oba. Eu acho que o Trump tomou esse tipo de medida pensando nas eleições que aconteceram. Algum atraso pode ocorrer, algum aumento de custo pode ocorrer, mas nada que vá mudar radicalmente o cenário de investimentos nos data centers que estão sendo construídos aqui”, pondera. Já a Associação das Empresas de Tecnologia da Informação e Comunicação e de Tecnologias Digitais do Brasil (Brasscom) disse, por meio de sua assessoria, que não comentaria sobre o assunto. O POVO também tentou contato com as principais empresas do setor de armazenamento de dados que atuam no Ceará, a Omnia e a Tecto Data Centers, e aguarda posicionamento para atualização posterior. (C

artigo.texto: Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said Tuesday it would be a âhistoric mistakeâ for the US to pull back on its AI infrastructure buildout following the data center backlash during the midterm elections. âI cannot fathom any scenario where the United States stops building data centers and allows another country like China to establish all the norms,â Jassy said at Semaforâs Silicon Valley & The World. The US would regret such a move âfor a very long time,â said Jassy, who has directed hundreds of billions into data centers around the world. Still, he acknowledged that tech companies need to âdo it better and partner more closely with our communities.â Given Nvidia is so central to the AI buildout, Jassy said he didnât think Jensen Huangâs departure would impact Amazon and pledged to continue working closely with the chipmaker. The growth in AI stems from âmore than one company,â he said. Nvidia GPUs help power AWS data centers and Amazon works with the chip giant on infrastructure and robotics. âTheyâll have to work out how they move forward as a company, but weâll be partners with them either way.â Jassy also said that Amazon, which currently doesnât let Metaâs Muse and other consumer agents access its site, is still talking to companies like Meta about how to open up the e-commerce giant to consumers who want to use the agents. He said the company would open up the site to agents if it could find a âgood exchange of valueâ and a positive experience for customers, which isnât happening at the moment.

artigo.texto: The data center capital of the world is pressing pause on legislative approvals for the digital infrastructure facilities through as late as September of next year. The Loudoun County Board of Supervisors voted 7-1, with one abstaining, Tuesday evening to halt consideration of legislative applications for data centers and substations, with a retroactive effective date of Sept. 15. Thirty-three legislative applications are currently active, according to the resolution. Supervisor Kristen Umstattd, who represents the Leesburg District, voted against the motion, and Supervisor Caleb Kershner, who represents the Catoctin District, abstained. "Just the fact of the matter is that this development of data centers has moved a lot faster than the board has been able to respond," Supervisor Juli Briskman, who proposed the review that culminated in the resolution, said just before the vote. "And we did have a lot of missed opportunities to respond and get this under control, as our constituents have been begging us to do, and this is a golden opportunity to do that tonight," added Briskman, who represents the Algonkian District. Loudoun County is in the second phase of its impact study that would establish new guidance and standards for data centers and substations. The result of that study is expected to be released next spring. The county's pause comes as communities across the U.S. are fighting to slow down the rapidly spreading asset class. Next door to Loudoun, Prince William County in September drastically shrank its map for data centers that are allowed by right. Montgomery County instituted an 18-month data center freeze in July. New York instituted a yearlong moratorium for large-scale data centers, also in July, and at least seven more states are considering similar measures, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures. Loudoun’s halting of legislative applications includes rezonings and special exceptions that need to be approved by the board. Administrative applications for things like site plans and subdivision plans would still be allowed to proceed. Data center moratoriums are not allowed in Virginia. But since the board has one year to review legislative applications under Loudoun's zoning ordinance, it's using that length of time to effect the pause. At Tuesday night's board meeting, Loudoun County Attorney Leo Rogers confirmed the legality of the pause that the county is undertaking, but said he does believe there is a "real threat of litigation" from data center applicants. The legislative effort dates back to July, when the supervisors asked county staff to look into whether instituting such a pause would be permissible. In September, after getting the green light from the county's attorney, the board voted to direct staff to draw up a resolution for the final vote. In March 2025, Loudoun took its first step in limiting data center development when it stripped by right zoning, requiring all data centers to go through a special exception process. Under that legislation, data centers in the works that had already been approved — 15 projects in the pipeline totaling 10.5M SF of development — can still proceed without going through that process. In 2025, Loudoun had about 53M SF of data centers, a 100% increase from five years earlier, according to county officials.

artigo.texto: Shelby Co asthma ER visits decline, as citizens question data center health impact Colossus One data center is not among the county’s major emitters, according to new health department data MEMPHIS, Tenn. (WMC) - Emergency room visits for asthma in Shelby County have declined from more than 20,000 in 2024 to just under 11,000 so far in 2026, the Shelby County Health Department announced during a meeting on pollution in Westwood on Wednesday night. The latest health department statistics also show Colossus One, the first SpaceXSI data center built in Memphis, is not considered one of the city’s biggest polluters. Data center critics have consistently cited worsening asthma in the community as their biggest health concern as gas turbines produce energy and pollution for Elon Musk’s data centers. The statistics presented at the meeting only apply to Colossus One in South Memphis. They do not apply to Colossus Two in Whitehaven, which is the world’s most powerful data center and is still expanding. Residents seek answers in Westwood Westwood is a community near the Colossus One data center in South Memphis. Residents have many questions since the data center boom in Memphis began in 2024. “Well, the biggest concern is pollution...,” Westwood resident Bettye Lewis told Action News 5. Clifford Lewis, also a Westwood resident, said, “It’s hard to tell whether some of the smells are coming from xAI or whether it’s coming from the waste treatment plant or another facility.” “First of all, I would say your concerns are legit,” said Dr. Bruce Randolph, interim director of the Shelby County Health Department, “I rode around yesterday along Stateline Road, Holmes Road and Tulane. I went through Boxtown and went by White’s Chapel. I rode through all of that to see for myself and you have reasons to be concerned. You’re right to voice your opinion. When I drove by TVA, I smelled the chemicals.” Major emitters named The health department listed these companies as the major emitters of pollutants in 2025: - Valero - Covoro Mining - Nucor Steel - The Allen Combined Cycle Plant - Mitsubishi Chemical The Colossus data center is considered a minor emitter. SCHD said the facility puts out less pollution than Kellog, Owens Corning, JM Smucker, Hershey and Exxon. “Yes, you should be concerned. But you need to be concerned about all of these major emitters, not just one,” Randolph said. Monitoring and testing Shelby County Mayor Mickell Lowery said the health department follows Environmental Protection Agency guidelines for measuring pollution. SCHD currently has 27 monitors at five locations. “But as the world changes…as technology changes…things may need to change as far as testing emissions, so we have to be on top of that,” Lowery said, “because if we don’t have a healthy community and we’re not protecting our water, our aquifer and our air, it’s for naught.” ZIP codes with most asthma ER visits These are the five ZIP codes with the highest number of emergency room visits for asthma year-to-date in 2026, according to SCHD: - 38127 – Frayser - 38109 – Southwest Memphis - 38128 – Raleigh - 38116 – Whitehaven - 38106 – South Memphis Poor communities are hurting the most. “We deserve to be healthy, wealthy, and wise,” said Dr. Karen Streeter, a newly elected Shelby County Commissioner now representing District 9. She organized the pollution meeting. More data centers planned The health impact of multiple data centers is still being studied. By the end of the year, SpaceXSI will operate six data centers in the Memphis metro area. “I’m not sure their pollution will be greater than what we already have...but hopefully, it will not,” Bettye Lewis said. How to report a concern Residents with a complaint or concern about something in their neighborhood can report it directly to the Shelby County Health Department at 901-222-9000. SCHD said it will send someone to investigate. To read the most recent SCHD report on environmental disparity, view it here: Click here to sign up for our newsletter! artigo.texto: The Hillsboro City Council voted Tuesday night unanimously to adopt Resolution 2941, extending the city’s temporary moratorium on new and expanded data centers and battery energy storage systems (BESS) for six more months. The vote came after a large crowd gathered at City Hall to be heard, with all testifying that the Moratorium passed nearly 4 months ago must be extended. Many of the same residents who have been boots on the ground all year showed up and spoke passionately, many holding nothing back. The extension extends the initial 120-day pause enacted in July—set to expire Nov. 24—and gives city staff time to complete environmental and economic impact studies before drafting a second phase of permanent land-use regulations. The council previously approved Phase 1 code amendments in October, restricting standalone data centers primarily to Industrial Park and Industrial Sanctuary zones and establishing a temporary 1,000-foot buffer from schools. While the 6–0 vote was unanimous—with Council President Rob Harris and Councilors Olivia Alcaire, Saba Anvery, Elizabeth Case, Cristian Salgado, and Kipperlyn Sinclair all voting in favor—the debate emphasized several policy questions and tensions on the dais. State Action vs. Local Protection: Councilor Salgado questioned whether extending the local moratorium was an unnecessary use of staff resources given Gov. Tina Kotek’s recent pause on certain state environmental permits and Enterprise Zone applications. City Attorney Chad Jacobs and planning staff clarified that state permits typically occur later in the development process and may not apply to smaller facilities. Without a local land-use moratorium, staff explained, a developer could still submit an application now to lock in Hillsboro’s current development code and wait out state-level pauses. Hillsboro’s Data Center Moratorium Overview: Funding and Study Timelines: City Manager Robby Hammond noted that the upcoming environmental impact study is expected to cost roughly $500,000 and will return to the council for contract approval within the next one to two months. Following a question from Council President Harris, Hammond confirmed that no General Fund dollars will be used; the vast majority of the cost will be covered by Enterprise Zone Community Service Fee reserves, supplemented by water funds for water-quality analysis. Staff said they are targeting four to five months for draft study deliverables to allow for public engagement within the six-month window. Salgado urged staff to include firm deadlines in the consultant contracts so residents do not have to repeatedly return to City Hall to advocate for further extensions. View this post on Instagram Battery Storage, Ethics, and Dais Tensions: Several councilors raised concerns that battery energy storage systems could be overlooked as consultants focus primarily on data centers. Councilor Sinclair requested that a BESS fire safety study and utility capacity data from PGE, Hillsboro Water, and Clean Water Services be incorporated into the process. Councilors Harris and Case also expressed interest in potentially decoupling BESS from data centers if battery storage regulations are completed sooner. Staff said they plan to evaluate BESS using national building code standards and in-house analysis, and confirmed the council could separate the two issues in the future. Sinclair also asked about ethics firewalls regarding the now-dissolved Silicon Forest Partnership, as well as the absence of a formal definition for “artificial intelligence” in the city’s development code. Economic and Community Development Director Dan Dias stated that while there could be overlap among regional consulting firms, the entities and scopes of work are separate and present no legal conflict of interest. View this post on Instagram Before the vote, Councilor Alcaire—noting it was likely her final official opportunity to address the issue—delivered a pointed rebuke of several colleagues on the dais, accusing them of failing to listen to residents and citing Forest Grove as a warning of siting data centers near wetlands. City staff will bring the environmental study contract back to the council for final budget approval in the coming weeks, with public review and Phase 2 code amendments expected to follow in 202

artigo.texto: Mercado global de bandejas para cabos (leitos para cabos): Tamanho, Tendências e Previsão até 2035 - Relatório completo em PDF · pacote de dados Excel · documento Word · apresentação executiva - Entrega por e-mail 24/7, inclusive fins de semana e feriados - Copiar e colar habilitado · formato pronto para impressão - Rodadas ilimitadas de esclarecimentos após a entrega Previsão do mercado de bandejas para cabos até 2035, impulsionada pela demanda por gestão de cabos em data centers Resumo Segundo o mais recente relatório da IndexBox sobre o mercado global de bandejas para cabos, o mercado chega a 2026 com fundamentos de demanda mais amplos, comportamento de compras mais disciplinado e uma arquitetura de oferta mais diversificada regionalmente. O mercado global de bandejas para cabos é um segmento fundamental da infraestrutura elétrica e do gerenciamento de cabos, oferecendo suporte estrutural rígido para o encaminhamento e a proteção de cabos de energia e de dados em edifícios, plantas industriais, data centers e sistemas de transporte. Em 2026, o mercado é moldado pela demanda constante de substituição em mercados de construção maduros e pela aceleração das instalações em projetos de infraestrutura digital e energia renovável. As bandejas para cabos — incluindo configurações tipo escada, calha, tela metálica, fundo sólido e ventiladas — são cada vez mais especificadas por sua capacidade de suporte de carga, propriedades de dissipação de calor e compatibilidade com práticas de construção modular. O horizonte de previsão até 2035 aponta para um crescimento moderado, porém resiliente, com os fundamentos da demanda migrando para lançamentos de cabos de maior densidade em data centers, códigos de segurança e combate a incêndio mais rigorosos em edifícios comerciais e a eletrificação de processos industriais. A escolha de materiais também está evoluindo, com as bandejas de alumínio e à base de polymer ganhando participação onde a resistência à corrosão e a redução de peso são relevantes. Este relatório oferece uma visão baseada em dados do tamanho do mercado, da segmentação, dos fluxos comerciais e da dinâmica competitiva, fornecendo a fabricantes, distribuidores e especificadores um arcabouço analítico transparente para a tomada de decisão até 2035. O cenário-base para o mercado mundial de bandejas para cabos prevê expansão constante de 2026 a 2035, com a demanda global crescendo a uma taxa composta de crescimento anual de aproximadamente 4,2%. O crescimento não é uniforme entre regiões ou tipos de produto; reflete, antes, uma rotação da construção comercial tradicional para aplicações em data centers, energia renovável e automação industrial. Nas economias avançadas, as atividades de substituição e modernização em edifícios e plantas existentes sustentam o volume de base, enquanto os mercados emergentes contribuem com demanda incremental por meio da construção de nova infraestrutura. A dinâmica do lado da oferta é moldada pela volatilidade dos preços do aço e do alumínio, pela utilização da capacidade de fabricação e pela transição contínua para acabamentos pré-galvanizados e com pintura a pó, que reduzem o tempo de instalação. Espera-se que a intensidade competitiva aumente à medida que fabricantes de metais e integradores de sistemas ampliem seus portfólios de gerenciamento de cabos por meio de aquisições e ofertas de serviços integrados. O índice de mercado, fixado em 100 em 2025, deve alcançar 151 até 2035, refletindo o crescimento acumulado de volume, e não a inflação de preços. Os riscos para as perspectivas incluem quedas no ciclo da construção, atrasos nos investimentos de capital em data centers e mudanças na política comercial que afetam os custos dos insumos metálicos. De modo geral, o mercado é mais bem caracterizado como maduro, mas em evolução, com potencial de alta atrelado às tendências de infraestrutura digital e eletrificação. Fatores de demanda e restrições Principais fatores de demanda - Rápida expansão de data centers de hiperescala e de colocation, que exigem gerenciamento de cabos de alta densidade e soluções de bandejas ventiladas para dissipação de calor - Eletrificação de processos industriais e modernização da automação, impulsionando a demanda por bandejas para cabos duráveis de aço e alumínio em ambientes de plantas - Instalações de energia renovável, incluindo parques solares e eólicos, onde os sistemas de suporte de cabos são essenciais para a coleta e a distribuição de energia - Códigos de construção e segurança contra incêndio mais rigorosos, que exigem suporte e separação adequados de cabos em construções comerciais e institucionais - Adensamento das redes de telecomunicações, incluindo small cells de 5G e expansão de fibra, que exige encaminhamento organizado de cabos em ambientes urbanos e suburbanos - Modernização da infraestrutura ferroviária e de transporte, incluindo sistemas de sinalização e energia que dependem de instalações robustas de bandejas para cabos Possíveis restrições ao crescimento - Volatilidade dos preços do aço e do alumínio, que comprime as margens dos fabricantes e atrasa as especificações de projetos - Ciclos longos de licenciamento e construção no setor imobiliário comercial, que podem adiar a demanda por instalação de bandejas para cabos - Disponibilidade de métodos substitutos de gerenciamento de cabos, como eletrodutos e canaletas, em certas aplicações de baixa densidade - Escassez de mão de obra qualificada em contratação elétrica, que pode retardar os prazos de instalação e afetar o cronograma dos projetos - Tarifas comerciais e requisitos de conteúdo regional que afetam os fluxos transfronteiriços de bandejas metálicas fabricadas Estrutura da demanda por setor de uso final Infraestrutura de data centers (participação estimada: 28%) Os data centers são o segmento de uso final de crescimento mais rápido para bandejas para cabos, impulsionado pela construção de instalações de hiperescala e de colocation para atender à computação

artigo.texto: ANTALYA, Türkiye, Nov 19: Nepal is seeking to turn its institutional preparations for participating in the carbon market into actual carbon credit transactions and climate finance by expanding cooperation with international buyers, investors and development partners. A discussion held at the Nepal Pavilion on Wednesday during the UN Climate Conference (COP31) explored ways to attract investment through the National Carbon Registry and implement Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. The event, titled 'Mobilising Climate Finance through Carbon Markets: Country Experiences, Challenges and the Way Forward', was jointly organised by the Ministry of Forests and Environment and UNDP Nepal. Government officials and carbon market experts from Nepal, Bhutan and the Philippines attended. Nepal launched its National Carbon Registry in March 2026 with technical and financial support from UNDP. The digital platform is designed to register carbon projects, record emission reductions, issue and transfer carbon credits, and ensure transparency in transactions. The registry provides the institutional foundation for Nepal's participation in international carbon markets under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, which allows countries to cooperate and exchange emission reduction outcomes to help limit global warming. COP31 launches platform to track cross-border carbon credits Presenting Nepal's policy and institutional arrangements, Ministry Undersecretary Dr Prakash Singh Thapa explained the registry's operational procedures, requirements for project developers and potential participation of international buyers. However, participants cautioned that establishing an institutional framework would not automatically attract investment. Nepal needs a credible pipeline of carbon projects, stronger institutional capacity, transparent benefit sharing and international partners willing to purchase high quality carbon credits. Deepak KC, climate change and resilience programme analyst at UNDP Nepal, said establishing the registry was only the first step towards developing a carbon market. "The priority now is to operate the system effectively, develop a strong pipeline of high quality carbon projects, attract private investment and create a supportive policy and regulatory environment," he said. He added that carbon finance should be viewed as a means of mobilising investment for Nepal's climate and development priorities and implementing its Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) 3.0, rather than simply trading carbon credits. Bhutan's experience also featured in the discussion. Yeshi Lhendup, deputy chief of Bhutan's Ministry of Finance, presented the country's progress in developing domestic carbon market regulations, policies and a national registry. Bhutan is working to connect its carbon market with international systems and increase participation by local communities and the private sector. Building on its experience under the Clean Development Mechanism, the country has moved some projects under the Paris Agreement framework and established bilateral carbon market cooperation with Singapore. It has also developed a separate platform to ensure transparency in carbon market activities and transactions. Another major challenge discussed was securing upfront financing for carbon projects. Their preparation, implementation, monitoring and verification require substantial investment. However, revenue comes only after emission reductions are independently verified and carbon credits issued, making initial financing difficult. Nasif Sofiane, regional lead for carbon pricing at the Global Green Growth Institute (GGGI), said innovative financing arrangements were needed to address the problem. Banks and investors are reluctant to commit capital without sufficient certainty about future project revenues. He also proposed combining smaller projects into larger investment portfolios. Nepal could, for instance, bring together brick industries, clean cooking technologies and small hydropower projects to attract investors and fund managers. Providing grants for project preparation, technical documentation and verification could also reduce investment risks and encourage private sector participation, he said. Representatives from the Philippines and international organisations, including Sandy Recabar of the country's Climate Change Commission and federal parliamentarian Kamal Subedi, also shared their views. Forestry, renewable energy, clean cooking technologies, electric transport, waste management and industrial energy efficiency are among the sectors with potential to generate carbon credits and attract investment in Nepal. Nepal's immediate challenge, however, is to move beyond institutional preparations and establish actual carbon transactions and investment partnerships through projects that deliver emission reductions alongside economic and social benefits.
