artigo.texto: Imagem ilustrativa Documento cita risco para o abastecimento de água e questiona o protocolo de R$ 10 bilhões assinado com a Atlas Renewable Energy Moradores, trabalhadores e entidades da sociedade civil de Uberaba lançaram uma petição pública que exige transparência e a realização de audiências públicas antes de qualquer licença, outorga ou benefício municipal para a instalação de megadata centers na Zona de Processamento de Exportação (ZPE) da cidade. O documento é uma reação ao anúncio da Prefeitura de que assinou um protocolo de intenções com a Atlas Renewable Energy para um megacomplexo de data centers, com investimento previsto de R$ 10 bilhões. Segundo os autores, poucas semanas antes do anúncio, o telejornal MGTV 2ª Edição noticiou o fechamento frequente de reservatórios e o pedido oficial para que a população economizasse água diante da crise hídrica. Choque de datas O principal argumento da petição é o descompasso entre dois cronogramas. Comunicados da Prefeitura, divulgados por veículos como o JM Online e o Regionalzão, projetam o início da operação do data center para 2028. Já a Resolução ARISB-MG nº 298, do Codau, prevê a conclusão das operações do Sistema de Abastecimento do Rio Grande apenas em 2030. Ao cruzar dados de consumo médio de água de Uberaba, do SINISA, com levantamentos técnicos divulgados pelo The Intercept Brasil, os autores calculam que o consumo diário de um megadata center equivale ao de 2.200 até mais de 36 mil residências. Para eles, operar a estrutura antes da conclusão da obra do Rio Grande colocaria em risco o abastecimento das moradias durante a estiagem. Protocolo não garante obra A petição também ressalta que o documento assinado é uma carta preliminar, sem obrigação de execução. Segundo os autores, citando o The Intercept Brasil e a BNamericas, a Atlas já divulgou anúncios bilionários semelhantes em Paracatu (R$ 35 bilhões), no Norte de Minas e no Rio de Janeiro, em disputa por clientes globais que ainda não fecharam contrato. Empregos e capital Com base em estudo da Fundação Getulio Vargas (FGV), o texto afirma que 85% das vagas geradas seriam temporárias, restritas à construção civil, e que menos de 4% seriam empregos permanentes em galpões altamente automatizados, beneficiados por isenções fiscais da ZPE e do regime federal Redata. A petição afirma ainda que cerca de 80% do capital investido não permanece na cidade, sendo destinado à compra de servidores e chips importados. Conta de luz e precedentes Os autores citam levantamentos da CBS News e da NPR segundo os quais o custo de obras de expansão da rede elétrica para atender centros de dados costuma ser repassado à tarifa dos consumidores residenciais. Afirmam também que, em cidades vizinhas como Paracatu e Uberlândia, projetos semelhantes avançaram sem audiências prévias e hoje são alvo de questionamentos na Assembleia Legislativa de Minas Gerais (ALMG) e de investigações do Ministério Público Federal (MPF). O que os signatários pedem - Transparência total: divulgação da íntegra dos protocolos de intenções e das estimativas de consumo de água e energia, sem cláusulas de sigilo comercial sobre recursos públicos e naturais. - Audiências públicas amplas: convocação pela Câmara Municipal e pelo Conselho Municipal de Meio Ambiente (Comam), com participação de moradores, sindicatos, universidades, produtores rurais e especialistas independentes. - Condicionante hídrica: proibição de licença ou operação de data centers de alto consumo antes da entrada em operação efetiva do Sistema Rio Grande, com exigência de refrigeração em circuito fechado, sem perda de água por evaporação. - Contrapartidas reais: definição clara de benefícios sociais, ambientais e de qualificação profissional para a população local. “Uberaba não pode decidir o futuro da sua água e da sua energia a toque de caixa”, conclui o texto, que convida a população a assinar e compartilhar. A Folha Uberaba solicitou um posicionamento da prefeitura e assim que for atendido, será inserido na matéria O link da petição: https://www.peticao.online/data_centers_na_zpe_de_uberaba_debate_publico_imediato?utm_source=whatsapp A prefeitura de Uberaba respondeu ao questionamento, veja a resposta na íntegras: A Prefeitura de Uberaba respeita o direito de manifestação do cidadão e está à disposição da comunidade para prestar esclarecimentos e dialogar. Nesse sentido, o Município informa que o projeto foi concebido desde a origem para promover o uso eficiente e responsável dos recursos hídricos, adotando soluções que reduzem a demanda por água e evitam a utilização da rede pública de abastecimento. O fornecimento de água ocorrerá por meio de fontes independentes, sem demanda direta sobre o sistema público de distribuição que atende à população e estando de acordo com todos os requisitos e formas de controle da legislação aplicável. Durante a operação, o sistema de resfriamento funcionará em circuito fechado, permitindo a recirculação contínua da água e reduzindo significativamente a necessidade de reposição. O projeto também prevê o reaproveitamento de água proveniente da Estação de Tratamento de Esgoto (ETE) para atividades de serviços gerais, como limpeza e manutenção, reduzindo ainda mais a necessidade de utilização de água potável. A combinação dessas soluções demonstra o compromisso do empreendimento com a eficiência, o reaproveitamento e o uso racional da água. Além disso, a instalação do empreendimento depende, entre outras etapas, do licenciamento ambiental, processo durante o qual o Conselho Municipal do Meio Ambiente (Comam) se manifestará por meio dos seus membros, que representam diferentes setores, incluindo a sociedade civil.

artigo.texto: Spartanburg County council takes up 6 data center development agreements Monday Residents speak for and against projects as council considers three final votes and three first votes SPARTANBURG COUNTY, S.C. (FOX Carolina) - Spartanburg County Council on Monday night took up six data center development agreements, with three up for final votes and three up for first votes, as residents spoke for and against the projects in council chambers. The agenda ran more than 700 pages and included 20 public hearings. Before the 5:15 p.m. public meeting, council met in executive session to discuss contractual terms of several development agreements. The three agreements up for final votes were scheduled for public hearings during the regular council meeting. Resident calls for council members to resign Spartanburg County resident Eric Allison, founder of the Facebook group No Data Centers in Spartanburg, has been leading opposition to data centers in the county. Allison called council members “cowards” and said every member should resign. “Our Spartanburg County Council, every member should be totally ashamed. They need to resign today. It’s a mess. In one meeting, 20 public hearings, 22 second and third votes to move projects forward. It’s absolutely insane,” Allison said. Allison said he believes council is sending residents a message: “We don’t listen to you. We don’t do what you want. We do what we want and our controllers want. Our ears are not for the people of Spartanburg County. Our ears are for other people.” Three of the 20 hearings involve data center development agreements. Valara agreement on South Pine Street The Valara data center at 4000 South Pine Street, which the agenda describes as a high-performance computing center, is under construction. Council took a final vote on a development agreement among the county, Numara LLC and Valara Holdings LLC. It was approved. The agreement will provide the company with long-term development certainty and establish limits on certain future county regulatory actions affecting the project. It will: - Lock in Valara’s development rights for 10 years, protecting the 457-megawatt project from certain future county regulations, moratoriums and zoning changes. - Require the county to determine within 10 days whether development applications are complete. Once an application is determined to be complete, the county would have 45 days to take final action. If the county fails to act within that period, the agreement says the application could be considered approved based on the submitted documentation. - Protect Valara’s ability to continue developing the property, including additional data center buildings, generators, substations and battery storage, subject to the agreement’s terms. In exchange, the company commits to noise mitigation, landscaping and at least one community meeting each year. The agreement calls for an investment of about $2.76 billion. The agreement identifies 27 full-time jobs as a target, not a guarantee. It also requires annual reporting to the county on investment, construction, utilities and employment. Fox Carolina contacted Valara by email to request an interview and a tour of the facility. Jones Road agreement A development agreement with 300 Jones Road Associates LLC for approximately 137 acres at or near 430 Jones Road also received final approval after a vote. The proposal calls for a data center with up to 65 megawatts of IT capacity, an anticipated investment of approximately $1.5 billion and 25 full-time jobs. The agreement also includes $9 million in community benefit payments over five years. The proposal has a history of county opposition. In June, Spartanburg County planning staff denied an earlier application for a data center at the Jones Road property, citing violations of the county’s Unified Land Management Ordinance. The county’s Board of Zoning Appeals upheld that denial on August 25. The developer is now pursuing the project under an exception to the county’s data center moratorium, adopted in September. The exception allows qualifying data centers of 65 megawatts or less on designated industrial park sites or former industrial properties to move forward if they meet additional requirements. The original denial was not overturned. Instead, the county subsequently adopted rules creating another path for certain smaller data center projects to seek approval through development agreements. Monday’s vote was the third and final reading. Tyger River Industrial Park proposals Project Spero was a proposed $3 billion data center development for the Tyger River Industrial Park. In February, Spartanburg County leaders announced they would not approve the tax incentives sought for the project, effectively derailing the proposal following significant public opposition. Jerry Tang, the executive associated with Project Spero, is now associated with four data center proposals in the same industrial park. One, AIB CLT1 at 389 Tyger River Industrial Drive, is an existing bitcoin mining operation proposing to convert its facility into a conventional data center. A final vote was held on Monday on a development agreement. It was approved. The proposed facility would have 50 megawatts of capacity and an estimated investment of $1.2 billion. The other three proposals, AIB CLT2, AIB CLT3 and AIB CLT4, were up for first readings. Each item on the agenda included a proposed special source credit agreement and development agreement. The agreements include tax incentives. Draft agreements indicate the incentives could run for 40 years. FOX Carolina contacted Tang by email to request an interview and a tour of the proposed development sites. Councilman and residents respond Spartanburg County Councilman Monier “Mo” Abusaft spoke with Fox Carolina before Monday’s meeting. artigo.texto: University of Dubuque students present semester-long data center research at community forum DUBUQUE, Iowa (KCRG) - As Dubuque County communities draft new zoning rules for data centers, University of Dubuque students shared semester-long research on the facilities with the public Tuesday night. The Data Center Community Forum at the Peter and Susan Smith Welcome Center featured projects from seven classes spanning aviation, environmental science, public policy, computing and theology. Junior Roland Preston, a flight operations and politics major from Des Moines, focused his research for his public policy and environmental ethics classes on the data center campus in Altoona, a facility he passes regularly on his drive home from college. “I chose the one in Altoona because I drive to and from Dubuque and back home in Des Moines, so I drive by that data center all the time,” Preston said. “So I wanted to actually take a look at that one specifically and kind of gather why was it built, what’s the impact on the local community, how’s the local community feel about it.” During his trips near the Altoona campus, Preston said he experienced firsthand one of the most common complaints raised by nearby residents. “If I get close to that campus in the Altoona area, you can hear it,” Preston said. “And I understand why people have concerns about it because it’s just this constant droning sound you hear. And I can imagine why it’s quite the inconvenience.” Dubuque County, the City of Dubuque and the City of Peosta all currently have temporary moratoriums halting data center construction while officials write ordinances governing water use, power demand and noise. Preston said those local pauses reflect how quickly the industry is moving compared to municipal policy. “This technology is outpacing our ability to regulate it,” Preston said. “And we need to stall it in its tracks right now, come up with a comprehensive way to regulate it, and then we can maybe allow it to keep happening.” “When Dubuque County, for example, talks about doing a moratorium on data centers, it is from that perspective that we have all these companies trying to come in ... and for them (the local governments) it feels like it’s the only way that they can put in meaningful regulation before companies start building,” he added. While Preston said he entered the semester with a favorable view of data centers, researching a specific facility gave him a more detailed understanding of community pushback. “When we talk about noise, talk about water issues, the impact on the community, I have a better understanding as to why people feel that way, especially now that I’ve taken a specific data center and looked at it very intentionally,” Preston said. Christine Darr, an associate professor of philosophy at the university, helped organize the forum after watching public meetings across the area grow increasingly heated. “We wanted to work together to help students understand a local issue, both locally and kind of nationwide,” Darr said. “We thought it would be a great opportunity to do some interdisciplinary work, so thinking about such a complex issue from a variety of perspectives, and then a great opportunity to kind of showcase our students and the great work that they do and offer something to the community.” Darr said combining fields like theology, aviation and environmental science was deliberate. “We thought it was an exciting opportunity to show how complex even something seemingly as simple as a data center might be,” Darr said. “And by bringing as many different disciplinary lenses, I think we did really kind of lift up all of the different ways that you can think about a particular issue, that nothing is one way or another way.” Following the student showcase, regional journalists Benjamin Fisher, Tom Kertscher of Wisconsin Watch and Grace Nieland of The Gazette held a panel discussion and Q&A on data center coverage and local policy. For Preston, presenting months of research to community members fulfilled a goal he set when he started college “It’s very nice researching something for months and then being able to talk to the public about it,” Preston said. Darr said she hopes attendees left the forum with a broader view of the debate. “I hope that people see that the issue is actually pretty complex, and also, I hope they walk away feeling as though they are part of a community that really cares about understanding issues, and trying to work together to understand things in a more nuanced way,” Darr said. Read More The battery materials firm Sila Nanotechnologies says it will sell up to $1 billion of its silicon anode materials to the battery maker Panasonic Energy. The deal is a sign that, despite slowing demand for electric cars and the automotive industry’s shift toward low-cost cathode chemistries, high-performance silicon-based anode materials are finding niches in the battery market. Silicon is almost necessary to achieve the performance required for batteries used by the defense industry, electric aircraft, and data centers, says Charlie Parker, principal consultant and founder of the battery intelligence firm Ratel Consulting. “Silicon is driving these emerging applications.” Silicon anode materials can store more energy than the same amount of graphite, the material typically used in the anodes of lithium-ion batteries. They also allow batteries to charge faster and pump out energy at a higher rate. The main disadvantage is that silicon costs more than graphite.

artigo.texto: The “blue wave” election this month was not just a nationwide success for Democratic candidates at all levels of government, but also local candidates who stood up against hyperscale data centers — the high-energy usage facilities that fuel big tech’s artificial intelligence services. This was true in several local races around Kentucky where specific data center projects have been proposed over the past two years, as companies and developers sought to take advantage of generous new tax breaks passed in Frankfort. One key example was in Cave City, the small tourist city along I-65 in Barren County where locals have fought a company’s proposal for a data center using 1.2 gigawatts of power. Over the objections of two-term Mayor Dwayne Hatcher, the city council voted 4-1 for a moratorium on data centers, drawing a lawsuit from the developer. Clifton Parsley, one of the city council members who voted for that moratorium, decided to run against Hatcher on that issue and won by a wide margin, despite large ad spending by a mysterious PAC supporting the incumbent mayor. The lone council vote against the moratorium also lost his office by not finishing among the top six candidates. Just a half hour down I-65, Bowling Green saw a similar result, as its city commission had voted down a proposed data center moratorium this summer. The two commissioners who voted for the moratorium finished with the most votes, while a pro-moratorium candidate finished third to replace a member voting against it. Comparable scenarios played out in local elections near proposed hyperscalers in Mercer, Simpson and Mason counties, with pro-data center incumbents losing out to candidates either outright opposing them or calling for more transparency. One of those successful candidates was Beth Corea from the tiny city of Burgin in Mercer County. She was a local organizer opposing the city’s efforts to annex a large area of farmland for a hyperscale data center who decided to run for city council and won — swept into office along with a new mayor and council fully opposed to annexation. Corea, a first-time candidate, said these local election results should send a bipartisan message to elected officials, including state lawmakers in Frankfort. “People aren't buying into this two-party, Hate Inc., us-versus-them anymore,” Corea said. “The us-versus-them now is the community, the public, versus the multimillion-dollar developers, the multimillion-dollar corporations coming in trying to get these tax breaks and lax regulatory frameworks for what they're bringing in.” The Kentucky General Assembly’s new session begins in January, where they are expected to take up legislation to put regulatory guardrails on data centers and consider repealing their 50-year exemption from use and sales taxes. House Bill 593 from this year’s session was an effort to put regulations in place to protect existing ratepayers from data centers’ increased energy demands and uphold local rules on where they can be located. The bill, sponsored by GOP Rep. Josh Bray of Mount Vernon, passed the House by a wide majority, only to stall in the Senate after opposition from Louisville Gas & Electric and Kentucky Utilities, the state’s largest private utility company. At the Kentucky Chamber of Commerce’s legislative preview conference this week, Bray said he plans to push “a more robust version” of HB 593 in the 2027 session. Legislative candidates, including some in the GOP supermajority, even campaigned on repealing data centers’ tax breaks — a position promoted by U.S. Rep. James Comer this week, when the Republican frontrunner announced his 2027 run for governor. “I think they're going to feel the pressure that political platitudes aren't enough now,” Corea said. “You got to show us policy, or we're going to vote you out. So it's time to remember who you represent and who you serve.” Burgin voters reject data center, sweeping in new leadership Corea, of Burgin, was pregnant and due to give birth shortly before the election when she filed for office, but was one of several candidates spurred to run for office based on how the city’s elected leaders were handling the data center project. “As events kept unfolding, it became clear that I wasn't going to get to choose the time; the time was choosing me,” Corea said. “That we needed people to step up and be the leadership that this town needs.” One of those successful anti-annexation candidates who won by a wide margin did not even have his name on the ballot. Joe Monroe was appointed interim mayor in July, shortly after the mayor resigned and the council advanced the annexation ordinance for the data center. Monroe subsequently stalled the ordinance, but pro-annexation council member George Hensley was the only candidate for mayor, and the deadline had already passed for candidates to be placed on the ballot. Monroe decided to file as a write-in candidate for mayor, and despite such candidates rarely winning races against on-ballot candidates, he won in a landslide, with 273 residents writing in his name and giving him 75% of the vote. Monroe’s victory was in spite of the fact that Community Growth Action — the same group supporting the pro-data center mayoral candidate in Cave City — spent hundreds of dollars on mailers for his opponent. Two pro-annexation Burgin council incumbents running for reelection placed last among the 11 candidates running, while Melinda Wofford — the lead opponent on the council — easily won the most votes. The other top six candidates to be elected to council included Corea and three other annexation opponents, along with an incumbent who recused himself from the votes. (“Substrate AI”), has signed an project commission agreement (the “Grid Connection Agreement”) with i-DE Redes Eléctricas Inteligentes, S.A.U., the electricity distribution system operator belonging to the Iberdrola group (“Iberdrola”), for the execution of the facilities required to connect to the distribution grid, associated with 5 MW of granted access capacity for its future AI data centre in Talavera de la Reina, Spain. This Grid Connection Agreement is part of Substrate AI's strategy to build its own AI infrastructure in Spain and support a more sovereign and competitive European technology ecosystem. The Grid Connection Agreement is a key step towards securing 5 MW of electrical connection capacity for the future data centre. Once built, Substrate AI will have one of the essential elements for the development of its project: the availability of sufficient electrical power to deploy its artificial intelligence (AI) computing infrastructure. The Talavera data centre forms part of Substrate AI’s strategy to develop its own technological infrastructure in Spain, contributing to the growth of European computing capacity and to the deployment of more sovereign, secure and competitive artificial intelligence. The future availability of these 5 MW through the Grid Connection Agreement represents a decisive step forward in the preparation of the project and enables Substrate AI to continue progressing towards the next milestones required for its launch. With this initiative, Substrate AI reinforces its commitment to Spain as a strategic location for developing artificial intelligence infrastructure and helping to build a European technology ecosystem with greater capacity and autonomy. For further information, please see Substrate AI’s website: www.substrate.ai.

Dozens of countries - from big emerging economies to the world's poorest nations - are calling for the UN's new carbon market to reassess climate integrity rules, in a push that campaigners and researchers have blamed on industry lobbying. At COP31 talks on the Paris Agreement Crediting Mechanism (PACM) this weekend, the Like-Minded Developing Countries – a group that includes Saudi Arabia, India and China – the Least Developed Countries (LDCs) and landlocked developing countries raised concerns about the requirements project developers must meet, according to sources familiar with the closed-door discussions. They warned about the cumulative weight of those requirements developed under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement as barriers to implementation. Several countries, including Singapore and some Latin American states, said rules must keep projects financially viable, while South Korea asked for proportionate requirements, the sources said. Their demands closely track arguments from carbon market industry groups, which claim PACM's conservative approach to counting emission reductions is so strict that few projects will ever come to fruition. Industry and NGOs lobby to weaken UN carbon credit rules in “coordinated” push In a letter published ahead of COP31, the lobby groups asked governments to "raise implementation concerns" and to request that the Supervisory Body - the UN body that oversees the market - assess the "combined impact" of its rules on the feasibility of projects. The letter was signed by the International Emissions Trading Association (IETA), a business group whose members include fossil fuel giants Shell, BP, Saudi Aramco and Chevron, along with the Project Developer Forum and the Wildlife Conservation Society, which develops forest conservation programmes. Draft text reflects industry demands Those demands are reflected in the first draft of the COP31 decision on the mechanism, published late on Saturday. To guard against over-crediting, PACM’s rules deliberately err on the side of issuing fewer credits when emissions cuts from projects are uncertain. The document asks the Supervisory Body to look at how these cautious assumptions add up across its rules and what that means for the number of credits, project costs and prices. The aim, it says, is to avoid "excessive compounding of conservative adjustments". Other parts of the draft tell the body not to make its rules too cautious or too rigid. That includes efforts to guard against the risk that carbon captured by a project is later released. Most of these passages add that environmental integrity must be maintained. Risk of another 'failure' "Weakening the rules is not climate ambition - it is a license to pollute,” said Erika Lennon, a senior attorney at the Center for International Environmental Law (CIEL). “As we are on the brink of permanently breaching 1.5C, we cannot afford to turn the carbon market into another loophole for polluters,” she added. Axel Michaelowa, research director at Perspectives Climate Research, said that if attempts to weaken the rules succeed, it could lead to another failure of an international carbon market. Demand for credits rests on trust, he said, and the slightest doubt over integrity erodes buyers' willingness to pay. Calls to revise requirements "must be supported by scientific evidence, not unsupported claims of under-crediting - especially when these assumptions come from private actors whose revenues depend on the volume of transacted credits rather than real mitigation outcomes," Michaelowa said. The EU, Switzerland and Senegal are among a handful of countries pushing back against demands to re-assess the market rules, according to the sources, and are opposing requests to weigh up the profitability of projects or to lower standards. Cookstove credits in focus At the centre of the fight are new methodologies for projects that aim to cut emissions by distributing cleaner cookstoves - one of the carbon market’s most popular credit types and also one of its most criticised for overstating climate benefits. A 2024 study in Nature Sustainability found cookstove projects had been over-credited roughly tenfold. Under the rules adopted by the Supervisory Body in October, cookstove project developers are required to set aside part of their credits in a buffer pool, in case the forests they claim to save later burn or are cleared. artigo.texto: W.Va. Treasurer prioritizing teacher pay, data center tax distribution for legislative session CHARLESTON, W.Va. (WSAZ) - West Virginia Treasurer Larry Pack presented his legislative priorities Tuesday, ahead of the state legislative session that begins in January. Pack’s priorities include: - More tax revenue from data centers going to county commissions and school boards, rather than the state, as laid out in H.B. 2014 - Pay raises for public school teachers - Eliminating the business inventory tax - Term limits for Board of Public Works officers, which include the Treasurer, Attorney General, and Secretary of State. Data center tax revenue Pack began highlighting the issue that county school boards don’t receive revenue from data centers in the lead-up to the 2026 general election. “The only money the Board of Education can get, any Board of Education can get, with respect to these data centers, is if they have an excess levy in the county,” Pack told WSAZ in October. “If the excess levy goes away, then the Board of Education does not get any of the money, with respect to the data centers.” Pack’s focus on the issue was concentrated in Mason County, who stood to gain or lose $90 million per year from its two data centers depending on whether its school board tax levy passed. It did. Tuesday, Pack said he’s advocating for the state policy to change, so county school boards don’t have to worry about a levy passing to benefit from data centers. “What [H.B.] 2014 does is take money away from county school boards, takes money away from county commissions, and puts it into the general fund for the state,” he said. “At a time when our school boards are struggling, why would we take money away from school boards?” Under the current bill, the data center’s host county receives 30 percent of the tax revenue, while 10 percent goes to all other counties, and the rest goes to the state - 50 percent of the tax revenue goes to the state’s Personal Income Tax Reduction Fund. “We don’t have a county that has water to every household, or sewer to every household. We don’t have a county that doesn’t complain about EMTs or having enough sheriffs. Why would we take money away from county commissions? They’re on the front lines,” he said. Sen. Eric Tarr (R-Putnam) told WSAZ he supports that change, and that the money could be “transformative” for a county. “It can have generational impact for the families that are there now and the great-great-grandchildren of those counties,” he said. “You can go in and say, ‘OK, well, now that we have our needs met, what are our wants?’ ” Tarr believes the money from the data centers could allow counties to decrease taxes for their residents. “When you have such a significant tax base being constructed with outside money coming into West Virginia, the opportunity to reduce all that taxation is significant,” he said. “And you can really create a competitive environment for businesses coming in to locate into those counties. And then you can grow out from that.” Tarr added: “You’re going to see county after county figuring out ‘how can we get one here? How can we get one in our county?’” Del. Sean Hornbuckle (D-Cabell) agreed that the proposal could be a good idea, emphasizing his belief that local control is crucial in the data center debate. “If we’re going to even have data centers, [counties] need to make sure they have their fair share,” he said. “The way that [H.B. 2014] was written was that the majority of it goes back to Charleston. That’s just unacceptable.” Pay raises for teachers Tuesday, Pack offered his proposal for pay raises for all public school teachers: the new minimum salary would be $50,000, and any teacher already making that amount would receive a $2,000 pay bump. “We have to attract new teachers, we have to retain our teachers we have, and we have to be competitive with our surrounding states,” Pack said. “You can drive across the line in the Eastern Panhandle and make $10,000 or $15,000 more. What person wouldn’t do that to bring more money into their family? We need to make sure that we’re competitive.” Eliminating the business inventory tax Pack said Tuesday he wants lawmakers to propose a constitutional amendment that would phase out the state’s business inventory tax over five years. According to Pack, West Virginia is one of few states that have a business inventory tax, which he called a “job killer” and a “growth killer.” “If we want manufacturing jobs, if we want small business to grow, we need to get rid of this business inventory tax,” he said. Pack said the phase-out would cost $100 million, but believes the investment that would come as a result of the elimination would make up for the cost. “We think the county commissions and boards of education can absorb that because we’ll get more growth,” he said. “We’ll get more jobs. We’ll have more investment in West Virginia.” Copyright 2026 WSAZ. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: The International Business Aviation Council (IBAC) is urging its affiliated national associations to lobby their governments to demand political pressure to block changes to the European Union Emissions Trading Scheme (EU-ETS). The group, which represents business aviation at ICAO, has backed the EBAA’s opposition to proposals made by the European Commission’s Climate Action directorate-general on the grounds that changes would disproportionately affect the industry to the extent that some operators could find it impossible to comply with requirements. Under proposals issued in July, the introduction of a new de minimis emissions threshold of 1,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide per company annually would bring many additional smaller operators under the EU-ETS mandate. According to IBAC, some members of the European Parliament want to further lower the de minimis threshold for EU-ETS compliance to just 250 tonnes. The group said this would bring around 1,000 more operators under the requirements of the legislation. The EC also wants the scheme to apply to all flights from the European Economic Area to third-country destinations within a 5,000-kilometer (2,700-nm) radius of Frankfurt, Germany. IBAC says this will significantly increasing the number of flights from outside the European Union that would be subject to requirements. As part of its rebuttal of the proposed changes, EBAA has also protested that they will subject business aviation to broader carbon-pricing obligations than airlines by being denied access to sustainable aviation fuel allowances and to the use of book-and-claim options. The group has also complained that the new structure would take no account of other passenger and carbon taxes levied by individual European Union member states, such as France, Portugal, Italy and the Netherlands. IBAC director general Kurt Edwards has accused the EC of “sectoral bigotry” in consciously discriminating against business aircraft operators, which he said will be harmful to the viability of some companies. Edwards said excluding the industry from book-and-claim accounting for emissions is especially unreasonable since its companies commonly fly to airports where SAF is not available. “In their supporting text, the European Commission said that business aircraft operators have the means and the resources to buy SAF without providing evidence of that,” he told AIN. “Why strip away the benefit of taking advantage of [SAF] technology?” In what IBAC said would be a further divergence from the ICAO-backed CORSIA approach to achieving net-zero emissions for air transport by 2050, the EC intends to reduce the mtow threshold for EU-ETS from 5,700 kilograms (12,540 pounds) to 2,500 kilograms. Edwards said this will mean turboprop aircraft such as the Pilatus PC-12 and Daher TBM 980 would be covered by the scheme and its high cost of compliance and administration. At the EBAA Week event in Brussels this week, IBAC representatives will introduce a new vehicle-tonne-kilometer metric that they are proposing for business aviation. According to Bruce Parry, senior advisor for industry affairs with Bombardier Aerospace, this would be a fairer way to calculate the sector’s emissions than the passenger-kilometer metric devised with airlines in mind. Edwards said the EC’s allegedly discriminatory efforts to make EU-ETS compliance harder for business aviation companies are also unnecessary since the industry is strongly committed to decarbonization. “Part of the reasoning for excluding our operators from SAF allowances is that they believe we are more likely to electrify [aircraft] sooner, but this simply isn’t the incentive they think it is,” he concluded. Ultimately, if the EC presses ahead with the proposed changes, IBAC has indicated that the industry may be forced to take legal action to challenge the new rules on grounds of discrimination. In June, lawyers acting for Dassault Aviation, with EBAA support, successfully challenged the process by which the European Commission had excluded business aviation from its “taxonomy” definition of environmentally sustainable activity. The European Union General Court in Luxembourg ruled that the industry had been excluded in an unfair and discriminatory way.

artigo.texto: Jasper residents get a crash course on data centers, but some say the presentation leaned one-sided JASPER, Ind. (WFIE) - Dubois County residents got a closer look at data centers Tuesday night, but some who attended said the event wasn’t as neutral as advertised. Officials and developers gave a presentation Nov. 17 at Jasper’s Thyen-Clark Cultural Center. They explained what data centers are and how they work, and they weighed the pros and cons. Nancy Eckerle, executive director of the Jasper Chamber of Commerce, said she hoped people came with open minds. “I hope people are just educated and informed that they come here with an open mind that they are not biased in their opinion, but maybe they learned something. Maybe they learned something. They didn’t know if they were against data centers maybe they’ll learn something that will just open their eyes a little bit and if they’re definitely for them, they may learn something that says you know maybe we don’t need that here or whatever it might be.” Presentation focused on property values, water and power The night’s main speaker was Paul Wyman, owner of The Wyman Group, a full-service real estate firm in north central Indiana. He went into detail on how data centers affect property values, water and power. Officials said the event was meant to be a neutral learning experience. Many in the audience said it wasn’t. They said they felt a bias in favor of data centers. Jasper resident Maggie Stimming said she agrees data centers are coming, but she questioned some of what she heard. “I agree with him that we are going to have data centers. I don’t think there’s any doubt about that. We’re not gonna turn the clock back. The horse is out of the barn and we will have data centers, but how we do them is I think what he was trying to get across how we do them and that’s a good point to make however, some of his examples I felt were not really very good.” Environmental questions dominate Q&A After the presentation, many in the audience asked questions. Many of them focused on how data centers would affect the environment. Others asked why demand for data centers is so high in the area. Some residents left concerned. They said many environmental topics were not addressed. Jasper resident Rock Emmert said diesel pollution was his biggest concern. “He touched on a lot of reasons and methods how communities can demand the best possible like the best practices or the best available control technology but he didn’t address about the pollution aspect of diesel. That was my biggest concern about the whole presentation. Absolutely zero concern for public health and pollution.” Now again, this was just meant to be an educational experience, and no plans for a data center were discussed. But if one ever comes, we will keep you updated. Copyright 2026 WFIE. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: AUBURNDALE, Fla. — The city of Auburndale is considering a pause on future data centers. This comes after the city received major pushback from the community over a proposed facility near Florida Polytechnic University. The project, known as the Auburndale Technology Center, would be housed inside two existing warehouses at 810 and 820 Pace Road. Since news broke about the data center earlier this month, Audrey Meadows and her husband, Daniel, have been focused on learning what could happen to their home. “Because we’re retired, we don’t get to leave every day and go away somewhere else. We have to live in it,” Audrey said. The Army veteran says she moved back to the rural area in 2018 to help take care of her mother. Her property has been passed down through generations, like many of the other homes along Marker Road. “Everything is all at least third generation. So, they’re not homes that ever come up for sale out there,” she said. “They get passed down through the family.” Meadows says her sons are supposed to be next in line, but she’s concerned the Auburndale Technology Center could move into the warehouses less than a mile away. “In five years from now, are they even going to want to live in it? And then can you sell it? Nobody else will buy it if it’s too noisy for you to live in,” she said. Texas-based development company Hillwood says the data center would have lower sound levels than a typical warehouse of its size. The facility is also expected to use less water than originally approved and have its own power supply through TECO. But after hearing from residents, Auburndale City Manager Jeffery Brown says leaders are considering a moratorium on future projects. “It would give us time to strengthen any shortcomings we find in our policy,” he said. “It would give us time to look at other places that have ordinances in place and pick the best of those to bring into an ordinance here.” Brown says that pause wouldn’t apply to the Auburndale Technology Center. The project is already in the permitting process, and the property is zoned to allow a data center. But Brown says the city will continue to make sure developers comply with local and state regulations. “One of the things we still have to do, we have to review the site plan, work with Hillwood on any deficiencies that are in that site plan,” he said. “We still have to get a consumptive use permit and approval through SWFWMD based upon the Florida statutes that show that it’s encumbering the city’s water system, or if it was, then what improvements have to be made to the water system that would be on Hillwood’s dime.” But Meadows believes the project should be put on hold until leaders come up with additional guidelines before it’s too late. “They’re rapidly hitting the point of no return,” she said. “Once that’s in, you can’t go back to make it a warehouse.” The city expects the moratorium to come before commissioners by the end of December, with a potential final vote in January. The public will have an opportunity to comment during both meetings.

artigo.texto: Swedish private markets fund manager EQT is acquiring US battery energy storage firm Flatiron Energy from Hull Street Energy (HSE). EQT said it has agreed to acquire Flatiron through its EQT Transition Infrastructure fund without disclosing financial terms. Flatiron, which was founded in 2021, develops and operates utility-scale energy storage projects across New England, New York and Mid-Atlantic power markets. Since HSE’s initial investment in 2022, Flatiron has expanded its portfolio nearly tenfold to 24GWh of capacity, been awarded 6GWh of long-term contracts and has 2GWh of batteries under construction. Flatiron joins an existing EQT battery storage platform that comprises Statera Energy in the UK and Ju:niz Energy in Germany. Benjamin Bygott-Webb, partner at EQT, said: “Battery storage has become essential to keeping the grid reliable and electricity affordable, as an ageing grid, a changing generation mix and rapidly growing power demand continue to put the system under strain. Flatiron has secured scarce, well-located sites and built a strong record in the communities where it operates. “Building on EQT’s deep experience investing in critical infrastructure, our expertise in scaling energy platforms and the opportunities for collaboration across the EQT infrastructure portfolio, we look forward to supporting the Flatiron team as they deliver their projects and bring more firm capacity to the region.” Sarah Wright, founder and managing partner at HSE, said: “This transaction underscores HSE’s approach to identifying attractive opportunities and creating long-term value in a rapidly growing and decarbonising power sector. “HSE is highly selective about the management teams we back, and Flatiron is an excellent illustration of why this matters. Because the Flatiron team has a strong track record in the sector and a rigorous, fundamentals-driven approach to setting strategy, they have been able to deliver material growth and value accretion.” Rob Brink, CEO of Flatiron Energy, said: “We started Flatiron with the mission to bring reliable energy where it’s needed most, in the communities that rely on it every day. “EQT is an exceptional firm with a strong track record of scaling platforms in the energy transition, and we couldn’t be more excited to partner with them on our next stage of growth.” Simpson Thacher & Bartlett and Santander served as legal and financial advisers to EQT, respectively, while Kirkland & Ellis and Guggenheim Securities advised Flatiron Energy. Faegre Drinker Biddle & Reath acted as legal counsel to HSE. To read the latest IPE Real Assets magazine click here.

The rule also imposes new licensing requirements specifically on exports to Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, and Brazil, which the U.S. views as having a higher-than-normal risk of chip diversion. [para. 2][para. 3] 3. Under the new framework, exporters must seek U.S. approval if they know covered chips or servers are destined for a data center providing more than 12 million in aggregate total processing performance (TPP) to China-linked companies. This threshold applies to an individual facility or a group of linked data centers, regardless of the data center's location, and covers computing provided directly or indirectly to companies headquartered in China. [para. 5][para. 8] 4. Based on Nvidia product specifications and industry estimates, the 12 million TPP threshold is roughly equivalent to about 750 Nvidia H200 chips. While this is small compared with the tens of thousands of chips typically needed to train the most advanced AI models, it could still support substantial inference workloads that require less concentrated computing capacity. [para. 6][para. 7] 5. Data-center operators face new obligations after chips are delivered. If an overseas facility begins providing computing capacity above the threshold to covered Chinese entities, the owner, operator, or another involved party must obtain a license. Existing data centers already providing such services have 90 days from the rule's effective date to seek approval if they wish to continue, or they risk future U.S. export restrictions. Commercial recommendation systems, such as those used by online retailers, are exempt. [para. 9][para. 10][para. 11] 6. The separate licensing requirement for Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, and Brazil could have a particularly large impact on Southeast Asia, which has become a major destination for AI data-center investment. Advanced chips shipped to these five countries will generally require U.S. approval, though companies headquartered in the U.S. or owned by U.S. parents can qualify for an exemption if they meet reporting requirements. Washington cited elevated risks of diversion to restricted users in these markets. [para. 12][para. 13][para. 14][para. 15] 7. Southeast Asia has grown rapidly as a computing hub as Chinese tech companies expand overseas and seek AI infrastructure. Singapore had more than 1.4 gigawatts (GW) of computing-infrastructure capacity in 2025, while Malaysia had about 1.06 GW, Indonesia 900 megawatts, and Thailand 620 megawatts. Regional capacity is expected to exceed 10 GW by 2030, up from more than 4.4 GW in 2025. [para. 16][para. 17] 8. Chinese technology companies including ByteDance, Alibaba, and Tencent have leased data-center capacity in Southeast Asia. Of roughly 1.5 GW of data-center projects approved in Thailand, as much as 60% to 70% are backed by Chinese investors or primarily serve major Chinese tech companies. In response, Malaysia plans legislation requiring data centers to disclose information such as operators, cloud customers, locations, electricity consumption, and GPU imports. Singapore said it is studying the new U.S. rules and engaging with affected companies and U.S. authorities. [para. 18][para. 19][para. 20][para. 21] 9. The rule also tightens requirements for semiconductor foundries and chip-packaging companies. Certain advanced chips designed by companies outside the U.S. and designated allied jurisdictions will be presumed to fall under U.S. export controls and to be intended for data-center use unless manufacturers or packaging companies can demonstrate otherwise. This builds on earlier restrictions aimed at preventing Chinese chip designers from using overseas foundries for advanced processors. [para. 22][para. 23][para. 24] 10. The Commerce Department formally rescinded the Biden administration's AI Diffusion Rule, a sweeping global framework unveiled in January 2025 that sought to divide countries into different tiers for access to advanced computing power. That rule never took effect; the Trump administration announced plans to abandon it in May 2025, arguing for a more targeted approach like the current interim rule. artigo.texto: BW ESS has partnered with French battery storage developer Wattmen to develop a battery energy storage system (BESS) portfolio of approximately 500 MW in France over the next three years. The partnership aims to expand BW ESS’ presence in the French energy storage market by developing large-scale, standalone battery storage projects connected to the transmission network. The collaboration will combine Wattmen’s local project origination and development expertise with BW ESS’ international experience in energy storage investment, project design and procurement. The companies will jointly work on advancing projects from the initial greenfield stage to ready-to-build status. This will include securing land rights, grid connections and the necessary regulatory authorisations required to move projects towards construction. The partnership will primarily focus on projects with connection capacities of at least 100 MW. The companies will priorities strategically located sites near grid connection points, with sufficient land availability to accommodate battery systems offering a minimum storage duration of four hours. This development strategy is intended to create a portfolio of large-scale energy storage assets capable of supporting the changing requirements of France’s electricity system. Under the partnership, Wattmen will lead local development activities, including identifying suitable project sites, negotiating land agreements, managing permitting processes and coordinating grid connections. The company will also work closely with landowners, local authorities and communities to facilitate project development. BW ESS will contribute its international energy storage experience, particularly in project design, investment and procurement strategy. The company operates across seven markets and brings experience in developing and managing battery storage projects at scale. Hazel Starmer-Jones, Development Director at BW ESS, said the partnership represents an important step in strengthening the company’s presence in France. She highlighted Wattmen’s technical capabilities and local market knowledge as important factors in selecting the development partner. Both companies aim to develop high-quality energy storage projects that can deliver long-term value while improving the flexibility and resilience of the French electricity system. Jean-Marc Guenée, CEO and Co-Founder of Wattmen, said the partnership combines complementary capabilities and a shared ambition to develop high-quality battery storage infrastructure. He noted that the collaboration would help advance strategically located projects and support the development of flexible energy infrastructure required for the energy transition. The agreement reflects BW ESS’ strategy of partnering with specialized local developers when entering and expanding in new markets. By combining local development capabilities with international investment and operational experience, the company aims to build a strong pipeline of energy storage projects. The latest partnership builds on BW ESS’ recent entry into France through the acquisition of two battery energy storage projects, each with a capacity of 100 MW and 400 MWh. These acquisitions, together with the new 500 MW development partnership, strengthen the company’s project pipeline and establish a foundation for further expansion in the French battery storage market. artigo.texto: Publicidade As novas restrições impostas pelos Estados Unidos à exportação de chips avançados para inteligência artificial adicionaram uma nova fonte de preocupação para os planos de expansão de data centers no Brasil e podem representar um obstáculo para a WEG (WEGE3), na avaliação do Bradesco BBI. A partir de 16 de novembro, fornecedores passarão a precisar de autorização do governo americano para exportar ao Brasil determinados processadores utilizados em data centers. A medida também alcança chips fabricados fora dos Estados Unidos quando desenvolvidos com tecnologia americana e faz parte dos esforços de Washington para evitar que empresas chinesas utilizem operações em terceiros países para contornar restrições tecnológicas impostas à China. Segundo a regulamentação do Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), Brasil, Singapura, Tailândia, Malásia e Indonésia foram classificados como países com risco acima do normal de desvio ilegal desses componentes para a China e Macau. Para o BBI, a notícia tem leitura negativa para a WEG, embora o banco não veja, por enquanto, necessidade de alterar suas estimativas, recomendação equivalente à compra ou o preço-alvo de R$ 62 para a ação. Na avaliação dos analistas, as restrições podem desacelerar a implementação de alguns projetos de data centers justamente em um momento em que o governo brasileiro tenta atrair investimentos para o setor por meio do programa ReData. Como a companhia fornece uma ampla gama de equipamentos para esse mercado, eventuais adiamentos poderiam postergar parte da demanda por seus produtos. O banco ressalta, contudo, que o impacto ainda é incerto e dependerá de fatores como a estrutura societária dos projetos, os usuários finais dos chips e as aplicações pretendidas. Além disso, a regulamentação prevê exceções para operações ligadas a empresas americanas e não representa uma proibição total das exportações para o Brasil. Continua depois da publicidade A preocupação surge em um momento de forte expansão do mercado local. Dados da Abinee citados pelo BBI mostram que as importações brasileiras de semicondutores somaram US$ 6,8 bilhões entre janeiro e setembro, alta de 51% na comparação anual. JPMorgan vê fundamentos intactos Apesar das preocupações de curto prazo envolvendo data centers, o JPMorgan segue otimista com a tese de investimento da WEG e reiterou recomendação overweight, equivalente à compra, elevando o preço-alvo para R$ 66 ao fim de 2027, ante R$ 56 anteriormente. O novo alvo implica potencial de valorização de cerca de 30% em relação aos níveis atuais. Para o banco americano, a empresa continua bem posicionada para acelerar o crescimento nos próximos anos, com expectativa de expansão da receita de 23% em 2027 e de 21% em 2028, depois de um crescimento estimado de apenas 3% em 2026. A tese é sustentada principalmente pelos negócios ligados a transformadores, sistemas de armazenamento de energia por baterias (BESS) e motores elétricos. Continua depois da publicidade Outro ponto destacado pelo JPMorgan é a proteção natural que a companhia possui contra a desvalorização do real. Mais de 60% das receitas da empresa são geradas fora do Brasil, sendo cerca de 30% provenientes da América do Norte. Segundo os cálculos do banco, cada depreciação de 5% do real acrescenta aproximadamente 4% ao EBITDA (lucro antes de juros, impostos, depreciações e amortizações) projetado da companhia. O JPMorgan também revisou para cima suas projeções financeiras após incorporar um cenário de câmbio mais depreciado. O banco elevou suas estimativas de EBITDA para 2027 em 6% e passou a trabalhar com crescimento de 27% nessa linha, além de prever lucro líquido e receitas acima do consenso de mercado para 2027 e 2028. Na visão dos analistas, a ação ainda negocia a múltiplos considerados atrativos, com desconto de cerca de 15% em relação à média histórica do período pós-pandemia. O banco argumenta ainda que a empresa tende a se beneficiar do atual ambiente doméstico por ser vista pelos investidores como uma companhia de alta qualidade, forte exposição ao dólar e menor dependência do ciclo econômico brasileiro. artigo.texto: SUBTULO: Conselho Municipal de Meio Ambiente busca análise do CNPEM, CPQD e PUC-Campinas sobre consumo de recursos e interferências em pesquisas científicas O Conselho Municipal de Meio Ambiente de Campinas (Comdema) publicou ofícios no Diário Oficial para convidar o CNPEM, o CPQD e a PUC-Campinas para avaliarem os impactos ambientais e nas atividades científicas do projeto de um mega data center na Fazenda Pau d'Alho, em Barão Geraldo. O empreendimento, da empresa Terranova, tem previsão de início em 2027 e pode alcançar 400 megawatts de capacidade até 2029, o que representaria 40% da capacidade atual de processamento de dados no Brasil. A Unicamp também participa das discussões por meio de pesquisadores. O Comdema está organizando um grupo de trabalho com especialistas em tecnologia, energia, recursos hídricos, legislação e saúde para apresentar um relatório técnico em até 90 dias. O conselho busca esclarecimentos sobre o consumo de até 3,24 milhões de litros de água por dia, a demanda de eletricidade, o aumento da temperatura no entorno, ruídos e vibrações que possam afetar equipamentos científicos sensíveis, além do descarte de resíduos eletrônicos e impactos urbanísticos. A Terranova informou que utilizará um sistema de refrigeração em circuito fechado para reduzir o consumo hídrico. A proximidade com o CNPEM, onde funciona o acelerador de partículas Sirius, motivou a consulta específica sobre vibrações e interferências. O CPQD foi convocado para avaliar eficiência energética e descarte de resíduos, enquanto a PUC-Campinas colaborará em análises ambientais e urbanísticas. Em agosto, o Comdema solicitou a suspensão dos licenciamentos da subestação de energia devido às preocupações com os recursos hídricos e elétricos. O Ministério Público de São Paulo (MP-SP) instaurou um inquérito civil em setembro para apurar a regularidade do projeto após denúncias. A Prefeitura de Campinas informou que apenas a subestação recebeu autorizações até o momento, seguindo a legislação municipal. A Terranova afirmou cumprir as exigências legais e destacou contrapartidas como preservação de áreas verdes, construção de vias públicas e estações de tratamento de água e esgoto. O projeto prevê investimento inicial de US$ 500 milhões e a geração de cerca de 3 mil empregos diretos e indiretos. Mín. 18° Máx. 25°

artigo.texto: As Electorate Rejects Terrestrial Data Centers, Satellite Industry Considers Space Compute Small onboard computers could analyze satellite imagery to flag crop problems for farmers and identify potential threats for defense agencies Akul Saxena NEW ORLEANS, Nov. 18, 2026 – Voters in 10 states backed restrictions on data center development on Nov. 3. Satellite executives say those restrictions strengthen the case for putting some computing equipment in orbit. Executives at the Broadband Nation Expo and Data Center Excellence event here took up what that rebuke means for computing in space Wednesday. Early compute applications Satellites collect more imagery than their radio links can send to Earth, said Rick Ward, founder and chief technology officer of OrbitsEdge, a Central Florida startup developing small computers that other companies can carry aboard their satellites. Processing the imagery in orbit and sending down only the results gets around that bottleneck. For a farmer, it’s the information that’s useful. “They need the information, not necessarily the pictures,” Ward said. Defense agencies are likely early customers, Ward said. Builders cannot start with gigawatt data centers, he said, so the first computing tasks have to be small ones where processing on board pays off. Early warning is another use case. A satellite that analyzes its own sensor data can send down an alert instead of raw imagery, skipping the wait to move the pictures to the ground first. "If you're doing something like Starshield, you need early warning protection first," Ward said. Starshield is SpaceX’s satellite line for government agencies. OrbitsEdge’s Edge1 design weighed less than 4.4 pounds and required 10 watts from its host satellite, Payload reported in June 2025. Meanwhile, Elon Musk’s rocket company applied to the Federal Communications Commission in January to operate up to one million data center satellites. That is about 59 times the 16,910 satellites the European Space Agency counted in orbit at the time, Broadband Breakfast reported. Moving from small onboard computers to facilities serving customers on Earth requires overcoming three major constraints: Cooling, launch costs and transmission delays. The case for orbit starts with scarce power on the ground A data center brings modest value to the town that hosts it, even when its value to the country is large, Ward said. That mismatch has made the facilities a hard sell locally, and it is the case for orbit, he said. Power is the other terrestrial bottleneck. A data center goes up in about two years, Ward said. Two nuclear reactors, by contrast, took close to 20 years, he said. For example, the two reactors at Georgia Power's Plant Vogtle took 15 years and $36.8 billion before entering service in 2024, took 15 years and $36.8 billion before entering service. Until new plants arrive, data centers on the ground rely on gas turbines and large solar arrays while their demand for electricity continues to surge, Ward said. Heat caps how big a machine can get Data centers on the ground often draw on local water to cool their servers while a spacecraft uses none. On Earth, servers shed heat three ways, through conduction, convection and radiation, Ward said. In space it’s only through radiation. Cooling 1 megawatt of computing takes about 13,000 square feet of panel, according to SatNews. That is nearly a quarter of a football field for 1 megawatt. Large data center campuses on the ground run to a gigawatt, 1,000 times more. Launch sets the price, and supply just tightened However, computing in orbit costs far more today than on the ground, Ward said. But the launch is a one-time bill, and hardware with few moving parts can run for decades. He called orbital compute a closed-loop system since “it's just mass." A Vulcan rocket failed Sunday, Nov. 15, destroying 40 Amazon Leo satellites, and could stay grounded for months. Falcon 9 launches from Florida paused for at least six weeks after Oct. 20 to make room for Starship. Altitude determines which computing tasks can go up The farther a satellite sits from Earth, the longer a signal takes to make the round trip. That delay, called latency, determines which computing tasks can run in orbit at all. A round trip to a geostationary satellite, about 22,236 miles up, runs 600 milliseconds or more. Low Earth orbit cuts that to 25 to 60 milliseconds. That gap matters for TCP, the protocol that carries most internet traffic. "There's no TCP-based network application that works better with more latency," said Grant Kirkwood, chief executive of Contrivian, which routes traffic across satellite and ground networks. Space traffic management Space traffic management matters more as the technology outruns policymakers, Ward said. The FCC has a role through licensing while civil traffic coordination moves from the Defense Department to the Commerce Department, said Tom Stroup, president of the Satellite Industry Association. A 2022 FCC rule requires low Earth orbit satellites to deorbit, or reenter Earth's atmosphere, within five years of mission end, replacing a 25-year guideline. The turnover in Congress With United Launch Alliance's Vulcan grounded and SpaceX's Falcon 9 paused in Florida, there are few rockets to go around. SpaceX can sell room on a launch to another company or fill it with its own satellites. Computing in orbit could easily take up all available capacity, Stroup said, which raises competition issues. New members of Congress take office in January. With that significant turnover, he said, policymakers will have a lot of questions about the industry. Some have called for breaking up SpaceX, which builds both the rockets and the satellites they carry. The model is working, Ward said, and splitting it would serve no real benefit because the pieces would very likely still be each other's customers.

artigo.texto: Data centers são apenas um dos dez pilares para o Brasil disputar a liderança global em IA Monica Miglio Pedrosa Para se destacar globalmente na transformação pela inteligência artificial, o Brasil precisa desenvolver capacidade própria de produzir conhecimento e tecnologia. O Redata (Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter) pode atrair investimentos para ampliar a infraestrutura necessária a essa ambição. Mas os data centers por si só não garantem autonomia sobre os modelos de IA que vão transformar os negócios e participar de decisões estratégicas nas empresas. O alerta é de André Luís da Fonseca, coordenador do Centro de Estudos em Estratégia e Inovação (CEEI) do COPPEAD/UFRJ. Segundo o pesquisador, os data centers podem ampliar a capacidade de processamento no país, mas manter os dados e a estratégia em tecnologias contratadas por empresas privadas estrangeiras. Além disso, de acordo com o periódico Technological Forecasting & Social Change, a infraestrutura é apenas um dos dez elementos para construir um ecossistema completo. Os demais são cultura, demanda, financiamento, instituições formais, intermediários, conhecimento, liderança, redes e talento. “A pergunta que o país precisa fazer não é apenas onde os servidores vão ficar, mas quem vai ser dono do conhecimento que roda neles. Capacidade de processamento sem capacidade de orquestrar a IA é aluguel de infraestrutura, não soberania”, afirma. Confira, a seguir, a entrevista exclusiva para a [EXP]. [EXP] O que a instalação de data centers representa para a participação do Brasil na indústria de inteligência artificial? [André Luís da Fonseca] A indústria da IA funciona sobre uma pilha de elementos. No nível mais básico estão o espaço onde fica o data center, a licença da prefeitura, a água usada para refrigerar os servidores e a energia elétrica que eles consomem. É uma camada sem a qual o restante não existiria, mas de menor valor agregado. Quando isso é feito por uma organização de fora, é quase como se estivéssemos exportando sol, água, uso da terra e autorização ambiental. Não tem muita diferença, para todos os fins práticos, de exportar soja. É quase como se tivéssemos um monocultivo agrícola, só que computacional. Isso contribui para o PIB, traz riqueza que de outra forma não viria e, portanto, é recomendável. A questão é passar a sensação de que estamos tendo uma participação na cadeia produtiva maior do que essa atividade de fato representa. Estamos pegando um pedaço da receita da indústria por meio do fornecimento desses recursos. Isso, por si só, não está diminuindo a dependência. Como avalia as contrapartidas de pesquisa e desenvolvimento previstas no Redata? Existem efeitos negativos associados ao uso do solo, da água e dos demais recursos de determinado lugar, assim como alguém poderia argumentar que uma plantação de soja tem efeitos ambientais negativos. Então, você exige uma compensação adicional. O Redata faz isso direcionando 2% da aquisição de hardware para investimento em pesquisa e desenvolvimento no Brasil. Esse investimento contribui para o ecossistema de desenvolvimento local, o que é uma coisa boa. E a oferta de 10% da capacidade ser oferecida ao mercado interno? O que ela representa? É preciso entender que estamos falando de vender uma parte da capacidade, não de dar. É como convidar alguém para montar um negócio no seu prédio e dizer que ele terá a chance de vender também para os moradores. Não sei se podemos atribuir tanta importância a esses 10%. Para o governo brasileiro, que tem a questão de manter o processamento dos dados públicos aqui, isso garante a possibilidade de comprar esse espaço. Garante que haverá capacidade disponível para rodar no Brasil o processamento de IA associado aos serviços do governo. Mas essa oferta não é exclusiva para o governo, já que a iniciativa privada no país também pode comprar e usar. Há outros benefícios econômicos que merecem ser considerados? No caso específico do Nordeste, há a possibilidade de aproveitar energia elétrica renovável que está sendo desperdiçada. Você leva o data center para perto da turbina eólica ou da usina solar e deixa de depender de linhas de transmissão para consumir aquela energia. Ela passa a ser monetizada, vendida na forma de computação, o que também é positivo. Não estou dizendo que isso não deva ser feito. Estou dizendo que tem muito mais a ver com PIB e geração de receita do que com diminuição da dependência. O problema é achar que estamos atingindo um resultado maior do que de fato estamos. Por que manter os dados no Brasil não resolve a dependência tecnológica? Estamos vivendo um aumento muito grande da dependência. Nossas atividades individuais e profissionais estão sendo estruturadas sobre uma cognição computacional que não controlamos. A empresa não controla e o país não controla. A simples possibilidade de um modelo deixar de estar disponível já é um problema. A questão é que estamos estruturando nosso trabalho e nossa pesquisa acadêmica cada vez mais em parceria com sistemas computacionais que não controlamos. Não é o fato de os dados estarem aqui que vai nos proteger disso. A tomada de decisão dos brasileiros está sendo feita em parceria com esses sistemas, e isso é uma fonte adicional de dependência. O dado pode estar aqui e continuar não sendo seu, continuar sem o seu controle. Não estamos falando de uma refinaria de petróleo que você pode expropriar e dizer que agora é sua. É uma máquina administrada por pessoas que estão em outro lugar e que tomam decisões com base em agendas que, eventualmente, não são as nossas. Que mudanças nas condições de uso desses sistemas podem afetar quem depende deles? Pode mudar o preço, a regra, as categorias sociais representadas naquele software. Podem mudar as políticas de tratamento dos dados que fornecemos o tempo inteiro. E a regulação, por si só, não resolve isso. O que resolve é ter alternativa. A própria maneira de tomar a decisão está sendo dividida com sistemas que não

artigo.texto: Hyperscale data centers’ energy consumption, carbon emissions newly estimated by researchers New research reveals the electricity consumption and carbon emissions behind America’s hyperscale data centers rivals that of some U.S. states For immediate release: November 16, 2026 Boston, MA—Over the course of a year, hyperscale data centers (HDCs)—the largest and most powerful class of data centers, supporting services such as cloud computing, large language model training, and global deployment of artificial intelligence (AI) tools—are powered mostly by fossil fuels and use as much electricity as entire U.S. states, according to a new study led by Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health and the Harvard Data Science Initiative. The study provides one of the first facility-level estimates of HDCs’ electricity use and carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions since the rise of AI. The study was published Nov. 16 in Nature Sustainability. “Data centers are growing incredibly fast, driven largely by AI, and decisions about where to build them and how to power them are being made right now. But there’s very little facility-level information about their environmental footprint,” said lead author Gianluca Guidi, postdoctoral fellow in the Department of Biostatistics. “Our study helps fill that gap.” “Our goal is to give the public, policymakers, investors, and developers a much more concrete, up-to-date picture than was available before,” added corresponding author Francesca Dominici, Clarence James Gamble Professor of Biostatistics, Population, and Data Science and director of the Harvard Data Science Initiative. “Decisions about where data centers go and how they’re powered are critical environmental and public health decisions, and they should be made with good data.” While data centers are known to require significant electricity to run, few studies have examined this topic facility by facility, estimating not just how much electricity each HDC uses, but what fuels generated this electricity. For this study, the researchers used satellite imagery to build a list of 403 HDCs across the U.S. and estimated annual electricity consumption for each facility between May 2024 and April 2025 under a range of operating scenarios. They then used Environmental Protection Agency data to attribute carbon emissions to each HDC based on the mix of power plants in its regional grid. The study found that these HDCs, depending on how hard they were running, together used between 68 and 99 terawatt-hours of electricity—with the upper estimate approaching the amount some states, such as Indiana, Michigan, and Tennessee, use in a year. During the study period, HDC electricity demand corresponded to approximately 1.8% of total U.S. electricity consumption, and was associated with about 25.7 million metric tons of CO2—an amount two to three times higher than an earlier estimate for 2018. Today, electricity demand and carbon emissions are likely much higher than they were during the study period, the researchers say. “What we’re seeing is already striking, but it’s only a snapshot of a rapidly expanding industry,” Guidi said. “The data center boom hasn’t slowed down since our study period ended in April 2025. New facilities have been built, existing campuses have expanded, and demand for AI computing continues to grow. That means the electricity use and carbon footprint we’re reporting could already be substantially larger now in 2026.” The study also found that roughly 54% of the electricity powering the HDCs was generated by fossil fuels—mainly natural gas (38%) and coal (15%)—and about a quarter of the electricity was in grid regions dirtier than average. The researchers noted substantial regional differences, with some HDCs relying much more heavily on carbon-intensive electricity than others. Many of the facilities were concentrated in geographic areas where electricity is generated heavily by coal-fired power plants. The researchers also noted that just four states—Virginia, Oregon, Ohio, and Iowa—accounted for more than half of the electricity use studied. The study had limitations, including that there wasn’t enough available data to study all HDCs in the U.S., and that the data did not allow them to differentiate between power used for general-purpose versus AI-specialized operations at each HDC. The researchers also noted that the study didn’t directly measure the health effects associated with HDCs, but that is a subject they plan to pursue in future research. “Quantifying health impacts is an important next step,” said Dominici. “First, carbon dioxide drives climate change, which affects health through heat waves, wildfire smoke, flooding, and other pathways. Second, the fossil fuel power plants in the regional electricity systems associated with this demand also release other pollutants, such as fine particulate matter, nitrogen oxides, and sulfur dioxide, that are directly linked to heart and lung disease and premature death. So when data centers draw heavily on fossil fuel power, the people living near and downwind of those power plants may bear health costs, even if they’re far from the data center itself.” Article information “Assessing the Carbon Emissions and Energy Consumption of US Hyperscale Data Centers,” Gianluca Guidi, Francesca Dominici, Tiziano Squartini, Callaway Sprinkle, Jonathan Gilmour, Kevin Butler, Eric Bell, Scott Delaney, Falco J. Bargagli-Stoffi, Nature Sustainability, November 16, 2026, doi: 10.1038/s41893-026-01985-7 The study was supported by the National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences–Harvard Center Pilot Project (P30ES000002), the National Institute on Aging (R01AG066793), and the National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences (R01ES034373).
