artigo.texto: The Chickasaw County Board of Supervisors appear to have the appetite to put together an ordinance dealing with data centers in the county. However, it appeared Monday that board members aren’t willing to enact a moratorium on allowing the facilities that have generated controversy and opposition in other parts of Iowa. Assessor Ray Armel, who also serves as the county’s land-use administrator, asked supervisors to look over examples of what other counties have done when it comes to rules governing data centers in the county. “They include in their moratoriums everything from bit drives to battery storage to solar … The majority [that I have] are just for data centers,” Armel said, “but I think if you want to get ahead on this, you should look these over.” Board Chairman Jake Hackman pointed out that some data center sites can take up between 500 and 600 acres of land, and opponents of data centers point out the use of natural resources — especially water — make them unattractive. Armel said that state lawmakers, who have passed property tax limitation laws in recent years, have expressed their frustrations that “counties and jurisdictions are passing some of these moratoriums and limitations, yet not accepting some of these facilities — whether it be solar, whether it be battery power, whether it be the bitcoin or what have you.” County Attorney David Laudner echoed Armel, and said it was important for supervisors to have a clear reason for enacting an ordinance or a moratorium. “I know a lot of people are against wind and were upset that the wind [turbines] came here,” Laudner said, “but they have provided quite a boon for some of the development and some money. Would the data centers do the same thing or would they not have much of an impact financially?” He emphasized that he “was not weighing in on” the issue, but that those questions need to be answered by supervisors. Armel said a data center would have a financial impact. “In my reading, what it showed and that wouldn’t necessarily be the case here, but [some places, there’s] up to a 30 percent reduction in property tax,” he said. Hackman said he would support an ordinance so that “we can make sure the current residents, county right-of-ways and intersections are protected,” and asked fellow board members how they felt about proceeding with putting an ordinance together. “I think we should have a couple weeks to look these over and make that decision,” Supervisor Steve Breitbach said. Fellow board members Travis Suckow said he was OK with adopting some kind of ordinance, but he also indicated he was firmly against a moratorium. “I don’t feel like we can — or should — tell property owners what they can and can’t do with their property,” he said. In the end, board members said they will look over the examples Armel provided and take up the issue again in the near future.

artigo.texto: Signs a long-term lithium supply agreement with CATL, which commands an approximately 40% share of the global EV battery market, covering lithium supply for 2026 through 2028 Extends raw material securing and development expertise from steel to lithium… further solidifying its sales foundation in China, the world’s largest EV battery market. Materializes CEO of POSCO Holdings CHANG In Hwa’s strategy to preemptively secure prime resources and build long-term partnerships with leading global customers, enhancing the competitiveness of the lithium business. POSCO group further strengthens its cooperation with CATL, the world’s largest EV battery company, through a long-term lithium supply agreement. CATL (Contemporary Amperex Technology Co., Limited), which accounts for about 40% of the global EV battery market, leads the industry by supplying batteries to major automakers in China and across the globe. Under the agreement, POSCO group supplies CATL with lithium required for EV battery production for 2026 through 2028. Both companies commit to solidifying their long-term partnership and working together to ensure a stable supply of raw materials. Supply under the agreement is already underway. POSCO group has been expanding its lithium business based on its capabilities in securing and developing raw materials, accumulated through its steel business. Building on its production base established through the preemptive securing of high-quality lithium resources, this agreement is expected to further solidify POSCO group’s sales foundation in China and strengthen its position in the global lithium market. This reflects CEO of POSCO Holdings CHANG In Hwa’s strategic focus on preemptively securing high-quality resources and building long-term partnerships with leading global customers. Moving forward, POSCO group will enhance the production stability and sales competitiveness of its lithium resources to drive profitability. At the same time, as Korea’s flagship supplier of critical resources, the group will contribute to stabilizing the global critical minerals supply chain.

artigo.texto: SAN DIEGO (KGTV) — Plans for what could be by far the largest data center in California are being considered in rural East County, and while the developer stresses it's only an early proposal, many who live there are already fighting against it. County records obtained by our media partners at KPBS, which ABC 10News has since reviewed, reveal a proposed data center called Project ECO with an electrical load of up to 500 megawatts — roughly four times the reported capacity of California's largest existing data center in Santa Clara County. It would be placed on 177 acres of land, less than a mile away from the home of Greg Curran, vice president of the Jacumba Sponsor Group which is leading the resistance. Jacumba is about 70 miles east of the city of San Diego, near the U.S.-Mexico border. You might recognize the unincorporated community from its well-known oasis, the Jacumba Hot Springs. In fact, that's part of what drew Curran there in the first place. "I just love soaking in the mineral hot springs and, you know, the area out here in the high desert," he said. "I just fell in love with it." Curran calls Jacumba the "perfect place to get away," but he and others fear this potential new development would change that. "This is the time to nip it in the bud," Curran said. Curran's neighbor Tanya Aiau, who lives in the Jacumba area even closer to the proposed site, shared her frustration as well. "If they start to build that, I'll literally have to move. I've got 30 acres. It's terrifying," Aiau said. IGNIS, a renewable energy company based in Spain, is the developer behind the project. ABC 10News spoke with a representative over the phone, Tahir Fazal, who made it very clear this is nothing more than a proposal to see if it's even feasible. Fazal said "pushback is very reasonable" and added that the company wants to stress "(we) will be very engaged with the community once (we) make the decision to move forward, if (we) make it." Curran knows what he would like the leaders of San Diego County's decision to be. "I think that we should put a moratorium on them. It's just too massive. It takes — it's mind-boggling the amount of energy that it needs," Curran said. Earlier this year, the City of San Diego and Escondido already approved moratoriums on large-scale data centers, and the City of Poway passed an ordinance to ban them outright. The county has already flagged water availability as a major concern and wants the electrical infrastructure to be reviewed. Residents tell ABC 10News they're also worried about air quality and noise, and more than anything, say it would be an industrial eyesore in an otherwise natural landscape. artigo.texto: In the midterm elections, voters gave America’s data center industry a beating. In 40 of 41 local ballot contests across 10 states, they backed restrictions or rejected measures favoring these sprawling developments. In Boulder City, Nevada, nearly 71% voted against allowing data centers in a large area of city-owned land. But now, the Trump administration is opening federal land to the same industry, including places where residents have spent months fighting to keep it out. In May, after fierce public opposition, Boulder City’s planning commission recommended rejecting a developer’s proposed data center on city land. But the company had also sought permission from the Bureau of Land Management to replace a solar project with a data center on nearby federal land. In June, BLM approved the change without a new environmental review, treating a massive data center as substantially the same project as a solar farm. “We were not consulted,” city attorney Brittany Walker told reporters. As one resident warned at a packed meeting, “Even if the project is now on adjacent BLM land, the impact does not stop at a property line.” An Interior appeals board halted the approval in September, and in October, the decision was set aside for further BLM review. The project remains alive, while meaningful environmental review and public participation remain unresolved. This is one project in a much larger building spree. The nonprofit More Than Just Parks has mapped more than 2,000 large data centers operating, under construction or proposed across the country, along with hundreds halted or delayed by community opposition. Each appears as a local land-use decision. Together, they represent a national transformation. In Utah, one company is seeking roughly 9,000 acres of BLM land for a nuclear-powered data-center complex. The Energy Department has selected four of its own federal sites for potential private data-center development. The buildings are just the beginning. They require power plants, substations, transmission lines, pipelines and water. A 2025 Energy Department report projects data centers could consume nearly 12% of America’s electricity by 2030. We’ve seen what happens when Washington embraces a colossal building spree — the last one to build as many federal dams as possible — without reckoning with the costs. In 1957, the federal Dalles Dam drowned Celilo Falls on the Columbia River, where Native families had fished for thousands of years. Treaty-protected fishing grounds vanished beneath the reservoir. Forty-nine years later, Google built its own data center in The Dalles, drawn partly by the region’s power infrastructure. Today, the Bonneville Power Administration markets electricity from 31 federal dams across the Northwest. The machinery of one great building spree is helping power the next. Those dams powered cities and irrigated farms. They also drowned Glen Canyon and more than 350,000 acres across seven Indian reservations on the Missouri River. The benefits spread far and wide. The people whose homes, fisheries and sacred places disappeared bore the cost. David Brower, who helped spare Dinosaur National Monument from another dam, later regretted his part in Glen Canyon’s destruction. He hadn’t even seen the place before its fate was sealed. “When we began to find out, it was too late,” he wrote. The secrecy is familiar, too. Google’s initial land deal in The Dalles was negotiated under “extreme confidentiality,” according to The Dalles Chronicle. In Tucson, officials and a utility signed nondisclosure agreements over a proposed data center. Residents did not learn what was coming until later, though packed public meetings helped to stop it. The Trump administration is working to speed up permitting for data centers. A 2025 executive order directed the Army’s civil-works leadership to examine a nationwide permitting pathway. The same Corps of Engineers that built The Dalles Dam is being enlisted to accelerate the next boom. Congress has an opportunity to intervene. Bills from Senator Ron Wyden, D-Oregon, and Rep. Rashida Tlaib, D-Michigan, would ban data centers on federal land. Rep. Dina Titus, D-Nevada, has proposed stronger environmental review and public participation for such developments. Midterm election voters made their wishes plain. Before Washington commits more public land, water and electricity, communities deserve a say in what gets built and who pays for it. Once the land is sacrificed, no public hearing can bring it back. Will Pattiz is a contributor to Writers on the Range, an independent nonprofit dedicated to spurring lively conversation about the West. He co-founded More Than Just Parks, a public lands advocacy and media organization.

artigo.texto: OS DATA CENTERS PODEM PREJUDICAR O PARTIDO DE TRUMP NAS ELEIÇÕES DOS EUA? O repórter do Estadão, Daniel Gateno, fala sobre o documentário “Estadão na América”, que estreia nesta semana, e o medo dos americanos com o futuro dos Estados. Gerando resumo De acordo com uma nova pesquisa, publicada nesta segunda-feira, 16, pela revista Nature Sustainability, os maiores data centers dos Estados Unidos são responsáveis por 25,7 milhões de toneladas de emissões de dióxido de carbono anualmente — quase tanto quanto países inteiros como a Bolívia ou a Dinamarca. O estudo apresenta as primeiras estimativas revisadas por pares das emissões de dióxido de carbono dos maiores data centers dos EUA desde o início do boom da inteligência artificial. Seus autores, uma equipe liderada por pesquisadores da Universidade de Harvard, examinaram o consumo de eletricidade e as emissões de carbono de 403 data centers entre maio de 2024 e abril de 2025. No total, essas operações consumiram quase 2% da eletricidade dos EUA, mais do que Nova York e Los Angeles juntas, e representaram cerca de 0,5% das emissões de dióxido de carbono dos EUA. O dióxido de carbono é o principal gás de efeito estufa responsável pelo aquecimento global. Os data centers em apenas três Estados, Virgínia, Iowa e Ohio, foram responsáveis por cerca de metade das emissões estimadas no estudo. Em Estados como o Oregon, os data centers são responsáveis por emitir menos dióxido de carbono por unidade de eletricidade consumida, porque uma parcela maior de sua energia é gerada sem combustíveis fósseis, constatou o estudo. Em todas as 403 instalações, 54% da eletricidade provinha da queima de combustíveis fósseis, principalmente gás natural e carvão. Um trabalho de detetive Grande parte da análise do estudo se resumiu a trabalho de detetive, ressaltando o sigilo sob o qual as empresas de IA têm permissão para operar. Sem uma lista pública de data centers para trabalhar, os pesquisadores começaram consultando um conjunto de dados comerciais cujas regras de licenciamento os impediam — e ao The New York Times — de publicar os endereços, nomes e proprietários das instalações. Os pesquisadores passaram horas estudando as plantas dos edifícios e imagens de satélite para confirmar a localização e o tamanho dos data centers, estimaram quanta eletricidade eles poderiam usar e, em seguida, calcularam suas emissões com base na matriz energética de cada rede elétrica regional. “O fato de termos que passar por um processo de reconstrução tão extenso apenas para entender onde a infraestrutura está localizada e qual a sua dimensão revela muito sobre a falta de transparência no próprio setor”, afirmou Gianluca Guidi, cientista de Harvard que liderou a equipe de pesquisa. Michael Thomas, que dirige a empresa de dados energéticos Cleanview e não participou do estudo, traçou um contraste entre data centers e usinas de energia, obrigadas a divulgar publicamente todos os tipos de detalhes sobre os impactos ambientais de suas operações. Coletar os detalhes das operações de um data centers, por outro lado, exige vasculhar milhões de documentos espalhados por bancos de dados municipais, estaduais e federais. “Talvez uns seis senadores tenham entrado em contato conosco. Eles perguntam coisas como: ‘Quantos data centers existem? Estamos tentando elaborar um projeto de lei’”, disse Thomas. “Por que o Senado está entrando em contato comigo e não a EIA ou a FERC?”, acrescentou, usando as siglas da Administração de Informação Energética dos EUA e da Comissão Federal de Regulamentação de Energia. Embora Estados como Virgínia e Ohio tenham começado a adotar uma supervisão mais rigorosa, Guidi afirmou que o governo federal deveria exigir que os operadores de grandes data centers divulgassem publicamente seu consumo de eletricidade e suas emissões. “As comunidades não deveriam precisar de uma equipe de pesquisadores de Harvard para analisar imagens de satélite a fim de compreender seu impacto ambiental”, disse ele. Os desenvolvedores de data centers dispõem de diversas ferramentas para ocultar os impactos de carbono e energia de seus projetos. Essas camadas de sigilo emergiram como um dos principais pontos de preocupação na crescente resistência a projetos de data centers em todo o país. Os eleitores optaram por limitar ou impedir o desenvolvimento de data centers em 40 das 41 iniciativas locais relevantes nas eleições de meio de mandato deste mês. “Acordos de confidencialidade, usuários finais ocultos e negociações a portas fechadas moldam as narrativas da oposição de forma mais consistente do que qualquer outra preocupação”, segundo um relatório recente da Relae, uma consultoria de clima e energia. Entre março de 2024 e o início de novembro de 2026, a oposição local bloqueou ou atrasou pelo menos 70 projetos de data centers para IA em 25 Estados, representando um investimento estimado em US$ 271 bilhões, de acordo com a pesquisa da Relae. Quatorze desses projetos estavam na Virgínia, o epicentro do boom dos data centers. Os data centers da Virgínia foram responsáveis por mais de um quarto das emissões estimadas no estudo. Na PJM Interconnection, a operadora da rede elétrica regional que atende a Virgínia, cerca de 60% da eletricidade que alimenta os data centers é produzida por combustíveis fósseis. Os números do estudo provavelmente subestimam todas as emissões de data centers dos EUA, porque a lista de instalações analisadas não representa um inventário completo. Ela exclui centenas de possíveis data centers que os pesquisadores não conseguiram verificar suficientemente, bem como instalações que não utilizam a rede elétrica, obtendo energia de geradores no local. É também um retrato de uma indústria que cresce a um ritmo vertiginoso. A instalação média no estudo tinha uma capacidade elétrica de cerca de 40 megawatts, enquanto projetos futuros, como o campus Hyperion de 5 gigawatts da Meta na Louisiana, terão mais de 100 vezes essa capacidade. artigo.texto: Siga Folha BV no Google Veja nossas notícias com mais destaque nas suas buscas. Siga Folha BV no Google Veja nossas notícias com mais destaque nas suas buscas. A WEG apresentou o W30Slim Smart EC, motor com inversor integrado e 175 milímetros de comprimento axial destinado a aplicações como ventilação e refrigeração de data centers. Divulgada pela fabricante em 10 de novembro de 2026, a solução reúne acionamento eletrônico e ventilação própria para facilitar sua integração aos equipamentos que mantêm os servidores em condições adequadas de operação. A família oferece potências de 1,5 a 10 hp, equivalentes a aproximadamente 1,1 a 7,5 kW. Esses números representam potência mecânica de acionamento, não capacidade de refrigeração. O catálogo posiciona o modelo em aplicações com ventiladores radiais: ele movimenta o conjunto responsável pela circulação de ar, dentro de um sistema térmico mais amplo. O que os 17,5 centímetros representam A medida destacada corresponde ao comprimento ao longo do eixo. Portanto, não descreve o diâmetro nem todas as dimensões externas do equipamento. Para fabricantes de sistemas de ventilação, essa característica pode ampliar as possibilidades de montagem em espaços restritos, embora o resultado dependa da geometria do conjunto. A WEG classifica o produto como o mais compacto, leve e eficiente de sua categoria. Entretanto, os documentos consultados não apresentam uma comparação reproduzível com concorrentes, identificando modelos, condições de ensaio e diferenças percentuais. A afirmação permanece atribuída à fabricante, sem validação independente apresentada nesses materiais. Inversor integrado controla a velocidade O inversor incorporado permite ajustar a rotação conforme o comando recebido, reunindo motor e eletrônica de acionamento em uma solução integrada. Isso oferece ao fabricante do equipamento uma forma de controlar a movimentação de ar conforme as necessidades operacionais, em vez de trabalhar exclusivamente com uma velocidade fixa. Entre as interfaces especificadas estão sinais de 2–10 V, corrente de 4–20 mA e PWM, além de comunicação Modbus. Na prática, esses recursos permitem receber comandos e integrar o acionamento à automação da instalação. A documentação também relaciona proteções contra sobrecarga, sobretemperatura, sobretensão, subtensão e rotor bloqueado. O catálogo apresenta alternativas de rotação nominal que chegam a 3.600 rpm, com faixas ajustáveis conforme a versão. A seleção precisa considerar simultaneamente potência, velocidade e alimentação elétrica; o limite de 10 hp não deve ser entendido como disponível em qualquer configuração. Ventilação própria e proteção opcional Outro diferencial é a construção TEFC, com ventilação própria. Segundo a WEG, o motor não depende do fluxo de ar produzido pela aplicação para manter seu desempenho térmico. Essa independência é relevante quando o posicionamento do acionamento dificulta a passagem de ar sobre sua estrutura. O catálogo informa operação em ambientes de −25 °C a 50 °C e regime S1, destinado ao funcionamento contínuo. A proteção padrão é IP55; IP66 aparece como opção. Assim, a resistência ampliada a poeira e jatos fortes de água precisa ser confirmada na configuração adquirida. A documentação menciona níveis de eficiência IE5 e IE6, mas não fornece, na apresentação geral do W30Slim, uma tabela completa de rendimento por carga e rotação. Por isso, essas classificações não permitem calcular diretamente a redução da conta de eletricidade de uma instalação. Demanda energética cresce, mas economia exige medição O contexto comercial é global. No relatório Key Questions on Energy and AI, de 2026, a Agência Internacional de Energia estima que os data centers consumiram 485 TWh em 2025 e projeta aproximadamente 950 TWh em 2030. Os valores abrangem o setor inteiro, incluindo instalações que não são dedicadas à IA. Para avaliar o impacto dessa tecnologia na infraestrutura de inteligência artificial, ainda faltam resultados operacionais do modelo: economia medida sob condições comparáveis, efeito sobre a eficiência total da instalação, preço e retorno do investimento. Os materiais consultados descrevem especificações e aplicações previstas, mas não apresentam esses indicadores em um data center identificado nem detalham prazos de fornecimento para projetos no mercado brasileiro. artigo.texto: Tulsa, Broken Arrow leaders weigh data center regulations amid growing public concerns As debate intensifies across Green Country over hyperscale data centers, Tulsa and Broken Arrow, the region’s two largest cities, have voted to pause consideration of any new data center proposals while they work on regulations. Broken Arrow City Manager Michael Spurgeon said the city’s decision followed packed City Hall meetings and concerns that have surfaced in other communities. Broken Arrow leaders halted data center discussions through the end of the year while the city develops an official plan for how to handle developers. “I know the council shares the same concerns that I have that the public has about the detrimental effect that a data center could have on a community when it comes to for example, our utilities, the water usage, utility rates,” Spurgeon said. He said the city wants to take a deliberate approach before moving forward. “We need to go about this in a very methodical way to look at every aspect of of what the impact would be, whether it's financial, whether it's environmental, whether it's long term,” Spurgeon said. In Tulsa, city leaders raised similar concerns, including the prospect of data centers being built near neighborhoods with limited ability for elected officials to weigh in. During discussion, Tulsa City Councilor Laura Bellis said, “I totally agree with you 100 percent about putting a data center next to large subdivisions. It's just nonsense to me.” Councilors also pointed to zoning rules that could allow data centers in multiple areas near neighborhoods with little to no need for city leaders to provide input. Tulsa City Councilor Vanessa Hall-Harper said, “I'm just raising a question that we have some kind of say in it or not. Where it's already zoned, I don't think we do.” As more cities and towns face data center proposals, a push is growing at the state Capitol to establish statewide guardrails. Tulsa state Rep. Amanda Clinton said communities can feel pressured by promises of economic benefits while lacking the resources to negotiate with major tech companies. “They're between a rock and a hard place. You know, they have this carrot being dangled out of there that they're going to get better schools, better sidewalks, better roads. And that's very tempting. But they also know that they share a city attorney with, say, 4 or 5 other towns. So they're not really quite equipped to go up against, you know, a Google or an Amazon. And they just feel like they're outgunned,” Clinton said. At Clinton’s request, the Legislature held its first-ever interim study on data centers last fall. Then last spring, lawmakers passed the first bill placing a limit on data centers by requiring them to produce their own electricity rather than drawing from the grid and increasing demand. “If these large tech companies want more electricity, fine. You pay for it. We shouldn't have to pay for it,” Clinton said. Clinton said lawmakers still need to address issues including water use, potential impacts on property values, and residents’ ability to learn about proposals. She also said data companies have realized that using non-disclosure agreements to advance projects in Oklahoma has not helped. “I think that people just don't feel like they have any say so they don't have any buy in. Like these decisions are being made for them and around them,” Clinton said. Clinton said she plans to file new bills on data centers in the coming legislative session. She also said that in multiple states, exit polling of midterm voters showed data centers ranked just under the war in Iran and inflation as a top concern. “This is not a Republican or Democratic issue. This is an issue about what we want for our future and for our communities,” Clinton said. Tulsa and Broken Arrow leaders are expected to finalize data center regulations in the coming months. City leaders say it is not a matter of if a new proposal comes, but when. “Sometimes it can seem like you're a little bit behind, but eventually you start to see the cities will catch up and start having regulations and ordinances in place that will actually govern how you how those businesses can move forward,” Spurgeon said.

artigo.texto: Publicidade Washington — Semanas depois de os eleitores demonstrarem forte insatisfação com os data centers nas eleições de meio de mandato, o Congresso debate uma ampla reformulação das regras federais de licenciamento que poderia ajudar as empresas de tecnologia a construir essas instalações mais rapidamente. O projeto de lei aceleraria as análises ambientais federais de vários projetos de energia, incluindo linhas de transmissão e gasodutos, facilitando para os desenvolvedores a obtenção da energia necessária para operar os data centers. Mas essa ajuda vem com uma enorme contrapartida: os data centers também teriam de pagar muito mais pela eletricidade, segundo uma disposição do projeto que cobraria das instalações uma tarifa adicional pelo acesso à rede elétrica. A medida alteraria décadas de regras federais do setor elétrico e poderia gerar uma economia de bilhões de dólares na próxima década para as famílias e outros consumidores. Leia mais: Boom de data centers de IA enfrenta reação negativa nas urnas dos EUA Leia mais: A SpaceX planeja investir US$ 74 bi na construção de data centers no Texas e Arizona A iniciativa de impor custos mais altos aos data centers evidencia como a política em torno da inteligência artificial se tornou complexa em Washington. Data centers gigantescos e ávidos por energia estão se espalhando rapidamente pelo país, pressionando as redes elétricas e provocando indignação em muitas comunidades. Neste mês, os eleitores aprovaram pelo menos 40 iniciativas locais para restringir essas instalações. Continua depois da publicidade Prós e contras Alguns ambientalistas que se opõem ao projeto de licenciamento o classificaram como um benefício para as empresas de tecnologia, argumentando que a legislação poderia acelerar o desenvolvimento de data centers abastecidos por gás natural. O projeto reduziria o alcance de leis ambientais federais para acelerar a construção de diversos tipos de empreendimentos, incluindo gasodutos, projetos eólicos e solares, linhas de transmissão de alta tensão, estradas, transporte público e moradias. Em contraste, os defensores apresentaram o projeto como uma oportunidade de endurecer as regras para as empresas de IA. “O período em que os data centers não pagavam sua parte termina quando este projeto for aprovado”, disse o senador Sheldon Whitehouse, democrata de Rhode Island e um dos autores do projeto. “A partir de agora, os data centers terão de pagar pelos custos adicionais que impõem à rede quando entram em operação. Eles não poderão transferir todos esses custos adicionais para a base tarifária da concessionária e fazer com que sejam arcados pelos demais consumidores.” Continua depois da publicidade O setor de data centers, por sua vez, permaneceu relativamente calado. Embora diversos grupos empresariais, sindicatos e algumas empresas do Vale do Silício tenham apoiado o projeto, uma das principais entidades representativas do setor ainda não o fez. A Data Center Coalition, cujos membros incluem Amazon, Google, Meta e Microsoft, afirmou que ainda está analisando a legislação. “Continuamos avaliando suas implicações com nossos membros, que estão fazendo sua parte para promover a acessibilidade e o crescimento econômico ao investir centenas de bilhões de dólares nos Estados Unidos todos os anos”, disse Jon Hukill, porta-voz da coalizão. Muitos data centers desenvolvidos para treinar e operar modelos de IA de ponta podem consumir tanta eletricidade quanto pequenas cidades, o que provocou debates sobre quem deve pagar pelos bilhões de dólares necessários para construir as usinas e linhas de transmissão de que precisam. Continua depois da publicidade Historicamente, as concessionárias distribuíram o custo das melhorias na rede elétrica entre todos os seus clientes. Mas, à medida que a insatisfação com os data centers aumentou, o presidente Donald Trump e vários governadores pressionaram as gigantes da tecnologia a assumir a conta e não repassar esses custos às famílias. A maioria das empresas de IA prometeu fazer isso, embora esses compromissos de proteção aos consumidores possam ser difíceis de fiscalizar. Inseridas nas 494 páginas do projeto de lei de licenciamento estão várias disposições destinadas a dar mais força a essas promessas. Cobranças extras Uma das medidas determinaria que a Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, a agência federal americana responsável pela regulação do setor de energia, emitisse novas regras em até 90 dias. Essas regras cobrariam dos data centers tanto os custos de eventuais melhorias na rede necessárias para atendê-los quanto os custos de utilização da rede elétrica existente. Continua depois da publicidade Isso derrubaria princípios regulatórios antigos, em vigor desde 1994, que proíbem as concessionárias de cobrar duas vezes dos clientes pela mesma capacidade da rede. Na prática, o projeto afirma que os grandes data centers são diferentes e deveriam pagar potencialmente o dobro do que pagam atualmente. “É uma grande mudança em relação à forma como temos administrado a rede até agora, na qual os benefícios são amplamente compartilhados e socializamos os custos”, disse Robin Millican, diretor de programas de pesquisa e parcerias estratégicas do Center on Global Energy Policy, da Universidade Columbia. Outras disposições dariam aos reguladores estaduais mais liberdade para cobrar dos data centers valores adicionais pelas usinas de energia de que precisam e utilizar o dinheiro para conceder créditos nas contas das famílias. Pela primeira vez, o governo federal também seria obrigado a monitorar o consumo de energia dos data centers. Os políticos têm colocado os data centers no centro das discussões em parte porque a dimensão do boom da IA ameaça sobrecarregar as redes elétricas. As gigantes da tecnologia também priorizam a velocidade e frequentemente estão dispostas a pagar mais para obter energia mais rapidamente. artigo.texto: ABB Key player in electrification According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Battery Circuit Breakers market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture. The global battery circuit breakers market is entering a phase of sustained expansion as electrification reshapes transportation, power generation, and industrial infrastructure. Valued for their ability to safely interrupt high direct current in battery-powered systems, these specialized protective devices are indispensable in electric vehicles, stationary energy storage, and renewable energy installations. Between 2026 and 2035, demand is forecast to rise at a robust pace, supported by policy-driven decarbonization targets, falling battery costs, and the proliferation of DC-coupled architectures. Asia-Pacific remains the largest and fastest-growing region, underpinned by China's dominance in EV and battery production, while North America and Europe accelerate investments in grid-scale storage and charging infrastructure. artigo.texto: Trending WHEELING - City officials in Wheeling have consistently heard from vocal opponents of data centers in recent months, but some of those same individuals stepped forward Tuesday night to express gratitude for comprehensive data center regulations introduced as new legislation before city council. Council heard the first reading of an ordinance to create Article 1365 of the city’s planning and zoning code, which outlines several pages of rules and regulations on data centers in Industrial districts. The legislation will establish a rigorous application process, requirements for development and performance standards, regulations for electrical power demands and water consumption, and guidelines on water reuse for closed-loop cooling systems. It additionally outlines rules for noise and air emissions, wastewater guidelines and regulations pertaining to other potential impacts associated with data center operations. For several months, local data center opponents have vocally stood against a planned development at the former Centre Foundry & Machine Company facility in the Wheeling neighborhood of Warwood along River Road. Silicon Foundation plans to redevelop the Centre Foundry site into a phased data center and energy technology campus. While opponents over the past several months have expressed criticism about the way the city has handled the situation surrounding the planned data center in Warwood, a handful of vocal community members came forward during Tuesday night’s meeting to acknowledge they view the new legislation as a step in the right direction. "This ordinance is a good effort to control if not prevent data centers in the city of Wheeling," said Warwood resident Polly Barks. "This effort to halt or mitigate Silicone Foundation’s disastrous effects on Warwood would not have happened without the sustained effort of our community, without coming together almost unanimously against data centers. I challenge any of you to find something that has been so uniquely unifying to the community, for better or for worse." Barks is among several Warwood residents who earlier this summer filed a civil lawsuit against Silicon Foundation in an effort to stop or at least pump the brakes on the development of the Centre Foundry site. She and others have been outspoken on the matter during public informational gatherings as well as during city council meetings. Barks and fellow colleagues have called for the city to pass a moratorium on data center development within the city - a move that Wheeling’s city solicitor maintains cannot be done legally. Officials have noted the Center Foundry site is properly zoned for data center use in an Industrial location. "Although it’s not a moratorium, I’m pleased that this provides a stop-gap that makes the city far less appealing to those coming in to exploit us for their own benefit to our detriment," Barks said. "Although I do disagree with the opening statement that, ‘the city recognizes that facilitating the development of data center service technology can be an economic development asset to the city and of significant benefit to the city and its residents. That’s subjective - we can agree to disagree on that." Barks applauded Ward 1 Councilman Tony Assaro, who represents the Warwood neighborhood, for listening to his constituents and representing their voice. "Tony has shown himself to be a faithful steward of the will of the people," Barks said. "For that we thank him and look forward to working with him further to make our community even better." Members of the Rules Committee of Council, the city administration, the city’s legal department and other council members all worked on the development of the data center regulations for several weeks. A draft of the document was made available on the city’s website, and city leaders welcomed suggestions from the public to make any adjustments to the regulations that may be deemed necessary or beneficial. The regulations were viewed as a result of community action, Barks noted, indicating the regulations attempting to address concerns expressed by vocal residents who do not want noise, higher utility bills, pollution or any other potential side effects data centers have reportedly brought to communities in other parts of the country. She credited people who wore anti-data center T-shirts, posted yard signs, signed petitions, attended events and let their voices be heard. "Residents have become activists," she said, noting this was the beginning of a fight against data centers throughout West Virginia, an effort unfolding "in a state that does not support the will of the people." Barks asked council to make a public statement about anticipated impact on the proposed data center at Centre Foundry. "Take credit for being the first city in West Virginia, to our knowledge, to adopt an ordinance against data centers, and lend your expertise elsewhere," she said. Amanda McWhorter of Triadelphia said she represents Ohio County on a statewide panel known as the West Virginia Data Center Accountability Project. "Thank you for listening to the community and working on this ordinance," McWhorter said. "I would love to be able to connect you to other communities, as well, with our group." McWhorter and Barks encouraged city leaders to work with other communities in the state and with Ohio County on similar efforts to regulate data centers on a local level. In West Virginia, House Bill 2014 - known as the Power Generation and Consumption Act of 2025, establishes state jurisdiction and outlines regulations on the state level for data centers planning to operate at 90 megawatts, which would be deemed as a "high impact data center." Wheeling’s new Article 1365 of the city planning and zoning code, could be used as a template for other communities faced with regulating the development of data centers below the "high-impact" threshold. artigo.texto: India is building its domestic carbon market under which agricultural carbon credits can finance climate-friendly farming. In this post, Suthar and Jangra highlight the importance of transparent prices, timely payments, data rights, and strict limits on corporate offset claims – without which there is a risk of greenwashing and transfer of climate risk from large polluters to the country’s smallest cultivators. A carbon-credit pilot involving 3,500 mango farmers in Karnataka’s Koppal district appeared to offer a useful bargain. Farmers would plant trees and manage biomass. The carbon stored through these activities would be measured, converted into credits, and sold. Farmers would earn additional income from land they were already cultivating. The payments did not arrive as quickly as expected. Officials attributed the delay to complex auditing, biomass assessment, and carbon-credit calculations. Farmer organisations questioned whether cultivators properly understood the system or knew when they would be paid. The pilot may eventually deliver benefits. Yet its early difficulties expose a central weakness in agricultural carbon trading: farmers must act before they know how much they will receive, when they will receive it, or how the value of their environmental work will be divided. This problem deserves attention as India builds its domestic carbon market. Carbon trading is not inherently greenwashing. A credible market can direct finance towards activities that genuinely reduce emissions. It becomes greenwashing when a company buys inexpensive credits, avoids difficult changes in its own operations, and then presents itself as environmentally responsible. For marginal farmers, the distinction is crucial. Their fields must not become places where corporations purchase reputational relief while leaving the agricultural and financial risks behind. The two markets must not be confused India’s Carbon Credit Trading Scheme contains two distinct parts: (i) The compliance mechanism applies to designated industries that must meet government-set emission-intensity targets. Companies performing better than their targets may earn certificates while those falling short may need to purchase them. (ii) The offset mechanism allows eligible projects outside the compliance system to generate carbon credits from verified emission reductions or removals. Agriculture is included within this emerging framework. The Bureau of Energy Efficiency has already listed an offset methodology for reducing emissions through improved management practices in rice cultivation. These mechanisms raise different questions. A compliance market can compel industrial facilities to meet regulated targets. Agricultural offsets allow corporations or other buyers to purchase reductions generated elsewhere. The greatest greenwashing risk arises when these offsets are treated as substitutes for reducing emissions within factories, transport networks, and supply chains. A farmer’s climate-friendly practice may be real. The corporate claim built upon it may still be excessive. Marginal farmers enter with weak bargaining power According to the government’s Situation Assessment Survey, 89.4% of India’s agricultural households own less than two hectares of land. These households enter carbon markets with limited savings, fragmented holdings, and little capacity to survive a failed crop or delayed payment. They do not negotiate with corporate buyers as equal market participants. A project developer generally designs the programme. A technical agency establishes the carbon baseline. An auditor verifies the claimed reduction. A registry issues the credit. An aggregator combines credits from hundreds or thousands of farms and negotiates with prospective buyers. The farmer changes the cultivation practice, supplies the land and provides the information needed to create the credit. But the farmer may never know the final selling price. Aggregation is often necessary because measuring and verifying carbon on each small plot would be expensive. It also creates an information imbalance. The intermediary knows how many credits were generated, what deductions were made, and what the buyer paid. An individual farmer may know only the amount transferred to their bank account. India risks recreating a familiar agricultural problem in a new market. Farmers produce the underlying value while intermediaries control the information, pricing, and final transaction. The company purchases a claim. The farmer accepts a constraint Agricultural carbon projects may require farmers to reduce tillage, alter water management, change fertiliser use, retain crop residue, plant trees, or adopt prescribed cultivation practices. Many of these changes can improve soil health and conserve resources. Their effects are not identical across farms. A method that works in one district may perform differently under another soil type, rainfall pattern, or pest regime. The farmer bears this uncertainty directly. A change in cultivation may require additional labour or machinery. It may alter weed management or increase costs during the transition. If the crop underperforms, the loss affects household income. If the activity fails verification, the expected carbon payment may disappear. The corporate buyer faces no comparable agricultural risk. It purchases a certificate and may use it in a sustainability report, advertisement, or net-zero claim. The environmental credit travels upwards. The production risk remains in the village. This imbalance is particularly troubling when carbon income is described as assured revenue. A payment that depends on future measurement, verification, market prices, and deductions is not assured income. It is a contingent claim the conditions of which are largely controlled by organisations outside the farm. Measurement can become another source of dependency A carbon market needs credible measurement. Buyers should not receive credits for reductions

artigo.texto: A Greenline, multinacional brasileira de tecnologia climática, passará a exigir cobertura securitária para todos os créditos de carbono mensurados e emitidos em suas operações. Desenvolvida com o apoio da corretora internacional Marsh e comercializada pela AKAD Seguros, a solução busca atender à crescente demanda de compradores corporativos por maior segurança jurídica, financeira e reputacional no mercado voluntário de carbono. Segundo a Greenline, a companhia será a primeira do setor a estabelecer a contratação de uma apólice como condição indispensável para a emissão de créditos na modalidade ex-post, na qual os ativos são gerados após a verificação dos resultados ambientais dos projetos. A iniciativa se dá em paralelo a questionamentos sobre a qualidade dos créditos negociados internacionalmente, a efetividade das iniciativas de conservação florestal e os riscos associados ao greenwashing, prática que consiste em atribuir a produtos ou atividades benefícios ambientais que não correspondem à realidade. A apólice contempla quatro modalidades de risco: descumprimento da entrega dos ativos contratados, falhas estruturais nos projetos, perda permanente de utilidade dos créditos, incluindo a desqualificação de metodologias ou autorizações governamentais, e despesas adicionais para a aquisição de títulos substitutos em caso de sinistro. Também estão previstas coberturas para gastos emergenciais destinados à contenção de danos ambientais, como operações de combate a incêndios florestais e auditorias realizadas após desastres naturais. Considerando o limite inicial de US$ 25 milhões por projeto e um preço de referência de US$ 10 por crédito, a proteção financeira corresponderia ao valor de ativos representativos de 2,5 milhões de toneladas de dióxido de carbono (CO2). “Controvérsias sobre a qualidade dos créditos, regularidade fundiária e o risco reputacional do greenwashing tornaram-se tópicos centrais em nossas negociações com grandes compradores corporativos”, afirmou Lucio Lopez, fundador e CEO da Greenline. “Tornar o seguro obrigatório em 100% das nossas operações não é apenas uma garantia financeira. É uma declaração de maturidade do setor. Estamos transformando ativos ambientais em instrumentos financeiros verdadeiramente bancáveis.” A contratação poderá ser estendida a projetos que já integravam a carteira da companhia antes da formalização da parceria, mediante avaliação individual da seguradora. Segundo a empresa, a padronização dos processos de mensuração e o uso de tecnologias de sensoriamento remoto favorecem a inclusão dessas operações. Concebido inicialmente para iniciativas de preservação de florestas nativas e redução do desmatamento, o produto também estará disponível para outras empresas do segmento de ativos ambientais, observados os critérios de aceitação de risco da AKAD.

artigo.texto: Two Nevada scientists tried figuring out how much water data centers use. It got complicated. Estimates of how much power Nevada's swelling number of data centers need have grown astronomically over the past two years. But the amount of water needed to cool and power them is opaque, even to scientists attempting to finalize a number. There are more than 75 data centers operating, under construction or planned across the state, primarily in the Las Vegas and greater Reno areas. And because little is known about site-specific cooling operations at each center, "We don't know how water-efficient these places are going to be," Sean McKenna, former director of the division of hydrologic sciences at the Desert Research Institute (DRI), told The Nevada Independent. McKenna and Erik Henzl, a research scientist and environmental economist at DRI, have spent more than a year correlating projected power needs to water usage for yet-to-be-built data centers in the state. The pair issued a report early this year, but their numbers were immediately rendered obsolete when NV Energy announced it had grossly underestimated how many power-hungry data centers were looking to come to Nevada. Henzl and McKenna reworked their numbers in a new report issued today. Their findings? How much water is needed depends on whether the data centers coming into Nevada utilize newer, water-efficient cooling technologies and how the power to run them is produced. Individual facility water usage is largely opaque, forcing the pair to instead base their projections on water estimates. "The energy demand has surged," Henzl said. "The water demand is more difficult to assess because of a dearth of information." With data centers moving toward more efficient technologies, the pair assumed medium or low water consumption by the centers, finding that under the updated power forecast put out by NV Energy, Nevada would require an additional 4,200-to- 12,800 acre-feet of water per year on top of existing consumption. At the higher end, that would be roughly how much Carson City's businesses and 58,000 residents use annually. "We're just kind of making our best guess on what we know," McKenna added. New power estimates blow old forecasts out of the water DRI's original report, which it issued in January, was the first Nevada-specific comprehensive analysis of data centers' water and power needs in the state. The report's findings were based on projections made by NV Energy in its 2024 Integrated Resource Plan (IRP), a roadmap outlining the utility's upcoming projects and needs. In that plan, NV Energy outlined 12 data center projects seeking power by 2033 with 5,900 megawatts (MW) of requested capacity, according to the report. But then NV Energy released an updated IRP this spring with drastically higher energy projections, largely driven by data center power needs, which are coming in much faster than NV Energy had previously anticipated. In its 2026 IRP, the utility outlined more than three dozen data centers seeking 16,530 MW of requested capacity by 2036. Projects range from smaller developments, such as BlueSky AI's planned 2.7 MW facility in Elko to Tract's 2,500 MW Virginia Highlands development. Various agencies and groups offer differing opinions on how many houses can be powered with one MW of power, but the general consensus is around a few hundred. Looking even further out, data centers, which currently account for 5 percent of NV Energy's sales, are expected to account for 64 percent of the utility's power sales by 2046. "NV Energy recognizes they will have to serve loads approximately 2.5 times current levels by 2046," according to the report. The big unknown Data centers are cooled differently depending on their age, local regulations, such as Southern Nevada's ban on evaporative cooling and other variables. Novva's 100 MW Las Vegas data center, for example, uses a closed-loop system. In 2025, it consumed less than 2 acre-feet of water. Google's data center in Henderson, however, uses an evaporative cooling system and consumed about 636 acre-feet of water in 2024. Henzl and McKenna had limited access to site-specific water usage, which McKenna said was "really a frustration with this report." What they do know is that direct and indirect water consumption — how much is used on site and how much is used offsite to generate power for the centers — are expected to increase under NV Energy's forecasts. Henzl and McKenna estimate that direct water use by data centers requesting to come into Nevada but not yet built, under a medium-usage model, could grow to nearly 12,800 acre-feet per year and indirect water usage could increase to nearly 22,000 acre-feet. "The big unknown is really this indirect or grid water use?" McKenna said. "Where does our power come from and how efficient are those generating sources? That's a big question." Behind-the-meter power In its 2026 IRP, NV Energy proposed adding nearly 12,000 MW of new power generation, primarily through solar, battery storage and natural gas, with some geothermal. But that isn't enough to meet the company's power demands plus the data centers' requested capacity. In response, impatient data center developers are turning to what is known as behind-the-meter power — power that is generated and consumed on-site. Behind-the-meter power allows data centers to produce the amount of energy they need without waiting in a queue with other large-load customers for NV Energy to have capacity to serve them. But because they aren't connected to NV Energy's system, the behind-the-meter systems bypass many state regulatory requirements. "The allure is speed to power," Henzl said. But with that speed comes uncertainty, including the amount of water needed to produce that power. "It's just a two-sided coin and it depends what that behind-the-meter source is," he said. artigo.texto: Ford has begun shipping battery cells made in Michigan using technology licensed from China's CATL, moving its next electric pickup from battery planning into prototype testing. The cells are destined for vehicles being developed at the company's Louisville plant in Kentucky. The announcement on 18 November concerns lithium iron phosphate, or LFP, cells from BlueOval Battery Park in Marshall. Ford owns the factory; CATL provides licensed technology and manufacturing expertise. That distinction sits at the centre of a project facing scrutiny over its Chinese connections. For Ford, the immediate customer is its own development programme. The shipments do not mean the Fathom pickup is on sale, or that the battery operation has reached its intended production rate. Michigan cells head for Kentucky prototypes Reuters reported that the first cells will support Fathom prototypes. CNBC said production at the roughly $3 billion Michigan facility started in October, with shipments now underway. Fathom is being developed on Ford's Universal Electric Vehicle platform. The company expects the pickup to reach customers in the fourth quarter of 2027, according to CNBC and Electrek, leaving further testing and manufacturing work before launch. The cells have a prismatic shape. Electrek reported that Ford chose this format to fit into the vehicle's structure and lower structural costs. It also said the company has not yet disclosed the pickup's battery specifications or driving range. LFP brings a different cost calculation Lithium iron phosphate avoids the nickel and cobalt used in other battery chemistries. Reuters described lower cost and durability as reasons carmakers are adopting it, while Ford links its choice to the effort to build less expensive electric vehicles. That is a manufacturing argument, not a promise that every cost saving will reach buyers. The new shipments establish a supply milestone for the development vehicles; they do not settle the final specification or ownership cost of a production truck. Ford's Alan Clarke told reporters that working with CATL offered a faster route to making affordable EVs in the United States. His comments describe why Ford chose a licensing arrangement rather than developing the manufacturing process entirely on its own. Planned output is not today's production The Marshall factory is designed for a rate of 40 cells per minute. CNBC reported an annual capacity of 20 gigawatt-hours for vehicles and Ford's energy-storage business, below the original plan of as much as 40 gigawatt-hours. The same report said Ford is still certifying processes and expects to increase output next year. Those qualifications matter when comparing a newly operating line with its planned capacity. The technology arrangement remains politically contentious. Reuters reported criticism from US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, while Ford has defended the domestic production and its decision to license CATL's expertise. A Ford spokesperson told Reuters the company still expects eligibility for a federal battery-manufacturing tax credit. The bottom line Ford now has Michigan-made LFP cells moving towards Fathom prototypes, an important step before its planned 2027 pickup launch. The next test is turning early shipments into repeatable production, while showing that licensed technology can deliver the lower costs behind the programme.

artigo.texto: An Arkansas ballot issue that did not pass in the Nov. 3 midterm election sparked debate about looming data center development across the state. Students expressed worries about environmental sustainability, public education and the growing influence of artificial intelligence. Issue 3 proposed creating an “economic development district,” which included several example facilities that would fit the zoning description. For some, the inclusion of “research, technology and development facilities” leaves room for potential data centers to be introduced. Had it passed, Issue 3 would have amended the Arkansas Constitution to allow local governments to create economic development districts and offer tax incentives to attract businesses. The amendment would have also authorized the legislature to create economic development programs using public money, including federal loans and grants. Nearly 50.7% of voters opposed the measure, according to results from the Arkansas Secretary of State’s office. Although Issue 3 did not specifically mention data centers, some students viewed the amendment as a possible way to make it easier for such developments to receive public incentives. Ethan Ericson, a UA senior data science major and first-time voter, said his concerns are focused on the speed and manner in which the infrastructure is being built. “The technology of data centers isn't necessarily a bad thing,” Ericson said. “The way that we're going about building out that infrastructure is irresponsible, in my opinion.” Ericson said data centers can strain communities and ecosystems when built in areas with limited water resources. He pointed to facilities that use water for cooling and do not reuse it through closed-loop systems. “If you dry up a whole basin, the operations like that are going to become a lot harder for those animals,” Ericson said, adding that environmental damage is a major concern. He said Arkansas should take particular care to protect its natural resources, especially as developers look to expand computing infrastructure. “I think it's especially relevant in Arkansas, with us being the Natural State, that we endeavor to protect our fragile natural environments,” Ericson said. Ericson doesn't question whether Arkansas should be building data centers. His question is whether the state is doing it with any real oversight. “The problem is that they are trying to do it really fast,” Ericson said. “I think they're being too hasty and they're not going through the proper steps to ensure a sustainable infrastructure of compute is built.” Renee Walden, a junior early childhood education major, said she opposes data center expansion in Arkansas, but said her concerns extend beyond environmental effects. Walden connected the growth of data centers to the increased use of generative artificial intelligence and its influence on students’ ability to think independently. She said while some uses of AI can be beneficial, such as medical tools used to help detect diseases, her criticism is directed at the growing use of generative AI for tasks that students could otherwise complete themselves. “I think that's really what education is about; it’s not, ‘I need to complete this task,’ but ‘What is this task helping me learn?’” Walden said. Walden said relying on AI to complete assignments can take away opportunities for students to develop critical thinking, analysis and comprehension skills. Walden also questioned whether public resources should be directed toward attracting data centers when schools and infrastructure remain priorities for communities. She argued that economic development incentives could come at the expense of public services. “I don't mind paying taxes if they're going to my schools,” Walden said. “But they're not going to my school. They're not going to my roads.” “The U.S. has a controversial history with voter legislation, especially the wording of it," Walden said. "It's written in legalese, which for the average voter, is quite literally unreadable." Walden said the vague wording made the category worth a second look. "What convinced me Issue 3 was about data centers is the project category, 'research, technology, and development facilities.' It feels like if it would have passed, it would be used as a backdoor for data centers."

artigo.texto: State launches India’s first SO2 Emissions Trading Scheme EMA is a collaboration between the Energy Policy Institute at the University of Chicago (EPIC) and the Abdul Latif Jameel Poverty Action Lab (J-PAL) to scale emissions markets across the Global South MUMBAI: The Maharashtra government on Tuesday launched India’s first sulphur dioxide (SO2) Emissions Trading Scheme with the Emissions Market Accelerator (EMA) to reduce industrial pollution. The scheme comes on the heels of the successful implementation and evaluation of the world’s first particulate (PM2.5) pollution market in Surat in 2019. EMA is a collaboration between the Energy Policy Institute at the University of Chicago (EPIC) and the Abdul Latif Jameel Poverty Action Lab (J-PAL) to scale emissions markets across the Global South. The Maharashtra Pollution Control Board (MPCB), which is implementing the scheme, has partnered with the University of Chicago Trust to incorporate artificial intelligence into environmental inspections. The announcement has come almost seven months after MPCB launched mock trading for the SO2 emissions trading market. According to its proponents, the new scheme will benefit approximately 130 million people by improving air quality in Maharashtra. Pankaja Munde, minister for environment and climate change, said at the launch, “We need to look at how technology, including AI, can help us monitor industrial pollution more intelligently.” Munde added that the state government’s role did not end with just regulating industries or controlling pollution. “We must also work alongside industry and encourage participation to create solutions that benefit both the environment and economic growth,” she said. Under the scheme, which covers 17 industrial sectors, MPCB will establish emission limits for participating industries and distribute emission permits, with each permit representing the right to emit a specified quantity of SO₂. Industries will have to monitor and report their emissions through Continuous Emissions Monitoring Systems, and at the end of each compliance period, surrender permits equivalent to their actual emissions. Industries that reduce emissions below their allocated permits can sell the surplus permits in the market. Conversely, industries that exceed their allocation can purchase additional permits from those with surplus. A statement from EPIC said that the selling of permits would create an economic incentive for “cleaner production and technological innovation”. For industries, the scheme provides a choice in how they meet environmental compliance requirements: either by investing in emission-control measures or purchasing permits. Siddhesh Ramdas Kadam, chairman of MPCB, said that the SO₂ emissions trading scheme was a “feather in the cap” for the state. “Our approach is not to control, but to grow together with industry,” he said. Professor Michael Greenstone, the Milton Friedman Distinguished Service Professor in Economics and director of EPIC and Co-Chair of EMA, said that a market like India could cut emissions while lowering costs for industry and helping the economy grow. Balaji Srinivasan, co-chair of EMA, who played a key role in coordinating the initiative, claimed that in the US, emissions trading had cut pollution by 96%. “So, other countries and Indian states are looking to the Maharashtra SO2 pollution market with enormous hope,” he said. Tithee Mukhoppadhyay, deputy executive director of J-PAL South Asia and advisor to EMA, said, “The Surat pilot proved that emissions trading cuts industrial pollution without hurting economic growth.” - ABOUT THE AUTHORSnehal Fernandes Snehal Fernandes is senior associate editor, who joined HT in 2006. She heads the Mumbai edition’s city reporting team that writes on civic and urban governance, transport and infrastructure, health, and education. She is also the National Science Editor. With a career spanning more than two decades, her expertise lies in writing on science and technology, space, environment, sustainable development, climate change, and nuclear energy. Her work consistently breaks down, and without oversimplyfying, science and research developments into an easy read for a broad audience. In 2009, she was among the very first journalist to report on the opposition to the Jaitapur nuclear power plant in Ratnagiri (Konkan) following the Indo- US civil nuclear agreement and consistently followed it with multiple stories from ground zero; wrote about the introduction and subsequent halt to the cultivation of genetically modified (BT) brinjal, and has interviewed Nobel laureates and award winning scientists. In 2012, she was awarded ‘The Press Club Award for Excellence in Journalism’ (Political category) for reports on the mining scam in Goa. Prior to HT, she wrote on education and transport at the Indian Express. She graduated in sociology from St Xavier's College, and firmly believes in the phrase by Karl Marx that ‘Religion is the opium of the people’. When she is not keeping a tab on the going-ons in Mumbai and the scientific world, you'll find her reading world news, or watching crime/espionage series or political dramas. She can repeatedly watch Kill Bill with the same interest as Planet of the Apes and Spiderman. artigo.texto: PAXTON — The Ford County Zoning Board of Appeals’ public hearing on proposed text amendments to the county’s zoning ordinances regulating energy storage systems was canceled just hours before it was scheduled to begin on Wednesday, Nov. 18. The hearing was initially rescheduled for Monday, Nov. 23, but then was “rescheduled for a future date” to be determined after the Ford County Chronicle objected to the Nov. 23 hearing date since it would not have allowed for the publication of a public notice in the newspaper at least 15 days in advance, as required by the Illinois Counties Code. “The law is very clear that (public notice of) any hearing of a ZBA in Illinois ‘shall be published at least 15 days in advance … in a newspaper of general circulation’ in the county,’” Chronicle Co-Publisher Will Brumleve wrote in an email to attorney Andrew Keyt, who advises the ZBA. “There are zero exceptions. Period.” While a public notice for the canceled Nov. 18 hearing was published in the Oct. 28 edition of the Chronicle — 22 days in advance — ZBA Chairman Emily Lattz said Keyt had advised that the publication of a new notice for the Nov. 23 hearing date was not needed — only the posting of a notice on the doors at the courthouse where the hearing is to be held. The yet-to-be rescheduled hearing will be held to hear evidence and make recommendations to the Ford County Board on text amendments to the county’s zoning ordinances regulating energy storage systems. “The proposed amendments include revisions to the application requirements, standards, regulations, safety requirements, fee requirements and related provisions concerning energy storage systems, including amendments intended to comply with recent changes to 55 ILCS 5/5-12024,” stated the notice published in the Oct. 28 edition of the Chronicle.

artigo.texto: Comissão de Meio Ambiente da FIERN debate segurança hídrica e condições para atrair data centers ao RN A segurança hídrica e os aspectos técnicos e regulatórios para a instalação de data centers no Rio Grande do Norte foram os principais temas discutidos na reunião da Comissão Temática de Meio Ambiente (COEMA) da FIERN, presidida pelo empresário Marcelo Rosado. A Secretaria de Estado do Meio Ambiente e dos Recursos Hídricos (Semarh) apresentou o trabalho de dimensionamento e manutenção dos reservatórios, além do planejamento para atender à expansão das atividades econômicas e ao abastecimento da população. “Eles mostraram o planejamento de como oferecer e ampliar a segurança, nesta área, para as novas indústrias, para as expansões residenciais, condomínios, loteamentos que poderão acontecer no estado do Rio Grande do Norte”, afirmou Rosado. O presidente da COEMA destacou que a sustentabilidade do sistema depende do uso adequado da água e dos recursos necessários para manter e ampliar a infraestrutura. Segundo ele, os investimentos precisam contemplar a redução do desperdício e o aumento da capacidade de armazenamento e abastecimento para atender à população e aos empreendimentos do estado. A apresentação sobre reservatórios, armazenamento, uso e distribuição da água foi conduzida pelo secretário de Estado do Meio Ambiente e dos Recursos Hídricos, Paulo Varella. Ele abordou iniciativas de recuperação de barragens, expansão de sistemas adutores, perfuração de poços e dessalinização. Entre as ações apresentadas está a previsão de recuperação de 28 barragens. Outro empreendimento apresentado foi o Projeto Seridó Norte, com 113 quilômetros de adutoras em execução. Os presidentes do Instituto de Desenvolvimento Sustentável e Meio Ambiente do Rio Grande do Norte (Idema), Werner Farkatt, e do Instituto de Gestão das Águas do Estado do Rio Grande do Norte (Igarn), José Procópio de Lucena, também participaram do encontro e destacaram a importância da sustentabilidade e do uso adequado dos sistemas hídricos. Data centers e atração de investimentos A discussão sobre data centers — instalações que abrigam equipamentos de processamento e armazenamento de dados — tratou das condições técnicas e ambientais para receber esses empreendimentos. Marcelo Rosado ressaltou que o Rio Grande do Norte tem diferenciais para disputar investimentos, mas precisa avançar nas políticas de atração e no debate sobre licenciamento. “Precisamos de mais discussão e, de alguma forma, criar políticas que consigam atrair mais investimento nessa área”, declarou Rosado, que também preside o Sindicato das Indústrias de Extração de Calcário, Fabricação de Cimento, Cal e de Argamassa do RN (SINECIM-RN) e é vice-presidente da FIERN. Na apresentação técnica, o especialista em gestão de data centers Júlio Lima abordou eficiência energética, fontes renováveis, resfriamento e uso responsável da água. Entre as alternativas apresentadas estavam o reaproveitamento de prédios e a adoção de sistemas de refrigeração que reduzam o consumo hídrico. Ele também destacou tecnologias voltadas à melhoria do desempenho ambiental das instalações e a importância de acompanhar indicadores que relacionam o consumo de energia, o uso de água e as emissões de carbono à energia utilizada pelos equipamentos de tecnologia da informação. Já o advogado e consultor jurídico Kepler Brito abordou a regulamentação do licenciamento ambiental de data centers aprovada pelo Conselho Estadual do Meio Ambiente (Conema). Ele explicou que o sistema de refrigeração é uma variável relevante na avaliação dos projetos, mas que a análise também deve considerar localização, consumo de água, efluentes, geradores, movimentação de terra e retirada de vegetação. “A resolução estabelece um enquadramento inicial, mas também preserva a análise técnica das características concretas do projeto. Estudos adicionais podem ser exigidos por decisão motivada e proporcional aos riscos, considerando o local, a tecnologia e outros elementos objetivos”, destacou Brito, em sua apresentação. Também participaram da reunião os presidentes do Sindicato da Indústria de Cervejas, Refrigerantes, Águas Minerais e Bebidas em Geral do Rio Grande do Norte (SICRAMIRN), Joafran Nobre; do Sindicato da Indústria de Panificação, Ivanaldo Maia; Francisco de Assis, representante do SINDIMÓVEIS na COEMA; e o assessor corporativo e gestor dos Conselhos e Comissões Temáticas, Ernani Bandeira.
